Over the years, Angola has sought to make its contribution to the building and consolidation of peace in Africa and in the world, but the current situation in no way reflects the aspirations of peoples for harmony and understanding among nations.

My country takes seriously our commitment to matters through the conflicts concerning peace, dialogue, respect for the norms governing international relations and the defence of International Law, sparing no effort to bringing the conflicting parties closer together and build consensus in Africa.
Our paradigm for peacebuilding initiatives is based on the search for realistic and sustainable solutions, within the principle of African solutions to conflicts in Africa.

We call for the effective implementation of Security Council Resolution 2719, which must ensure predictable, adequate and sustainable financing for African Union-led peace support operations authorized by the United Nations Security Council, because investing in Africa’s capacity to prevent and resolve conflicts is also an investment in international peace and security.

This session of the General Assembly is of particular significance to my country, as it is taking place in the year in which we celebrate the fiftieth anniversary of the Republic of Angola’s admission as a full member of the United Nations Organization, in December 1976.

At that time, it was a historic achievement for the Angolan people, who waited more than twelve months from the date of the proclamation of their National Independence for the country to be accepted as a full-fledged member of the international community.

That event, of great significance for the history of my country, took place in a global context in which Angola became a victim of confrontation between the world powers, in the struggle for control of spheres of influence within the spirit of the Cold War.

Our entire journey towards the attainment of peace in 2002 was closely linked to the disputes of that period, which hampered the fulfilment of the dreams of Angolans and their plans to build a prosperous nation committed to its development.

These facts belong to the past, but they have left us with a wealth of experience and lessons that we have drawn upon to build peace, understanding and reconciliation among all Angolans and to chart the course of our foreign policy.

Peace and national reconciliation is now a reality, as shown demonstrated through concrete gestures, including the holding of award ceremonies honouring the main political leaders of and representative members of all segments of civil society, within the framework of the 50th anniversary of National Independence.

ALBANIA AT THE UNITED NATIONS Artificial Intelligence, Automation, Manipulation and the Sovereign Imperative New York, General Debate of the 81st Session Well, it is my turn to preach in this desert where we gather every year, and I take that as the privilege of the few.
Mr. President, Dear representatives of the Peoples of the United Nations, Gunpowder changed the battlefield.
Nuclear fission changed the meaning of human survival.

Artificial intelligence is changing something even more intimate: who can enter the mind of a citizen, imitate a trusted voice, manufacture a reality calibrated to one person’s fears, and do so millions of times at once.
Albania is not a developer of frontier models.
But we are a nation that has already lived the future others are still debating.
And I have come here with a simple message: The greatest immediate danger is not that artificial intelligence will stop obeying humanity.
The greatest danger is that it will obey the wrong human beings perfectly.
The challenge comes in three layers: what artificial intelligence does instead of us, what it does to us, and who gains the power to reach us.
First, what it does instead of us.
The public debate imagines machines that awaken, acquire ambitions and turn against their creators.
But the systems confronting us today do not wake up with hatred in their hearts. They multiply ours.
They have no ambition of their own.
They serve the ambitions of others.
But they can be deployed by a state.
They tell no lie for their own benefit.
But they can tell a billion lies on our behalf.
The machine has no conscience, but it can borrow the reach of a government, the precision of a weapon and the intimacy of a friend.
At the same time, the economic incentives surrounding artificial intelligence increasingly reward the replacement of human effort, rather than the enlargement of human capacity.
Write the code so that I do not have to understand it.
Draft the report so that I do not have to think through it.
Make the judgment so that I do not have to assume responsibility for it.
When success is measured only by how much work the machine removes from the human being, we may create more efficient institutions but less capable people.
A civilisation that outsources effort may eventually outsource knowledge.
A civilisation that outsources knowledge may eventually outsource judgment.
And a civilisation that outsources judgment will discover that it has also outsourced responsibility.
We can build artificial intelligence that teaches rather than merely answers, guides rather than commands, and strengthens the human being instead of making the human being dependent upon it.
The question cannot be only: How quickly did the machine complete the task?
We must also ask: What did the human being learn?
And who answers when it is wrong?
Albania became the first country to bring an artificial intelligence instrument into the architecture of government through Diella, our artificial intelligence minister.
We did not do this to transfer sovereignty from people to a machine.
We did it to make public services more accessible, procedures more transparent and the state more accountable.
Behind every consequential public decision there must remain a legal mandate, a human institution and a name that can be called to answer.
The second layer is what artificial intelligence can do to us.
Artificial intelligence inside an accountable state can reduce the distance between citizens and public services.
Artificial intelligence outside accountability can eliminate the distance between a lie and the human mind.

A fabricated narrative of an Israeli invasion of the Albanian coast, an invasion that had never occurred, was manufactured, personalised and delivered through voices, pages and channels citizens already trusted.
One citizen received a story of national betrayal.
Another received a story of religious provocation.
Another received a conspiracy of foreign occupation.
Different fabrications entered different emotional worlds, all serving the same strategic lie.
Citizens protested against a phantom enemy.
Antisemitic tropes entered our public discourse.
Fear became anger, anger became mobilisation, and fabrication became political reality.
This was not a laboratory experiment.
It was a Tuesday in Tirana.
The algorithm did not invent the objective.
The algorithm did not develop hatred.
It discovered how to activate ours.
This is systematic fraud as a service.
Election interference no longer requires one television station or one piece of propaganda repeated to an entire population.
It can now operate at the resolution of one voter.
Two neighbours may stand in the same street, vote in the same election and inhabit entirely different realities, each manufactured specifically for them.
When that happens, democracy does not merely lose a debate.
It loses the common ground on which debate is possible.
Sovereignty no longer erodes only at the border.
In the twentieth century, sovereignty meant control over land, territorial waters and national airspace.
In the twenty first century, it must also mean the capacity of a free society to defend the conditions under which its citizens form their own judgments.
And then comes the third layer: reach.
For centuries, the great threat to freedom of speech was censorship.
Today, freedom of speech is also threatened by the weaponisation of freedom of reach.
Speech is the right to express an idea.
Reach is the power to place that idea before millions of people.
Reach can be purchased, automated, manipulated and secretly assigned by platforms, corporations, criminal networks and foreign states.
The right to speak is universal.
But there is no universal right to anonymous, unlimited and artificially amplified reach.
When one lie can be multiplied a billion times, truth does not need to be censored.
The citizen remains formally free to speak, but speaks into a storm that no human voice can match.
Freedom of speech can therefore be defeated without banning a single book, imprisoning a single journalist or deleting a single post.
The answer to bad speech remains more speech.
But the answer to covert, industrial amplification must be exposure.
Was it spread by people or machines?
Was the apparent public reaction authentic, coordinated or foreign-directed?
Defending democracy does not mean controlling what people are allowed to think.
It means revealing the hidden powers seeking to control what people are made to see.
If we protect freedom of speech while leaving the control of reach completely opaque, we defend the door while surrendering the room.
Some respond by demanding that artificial intelligence be slowed or stopped.
A pause by democracies will not produce a pause by dictatorships.
A moratorium observed by responsible states will not restrain hostile powers, criminal networks or industries of manipulation.
We cannot regulate ourselves into helplessness.
On this essential strategic question, President Donald Trump is right: we cannot stop. We must accelerate.
But acceleration must have a direction.
We need artificial intelligence that is verifiable, transparent and accountable, built by free societies, shared among allies and placed in the service of citizens.
The answer to weaponised automation is not technological surrender.
It is better artificial intelligence in the hands of those who remain accountable under law.
Sovereign artificial intelligence does not mean isolation.
It means that no nation should be helpless before systems it cannot understand, inspect or challenge.

Every country must be able to protect its language, authenticate public communications, detect coordinated manipulation, preserve evidence and inform its citizens without depending entirely on the commercial priorities of a distant corporation.
This is why Albania is building an artificial intelligence based digital Mirror.

The Mirror will identify manipulation in real time, test claims against authoritative information, reveal coordinated patterns and help citizens understand not only what they are seeing, but also how and why it reached them.
It will not tell citizens what they must think.
Truth cannot be decreed by a government.
It must be evidenced, sourced, tested, challenged and defended in the open.
The Mirror is not intended to become an arbiter of opinion.
It is intended to become an infrastructure of transparency.
It does not seek to create a ministry of truth.
It seeks to defend society against an industry of lies.
Albania therefore calls for an international compact for sovereign and democratic artificial intelligence.
First, citizens must know when politically consequential content has been artificially generated or materially manipulated.
Second, the architecture of reach must become transparent.
Citizens and states must be able to know who created, financed, targeted and artificially amplified consequential political content.
Third, every consequential use of artificial intelligence by a public institution must preserve a clear chain of human and legal accountability.
Fourth, democracies must create a shared early warning system so that evidence of artificial intelligence driven manipulation can travel between allies as quickly as the manipulation itself.
And smaller nations and smaller languages must not be abandoned outside this protective architecture.
Digital sovereignty cannot become a privilege reserved for the richest states.
Those attacking our societies already cooperate across jurisdictions.
Our democracies must learn to do the same.
This is not ultimately a contest between humanity and machines.
It is a contest between different human purposes, each amplified by machines.
Between those who use artificial intelligence to enlighten and those who use it to obscure.
Between those who use it to empower citizens and those who use it to manipulate them.
Between those who accept responsibility and those who hide behind automation.
We should not fear that machines will become too human.
We should fear that human beings will become invisible behind machines.
Excellencies, Every generation is called upon to defend freedom in the territory where freedom is most threatened.
For one generation, that territory was the battlefield.
For another, it was the ballot box.
For ours, it will increasingly be the human mind.
Let us ensure that no citizen is left alone before an algorithmic army.
Let us ensure that no small nation is forced to rent its understanding of reality from beyond its borders.
Let us ensure that no democracy wakes up after an election to discover that its people exercised their freedom of choice inside a world secretly designed for them by someone they could not see.
Artificial intelligence will not decide whether this century belongs to liberty or manipulation.
The question is whom it will obey, under what law and in the service of what human purpose.
We choose acceleration, but not surrender.
We choose innovation, but not abdication.
We choose augmentation, not the atrophy of human capability.
We choose sovereignty, but not isolation.
And precisely because we choose it, we refuse to confuse it with the unchecked freedom of machines, money and foreign powers to reach everyone, everywhere, without disclosure.
We choose truth, not because truth is always easy or comfortable, but because without a shared commitment to reality, there can be no shared public life.
And without a shared world, there can be no United Nations.

81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly Address by the Head of Government, H.E. Mr. Xavier Espot Zamora New York, 23 September 2026 Mr. President, Mr. Secretary-General, There is an idea that has accompanied Andorra for more than two hundred and seventy years and that continues to shape the way we understand politics.

The Manual Digest, one of the great works of our institutional heritage, through which Antoni Fiter i Rossell condensed and recounted the essence of Andorran identity, reminds us that the legitimate exercise of power only makes sense when it places the common good above any other interest.

This idea, written in 1748, long before modern international organizations came into existence, remains remarkably relevant today, because multilateralism is nothing more than the application of this same principle to relations among nations: the understanding that the common good of the international community is inseparable from the well-being of each of our countries.
In Andorra, this approach to politics has enabled us to preserve more than seven centuries of peace, dialogue and coexistence.
Not because history has been easier for us, but because we have learned that the best way to protect freedom is to build trust, seek balance and make compromise a form of governance.
Perhaps it is precisely this experience that a small country such as ours can share with this great Assembly today.
I am convinced that your experience in multilateralism will help strengthen the role of the United Nations at a particularly decisive moment for the world and for this Organization itself.
The theme you have chosen for this session, “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: An Effective and Inclusive United Nations for All,” accurately captures the challenges of our time.
The crisis we face is not only geopolitical, economic, climatic or technological.

Above all, it is a crisis of trust: among States, between institutions and citizens, and above all in the ability of the international community to fulfil the promise that gave meaning to the creation of the United Nations: to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war, to uphold the inherent dignity of every human being, and to promote an international order founded on human rights.
Trust is an intangible asset, perhaps the most valuable of all.
It takes great effort to build, yet very little to destroy.

When international commitments are relativized; when the Charter of the United Nations ceases to serve as the shared framework guiding the actions of States; when international humanitarian law is violated with a frequency that risks normalizing horror; or when civilians cease to be protected and instead become targets, what is weakened is not only peace itself, but also confidence in the international order and in all the organizations that represent and promote it.

From this Assembly, Andorra wishes to reiterate a conviction it has upheld for more than three decades: for small States, multilateralism is not a strategic option but a guarantee that all countries, regardless of their size, can make their voices heard on an equal legal footing.
It is the clearest expression of the principle that the force of law must always prevail over the law of force.
It is precisely for this reason that we continue to firmly defend the need to uphold the Charter of the United Nations, international law and international humanitarian law.

We support, more than ever, the efforts of the International Criminal Court to identify those responsible for the gravest crimes and we condemn any act of aggression that violates the sovereignty and territorial integrity of a State.

In this sense, we continue to express our solidarity with the people of Ukraine in the face of the consequences of a war that has lasted far too long, and we reiterate our support for efforts aimed at achieving a just, comprehensive and lasting peace, in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations and international law.
We do so for the people of Ukraine, and also for all territories where conflicts continue to persist.

Likewise, we reaffirm that a negotiated solution based on the coexistence of two States, Israel and Palestine, living side by side in peace, security and mutual recognition, remains the most solid path towards achieving a just and lasting peace in the Middle East.
We also hope that a peaceful solution can be found in Lebanon that fully respects the sovereignty of all countries involved.
PAUSE We cannot resign ourselves to turning human suffering into a statistic.
Behind every victim lies a life cut short; behind every child killed, a future that disappears; behind every school or hospital destroyed, a part of our shared humanity that has failed.

For this reason, we are particularly concerned by the increase in attacks against civilians, humanitarian personnel and United Nations staff, who carry out their mission, often under extreme conditions and at extraordinary personal risk.
We are especially alarmed by the conclusions of the Secretary-General’s latest reports on children in armed conflict and on conflict-related sexual violence.
The figures presented are not only dramatic; they are morally unacceptable.
For the first time, in many cases, the primary perpetrators of these violations are the States themselves, which should be the foremost guarantors of the protection of their citizens.
Faced with this reality, Andorra will continue to act.

We have increased our contribution to the Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict, strengthened our support for UNICEF programmes, and actively participated in the negotiations of the future Convention on Crimes Against Humanity, with particular attention to the protection of children.
The 2030 Agenda remains the most ambitious collective commitment ever undertaken by the international community.
It is not merely a set of technical objectives, nor simply an international planning framework.
It is a promise: the promise that the place where a person is born should not determine their opportunities, their life expectancy or their future.

The effects of global warming are being felt across many regions of the world, from coastal areas and river deltas to the most vulnerable territories, which are increasingly exposed to extreme weather events.
Andorra experiences them from its mountains.
Our geographical realities are very different, yet we share the same certainty: climate change is no longer a scientific projection.
It is a reality that is already transforming people's lives.

This year, Andorra had the honour of hosting the global meeting of the Mountain Partnership, culminating in the adoption of the Andorra Declaration, which highlights the importance of improving connectivity in mountain areas, narrowing the digital divide, and strengthening resilience to natural hazards through early warning systems and adapted infrastructure.
We undertook this effort convinced that mountains can no longer remain a peripheral element of the international climate agenda.

They are far more than landscapes: they are freshwater reserves on which hundreds of millions of people depend, havens of exceptional biodiversity, and a privileged indicator of the effects of global warming.
This very summer, we experienced temperatures that exceeded all known records.

We have witnessed with concern the major wildfires that have affected regions very close to our country, and the catastrophe in Nepal has highlighted the dramatic effects that rising temperatures are having on glaciers and, consequently, on mountain regions.
And we have once again confirmed that climate change is not a challenge for future generations.
It has been part of our present for a long time, and we must continue working to ensure that the voices of mountain territories are heard in the major international climate negotiations.
Our contribution may be modest in scale, but it is ambitious in commitment.
We are moving towards a more resilient energy model, increasing year after year renewable energy production, and preparing our third Voluntary National Review on the Sustainable Development Goals.
Ladies and Gentlemen, Artificial intelligence represents one of the most profound transformations humanity has ever known.
It opens extraordinary opportunities for scientific progress, medicine, education and the fight against climate change.
Yet it also compels us to ask a question that no previous generation has had to face with such urgency: How can we ensure that technological progress remains human progress?
This is the debate that truly lies before us.
It is not a debate about machines; it is a debate about ourselves.

We must ensure that artificial intelligence expands opportunities rather than inequalities; that it protects human rights rather than putting them at risk; that it strengthens our democracies rather than weakening them; and that it preserves the cultural and linguistic diversity, which constitutes one of humanity’s most valuable heritages.
For a country such as Andorra, this last aspect is particularly relevant.
The digital revolution must not lead to cultural homogenization that condemns languages with fewer speakers to invisibility.
That is why we advocate for global digital governance that fully incorporates respect for multilingualism, cultural diversity and equal access to knowledge.

And this is why Andorra will continue to work, both within the Group of Friends of Multilingualism and the Group of Francophone Ambassadors, to ensure that new digital tools, as well as the United Nations itself, continue to reflect the plurality of peoples and cultures that we represent.

Ladies and Gentlemen, This Organization exists because the international community understood that the destiny of peoples is shared; because no nation can prosper while ignoring the suffering of others; because the security of one depends on the security of all.

In this regard, I would first like to refer to the excellent UN80 Initiative, which proposes improvements to the work of the Secretariat, a stronger mandate lifecycle and a simplification of structures to avoid duplication.
Secondly, I would like to emphasize the need for reform of the Security Council so that the Organization reflects the realities of today rather than those of eighty years ago.

The most important reform, however, is to ensure that this Organization remains a space where States not only defend their legitimate interests, but are also capable of exercising a shared responsibility in addressing the great challenges facing humanity and, above all, continue to believe that what unites us is stronger than what divides us.

Since 2017, he has exercised his mandate during one of the most difficult and uncertain periods the international community has known, consistently defending the principles of the United Nations Charter and reminding us, even when it seemed most difficult, that multilateralism remains the best hope for preserving peace, dignity and cooperation among peoples.
I hope that the next Secretary-General elected will possess the same capacity and ambition to strengthen the Organization and to confront, with determination, the challenges facing humanity.
This will be the last time that I have the honour of addressing this General Assembly as Head of Government of the Principality of Andorra.
It will be my eighth intervention before this Assembly: six times in person and, unfortunately, twice virtually because of the COVID-19 pandemic.

On eight occasions, I have had the privilege of bringing the voice of my country to this forum, sharing its convictions and defending its interests with the certainty that the greatness of a nation is not measured by its size, nor by its economic or military power, but by the strength of its values and by its willingness to contribute to the common good.
And I continue to believe, as I did on the first day, that the United Nations is indispensable.
Not because it is perfect, but because it remains the finest expression of an extraordinary idea: that, despite our differences, dialogue will always be more powerful than force.
It has been one of the greatest honours of my tenure as Head of Government of Andorra to represent and serve my country from this podium.
The recently deceased Franco-Iranian artist Marjane Satrapi once wondered whether we may have misunderstood the very purpose of education.
Perhaps, she said, before teaching our children how to achieve economic or professional success, we should teach them that true success lies in humanism.

The history of humanity cannot be understood without the extraordinary capacity of human beings to create communities, cooperate and build societies through intelligence and language, but also through empathy.
We have come this far because we understood that intelligence allows us to organize ourselves, language enables us to communicate, and empathy teaches us to care for one another.
In doing so, we discovered one of civilization’s greatest achievements: that when someone is vulnerable, the community does not abandon them; it protects them.
Likewise, in the face of the great challenges of our time, no nation can save itself alone.
That is why the future of Andorra and all other nations lies within the United Nations, and, I hope one day, in our case, also within the European Union as an associated State.
Because regardless of whether a country is richer or poorer, we will only be able to shape our common future if we deepen the ties between our peoples, both globally and regionally.
If we preserve this conviction, we will continue to find pathways towards prosperity, peace and justice.
For the future will not depend only on the intelligence we are capable of creating; above all, it will depend on the humanity we are capable of defending and preserving.

Statement by the United Arab Emirates At the High-Level General Debate of the 81st Session of the General Assembly Delivered by: His Excellency Khalifa Shaheen Al Marar Minister of State New York, September 28, 2026 Mr. President, Our region and the world are undergoing a period of rapid transformation, marked by intensifying challenges and divisions.

Amid all this, the United Arab Emirates stands tall — guided by a clear vision and unwavering determination to transform challenges into opportunities, turn ambitions into achievements, and open new horizons for peace, development, and prosperity for our people, the peoples of the region, and the world.

This stems from our principled approach rooted in de-escalation, bridge-building, the promotion of diplomacy and dialogue, the peaceful settlement of disputes, and the rejection of the unlawful use or threat of force, as well as coercion.
This approach is grounded in full respect for the relations, sovereignty of States, good-neighborly international law, and the Charter of the United Nations.

These values have long underpinned our domestic and foreign policies: As Iran continues its occupation of the three Emirati islands — Greater Tunb, Lesser Tunb, and Abu Musa — which we reject, the United Arab Emirates has consistently called for a peaceful settlement of this conflict, whether the through direct negotiations or by recourse International Court of Justice.
to Amid growing threats to navigation in our region and beyond, my country has continued to emphasize the principles of freedom of navigation and the right of transit passage.

We stress the need to secure and protect the safe flow of supply chains, trade, and energy in accordance with international law, including the law of the sea, and the principle of state sovereignty, recognizing these as pillars of food security, development, and prosperity of nations.
The United Arab Emirates has continued to support every sincere effort to achieve peace, particularly in Yemen, Libya, the Sahel, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Myanmar, Haiti, and elsewhere.

We have also supported efforts to reach a sustainable political solution to the Question of the Moroccan Sahara, based on the Moroccan Autonomy Initiative, while affirming the Kingdom of Morocco’s sovereignty over this territory.

We have remained steadfast in our role as a trusted international mediator, successfully conducting twenty-six mediations that facilitated the exchange of nearly eight thousand prisoners between Ukraine and the Russian Federation, ensuring their safe return to their homelands and families.
The UAE has also stood ready to support nations undergoing positive transformations — such as Syria and Lebanon — as they move towards a secure and stable future.
Regarding Sudan, my country has underscored the imperative of ending the humanitarian catastrophe, securing a permanent and unconditional ceasefire that would bring an end to the civil war.

This includes launching a comprehensive and credible political process, led by civilians, which would culminate in the formation of a civil government independent of both parties to the conflict and of extremist groups.
It is crucial to ensure that neither side of the conflict has a role in the new civilian government.

The future of Sudan must be decided solely by the Sudanese people, and the international community must press the leaders of Port Sudan authorities and those of Rapid Support Forces, as parties to the conflict, to engage seriously with international initiatives.
As for Gaza, the UAE was among the first to support the framework established by the international community to end the horrific war.

We have stressed the need to fully implement the comprehensive plan to end the conflict in Gaza — and the associated roadmap — including Israel’s withdrawal from the Gaza Strip, the disarmament of Hamas, and the advancement of a serious political horizon leading to a just and lasting settlement of the Palestinian Question based on the two-state solution.
This entails the establishment of an independent, sovereign Palestinian state living side-by-side with Israel in peace and security.

We also underscore the importance of ensuring the unification of Gaza and the West Bank under a Palestinian authority that, once reformed, will be capable to fulfill its responsibilities and ensure that arms remain solely under its control.

We further underscore the urgent need to halt Israel's dangerous escalation in the West Bank and its settlement activities — which are accompanied by the rise of settler violence, terrorism, and the siege of Palestinian villages, as well as the ongoing violations in East Jerusalem and at holy sites and the attempts to impose new historical and legal realities on the ground.
My country condemns all such actions in the strongest terms.
For decades, the UAE's commitment to the Palestinian people has remained unwavering.
Today, that commitment continues through our role as the largest provider of humanitarian aid to Gaza, along with our humanitarian and development projects in the West Bank.

This role reflects the core values of our foreign policy, which is driven by the spirit of giving through effective international partnerships while the principles of international humanitarian law and the protection of civilians.

As the United Nations prepares to transition to new leadership, we look forward to the next Secretary-General using his or her good offices to activate preventive and mediation mechanisms before the first signs of crises emerge, rather than merely reacting once they have erupted.
Crises must be addressed at their roots, not simply managed.
Mr. President, My country has refused to let the crises surrounding us undermine the world-leading achievements we have built over decades.
On the contrary, we have pressed ahead with progress across every sector — for this nation was forged not in the absence of challenges, but in defiance of them.
The peoples of our region aspire to stability and prosperity in an environment defined by cooperation, moderation, and tolerance — not by violence, hatred, extremism, or terrorism.

The UAE model has demonstrated its resilience and its capacity to deliver tangible results by investing in the key pillars of national strength, foremost among them strategic independence, industrial capabilities, advanced defense systems, and world-class infrastructure and logistics.

This is complemented by the empowerment of human capital, the cultivation of a knowledge-and innovation-based economy, and the harnessing of the opportunities offered by the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreements (CEPAs) concluded with thirty-eight nations—among other frameworks—to diversify markets and supply chains and broaden horizons for trade and investment.
We will continue to cement the UAE's role as a global hub connecting markets and capital, opening ever-broader horizons for growth.

This is the promise the UAE makes to its people and to all who call it home — and it is the bedrock of our international partnerships, particularly with the nations of the Global South and Africa, which have matured into an enduring strategic cooperation rooted in mutual respect and shared interests.
The UAE continues to expand its investments in artificial technologies, healthcare, and intelligence, emerging education.

We are also strengthening our position as a trusted and responsible leader in the energy sector — balancing the needs of today with bold investment in the solutions of the historic tomorrow and driving commitments of the 'UAE Consensus' toward long-term collective action.

This year, the UAE is preparing to co-host with Senegal the UN Water Conference, recognizing the importance of concerted, coordinated international action in confronting the challenges of water, climate, and food security.
We are confident the conference will mark a vital milestone in advancing real, practical solutions for water security.

These efforts embody our firm commitment to turning the challenge of water scarcity into an opportunity for innovation and joint international action, including through the Mohamed bin Zayed Water Initiative, which harnesses innovation, partnership, and investment to deliver lasting, sustainable solutions for present and future generations.

Two days ago, Abu Dhabi also hosted the opening of the 15th UN Congress on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice, highlighting the need to keep pace with rapid technological advancement and to protect societies from the impacts of crime, violence, and exploitation.
At the same time, we are investing in the values of tolerance, peaceful coexistence, and inclusion through partnerships that bring together diverse nationalities and faiths.
We are building a society in which women participate fully, equally, and meaningfully, and in which young people are genuine partners in shaping their future.

In conclusion, Mr. President, my country will remain committed to the path of moderation, the rejection of violence and extremism, and the investment in people and in the vast potential with which our region is so richly endowed.
We extend our hands to our partners in the region and across the world to build rather than to destroy, and to unite rather than to divide.

AN ABSURDITY, SOMETHING THAT IT SEEMS FEW HAVE TAKEN THE TIME TO REFLECT UPON, EXCEPT THOSE OF US WHO HAVE THE PASSION OF READING JORGE LUIS BORGES AND LOVE HIS VIEW OF VALIDATING AN IDEA BY TAKING IT TO ITS LIMIT.

IN SHORT, THESE TECHNOLOGICAL IMPROVEMENTS NOT ONLY HAVE NOT RESULTED IN ANY OF THE CATASTROPHES WITH THE that they have tried to sow terror in us, but that moreover, each of them also ended up expanding what the human being was capable of doing.
Now man has built machines capable of carrying out tasks that until very recently seemed reserved to his own intelligence.
And where many see a threat, we see a frontier.
Artificial intelligence can multiply our productivity by orders of magnitude that we still do not understand.
Invoking Adam Smith, artificial intelligence will be the pin factory of the twenty-first century, and much more.
It can transform our economies, our medicine, our education and even our way of governing.
But prudence does not mean fear.
And, what is more, fear, from no point of view, should automatically become obedience.
In fact, the dystopian scenarios that are usually invoked to instill fear and foster State control make no sense from the economic point of view.
The answer lies in Adam Smith.
Artificial intelligence, just like the division of labour in the case of the pin factory, is an accelerator for productivity growth.
However, Smith pointed out that the division of labour is limited by the size of the market.
Therefore, growth will be extinguished together with its counterpart of genuine demand, without fiscal deficits or spurious issuance of money.

But not only that; moreover, those projects have to be financed and that is done with the resources of human beings, that is, their initial endowments and the level of wealth, which is the counterpart of the size of the market.

What is more, the purpose of producing more is a higher level of consumption; however, the satisfaction that it generates grows at a diminishing rate, while the loss of satisfaction from giving up leisure for greater production grows disproportionately.
Therefore, that point where what is gained through a greater amount of consumption is equated with the loss of leisure leads the system to an equilibrium position with no room for dystopian terror.
That is why, when we hear that the State must control artificial intelligence, it is worth remembering something elementary: the State is not an abstract creature, but men, officials and bureaucrats.
And to grant it control over innovation is to grant some, in the best and most naive of cases, the power to limit what others can create.

History gives us reasons to examine such power carefully: for centuries, fear of tomorrow was an argument for restricting freedoms in the present, with the same promise: give us part of your freedom and we will protect you from this new threat.
We will apply a different principle... in the face of uncertainty, we propose determination.
In the face of fear, courage.
In the face of decline, ambition.
And in the face of resignation, we propose optimism.
That is why I say to you, in the face of artificial intelligence, Argentina will place itself at the vanguard of freedom.
We have the critical minerals, the energy, the talent and the capacity to compete in every link of that value chain.

And we want to be the most competitive place in the world to develop it, with a cutting-edge legal framework, the commitment not to regulate preventively, limited liability for companies operating with AI agents, and tax benefits.

Because artificial intelligence is not a geopolitically neutral matter: it is necessary for the West to lead the development of technology, in order to ensure that it is in keeping with our fundamental libertarian values, such as respect for life, liberty, private property and the notion of human dignity.

In this, we fully share the vision of President Trump Mr. President; We are living through one of those strange moments in history in which one world begins to disappear before the next has finished being born.
But they are also extraordinary moments.
Because during long periods of stability, nations administer the world they inherited.
In periods of transformation, some have the opportunity to build the world to come.
Argentina wants to be one of them.
We will continue to form part of multilateral forums, in good faith, because there are problems that require joint work.
But we do not confuse cooperation with subordination: we believe in alliances and, before anything else, in nations.
Argentina speaks of this with the experience of one who knows its own mistakes.
We know the cost of isolation.
We know the cost of destroying a currency.
We know the cost of turning the State into a permanent obstacle to human initiative.
For a century we tried almost every way of preventing our own greatness.
And we survived, not intact, but we survived.
And perhaps for that reason today we understand something that other nations may forget: decline is not a destiny, but the result of repeated decisions.
And if that course can be chosen, it can also be changed.
That is what Argentina is trying to do.
We have the energy the world will need. We have food.
We have the South Atlantic and we are a natural gateway to Antarctica.
And we have something that for too long we lacked: the will to transform our possibilities into national power.
We want a prosperous, influential and powerful Argentina.
Not to subjugate others, but to be free.
Not to conquer others, but so that our destiny may be decided by Argentines.
Therefore, to the free men and women of the world, to To the scientists, to the entrepreneurs, to the creators, to those who dreamed of a land where they could begin anew, I say: look to the south.
You will find a vast land, of fertile fields, of oil, of minerals, and of human talent.
A land that received millions who crossed oceans in the hope that their children would live better than they did, and built one of the most prosperous nations on Earth.
We have the responsibility to live up to that.
We do not know exactly what the world that is being born will be like.
But we do know what kind of nation we want to be when it arrives.
A free nation. A prosperous nation. A sovereign nation.
A nation capable of defending what is its own and open to the world.
A nation that is not afraid to once again utter a word that for too long seemed forbidden: greatness.
No nation has a guaranteed place in history: it is built generation after generation, with work, with freedom, and with the will of a people who refuse to accept that their best days are behind them.
We believe that Argentina still has a great history ahead of it.
And we have decided to go in search of it.

Honorable President of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen; The peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan, established on August 8, 2025, with the support and personal engagement of US President Donald Trump, has opened up new opportunities for our region, the South Caucasus.
On this occasion, I would firstly like to address what President Trump referred to from this podium two days ago.

I have said it and I reiterate it now: the breakthrough in the establishment of peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan simply would not have been possible without President Trump’s personal engagement and his resolute commitment to establishing peace.
President Trump’s personal presence, by the way, has practical and symbolic expressions on the ground as well.

The fourth paragraph of the Peace Declaration adopted at the Peace Summit held at the White House on August 8, 2025 states (quote): “The Republic of Armenia will work with the United States of America and mutually determined third parties, to set forth a framework for the “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” (TRIPP) connectivity project in the territory of the Republic of Armenia.
We confirm our determination to pursue efforts in good faith to achieve this goal in the most expeditious manner.”
The implementation of the TRIPP project is thus becoming a reality with tangible steps.

The Framework Agreement on Strategic Cooperation on the “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” project signed between Armenia and the United States of America will soon be ratified by the National Assembly of the Republic of Armenia.
We are currently working with the United States government to establish the TRIPP development company and sign a shareholders agreement.
Accordingly, Armenia will initially have a 26 percent stake in the TRIPP development company, and the United States will have a 74 percent stake.
The agreement provides that in the event of its extension, in the 50th year, the Republic of Armenia’s share will become 49 percent, without additional investment.

One of the practical expressions of the TRIPP project will be the implementation of paragraph 3 of the Peace Declaration, adopted by me and the President of Azerbaijan on August 8, 2025, and signed by the President of the United States as a witness.

Paragraph 3 of the Declaration states (I quote): “We reaffirmed the importance of the opening of communications between the two countries for intra-state, bilateral, and international transportation for the promotion of peace, stability, and prosperity in the region and in its neighborhood on the basis of respect for the sovereignty, territorial integrity, and jurisdiction of the States.

These efforts are to include unimpeded connectivity between the main part of the Republic of Azerbaijan and its Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic through the territory of the Republic of Armenia with reciprocal benefits for international and intrastate connectivity for the Republic of Armenia.”
The implementation of the TRIPP project will be of historic importance for the Republic of Armenia.
For the first time since the early 1990s, Armenia will get railway connection with Azerbaijan, and thus with Russia, Central Asia and China.

However, it should be emphasized that after the Peace Summit on August 8, 2025, Azerbaijan opened its railway to Armenia, and now we have a railway connection with Azerbaijan through the territory of Georgia.

The implementation of the TRIPP project will create a direct railway connection between Armenia and Azerbaijan, as well as a railway connection from Azerbaijan to Azerbaijan through the territory of Armenia and from Armenia to Armenia through the territory of Azerbaijan, because Armenia does not have a railway connection between its northern and southern regions, and this is practically possible only through the territory of the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic of the Republic of Azerbaijan, while Azerbaijan does not have a railway connection with its Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic and this is practically possible only through the territory of Armenia.

In the near future, we will restore the railway sections of Meghri and Yeraskh in the Republic of Armenia that existed during the Soviet Union and were later destroyed, and the railway connections I mentioned will be opened.
But this will also have a huge international significance, because in parallel with the construction of the aforementioned railways, we are waiting for the opening of the Armenia-Turkey railway.

Together with the TRIPP project, this could become one of the most important events in the field of international logistics in recent decades, because thus a new railway connection will be opened between China, Central Asia, Turkey and the European Union.

All this opens up another crucial opportunity for international logistics, because the restoration of the railway connection between Armenia and the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic of the Republic of Azerbaijan restores the railway connection between the Persian Gulf and the Black Sea.

This is an important nuance, because it shows why and how the implementation of the TRIPP project promises great benefits to all countries in our region, and these potential benefits can become a cornerstone of long-term stability and peace.

After almost 35 years of conflict, we are now discussing issues of building pipelines, power lines, and roads in addition to the east-west railway within the framework of the TRIPP project, and this will enable not only the Republic of Armenia, but also the entire South Caucasus to become a Crossroads of Peace.

Honorable President of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, Excellencies, All of this reflects the optimism that has been established in our region and in the Republic of Armenia since the Washington Peace Summit on August 8, 2025.

The citizens of Armenia reaffirmed their optimism in the parliamentary elections held on June 7 of this year, where the overwhelming majority of voters voted in favor of the slogan “Own up the peace,” enabling the “Civil Contract” party to form a parliamentary majority.

The elections took place under special circumstances of external information manipulation, and a number of external and internal forces were developing and implementing a plan to seize the state, using mass disinformation, hybrid and other tools, as well as the distribution of mass voter bribes.

But the democratic and institutional reforms we have implemented in recent years proved their strength, and Armenia's state institutions demonstrated high resilience, preventing state capture and giving the people of Armenia the opportunity to have their say.
The people of Armenia have owned up the peace, and we must consistently engage in the further strengthening and institutionalization of peace.

In the relations between Armenia and Azerbaijan, the clarification of the fate of several thousand missing persons is a matter that needs to be addressed, on which we have reached an agreement to cooperate with Azerbaijan.
Armenia is ready to continue and deepen cooperation with Azerbaijan on the issue of demining.
And of course, people in the Republic of Armenia are waiting for the return of Armenians who were detained in Azerbaijan as a consequence of the conflict.

Along with these issues still being unresolved, another reason that fuels pessimists is the use of conflict rhetoric from time to time in certain circles of Armenia and Azerbaijan, sometimes at the official level.

I think that we, I mean Armenia and Azerbaijan, have achieved more than sufficient results, which should be more valuable for us than the use of conflict rhetoric, whether it is about history or historical-cultural monuments or anything else.
Nurturing the peace, strengthening and making it institutional should be the main theme of cooperation between Armenia and Azerbaijan.

For two and a half years now, there have been no casualties or injuries as a result of cross-fire between Armenia and Azerbaijan, and I believe this is the greatest value that has been created as a result of the recent years.

We have never had such a period in the relations between independent Armenia and independent Azerbaijan before, even though Armenians and Azerbaijanis have centuries of experience of peaceful coexistence.

Our task, however, is not to restore that historical experience, but to build interstate relations on the basis of that experience of the peoples, based on respect for each other's territorial integrity, sovereignty, and political independence.

This, by the way, is exactly the rhetoric that Armenia and Azerbaijan have already agreed upon and initialed in the text of the agreement on establishing peace and interstate relations between the two countries.

The signing and ratification of the agreement, which was initialed at the Washington Peace Summit, is the next major topic in the joint agenda of Armenia and Azerbaijan, and we will consistently continue to work in this direction.
The balanced and balancing foreign policy adopted by Armenia stems from the logic of multipolarity, which is one of the key principles of the United Nations.

In recent years, we have established strategic relations with Georgia, France, China, the Netherlands, Kazakhstan, Germany, Luxembourg, the United Kingdom, Bulgaria, Croatia, Lithuania, the United States of America, and the European Union.
Today, by the way, the European Commission approved the decision to adopt autonomous trade measures for Armenia, which is yet another manifestation of the new quality of Armenia-EU relations.

Our relations with Russia are in a transformation phase, and this is a natural process, because throughout the entire preceding period, the largest factor influencing relations between Armenia and Russia was the Armenia-Azerbaijan conflict.

Now that we have established peace with Azerbaijan, Armenia-Russia relations will naturally change, and it is our desire that these relations develop on the basis of the principles of friendship and mutual respect.

We will, of course, continue to develop our relations with our partners located closer to or farther from Armenia, and in this regard, I would like to highlight the countries of Central Asia, with which our relations are also highly dynamic.
But I also cannot but emphasize that the normalization and deepening of relations with our neighbors are nevertheless of key importance for our foreign policy vision.
I have already spoken about the dynamics of our relations with Azerbaijan.

We have a high-level dialogue with Turkey, and I want to confirm the words expressed by President Erdogan from this podium the other day, that we are resolutely pushing forward the process of normalizing Armenia-Turkey relations.
Our relations with our two other neighbors, the Islamic Republic of Iran and Georgia, remain of exceptional importance to us, and our good neighborliness continues to develop and deepen.
The Republic of Armenia considers its contribution to the region’s stability and development to be our key task in international peace, stability, and development.

Honorable President of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, Excellencies, This October, Armenia will host the 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity, and I invite you all to participate in this very important event for Armenia and for the international biodiversity agenda.
Can multilateralism still protect the weak as well as the strong?
Can international law restrain power, rather than merely record its consequences?
Can development remain a promise for all, rather than a privilege for some?
For Antigua and Barbuda, these are not philosophical questions.
For Small Island Developing States, they are questions of survival.
As we begin the eighty-first session of this General Assembly, we stand between two eras: one ending, and another waiting to be shaped.
For my country, that appreciation is deeply personal.
The entire population had to be evacuated. Homes were destroyed. Livelihoods disappeared.
An island community was brought to its knees.
And he understood what Small Island Developing States have been telling the world for decades: climate change is not waiting for the future.
It is already destroying lives, economies and communities.
He continued to stand with SIDS.
He returned to Antigua and Barbuda for the Fourth International Conference on Small Island Developing States.
He championed vulnerable countries and supported the international effort that brought the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index into being.
Whether confronting climate change, challenging inequality or calling for reform of the international financial system, he was a fearless and principled advocate.
He never relented in demanding a fairer world, and he consistently placed the concerns of small island states before the international community.
But gratitude for the past must now be matched by courage in shaping the future.
The next Secretary-General will inherit a United Nations confronting wars and conflicts that devastate lives and undermine international stability.
Deep geopolitical divisions, financial constraints, the climate emergency and declining trust will test the Organization’s capacity to respond.
Excellencies, the choice before us is about more than selecting an individual.
It is about the future direction of this Organization.
That is why Antigua and Barbuda has nominated María Fernanda Espinosa to serve as the next Secretary-General.
We believe she is the right leader for this moment.
After more than eighty years, no woman has ever served as Secretary-General.
Our case for María Fernanda Espinosa rests on more than gender.
It rests on competence, experience, independence and leadership.
At a time of fragmentation, the United Nations needs a credible bridge-builder capable of restoring confidence in multilateralism.
Antigua and Barbuda believes that María Fernanda Espinosa can provide that leadership.
Technology is racing ahead of governance.
Artificial intelligence offers extraordinary possibilities, but it also raises profound concerns about who will control its development and share its benefits.
Small states must not be left as spectators in this new era.
Nor can we accept an international system in which rules are binding upon the weak but negotiable for the powerful.
Sovereignty cannot depend upon power, nor justice upon the identity of one’s friends.
Antigua and Barbuda commands neither a great army nor a large market.
International law, cooperation and multilateralism are fundamental to our security and stability.
For us, the United Nations is not optional.
It is essential to our survival.
We support a more efficient, coherent and accountable United Nations.
But efficiency cannot become another word for retreat.
The UN80 reform process must be judged by whether this Organization serves people better.
For SIDS, that means protecting the development pillar, advancing implementation of the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS, and bringing effective support closer to those who need it.
Trade disputes, tariffs and economic fragmentation raise the costs of food, transport and development.
Too often, small states pay the price for disputes we did not create.
We call upon the major economies to choose dialogue and cooperation.
Fairness must also govern international finance.
A hurricane does not check GDP before destroying a school.
A rising sea does not consult income classifications before entering a home or village.
That is why the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index matters.
It provides a fairer measure of the structural vulnerabilities that GDP alone cannot capture.
Nowhere is the urgency greater than in the climate crisis.
For Small Island Developing States, climate change is not a warning about tomorrow.
Warmer oceans fuel more destructive hurricanes. Coastlines are retreating.
Salt water contaminates freshwater supplies, forcing countries such as mine to rely on increasingly costly means of securing safe water.

The General Assembly’s High-level Meeting on Sea Level Rise placed before the international community fundamental questions of statehood, sovereignty, maritime rights, displacement, culture and identity.
Climate change must never be allowed to erase a nation’s sovereignty, its statehood or the rights of its people.
Antigua and Barbuda and other vulnerable states sought clarity on the obligations of States in relation to climate change.
The International Court of Justice has now spoken.
Climate obligations are not acts of generosity.
They are responsibilities under international law.
For small states, international law is more than a moral aspiration.
For SIDS, climate justice is survival.
Our survival is inseparable from the ocean.
The entry into force of the BBNJ Agreement is therefore an important achievement for multilateralism.
But implementation will be the real test.
SIDS must share fairly the benefits arising from marine genetic resources.
Capacity-building must be meaningful, and marine technology must be accessible.
Climate justice cannot be separated from historical justice.
The Caribbean did not arrive at this moment on equal terms.
Centuries of enslavement and colonial extraction transferred wealth from our societies and denied generations the means to build prosperity.
Political independence did not erase that harm.
Today, countries that contributed least to climate change must borrow at high cost to rebuild from disasters driven overwhelmingly by emissions accumulated elsewhere.
That is where climate debt meets historical debt.
Antigua and Barbuda stands firmly with CARICOM and Africa in demanding reparatory justice for people of African descent.
Reparatory justice requires acknowledging responsibility, repairing continuing harm and correcting structures that still reproduce inequality.
Expressions of regret are not enough.
Justice requires honest dialogue followed by concrete measures for repair, restitution and development.
Reparatory justice is not a favor.
It is a claim grounded in responsibility, equality and human dignity.
Development finds its true meaning in the lives and dignity of people.
Non-communicable diseases cut short too many lives and diminish the quality of life of too many of our citizens.
Preventing these diseases, detecting them early and ensuring effective treatment are national development priorities.
Preventable vision impairment denies thousands of our people opportunities to learn, work and live independently.

Antigua and Barbuda will continue to champion mental health, strengthen our universal health programmes to address non-communicable diseases, and place eye health firmly within our development priorities.
This November, Antigua and Barbuda will host a Global Eye Health Summit to move the international community from advocacy to action against the growing burden of preventable sight loss.

We invite Member States and partners to join us and support an Eye Health Compact that expands access, strengthens prevention and treatment, mobilizes finance, and integrates eye health into development.
Two years ago, the international community gathered in Antigua and Barbuda and adopted the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS—ABAS—our ten-year framework for sustainable development and resilience.
Now comes the harder part: implementation.
SIDS need finance, technology, capacity and institutions that recognise vulnerability.
The SIDS Centre of Excellence will help turn ABAS commitments into practical solutions through better data, innovation, investment and support for debt sustainability.
ABAS must move from commitment to implementation—and SIDS must move from vulnerability towards resilience.
International financial architecture must also change.
The Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development in Sevilla placed debt and development finance closer to the center of the international agenda.
That progress must now become action.
Small states cannot develop sustainably when they must repeatedly borrow to rebuild.
We cannot fulfil the promise of ABAS while carrying unsustainable debt.
Nor can we build resilience when the cost of capital itself penalizes vulnerability.
For too long, the international financial architecture has asked vulnerable countries how much debt they can carry.
It must also ask how much development they can achieve.
How can countries realize their potential when debt service, repeated shocks and high borrowing costs consume the resources needed for schools, hospitals and resilient infrastructure?
Finance must create fiscal space for development.
Vulnerable states need greater access to long-term, affordable and predictable financing, together with debt solutions that respond to their real circumstances.
We call for the launch of the intergovernmental process on debt agreed in Sevilla.
There can be no sustainable development without peace.
But peace begins long before guns fall silent.
It begins when young people see a future; when societies provide food, education, employment and opportunity; and when injustice is addressed before it becomes instability and conflict.
In a fractured world, the United Nations must renew both its operational relevance and its moral clarity.
It must help forge a new compact between developed and developing countries, connect finance to resilience, and support local leadership with global solidarity.
Development is an instrument of peace.
The United Nations must invest as seriously in preventing wars as it does in responding after they begin.
Diplomacy, mediation and development must be central to that work.
Throughout every crisis, one principle must remain constant: international law must apply equally to all.
The credibility of the international system depends upon that consistency.
United Nations reform must extend to the Security Council—its composition, its decisions and its capacity to act.
Antigua and Barbuda welcomes the initiative led by France and Mexico calling on permanent members to refrain voluntarily from using the veto in situations involving mass atrocities.
We will join the growing number of Member States supporting this call.
The veto must not paralyse the Council or prevent it from fulfilling its responsibility to maintain international peace and security.
Africa’s continued exclusion from permanent membership is an injustice that must be corrected.
Africa must have permanent representation of the Council.
Small Island Developing States must also have an assured voice at this table.
Antigua and Barbuda calls for a dedicated SIDS seat on a reformed Security Council.
The Council’s credibility depends equally on its response to those who urgently need its support.
The crisis in Haiti is a human tragedy and a challenge to Caribbean stability and democratic progress.

We call on the Security Council to renew the mandate of the Gang Suppression Force and international partners to provide the personnel, equipment and sustained financing needed to make that mandate effective.
The hardship facing the Cuban people also demands our attention.
Antigua and Barbuda calls on the United States and Cuba to return to the table of diplomacy and work as good neighbors towards resolving their longstanding differences.
The Cuban people must not bear collective punishment for political disagreements.
Their well-being must remain central to efforts to find a peaceful and lasting solution.
Across our region, our purpose is clear: to protect human dignity, strengthen stability and ensure that dialogue and cooperation prevail.
Excellencies: The world is changing—its climate, its technology and its balance of economic power.
This United Nations must change with it.
But its founding principles must endure: the equality of nations, the dignity of peoples, the sovereignty of States and respect for international law.
Mr. President: Let United Nations reform strengthen multilateralism.
Let international law protect every nation.
Let finance serve development rather than deepen debt.
Let us implement ABAS, protect our ocean and invest in human dignity.
And as this Organization prepares for new leadership, let us choose leadership equal to this moment.
History will not judge us by the number of resolutions we adopt.
It will judge us by whether we acted when the seas rose, inequality deepened, international law was violated and multilateralism faltered.
Let us enter this new era with courage in our leadership, fairness in our decisions and hope in our common future.
And it is our hope that this United Nations can still fulfil the promise of its Charter.

My dear colleagues, this evening I want to talk about the need for nations to work together on the new challenges that we face climate change, emerging technology and the breakdown of international rules.
Eight decades ago, the citizens and leaders of our nations made a solemn promise to future generations.
Having known the untold sorrow of two devastating global conflicts in their lifetimes, they vowed to work together to prevent another.

The pioneers who built this institution from the ruins of war, proud Australians among them, were also coming to terms with two terrible truths the horrors of the Holocaust and the unprecedented horror of nuclear weapons.
A depth of evil and a scale of destruction beyond imagining even a decade earlier.
Yet rather than recoil from that reality, our leaders stood together to face it, learn from it, and most importantly, guard against its return.
And instead of surrendering to fear or dealing in retribution, or abandoning their fate to a world governed by force alone,
they came together to renew and affirm their faith in humanity, in the essential and equal dignity and worth of every individual,
in the sovereignty of every nation and in the capacity and indeed the responsibility of all of us to give the Universal declaration of human rights,
life and weight and real meaning by engaging in the dialogue that builds trust and deepens understanding and backing those words with actions.

In this moment, we need to lean in and strengthen and modernise the fundamental parts of the UN system that help to build peace and promote economic development and sustainability, sovereignty, prosperity and peace are never guaranteed.

They must be created, nurtured and protected by each generation, supporting the jobs, homes, schools and healthcare that represent the fullest expression of the UN's commitment to the economic and social advancement of all peoples.
We know that the surest way to minimise the potential for conflict is to create the prosperity, opportunity and economic justice on which lasting peace depends.
That means cooperating on the urgent challenges that confront each of our sovereign nations, and creating solutions that work for our citizens.
This was the founding purpose of the United Nations.
And for the leaders who have gathered here this week, this remains the test of our time.
A test we can and we must pass.
Whether it is climate change or artificial intelligence.
There is always the temptation to say that our generation is being confronted by issues that our predecessors could not possibly have imagined while dealing with the world they would not recognise.
But for all the transformation the past eight decades have brought, the fundamental, fundamental stakes haven't changed.
And just as its values, our values, our ideals, our commitment to dialogue and cooperation proved equal to that task, then we can rise to meet these new challenges now.
We can reaffirm our national sovereignty and our shared humanity.
We can seize and share and shape the opportunities this moment holds in the interests of our citizens.
But we can only do it together.

From the very first days of this forum, Australia has always known that we understand that the UN mission cannot be entrusted solely to the great powers or the biggest countries, or even the loudest voices alone, nor can it be subcontracted to the world's richest companies, or dictated by the pace of technology.
Then now and always, shaping a secure, peaceful and prosperous world is a task for all of us.
And that world must be driven by the values and aspirations of all of us.
We all have a part to play.
And that is why Australia is seeking a non-permanent seat on the UN Security Council for 2029 2030.
The world faces tough times and Australia wants to respond to partner and to make a difference.
Should our Security Council bid prove successful.
Our purpose and approach will be consistent with how we have always conducted ourselves at the UN.
And we will protect what matters most.
Mr. president, a safer world is one governed by rules, not by power and force alone.
It is a world in which all countries have the freedom to decide their own future.
As a member of the UN Security Council, Australia will safeguard the rules that protect us all by upholding international law, including the UN charter and the sovereignty of all states.
We will amplify the voices of small states and middle powers to ensure a wider range of perspectives shape the council's decisions.
We will work to prevent crisis, resolve resolve conflicts and protect civilians through diplomacy, peace building and practical action.
Our objective will be to support a more effective, representative and responsive UN that is equipped to address the fast growing challenges of today. Listening, partnering. Protecting colleagues.
New issues are becoming international issues demanding our full attention.

Climate change, where the science foretold of the increase in frequency and intensity of extreme weather events that we are now experiencing emerging technology, including artificial intelligence, which is evolving at a furious pace, and the breakdown of trust, civility and social cohesion, which is promoting conflict within and between countries.
Clearly, the multilateral system we have all known and benefited from is under immense strain.
To promote the peace, to create a world of human dignity, to do justice to the UN's mission, we must embrace change and we must embrace reform.
Australia supports the rules and institutions that underpin open trade and connectivity.
That order, based on agreed rules and institutions, faces massive disruption.
This doesn't mean abandoning multilateralism, it means working to reform it.
So it's up to the challenges ahead and building beyond multilateralism, with new coalitions and partnerships to address and solve complex problems.
As a middle power, Australia is showing leadership and working with others on fresh ideas to tackle the big issues now facing the world in our region, the Indo Pacific.
We are elevating relationships that help to build sovereign capability and offer nations sovereign choice free from coercion, so that our partners can address the big issues confronting them.
Economic security, human development, energy security, transnational crime, sovereign capabilities, trade and investment, and science and technology.

Whether it's our support for our Pacific family, our partnerships in South East Asia the elevation of our relationships with Japan, India and the Republic of Korea, or the deepening of our partnerships with Europe and Canada.
We seek to amplify the voices of small and mid-sized states to ensure council decisions are informed by the widest possible perspectives.
Working strongly together on issues that matter to us, to them, and to the world.
We are developing these new partnerships while continuing to work closely with our principal ally, the United States, and our major trading partner in China.
Australia stands for a safer world where no country dominates and no country is dominated.
Crises are prevented, disputes are settled through rules and dialogue, and institutions deliver outcomes.
There are so many issues to confront urgently and cooperatively.
Last year at this assembly, Australian parents spoke to world leaders about their campaign, resulting in our nation's social media ban for under 16.
Those parents channelled their personal grief into a powerful call for global action.
Already, more than 20 countries are bringing in or have brought in age restrictions on social media.
And with the European Community taking action, there are many more to come.
More recently, our government has announced a digital duty of care.
Its purpose is to deliver control back into the hands of people by empowering them to determine what appears in their feed, giving them the choice.
The technological development that must now be the subject of public discussion is artificial intelligence.
AI can improve lives, boost growth and productivity, provide revolutionary breakthroughs in healthcare and other fields.
But leaders of AI companies themselves have warned of the potential risks to allow frontier AI to develop too fast without guardrails.
Recently, an artificial intelligence agent infiltrated an Australian government website.

This is unacceptable, and it is why Australia has been leading the way in establishing Australian standards for AI standards to ensure that AI will work and deliver for people, not the other way around.
We can't ignore AI or prevent it.
And it's why we joined with other nations this week to call for action to shape artificial intelligence development, rather than be passively shaped by it.
Australia is a nation built on fairness and opportunity that promotes equality and respect for all people.
We work to prevent conflict, protect civilians, and defend the rules that protect us all.
We uphold international law, including the UN charter, and support bold, practical reform to ensure the UN can best fulfill its mandate into the future.

We are strong supporters of freedom of navigation and overflight for all nations, just as we are in our efforts to combat nuclear proliferation We oppose Russia's continued illegal, unprovoked and immoral invasion of Ukraine and reiterate our calls for Russia's immediate, complete and unconditional withdrawal and an end to attacks upon civilians and civilian infrastructure.

This week, Australia endorsed the 2026 International Crimea Platform joint statement reaffirming our respect for Ukraine's sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders.
And we signed a new bilateral security agreement with Ukraine to complement the humanitarian and military support that we have provided.
When countries facing disaster and conflict reach out for help.
Australians always respond generously with humanitarian assistance.
We have a solemn duty to protect those who undertake this vital work.

Last year, following the killing of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom and the deaths of over 1000 other humanitarian workers in the last three years, Australia and eight partner nations led the development of a declaration for the protection of humanitarian personnel.
Now supported by 130 countries, that declaration outlines practical measures to ensure stronger accountability, safer access and better protection for aid workers operating in conflict zones.
Again, listening, partnering, protecting Australian values at work, in practice. Colleagues.
Last year, Australia took the considered decision to join other partners and recognise the state of Palestine.
It was motivated by the determination to try and end a cycle of violence that has stolen too many innocent lives.
