We know the only viable path to peace and security in Palestine, in Israel and in the broader Middle East is through a two state solution where the people of Israel and the people of Palestine can raise their children in freedom and safety.
We will continue to speak out against actions that damage that prospect of peace, including illegal settlements in the West Bank.

Just as we continue to oppose any role for the terrorists of Hamas in Palestine's future, the conflict in Iran has taken a severe toll on the Middle East and has had a devastating impact on the global economy.
Australia has been consistent in our calls for a ceasefire and for the Strait of Hormuz to reopen and restore the freedom of navigation and trade.
And we continue to call for Iran to halt its indiscriminate attacks on the region and to abandon any program to obtain nuclear weapons.
Colleagues, Australia's approach to diplomacy is both local and global.
Our geography gives us a unique perspective as a Pacific nation, inhabiting an entire continent and connected to South east Asia, the Indian Ocean and Antarctica.
We feel joined to our region not just by geography, but by our close human connections, including family.
We are one of the world's most successful multicultural democracies, proudly home to the oldest continuous civilisation on earth.
Our First Nations Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, and home also to people from more than 300 different ancestries.

With more than half of our population either born overseas or having at least one parent born overseas, we are investing in the multilateral system by elevating Pacific voices in shaping global decision making.
Working with them to advance their development needs and counter the transnational organised crime that is spreading across the beautiful Pacific Ocean that we share.
And addressing climate change, which threatens their very existence through rising sea levels and increasing salinity.
Accepting the science of climate change and acting upon it is rightfully the entry point for engaging with these vital nations of the Pacific.
Or as we call it, the Blue Continent.
It's why we are partnering with the Cop 31, President Takaya and Pacific Nations to sponsor a Pacific Pre-cop meeting in Fiji and Tuvalu.
Pacific countries have long been leaders on climate action.
Their voices are central to shaping the global response.
And we proudly work with them.
Mr. president, Australia's purpose in its relations with the United Nations is clear and our approach is principle.
We partner as equals and we protect what matters most.
We engage across regions, listen to different perspectives, and we build trust.
We champion the rights, sovereignty, and agency of all, particularly smaller and mid-sized nations.
We are a reliable, practical and transparent partner, and we play our part to protect the people of the world by taking on the difficult challenges shaping their lives and the health of their planet.
With innovative ideas and approaches Australia helped create the United Nations to bring an end to an era of destructive conflict, and to build something better for all of us.
A world where prosperity is driven by shared opportunity and peace is secured by collective responsibility.
Australia is stepping up to play our part.
193 States that have signed up to the UN Charter.
That have signed up to one essential principle: That relations between States are not governed by sheer power, but by rules.
Today, this commitment is being tested. By conflicts.
By shifts in power. By new technologies.
And our global institutions are struggling to keep pace.
So, let me ask question that I believe sits underneath everything we are discussing this week: Who decides?
Who decides whether a border is a line to be respected or a target to be crossed?
Who decides whether a human being or a machine pulls the trigger?
Who decides who gets heard, and who is left waiting outside the room?
For more than eighty years, this organisation has stood for one answer: power must be bound by rules agreed together.
That answer secured Austria's sovereignty and our prosperity. It still does.
We are a nation of nine million people.
An open, liberal democracy, and we are proud of it.
Alone, we cannot keep trade routes open, stabilise energy markets, or prevent wars.
Like most countries in this hall, we depend on a world in which borders are respected, agreements are kept, and strength is bound by law.
When that order weakens, the gravest price is paid by those least able to bear it: by countries already in crisis, by populations heavily dependent on food imports and by people caught in conflict.
In Austria we are fortunate to live in peace.
But the consequences reach us, too: energy prices rise, factories close, and families forced to flee war and seek safety in Europe.
This is why the United Nations matters.
This is why we are a proud host country of the Organization.
Why we - successfully - campaigned for a seat on the UN Security Council.
Austria will be a reliable partner in the Security Council during the next two years.
Austria – throughout its campaign – has made a promise: To spare no effort on the Security Council to protect our common rules.
To engage in dialogue with everyone.
And to rebuild trust in our global order that has been eroded by a dangerous zero-sum logic.
THE RULES ARE BEING TESTED But for all of us the road ahead is not easy.
Because today, that order is being tested, in conflict after conflict.
For more than four years, Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine has violated the UN Charter, and it still does.
During my last visit to Kyiv, I witnessed the pain it causes firsthand.
Austria’s position remains clear: we will not accept a change of borders by force.
We need an urgent ceasefire to create a credible path to negotiations between the parties.
In the Middle East, the continuous escalation teaches us a similar lesson.
After years of bloodshed and suffering, it is obvious: no one can bomb their way to peace.
We want a prosperous and safe Israel.
But the same applies to the Palestinians and to Israel’s neighbours.
Israelis and Palestinians deserve to live side by side in peace and security, with a credible path to a two-state solution.
Any unilateral actions that undermine this prospect – including the continued settlement expansions in the West Bank – only perpetuate the conflict and must be firmly rejected by all of us.
Palestinians in Gaza desperately need peace and stability, with Hamas disarmed and the IDF withdrawing from the Strip.
Iran and the United States must come back to the negotiating table: to end the suffering, to credibly revive the nuclear talks and to stop holding global supply chains hostage to political ends.
Especially when there are bilateral deadlocks and conflicts are impacting the whole world, we must pursue for multilateral solutions.
In Lebanon, we need a sustainable arrangement to support the LAF in disarming Hezbollah.
The withdrawal of UNIFIL must not create a vacuum that will leave the region worse off than before.

The same set of international rules must protect civilians in Sudan, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in Yemen, Haiti, Myanmar, Ethiopia and other conflicts that receive far too little international attention.
International law must apply to all states.
And where violations occur, there must be responsibility and accountability.
This is why Austria will also continue to stand firm in protecting the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court.
They need institutions capable of upholding them.
And today, the United Nations too often falls short.
Not because it has failed – because we have let it stand still.
There is no alternative to the UN.
There is only the work of making it work.
CHANGING HOW THE UN WORKS The United Nations was not created to discuss international problems.
It was created to solve them.
Yet as conflicts and injustice multiply, the UN too often fails to act.
Inside this building, that failure can look like another meeting without a decision.
Outside these walls, it means that wars continue, help does not arrive, and more families bury their dead.
For these families, UN procedures do not matter.
What matters to them is whether food arrives, whether a doctor reaches them, whether peacekeepers protect them.
Reform must therefore pass a simple test: does it make the United Nations more able to deliver when people need it?
Austria has been a strong supporter of the reform efforts of the Secretary-General.
And, as an incoming member of the Security Council, we are committed to protect the principles of the Charter.
To show to the world, that the Council can act.
And to work towards making the decisions we take there more inclusive.
ADDRESSING NEW DANGERS The United Nations was built to confront the dangers of 1945.
Today, we must face new and rapidly emerging dangers: one of the most urgent threats today is the loss of human control over weapons.
Every Austrian knows the Terminator movies, about a machine, sent to kill humans.
This killer robot was played by a famous Austrian-born, Arnold Schwarzenegger.
In the movies, Skynet learns to choose its own targets and starts a war.
Today, it is not fiction any more.
Today, weapons with increasing autonomy are already used on the battlefield.
The direction is clear: machines are gaining more freedom to find and strike targets.
But a machine cannot understand surrender or mercy.
It cannot face a court or answer for a death.
It must never have the final say over who lives and who dies.
We therefore need international rules for autonomous weapons, built around one clear principle: no machine may decide to take a human life.
Some will say that agreement is impossible when technology moves so quickly and major powers distrust one another. History says otherwise.
Austria was still occupied, while the superpowers were testing hydrogen bombs.

And yet, from this podium, Eisenhower named two things that did not yet exist: negotiations to restore Austria’s independence and: an international agency that would bring nuclear technology under international oversight.
To serve, as Eisenhower said: “the needs rather than the fears of mankind”.
Two years later, the IAEA began its work and Vienna became its home.
The world did not ban atomic energy.
It built rules for its peaceful use.
But those rules came only after Hiroshima and Nagasaki had shown the terrible cost of waiting.
We cannot afford to wait for a catastrophe to happen.
With artificial intelligence, we can still act first.
For this reason, Austria joins the UN Secretary-General and the President of the ICRC in calling for a legally binding instrument with clear prohibitions and restrictions on autonomous weapons.
We need binding rules that keep human beings in control and ensure accountability.
And we must not drag this out.
CLOSING: AUSTRIA’S CONTRIBUTION TO PEACE Every rule and reform I have spoken about serves one purpose: peace.
During our Security Council term, Austria will make emerging technologies, the protection of civilians, children in armed conflict, and women’s full participation in peace processes priorities.
Children must never be treated as collateral damage.
Women must have a real voice at the negotiating table, as leaders and peacebuilders, not as an afterthought.
It is the refusal to give violence the last word.
During the Cold War, states that deeply distrusted one another still met in Vienna.
Austria will keep that door open whenever dialogue can prevent bloodshed.
And peace rests on human rights.
In Vienna in 1993, the United Nations affirmed that those rights belong to every person, everywhere.
That principle is not settled history.
It is a responsibility we must defend today.
I began by asking who decides.
Let me end with Austria’s answer.
The strongest voice in the room must not decide alone.
Nor should those with the most tanks or the deepest pockets.
There are 193 countries in this hall.
Most of us cannot impose our will on others.
Most of us do not want to live in a world where some can.
Technology must remain under human control.
Responsibility must always be owned by us, by humans.
And, ultimately: Nations must speak so weapons remain silent.
Ladies and gentlemen, As global challenges become increasingly complex, no country can address them alone.
And yet, the growing limitations of multilateral mechanisms continue to undermine our collective ability to respond effectively to current and emerging threats.

Meeting these realities requires joint action, but true transformation is impossible without first restoring trust in the international order and demonstrating that multilateralism can once again deliver tangible results for all.

In an era marked by division, growing intolerance and stark double standards, Azerbaijan advocates for a reinvigorated and reformed multilateral system, underpinned by strict adherence to consistent and non-selective application of universally accepted norms and principles of international law.
Azerbaijan supports a more effective UN capable of delivering tangible results for Member States, especially in peace and security, development, climate resilience, and humanitarian action.
Through inclusive multilateralism, all States, large or small, particularly developing countries, must have the opportunity to participate equally in global decision-making.
In this context, reform of the UN Security Council is essential to make it more representative, effective, and responsive.
Restoring global trust begins, first and foremost, with respecting international law, sovereign equality, and peaceful coexistence.
It is exactly these principles that are guiding our efforts for peace and stability in the South Caucasus.
Even though the decades-long conflict with Armenia brought immense tragedy to our people and left deep scars across our land, Azerbaijan has chosen to look ahead and turn the page of enmity.
We offered Armenia peace fully in line with norms and principles of international law, based on mutual recognition of and respect for each other’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

Our normalization efforts produced historic results at the Washington Peace Summit last August, where the leaders of Azerbaijan and Armenia signed a Joint Declaration witnessed by President Trump of the United States of America.
Through this Declaration, both sides confirmed the end of the conflict and their will to jointly chart a peaceful and prosperous future.
The sides also initialed the Agreement on Establishment of Peace and Inter-State relations.
Today, we have achieved de facto peace.
Moreover, by unilaterally lifting transit restrictions, Azerbaijan facilitates transportation of goods to and from Armenia.
We have also established bilateral trade.
Azerbaijan provides strategically important oil products to Armenia on a regular basis despite increased volatility in markets and growing international demand for these commodities.
As we proceed with the peace agenda initiated by Azerbaijan, our entire region is now turning into a promising anchor of stability, connectivity, and tangible economic dividends.

To make this process irreversible, it is of crucial importance to eliminate the remaining obstacle, which will allow finalization of the normalization process through the signing of the already initialed bilateral agreement.

Complementing the regional normalization process, Azerbaijan’s post-conflict rehabilitation agenda aims to ensure that hundreds of thousands of Azerbaijanis can eventually exercise their right to a safe and dignified return to their homes.
Due to large-scale reconstruction efforts taken by the Government, life is now returning to our liberated territories.
Azerbaijan is rebuilding the entire region through “smart cities” and “smart villages” powered by green technology.
Areas that were once rubble and ashes are now rising as modern settlements.
Today, more than 90,000 people live, study, and work in the liberated territories.
Regrettably, a massive contamination of the territories of Azerbaijan with landmines and other explosive devices remains a serious obstacle.
This significantly obstructs the reconstruction and return process.
Since the liberation of occupied territories in 2020, more than 400 individuals, including women and children, became victim to landmines.
The cumulative toll of landmines over the past 30 years exceeded 3500 persons.

Given the scale of the problem, Azerbaijan considers mine action an essential prerequisite for fulfilling human rights and has formally declared humanitarian demining its 18th National Sustainable Development Goal.

Similarly, the need to clarify the fate and whereabouts of nearly 4000 Azerbaijanis who went missing due to the conflict is essential, not only for accountability and the rights of the victims and their families, but also for post-conflict reconciliation and normalization.
In the face of increasingly complex global challenges, our collective response must be inclusive, equitable and universal.
Azerbaijan’s own experience reflects these principles.
Our society is inherently multicultural and multi-confessional, shaped by centuries of peaceful coexistence of diverse ethnic, cultural and religious communities.
This tradition is reflected in Azerbaijan’s international initiatives, including the World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue.

Launched in 2008, in the framework of the “Baku Process”, the Forum has evolved into a prominent global platform for advancing intercultural dialogue and cultural diversity, receiving international recognition, including through a series of United Nations General Assembly resolutions.

Building upon these values, under the leadership of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, H.E. Mr. Ilham Aliyev, Azerbaijan has taken important steps to strengthen international solidarity, to build bridges and to mobilize collective responses.

This commitment has also been demonstrated through successful hosting and steering of major global gatherings, including COP29, the 13th session of the World Urban Forum, results-oriented chairmanships of the Non-Aligned Movement, the Organization of Turkic States and the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia, and Azerbaijan’s increasingly active engagement across other international platforms.

Azerbaijan’s full-fledged membership in the Consultative Meeting of Heads of State of Central Asia and the C6 format will enhance our contribution to cooperation and connectivity within the region and beyond.
COP29 provided a good example of this approach in practice.
As host and Presidency, Azerbaijan guided negotiations towards ambitious and balanced outcomes while working to ensure that all voices were heard.

The conference delivered several historic agreements, full operationalization of Article 6 carbon-market mechanisms, and further advancement of arrangements supporting the Loss and Damage Fund for vulnerable communities affected by climate change.
Azerbaijan continues to build on its legacy, with particular focus on translating negotiated outcomes into practical implementation.

This September, for the first time, Baku hosted the UNFCCC Climate Week, bringing together governments, international organizations, the private sector and other stakeholders to advance implementation and practical solutions.
Azerbaijan’s commitment to international solidarity and cooperation is equally reflected in our development and humanitarian assistance.
In recent years, Azerbaijan has significantly expanded the scope of its international aid, with particular attention to Small Island Developing States and African partner countries.
Since 2020, we have provided humanitarian, economic and technical assistance worth approximately USD 400 million to more than 140 countries.

As we mark the 40th anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development, Azerbaijan reaffirms its commitment to partnership-based approaches founded on solidarity, mutual respect and shared development priorities.
As we inch closer to 2030, it is becoming ever more apparent that the world remains off track in implementing the Sustainable Development Goals.

Azerbaijan is firmly committed to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, having integrated the SDGs into its national development strategies, institutional frameworks, and Voluntary National Review processes, while placing particular emphasis on connectivity, green growth, digitalization, and sustainable urban development.
In less than two decades, Azerbaijan’s GDP has increased threefold, while the poverty rate has declined from 49% to around 5%.
At the same time, Azerbaijan maintains one of the lowest levels of public external debt globally.
Our commitment also extends to advancing sustainable development through effective and accountable institutions.

At Azerbaijan’s initiative, on 30 March 2026, the UN Human Rights Council adopted by consensus, for the third time, the resolution entitled “Promoting Human Rights and the Sustainable Development Goals through Transparent, Accountable and Efficient Public Service Delivery.”

Co-sponsored by more than 100 Member States, the resolution underscores the essential role of citizen-centered, transparent and efficient public institutions in advancing human rights and accelerating progress towards the SDGs.

Azerbaijan’s innovative ASAN and DOST models of transparent, accessible and citizen-centered public service delivery have gained international recognition and are increasingly being adopted by dozens of partner countries.
Sustainable urbanization is another important pillar of our approach to the 2030 Agenda.
Resilient cities are essential to improving quality of life, strengthening communities and promoting inclusive economic and social development.
In this context, Azerbaijan’s successful hosting of the 13th session of the World Urban Forum marked an important contribution to the global urban agenda.

The key outcomes of the Forum – the Baku Call to Action and the Chair’s Summary – subsequently contributed to the High-level Meeting of the General Assembly on midterm review of the New Urban Agenda, held in New York in July this year.
At the same time, environmental protection remains an important national and regional priority.
We are particularly concerned by continuing decline of the Caspian Sea, with serious implications for biodiversity, livelihoods and economic activity across the region.
As a challenge shared by all Caspian littoral States, it requires a coordinated, collective and sustained response.
While remaining firmly committed to our climate goals, we must also recognize that, in the immediate term, development cannot realistically proceed without traditional energy sources.
Energy security, moreover, is closely intertwined with peace, regional connectivity, and sustainable economic development.

As a reliable natural gas supplier to 16 countries, Azerbaijan ranks among the leading pipeline gas suppliers globally and plays a strategic role in strengthening energy security and diversifying supply routes across Europe and beyond.
Azerbaijan’s contribution to global energy security is increasingly complemented by its growing role in the clean energy transition.

We are investing in renewable energy, commissioning major solar and wind projects, expanding hydropower capacity and developing new clean energy initiatives together with leading international partners.
Agreements already signed envisage around 6 GW of additional solar and wind capacity by 2030.
By 2030, renewables are expected to generate almost 40% of Azerbaijan’s electricity.
Expansion of renewable power generation will create new opportunities for Azerbaijan to export green electricity to European markets.
This way, our role as a reliable energy partner is evolving alongside the global energy transition.
Energy connectivity is part of Azerbaijan’s broader vision of connecting regions, markets and economies.

Azerbaijan has emerged as a key transport and logistics hub between Europe and Asia, contributing to major trans-regional connectivity initiatives, investing in modern transport infrastructure and expanding cooperation with regional partners.
Since 2022, we have witnessed an increase in cargo volumes along the Middle Corridor by almost 90%.

Strategic infrastructure projects along the Middle Corridor spearheaded by Azerbaijan, including the Baku International Sea Trade Port and the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars railway, are helping to create more resilient, diversified and sustainable supply chains between Asia and Europe.
This growth demonstrates the Middle Corridor’s considerable potential as a key driver of regional connectivity, trade facilitation and sustainable economic development.
Our connectivity agenda extends beyond energy and transport.
Digital connectivity offers another important area for regional cooperation.
Azerbaijan is advancing new digital links across the region through ambitious initiatives, such as the Digital Silk Way.
This project envisages an advanced fiber-optic network across the Caspian Sea, further strengthening Azerbaijan’s role as a regional digital hub and a key link between Europe and Asia.
This broader connectivity agenda is also closely linked to the emerging peace architecture in the South Caucasus.

The “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” (TRIPP), another key outcome of the 2025 Washington Summit, is expected to facilitate unimpeded multimodal connectivity between the main part of Azerbaijan and its Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic and unlock new opportunities for regional trade, economic integration and prosperity as part of the Zangazur corridor.

In conclusion, I wish to reiterate that our shared challenges demand renewed global solidarity, more effective and trusted multilateralism grounded in international law, and a reinvigorated system of cooperation.
Trust, however, must be restored through concrete actions.
Peace must be built on the ground, commitments must be translated into real outcomes, and sustainable development must deliver meaningful improvements in people’s lives.

Azerbaijan has consistently upheld the purposes and principles of the UN Charter and demonstrated its firm adherence to international law, including respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, non-interference in the internal affairs of States, sovereign equality, dialogue and cooperation, as well as the faithful, consistent and non-selective implementation of agreed commitments.
This is the multilateralism we believe in – principled, inclusive and, above all, capable of delivering tangible results.

STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF REPUBLIC OF BURUNDI AND CURRENT CHAIRPERSON OF THE AFRICAN UNION AT THE GENERAL DEBATE OF EIGHTY-FIRST SESSION OF THE UNITED NATIONS GENERAL ASSEMBLY New York, 23 September 2026 In the name of God, the Almighty, the Most Merciful,

His good offices, exercised with wisdom, humility and determination, have made it possible to bring closer together the most divergent points of view and to provide valuable support to nations, especially to countries of the South, in their quest for stability and prosperity.
Burundi, which has always been able to count on the benevolent support of the United Nations, wishes to salute his leadership and his unwavering attachment to principles multilateralism.

3. The theme of this eighty-first session, “Restoring trust, steering transformation: a United Nations Organization that serves all” comes at a time when our world is faced with multiple crises, aggressions against States, internally armed conflicts fuelled from the outside, and expansionist conflicts causing distrust among States and leading to the inability international community to settle these crises by peaceful means.
4. In this context, a fundamental question arises: how can we restore trust in multilateralism and ensure that international institutions truly meet the expectations of all peoples?
Our answer is clear: we must strengthen multilateralism, reform global governance and place human dignity at the heart of our collective action.
Peace is the source of all good.
Peace in our hearts, peace in our societies, peace in our countries.
Let us begin by restoring peace in our own enclosure.
Let us consolidate peace in our respective countries, restore trust among our peoples, and restore the image of humanity around us.
6. In this year when Burundi holds the current chairmanship of the African Union, we are particularly aware of the responsibility incumbent upon us.
As the African Union champion for the youth, peace and security agenda, I organized this year once again a continental youth dialogue coupled with the Women, Peace and Security agenda.
During this dialogue, I sensed the enthusiasm of young people and women to create a community of shared destiny in the spirit of Ubuntu.
7. In these young people I sensed the will to connect with one another and to live together.
But, unfortunately, there are still States that prevent their citizens from living together with other peoples as brothers.
They develop and foster xenophobia and intolerance.

They divide through the omission of preventive and corrective measures, by putting forward levels of development, saying this one is rich, that one is poor, thus creating a gap between peoples on the basis of wealth and material possessions.
And on that basis, they come to regard themselves as saints, reproaching others for being inferior.
How can we create trust between States without beginning with the connection and cohesion of our peoples?
We, leaders, must revive within ourselves that spirit of Ubuntu, the Ubuntu with which God created us.
Indeed, God did not create a selfish man; He created a man of Ubuntu, the Ubuntu that I see in you and that you find in me.
Ubuntu is the common denominator that must regenerate trust among all human beings.
8. As an African and bearer of the African word at this time when I hold the rotating chairmanship of the African Union, I also have a duty to declare it.
We are here to carry a conviction: Africa must be listened to more, better represented and more closely associated with the decisions that determine the future of our planet.
That is what must create trust between Africa and the other continents, as well as with international institutions.
9. We no longer want to see the Human Rights Council become a forum for oppressing countries deliberately chosen because they defend and fight for the interests of their peoples.
We want to see this Council work for justice and fairness for all States, without distinction.
10. The law international human rights law must be applied, without exception, to all the States of the world, both in its corrective function and in its regulatory function.
The Human Rights Council cannot be instrumentalized by certain countries to the detriment of other States, since all Member States of the United Nations enjoy sovereign equality.

Burundi wishes to reiterate, consistently, its opposition to the imposition of a “Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Burundi”, who was designated for it outside any dialogue and any prior consultation.

11. Burundi is a responsible country that respects Human Rights; for decades it has fought against impunity, ensured respect for the rights and freedoms of all and guaranteed security as well as non-repetition of the crimes it experienced in the past.
12. Africa intends to be a full-fledged actor and not a mere observer, called upon to applaud decisions in the formulation of which it was not associated.
It asks for justice, equity and representation.

We therefore reaffirm, with force, the need for reform of the United Nations Security Council, in order to allow permanent African representation and more equitable participation of the continent in the decision-making mechanisms of the international community.

13. In this regard, Burundi considers that discussions on reforms must also address the financial viability of the United Nations system, by strengthening the predictability, transparency and sustainability of its financing.
It would not be consistent to entrust the Organization with ever greater responsibilities without guaranteeing it the resources necessary for their implementation.
We therefore call on Member States, especially the wealthiest, to show responsibility and solidarity in order to preserve the financial stability of the Organization.

14. In this dynamic of reform, strengthening and consolidation of our Organization, Burundi also wishes to contribute to the debate on the selection process of the next Secretary-General of the United Nations.

In the current international context, marked by profound geopolitical divisions and growing challenges for multilateralism, this process must be conducted in a spirit of transparency, openness and collective responsibility.

15. Burundi considers that this process must be based above all on qualifications, experience, integrity, independence of judgment, diplomatic ability and the capacity to bring together the positions of all Member States.

16. We need a true bridge-builder, a person capable of engaging in dialogue with all, of bringing positions closer together when divergences appear insurmountable, but also of showing firmness, courage and independence when it comes to defending the principles of the Charter of the United Nations and upholding the collective interest.
17. Peace remains the primary condition for development.

The African Union is deeply concerned by the persistence of conflicts and crises that continue to cause massive population displacements, destroy infrastructure and deprive millions of children of their right to education and to a better future.
We pay particular attention to the situation in the Great Lakes, in the Sudan, in the Sahel, in Somalia and in all regions confronted with violence and instability.
18. We reaffirm our commitment to the search for African solutions to African problems, in compliance with international law and the Charter of the United Nations.
We therefore call for the strengthening of the partnership between the African Union and the United Nations in the prevention, mediation and peaceful settlement of conflicts.
Burundi, drawing on its experience, will continue to contribute to peace efforts on the continent.

As decided in Luanda during the 21st session of the Extraordinary Assembly of Heads of State and Government of the African Union, Africa must not only learn to manage conflicts; it must strengthen its capacity to prevent them.

We also call on the international community to provide greater support to African peace and security mechanisms, in particular through predictable and sustainable financing of peace operations led by Africa.
20. I would be remiss if I were to address this august assembly without speaking about the issue of water.
The African Union has placed the year 2026 under the theme of sustainable water availability and access to safe sanitation systems, in order to achieve the objectives of Agenda 2063.
This choice is particularly significant because water is life, water is health, water is food security, water is energy, and water is also, in certain regions, a question of peace and stability.
21. We therefore call for strengthened international mobilization in favour of universal access to drinking water and sanitation, particularly in rural areas and the most vulnerable communities.
We invite our partners to consider water not only as a natural resource, but as a strategic investment in peace, health and sustainable development.
22. As regards socio-economic development, the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals and Agenda 2063 requires financial means commensurate with the ambitions.
Now, many developing countries face considerable budgetary constraints, high financing costs and the burden of debt.
We therefore call for a reform of the international financial architecture so as to make it fairer, more inclusive and better suited to the realities of developing countries.
Such a reform must in particular make possible access to predictable, affordable, sustainable financing, which is indispensable for accelerating the implementation of the SDGs and Agenda 2063.
23. We must also make Africa more active.
In this regard, Africa, with its fifty-five States and more than one billion four hundred million inhabitants, cannot remain on the margins of the bodies where the rules of world trade are drawn up.

On behalf of the African Union, I reiterate our continent’s call for full and equitable representation within the World Trade Organization: this is not a favour that we are requesting, but justice that we demand and a guarantee of progress for the multilateral trading system as a whole.
With the African Continental Free Trade Area, our continent has already demonstrated its capacity to build rules and integrate markets; it is now for global trade governance to draw on this.
But, to succeed, we must be more resilient in order to preserve the environment favourable to agriculture, which is a source of life and food security.
Indeed, Mr. President, climate change particularly affects the most vulnerable populations.
Africa contributes little to historical greenhouse gas emissions, but it is already suffering serious consequences from them.
We therefore call for strengthened international solidarity in the areas of adaptation, climate finance and technology transfer.
24. Food security must become a strategic priority because no sustainable development is possible when millions of families do not have sufficient and nutritious food.
25. In conclusion, I wish to raise the issue of youth, that most precious capital on which the entire international community can and must rely.

26. I speak today not only as a convinced friend of young people, but also on the basis of a lucid observation: our intellectual youth has become the object of sustained, deliberate and organized covetousness on the part of most of the wealthiest nations, whereas its primary vocation should be to serve its parents, its loved ones and the homeland, which have invested so much in its education.
Many African States devote considerable resources to education, vocational training, entrepreneurship, science, digital technology and innovation.

However, while our African nations, like Burundi, make these major sacrifices to build their future, these young talents are prematurely drawn away by actors offering better material and financial conditions, without having made any prior investment in their educational path.
Let us be perfectly clear: it is imperative to establish a fair partnership so that our countries receive equitable compensation for the investments made in the training of our youth.
27. The other actions that we must all undertake also consist in giving young people a real place in decision-making, peace and development processes.
Youth must not be considered solely as beneficiaries of public policies.
They must be integrated both upstream and downstream in their processes of design and implementation.
This is what would make it possible to create a certain future and restore hope to this youth.

28. This emerged from the discussions during the 5th edition of the Continental Dialogue on Youth, Peace and Security, which was held in Bujumbura from 10 to 12 August 2026, and which highlighted the existing link between water, peace, conflict prevention and the inclusive leadership of young people and women.
The work of this dialogue showed that there can be no lasting peace in Africa without the full, effective and institutionalized participation of its youth.
For too long, we have spoken of youth as a generation called upon to take over tomorrow.
But African youth is not only the future of our continent, it must also be its present.
29. We therefore call for the strengthening of the continental Youth, Peace and Security Agenda and for it to be given resources commensurate with its ambitions.
We have a duty to create more spaces enabling young people to contribute to conflict prevention, mediation, reconciliation and peacebuilding.
As Chairperson of the African Union and Champion of the Youth, Peace and Security Agenda, I intend to continue to carry this ambition forward.
30. Lastly, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, speaking of Burundi, we are pursuing with satisfaction its economic and social transformation within the framework of its Burundi Vision 2040-2060.
We are determined to transform our agriculture, to develop our infrastructure, to improve access to energy and water, to strengthen education and health, and to promote a dynamic private sector.
Our ambition is that of an emerging Burundi by 2040 and a developed Burundi by 2060.

31. We invite our partners to support this transformation not only through multifaceted assistance, but also through investments, technology transfer, capacity-building and the development of mutually beneficial partnerships.
The 2040-2060 Vision now constitutes a central framework for national development planning.
32. The African Union and the United Nations share a special responsibility in building a more peaceful and more just world.
We must strengthen our partnership in the areas of peace and security, sustainable development, health, climate, youth and global governance.
33. The UN-AU partnership must be founded on mutual respect, complementarity and greater African ownership of solutions to the continent's challenges.
34. Africa wants to be a strategic partner and a full-fledged actor in multilateralism, and not simply a space for intervention by the international community.
35. Burundi, in assuming the presidency of the African Union, is choosing unity, solidarity and action.
We are choosing an Africa at peace. An integrated Africa.
An Africa that transforms its resources.
An Africa that gives its youth the means to create and innovate.
An Africa that controls its destiny.
And we are choosing renewed multilateralism, in which every region, every people and every nation count.
36. For Africa, we want a United Nations that is more representative, more effective and closer to the peoples.
We want Africa to be better represented within global decision-making bodies.
We want a global partnership founded not on dependence, but on solidarity, shared responsibility and investment in the future.

37. On behalf of the Burundian people and in our capacity as current Chairperson of the African Union, we call on all our partners: “Let us make this period of transformation an opportunity to build a more just world, a stronger Africa and a better future for future generations.”

38. Burundi and the African Union express the hope that the general debate of this 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly will be the starting point for strengthened multilateralism, a United Nations within which every State and every region count.
This is the guarantee of stability, greater solidarity, greater well-being and sustainable development on our planet.

Belgian statement at the General Debate of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly Mr President, Mr Secretary-General, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, Maurice Maeterlinck, born in Ghent and awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1911 (nineteen eleven), wrote a strange, almost unsettling play entitled The Blind.
Twelve people find themselves in a forest on an island.
The guide who led them there is sitting among them.
He is dead, but they do not yet know it.
They are waiting for him to return.
They hear the wind, the sea, the voices around them.
They know they are not alone, yet they can barely tell where the others are.
At one point, one of the characters says: “Years and years we have been together, and we have never seen each other!”
That line comes back to me when I look at our world.
We exchange statements, messages and positions.
At times, we spend hours around the same tables.
And yet, being in the same room does not mean that we understand one another.
Do we still take the time to hear what others are telling us?
To understand what they fear, what they need, and what the world looks like from where they stand?
That, to me, is where diplomacy begins.
But when we no longer do.
Diplomacy is not about erasing disagreements, nor about abandoning our principles to secure consensus at any cost.
It is about continuing to speak, continuing to listen, and finding ways to manage our differences without allowing them to lead to a breakdown in relations or to confrontation.
In the play, one of the characters says something very simple: “Let us try to draw a little closer.”
Maeterlinck wrote those words more than a century ago.
Yet they feel entirely relevant today.
Drawing closer does not mean thinking alike.
It means refusing to let distance turn into indifference, then mistrust, until eventually we stop speaking altogether.
It is one of the paradoxes of our time.
We have never been more connected, yet we do not necessarily understand one another any better.
Our economies, societies and technologies have become deeply interdependent, even as the temptation to turn inward returns with force.
In other words, we depend on one another more than ever, at the very moment when we are sometimes tempted to believe that we can do without one another.
The more interdependent we become, the more we need common rules.
Not to impose a single vision of the world.
But to ensure that we can manage our disagreements without allowing the law of the strongest to become the only law that matters.
In the play The Blind, the characters have lost the person who was meant to show them the way.
We are not in the same position.
No one will come and decide for us which direction to take.
But that does not mean we can move forward without bearings.
Faced with wars, humanitarian crises, climate disruption, pandemics and technological upheaval, the question is ultimately quite simple: do we still have a common compass?
For Belgium, the answer is yes.
That compass is the Charter of the United Nations.
But a rule has value only if it continues to apply when respecting it becomes difficult.
It is precisely when the law runs counter to a State’s immediate interest that we discover whether it truly matters.
When a signature loses its value the moment it becomes binding, when a treaty holds only for as long as it suits the party that signed it, it is not merely a legal text that is weakened.
It is trust in a promise made.
And with it, the security of all those who believed they could rely on that promise.
This is why Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine concerns far more than two States.
When a border can be changed by force, every border becomes less secure.
No one in this room needs reminding that international politics is shaped by power and by interests.
The Charter does not wish those realities away.
It draws a line around what power may be allowed to do.
For Belgium, that line matters in very practical terms.
We are an open country, with an economy tied to the world and a security bound up with that of our partners.
We depend on States keeping their word, on agreements surviving changes in the balance of power, and on borders not being redrawn at gunpoint.
International law reflects our values, certainly.
That is why Belgium stands firmly with Ukraine.
Any lasting peace must be grounded in the Charter of the United Nations and in respect for Ukraine’s sovereignty, political independence and territorial integrity.
But we cannot uphold these principles on my continent alone – in Europe – and treat them as optional elsewhere.
Sovereignty, territorial integrity and the right of peoples to determine their own future do not change meaning when we cross the borders of our continent.
The same standard must guide us when it comes to international humanitarian law.
Its rules do not apply only when they suit us.
They exist precisely for the moments when respecting them becomes difficult.
In Palestine, Sudan, Myanmar, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Haiti, and so many other places scarred by war or armed violence, the circumstances differ.
But no human life is worth less than another.
Humanitarian aid must be allowed to reach them.
This year again, hundreds of millions of people need humanitarian assistance while the resources available to help them are shrinking.
When funding runs out, what do we tell the mother who has walked for hours to reach a clinic with her sick child?
What do we tell a family waiting for food?
That there will be no delivery tomorrow?
We cannot ask humanitarian workers to give those answers because we have chosen to cut their funding.
This is not the time to treat humanitarian aid as an optional expense.
It is neither a reward nor a bargaining chip.
A hungry child is not responsible for the position taken by his government.
That child has the right to eat, the right to receive care, and the right to be protected.
That is why I urge every one of us not to cut humanitarian funding.
International law does more than contain violence.
It also enables trade, exchange and movement.
That brings me to a freedom that may at first sound rather technical: freedom of navigation.
For my country, it is anything but technical.
As early as the nineteenth century, the port of Antwerp had immense potential.
But ships sailing up the River Scheldt had to pay a toll.
In 1863 (eighteen sixty-three), an international agreement abolished that toll once and for all.
The abolition was to apply to “all flags”.
An international route has real value only if it remains open.
Passage cannot depend, each time, on a fresh contest of power.
That is precisely what freedom of navigation represents today.
It is not merely the abstract right of a ship to travel from one point to another.
It allows economies that may share neither the same interests nor the same alliances to remain connected.
It allows a landlocked State to take part in global trade.
It allows grain, medicines, gas and industrial components to cross several maritime areas without their passage having to be renegotiated at every stage.
That seems perfectly normal while everything is working.
It takes only one route closing for us to remember how much it matters.
Think of the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the entrance of the Red Sea, the Suez Canal, the Bosporus, the Strait of Malacca or the Panama Canal.
More than 80 per cent of global merchandise trade by volume is carried by sea.
When a ship is attacked, when a strait becomes dangerous, or when a carrier has to sail around an entire region, the effects are felt thousands of kilometres away.
But also in the price of energy, fertiliser and food.
The price of a tank of fuel.
The price of a loaf of bread.
And very often, the countries with the least economic room to maneuver bear the greatest burden in proportionate terms.

The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea confers rights, but it also imposes obligations: the safety of navigation, the protection of the marine environment, and respect for the rights of coastal States.
A smaller navy does not mean fewer rights.
Nor does a larger one confer the right to impose its will.
No country should have to surrender the rights the law gives it simply because another can send more ships.
But keeping our sea routes open also means keeping them safe, all the way into our ports.
The International Ship and Port Facility Security Code, the ISPS Code, offers a very concrete example of what multilateralism can achieve when it works.
Piracy, terrorism and crime are scourges that we must fight together.
Freedom and security are not opposing ideas.
Security is a condition of freedom.
I dwell on freedom of navigation because it illustrates something larger.
We can defend our interests while accepting that others have rights too.
And when rules are clear and predictable enough, a space of competition can still remain a space of cooperation.
The ocean, moreover, are far more than the highways of our trade.
They feed populations, regulate our climate, and absorb much of the excess heat caused by global warming.

For many small island States, rising sea levels affect the land on which their citizens live, their economy, their culture and, in some cases, their very ability to remain where their families have lived for generations.
The freedom to use the ocean therefore comes with a responsibility: to preserve it.
And on this point, allow me to be optimistic.
The BBNJ Agreement entered into force this year, after almost twenty years of negotiations.
Measured against a political cycle, that is close to an eternity.
Measured against the building of international law, it is sometimes the time needed to reach a compromise strong enough to last.
The Agreement proves that, even today, we continue to build international law rather than dismantle it.
Belgium has invested greatly in this process.
It helped launch the Blue Leaders, a coalition of countries working to protect at least 30 per cent of the ocean by 2030 (twenty thirty) and secure an ambitious high seas treaty.
The BBNJ Agreement now gives us an essential tool to advance towards that protection goal.
But twenty years of negotiations must not be followed by years of waiting.
It is in that spirit that Belgium is offering to host the treaty’s future secretariat in Brussels.
We are ready to enable it to work from day one.
It will be able to draw on our scientific expertise and on a community that brings together international organisations, embassies and civil society.
So that what we have agreed together becomes real protection at sea.
Beneath those same ocean run other vital routes: the cables that connect our continents and carry much of our digital communications and energy.
Here too, our interdependence is plain to see.
A break, an act of sabotage or an attack can have consequences thousands of kilometres away.
But our responsibility in the digital world does not end with infrastructure.

Artificial intelligence already confronts us with another question: how can we make full use of the possibilities created by innovation without allowing technology to move faster than our ability to protect people?
I am thinking in particular of children, who are growing up in a world where AI can open extraordinary possibilities, but also create new vulnerabilities.
We must neither hold back innovation out of fear nor assume that it will regulate itself.
At sea as in the digital world, freedom needs rules if it is to remain freedom.
interdependence without speaking about People have always moved, and they will continue to do so.
Governments have a duty to manage that movement and to ensure that migration takes place safely, regularly and in accordance with the law.
Order is itself a matter of human rights.
When migration is left in the hands of smugglers and traffickers, people are exploited, placed in danger and sometimes lost at sea.
But the way in which governments maintain order matters just as much.
States have both the right and the responsibility to manage their borders.
They must do so in full respect of international law and fundamental rights.
A person’s legal status may change.
That is why countries of origin, transit and destination must work together.
Safe, orderly and regular migration and respect for human rights are not competing ambitions.
They must go hand in hand.
We can either manage our interdependence, or be at its mercy.
Health crises have taught us the same lesson.
Those who refuse to cooperate weaken themselves.
But if our commitments are to hold, we also need institutions capable of upholding them.
This year, we mark the 80th anniversary of the International Court of Justice.
It settles legal disputes submitted to it by States, peacefully and in accordance with international law.
The International Criminal Court has a different mandate: to fight impunity by prosecuting and trying individuals accused of the gravest international crimes.
Their independence must be defended equally.
Both courts rest on the same idea: power cannot be its own judge.
That remains true even when we dislike their rulings or proceedings.
When judges or staff members of an international court face sanctions or pressure for carrying out their mandate, Belgium will always stand with them to protect them.
But the promise of the law does not end in courtrooms or in relations between States.
The right to think and speak freely.
And the freedom not to believe.
It concerns the ability of every woman to decide the course of her own life and take her equal place in society.
The ability to love the person we love without fear of prison, violence or persecution.
These freedoms belong to no single continent.
They rest on an elementary conviction: a person’s dignity does not depend on their sex, their origin, their sexual orientation, or what a government thinks of them.
Human dignity does not require us to be alike in order to be equal.
That conviction also guides our diplomacy.
Dialogue is not the opposite of resolve.
It also requires institutions capable of functioning.
Defending the United Nations does not mean pretending that everything within it works well.
But there is a difference between reforming an organisation and weakening it.
We cannot ask more of it, steadily strip away its resources, and then express surprise when it is not effective enough.
Reform must preserve what gives the Organisation its purpose: peace and security, human rights, and development.
It must also ensure better representation for every region of the world.
More than eighty years ago, Paul-Henri Spaak led the Belgian delegation to the San Francisco Conference that gave birth to the United Nations.
A few months later, he became the first President of this General Assembly.
Belgium was emerging from war and occupation.
That is precisely why multilateralism seemed the obvious choice to us.
We are not here to preserve an institution for its own sake.
We are here to preserve what it must make possible.
Ladies and Gentlemen, Before we were presidents, ministers, ambassadors or diplomats, we were all children.
And despite all that sets them apart, the people we represent often want remarkably simple things.
To come home in the evening.
To watch their children grow up and send them to school without fear. To work.
To love the person they love.
To make plans for next year.
Not to live with the thought that war, hunger, disease or violence could make everything disappear overnight.
That is the most concrete definition of peace: being able to live your life without constantly fearing that you will lose it.
We can build peace, and we can damage it.
We can pass it on, or leave the next generation with the task of starting all over again.
At the beginning of this speech, I spoke of Maurice Maeterlinck’s play The Blind.
Its characters were waiting for someone to show them the way.
No one will come and decide for us what kind of world we want to live in.
But we are not without bearings.
Above all, we have a responsibility to use them both.
A compass cannot prevent a storm.
It helps us hold our course when the storm comes.

– Ladies and Gentlemen, It is with particular honor that I take the floor before this august Assembly to convey to you the warmest greetings of the Beninese people and to bring before you the voice of Benin: a voice resolutely committed to peace, dialogue and multilateralism; a voice that also intends to play its full part in the collective reflection on the future of our Organization and on that of our world.

At the end of two (02) terms served during one of the most trying periods in our contemporary history, Benin salutes his constancy and his commitment to multilateralism and to respect for the Charter of the United Nations.
At a time when the temptation to withdraw is strong, he has consistently defended the idea that, in the face of crises, no nation can durably build its security and prosperity in isolation.
– Ladies and Gentlemen, There are moments when History compels us to choose not only what we want to do, but also what we want to become.
It is with this question in mind that Benin is taking part in this session, animated by a deep conviction: the future is not awaited, it is prepared.
It inspires the Benin 2060 Vision, which projects our Nation toward the centenary of its accession to independence.
But this ambition concerns not only our national destiny.
It also determines the way in which we look at the world, which is itself at a crossroads.

We are confronted with wars that are dragging on, the spread of terrorist threats, persistent geopolitical tensions, widening inequalities, debt that is reducing the capacity for action of many States, as well as climate disruption whose consequences affect the most vulnerable first.
At the same time, a technological transformation of considerable magnitude is accelerating.
Artificial intelligence is already transforming knowledge, work, the economy, education and information.
Never has humanity had so many means at its disposal to act upon its destiny.
And yet, perhaps never has it been confronted, with such urgency, with the need to decide collectively how these means must be placed at the service of the common good.
That is why the theme of this 81st session: “Restoring trust, managing transformations: building a United Nations Organization serving all” resonates with particular force.

The real challenge of our time is therefore not only to manage the successive crises, but also to recover our collective capacity to anticipate, to decide and to act before crises become irreversible.
It believes in it not out of nostalgia for the world of 1945, but because the world of 2026 more than ever needs a space where States can speak to one another, listen to one another and act together.
But defending multilateralism also means looking at the United Nations with lucidity.
It is strengthened when our Organization is capable of responding to the expectations of those it serves and of producing concrete results.
It is in this spirit that Benin supports the efforts undertaken within the framework of the UN80 Initiative.
We must seek greater effectiveness, coherence, transparency and accountability.
But we must keep in mind one essential requirement: reforming the United Nations must not mean only reducing its costs.
Above all, it must mean increasing its impact.
A more effective United Nations must be better able to prevent conflicts, respond to humanitarian crises, support development and anticipate the transformations that are already shaping our future.
It must also remain faithful to the principles that underpin its legitimacy: universality, the sovereign equality of States, solidarity and respect for the Charter.
– Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, There is one reform without which all the others will remain incomplete: that of the governance of international peace and security.
The Security Council remains largely a reflection of a balance conceived in a world that is no longer that of today.
Africa still has no permanent seat.
This situation raises a question of justice, equity and, beyond that, of the legitimacy of the multilateral system itself.
Benin reaffirms its full support for the common African position, as set out in the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration.
We are not asking for a privilege: we are asking that the governance of international peace and security be more reflective of the world it claims to serve.
For Benin, the question of security has a particularly concrete dimension.
It seeks to exploit vulnerabilities, to make light of borders, and to gradually extend its hold into new areas.
Benin fully measures the gravity of this threat.
In this regard, I should like solemnly to pay tribute to the courage and dedication of our defence and security forces, as well as to the resilience of the Beninese People.
We are strengthening our defence and security capacities.
We are consolidating surveillance of our territory and our borders.
We are intensifying our cooperation with our neighbours and our partners.
But the experience of our region teaches us one essential thing: faced with a threat that is evolving rapidly, we must learn to act more quickly before it turns into a crisis.
That is why we must make prevention, warning and early action the three (03) phases of one and the same security policy.
This requires better intelligence-sharing, stronger cross-border cooperation, and improved coordination among national, subregional and continental mechanisms.
Solidarity among States, regional cooperation, the action of the African Union and the support of the United Nations must therefore be better articulated.

But prevention cannot be reduced to a security issue, because while security requires means of defence, it is strengthened through development, social cohesion and the effective presence of the State.
Education, employment, infrastructure and the prospects offered to young people also contribute to preventing the vulnerabilities that terrorist groups seek to exploit.
Collective security cannot be sustainable without economic and financial security.
There is indeed another fragility threatening international stability: the fragility of development financing.
Many developing countries today are faced with a particularly difficult equation.

They must simultaneously accelerate their development, finance their energy transition, adapt to climate change, invest in health, education and the digital sector, while also responding to growing social needs.
Yet these requirements are accumulating in a context in which access to financing remains more costly and fiscal space is often more limited.
This situation is neither sustainable nor equitable.

Benin therefore calls for the determined pursuit of the transformation of the international financial architecture, in order to enable developing countries to access financing that is more accessible, more predictable and better suited to their development trajectories.
We must also have the ambition to invest more in development, for investing in development means investing in peace, in security and in stability.
The climate issue also illustrates this requirement of justice.
Africa contributes relatively little to global greenhouse gas emissions, even though it is already bearing the full brunt of the consequences of climate disruption.
We are not asking for a right to pollute.
We are asking for a right to development.
We want adaptation, resilience-building and the issue of loss and damage to be addressed with the urgency required by the reality experienced by our populations.
We also want the energy transition to be an opportunity to industrialize, create jobs and strengthen access to energy.
For us, climate justice does not consist in setting development against transition.
It consists in enabling developing countries to build a growth model that is more resilient, more inclusive and more sustainable.
We must also prepare for the next great transformation: that of artificial intelligence, which can become one of the most powerful accelerators of human development.
It can broaden access to knowledge, improve health systems, support farmers and make administrations more effective.
But it can also reproduce or amplify existing divides.

If Africa remains merely a consumer of technologies designed and controlled elsewhere, a new form of dependency could emerge: dependency linked to data, infrastructure, computing capacities and critical technologies.
Benin therefore advocates international governance of artificial intelligence that is inclusive, responsible and development-oriented.
Africa must not be only a market for the technologies of tomorrow.
It must also be able to be a space for creation, innovation and production.
It is on that condition that artificial intelligence can become not a new factor of division, but an instrument of emancipation, progress and shared development.
Confidence in international institutions is also linked to the confidence that peoples place in their own institutions.
Benin, for its part, is continuing the consolidation of its institutions and its democratic framework, in keeping with its Constitution and legal order.
We consider that stability, public accountability and citizen participation constitute essential conditions for sustainable development.
Our experience reinforces us in one conviction: the strength of institutions is one of the foremost infrastructures of peace.

We are convinced that if national trajectories may be different, they must nevertheless converge towards the same objective: to offer every people the necessary conditions to build its future in peace, dignity and stability.
Allow me now to address a dimension that touches at the heart of Benin’s identity.

Our country is a land of memory, marked by greatness, resistance, but also by a tragic and painful history: that of daughters and sons torn from their lands, separated from their families and scattered throughout the world.
That history has left deep wounds.
It has also created, over the generations, a diaspora whose link with the continent has never been extinguished.
We can neither rewrite that history nor erase the wounds of the past.
But we can choose what we make of it.
Benin has chosen to make it a bridge.

We want to offer those who wish to reconnect with their African history the possibility of reweaving a living bond with the continent, with the land of their ancestors, from which they were torn away.
The possibility, under the conditions provided for by our legislation, of acquiring Beninese nationality thus carries a dimension that goes beyond the sole administrative act.
It is part of a desire to rebuild a relationship, to renew a bond and to transform a painful memory into a relationship oriented towards the future.

To this diaspora, which everywhere in the world looks towards Africa, Benin wishes to say this: you are the heirs of a painful history, but you can also become the actors of a new history in which memory would no longer be only the remembrance of what was lost, but also the point of departure for what can be rebuilt.
It is with this perspective that Benin intends to make reconnection with Afro-descendants not a simple return to the past, but an opening towards a shared future.
Benin does not want only to be a land of memory.
It wants to be a land of reunion, transmission and future.
Let us instead look at it with lucidity, with confidence and above all with responsibility.
We already know much of what the future holds for us:
(i) the climate will continue to change,
(ii) technology will continue to transform our societies and our economies,
(iii) Africa will carry greater weight in the demographic and economic balances of the world,
(iv) security threats will continue their attempts to cross borders...
But above all, we know one thing: no State will be able to respond to these challenges alone.
And above all, let us prepare to pass things on.

For the responsibility of a generation is not only to receive the world from those that preceded it, but to have the courage, the vision and the determination to make it better for those that will follow it.
It is this responsibility that Benin intends to assume: for itself, for Africa and within the United Nations.
Restoring trust means recovering the ability to act together.
Managing transformations means choosing to prepare for them rather than to undergo them.

And making the United Nations an Organization at the service of all means ensuring that multilateralism recovers, in the lives of peoples, the strength and usefulness that are the basis of its legitimacy.
Benin is ready to play its full part in this.
It is with hearts filled with the memory of thousands of children, women and men of Burkina Faso, Mali and the Niger, innocent victims of terrorism, that I take the floor.

But it is also with the pride drawn from the resilience of the peoples of the Sahel, and the hope inspired by the bravery of the defence and security forces of the Confederation, as well as by the crucial role played by the Volunteers for the Defence of the Homeland, that I am entrusted with the noble mission of delivering this statement.
I would also like to spare a reverent thought for the bereaved families, the stricken communities and all those whose lives have been affected by terrorist barbarity.
For more than a decade, this blind violence has been sustained, armed, financed and instrumentalized by criminal networks and their supporters, determined to subjugate the Sahel through fear.
But let them hear it here: they will not succeed.

I bow with deep respect before the memory of the defence and security forces of the Confederation of Sahel States, our Volunteers for the Defence of the Homeland, and all our patriotic forces who fell on the field of honour.
In evoking their memory, I offer a reverent thought for Army General Sadio CAMARA, cowardly assassinated on 25 April 2026 for his commitment to peace in Mali and in the Sahel.
The supreme sacrifice that our heroes have made is the seed of the freedom, justice and sovereignty to which our oppressed peoples aspire.

It is the daily sustaining source of our collective determination to regain the integrity of our territories, to defend our dignity and to guarantee our sacred right to live free, in peace and in security.
To the people of the Confederation of Sahel States, including its diaspora, I pay solemn tribute and renew to them my pride.

The courage, resilience, commitment and mobilization that they demonstrate every day, in support of the efforts of the Heads of State of the AES Confederation, remain the centre of gravity of our march towards sovereignty, stability and development.

To all the peoples of Africa and of the world who share our struggle and who recognize themselves in the ideal of peace, dignity and freedom championed by the AES Confederation, I reiterate my gratitude.

The confederal dynamic undertaken and assumed by our States, far from being isolation, is the expression of the refusal of fatality and chronic tutelage, as well as the rejection of selective indignation in the face of human tragedy.
It is the sign of the shared will of our States to break out of the vicious circle of structural domination and exploitation deeply rooted in colonialist and neo-colonialist vestiges.
It carries within it the hope of the rebirth of the central Sahel, long labelled with every demeaning qualifier.

The new march embarked upon since 16 September 2023 through the adoption of the Liptako-Gourma Charter, consolidated by the establishment of the Confederation of Sahel States on 6 July 2024, has revealed a new horizon for the peoples of the AES.

Every stretch of territory regained, every terrorist base destroyed, every battle won over the forces of evil, every school reopened, every village resettled, every reform initiated, brings us closer to that new horizon defended with determination by Comrade Captain Ibrahim TRAORE, Army General Assimi GOITA and Army General Abdourahamane TIANI.
Under their enlightened leadership, through thick and thin, the Alliance of Sahel States asserts itself every day by taking charge of and assuming its destiny.
A destiny of dignity, prosperity, freedom and justice.

It asserts itself through the mobilization of one people in a common space for a shared destiny: “One people, one space, one destiny”: this motto guides each of our actions and is embodied in the operationalization of the unified Force of the Confederation, just as it is embodied in the creation of the Confederal Bank for Investment and Development.

It is embodied in the consolidation relations between all the institutions of the countries of the AES, just as it is embodied in the strengthening of the age-old historical ties between the communities and the driving forces of our area.

Lastly, this motto lives in the diplomatic cohesion of the three States, illustrated in the finest way by this very statement delivered on behalf of the States of the Confederation of AES, on behalf of the Peoples of the Confederation of AES and on behalf of the Diaspora of the Confederation of AES.
AES welcomes the choice of the theme of the present session: “Rebuilding trust, managing transformation: an Organization for all”.
In itself alone, this theme is an undeniable admission:
- the admission of trust eroded among members because of double standards, partial positions, institutionalized injustice, and the instrumentalization of institutions and procedures;
- the admission that our Organization is struggling to adapt to the changes, yet obvious, of a constantly evolving world; and
- the admission of recognition that our Organization, alas, is no longer for all, but belongs more to actors chosen according to their power and their interests.

The verses of hope set out in the Charter of the United Nations and praising peace are scorned, international law is martyred and tortured by members whose propensity for domination, neocolonialism and hegemony is beyond question.
Yes, trust must be rebuilt; this is an ambition that we share.

But this suggests that our Organization must cease to be the mouthpiece or showcase of a few powers in order to become the common home of peoples, equal in dignity, equal in rights and equal in sovereignty.
It is in the light of this requirement, and of what is at stake in the Sahel, that we are taking part in these deliberations.

For the Confederation of Sahel States, rebuilding trust necessarily goes hand in hand with the immediate cessation of State support for terrorists, for terrorism cannot continue to be an instrument of the foreign policy of certain powers.
The Confederation of Sahel States is not confronted with a mere addition of isolated terrorist groups.

We are facing a persistent enterprise of destabilization, supported by considerable means and directed against the right of our peoples to live in peace, to choose their leaders, to dispose of their resources and to exercise their sovereignty fully.

The terrorist attacks, in particular those perpetrated on 25 April and 4 July 2026 in the Republic of Mali, on 18 June and on 29 and 30 August 2026 in the Republic of the Niger, perfectly illustrate this finding.
Let us say it bluntly: the supply chains, the technical capacities and the coordinated use of such conventional means do not arise out of nothing.
Behind the terrorist’s murderous arm there emerge structured support networks, including State support, driven by the desire to regain lost advantages and privileges.

We call on the international community to face the facts, to investigate seriously and to condemn, without geopolitical calculation, all those who finance, arm, provide intelligence to or protect terrorists.
Silence, in the face of such actions, is no longer prudence but complicity.

Rebuilding trust also goes hand in hand with strict respect for the sovereignty of States; it goes hand in hand with the development of partnership and not subjugation; it goes hand in hand with justice freed from neocolonialist designs.

This is contrary to the instrumentalization of certain international human rights protection mechanisms for purposes of political pressure against our countries, such as the ill-chosen role of the European Parliament in justifying a possible neocolonial offensive through its ill-founded resolutions against the Sahel.
Trust cannot be reborn in an Organization that invokes law for some and tolerates arbitrariness for others, that demands of the weak what it does not dare ask of the powerful.
