The promotion and protection of fundamental rights constitute, for our States, a responsibility that is fully assumed.
We exercise it in a context of extreme violence imposed on our populations by terrorists.

When our States adopt exceptional measures, strictly governed by their national legislation and their international obligations, they act to protect populations, preserve public order and guarantee national security.
For the first human right is the right to life; the first freedom of a people is not to live under terror.
We note that these measures are too often the subject of partial and selective readings, without sufficient consideration for realities on the ground.
The Confederation reaffirms its commitment to an impartial, objective and non-selective approach to human rights.
It calls for dialogue based on mutual respect, good faith and the rigour of facts.
We accept impartial and objective examination; however, we reject political prosecution.
Yes to respect for the law; but we reject its instrumentalization.

It is precisely because of serious shortcomings, persistent selectivity and politicization that has become manifest that our States have sovereignly decided to withdraw from the International Criminal Court and have formally notified their withdrawal from the Rome Statute.
International justice, yes; variable-geometry justice, no. The Confederation remains committed to independent, impartial and credible multilateral institutions.
The Confederation of Sahel States stands against domination, exploitation and contempt.

It subscribes to the vision of an Africa restored in its dignity, which chooses its own path, which takes charge of itself, which frees itself from the constraints and burdens of the past, in order to be master of its destiny.

In this regard, the Confederation of Sahel States welcomes the adoption, on 25 March 2026, by the United Nations General Assembly, of the resolution recognizing the transatlantic trafficking of Africans reduced to slavery and the system of racial enslavement as the most serious crime against humanity.
This historic recognition, part of a noble march, must open the way to truth, memory, reparations and a real transformation of the international relations inherited from slavery and colonization.

This is also an opportunity to welcome the recent adoption, just three weeks ago, on 04 September last, of resolution A/80/L.104, aimed at restoring its natural greatness to Africa after several centuries of underestimation and minimization of the size of our dear continent.
With regard to peace and international security, our world remains confronted with the multiplication of armed conflicts, the emergence of new crises and the return of the law of the strongest.
Unilateral approaches, sanctions outside the law, selective interventions and double standards weaken the international order and severely test the multilateral system.
The Confederation of Sahel States calls for the immediate cessation of violence against civilian populations, for unhindered humanitarian access and for a just and lasting political solution.
The inability of the Security Council to prevent or durably resolve these crises reveals the limits of a system that too often protects the interests of powers to the detriment of human life.

With regard to development, the Confederation remains concerned by the worsening of climate vulnerabilities, the multiplication of humanitarian crises, and the malicious use of information technologies and artificial intelligence for purposes of manipulation and destabilization.
The conclusions of the High-level Political Forum of July 2026 confirm that the international community remains far from the Sustainable Development Goals.
Four years from the 2030 deadline, the time is no longer for ritual declarations: it is for action, equitable financing and economic justice.
Faced with these challenges, collective, ambitious and solidary responses are required.

The Pact for the Future, Seville Compromise, the Doha Programme of Action, the UN80 initiative and the Awaza Programme of Action for Landlocked Developing Countries can help make the multilateral system more effective, more inclusive and more results-oriented, on condition that they do not remain promises.

Our priorities must be clearly defined: reduce the digital divide, strengthen climate resilience, invest in human capital, consolidate health and education systems, support industrialization, ensure the effective participation of young people and women in decision-making.

International solidarity is necessary; but the experience of the Confederation of Sahel States also demonstrates that the mobilization of internal resources, based on trust, national solidarity and citizen participation, is the first lever of economic liberation.

The Confederation of Sahel States supports the efforts undertaken within the framework of the UN80 Initiative, convinced that our Organization must undergo a profound transformation to respond to contemporary challenges.
But reform must not be a pretext to further reduce the presence of the United Nations in countries.
It must be political, democratic and courageous in the redistribution of voices, responsibilities and powers.
The reform of the Security Council can no longer wait.
It must strengthen transparency and accountability, put an end to double standards, and adapt the Organ to geopolitical reality.
The Confederation of Sahel States reaffirms reiterates its support for the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration.
The credibility of the United Nations will depend on its capacity to uphold, with the same rigour and without distinction, the Charter, international law and the sovereign equality of States.

In this spirit, the Confederation of Sahel States reiterates its call for the lifting of all unilateral coercive measures contrary to international law, including the embargo imposed on Republic of Cuba.

Reform of global governance must also transform international financial architecture: more equitable representation of developing countries in international financial institutions, fair treatment of debt, real access to development financing, fairer international trade and respect for national priorities.

The Confederation of Sahel States remains resolutely committed to working, alongside all Member States of the United Nations, for the advent of a more just, more equitable and more united international order, founded on the dignity of peoples, the sovereign equality of States, international justice and the peaceful settlement of disputes.
But our cooperation will never be synonymous with submission, and our openness will never mean the abandonment of our vital interests.

It is only on this condition that we will be able to restore trust among Nations, restore credibility to our Organization, and offer present and future generations a safer, more prosperous world that is more respectful of the aspirations of all peoples.
We ask no one for permission to exist.
We seek from no one a certificate of sovereignty.
We move forward, united and standing tall, because our cause is just and because our future belongs to us.

Ladies and Gentlemen Heads of Delegation, Ladies and Gentlemen, At the national level, I should now like to draw the attention of our august Assembly to a number of considerations regarding the situation in my country.
Burkina Faso has embarked on a dynamic of profound transformation, driven by the progressive popular Revolution.
At a time when we are preparing to commemorate its fourth anniversary, we can, with responsibility and lucidity, note the progress made in several areas of national life.
On the economic front, Burkina Faso is resolutely pursuing its efforts towards a structural transformation of its economy and development based to a greater extent on its own potential.

In synergy with the other member States of the Confederation of Sahel States, our country is working to strengthen its productive capacities, enhance the value of its national resources and further promote the local processing of our raw materials.

In the agricultural and industrial sectors in particular, important presidential initiatives are being implemented in order to stimulate national production, create jobs and strengthen the participation of our populations in economic activity.

Under the leadership of Comrade Captain Ibrahim TRAORE, President of Faso, Burkina Faso has chosen to place the people at the heart of every dynamic, by encouraging the creation of new production and processing units and by promoting better enhancement of the value of our resources.
Through hope-bearing initiatives, in particular the six major presidential initiatives, our economy is being energized and gradually consolidated.

Our ambition is to strengthen the foundations of endogenous, sustainable and inclusive development, while continuing the profound refoundation of our society and the strengthening of our economic sovereignty.
This transformation also concerns infrastructure, the development of which is gradually accompanying the dynamic of modernization and structural transformation of our economy.
In this regard, the RELANCE Plan 2026-2030 constitutes a major framework for consolidating this orientation and supporting the changes undertaken in our country.

By relying first and foremost on our own strengths, by choosing to exploit and process our resources locally, we intend to create more value within our economy and ensure that the wealth of our country primarily benefits our populations.

On the security front, Burkina Faso, in coordination with the countries of our confederation, is continuing its efforts to restore lasting peace, security and social cohesion throughout its territory.
More than 74 per cent of the national territory is now under its control.
Our Defence and Security Forces, as well as our Volunteers for the Defence of the Homeland, are continuing their operations against terrorist groups and criminal gangs.

These developments are reflected in particular in the recapture of several villages and localities, the gradual return of thousands of persons to their places of residence, the reopening of dozens of schools, as well as the resumption of activities in several health centres and the gradual re-establishment of the administration.

These gains, which continue to be consolidated, are the fruit of the efforts and sacrifices made by our people, as well as the commitment of all those mobilized for the restoration of peace and security.
In the Middle East, we remain particularly concerned by the situation of the Palestinian people and the suffering endured by the civilian populations of Gaza.

Faced with this tragedy, Burkina Faso reaffirms its commitment to a lasting political solution based on the coexistence of two States, Israel and Palestine, living side by side in peace and security, in accordance with international law and the relevant United Nations resolutions.

In another area, Burkina Faso remains concerned by the consequences of unilateral coercive measures imposed on certain States, in particular Cuba and Nicaragua, the repercussions of which severely affect populations.
In this regard, we call for priority to be given to dialogue, cooperation and mutual respect among States.

With regard to the question of Western Sahara, Burkina Faso, faithful to the principles enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations, reaffirms its attachment to the political process conducted under the auspices of the Secretary-General of the United Nations.
We encourage the continuation of efforts aimed at achieving a negotiated political solution between the parties, in accordance with the relevant resolutions of the Security Council.
Likewise, we reaffirm our attachment to the principle of one China.

Through these various considerations, Burkina Faso wishes to reaffirm an essential conviction: our Organization will be able to respond fully to the challenges of our time only if it remains faithful to the principles that presided over its creation.

We remain convinced that, through dialogue, solidarity and determination, the United Nations together with our peoples can overcome the trials they face and build the foundations of a future of peace, dignity and shared prosperity.
One People - One Space - One Destiny.
Long live the Confederation of Sahel States standing upright Long live the Sahel standing upright.
Let me begin by paying my deepest respect to all the martyred freedom fighters of Bangladesh.
I respectfully remember the contributions of those who have made the ultimate sacrifice in the struggle to establish democracy, justice and people's rights in our country since independence.
I also pay my sincere respect to all those who were martyred and injured in the mass uprising of courageous students and people in July–August 2024 against fascism.
After more than a decade and a half of movement and struggle against fascist rule and exploitation, and through the sacrifice of thousands of lives, Bangladesh is now free from fascism.
In a free, fair and impartial national election held on 12 February this year, the people entrusted the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) with the responsibility of governing the country.
I congratulate the democracy-loving people of Bangladesh.
We believe that the people are the source of all our political power.
Standing on this world stage of the United Nations, I am somewhat nostalgic at this moment.

It was from this very world stage that my father, Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman, the proclaimer of Bangladesh's independence, and my mother, former Prime Minister late Begum Khaleda Zia, addressed the world on behalf of the country and its people.
Today, I too stand here to speak for the interests of my country and its people, and in the hope of a peaceful world community.
In this age of globalisation, whatever happens in any part of the world has, to varying degrees, a negative impact on every country.
Human-made conflicts have created situations of unrest in many countries.
Vast numbers of people are being displaced, giving rise to humanitarian crises.
Wars and conflicts are placing immense pressure on the global economy.
Energy security concerns, disruptions to global energy supply systems and rising inflation are worsening the economic situation.
We believe that every conflict should be resolved through dialogue, diplomatic processes and mutual cooperation.
Equality, fairness, protection of mutual interests, and respect and dignity among disputing states should form the basis of bilateral and multilateral relations.
We aspire to a peaceful world, a humane global community where, rather than weapons of destruction, reason and debate, diplomacy, education and humanity become the instruments of change.
Bangladesh sees the United Nations as the centrepiece for establishing an accommodative global community based on mutual respect for one another's independence and sovereignty.
The tendency to divert development budgets towards military expenditure in different parts of the world reverses the direction of our journey towards global peace.
As a peace-loving nation, Bangladesh remains committed to the goals of complete and general disarmament, preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons, and arms control.

I reiterate Bangladesh’s support for any initiative at the United Nations dedicated to establishing world peace and serving humanity.The people of Bangladesh, who believe in democracy, remain deeply concerned about the plight of the freedom-seeking Palestinian people.
Bangladesh once again reaffirms its unwavering support for their legitimate demands, including their right to self-determination and their right to establish an independent State of Palestine.

In the prevailing global circumstances, the theme of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly, “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All”, is highly relevant and timely.
Bangladesh remains steadfast in its commitment to multilateralism in maintaining international peace and security.
As Vice-Chair of the Peacebuilding Commission, Bangladesh continues to serve as a strong voice for sustainable peace, conflict prevention and inclusive peace.
As a consistent contributor to United Nations peacekeeping missions, Bangladeshi peacekeepers are serving humanity in different parts of the world.
The courageous participation of Bangladeshi women in peacekeeping missions, even under adverse circumstances, reflects our strong commitment to advancing the agenda of “Women, Peace and Security”.
This year, Bangladesh is observing the 40th anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development and the 25th anniversary of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action.
Migration is as old as human civilisation.
In many countries around the world, migrants make important contributions to the economies of both their countries of origin and their countries of destination.
The government of Bangladesh is committed to ensuring regular, safe and orderly migration.
Bangladesh expects stronger global cooperation to ensure the rights, dignity and well-being of migrants.
For more than nine years, Bangladesh has been sheltering more than 1.2 million forcibly displaced Rohingya from Myanmar.
This has placed immense pressure on our resources, environment, security and local communities.
As a densely populated country, Bangladesh believes that the source and origin of the Rohingya crisis lie in Myanmar; therefore, its solution also lies there.
The only solution to this problem is the early safe return of the displaced Rohingya people to their homeland, Myanmar.
For a lasting solution to this crisis, Bangladesh expects firm and effective support from the United Nations and the international community.

At the same time, I call upon the United Nations and the international community to continue life-saving assistance programmes for the displaced Rohingya people until they can be repatriated to their own country, Myanmar.
If the international community fails to ensure justice for the displaced Rohingya people, this could turn into a humanitarian crisis in the near future.
Bangladesh is one of the countries most vulnerable to the adverse impacts of climate change.
Although Bangladesh has contributed little to global carbon emissions, it is bearing the adverse consequences of climate change.
In these circumstances, Bangladesh has chosen the path of building resilience and developing the capacity to survive and adapt.
Therefore, Bangladesh expects stronger global action at COP31 on climate justice, climate finance and adaptation support.
The government of Bangladesh has strengthened its programmes for environmental protection.
As part of these efforts, the government has launched a programme to plant 250 million trees across the country over the next five years.
Emphasis has been placed on the use of clean energy and solar energy.
With the aim of freeing the country from the scourge of floods and droughts, the government has also launched a programme to excavate 20,000 kilometres of canals across the country.

The government has also begun work on the Teesta Master Plan and the Padma Barrage project to increase freshwater flows into the world's largest mangrove forest, the Sundarbans, and to conserve water through large reservoirs.

At the same time, while strengthening domestic measures for water conservation and pollution prevention, the Government has reaffirmed its commitment to cooperation on transboundary water management by signing the 1992 Water Convention.
After ending more than a decade and a half of fascist rule and exploitation, Bangladesh became free from fascism in 2024.

Having been freed from the scourges of enforced disappearances, killings, abductions, corruption, plunder and money laundering that had become the norm under fascist rule, Bangladesh is now once again embarking on the path of democracy.
To repair a Bangladesh battered by fascist rule and exploitation, the Government is pursuing a 3-R strategy: Recovery, Restoration and Reconstruction.
A vast horizon of opportunities has now opened before Bangladesh.
Taking advantage of the demographic dividend, the Government has begun implementing extensive programmes to transform the country's working-age population into a skilled human resource.
The Govenrment has also undertaken some forward-looking initiatives to create into a large-scale employment opportunities and ‘Manufacturing Hub’.
In this endeavour, Bangladesh wants its development partners by its side.
To create opportunities for young entrepreneurs, researchers and innovators in the country to pursue start-up initiatives, the Government has allocated US$4 billion in the current fiscal year.
More than half of the country's population is female.
Therefore, women are at the forefront of all government plans for socio-economic transformation.
The government is giving priority to women's education, women's employment and the creation of women entrepreneurs.
To promote women entrepreneurship, particularly in the small and medium-sized industrial sector, the Government has expanded opportunities for cash financing for women.
Free education opportunities up to the undergraduate level have been opened to women.
The government seeks to ensure not only electoral democracy but also the democratisation of the economy, so that the benefits of economic growth and prosperity reach every family and every citizen.

To achieve this goal, the government has already launched assistance programmes for economically disadvantaged people through various social protection programmes, including the Family Card, Farmers’ Card, Sports Card and e-Health Card.
The government considers the Family Card, issued in the name of the female head of each household, a symbol of women's economic empowerment.
It is also in the government's plans to introduce a Universal Card by integrating the various cards introduced to provide support in different sectors.
The government is implementing the 31-point programme presented to the people before the national election of 12 February 2026.

At least 73 per cent of the activities under the Government's 31-point programme have a direct alignment, and 27 per cent an indirect alignment, with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals and their guiding principle of “Leave No One Behind.”

The government hopes that through the implementation of these programmes, development disparities between urban and rural areas will be reduced, while accountability and inclusive, sustainable development will be advanced across all areas of the 2030 Agenda.
The government of Bangladesh has accorded special importance to education, health and sports.
The highest budgetary allocation in the country's history have been made in the education sector.
Our plan is to increase budgetary allocation to education to 5% of GDP within next five years.
A curriculum has been developed with emphasis on technical and practical education to ensure an employment-oriented education system with strong ethical values.
From the first grade, primary-school students are being provided with schoolbags and clothing, that is, school uniforms, as well as free lunch.
The government hopes that this will increase school enrolment and improve the quality of education.
To establish sports as a profession, sports has been included as a subject in the education curriculum for the first time.
As part of this initiative, more than 2 million students participated in a month-long nationwide football tournament for school students held last June.
Science and technology will shape the future of the world.
We are entering a new era of artificial intelligence, biotechnology and science.
Technology is advancing very rapidly, but its opportunities are still not equally accessible to all.
Bangladesh's large young population and growing digital capabilities have created new possibilities for us.
To harness these opportunities, access to advanced technology, knowledge and research must be brought within everyone's reach.
We do not want today's digital divide to become tomorrow's artificial intelligence divide.
Bangladesh respects innovation and intellectual property.
At the same time, it is essential to ensure technology transfer, skills development and affordable access to modern technologies for developing countries.
No country should be left behind in this scientific advancement.
Bangladesh stands ready to work together to build a fair and prosperous future for all.

It is now time for the United Nations to adopt an effective policy framework so that the benefits of the development and rapid expansion of artificial intelligence and social media can be harnessed positively across countries.
Bangladesh is awaiting graduation from the list of Least Developed Countries (LDCs).

For Bangladesh, as well as for all other countries undergoing this process, sustained support in areas such as assured financing, greater market access, technology transfer and capacity-building is essential to make the graduation process sustainable.
In the present world order, all countries are interdependent.

Bangladesh believes that, particularly at the regional level, we can help one another achieve prosperity through the facilitation and expansion of trade, effective connectivity and meaningful cooperation.
The COVID-19 pandemic claimed the lives of millions of people around the world.
But it also sent a message to the world: for the global community to survive, mutual assistance, empathy and cooperation are indispensable.
It is essential to ensure sustainable production of vaccines, therapeutics and diagnostic equipment in developing countries so that these are readily accessible to all.
A state can never become strong by keeping its citizens powerless.

Through ensuring the political and economic empowerment of the people, we want to build a prosperous, self-reliant, welfare-oriented democratic state where everyone, irrespective of political affiliation, religion or ethnicity, can live with security and peace, and with equal rights, honour and dignity.
Bangladesh continues to make progress in all areas, including democracy, human rights, good governance, accountability, political stability and the investment environment.
The government is working to establish a safe and stable Bangladesh with a business- and investment-friendly environment.
In today's democratic Bangladesh, we welcome partnership, innovation, and both domestic and foreign investment.

We want to build a Bangladesh where young people can pursue their dreams without fear or hindrance; where women can lead their lives with confidence; where every child grows up with the opportunity to realise their full potential; and, above all, where people are assured of a safe and peaceful life.
That is why we say: “Bangladesh First — Bangladesh for All.”
I conclude my address by reaffirming Bangladesh’s unwavering commitment to the values and principles of the United Nations in order to build a peaceful world.
Today, the world needs not only more dialogue, but also more trust, more responsibility and more capacity to act together.
Multilateralism has meaning only if it leads to decisions and if decisions lead to action and results.
The human being must be at the heart of this common response: his life, his dignity, his rights and his opportunities.

This requires an international order based on the Charter of the United Nations and international law, and a United Nations that not only formulates principles, but has the power and the capacity to uphold them.
An organization that defends multilateralism, and that means a world order of rules by all and for all, for small and large countries alike, without double standards.
Bulgaria will continue to be a steadfast defender of this order and of a strong, effective and active United Nations.

Today, the United Nations must prove not only its ability to bring States together, but also its ability to act – through joint efforts, it is our duty to transform the world from one of disorder into one of international law and lasting peace.
The Pact for the Future provides important guidance, but it must be supported by real reform.
The Security Council must reflect today’s world, with fairer regional representation and increased legitimacy and effectiveness.
Bulgaria supports its enlargement in both categories of membership, including with at least one additional non-permanent seat for the Group of Eastern European States.
The UN80 initiative is an opportunity to make the Organization more effective, better coordinated and better able to fulfil its mandates.
But reform without resources is not possible.
Predictable and sustainable financing is necessary for the United Nations to be able to discharge the responsibilities entrusted to it by States.
The upcoming election of a new Secretary-General will also be a choice for the direction of the Organization.
We expect his successor to have the vision, the courage and the leadership needed to restore trust, overcome divisions and act for change.
Your Excellencies, Peace and security are among the principal responsibilities of the international community.
Faced with conflicts that have claimed the lives of thousands of people and caused enormous destruction, we must redouble our efforts to prevent and end hostilities.
The main challenge remains the war against Ukraine, the consequences of which extend far beyond the immediate combat zone.
Is it not time to rethink European security policy?
Bulgaria, as a member state of the European Union, is raising its voice and proposing that we also have a debate on this subject and on the broader goal of the future of post-war Europe.
And to begin the debate, it is high time to transfer the conflict from the military sphere to the political and diplomatic domain.
This is about negotiations, which require dialogue and at least a minimum of trust, underpinned by appropriate guarantees.
The fate of Ukraine cannot be decided without Ukraine.
But Europe cannot be a mere observer; it must be a real participant in the negotiations on the post-war security architecture on the continent after the end of the war.
Europe must be in a position to guarantee its own security.

Military security should be complemented by the second pillar of security, the contractual-legal pillar, which should guarantee that strengthening defence potential brings more security rather than a new arms race.
For Europe’s security, we must add strong diplomacy to military and economic security.
It would be irresponsible if, after the end of the war in Ukraine, we were unable to offer European citizens anything better than a new and worse Cold War.
We need a vision for the day after according to the formula “a Europe of peace through deterrent defence and shared security”.
From this highest platform, we make an appeal to guide us on the path towards this goal!
Bulgaria considers that the security and stability of the Black Sea region are an integral part of its national security in all its dimensions.
The war between the Russian Federation and Ukraine has spilled out of the territorial waters of the parties to the conflict, which directly affects Bulgaria today.

However, the problem of the Black Sea has shifted from regional to global because, with the regional negative consequences combined with the war in Iran and the aridity of the Danube, it is leading to a food crisis in the world, mainly in the Middle East and Africa.
The inability to export grain and fertilizers poses a real risk of famine this winter in a number of countries in those regions and of jeopardizing the 2027 harvest.

Bulgaria cannot and does not want to remain indifferent and, applying the practical diplomacy approach, is preparing an initiative for which it will strive, together with the countries of the region and all interested parties, to reach an agreement and common action in order to ensure the freedom/security of navigation in the Black Sea.
We are convinced that this issue deserves the attention of the United Nations.

Bulgaria therefore calls for the Black Sea to be transformed from an area of increased risk and threat into an area of “shared security” — an area of security, an area of free transport, energy, trade, digital corridors, tourism, an area where different cultures, religions and political systems meet in peace.
The Middle East also needs political solutions and de-escalation.
A new cycle of destruction, humanitarian crisis and violence cannot be permitted in Gaza.
It is necessary to create the conditions for stabilization and reconstruction, for credible security guarantees for Israel and for effective Palestinian governance.
Bulgaria condemns the terrorist actions of Hamas and insists on its complete and unconditional disarmament.
The organization has no place in the governance of Gaza.
We remain convinced that the only durable solution is for two States, Israel and Palestine, living side by side in peace and security.
This is the only way to give both peoples the prospect of a dignified life and a peaceful future.
Political decisions to achieve stability must also be at the forefront in Lebanon, Syria and Yemen.

In the context of developments around Iran, the security of global maritime routes and, first and foremost, the route through the Strait of Hormuz have highlighted the global dimensions of this issue.

As we have repeatedly stressed publicly in international forums, Bulgaria strongly supports the freedom and security of international maritime transport and insists on full respect for the applicable international law and the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.
There are also major challenges in Africa.

In the Sudan, the Sahel and the Great Lakes region, political processes, the protection of civilians and the strengthening of State institutions, long-term development efforts and economic opportunities are needed.
Security requires that we limit the risks arising from weapons of mass destruction and their proliferation.

Bulgaria remains committed to strengthening the international architecture of non-proliferation, disarmament and arms control and the three pillars of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons.
We support the objective of a world without them, which must be pursued through pragmatic measures: greater transparency, verifiable control and limitation of arsenals.

Global conflicts have introduced new threats hitherto unknown, even threatening nuclear security through irresponsible attacks against nuclear sites and lines vital to their safety support, such as attacks against the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant and other Ukrainian nuclear power plants.

On the other hand, compliance with the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons is the essential condition for Iran, which must above all strictly comply with its international obligations and reach a durable nuclear agreement under the control of the International Atomic Energy Agency.
We have repeatedly called for this and it remains valid to this day: The DPRK should cease its nuclear and missile programmes.
Today’s security requires that we act in time.
This implies strengthening diplomacy, mediation and political dialogue, but also effective control of arms proliferation and of the military application of new technologies.
Artificial intelligence must be developed within the framework of international law and under effective human control, and outer space must remain a space for peaceful and safe use.
The same principle must guide our response to terrorism, radicalization, disinformation and cyberthreats.
No country can do this alone.
Strong institutions, effective United Nations peacekeeping operations and closer international cooperation are needed.
Bulgaria will continue to defend this approach.
Lasting security is built not only by responding to crises, but also through our ability to prevent them.

Excellencies, As a member of the United Nations Human Rights Council in 2024-2026, Bulgaria is working for a public environment in which discrimination, racism, anti-Semitism and hate speech have no place.
Freedom of the media, the protection of journalists and access to reliable information constitute an essential element of this environment, particularly in the face of growing disinformation.
This commitment also implies ensuring that everyone has the opportunity to participate and to be heard.

The rights of the child and access to education, the equal participation of women and girls in societal processes and the full inclusion of young people in them are essential to building societies in which everyone is part of the decisions that determine their future.
Bulgaria supports concrete international efforts in this direction, from guaranteeing every child’s right to education to the consistent implementation of the women and peace and security agenda.
The protection of human rights is measured not only by the commitments made, but also by the real possibilities for participation, education and a life in dignity.
This is our common goal: societies in which differences do not divide, hatred does not define, and the rights and dignity of every person are protected.
Sustainable development is not an abstract goal.

It means enabling people to live in dignity, to receive quality education and health care, to have employment and prospects, and enabling societies to face crises and change without leaving anyone behind.
That is why Bulgaria remains committed to implementing the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and to accelerating progress in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals.
Environmental responsibility is one of the fundamental principles of sustainable development.
Unfortunately for us, in the context of the war against Ukraine, such a subject is becoming increasingly urgent.
The resilience and balance of the marine ecosystems of the Black Sea are threatened by the harmful consequences of the military conflict.
Bulgaria strongly urges political engagement and compliance with General Assembly resolution 77/104, adopted on 7 December 2022, on the protection of the environment in relation to armed conflicts.
For Bulgaria, investment in education, science and culture is an investment in the long-term viability of societies.
They not only preserve knowledge and identity, but also give people the ability to adapt and create.
Bulgaria will continue to honour this commitment also at the international level.

Our election as a member of the Intergovernmental Committee for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of UNESCO for the period 2026-2030 is an opportunity to make this commitment an even more active contribution.
Sustainability means being prepared for the changes that are already under way.
The climate is changing, health crises can affect the whole world, and new technologies are changing the way we work and live.
We cannot stop change, but we must manage it so that it works for people.
This means a just green transition, better global connectivity, and preparedness for a common response to health crises.
The assistance of artificial intelligence will be indispensable if it develops our capacities without undermining security and trust.
Bulgaria will continue to contribute to the international dialogue on this subject, including by participating in the preparation of the second global dialogue on AI governance in 2027.

Excellencies, All these efforts lead to a common goal, to a world in which peace, security, human rights and development are mutually reinforcing and complementary, and where international law protects human dignity.
Let us ensure that the United Nations is not only a forum for discussing crises, but a driver of their prevention and peaceful settlement.
Because the future does not necessarily belong to the strongest, it will belong to those who succeed in building trust.

There is no greater responsibility to our peoples than to deliver to future generations a world in which cooperation is stronger than confrontation, dialogue stronger than hate speech, and peace stronger than war.
And Bulgaria is ready to contribute to this not only as a consumer of security, but also as a producer of security.
You have chosen for this session a theme that speaks directly to the challenges before us: “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that delivers for All.”
Trust is not restored through statements or by repeating appeals.
It is restored by upholding the law and translating the decisions of this Organization into effective protection for people’s lives, rights and livelihoods.
We meet at a time when the Arabian Gulf is facing a security situation of a severity not witnessed in decades.

The States of the Gulf Cooperation Council and the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan have been subjected to waves of unjustified Iranian attacks involving ballistic missiles and drones, targeting civilian infrastructure, residential areas, ports, airports and energy facilities, in flagrant violation of international law and the Charter of the United Nations.
These are indiscriminate attacks without justification under any law.

My country also condemns the attacks carried out by the Iran-backed terrorist Houthi militia against civilian objects and Islamic holy sites in the brotherly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and their threats to freedom of navigation in the Bab Al Mandab and the Red Sea.
Allow me to put the facts before you in numbers.
Our countries have been subjected to nearly 7000 attacks, involving 1,700 ballistic missiles, 80 cruise missiles and 5,220 drones.
Two thousand cargo vessels and tankers, with 20,000 seafarers on board, have also been detained, while 72 commercial vessels have been targeted, resulting in the deaths of 22 seafarers.
Behind every figure is a ship, a port, a market, and families waiting for those that provide for them to return home.

Commercial vessels have been targeted in the Strait of Hormuz, mines have been laid in an international shipping lane, and restrictions on passage have been imposed in contravention of international law.
The consequences extend far beyond the Arabian Gulf, affecting energy and food prices, shipping and insurance costs, and supply chains across the world.

As the Kingdom renews its full solidarity with the brotherly countries subjected to these attacks, it commends the professionalism and readiness of the Bahrain Defence Force, and the air defence forces of brotherly countries, in confronting these attacks.

It reaffirms the right of these States to take all lawful measures to defend their sovereignty and territorial integrity, in accordance with Article 51 of the Charter of the United Nations and the Joint Defence Agreement of the Gulf Cooperation Council States, while continuing to exercise the utmost restraint and seeking to ensure that security and peace prevail for the benefit of the people of the region.
The position of the Kingdom of Bahrain is grounded in law, not in taking sides.
The Strait of Hormuz is an international strait, and the right of transit passage through it is established for the vessels of all States under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.
That right may not be suspended or obstructed, nor may conditions be imposed upon it unilaterally by any State.
Accordingly, the Kingdom categorically rejects any permit or fee regime imposed on passage.
It rejects the use of international waterways as instruments of pressure, economic coercion or the seizure of vessels.
Such actions would set an extremely dangerous precedent, because what is accepted today in one strait may be demanded tomorrow in every international waterway upon which global trade depends.
Alternative routes cannot be treated as a solution to conduct that violates international law.
Mitigation measures are an emergency response.
They should not be used as a pretext to claim that the Strait is no longer necessary, or to accept a new status quo.
The right of passage does not cease to exist because alternatives are available, nor does a violation cease to be a violation because those affected have found ways to reduce their losses.
This threat is not confined to the Strait of Hormuz.
Security Council resolution 2817 also referred to the Bab Al Mandab, recognizing that a threat to one waterway is a threat to navigation through all waterways.
The security of navigation in the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden and the Bab Al Mandab forms part of a single system.
We are not defending a regional interest, but a rule that applies to every international waterway, and if it applies to our strait alone, it would cease to be a rule.
The Kingdom of Bahrain has not confined itself to stating its position in principle.

On behalf of the Gulf Cooperation Council States and the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan, and by virtue of its current presidency of the Gulf Cooperation Council and its non-permanent membership of the Security Council, Bahrain led efforts resulting in the adoption of Security Council resolution 2817, with the historic and unprecedented support of 136 states, which condemned the attacks against our countries, reaffirmed their sovereignty, and rejected any action intended to close the Strait or obstruct navigation through it.
The Kingdom also introduced a draft resolution under Chapter VII of the Charter to protect commercial navigation.

The resolution adopted by the Council of the International Maritime Organization on 19 March, together with Human Rights Council resolution 61/1, further demonstrated that the international rejection of such conduct extends beyond the Security Council.
We stress the need for the full implementation of these resolutions in a manner that ensures those responsible are held accountable and compensation for the damage caused.
On the seventeenth of this month, the Kingdom convened an Arria-formula meeting of the Security Council dedicated to freedom of navigation.
We heard from 53 affected States, the maritime transport sector and relevant international bodies.
All delegations expressed one clear conclusion: freedom of passage through international straits is a prerequisite for global economic prosperity.

The Kingdom contributes to the protection of a rules-based maritime order across an area exceeding three million square miles through its hosting in Manama of the headquarters of the Combined Maritime Forces, comprising 47 nations.

In this context, the Kingdom welcomes the establishment of the Multinational Maritime Defence Alliance led by the brotherly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and is proud to participate as a founding member, in support of efforts to safeguard international trade routes and global energy supplies, in accordance with international law.
As efforts continue in the Security Council, this General Assembly has an equally important role to play as the forum in which all States stand as equals.

From this podium, we call upon Member States to support a firm, collective position which upholds freedom of navigation and the right of transit passage in accordance with international law, and which affirms that the security of maritime passages is a collective responsibility that cannot be made subject to bilateral arrangements.
This is what restoring trust means in practice.
This is not a call dictated by the present crisis.

From this very podium two years ago, His Royal Highness Prince Salman bin Hamad Al Khalifa, Crown Prince and Prime Minister, said that the systems established to safeguard the international order were under severe strain, and that this Organization must evolve to confront growing threats.
He called for comprehensive, consensus-based reform encompassing all decision-making bodies, including the Security Council.
What has happened since then has not altered that conviction.
The test of the United Nations’ credibility is not only confined to our waters.
The Palestinian cause remains at the heart of our concerns.

The Kingdom reaffirms its steadfast position in support of the establishment of an independent and geographically contiguous State of Palestine, living alongside the State of Israel in peace and security.

The Kingdom has also joined the Board of Peace as a founding member, pursuant to Security Council resolution 2803, reaffirming its unwavering support for the rights of the brotherly Palestinian people.

The Kingdom also reaffirms its support for the unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Syrian Arab Republic, as well as for efforts to lift sanctions in a manner that enables the brotherly Syrian people to rebuild their country.
In Sudan, we call for an immediate ceasefire, the protection of civilians, unhindered humanitarian access, and a political solution that preserves Sudan’s unity and the institutions of the State.

In Yemen, we renew our support for a political solution under United Nations auspices, led by the legitimate Government, and express our appreciation for the efforts of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in this regard.

Our position on other conflicts, including the conflict in Ukraine, is guided by the same principles, regardless of the parties involved: adherence to the Charter, respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, and the peaceful settlement of disputes.
The Kingdom of Bahrain, where mosques, churches and temples have stood side by side for generations, believes that tolerance and coexistence are not simply policies to be adopted.
They are part of the identity of Bahraini society and a foundation of our national unity.
It was in this spirit that the Kingdom introduced the initiative adopted by the General Assembly designating 28 January as the International Day of Peaceful Coexistence.

His Majesty the King also issued the Kingdom of Bahrain Declaration on religious freedom and freedom of belief; the King Hamad Global Center for Coexistence and Tolerance was established; and the King Hamad Award for Coexistence and Tolerance was launched.
The same approach underpins our development journey.
The Kingdom continues to advance its Economic Vision 2030, pursue its commitment to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals, and strengthen the status and advancement of Bahraini women.
The Kingdom embraces the Women, Peace and Security agenda, and the Youth, Peace and Security agenda, and both are priorities during its membership of the Security Council.
No discussion of development today is complete without addressing the technology that is reshaping it.

From this podium two years ago, His Royal Highness the Crown Prince and Prime Minister called for the adoption of an international treaty governing the development of artificial intelligence, to ensure that this technology contributes to peace rather than exacerbating conflict.
Since then, the General Assembly has taken positive steps.
Dialogue can bring positions closer, but it does not create obligations.

The aim is not to halt a technology that no one has the power to halt, but to ensure that its growth is surrounded by safeguards, just as the international community surrounded nuclear energy with safeguards that preserved its benefits without preventing it.
This technology recognizes no borders; a safeguard adopted by a single state is no safeguard, just as a rule that applies in a single strait is no rule.
We therefore renew our call for a binding international framework to ensure that this technology becomes a driver of innovation rather than division.
And this, in our view, is what it means to manage the transformation that you chose as the theme of your session.
However far apart they seem, all these issues are bound by one fundamental truth: security and prosperity are not parallel objectives.
They are a single objective pursued along two paths.
There can be no prosperity without security, and no sustainable security without interconnected economies and societies at ease.
This is not a Gulf perspective dictated by geography.

It is a lesson humanity has learned from its wars, and one Europe learned when it built its peace not through treaties alone, but on interests so intertwined that separating them became costlier than preserving them.
It is in this light that we view freedom of navigation.
A waterway is not merely a security issue of concern for coastal States.
It is an artery of development through which the food, medicine and energy of nations flow.
When a single waterway is disrupted, the cost is felt by a family in a country that does not have a coastline.
An economy that is difficult to disrupt is difficult to coerce, and interdependence, once firmly established, becomes a shield against coercion.
This approach is not a position shaped by the circumstances of the moment.

It is what His Majesty King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa, King of the Kingdom of Bahrain, has consistently advocated for, out of a conviction that the security and prosperity of this region are two faces of a single truth, and that a just peace and lasting stability are the path towards a dignified life for all the peoples of the region, whatever their faiths and cultures.
It is on this basis that we reaffirm that what the United Nations needs today is not more resolutions, but a greater capacity to implement them.
A resolution adopted but not implemented has no value, and a right that is recognized but not protected has no meaning.
I conclude by saying that the Kingdom of Bahrain continues to be guided by His Majesty’s vision.
For peace, as His Majesty sees it, is not declared but built.
It can rest only on respect for human beings in their dignity and their beliefs, and on dialogue that is not a concession, but a strength.

The Kingdom will remain faithful to its international commitments and covenants, committed to international law, freedom of navigation, and a just, comprehensive and lasting peace, true to His Majesty’s approach and to the conviction that the security of our region and the prosperity of its peoples are a shared responsibility that can only be safeguarded through our collective efforts.
The Bahamas pledges to you, its full support.
Every generation inherits a promise it did not make.
The promise of our generation was made eighty-one years ago, with the founding of this United Nations, from the ashes of the worst war in human history.
Its ideals have proven its worth.
No nation is too small to be sovereign.
No people too poor to be equal.
And the strong should be bound by the same law as the weak.
Sad to say, the United Nations has drifted away from its promise.
The Bahamas comes today to insist on it.
All week we have been told this is an age of uncertainty.
With respect, I do not agree.
Uncertainty is the language of those who have already decided, and do not wish to say so.
Rules are giving way to deals, and the benefits of the deals go to whoever holds the most leverage.
Once again, we hear the language of Spheres of Influence.
For 500 years, the Caribbean was somebody's backyard.
We did not win our freedom to once again become somebody's backyard.
The message to small nations is very clear.
Be as sovereign as we allow you to be.
A sovereignty that must ask permission is not sovereignty.
Our ancestors did not break their chains so that their children could become tenants.
The only uncertain thing is how we respond to the opportunities and challenges of this time.
People often say that the world lacks political will.
The world has never lacked political will.
In 2008, when the banks of the richest nations were failing, trillions of dollars were found in a matter of weeks.
When a global pandemic reached the capitals of the powerful, the political will returned.
Somewhere, a bank is always too big to fail.
But a nation should never be too small to be left behind.
What the world lacks is not political will for change.
A change in who writes the rules.
A change in whose suffering counts.
A change in who decides, and who pays.
Political change is a decision about who holds power.
And Mr. President: That is what I have come to speak about today: Power!
Two and a half thousand years ago, the envoys of Athens stood before the small island of Melos and told its people a simple truth about power.
The strong do what they can.
The weak suffer what they must.
Eighty-one years ago, in San Francisco, humanity wrote a different law.
Not equality of size or wealth. Equality of standing.
The United Nations was the world's answer to Melos.
But in 1945, nearly one in three people on earth still lived under colonial rule, the people of my islands among them.
The Bahamas was not in that room.
But we were on the map.
Not granted from above. Demanded from below.
On the eighteenth of September 1973, The Bahamas took its seat in this Assembly.
Then in 1985, Commonwealth leaders met in my own capital and agreed The Nassau Accord against apartheid.
We were told pressure would never work.
Less than five years later, Nelson Mandela walked free.
None of that happened because the powerful suddenly found their conscience.
It happened because the balance of power in the room was changed.
That is the lesson of history.
Change is not given, it is organised.
It is not the small states who are dismantling the rules-based order.
Small countries cannot dismantle a rules-based world.
But we will be the first to be crushed beneath its collapse.
Great powers can survive the end of the rules. Small states cannot.
For us, a rules based world is our shield.
The rules have not always been applied fairly.
But the answer is not a world without rules.
It is rules that bind the strong as firmly as the weak.
International order, where rules apply only to the weak, is not order.
When The Bahamas defends multilateralism, we are not defending a bureaucracy.
We are defending the only successful arrangement in which a nation of four hundred thousand people can stand at this podium as the sovereign equal of a nation of a billion people.
A world without rules is not a free world. It is Melos.
I do not appeal to conscience.
Small states have done that for decades.
Today, I appeal to your interests.
What is in your best interest?
No wall is high enough to keep out rising warming seas.
No border strong enough to stop a pandemic.
Narrow self-interest asks what you can take today.
Enlightened self-interest asks what kind of world you will have to live in tomorrow.
The international, rules-based order benefits all.
They are not arbitrary having been arrived at through lived experience.
Every rule you break today is a rule you will need tomorrow.
Every institution you starve is one you will one day call upon.
Every small nation you abandon is a crisis you will one day inherit.
Defending the rules is not a favour to the small.
It an insurance for the strong.
Nowhere is that truer than the climate crisis.
Here too, we are told there is uncertainty. There is none.
And it does not recognise a veto.
In 2024, for the first time, the world was more than one and a half degrees warmer for an entire year.
The line which small island states fought to write into the Paris Agreement, has already been crossed.
A new report released only days ago warns that the El Niño phenomenon, now heating the planet, is likely to cost some four hundred and fifty thousand lives by next February.
In 2019, Hurricane Dorian inflicted damage and losses on The Bahamas equal to roughly a quarter of our national output.
Families watched the sea take the only land they had.
Most of my country sits barely above sea level.
For us, a rising ocean is not a forecast.
It is a boundary inching towards our doorsteps.

That is why The Bahamas proudly endorses yesterday's Declaration on Sea-Level Rise, which affirms that our statehood, our boundaries and our seat in this Assembly will not be washed away by the sea The science is certain.
Last year, the International Court of Justice made clear that the law is also certain.
The people who bear least responsibility are asked to adapt first, pay more, and recover from disasters they did not cause.
People who lose their homes do not disappear.
They move, and they arrive at someone's border.
Prevention costs less than rebuilding or relocating.
But no nation, acting alone, can hold back the tides.
Nor can we build resilience inside a financial system designed at Bretton Woods in 1944, which still declares us too prosperous to help, until the next storm makes us poor.
The Loss and Damage Fund exist.
What is missing is the power shift to make them operational and real.
The next contest for power will not only be fought over land and sea.
It will be fought over data.
Our citizens’ data crosses the world without a visa and without a vote.
It leaves our shores as raw material, and returns as products we must buy.
We have seen this pattern before.
My islands once exported salt, sponge and sisal.
It does not arrive with ships and flags.
It arrives in a box on a screen and a button that says, I agree.
I am talking about the capacity of a people to govern their own digital lives.
People whose daily lives and histories are being mined, should decide where their data lives, who may use it and on what terms.
Those people should be able to share in the value which their data creates.
It means building artificial intelligence that understands our languages, our laws and our lives, not only the lives of those in the wealthy North and dominate languages and cultures.
And it means taking part in the digital age on our own terms, not as consumers of other people's systems, but as builders of our own.
Data is the newest raw material in the global economy.
The old empires took our lands, plundered them and renamed them.
The new ones seek to take our data, and hand us back a picture of ourselves, one we did not paint.

In this modern age, are we expected to be simply the unquestioning suppliers of data, or can we not rightfully expect to participate in processing our own data so as to refine it, govern it and profit from it?
We do not think it outrageous to demand that small states help write the rules of this new age, not simply be shown where to sign.
That is why The Bahamas asks you to support the nomination of Mr. Stephen Bereaux for Deputy Secretary-General of the International Telecommunication Union.
The Security Council was designed by the victors of a war that ended eighty-one years ago.
Five nations still hold a veto over the peace of one hundred and ninety-three.
Most of the nations in this Hall did not exist when that arrangement was made.
An institution that cannot reform itself cannot hope to reform the world.
Power without legitimacy is not order. It is control.
And a peace kept only by the powerful is not peace. It is permission.
That is why The Bahamas seeks a seat on the Council for the 2032–2033 term.
The Bahamas does not seek a seat on the Council to sit quietly inside that arrangement.
We seek it to help change it: a Council that reflects the world as it is, and that gives small island states a dedicated seat at the table where our survival is decided.
Change must also reach the leadership of this Organization.
The Bahamas supports the candidature of Her Excellency Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of Guyana for Secretary-General.
A former Foreign Minister who has presided over the Security Council, she understands what rules mean for nations with no other protection.
In eighty-one years, this Organization has had nine Secretaries-General.
None has come from the Caribbean.
The Bahamas believes the time has come for both to change.

In our own hemisphere, The Bahamas again calls for the lifting of the strengthened blockade against Cuba, an end to the fuel blockade, and Cuba's removal from the unilateral list of alleged state sponsors of terrorism.
We call on all states to respect Latin America and the Caribbean as a Zone of Peace.
And we must speak of Haiti.
Haiti was the first nation on Earth born from a successful revolt by enslaved people.
For that act of courage, it was made to pay.
In 1825, under the guns of a foreign fleet, Haiti was compelled to compensate its former colonisers for its own freedom.
It took Haiti more than a century and a half to pay that compensation.
If you want to see what sovereignty costs when it is only allowed, and never respected, look at Haiti.

When the Security Council meets on the 30th of September, we urge it to renew the mandate under Resolution 2793, and to give the Gang Suppression Force the resources to deliver, in a partnership that respects Haitian sovereignty.
The injustice of this century has a history.

This month, CARICOM advanced its Ten-Point Plan for reparatory justice, building on this Assembly's recognition, in March, of the trafficking and racialised enslavement of Africans, as crimes against humanity.
The wealth of empires was built on the stolen lives of our ancestors, including enslaved children.
It is important that the former colonisers have recognised this atrocity, as recognition was a vital step.
But recognition without repair is only a sentence on a page.
We call on the nations that profited to engage seriously with reparatory justice: truth, apology, restoration and development.
The founders of this Organization made their promise in the ruins of war.
We should not need ruins to find our own courage.
The United Nations was not created to manage the decline of its own promise.
It was created to build on it.
The only uncertain thing is how we respond.
I challenge you, I dare you, I encourage you, I demand of you: Let history record that we responded through change.
We are a symbol of a nation that has survived severe trials but has not lost its path towards a better future.
In the period from 1992 to 1995, my country was subjected to aggression, joint criminal enterprises, genocide against Bosniaks, crimes against humanity and other war crimes.
Following the end of the aggression in 1995, destructive forces have sought, through blockades, obstruction and other means, to halt the progress of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
They are slowing down our path towards a modern European state, but they cannot stop it.
Today, Bosnia and Herzegovina stands at the doorstep of the European Union (EU) and the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO).
These are our strategic foreign policy objectives, unanimously defined by the state authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
Unfortunately, there are still those seeking to realise greater-state projects at the expense of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
During the aggression, they attacked our country by military means; today, they do so by political, diplomatic and other means.
It is very important that the UN courts have established the nature of the war waged against the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
Final judgments, including those concerning joint criminal enterprises, have established that this was an international armed conflict.
Judgments of the highest UN courts have established that genocide was committed against Bosniaks.

They also stand as judgments on the greater-state policies that, through a joint criminal enterprise, sought to divide and destroy Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent, sovereign, indivisible and internationally recognised state.
We live in a world of injustice, insecurity and intolerance.

The strengthening of authoritarian populism, the aggression against Ukraine, the suffering in Gaza, the war in the Gulf region, the catastrophic situation in Sudan and other flashpoints have brought humanity into a profound crisis, marked by great uncertainty and fear.
We must not remain silent in the face of injustice.
The world did not respond adequately to the aggression against Ukraine and the genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, just as it did not during the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The aggression of the Russian Federation against Ukraine is a flagrant example of a violation of the UN Charter and international law, while Gaza is humanity’s greatest defeat in the twenty-first century.
The greatest global crises are directly interconnected and have the same root: the erosion of international law.
Disrespect for international law cannot lead the world towards prosperity and a better future.
Without contemporary humanity, we cannot solve its problems.
Instead of force, we need respect and the strengthening of the existing international norms, rules and institutions that we have built over more than 80 years.
The multilateral system today faces a serious challenge – a crisis of institutional trust.
Trust is weakening because some actors in the international community undermine the values enshrined in the UN Charter.
The future of humanity does not lie in policies of violence and human rights violations.
Conflicts and wars are not the purpose of our civilisation.
Let us build a culture of dialogue, cooperation and peace.
In this context, I believe it is of utmost importance to:
▪ reaffirm the importance of the UN Charter;
▪ revitalise the role of the UN as the global centre for coordination and cooperation;
▪ support the reform process and strengthen the credibility of the UN;
▪ consistently implement the Sustainable Development Goals;
▪ build mutual trust, inclusiveness and a democratic vision of leadership;
▪ and strengthen preventive diplomacy at a time of numerous tensions and conflicts.
Let respect for international law, peace, solidarity, sustainable development and justice be the path that we follow together.
We in Bosnia and Herzegovina call upon all UN Member States to focus on:
▪ reaffirming relations between states on the basis of international law;
▪ ensuring respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms;
▪ combating hate speech and all forms of discrimination;
▪ strengthening policies for the prevention of genocide, crimes against humanity and other war crimes;
▪ advancing the rights of women and children;
▪ and strengthening gender equality, better healthcare and education.
The world must return to the fundamental principles upon which the UN is founded.
These are not unrealistic propositions; they are the only possible foundations of a stable world.
Bosnia and Herzegovina is a reliable and responsible member of the UN.
Among other things, I would like to remind that Bosnia and Herzegovina is:
▪ aware of climate change and committed to contributing to global efforts;
▪ committed to the transition towards renewable energy sources and the reduction of harmful gas emissions;
▪ and determined to combat all forms of terrorism.
We in Bosnia and Herzegovina know that peace cannot be taken for granted.
Peace must be safeguarded every day.
It requires responsibility of political leaders, respect for the law and a readiness for dialogue.
There must not be one standard for large states and another for small states.
If we want to preserve trust in the international order, the rules we establish together must be applied equally.
Bosnia and Herzegovina is the only country in Europe where genocide was committed after the Second World War.
In May 2024, the UN General Assembly adopted the Resolution designating 11 July as the International Day of Reflection and Commemoration of the 1995 Genocide in Srebrenica.
This Resolution represents a profoundly moral and civilisational act by the UN General Assembly.
The adopted Resolution is equally important for the UN and for Bosnia and Herzegovina.
It is particularly dangerous that the leadership of the Republic of Serbia glorifies the convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić.
The monster Ratko Mladić is not a hero, but a convicted war criminal.
The institutional glorification of this war criminal is an anti-civilizational and unacceptable act.
It amounts to identifying Serbia’s state leadership with one of the worst butchers in European history.
It is an indication that Serbia has not abandoned the ideology and policies that lead to aggression and genocide.
It is a direct assault on the values of the UN, whose court delivered a final judgement against this war criminal.
Let me remind you that Serbia is the only state in the world that has been found by a UN court to have violated the UN Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide.
I call on the UN and EU and other international actors to clearly condemn this conduct and take concrete measures against those who institutionally glorify convicted war criminals.
Unfortunately, the ideology and policies that led to the genocide against Bosniaks continue to threaten Bosnia and Herzegovina.

From the podium of the UN General Assembly, I wish to publicly warn the international public that the current leadership of the Bosnian entity Republika Srpska continues to threaten the peace and security of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the region.
We must stop this destructive policy together.
The victims of the genocide and the employees of the Memorial Centre Srebrenica are facing unacceptable pressures from the police of the Republika Srpska.

We must not allow that the police and other institutions of Republika Srpska which committed the genocide against Bosniaks, today threaten the survivors and those that are preserving the memory on the victims of the genocide.
Those seeking to destroy the Dayton Peace Agreement are attempting to create the conditions for the secession of the Bosnian entity Republika Srpska.
In the period ahead, they will intensify their activities, primarily with the aim of:
▪ weakening and abolishing the mandate of the High Representative of the international community, which is also envisaged by the Dayton Peace Agreement;
▪ weakening the institution of the Constitutional Court of BiH;
▪ and seizing the state property of Bosnia and Herzegovina, contrary to national and international law.
Bosnia and Herzegovina is an unconquerable state.
There is not a single map of Southeast Europe from the past 1,000 years on which Bosnia or Bosnia and Herzegovina does not appear.
Bosnia and Herzegovina is home to people who love freedom more than their own lives.
Finally, as the Chairman of the Presidency of BiH, I wish to emphasise that I am proud of the brave people of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
These are people who have suffered injustice, yet they continue to fight for justice.
These are people who have been victims of lies, yet they continue to fight for the truth.
These are people who support the struggle for justice, freedom and human dignity throughout the world.
These are the honourable and proud people of my homeland, Bosnia and Herzegovina.
STATEMENT by the Minister for Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Belarus M.V. Ryzhenkov 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly General Debate Mr. President!
The theme of the session as a diagnosis Let us begin with the theme of the current debate — “Restoring trust, steering transformation: an Organization working for all.”
It is an interesting theme and allows for a substantive discussion.
Indeed, trust among States today is at its lowest point since the Cold War.
More and more voices are saying that the United Nations is not working for all and is not capable of steering change.
In large part, this is because we, the Member States, have become mired in endless discussions but have still not given the Organization a real opportunity to act.
That is precisely why the theme of this session today sounds like a sentence on our collective indecisiveness and at the same time like a diagnosis requiring urgent treatment.
We are surrounded by a systemic crisis in international relations.
We see it everywhere: the air is filled with anxiety.
From Europe to the Middle East, from Asia to Africa and Latin America.
The world is being overwhelmed by wars and conflicts.
They take lives, separate families, turn flourishing cities into ruins, and generate ever new waves of mass forced migration.
Global supply chains are being disrupted.
The energy crisis is intertwined with the food crisis.
All this hits the most vulnerable segments of the population particularly hard.
An even more alarming signal is the collapse of the system of strategic stability.
For the first time since the 1970s, there are no longer any legally binding limits on strategic arms between the largest nuclear Powers.
No treaties, no verification mechanisms, no predictability.
Humanity is once again balancing on the edge of existence, which we had hoped to leave forever in the last century.
How did we reach such a point?
And this is not a coincidence of circumstances.
It is the natural result of actions by certain States aimed at deliberately undermining the system of international relations.
So that the world would develop not according to the laws of peaceful coexistence, but according to the principle of the right of force and political egoism.
If we truly want to restore trust, we must not hide behind diplomatic courtesies, but honestly name the causes of the crisis.

The root of mistrust: hegemony instead of law In 1945, in San Francisco, at the founding conference of the United Nations, United States President Harry Truman spoke words that today sound like a prophecy: “Power as we are, we must deny ourselves the license to do always as we please.”
If all those whose power is great had acted in this way, we would have avoided many wars and conflicts.
Unfortunately, the aspiration to live at the expense of others has remained the main narrative of the collective West’s development.
During the Cold War, the balance of power was ensured by a system of checks and balances between two opposing political systems.
But since the 1990s, when that equilibrium collapsed, the policy of unlimited superiority began to grow rapidly.

And over the past three decades this policy has reached its apogee: Western countries have in effect trampled on international law and begun forcing everyone to act on the basis of so-called “rules”, destroying countries they disliked and suppressing peoples that would not submit.
These rules are like road signs in a city that they themselves designed.
For themselves, a green light always.
But the matter is not one of metaphors.
The matter is facts known to everyone.
Yugoslavia, Iraq, Libya, Syria, Venezuela, Cuba, Iran, Palestine — this is far from the full geography of the countries that were or remain in the focus of Western interest.
And now add to this unfair global trade, where the rules are written to suit the interests of transnational corporations.
Also add illegal unilateral sanctions that are suffocating entire peoples.

And the unlawful actions of the Western members of the Security Council have further contributed to the destruction of security and stability in international relations — and the trend is only intensifying.
And where has the United Nations been all this time?
The Organization has practically not participated in conflict settlement.
Its role has most often been reduced to expressions of concern and appeals addressed to those who have already suffered.

A particularly disturbing role today is being played by the leadership of the European Union, which, through an unrestrained desire to preserve its slipping hegemony, is trying to obstruct global stability and the maintenance of peace.
And in pursuing this goal it is ready to sacrifice the well-being of its citizens.
And do the peoples of Europe really crave some kind of revenge against Russia, especially at the price of their own impoverishment?
Do they really want to be cannon fodder in a war that European Union politicians are allegedly preparing for by 2030? Of course not.
But in Brussels someone very much wants to play at soldiers and secure his grandeur in history.
This has happened before — and more than once.
And how it ended — we know.
Sensible politicians in Europe today are an endangered species.
