And those who still dare to speak the truth are quickly taken out of the game.
The script is well rehearsed: manipulation of public consciousness, bribery, unfounded persecution, actions threatening life.
Many in the West are clinging with their last strength to their domination.

For they are already beginning to be called to account for the centuries-long plunder of colonies, for the destruction of the cultures, traditions and identities of subjugated peoples, for the slave trade that took millions of lives.

This is the context in which the resolution adopted by the General Assembly in March of this year declaring the trade in enslaved Africans and the racial enslavement of Africans to be a crime against humanity was framed.
Belarus supported this resolution without hesitation.
And this is not simply a diplomatic gesture — it is the voice of a country that itself passed through a similar hell in history.
We know what genocide is — one third of our population during the war was cold-bloodedly killed and tortured by “civilized” Europeans united by Hitler 85 years ago.
Now their descendants tell us that they have nothing to do with it and their grandfathers had nothing to do with it.
But it was not the Führer who set fire to a village house with Belarusian children, old people and women inside.
We know what the plundering of cultural heritage is — our wealth, resources and works of art were taken to the West.
Young people were forcibly deported into slavery to the same place — to Europe.
And today, having come under unprecedented sanctions, we have once again felt what it means to be a target.
Therefore, we support with particular feeling those who demand historical justice, including on the subject of reparations raised by the African Union.
But reparations are not not only finances.
It is also respect for memory.
It is the return to peoples of their own history.
How many more names remain on the map of the world that have erased the memory of millennia?
A simple example: the great waterfall that the peoples of Zimbabwe for centuries called Mosi-oa-Tunya — “the smoke that thunders.”
The colonizers “discovered” it and named it in honor of their queen, who in Africa had never even been.
Is this not theft of identity?
The Western elites do not like the new multipolar world, in which their voice ceases to be decisive.
But instead of adapting to positive changes, they continue to sow chaos and instrumentalize instability.
For us in Belarus this is seen most vividly in the example of Ukraine.
Does the West strive for peace there?
Its goal is to inflict a civilizational defeat on Russia.
To weaken, humiliate, break it and continue living at the expense of Russian resources.
But not at the cost of the lives of its own citizens, but of ordinary Ukrainians.

It makes it possible to create an image of the enemy, to mobilize one’s own population under the pretext of a collective threat, to write off economic failures, to justify militarization and to enrich oneself.
That is why a conflict is needed — managed, frozen, eternal.
But if the West wants to take a worthy place in the emerging multipolar system, it needs to change.
To understand that the future of our Planet lies in cooperation, not in confrontation.
Yes, it will have to move over on the global “bench” of international relations — and very seriously.
It will need to abandon the policy of neocolonialism, to forget about the self-isolation to which the EU is condemning itself by creating a new iron curtain on the border with Belarus and Russia.
But in essence — with the whole space of great Eurasia, which lies beyond us.
The United Nations: transformation or decline About the United Nations.
Is our Organization keeping pace with the times?

Forty-five years after independence, Belize continues to pursue the peaceful settlement of its territorial disputes with Guatemala and with Honduras.
Belize has chosen, and will always choose, law over force.

Belize informs this Assembly of a serious breach of international law committed on the night of 23 September 2026, when a Guatemalan military aircraft entered Belize’s sovereign airspace and intentionally disabled its transponder.

This act violates the Chicago Convention on International Civil Aviation, customary norms governing state aircraft, and the inviolability of territorial sovereignty protected under Article 2(4) of the United Nations Charter.
This incursion is not an isolated event.

It forms part of a continuing pattern in which Guatemalan state vessels and personnel operate unlawfully in Belizean territorial waters of the Sarstoon River, which forms part of Belize’s border with Guatemala, in defiance of obligations—binding on both Parties—to refrain from any action capable of aggravating or extending the dispute presently before the International Court of Justice.
The case is scheduled for hearing in February 2027.
Guatemala’s conduct risks prejudicing the Court’s authority and undermines the principle of peaceful settlement of disputes enshrined in Article 33 of the Charter.

Belize therefore calls upon Guatemala to immediately cease all incursions by air, land, or sea; to comply fully with its obligations under the UN Charter, the Chicago Convention, and the OAS Confidence-Building Measures; and to respect the integrity of the ICJ process.
Belize further requests heightened monitoring by the United Nations and the OAS to ensure that no Member State uses military force or intimidation to influence judicial proceedings.
We await the Court's judgments with confidence, and we look forward to borders that are respected by all.

Families around the world are paying for the rising the price of fuel, fertilizers, and food.
The war between Russia and Ukraine has dragged on for five years, in a humanitarian drama that continues to claim lives.
We all know that there will be no winners on the battlefield.
Initiatives such as the Friends of Peace Group, created by Brazil and China, reveal that there are forces in the international community willing to work towards dialogue.
In Latin America and the Caribbean, geographical proximity to the world's greatest military power is inescapable.
Especially in a context of renewed hegemonic temptations.
Brazil does not fit in anyone's backyard.
We need partners with a positive agenda that fosters development.
Ideological differences should not hinder higher integration amongst neighbours.
The countries in the region have experienced the horrors of authoritarian regimes.
We have come a long way to restore popular will.
Democracy is once again under threat.
We witness once more foreign interference in electoral processes.
Dividing the world into zones of influence and neocolonial incursions for strategic resources are anachronistic gestures.
The Venezuelan people deserve to define their own destiny.
Nicaragua will not solve its problems by preventing the opposition from running in the elections.
The crisis in Haiti continues to test the limits of the international community’s indifference.
In Cuba, the world watches in horror as collective punishment is imposed on 10 million people by an illegal economic and energy embargo.
Brazil does not underestimate the challenge represented by organized crime.
We are ready to face the criminal organizations that terrorise our local communities.
Police officers do not make it back home.
But we will not outsource the responsibility of defending its borders and guaranteeing our population the right to live without fear.
We do not need aircraft carriers guarding our waters.
We need cooperation to block the flow of weapons and money that feeds crime.
That’s the spirit of the proposal that I personally handed to the US President.
We want to fight money laundering carried out by Brazilian criminals abroad.
For a long time, Brazilian states acted each in their own way.
Crime made the most of the lack of coordination.
In Manaus, we created the Amazon international police cooperation centre, bringing together public safety authorities from 9 Amazon countries.
In 2025, we carried out the biggest operation against organized crime in Brazil’s history.
We broke records of drugs seizures, as well as unlawful assets and resources.
We are facing all levels of crime, including crime tycoons.
The anti-faction law we have just passed, establishes heavier sentences for organized crime than those carried by terrorism.
Organized crime and corruption walk hand in hand.
The fight against corruption shall remain relentless, no matter who it hurts.
No one is above the law.
Ladies and Gentlemen, The pillars of multilateralism are being eroded.
The World Trade Organization is being kept on life support.
When governments capitulate vis-à-vis those who use tariffs as weapons of coercion and blackmail, consequences are harmful.
In the age of misinformation, obscurantists resist the evidence of science.
We will never forget the millions of lives lost due to the negligence in the fight against COVID-19.
Anti-vaccine campaigns are bringing back diseases we thought were eradicated.
Weakening the World Health Organization makes everyone more vulnerable.
Until recently, the response to climate change was firmly established at the centre of the international agenda.
This year, however, the topic disappeared from the debates of the G7 and G20, forums that bring together the largest carbon emitters.
It's time to resume the offensive and inflict a defeat on denialism.
Nature reminds us every day that we live on one planet.
The glaciers in the Himalayas are melting.
A Super El Niño may cause torrential rains, droughts, and forest fires in different parts of the globe.
Its effects will hit the most vulnerable the hardest.
Brazil has been demonstrating that it is possible to combine economic growth with reduced emissions.
We have achieved self-sufficiency in oil and will continue to explore the potential of new reserves, such as those in the Equatorial Margin.
But we will not abandon the environmental agenda.
We will move forward with the roadmap for the decarbonization of the Brazilian economy.
The Tropical Forest Forever Facility, launched at COP30 in Belém, shows it is possible to change old paradigms.
The forest is worth more standing that destroyed.
We will continue to reduce deforestation, which has been cut in half in the Amazon, reaching its lowest level in 11 years.
We have the moral authority to reject protectionist measures disguised as commitment to the environmental cause.
Brazil is a global reference in green energy.
We have the critical minerals and rare earths the world needs to make the energy transition.
Our natural wealth belongs to the Brazilian people – and it is in their benefit that it will be exploited.
Access to our minerals will be contingent upon mandatory value generation in our territory, technology transfer, and the supply of strategic national sectors.
We are living through an unprecedented technological revolution, with great risks and opportunities.
It would be an unforgivable historical omission not to address the challenge of regulating Big Techs and Artificial Intelligence.
A handful of techno-oligarchs want to resurrect a version of digital ultraliberalism, without rules or transparency.
They are promoting a race with no ethical boundaries, bypassing the United Nations and the Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence.
As Pope Leo XIV warned, "decisions about technology should never be separated from awareness and responsibility”.
Companies that are aware of the risks of their products are transferring the impossible task of confronting algorithms to families.
The billion-dollar betting industry turns addiction into profit.
Its exponential dissemination is increasing debt levels and destroying homes.
Brazil will not tolerate this business model.
We passed one of the most advanced pieces of legislation in the world to protect children, adolescents, and women in the digital environment.
We will ensure fair compensation for artists, musicians, and audiovisual content creators.
We will not give in to pressure from multinationals that want to privatise our PIX, a free public payment infrastructure that has made financial inclusion a reality for millions of Brazilians.
Ladies and Gentlemen, The Sustainable Development Goals are currently under attack from reactionary forces that wish to normalise injustices.
Inequality and underdevelopment are the result of political choices.
It is possible to include the poor in the budget and make the rich pay their share.
It is necessary to cut privileges and invest in free quality education and healthcare.
There is a legitimate desire for change throughout the world.
But change is not the same as going backwards.
It's not about taking away rights.
It is not about reviving theories of racial supremacy or female subjugation.
It's not about recolonising the Global South.
Change means moving towards a more participatory future and more achievements.
It is about creating and sharing effective public solutions to development challenges through a democratic, strong, efficient, and capable state.
It's about betting on the spirit of solidarity and cooperation with Africa, Asia, and Latin America and the Caribbean.
Initiatives, such as the Global Alliance Against Hunger and Poverty, launched by Brazil, and the UN Intergovernmental Panel on Inequality, launched by South Africa, stem from this political will.
Brazil is in a hurry to become a developed and socially fair nation.
We have adopted an economic model based on income distribution, job creation, and wage increases.
We are invested in improving productivity, expanding credit, and building a robust social safety net.
Brazil has returned to sustainable growth.
We are the third largest destination for foreign direct investment.
Despite the high tariffs imposed against our economy, this year we shall break a new record in our exports.
There is still much to be done.
The world of work is undergoing a transformation.
Older people want to stay active.
Young people want to become entrepreneurs.
Workers need time to rest, improve their skills, and spend time with their families.
In Brazil, achieving this goal requires ending the so-called 6x1 working schedule to guarantee workers two days off per week.
This change is crucial to alleviate the domestic burden that still falls on women.
We are building a Brazil where women don't need permission to occupy positions of power or enter the job market.
A country free from femicide, where no woman, inside or outside their home, lives under the threat of violence.
This is a cause that the whole world needs to embrace.
When he was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, Dr. Martin Luther King stated that “What self-centred men have torn down, other-centred men can build up”.
The UN was born under the sign of hope.
Over eight decades, it has contributed to decolonisation, promoted human rights, and supported sustainable development.
It has protected migrants and refugees, and condemned racism, antisemitism and religious intolerance.
These were achievements of leaders who took up to this podium driven by indignation at the injustices of their time.
Men and women who refused to accept war as destiny, colonialism as a right, apartheid as a legitimate system.
It was from this ability to say "no" to inequalities that some of the greatest transformations we have experienced were born.
Faced with the paralysis of the United Nations, we need to rediscover the political will so that it may once again become a temple of peace.
I want to conclude with a message from my country to everyone who is listening.
On October 4th, millions of Brazilians will go to the polls to define their destiny.
They are not just voting for president of the republic, state governors, and representatives of the Legislative Branch.
They will decide between democracy and denialism.
If Brazil will move towards a future with more opportunities, or back to a past of exclusion.
We shall have competitive and transparent elections, where every candidate benefits from the broadest freedom of speech.
We know that some abuse this freedom, to associated themselves with foreign interests against the country.
We do not underestimate the challenge of misinformation networks that aim to distort public debate during the campaign.
But we have a modern and robust election system.
Under the watchful eye of a pluralistic citizenry and a free press, we will not allow the enemies of democracy, whether domestic or foreign, to undermine popular will.
Brazil continues to be a sovereign country.
Nobody...!!! Nobody will turn us away from this path.

Mr. president, excellencies, my friends, we meet at a time when the obstacles confronting human progress are multiplying, obstacles to peace, obstacles to food and clean water, obstacles to finance, medicine and education, obstacles to movement and opportunity.

Obstacles to technology, to the knowledge and infrastructure needed to use it, and increasingly, obstacles between nations, between communities, and between people who no longer agree on the same facts or trust the same institutions.
War continues to destroy lives and communities.
Even though the international community possesses more tools than ever, ever before to prevent conflict and to facilitate dialogue.
Even though the science is clear enough for us to act, and many of the solutions are already known.
And despite unprecedented global wealth, millions remain without reliable access to food, water, health or shelter.
These challenges, my friends, are creating the crises of which we constantly speak, and at the same time, new challenges are emerging.

Artificial intelligence is opening extraordinary possibilities in health, education, science, and productivity while also creating new risk of exclusion, exploitation, surveillance and the distortion of truth.
And yet, the cooperation needed to confront these challenges is under strain.
It is why I believe the theme this year is so apt. Restoring trust. Managing transformation.
A united nation that delivers for all.
The theme reminds us that we have institutions created to preserve peace, to advance development, and yes, to protect human dignity.
The institutions are these very United Nations.
We have shared principles grounded in sovereign equality, and in the recognition that our responsibilities extend beyond borders.
The reality is that we understand that there is, regrettably enough, for us to be able to invest in prevention rather than waiting to finance reconstruction.
We understand enough about the climate crisis to reduce the emissions that are warming our planet, and take the necessary steps for our populations to adapt.

We equally now understand enough about the rapid development of AI to know that as we welcome its promise, we must anchor its development in a universal, humanizing framework that does not imperil our existence as human beings.
The failure, my friends, to address these challenges, therefore, is not one simply of knowledge or capacity.
It is a repeated failure to convert what we know into what we do.
To turn principle into practice and global capacity into solidarity So beneath our many crises lies yet another one.
And yes, it is a crisis of responsibility.
The transformation we seek for a better world will only happen when we trust each other.
And we accept our responsibility for each other.
We in the Caribbean understand something about the necessity of living together.

Barbadian novelist and essayist George Lamming once described the Caribbean as perhaps the first global experiment in human history, bringing together, and I quote, every branch of the human family, from the indigenous peoples of the Americas to the diverse peoples from Africa, Europe and Asia.

It is as though that we, through this tortuous and shared history of migration, conquest, slavery and the difficult work of constructing a common national and regional destiny that we give the world an example to follow.
Against all the odds, the Caribbean produced what Lamming called a new kind of global family.
Our history has taught us that difference need not mean division.
That coexistence requires dialogue and negotiation, and that those without the power to compel must learn the power of persuasion.
In this spirit I'd like to thank Her Excellency Annalena Baerbock for her leadership of the General Assembly's 80th session and for helping to advance the work of the Member States on UN reform.
We look forward to your stewardship of this assembly, and we move to restore trust and indeed to carry reforms from proposals to implementation.
We cannot move swiftly to reorganise offices and reporting lines while allowing the most consequential questions of power and representation to remain unresolved. Transformation and development.

Peacekeeping and humanitarian aid cannot succeed if member states are unwilling to fund it Let's be very clear no organizational chart can overcome the refusal of states to respect decisions that they find inconvenient.
We cannot continue to ask international organisations to do more, while failing to provide them with the resources necessary to fulfil the mandates that we ourselves have agreed.
And if member states believe in the institutions that they have created, then we must also be prepared to sustain them.
Barbados has consistently met that responsibility, and I give this body the assurance that we will continue to do so.
Our commitment to multilateralism, to an international rules based order, must be measured not only by what we ask of these institutions, but by our willingness to support them.
So yes, let us improve the machinery, but let us also reform the exercise of power.
The Security Council still has 15 members, five of them permanent.
Africa, with 54 states has no permanent seat.
And you've heard speaker after speaker after speaker come to this platform to say that this must change.
Small island developing states equally confront threats that now reach squarely into the council's mandate from climate and security and illicit armed arm flows to organised crime and displacement.
And yet, despite constituting one quarter of the world's states, we have no assured representation within the councils.
This, to my friends, must change.
And the world we know has already changed.
The council has not changed with it.
But reform is not only about who sits at the table, it is about how power is exercised.
Barbados is therefore joining 123 other member states in supporting the Franco-mexican initiative on the use of the veto in the cases of mass atrocities.

Its principle is fundamental where populations face genocide, crimes against humanity, or large scale war crimes, the veto should not be allowed to paralyse the Security Council when action is most urgently needed.
This is why people are losing trust in the United Nations and its council.
Mr. president, it's not fair to the majority of member states who still believe in the promise of this body, even as we call for greater equity with the reform of the Security Council.
We must equally reform the Secretariat to better support peacekeeping and the resolution of conflicts.
We've been told that there are more conflicts today than at any time since the United Nations was established, and regrettably, these conflicts are in almost every corner of the planet.
The Oslo Peace Institute reported that in 2025 last year.
I'm told that this makes it the third most violent year in the post-Cold war era.
My friends, the scale of human tragedy is mounting, and whether it is in Gaza or the West Bank or Lebanon, or Yemen or Sudan or Ukraine or elsewhere.
That there was a risk of conflicts in the Middle East widening even further, and the conflicts continue.
These fears, regrettably, have come to pass and with a global impact. Nevertheless.
Indeed, conflicts are more protracted and more fragmented.

And when coupled with hunger and unsustainable debt and a warming planet, it becomes a veritable hell for the citizens of those countries Increases in energy and transport costs and in interest rates have spurred inflation.
It means that no one, even on the other side of the world, can escape the hardships in meeting their daily needs.
The truth is, until there is a two state solution that respects the rights and territories of both the Israelis and Palestinians, we will continue to live on the edge in this world.
And you may well ask, how have we gotten here?
We need to address with laser like focus each and every one of these conflicts.
And let us let the UN deliberately and systematically deploy nimble mediation teams led by political leaders, current and retired.
On behalf of the Secretary General and enjoying the Secretary General's confidence and authority and the respect of Member States.
This, my friends, will help lift the heavy weight necessary to end these multiple conflicts and to bring peace and dignity to those affected populations.
We know that many hands make light work and we can't ignore it.
These conflicts need to be supported by a quicker and technology enhanced observer force, capable of rapid deployment to monitor and support ceasefires and peace agreements to be given the resources.
These peacekeeping forces must be given realistic mandates, predictable financing and true partnership.

Let us work my friends together with the parties to these conflicts, to build dialogue and to bring opportunities for investment and jobs to the affected populations so that they too, can live properly.

And as for the wider international legal order, we know that countries of every size and capacity depend on a system in which rules are made collectively and applied consistently and fairly But if we don't act early enough, we have trouble.
And that is why we say that the UN must receive the resources and the resolve to act before the guns speak, and not after the guns start to fly.
My friends, without an equitable rules based order, smaller states like mine will simply cease to exist in this world.
And that is why Barbados is a co-sponsor of the P4M, a group focused on strengthening multilateralism and to beat back the undertakers who are waiting to bury it.
We also say thank you for taking the journey without diverting from the principles and the core values of this charter.

As the United Nations undertakes the important task of selecting its next secretary general, Barbados joins its sister member states in the Caribbean community in pledging its full support for the candidature of Ambassador Carolyn Rodriguez Burkett of Guyana.

At a moment when the international community is being called upon to renew its faith in multilateralism, we believe that Ambassador Rodriguez Burkett brings to this task the experience, the skills and the understanding to serve the entire membership of this organization.
I'd like, sir, to turn to the topic of artificial intelligence, which is one of our new challenges.
AI is already transforming how we work, learn and govern, and it is clear that its potential is extraordinary.
We have found that it has great capacity to detect disease earlier, predict disasters, improve agriculture, and expand access to education and public services.
And yet, these same extraordinary systems can just as quickly reproduce discrimination, widen surveillance, and spread falsehoods faster than institutions can respond.
We must not allow a new technological age to reproduce all hierarchies of access and power.
And this is why Barbados is so honored to host the second in-person meeting of the Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence, which will be held in November of this year.
In this growing age of AI, governance cannot be left to voluntary corporate practices or to a small number of technologically advanced states.
We need globally agreed rules that protect human dignity, preserve meaningful human oversight, and ensure that the benefits of AI are shared widely and equitably.
I caution a technology that will affect every state must be governed by the rules that every state has had the opportunity to shape.
Mr. president, exactly 65 years ago that great Caribbean, French, African intellectual and psychiatrist Frantz Fanon published what has now become a classic, The Wretched of the earth.
And across the vast range of observations and analysis that he made in that extraordinarily lucid and prescient book, he said the following.
What matters today is the issue which blocks the horizon is the need for a redistribution of wealth.
Humanity will have to address this question, no matter how devastating the consequences may be.
My friends, this was true in 1961 and sadly remains manifest today.
This is why Barbados throws its full support behind the establishment of the International Panel on Inequality that is being proposed.
Growing inequality is at the centre of geopolitical discussions, tensions, distrust in institutions and indeed the increasing number of conflicts that we see.
It is for this reason that we reject the notion that governments must refrain from policy interventions that are essential to creating a level and fair playing field for ordinary citizens.
We know that it is the policy choices of government that has led to this injustice, and it is the policy choices of governments that must now remove it.
For us, this is as important a battle of the as the climate crisis.
Mr. president, that brings me to that crisis.
Minister Murat Kurum, representing the incoming Cop 31 presidency, has put the challenge plainly the time for simply setting out goals is behind us.
Anyone who experienced this summer in Europe and elsewhere knows that it was the hottest on record, and the super El Nino has not even yet hit.
The proposed action agenda places methane reduction at the centre of climate implementation, and we welcome that focus.
It is true that carbon dioxide must remain central to the global energy transition, but emissions are not falling quickly enough, and the full benefits of action will take time to emerge.

So, Mr. President, under Barbados's presidency of the Cvf Climate Vulnerable Forum and its G20 countries, 74 countries got together and advanced the call to pull the methane emergency brake at the G20 Ministerial Dialogue in April of this year.
The finance ministers agreed that methane reduction must be treated not only as an environmental priority, but also an economic, fiscal and public health opportunity.
We must now implement the climate.
Vulnerable countries need to mobilise approximately $490 billion each year by 2030, and yet the current inflows are roughly $90 billion.
As a young people in Barbados would say, the math simply ain't math.
We must also correct the inequity of the borrowing costs that these countries face.
It is almost 1.2 percentage points higher for climate vulnerable countries than for advanced economies.
Now that figure seems small to you, but that actually generates an estimated $62 billion more a year in excess interest payments each year.
So that, believe me when I say that change is possible.

As we have seen consistently with measures from the Bridgetown Initiative in less than one year, Barbados as chair of the climate Vulnerable countries, the G20 countries, along with the OPEC fund for International Development, designed and launched the Vulnerability to Viability Compact on four pillars, bringing about 74 countries along with 16 development finance institutions globally, to expand access to affordable long term capital for education projects, health projects and water infrastructure.
The Cvf also had its governors of the central bank meet to establish the lifeline Fund, which will shortly be operationalized.
It seeks to provide rapid liquidity when climate shocks create balance of payments pressures for countries.
So we are moving to help ourselves.
We have been resolute, and the reason for it is that we know that you cannot build hospitals and schools and water infrastructure with ten and 15 year money.
It crowds out critical investments for our people and leaves you flat footed.
And that is why this important initiative represents real progress.
But mechanisms such as this one cannot, on their own, address the underlying flaws of the international financial architecture.
I repeat that for almost five years, the Bridgetown Initiative has consistently argued that climate resilience, debt sustainability and access to affordable finance cannot be treated separately.
For many vulnerable countries, the problem is not simply the availability of capital, but whether we have the fiscal space to borrow and to invest on reasonable terms.
Mr. president, as I turn to my region in the Caribbean, I'd like to highlight a series of crises that continue to threaten our peace, stability and development.

Let me say at the outset that when I speak about letting many hands make light work, when it comes to conflict resolution, that this is one of the areas in which the political leaders of the Caribbean can play a pivotal role in its own region.

Firstly Haiti, the security crisis continues to retard political renewal and economic recovery, and still the preparations for a return to constitutional government, yes, are moving forward even with great difficulty.
But those efforts cannot succeed unless security improves, particularly in the areas containing more than half of Haiti's electorate in the capital and surrounding areas.
Barbados, therefore supports the full deployment that has been 2 to 2 long promised, and the renewal of the mandate of the gang suppression force.
Let me remind you that it was in 2022 that this recent, more heightened state of insecurity began with the fuel riots just before the General Assembly met in 2022, and in 2026.

We have not kept faith with providing the level of security that would minimize the loss of life At the same time, we have to give thanks where thanks is due and there are member states who have contributed in whatever way to help in Haiti find its path.
This includes, of course, the Caribbean community's Eminent Persons group, which has been helping to build consensus and maintain engagement with key international partners in the last few years.
In addition, Mr. President, we are deeply concerned by the worsening humanitarian pressures facing the people of Cuba.
Too many people are suffering. Too many people.

Restrictions on trade, finance and access to fuel are intensifying hardship not only for Cuban citizens, but for all others who study and live there Barbados has each year opposed the use of the embargo and other unilateral coercive measures against Cuba.
And as always, we call for constructive engagement, constructive engagement grounded in dialogue, sovereign equality and respect for international law.
That is why we are here as individual states.
We will also extend our continued solidarity to the people of Venezuela, who, regrettably, are recovering from the devastating double earthquakes in June.
Barbados was proud to stand with our neighbour in the immediate aftermath, dispatching our field hospital and personnel to Venezuela.
We remain committed to supporting them in their longer term recovery.
A stable, sovereign, peaceful and democratic Venezuela is vital to the security and prosperity of not just Latin America, but the wider Caribbean.

In this regard, however, I must take this opportunity to reiterate Barbados steadfast support to its sister of Caricom, its sister Caricom country Guyana, as it seeks to bring a peaceful resolution through the International Court of Justice for the long, outstanding territorial controversy with Venezuela.
This is in the interests of the people of Guyana, the people of Venezuela and the wider people of the Caribbean and Latin America.
The Caribbean, my friends, must remain a zone of peace.
We cannot accept our region becoming a theatre.
We cannot accept our region becoming a theatre for confrontation, or for the unilateral and unjustified use of force.
On March 25th of this year, a historic resolution was passed in this General Assembly.

The overwhelming majority of states acknowledged the truth that we in the Caribbean long knew the trafficking of enslaved African and racialized chattel enslavement of Africans is the gravest crime against humanity.
Regrettably, we still carry the scars.
I reminded us that it was my country, Barbados, that passed the first slave code that the world knew in 1661 to deal with chattel slavery.
Others, regrettably followed, including the infamous Code Noir of 1685.
That Code Noir was only repealed this year, and then hence the wounds are still raw.
We in Barbados accept the moral responsibility of removing the cross of slavery with its horrific consequences.
We must affect healing through Reparatory justice, for it is the right thing to do.
As a result, in July of this year, Caricom Heads of Government approved the revised Caricom ten Point Plan for Reparatory justice for the Caribbean, for Africa, and for those countries concerned.
The honest engagement must begin, and I thank President Mahama of Ghana for coming to the table with the force with which he has come.
We do not ask for reparations without accepting responsibility for our own self repair, which we have undertaken for decades.
I want to be very clear about this, Mr. Speaker.
Mr. president, I make the same mistake as President Mohammed. We are parliamentarians.
I want to make this clear.

Let there be no doubt, Mr. President, that the mindset that established, justified and sustained slavery is the same mindset that sustains the inequities and the inequities within the power structures of this very institution and within the international financial architecture.
It is the same mindset that caused a global map to remain grossly inaccurate on the size of Africa for centuries.
As if the true size of Africa would intimidate the rest of the world into understanding its power.

Mr. president, if we want to restore trust in these United Nations and we want to manage transformation, as is your theme, and we want a UN that truly delivers for everyone, then at its core, we must treat every human being as having equal value and deserving respect.
And I can find no better reference than His Majesty Haile Selassie speaking in this very assembly on the 4th of October, 1963.
And those who know the words can say it with me until the philosophy which holds one race superior and another inferior, is finally and permanently discredited and abandoned everywhere, is war until.
Until there are no longer first class and second class citizens of any nation, until the color of a man's skin has of no more significance than the color of his eyes.
There will be no trust and no transformation.
And in the words of that iconic song made famous by Dionne Warwick, what the world needs now is love. Sweet love.
It's the only thing that there's just too little love.
No, not just for some, but for everyone Love and a little kindness.
The 9th of December this year will mark 60 years since Barbados took its place in this organisation, emerging into independence after 340 years of imperial subjugation.

On a wintry 9th of December 1966, just nine days after we achieved independence, and on the very day of our admission to the United Nations, our first Prime Minister, the right excellent Errol Barrow, set out what, coupled with the principles of this organisation has remained our guiding principle in dealing with the world that Barbados is a friend of all and a satellite of none.
Indeed, Prime Minister Barrow spoke of a world marked by profound inequalities in wealth and opportunity, which Fanon had highlighted only five years earlier.
In the text I quoted and drawing from Prime Minister Barrow's language, where he quoted from the Hebrew Bible.
He warned that newly independent countries could not remain hewers of wood and drawers of water, while the wealth of the world flowed elsewhere.
He saw the United Nations as having to put the eradication of poverty at the centre of its role.
Do not question, therefore, why we view it as our duty to fight increasing global inequality.
Much good has been done by this UN in the last 60 and 80 years.
During this time, our membership in the United Nations has been essential to Barbados expression of its sovereignty and its participation as an equal member of the international community.
These halls have given us a place to speak in our own name, to defend the interests of our people and others, and to help shape the decisions that affect us all.
This un, this United Nations must continue to stoke those fires for a transformed and inclusive world.
Mr. President, The theme of this Session speaks directly to something the world is losing far too quickly: Trust.
It is difficult to build, easy to fracture and, once lost, very hard to restore.
Without it, treaties risk becoming little more than words, institutions become arenas for accusation, and countries increasingly feel compelled to rely only on themselves.
At a time of profound transformation, rebuilding confidence among nations lets us confront change and uncertainty together.
Today, we not only see declining confidence between countries, but also a growing crisis of faith in the rules meant to bind us together.
When nations begin to believe that rules are applied differently depending on power or circumstance, the instinct is to turn inward and act alone.
And the international order becomes more fragile, leaving smaller and more vulnerable States particularly exposed.
For Brunei Darussalam, multilateralism is not an intellectual concept.

It is the assurance that sovereignty and territorial integrity will be respected; that every nation, irrespective of size, has a voice; and that international law protects the weak as surely as it restrains the strong.
The Charter of the United Nations must therefore remain our common foundation.
It cannot mean one thing in one crisis and something different in another.
Its principles must be upheld consistently if this Organisation is to retain its legitimacy and credibility.
Few issues demonstrate this more painfully than the question of Palestine.
For generations, the Palestinian people have waited for justice, statehood and dignity.
They cannot be asked to wait indefinitely for rights that are already theirs.
In Gaza, the scale of human suffering and destruction is intolerable.
Civilians, including far too many children, continue to bear the heaviest cost.
Medics, journalists, humanitarian workers and United Nations personnel have also lost their lives while carrying out their duties.
In the West Bank, Palestinians continue to endure occupation, expanding illegal settlements, settler violence and displacement from their homes and land.
Whether in Gaza or the West Bank, these are not merely numbers.
And their suffering exposes a fundamental truth: international law and the principles of the Charter must apply equally to everyone.
There cannot be one standard for some, and another for others.
A just and lasting peace therefore requires more than managing the consequences of conflict.

It requires addressing its root cause and realising the Palestinian people's legitimate right to self-determination and an independent State of Palestine based on the pre-1967 Borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital.
Without justice for the Palestinian people, there can be no lasting peace.
This remains a defining test of the credibility of the United Nations and, particularly, the Security Council.
And the conflict is no longer confined to Palestine.
Its consequences are now spreading across the region.
In neighbouring Lebanon, United Nations peacekeepers have also lost their lives while serving the cause of peace.
It is in this wider context that Brunei Darussalam co-sponsored Security Council Resolution 2823, strengthening accountability for crimes against United Nations peacekeepers.
Those who serve under the United Nations flag must be protected.
The protection of those who serve peace, and the protection of innocent lives, especially children, must remain at the heart of this Organisation.
Rebuilding confidence does not mean returning to a world that no longer exists.
It means equipping ourselves to face the world that is emerging.
From conflicts and climate change to sustainable development and emerging technologies, the challenges before us are increasingly complex and interconnected.

In Southeast Asia, ASEAN offers a practical example of how these principles can be applied at the regional level.
Despite our differences, ASEAN has chosen dialogue, restraint and continued engagement.
This year marks the 50th anniversary of the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia, or the T.A.C.

ASEAN’s experience shows that institutions remain relevant when rules are respected, dialogue stays open, and differences are managed peacefully.
The same must be true for the United Nations.
Reform must not become an exercise in rearranging structures while confidence outside this Hall continues to erode.
Transformation must strengthen the United Nations' ability to prevent crises, respond effectively to Member States, and deliver outcomes that make a meaningful difference to people's lives.
Brunei Darussalam therefore supports initiatives such as the Pact for the Future and the UN80 Initiative.
Ultimately, reform must achieve more than efficiency.
It must strengthen this Organisation's credibility and its capacity to deliver.
A United Nations that delivers for all must ultimately deliver for the people.
That is the spirit of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.
At its heart is a simple promise: that progress today should not come at the expense of tomorrow.
For Brunei Darussalam, preparing for the future begins with our people.

Together, these goals reflect our conviction that national progress cannot be measured by economic growth alone.

It also means ensuring they have the security and stability to build their lives with confidence, supported by strong communities, quality healthcare and essential services, social protection, and a cohesive, resilient society.
For Brunei Darussalam, stability and development go hand in hand.
Stability gives people the confidence to plan for tomorrow, and development gives them the opportunity to build that tomorrow.
Both must be sustained by a dynamic, diversified and resilient economy that creates meaningful opportunities and quality employment.
Together, they create the conditions in which people can realise their full potential.

Our ambition is therefore not merely to build a more prosperous country, but a society in which people feel secure in the present, confident about the future, and equipped to shape that future for themselves.

That is why “no one left behind” must be more than a phrase.
It must be reflected in the choices we make and in the outcomes we deliver.
The realities before us are complex.
But the principles that should guide us remain clear.

Confidence in the international system is strengthened when promises are kept; when international law is applied equally; when dialogue is chosen over force; when sovereignty is respected; and when every nation, large or small, knows that its voice matters.
Therefore, to build a United Nations that delivers for all, we must always remember who “all” means. Not institutions. Not statistics.
The United Nations we build today will shape the world the next generation inherits.

We owe them a world in which cooperation remains stronger than conflict; where dialogue remains preferable to confrontation; where international law does not bend according to size or strength; and where justice is not determined by power.
The world does not need another promise that we fail to keep.
It needs us to honour the promises we have already made.
That is how credibility is restored.
That is how multilateralism and international law remain relevant, and that is how we build a United Nations that truly delivers for all.

Her tenure reminds us of an unfinished chapter the history of this Organisation.
Eight decades later, the United Nations has yet to be led by a woman as Secretary-General.
Mr. President, theme of this session, "Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All", aptly captures the central challenge before us.
• Restoring trust requires fidelity to the UN Charter and international law;
• Managing transformation requires institutions capable of adapting to a rapidly changing world; and
• Delivering for all requires us to move beyond declarations towards tangible improvements in the lives and livelihoods of our peoples.
4. Ultimately, our declarations, communiqués and resolutions must travel the difficult road from this Assembly Hall to the daily lives of the peoples we represent.
Persistent conflicts, geopolitical tensions and growing divisions have tested trust between nations.
Concurrently, our world is undergoing transformation driven by technology, climate change, demographic shifts and changing patterns of economic power.
6. The pertinent question is how we strengthen multilateralism so that the United Nations can deliver meaningful results for all Member States.
7. Humanity has travelled far enough to know that on the great challenges of our age, none of us can go it alone.
Whether a nation of a billion people, or, like Botswana, with just over two and a half million people, we share one fragile planet and one imperfect but irreplaceable United Nations.
8. The choices we make will determine whether multilateralism restores trust, manages transformation and delivers for all, or becomes a cautionary tale of promises made and forgotten.
Botswana comes to this podium with the power and weight of genuine conviction.

9. When Botswana gained independence in 1966, we carried a founding belief that our security and prosperity would come from disciplined integration into a community of nations governed by rules that all had agreed to honour.
We honoured our treaty obligations and opened our economy in accordance with the norms this Organisation exists to uphold.
We regarded compliance with international law as one of Botswana’s strongest protections.

10. That is the tradition I bring to this podium representing a nation staking its existence on the promise that shared rules, faithfully observed, remain humanity’s best instrument for peace and prosperity.
That tradition tests whether trust between nations, large and small, can be restored.

11. Mr. President, restoring trust must begin with restoring respect: respect for sovereignty, territorial integrity, and equal dignity of every nation, regardless of its size, wealth or military power.
For smaller States such as Botswana, a rule-based international order is an essential safeguard.
It assures us that international relations will be governed by the strength of agreed principles.
12. Botswana believes that rules that bind only the weak are not rules; and principles applied selectively soon cease to command respect.
That is why Botswana calls on this General Assembly, the Security Council, and every organ of the United Nations, to recommit to dialogue as the first instrument of diplomacy.

13. Botswana has sought to live by this principle as a host to the Southern African Development Community (SADC) Secretariat, through our contributions to regional mediation and election observation, and through our consistent commitment to the peaceful settlement of disputes.
14. Mr. President, even as we work to restore trust, our world is transforming.
Climate change is no longer tomorrow’s warning.
It is today’s drought in Africa, floods in Asia, rising seas in the Pacific, and wildfires in Europe and the Americas.
15. For Botswana, custodian of the Okavango Delta, (a UNESCO World Heritage Site) and the Kgalagadi ecosystem, climate change directly affects livelihoods, water security and biodiversity.
Botswana remains committed to the 30-by-30 target and the sustainable management of our natural capital.
16. Mr. President, Africa has the youngest population on Earth.
That is an extraordinary asset if we invest in it.
But what is a demographic dividend today can become a demographic crisis tomorrow if opportunity does not keep pace with aspiration.
17. Youth unemployment remains one of the most urgent challenges of our time.
Managing it is a shared responsibility.

Botswana calls upon the United Nations Development Programme, the International Labour Organisation, and all relevant multilateral institutions to make technology transfer, skills development and capacity-building funded priorities.
18. As we will all agree, the credibility of our multilateral commitments will be properly tested in development finance.
When countries have the means to invest in their people, and when international institutions respond effectively to shared threats, trust is strengthened.
But when commitments remain out of reach for those who need them most, confidence in the system weakens.
Getting these fundamentals right is central to restoring trust, managing transformation, and building a United Nations that delivers for all.

19. The global financial architecture must, therefore, evolve to reflect the economic realities of the 21st century, including financing demands created by climate change, technological transformation and the imperative for sustainable development.
Developing countries frequently face borrowing costs several times higher than those of wealthier nations because the system was not designed with the circumstances of the Global South in mind.
20. Debt sustainability is a question of development and fairness.
When nations spend more to service debt than invest in education, job creation, or provision of healthcare, trust in the system erodes.
Botswana calls upon this Assembly and the international financial institutions to pursue reform of global financial governance.
This would give developing countries a meaningful voice, and provide fair and predictable access to concessional finance.

21. We further call upon the United Nations and its financial partners to mobilise private capital through innovative and blended financing arrangements that de-risk productive investment developing economies.
This is enlightened fairness and sound economics.
Capital should help create opportunity where its impact can be felt.
22. Mr. President, health is where the promise of international solidarity is tested most directly, and Botswana speaks from hard-earned experience.
Three decades ago, our country faced an HIV/AIDS epidemic of such severity that some questioned our long-term national resilience.
23. Through determined national leadership, bold public investment and sustained global partnership, Botswana built one of the world’s most comprehensive HIV/AIDS treatment programmes.

We achieved the UNAIDS 95-95-95 targets ahead of schedule, and we became the first African country to achieve World Health Organisation Silver Tier status for elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HIV.
24. Our experience demonstrates that when national ownership and international solidarity converge, seemingly impossible challenges can be overcome.
This kind of practical solidarity restores confidence in multilateralism.
We stand ready to share the lessons of this experience through South-South and triangular cooperation.

25. Botswana attaches particular importance to preserving UNAIDS, an indispensable partner in our national response through evidence-based policymaking, technical assistance, resource mobilisation and global advocacy.

That partnership helped to mitigate an epidemic by means of one of the world’s most successful national responses, and placed Botswana firmly on the path towards ending HIV/AIDS as a public health threat by 2030.
26. Mr. President, Botswana supports reforms that strengthen the effectiveness, coherence and responsiveness of the United Nations system.

27. We also believe that efficiency gains should be redeployed to strengthen the capacity of Organisation to prevent conflict, address emerging security threats and deliver meaningful results in programme countries, in line with the UN80 Vision.

28. It is in this spirit that Botswana accords the highest priority to its partnerships with the United Nations Office of Counter-Terrorism (UNOCT), UN-Habitat, the International Trade Centre (ITC), the International Organisation for Migration (IOM), among others.

29. We particularly recognise UNOCT’s leadership role in strengthening the United Nations’ collective efforts to prevent and counter terrorism and violent extremism, and in translating international commitments into practical support for Member States.

30. Botswana remains committed to further deepening its cooperation with UNOCT and the wider United Nations system through capacity-building, technical assistance, knowledge-sharing and the exchange of good practices.
Such partnerships demonstrate that a responsive United Nations can build trust, strengthen national capacity, and foster peace and security.
31. Mr. President, no reform agenda, including UN80, is complete without addressing the longstanding inequities within the Security Council.

In this regard, Botswana reaffirms its support for comprehensive Security Council reform, and aligns itself with the Common African Position as articulated in the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration.
32. We believe that a Security Council that continues to exclude Africa and Latin America from permanent membership cannot credibly claim to reflect contemporary geopolitical realities.
33. We also call on the United Nations to continue to explore the creation of an inclusive international framework on emerging technologies, including Artificial Intelligence.
We recognise technology as a bridge that narrows global inequality.
This extends to critical minerals, rare earths and energy resources that power the technological revolution, many of which come from developing countries.

34. Therefore, developing countries must have a meaningful voice in setting the standards and safeguards that will govern these technologies, ensuring that they expand opportunities, support decent work, and strengthen public services, while protecting human dignity, rights and security.
35. Mr. President, I wish to reaffirm Botswana’s commitment to multilateralism.
We believe that shared challenges require shared solutions.

We also believe that implementing the Pact for the Future, together with the UN80 Initiative, offers an opportunity to translate our shared commitments into practical improvements in the functioning of the United Nations.
36. In conclusion, Mr. President, I reemphasise that restoring trust, managing transformation, and delivering for all, are interconnected.
• We restore trust when we uphold our commitments, respect the UN Charter, and apply international law consistently;

• We manage transformation when change creates opportunity rather than deepen inequality, when developing countries have a meaningful voice in shaping the systems that affect their future, and when technological and economic progress serve humanity as a whole; and
• We deliver for all when our decisions translate into tangible improvements peace, security, development, health and human dignity.
37. The difference our decisions make in the lives and livelihoods of people is the standard against which the credibility of the UN must be measured.
38. Botswana is ready to work with all Member States.
We may be small in size, but we are steady in principle.
39. Let us ensure that history remembers this 81st Session for the trust we rebuilt, the promises kept, and the future created.
I take the floor on behalf of the Central African Republic, with the full sense of responsibility bestowed by this podium and the pride of a people that has never given up hope.
Mr. President, this session is taking place at the time of a twofold need: to restore trust and to manage transformation, to understand the urgent need for action.
Let us gaze upon the world as it is, first.
It has been a long time since peace has seemed so fragile.
On all continents, conflicts are multiplying, becoming entrenched, and fueling one another.
Each has its reasons, its history, its instigators, but they all have one thing in common: they are costing civilian lives, destroying schools and hospitals, and displacing entire families.
Disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz are causing energy and fertilizer prices to skyrocket.
Terrorism, trafficking, and armed groups are flourishing in zones beyond state control.
However far they may be from the front line, no state is safe from the repercussions of these conflicts.
At the same time, divisions within the Security Council— the body charged with protecting international peace and security— are paralyzing action where it is the most urgently needed.
International law is supposed to protect the weak from the ambitions of the powerful, and yet it is increasingly being dismissed as optional.
This is the paradox of our time.
We have never had so many reasons to act together, and we have never found it so difficult to do so.
This paradox comes with a price, and this price is primarily being paid by the most vulnerable.

According to the UN itself, more than 147 million people in 19 countries and territories experienced acute food insecurity caused by conflict in 2025, and yet at a time when need is soaring, resources are shrinking.
Humanitarian funding has fallen to its lowest levels since 2016.
Peacekeeping operations, including in my own country, have been forced to cut back their patrols, shut down bases, and suspend local dialogue initiatives.
Each budget cut adopted in New York or in some faraway capital is an opportunity for armed groups on the ground.
The trap is an insidious one.
A fragile country needs security to develop, and it needs development for stability.
When health care, education, roads, energy, and youth employment are placed on the back burner, it is not only the SDGs that move out of reach; it is peace itself that is jeopardized.
I would like to emphasize that abandoning fragile countries will not lead to savings.
It is simply putting off a bill that will have to be paid with interest.
The CAR understands this trap, and it also knows how to escape it.
It has undergone trials that remain fresh in our memory and has learned a lesson: peace cannot be decreed; it must be built day after day through dialogue, justice, and shared development.
No peace imposed by force can be lasting.
Only a negotiated peace that is just and inclusive can truly restore trust between nations.
That is why we made the difficult and often criticized choice of an inclusive political dialogue, negotiated disarmament, and national reconciliation, instead of a military response alone.
This olive branch policy has led to tangible results that I would like to share with this Assembly.

Out of the 14 armed groups that signed the Political Agreement for Peace and Reconciliation, 11 have already voluntarily disbanded as part of the disarmament, demobilization, reintegration, and repatriation program.
The last two groups involved in this process are continuing the process of disbandment in accordance with the Jamena Accord.
I say this with the conviction of lived experience: holding out one's hand to yesterday's opponent is not a sign of weakness.
It is often the safest path toward a lasting peace.

And that is why I renew the proposal that the CAR has been making for several sessions now, to establish a global conflict prevention and mediation mechanism with predictable financing, and that is managed with complete transparency.
Mr. President, we cannot restore trust without tackling climate change with the same resolve.
There cannot be lasting security without climate security.
There cannot be climate security without climate justice.

My country will bring three demands to the 31st Conference of the Parties in Antalya, Turkey: that the Loss and Damage Fund become fully operational and accessible; that adaptation financing should no longer be the forgotten stepchild of climate finance; and that the countries of the Congo Basin, the second-largest lung of the planet, should finally be justly compensated for the services they provide to humanity by protecting their ecosystems.
This demand for justice also applies to global health.
We call for equitable access to vaccines and health care technologies, and for strengthening health systems in the most vulnerable countries.
Restoring trust, Mr. President, is not limited to interstate relations.
First and foremost, it is built within our own borders between the state and its citizens.

This is the goal of our National Development Plan 2024-2028, which has five pillars: security and governance; human capital; resilient infrastructure; economic production; and environmental sustainability.
These pillars are not only a planning framework, but are also a renewed social contract with our population.
At the heart of this ambition lies our youth.
Our youth is our greatest asset, our greatest responsibility.
A well-trained and employed youth, involved in decision-making, is the best guarantee against recruitment by armed groups.
The same is true for women, whose role in peacebuilding is not a bonus but a prerequisite.

The population of Biro has more than doubled, exerting intolerable pressure on water resources and on already strained services.

The town of Amdafuk last June experienced an escalation of violence that put more than 11,000 of our compatriots on the street, while the arrival of Sudanese livestock farmers fleeing with their flocks has inflamed new tensions with our rural populations over access to water and land.
Tensions that armed groups eagerly exploit.
My country, with its legendary hospitality, is not complaining.
We are asking for regional and international solidarity to be commensurate with the challenges we are facing.
The CAR, like all sovereign nations, aspires to take full charge of its own security.

This transformation first requires a bold Security Council reform.
We cannot claim to represent the world of 2026 with the proportions of 1945.
A continent of more than 1.3 billion inhabitants, whose crises make up a large portion of the Council's work, ought to have at least one permanent seat in it.
The Pact for the Future has opened a window, but two years after its adoption, negotiations on Security Council reform are still ongoing.
The decision that is urgently needed has yet to be made.
The African position, represented for years now by the Eslaouini Consensus and the CERT Declaration, is not a favor we are asking.
It is a demand for justice and effectiveness.
Transformation, next, requires peacekeeping operations with realistic mandates and predictable financing.
We support strengthening the UN-African Union partnership, including through predictable financing for African-led operations.

These reforms are not favors; they are investments in the world's stability.

Mr. President, digital transformation and the rise of artificial intelligence are rightly considered to be one of the great promises of our time.
The Global Digital Compact must become a reality: affordable connectivity, skills transfer, data protection, and a governance of AI in which developing countries decide instead of simply being users.
The transformation also requires facing history with lucidity.
The wounds left behind by colonization are still being felt on our continent.
Reparations are not simply reopening a feud of the past.
They are a demand for justice for the future, recognition of the wrongs committed, restitution of cultural goods and archives, equitable cooperation, debt relief.
The African Union has prioritized this, and the CAR fully supports these efforts.
Transformation calls for real respect for the sovereignty of states.
Sanctions and restrictions must be tools for peace and must be adjusted in accordance with the progress made.
They must not be retaliatory measures serving geopolitical interests.
Mr. President, we are at a crossroads.
It is now time for decision.
That is why the CAR calls upon the UN to act.
Saving the world is not a task for one nation or one continent.
It is our collective will to action.
Let this 81st Session be one in which we stop taking stock and begin taking action.

You're welcome to attend the forum and join in the discussion about the way forward in global governance.

No matter how the international dynamics evolve, China remains unchanged in its pursuit of peace and development and its dedication to safeguarding, fairness and justice, and in its commitment to multilateralism.
China will join hands with all other countries to build a community with a shared future for humanity and make the world a better place for all of us. Thank you.
Mr. President, This session is being held in a very worrying international context.
Conflicts and flashpoints are multiplying, geopolitical divisions are deepening, while the rise of terrorism and violent extremism threatens an ever greater number of territories.
At the same time, climate upheavals are hitting our countries hard, not to mention the humanitarian crises and the deep inequalities that are weakening our societies.
Added to this are the real risks of destruction of humanity linked to the uncontrolled development of artificial intelligence.
The world is therefore at a difficult turning point.
It is thus witnessing, almost helplessly, the gradual fragmentation of its peace architecture and an alarming reconfiguration of the international arena.
Before our eyes, multilateralism is being severely tested, weakened by an erosion of trust among nations and in the institutions that safeguard the world order.
In these times of multilateral fracture, we must imperatively find appropriate solutions to put an end to these dangerous escalations, give priority to dialogue and revive trust.

With regard to international institutions, that trust is measured by their ability to translate the universality of their principles into concrete action and to treat every State, large or small, with the same requirement of fairness.
The trust of peoples, for its part, is nourished by tangible results, by the certainty that the decisions taken in their name effectively serve their security and dignity and protect their future.
The theme chosen this year thus accurately reflects these expectations of our time.

It invites us, precisely, to the imperative of restoring trust in our collective ability to respond effectively to global challenges, to support the current changes and reforms in the architecture of the United Nations, so that our Organization may once again be capable of providing concrete solutions to the concerns of all peoples.
For Côte d’Ivoire, this means that multilateralism must be revitalized and, consequently, that diplomacy must be restored to its proper place and credibility for the effectiveness of its action.
In view of these challenges, an immense task awaits the next Secretary-General of the United Nations, whose selection process is now fully under way.

Côte d’Ivoire hopes to see this process lead to the designation of a person of very high stature, whose moral values, independence of mind, diplomatic experience and sense of dialogue will enable the United Nations to continue, with ambition and effectiveness, its mission in the service of peace, development and solidarity among nations.
International developments remind us every day of the human, political and economic cost of protracted conflicts.

Côte d’Ivoire remains deeply concerned by the resumption of hostilities in the Near and Middle East, the consequences of which weigh on peace and on food, energy and economic security throughout the world.
The dramatic situation prevailing in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and in the Sudan is equally worrying, with grave and unending humanitarian consequences.
All these persistent confrontations are aggravating the suffering of populations and producing harmful effects that extend far beyond the borders of the States concerned.
Accordingly, we call for dialogue to prevail over arms.
To the Haitian people, we also extend our solidarity.

Côte d’Ivoire will continue to contribute to the ongoing initiatives aimed at supporting the Haitian authorities and international partners in restoring security in that brotherly country, in order to restore democratic legitimacy to its institutions.

This is an opportunity for my country to reaffirm its commitment to the peaceful settlement of disputes, in accordance with the Charter of the United Nations, and to lend its full support to the many mediation efforts undertaken by the United Nations, the African Union and the competent regional organizations.
Ladies and Gentlemen, Africa is bearing the full brunt of the retreat of multilateralism and the difficulties the United Nations has experienced in recent years.

Owing to the lack of support from certain partners and from the United Nations, several African countries are struggling to resolve conflicts on a lasting basis and to bear the cost of the various counter-terrorism and peacekeeping operations.
Meanwhile, violent extremism, transnational organized crime and illicit trafficking of all kinds continue to weaken several regions of the Continent, particularly the Sahel.

Our experience and the reality on the ground show that no State can, on its own, durably overcome such threats, which require greater regional cooperation and international solidarity for appropriate responses.

These threats also call for investment in conflict prevention and for addressing upstream the fragilities on which crises feed, particularly poverty, inequalities, youth unemployment and other forms of marginalization of all kinds.
In this regard, we commend the efforts of the United Nations, the African Union, ECOWAS and all partners engaged in the security and stabilization of our region.
The expected effectiveness of these Institutions therefore calls for them to be more representative, more inclusive and more in tune with the demands of our time.

Indeed, it is becoming increasingly difficult to explain to younger generations that the Organizations created in the aftermath of the Second World War can no longer faithfully reflect the political, demographic and economic realities of the twenty-first century.

My country once again reaffirms its support for an ambitious reform of the Security Council, in order to ensure Africa permanent representation within this important organ whose decisions directly affect our peace and security.
It is for this reason that Côte d’Ivoire welcomes the progress made through the Pact for the Future and calls for its prompt implementation.
The real challenge is no longer to adopt new commitments, but to translate those already undertaken into tangible results for the well-being of our populations.
Peace cannot be lasting without truly inclusive and equitable development.
As the 2030 deadline approaches, the progress made in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals remains insufficient, while financing needs remain considerable in many developing countries.

The Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development rightly recalled that the necessary resources exist, but the challenge now lies in our collective ability to mobilize and direct them with greater equity, solidarity and effectiveness in the service of sustainable development.

Côte d’Ivoire therefore calls for an ambitious reform of the international financial architecture and for a renewed global partnership, in order to ensure developing countries more equitable access to the resources necessary to finance infrastructure, health, education, energy, industrial transformation and the creation of decent jobs for young people.
Climate challenges require the same mobilization.
Africa contributes the least to global greenhouse gas emissions, yet remains among the regions most severely affected by their consequences.
Droughts, floods, land degradation and disruption of food systems directly threaten the livelihoods and means of subsistence of millions of people.
In this context, respect for international commitments in the areas of climate financing, adaptation and technology transfer constitutes an imperative of justice and solidarity.
The transformation of our world is also technological.
Artificial intelligence and the digital revolution are opening up considerable prospects in many areas of our contemporary world.
However, these technological advances can also deepen existing divides if their development and access remain unevenly distributed.

In this regard, Côte d’Ivoire supports the efforts of the United Nations aimed at promoting global governance of artificial intelligence that fosters innovation, while protecting human dignity, international security and sustainable development, in a spirit of inclusion, ethics and equitable sharing of the benefits of technological progress.

Mr. President, The trust that we seek at the international level must also be built within each of our States, through the strength of our institutions and our ability to create the conditions for sustainable and shared development.
For its part, my country is continuing, under the leadership of President Alassane OUATTARA, its march towards a stronger and more diversified economy, while ensuring peace and stability.

This ambition is now being advanced through Côte d’Ivoire’s 2026-2030 National Development Plan, which is part of a long-term vision, in line with the United Nations 2030 Agenda and the African Union’s Agenda 2063.
Our ambition remains to build a prosperous and united nation, where economic growth translates into more opportunities, social progress and well-being for all our populations.
At a time when the United Nations has entered its ninth decade of existence, we have a collective duty to demonstrate that multilateralism remains the best response to the challenges of our time.
We must choose dialogue rather than confrontation, cooperation rather than withdrawal, solidarity rather than indifference.

We must restore trust among nations, ensure that law prevails over force, place the human being at the heart of our decisions and make our diversity a source of richness rather than a cause of division.
Then the United Nations will continue to embody the hope of peoples and to fulfil the promises that gave rise to its creation.

Côte d’Ivoire, faithful to its values and deeply committed to peace, dialogue and multilateralism, will continue, with humility but with determination, to contribute to this collective endeavour, because we believe that the destiny of humanity remains profoundly shared.
Finally, it is for us to ensure that the United Nations remains, for present and future generations, a true crucible of human dignity and the guarantor of a better world.
YOU HAVE SEEN FIT TO PLACE THIS SESSION UNDER THE REFERENCE THEME AIMED AT RESTORING TRUST, MANAGING TRANSFORMATION FOR A UNITED NATIONS ORGANIZATION THAT DELIVERS RESULTS FOR ALL.
CAMEROON APPRECIATES THE RELEVANCE OF THIS THEME AND ITS ACUTENESS IN THE CURRENT CONTEXT.

WE ARE INDEED FACING, TOGETHER, THREE INSEPARABLE IMPERATIVES: FIRST, RESTORING TRUST AMONG STATES; SECOND, RECONCILING PEOPLES AND NATIONS WITH MULTILATERAL INSTITUTIONS; AND THIRD, ENSURING THAT RECENT TECHNOLOGICAL ADVANCES SERVE ALL HUMANITY.

WE ARE LIVING INDEED IN AN AGE IN WHICH THE FEATS OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY HAVE MADE POSSIBLE AN IMPRESSIVE FLOWERING OF USEFUL KNOWLEDGE, SUCH AS THE CURRENT EMERGENCE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TO ADDRESS THE MULTIPLE CHALLENGES FACING HUMANITY.
