OVER THE RECENT DECADES, WE HAVE ADOPTED AGREEMENTS IN DIFFERENT FIELDS AND HAVE CONTINUED TO CREATE THE CONDITIONS FOR A MORE JUST WORLD IN WHICH ALL MAY LIVE IN PEACE AND SECURITY.
HOWEVER, DESPITE OUR EFFORTS, WARS AND CONFLICTS OF ALL KINDS PERSIST.
HUMANITARIAN DISASTERS, SELFISHNESS AND INTOLERANCE ARE INCREASINGLY PRESENT.
WE ARE WITNESSING, POWERLESSLY, THE DECLINE OF INTERNATIONAL SOLIDARITY AND MULTILATERALISM IN THE FACE OF THE RISE OF BLOCS CLASHING OVER ISSUES THAT CONSOLIDATE THEIR SPECIFIC INTERESTS.
IT IS TIME TO RETURN TO THE VERY SPIRIT AND FOUNDATIONS OF THE Charter of the United Nations.
AT THE SAME TIME, CLIMATE DISRUPTION IS WORSENING AND CONSTITUTES A PLANETARY CONCERN.
FLOODS, DROUGHT AND FOREST FIRES ARE RECURRENT AND SPARE NO REGION OF THE WORLD.
THESE PHENOMENA DEPRIVE MANY POPULATIONS OF THE BENEFITS THEY COULD LEGITIMATELY HAVE DRAWN FROM THE PRODIGIOUS TECHNOLOGICAL PROGRESS ACHIEVED.
FACED WITH SUCH A SITUATION, IT IS THE DUTY OF US ALL TO WORK TOGETHER TO MEET THESE CHALLENGES AND RESPOND EFFECTIVELY TO THE EXPECTATIONS OF OUR PEOPLES.
THE UNITED NATIONS OFFERS US, IN THIS REGARD, AN IDEAL FRAMEWORK FOR DISCUSSION AND COMPROMISE TO FIND SOLUTIONS TO THESE CHALLENGES THAT CONFRONT US ALL.
CAMEROON IS FIRMLY COMMITTED TO THIS PATH AND SUPPORTS THE UN80 INITIATIVE, AS WELL AS ANY OTHER APPROACH THAT CONTRIBUTES TO STRENGTHENING INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION AND SOLIDARITY.

WITH ONLY A FEW YEARS LEFT BEFORE THE DEADLINE OF THE 2030 AGENDA, WE CAN SEE, DESPITE REMARKABLE EFFORTS, THAT PROGRESS STILL NEEDS TO BE MADE TO ACHIEVE THE Sustainable Development Goals WE HAVE SET FOR OURSELVES.
THE RESOURCES TO ACHIEVE THIS ARE, HOWEVER, AVAILABLE ON A GLOBAL SCALE.
IT THEREFORE FALLS TO US TO IMPROVE THE CONDITIONS FOR THEIR ACCESS AND USE.
IN THIS REGARD, DEVELOPMENT FINANCING SHOULD NOT BE REGARDED AS AN ACT OF CHARITY.
IT CONSTITUTES AN INVESTMENT IN STABILITY, SHARED PROSPERITY AND COLLECTIVE SECURITY.
THAT IS WHY CAMEROON CALLS FOR THE PROMPT AND FULL IMPLEMENTATION OF THE COMMITMENTS MADE IN SEVILLE IN JULY 2025 ON FINANCING FOR DEVELOPMENT.
THIS IMPLIES, IN PARTICULAR, THE NECESSARY UNDERTAKING OF A REFORM OF THE INTERNATIONAL AND MULTILATERAL FINANCIAL ARCHITECTURE TO GIVE A FAIRER PLACE TO THE COUNTRIES OF THE SOUTH.
WE MUST ALSO GIVE NEW IMPETUS TO INTERNATIONAL TRADE, INDUSTRIALIZATION, THE LOCAL PROCESSING OF RAW MATERIALS AND THE STRENGTHENING OF REGIONAL INTEGRATION.
IT WAS INDEED THIS DYNAMIC THAT GUIDED THE WORK OF THE FOURTEENTH MINISTERIAL CONFERENCE OF THE WORLD TRADE ORGANIZATION, WHICH CAMEROON HAD THE PRIVILEGE OF HOSTING FROM 26 TO 29 MARCH 2026.

CAMEROON ALSO INTENDS TO CONTRIBUTE TO THE FULL EXPANSION OF THE African Continental Free Trade Area, ACRONYM AfCFTA, OF WHICH IT IS AMONG THE FIRST COUNTRIES ON THE CONTINENT TO HAVE RATIFIED THE STATUTES, IN ORDER TO STRENGTHEN INTRA-AFRICAN DEVELOPMENT AND TRADE COOPERATION.
MOREOVER, MY COUNTRY REITERATES ITS SOLIDARITY IN SUPPORT OF THE COMMON POSITION OF THE AFRICAN UNION FOR BETTER REPRESENTATION OF AFRICA WITHIN THE UNITED NATIONS SECURITY COUNCIL.
ALSO, MY COUNTRY INTENDS TO MAINTAIN ITS PARTICIPATION IN UNITED NATIONS PEACEKEEPING OPERATIONS, IN THE TRAINING AND CAPACITY-BUILDING OF AFRICAN PERSONNEL CALLED UPON TO SERVE IN THEM.
IN THIS REGARD, I WOULD LIKE TO WELCOME THE EXEMPLARY COOPERATION THAT CAMEROON MAINTAINS WITH THE UNITED NATIONS IN THIS AREA.

IN SO DOING, IT REAFFIRMS THE DETERMINATION WITH WHICH IT WILL UNSWERVINGLY PURSUE, WITH THE MEMBER STATES OF the Lake Chad Basin Commission, THE UNRELENTING FIGHT AGAINST TERRORISM AND THE STABILIZATION EFFORTS IN THE AREAS AFFECTED AROUND LAKE CHAD.
AT THE DOMESTIC LEVEL, THE GOVERNMENT OF MY COUNTRY IS WORKING TOWARDS A RETURN TO A NORMAL SITUATION IN THE NORTH-WEST AND SOUTH-WEST REGIONS.
THE GOVERNMENT’S EFFORTS TO COMBAT INSECURITY AND TO ACHIEVE THE SOCIAL REINTEGRATION OF PERSONS WILLING TO RENOUNCE VIOLENCE HAVE ALREADY PRODUCED TANGIBLE AND OBSERVABLE RESULTS ON THE GROUND.
IT SHOULD BE EMPHASIZED THAT THE CAMEROONIAN AUTHORITIES HAVE CEASELESSLY MULTIPLIED AND CONSOLIDATED THESE RESULTS.
I CAN ASSURE YOU OF CAMEROON’S CONSTANT COMMITMENT TO SOLIDARITY FOR DISPLACED POPULATIONS, REFUGEES AND HOST COMMUNITIES, DESPITE THE MULTIPLE AND SIGNIFICANT CONSTRAINTS ARISING THEREFROM.

IN AN INCREASINGLY UNSTABLE WORLD, WE MUST DO EVERYTHING POSSIBLE TO CREATE CONDITIONS CONDUCIVE TO PEACE, SECURITY AND THE STABILITY OF THE INTERNATIONAL POLITICAL ENVIRONMENT WITH A VIEW TO ENSURING THE WELL-BEING OF ALL.
WE HAVE THE OPPORTUNITY TO DO SO.

LET US THEREFORE POOL AND COMBINE OUR RESOURCES TO MEET THIS COMMON CHALLENGE TOGETHER, IN ORDER TO RESPOND TO THE UNCEASING CALLS OF OUR PEOPLES, WHO ASPIRE ONLY TO LIVE IN A WORLD OF PEACE, SECURITY AND PROSPERITY FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE GENERATIONS.
Over a decade marked by wars, the pandemic, the climate emergency and heightened geopolitical tensions, he has consistently defended peace, human dignity and international cooperation.

The theme of this session — “Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations Organization that serves all” — aptly expresses the challenge that we must collectively meet in order to revive the hope that our Organization inspired at the time of its creation.

For the Democratic Republic of the Congo, this session is once again an opportunity to reaffirm its faith in multilateralism founded on the constant pursuit of peace and justice that opens the way, not to the prosperity of a few, but rather to the creation of a truly shared horizon among peoples and for future generations.
This faith nevertheless obliges us to look lucidly at the transformations of the world and to question our Organization’s ability to evolve with it.

For our peoples, for their part, have never ceased to believe in the necessity of international cooperation; a cooperation that in the most difficult hours mobilizes promptly but that can also, in certain respects, seem to delay elsewhere; when territorial integrity is defended vigorously in one crisis and seems negotiable in another; when the suffering of civilians calls for action in one place but appears to accommodate waiting in another.
There can in reality be no lasting trust when the force of our proclaimed principles varies according to peoples, crises or circumstances.
In a constantly changing world, our peoples’ trust in multilateralism begins where the application of a law that varies according to geography, economic power or the play of alliances ends.

Our transformation must in fact rest on the requirement to restore the Charter in its full force, in particular through respect for: the principle of the sovereign equality of States, the peaceful settlement of disputes, the prohibition of the use of force, respect for territorial integrity and the dignity of the human person.
Such must be the ambition of the United Nations.
There can be no restored trust in our Organization, and it can even less be transformed, so long as it continues to reflect a world that has ceased to exist.
The world of 1945 is no more.
The digital revolution, the energy transition and climate disruption are today reshaping its balances.
Yet the institutions charged with supporting these transformations too often remain the reflection of an order that no longer exists.
Artificial intelligence today provides one of the most striking illustrations of this.
It offers immense possibilities, but also the risk of new divides.
Its governance cannot be the preserve of a few powers or companies: developing countries must be able to participate in defining its rules and to gain access to the capacities that determine its use.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo supports the United Nations global dialogue on the governance of artificial intelligence and the creation of a global capacity-building fund.
The digital divide must not become an intelligence divide.
This requirement for inclusion must above all find expression in global governance.

Africa has asserted itself over time as an essential demographic, diplomatic and geopolitical force, yet to this day it remains insufficiently represented where decisions are taken that commit the future of the world.
Indeed, how can one fail to mention the historical anomaly constituted by the absence of Africa among the permanent members of the Security Council?
The admission of the African Union to the G20 certainly marked an important step forward.
However, it cannot contain this requirement for representation.

As a member of the Security Council for the period 2026-2027, we reaffirm our adherence to the common African position, enshrined in the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration: two permanent seats for Africa, with all the prerogatives attached thereto as long as the right of veto continues to exist, as well as two additional non-permanent seats; this in order to make the Council more representative, more legitimate and, ultimately, more effective.
This requirement for representation goes hand in hand with that of responsibility.

And it is in this spirit that the Democratic Republic of the Congo intends fully to exercise its own, notably in the choice of the next Secretary-General, whose mandate will have to continue the effort to transform our Organization and adapt it to the priorities of a world undergoing profound change.

We carry this same ambition within La Francophonie through the candidacy of Ms. Juliana Amato LUMUMBA for the post of Secretary-General of the OIF, with the vision of a renewed Francophonie, closer to the peoples and capable of strengthening trust among its members and in the face of the challenges before us.

For the Democratic Republic of the Congo, it is precisely in the gap between the trust that we call for to be restored and the transformations that we aspire to support that the full scope of our international commitments is measured.
Our country lies at the heart of several of these transformations and, at times, at the very crossroads of their contradictions.
Few situations illustrate as painfully the gap between international commitments and lived reality as that in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
For more than three decades, millions of Congolese women and men have suffered attacks, forced displacement and bereavement.
Territories are occupied, families scattered, women and girls are victims of sexual violence, while children are recruited or deprived of schooling.
At the same time, the plundering of our resources continues to feed international trade channels.
My country remains confronted with a war of aggression waged by Rwanda under cover of AFC/M23, in violation of its sovereignty and territorial integrity, as documented by the United Nations.
The atrocities perpetrated by other armed groups, notably the ADF and CODECO, further aggravate this humanitarian crisis.
Faced with this ordeal, the Democratic Republic of the Congo has chosen the path of diplomacy, without ever renouncing its rights.

The peace agreement signed in Washington on 27 June 2025, the commitments undertaken within the framework of the Doha process and the harmonized roadmap of the African Union have opened prospects that we support consistently.
I welcome the engagement of the United States of America, the State of Qatar, the African Union, the African facilitators, regional partners and all those who are sincerely working to restore peace.
However, we owe it to the truth to acknowledge that, for millions of Congolese, this peace still remains a promise.
Security Council resolution 2773 (2025) nevertheless charted an unambiguous path.

It demands the effective cessation of hostilities, the withdrawal of Rwandan forces from Congolese territory, the end of all support to armed groups, the disengagement of AFC/M23, the dismantling of parallel administrations, the restoration of State authority, unimpeded humanitarian access, as well as the safe and dignified return of displaced persons and refugees.
We do not expect new texts to replace those that have already been adopted.

On the question of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda, long invoked by Kigali to justify its military presence on our territory, the Democratic Republic of the Congo is assuming its responsibilities.

The protocol signed by the political and military leadership of the FDLR on 30 May 2026 provides for their disarmament, demobilization and the cantonment of its combatants with a view to their repatriation or relocation, without prejudice to judicial proceedings for serious crimes, and this until the dissolution of the movement.
The repatriation, on 8 September, with the support of MONUSCO, of 120 persons associated with the FDLR constitutes an initial concrete expression thereof.
The question of the FDLR can therefore no longer serve as a pretext for maintaining a foreign military presence on our territory.

The coordinated implementation of the Washington, Doha and African Union mechanisms must therefore rest on a precise timetable, independent verification, regular information-sharing and effective consequences in the event of violation.
In this context, MONUSCO retains an essential role in the protection of civilians, the monitoring of the ceasefire and support for the agreed mechanisms.

Any evolution of its presence will have to be determined by the security conditions on the ground, the strengthening of national capacities and the guarantee that no vacuum will be left to the detriment of the populations.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo will continue, for its part, fully to assume its responsibilities, notably through the continuation of reforms of its defence and security institutions, the strengthening of State authority and the reconstruction of territories affected by conflict.

And because the peace sought in the subregion must also go hand in hand with cohesion within our Nation, the President of the Democratic Republic of the Congo launched, on 28 August, a National Dialogue for peace, cohesion and the refoundation of the State.
This dialogue is open to the political and social forces committed to the Republic, the Constitution, the integrity of the territory and the rejection of violence.
It aims neither to circumvent the institutions nor to organize a power-sharing arrangement.
It must enable us to address the structural causes of our fragilities, consolidate national unity and build a State that is fairer, more present and more protective.
Our hand remains extended to all the children of the Congo who choose peace, republican debate and loyalty to the homeland.
We will speak among Congolese with frankness and responsibility.
But no internal dialogue can transform external aggression into a mere domestic dispute.
Likewise, no external aggression should exempt us from correcting our own weaknesses.
National cohesion and the defence of territorial integrity are not opposed: they reinforce each other.
For the peace we seek cannot be limited to the cessation of hostilities.

It must also enable our country to take full possession once again of its future, by transforming the wealth that has for too long fuelled conflicts into instruments of development and shared prosperity.

There is another paradox that my country’s experience shows the world: some of its resources that fuel conflicts on its territory are also those on which a growing share of the transformations of the world economy depends.
The governance of strategic resources must henceforth be an issue of peace, development and global security.

The energy transition, the electrification of transport, energy storage, as well as the expansion of digital infrastructure and artificial intelligence are accelerating demand for copper, cobalt, lithium, nickel and other critical minerals.
As the world’s leading producer of cobalt and a major copper power, the Democratic Republic of the Congo is at the heart of this transformation.
Congolese cobalt already contributes to the operation of batteries, electricity grids, digital equipment and technologies indispensable to the decarbonization of the world economy.
It would be both unjust and dangerous for value added, jobs, know-how and technologies to remain concentrated far from the communities that make this transformation possible.
A decarbonized economy will not be built with blood-stained minerals.
Nor will the transition be made just by reproducing, under a green colour, the dependencies of the past.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo therefore rejects the old model that confines producing countries to raw extraction, while processing, research, technology and the bulk of profits are concentrated elsewhere.
Our ambition is clear: we no longer want to be only the subsoil of the world economy; we intend to become a workshop, a laboratory and a sovereign partner in it.

We want to process more cobalt and copper on our territory, develop battery precursors and industrial components, train our engineers, support our researchers and integrate our enterprises into global value chains.
We want to build, with our African and international partners, competitive regional sectors that create jobs, skills and shared prosperity.
This ambition first requires us to assume our own responsibilities fully.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo is continuing the modernization of mining governance through the transparency of contracts, extractive revenues and beneficial owners, the strengthening of the mining cadastre, the deployment of traceability mechanisms and the fight against fraud.
It is also accelerating the formalization of artisanal mining, the supervision of traders, the organization of cooperatives and the securing of mining areas.
In this regard, the fight against child labour in mines constitutes a moral and national obligation.

With the International Labour Organization, UNICEF and our other partners, we are strengthening mechanisms for identification, monitoring and remediation, the training of inspectors, the schooling of children and the economic solutions offered to their families.
Our objective admits of no ambiguity: zero children in the mines.
This responsibility falls to the Congolese State.
But it also involves companies, traders, refiners, manufacturers, financial institutions and destination markets.
The first test of a responsible chain is not the electric vehicle at the end; it is the child who no longer goes down into the mine at the beginning.

That is why the Democratic Republic of the Congo proposes the development, under the auspices of the United Nations, in partnership with the African Union and in consultation with producing, processing and consuming countries, of a Global Framework for fair, traceable and resilient critical mineral value chains.

Based on the sovereignty of producing States, it must guarantee the traceability of minerals, the responsibility of economic actors, the protection of workers and communities, as well as a fairer sharing of value through local processing and technology transfer.
The Lobito Corridor must become one of the instruments of this ambition.
We welcome the commitment of Angola, Zambia, the United States of America, the European Union, the African Development Bank, financial institutions and the private sector to its realization.

The rehabilitation of rail links, the modernization of infrastructure, the facilitation of trade and energy investments can open up our territories, reduce logistical costs and stimulate regional trade.
But our vision goes far beyond the accelerated export of raw materials.
A corridor that merely shortened the path from the mine to the port would only reproduce the past.

The Lobito Corridor must become a true backbone of regional industrialization with the support of investors with whom we hope to build transparent, sustainable and mutually beneficial partnerships for the well-being of our future generations.

As you will have understood, the transformation that we seek at the scale of our organization, we chose first to initiate at home, in the conviction that by investing in our population, the foremost wealth of our Nation, we will succeed in building the foundations of renewed trust and lasting prosperity.
Introduced in 2019, free primary education has enabled more than 5 million additional children to gain access to school.
During the 2023-2024 school year, more than 21 million children were attending primary school, compared with fourteen million seven hundred thousand four years earlier.
This quantitative progress must now be translated into quality.
We are continuing the construction and rehabilitation of schools, and have recently launched the rollout of school canteens.
Because access is not enough: every child must be able to learn in a safe, inclusive, equipped school open to the tools of its time.
This requirement applies in particular to girls, children with disabilities, displaced children and those whose schooling is threatened by conflict.
The same ambition guides our health policy.

We are continuing the gradual extension of universal health coverage, notably through free maternity care, the improvement of maternal and neonatal care, vaccination, access to essential medicines, the strengthening of health personnel and the expansion of social protection.
Each health crisis confirms the same truth: health sovereignty is built before the emergency.
It rests on accessible health systems, robust epidemiological surveillance, effective laboratories, sufficiently funded research and, above all, the trust of populations.
In this regard, the Ebola virus disease outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo strain remains a major ordeal.
For the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the fight against this epidemic constitutes an absolute priority.

Having contained sixteen previous outbreaks, the Democratic Republic of the Congo is mobilizing recognized scientific and operational expertise; and thanks to national mobilization and the support of our partners, the response undertaken has recently been producing tangible results.
Moreover, clinical trials are simultaneously evaluating vaccines and treatments adapted to this strain.

I would like to pay tribute to Congolese and foreign health personnel, to researchers, to communities and to our partners, in particular the World Health Organization and the African Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), for the valuable support provided to the Democratic Republic of the Congo in eradicating this disease and in strengthening its resilience.
This requirement of resilience does not stop at the borders of health alone.
It is imperative in the face of climate disruption, the effects of which are already placing our societies under growing pressure.
Floods, droughts and erosion, not to mention population displacement, threaten our stability.
In the face of these upheavals, not all countries bear the same responsibility or the same burden.
Those that contribute the least to global warming often suffer its heaviest consequences.
This paradox is all the more striking because some of these countries are also among the principal guardians of the natural assets on which our common future depends.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo is one of them.
It contains an essential part of the Congo Basin, one of the planet’s great climate regulators.
Its forests, its peatlands, its fresh waters and its biodiversity render considerable ecosystem services to humanity.
This global heritage will continue to be preserved, while maintaining that the communities that ensure its protection should be able to derive benefit from it.
Climate financing in this regard represents a fair solution.
It should, however, be accessible, predictable and proportionate to the services rendered.
Indeed, climate justice cannot consist in indebting further those who already bear the cost of damage they did the least to cause.

In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, this ambition is taking shape in particular through the Kivu-Kinshasa Green Corridor, which combines preservation of ecosystems, economic development and the improvement of the living conditions of the population.
With a production of 60 megawatts of electricity, this initiative also carries, by 2027, the ambition of creating 25,000 jobs and protecting 5,000 square kilometres of natural forest.
The climate crisis is also a water crisis.

Following on from the African Water Forum held last July in N’Djamena, the Democratic Republic of the Congo has proposed the creation of an African Coalition for Water Security, intended to strengthen regional cooperation and to mobilize the financing necessary to make water a lever for development and the prevention of tensions.
Four years before the 2030 deadline, the Congolese roadmap for accelerating the Sustainable Development Goals assesses our needs at more than 70 billion dollars.
We are strengthening our domestic revenues and improving the quality of public expenditure.
But a country simultaneously confronted with war, epidemics, poverty and climate shocks cannot alone bridge such a gap.
At the same time, official development assistance fell by more than 23 per cent in real terms in 2025, the largest annual contraction ever recorded.
This contraction weakens development efforts and compromises the prevention of crises whose consequences far exceed national borders.
Assistance remains indispensable, but it will not be enough.

The Seville Commitment must now be translated into better access to concessional financing, greater mobilization of the multilateral development banks and debt relief mechanisms that preserve the investment capacities of our States.
Lastly, no financial architecture will be sustainable without tax justice.
International cooperation must combat illicit financial flows, tax evasion, transfer pricing manipulation and the laundering of proceeds derived from natural resources.
Stolen assets must be swiftly identified, frozen and returned.
Every penny recovered can finance a vaccine, a school textbook, a borehole or a road.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo knows that the trust which it calls for to be restored on the international stage must first and foremost be earned through the commitments it honours on its own soil.
That is the meaning of the efforts it is undertaking to consolidate peace, strengthen its institutions and make its natural and human wealth the foundations of shared prosperity.

Our experience teaches us, however, that no national transformation can fully bear fruit in an international order whose principles continue to be applied unequally and whose institutions are insufficiently adapted to the realities of our time.
That is why our ambition for the United Nations is inseparable from the one we hold for our own country.
We want a transformation that inspires trust because it keeps its promises, and a trust that makes lasting transformations possible.
At a time when humanity is wavering between fragmentation and cooperation, it is therefore incumbent upon us to make this ambition a collective responsibility.
Restoring trust means applying the law when it is costly, and not only when it is convenient.
Supporting transformations means sharing their benefits fairly.
Putting the United Nations at the service of all means guaranteeing that no people is too remote to be protected, too deprived to be heard, or too rich in resources to remain sovereign.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo intends to play its full part in this endeavour.
At the heart of Africa, it will pursue its own transformation while contributing to that of our Organization, in the conviction that justice done to the latter will strengthen the security of all.

For it is by restoring to institutions the strength of their principles, to peoples proof of our word, and to future generations the right to hope that we will restore the full meaning of the promise of the United Nations.
In this spirit, the Republic of the Congo is following with particular attention the selection process for the next Secretary-General of the United Nations.

We consider that Africa, a continent at the centre of the issues facing the United Nations and of global geostrategic challenges, must remain at the heart of the mandate of the future Secretary-General.

The next Secretary-General must carry a truly universal vision of the United Nations: a vision that leaves no continent at the periphery, and in which Africa’s place, responsibilities and legitimate interests are fully taken into account.
For the Republic of the Congo, restoring trust and managing the transformation of our international institutions represent a collective imperative.

The theme of this session — “Restoring trust, managing transformation” — resonates as a call for lucidity and courage in a world where trust is eroding, where tensions are intensifying, where power relations and double standards threaten to supplant the spirit and letter of the Charter of the United Nations.
Never has humanity had such need of renewed, inclusive and representative multilateralism, capable of reflecting the reality of a multipolar world in which Africa must occupy its full place.
This renewal requires a profound reform of international institutions, first and foremost the Security Council.
Africa, borne by the power of its history, the momentum of its demography and the solidity of its geopolitical weight, can no longer remain on the margins of the decisions that shape its destiny.
It must be an actor, fully and legitimately.
In accordance with the Ezulwini Consensus, its demand for two permanent seats endowed with the right of veto is not a claim: it is a right.
A just right, a well-founded right, a right commensurate with the balances of the twenty-first century.
The institutions must change with it.
Africa is not asking for a favour.
It is asking for its rightful place.

The Republic of the Congo, in its capacity as a member of the Committee of Heads of State and Government of the African Union on the reform of the United Nations Security Council (C10), will not compromise on this common demand.
The Republic of the Congo reaffirms its readiness to serve the international community.
With your support, it renews its aspiration to serve as a non-permanent member of the Security Council of the United Nations for the period 2030–2031.
This candidacy is based on a long diplomatic tradition, on our constant commitment to peace and on an exacting conception of international responsibility.
For more than five decades, our diplomacy has contributed consistently and effectively to several peace processes on our continent, with implications at the global level.

• The contribution to the liberation of Namibia and the withdrawal of Cuban troops from Angola under the Brazzaville Protocol of 1988, with Angola, Cuba and South Africa as the principal parties, under joint mediation by the Congo and the United States, and with an important role for the United Nations;
• Efforts towards the cessation of hostilities in the Central African Republic;
• Initiatives in support of reconciliation in Libya, for which my country holds the responsibility of chairing the African Union High-Level Committee on that country;
• Peace efforts in the Great Lakes region.
Our diplomacy is not a diplomacy of confrontation.
It is a diplomacy of dialogue, mediation, mutual respect and the search for African solutions to African problems.
We reaffirm here the pan-African vocation of our diplomacy.
Sovereignty is not a refusal to cooperate.

Sovereignty is the capacity of a people and a nation to determine freely their priorities, to defend their legitimate interests, to choose their partners and to preserve their independence of decision.
It is this conception of sovereignty that the Republic of the Congo defends.

We intend to pursue a foreign policy based on non-alignment, the diversification of our partnerships, mutual respect among States and the refusal of any interference in the internal affairs of nations.
We are open to the world, but we want to remain masters of our choices, of our destiny.
The Republic of the Congo is not meant to choose one side against another.
It sees itself as a link between Nations.
The Republic of the Congo has embarked on a path of profound transformation through Our Roadmap, “Let Us Accelerate the March Towards Development”, structured around several priorities:
We are building a Congo that is no longer content merely to export its raw materials, but that further processes its wealth on its own territory.
This is the meaning of our interest in special economic zones, because our vision of political sovereignty must go hand in hand with economic sovereignty.

It should be noted that Our vision, “Let Us Accelerate the March Towards Development”, is part of the dynamic of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the African Union’s Agenda 2063 on “The Africa We Want”.
But let us be lucid and pragmatic.

The development ambitions of the Republic of the Congo — like those of many African countries — are today being held back by the burden of debt, the inequalities of the international financial system and the consequences of climate change.
Four years before the 2030 deadline for the SDGs, we cannot afford a new collective fiasco.

The Republic of the Congo therefore calls for an ambitious international response to the question of the debt of developing countries, including through relief mechanisms and, where circumstances justify it, debt cancellation making it possible to free up resources for the investments essential to the SDGs.
Africa is not a periphery of the world.
It is one of its centres of gravity, the source of the renewal of multilateralism.
When Africa speaks with one voice, it advances the international agenda, inspires the world, asserts itself and opens new perspectives.
Three major initiatives carried forward by our countries bear witness to this:
• the United Nations Decade for Afforestation and Reforestation (2027–2036), carried forward by the Republic of the Congo;
• resolution 80/250 relating to the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans as a “crime against humanity”, carried forward by Ghana; and
• the “Correct the Map” resolution, carried forward by Togo.
These initiatives demonstrate that Africa contributes to defining the international agenda.
It is in this spirit that the Republic of the Congo will continue its Pan-African commitment.

The abolition of visas for Africans as from 1 January 2027 reflects Our desire to revive Pan-Africanism and the ideals of our Founding Fathers, to strengthen free movement on our continent, to build intra-African tourism, to make exchanges and solidarity among African peoples more inclusive, while preparing the African Continental Free Trade Area — the AfCFTA.
The duty of remembrance also requires us to face our history.
Near Pointe-Noire, in the Republic of the Congo, there rises a project of historical significance: the Loango Bay Memorial.
From this land departed many human beings torn from their families, their culture and their homeland by the transatlantic slave trade.
Loango must become a place of truth; A place of memory; A place of contemplation; But also a place of rebirth.
Our ambition is for Loango, like Gorée in Senegal, Cape Coast in Ghana or Ouidah in Benin, to be a bridge between Africa and its diaspora.
That people of African descent from all over the world may there recover a part of their history, their identity and their dignity.
That is also the meaning of our commitment in September 2025 in Harlem with people of African descent.
The Republic of the Congo also reaffirms its desire to mobilize Congolese abroad in the work of transforming Our country.
Our diaspora constitutes a human, intellectual, scientific, cultural and economic asset.
Its skills, its experience, its investments and its commitment are indispensable to accelerating our development.
The Congo needs all its children, its precious human capital.
The Republic of the Congo is a land of opportunities.

It has significant natural resources, critical minerals, considerable agricultural potential, tourism potential still largely to be developed, expanding infrastructure and a major geostrategic position at the heart of Central Africa.
We invite investors and development partners to support this ambition, notably through mutually beneficial public-private partnerships.
We want partnerships that create added value, develop national skills, promote technology transfer, respect our interests and contribute sustainably to our economy.
The Republic of the Congo also bears a particular responsibility with regard to the Congo Basin, the second ecological lung of the planet.
This exceptional heritage constitutes a major reservoir of biodiversity and plays an essential role in regulating the global climate.
The Congo Basin is one of Africa’s principal responses in the fight against global warming.
We cannot continuously accept that the countries that preserve these ecosystems bear alone the cost of this responsibility.
International solidarity must also have a price.
• fair and predictable remuneration for ecosystem services and carbon;
• increased capitalization of the Blue Fund;
• recognition of the Congo Basin as a global priority and strengthened international cooperation dedicated to its preservation.
We regret the absence in the Republic of the Congo of a United Nations institution dedicated to this cause that is commensurate with the strategic importance of the Congo Basin.

The Republic of the Congo also calls for the official launch of the United Nations Decade for Afforestation and Reforestation, and for the development of ambitious national road maps for its implementation.
Beyond its majestic rivers, its age-old forests and its ancestral lands, Congolese territory represents far more than a geographical space.
It is the bedrock of our Nation; It is the foundation of our identity; It is the territory of our sovereignty.
The Republic of the Congo will always defend the integrity of its territory, the security of its borders, the control of its natural resources and the freedom of its strategic choices.
It is the responsibility that we owe to the generations that came before us and the heritage that we must pass on to future generations.
As a fervent defender of peace on the international stage, the Republic of the Congo calls:
• for talks between the Russian Federation and Ukraine;
• for de-escalation in the Strait of Hormuz;
• for a just and lasting political solution in the Middle East;
• for the stabilization of the eastern part of the Democratic Republic of the Congo;
• for the lasting return of peace in the Sudan;
• for the continuation of reconciliation in Libya;
• for the lifting of the embargo against Cuba;
• for the return of peace and stability in the Sahel.
We reaffirm that: Peace is not weakness; Negotiation is not renunciation; Dialogue is not capitulation.
In this spirit, the Republic of the Congo will continue to give priority to mediation, dialogue and the search for political and peaceful solutions.

In order to build a prosperous and peaceful Africa, from Libya to the Sahel, from the Sudan to the Great Lakes region, we reiterate our readiness to support our brotherly countries in resolving crises and towards a return to peace and stability.
Through our history, we know that peace is always more difficult to build, but that it remains the only victory that benefits everyone in a lasting way.
In this same spirit of responsibility, the recurrent Ebola crises and repeated pandemics remind us that the threats we face are no longer only military or economic.
Health security has become an essential component of collective security.
In this regard, the Republic of the Congo will play fully its part in consolidating the seat of the WHO Regional Office in Brazzaville, in accordance with the Headquarters Agreement of 1952.
We also call for international governance of artificial intelligence and outer space.
These technologies must remain at the service of humanity, progress and the emancipation of peoples.
Technological progress must not become a new instrument of domination.
Africa too must be a place of creation, innovation and digital sovereignty.
In conclusion, the Republic of the Congo will remain faithful to its principles: peace, development, sovereignty, good-neighbourliness, dialogue, cooperation and mutual respect among Nations.
We will continue to defend our national interests while assuming our international responsibilities.
We will continue to believe in Africa and in our common destiny.
And We will continue to choose the United Nations as the privileged space for dialogue among peoples.

Ladies and gentlemen, I appear today before this assembly representing the president of the Republic of Colombia, Abelardo de la Espriella, who has asked me to be here on his behalf and bring before you a message written by him.
From this moment on, what you will hear are the words of the president of the Republic of Colombia.
I have asked the Vice President of the Republic, José Manuel Restrepo, to read this message on my behalf.
I have done so because I assured the Colombian people that I would not leave the country during the four years of my term, and I am keeping that promise.
47 days ago, a new government took office in Colombia.
Three days later, at 7:34 a.m., the earth shook.
A 7.4 magnitude earthquake struck my country in a matter of seconds.
Homes, hospitals, schools, roads and bridges had been totally destroyed or severely damaged.
The Colombian Geological Service confirmed that this was the strongest magnitude earthquake recorded in Colombia so far this century Hundreds of Colombians lost their lives.
4500 were injured and more than 452,000 people were affected.
They represented the life savings assets of these people.
The government that had barely started its work was forced to confront one of the greatest natural disasters in our recent history.
There was no time to ask whether we were ready.
We had to act, and we did so.
I gave one unequivocal instruction we had to save human lives.
There was time for everything else.
Appointments to posts could wait, meetings could wait.
But my fellow fellow Colombians trapped underneath the rubble could not.
The government deployed to the affected areas alongside the security forces, emergency services, volunteers and rescue workers.
And from the very beginning, we started receiving the generous assistance from friendly countries and international organizations such as all of you.
The earthquake claimed the lives of many of our fellow Colombians and destroyed thousands of homes and buildings and much infrastructure.
But it also reminded us once again of something that Colombians are very familiar with.
We might fall, we might suffer, and we might weep.
But what we cannot and what we do not know how to do is give up.
But I'm not only going to talk to you about this tragedy.
I want to refer to what Colombia decided to do in its aftermath.
On the 7th of August, I took over a country that had begun to lose something far more difficult to rebuild than a road or a building. That is trust.
Trust in the law that should protect our citizens.
Trust that working, studying, and doing things well are worthwhile.
Trust in a state that lives up to its duty.
No country, no country can prosper when its people cease to trust in it.

That's why the government that I lead has tasked itself with taking up every possible decision to enable Colombia to believe in itself again, and to ensure that the world can believe in Colombia again.
And I call that overarching purpose the patria milagro, the miracle nation.
The first step is a basic one restoring security.
For far too long, Colombians have had to live alongside situations that no society should accept as normal.

A rural farmer having to ask permission from a terrorist group to work on his land, a shopkeeper having to hand over part of the fruits of his labor to extortionists, a mother increasingly gripped by fear every time their child goes out to play in the park.
That is not, and it cannot become the norm.

Consequently, from the very beginning of my government I gave the security forces one clear instruction to regain territorial control, to fully restore the state's authority and to confront the structures using terrorism.
My government is determined to do away with euphemisms.
Organizations that murder, that kidnap, that use explosives, that recruit children, and that deliberately resort to terror to subjugate a society are terrorist groups.

That is what we call them, and we are facing up to them with the full, legitimate force of the state, within the Constitution and within the law But there is another reality that is very often overlooked.
The illicit drugs produced in Colombia don't end up in Colombia.
Drugs trafficking is a transnational criminal enterprise.
Its money moves through international financial systems, and its networks operate across numerous countries.
I will do everything necessary to combat that scourge, but a transnational threat requires the international community to play its part as well.
Security, while essential, is not enough.
A territory that provides no opportunities remains vulnerable.
My administration is therefore also focused on ensuring that Colombia grows again.
For years, we have discussed how to better distribute what we have.
That is a legitimate, necessary discussion, but it's absolutely not enough.
We also need to ask ourselves, how are we going to produce more?
What they have to do is lay the foundations for it to occur.
In our miracle nation, we want an idea to be able to come, a business, a business to create jobs, and for jobs to become well-being for our people.
To those of you anywhere else in the world who are wondering where to invest, I would like to invite you to look at Colombia.
It's a country with access to two oceans, productive land, energy resources, enormous biodiversity, an excellent geographical position, and a government that champions private enterprise.
But above all, look at our people.
Colombia does not want to watch the technological transformation of our time from the sidelines.
We want to be a part of it.
We want to train young people for super intelligence, for robotics, for data science, for agro industry for engineering, and for the new economy.
Millions of Colombians are not asking the state to sort out their lives.
They're asking the state to give them the opportunity to build those lives.
And that is what gives meaning to what I have called the miracle nation.
This isn't the name of a government, nor is it a naive promise that our problems will just disappear.
This is the country that we're going to build.

It's a country where security allows us to reclaim our territories threatened by terrorism, where trust attracts investment, where investment creates jobs, and where growth leads to better living conditions.
It is a schoolteacher in Mompos Bolivar, teaching with the tools of the 21st century.
A young woman in Pasto, Narino, preparing to be a part of the future industries This is the miracle nation that we've already started to build.
I'm well aware that 47 days is far too little time to change a country, but it is enough time to change the course of a country.
And I want Colombia to once again enjoy strong growth.

That growth should lead to a job for a young person, a home for a family, timely access to medicines, a harvest that finds a market, and Colombians who, thanks to their own efforts and dedication, can escape poverty.
This is our miracle economy, an economy that grows so that people can grow with it Our relationship with the world is also a part of this purpose.
Over the last few weeks, we have seen this very tangibly.
When friendly countries and international organizations came to our aid following the earthquake.
This solidarity makes full sense when it reaches people, when it solves problems, and when it produces results.
And it is precisely because I recognize the value of that cooperation that today I want to speak frankly about the UN.
I've been critical about this, of this organization.
I was critical of it before I became president, and it would be inconsistent to address this Assembly today and conceal my attempt to seal my convictions.
This criticism isn't born out of whim or hostility towards the United Nations.
It's based in political, institutional, doctrinal considerations.

I believe in the UN as an organization, and it is precisely for that reason that I believe it's legitimate to ask whether the institutions that we've been building are effectively responding to the problems that that it was created to address.
The charter itself is very clear here.
This organization was born to maintain international peace and security, to foster friendly relations among nations, and to promote cooperation in resolving the major common problems.
Eight decades on, the question cannot be whether those purposes remain valid.
Of course they do The questions have completely changed, though.
Is the UN fulfilling those purposes with the effectiveness demanded by today's world?
Are there bureaucratic structures that have become excessively cumbersome?
Are we dedicating too many resources, too much energy to administering procedures and or too little to resolving problems?
Are we measuring our results rigorously enough?
Another matter that I wish to address is human rights.
Colombia defends human rights and will continue to do so.
But my country believes that protecting human rights loses credibility when it becomes subjected to political calculation.
I categorically reject human rights being used as a banner raised against some and lowered against others.
Nor can human rights become an instrument rewarding friends, punishing adversaries, or, worse still, remaining silent in line with the political circumstances of the time.
Our duty is to prevent politics from weakening the defense of human rights.
If we want the system to be respected, it needs to be serious, consistent and equally demanding on all of us.
My country is consistent, and therefore we want to ensure that we have a credible defense of human rights.
And in this, just as in so many other areas, the United Nations still has some room for improvement in that connection.
We trust in a democratic transition in Venezuela, a swift, safe, far reaching transition.
There's another doctrinal concern that I wish to raise just as honestly globalism.
Allow me to begin by clarifying what I mean by that.
I'm not talking about international trade or cooperation among states, nor am I talking about a humanity that shares common problems and responsibilities.

All of those things are absolutely necessary I'm talking about a concept according to which nation sovereignty, distinct identities, traditions, and the values of peoples are obstacles that gradually give way to increasing political and cultural uniformity decided by supranational bodies.
I don't share in that doctrine, which I consider perverse and harmful.
For me, multilateralism isn't about dissolving nations, but rather about facilitating cooperation among them.
Loving one's homeland isn't compatible with respecting others, defending history, culture, values, and traditions doesn't mean disparaging those of another.
International cooperation is richer when those who sit around this table know who they are, where they come from, and what the people in whose name they speak represent.
Several of the questions that I've asked are not unfamiliar to this organization.

The UN 80 initiative has placed on the table issues of duplication, fragmentation, administrative burden, and the way mandates function as part of an effort to make the United Nations more efficient and more effective.
Acknowledging an institution's imperfections doesn't mean overlooking its value.
On the contrary, it might be a way of strengthening it.
It has never been my style to hide behind political correctness or to tell my interlocutors what I imagine they want to hear.
I'm not looking to please anyone, but rather to set out the position of the Republic of Colombia respectfully, cordially and clearly.
All can be improved perfected, and the United Nations is no exception.
There is one specific area that Colombia wishes to reflect on further.
That is the international fight against terrorism.
This organization has done significant work here.
Since 1963, the international community has developed 19 universal legal instruments aimed at preventing different terrorist acts.
However, after decades of discussion, there is still no legal definition of terrorism that is universally agreed by member states.
The UN Office of Counterterrorism itself has recently flagged that the lack of a universally agreed definition begets legal uncertainty.
Discrepancies among national laws and causes difficulties in international cooperation.
The Republic of Colombia believes that the time has come to move ahead.

We need a common international definition that is sufficiently clear and precise, compatible with international law and fundamental safeguards, but also useful enough so that states can cooperate effectively in combating acts of terrorism.
A serious definition should avoid two extremes.

On the one hand, a political disagreement being arbitrarily characterized as terrorism, and on the other hand, allowing an organization to hide murders, kidnappings, bombings, or deliberate attacks against civilians behind a political label in order to evade the legal consequences of its actions.
Terrorism must be condemned regardless of the perpetrator, where it is committed or the cause they invoke.
The United Nations has repeatedly reaffirmed that terrorism, in all its forms and manifestations, represents one of the most serious threats to international peace and security.
Now, a better definition is not enough.
States need better tools to combat this phenomenon.
We need faster mechanisms for exchanging information and intelligence.
We need better judicial cooperation, effective tracing, freezing, seizing instruments for assets related to terrorist financing.
And we need closer cooperation to deal with networks that operate simultaneously across different countries.
Colombia stands ready to participate actively in that discussion.
My country wants to see United Nations, where the effectiveness is measured less by the volume of documents it produces, and far more by the results that it delivers.
A UN that is less inclined to multiply processes and more determined to translate international cooperation into concrete action.

That is the sort of multilateralism that Colombia is ready to defend, one that respects the sovereign equality of states as the charter itself provides, but one that is also capable of acting effectively when threats recognize no borders, drugs, trafficking, terrorism, transnational organized crime and illicit economies are precisely those threats.
Specifically, my government's foreign policy is guided by national interests by the defense of our sovereignty, and by the pursuit of results.
That national interest I refer to also has a specific objective that is ensuring the prosperity of our people.
Foreign policy should serve to create jobs, to attract investment and technology, to open markets, and to create opportunities for Colombians.
With that goal in mind, I wish to extend an invitation to the world.
Come to Colombia, invest in Colombia grow and prosper with Colombia Believe in Colombia.

I don't promise you a perfect country, but I can assure you that I am working tirelessly to build you a nation that is, to build a nation that is safer, more prosperous, and with more opportunities for its people.

Colombia does not come before the world today to ask others to do for us what it is our responsibility to do for ourselves rebuilding our country, restoring security, growing the economy, protecting our institutions, and giving opportunities back to millions of people are first and foremost responsibilities that fall to Colombians.
But we also know that no nation can turn its back on the world.
We need partners and friends with whom we can trade, invest, exchange knowledge, and address common threats.
That is the Colombia that I present to you today, a country that is well aware of its difficulties, but also of its enormous potential.
A country that doesn't try to hide its problems, but rather to confront them.
A country that is getting back on its feet and knows where it wants to go.
To the nations represented here, I extend my hand respectfully and through friendship.
Colombia wants to work with you on everything that we can build together.

I want within a few years, when the world looks again at my country, I want them to see a nation that is safer, more prosperous, more well respected and above all, far more confident in its own abilities.
And if that is the Colombia that the world sees, there'll be no need to explain what I meant when I spoke of the Patria Milagro, the miracle nation.

At a time when he will hand over the baton of our Organization // in a tense and uncertain international context, // I express my very best wishes for success to the person who will succeed him in his functions.

Faced with a global context // marked by a crisis of confidence in international institutions, // often perceived as privileging the balance of power // over law, // our Organization must rise above partisan interests.
In shà Allah, the next leadership // will know how to embody the unity and renewal of a multilateralism // that is more credible.

Indeed, it will be essential // for that voice to defend the aspirations of developing countries // with particular attention to island and vulnerable States, // in order to forge responses of solidarity to the challenges that bind us.
For 81 years, // this General Assembly has remained the central pillar of multilateralism.
Yet, // as we gather in New York, // humanity stands at a crossroads.
Indeed, one lucid observation is called for: // despite our efforts, // the Sustainable Development Goals of the 2030 Agenda // remain out of reach.
Widening inequalities, // the climate emergency and the fragility of international peace require of us a new lucidity.
In this uncertain world, // it is imperative to restore confidence, // mutual respect and the equality of all before the law.
Such is, // at the heart of this 81st session, // our collective responsibility.
One year ago, // in this very hall, we called for peace to be made the foundation // of our development and of human rights.
// Twelve months later, // it must be acknowledged that there is a gap between our commitments and reality.

Everywhere in the world, // from the Middle East to the Sahel, // by way of the Great Lakes, // Eastern Europe and Latin America, // civilian populations continue to pay a heavy price for conflicts whose interests are often unacknowledged.

// The deadly war in the Middle East, // marked by massive civilian losses // and the destruction of critical infrastructure, // which has led to the paralysis of the Strait of Hormuz, // has spread to Syria and Lebanon // as a result of military operations carried out by Israel, // and is generating major consequences // for the global economy.

In addition to the global shock wave it has caused, // this conflict poses a direct threat // to the food and energy security // of vulnerable countries such as the Union of the Comoros, // which depend heavily // on imports and on the purchasing power of our populations.
This requires greater international solidarity in the face of this shared insecurity.

Allowing the conflict in the Middle East to persist // directly weakens the United Nations // by calling into question its capacity // to maintain world peace // and by eroding its credibility // among the peoples we represent.
The theme of this 81st session recognizes this rupture and admits that something has broken.
That is why it is imperative to restore confidence, // no longer through new promises, // but through acts guaranteeing the primacy of law and collective security.

It is time to move beyond power relations // in order to found a new human ethic, // transcending divisions, // questions of race, colour and belief // and anchored in the preservation // of our common ecosystem.

Created in 1945 upon the ruins of the Second World War, // our Organization has the vocation of guaranteeing peace, // security and the sovereign equality of States in strict compliance with international law.
// Without these principles, // it would be nothing more than an empty forum.
// Now, since our last meeting here, in September 2025, the genocide in Palestine continues its macabre work.
Hundreds of thousands of Palestinian civilians, women, children and elderly people have lost their lives, and entire populations are on the verge of extermination.

The international community will regain its credibility first through the action it undertakes urgently to silence the guns, preserve the lives of civilians, Israelis, Palestinians, Lebanese, Syrians, and ultimately achieve the implementation of United Nations resolutions, which advocate in particular the two-State solution, Israeli and Palestinian, coexisting peacefully.
This is a prerequisite for the other transformations capable of meeting, with justice, the climate challenges, the issues of artificial intelligence and the imperatives of sustainable development.
From then on, we will be able to make the right to development the pillar of multilateralism, by facilitating access to sustainable financing and reducing global inequalities.
Allow me to quote a great African writer, Chinua ACHEBE, who said this: “When we gather in the village, in the moonlight, it is not because of the moon.
Every man can see it in his own courtyard.
We come together because it is a good thing to do.
Let us therefore continue in a spirit of teamwork and draw upon the power of solidarity.
If we smile together, it is not because we have no problems, but because we are stronger than the problems.”

For half a century, the Comorian State, still in search of its sovereignty, within its borders recognized by international law, has remained under illegal French occupation, despite the many relevant resolutions of our Assembly.
The Comorian side, which has always favoured the peaceful settlement of this dispute, has always believed and considered that there is no other alternative than dialogue.
This dialogue, we have engaged in with France for two decades, in order to arrive at a peaceful resolution of this dispute, described as unpleasant by the late French President François Mitterrand.
We regret that this dialogue has not succeeded.
On the contrary, French unilateral actions, particularly on the African continent, run counter to our expectations.

We deeply deplore the inclinations of certain neighbouring, brotherly and friendly countries, which have always defended the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Comoros, to establish relations with an occupied part of our territory.
We call for the solidarity that African countries have always shown in defending their sovereignty in general and, in particular, the territorial integrity of the Comoros.

We firmly condemn initiatives for cooperation with the local authorities of Mayotte, as well as the recent statements by the French Prime Minister linking development assistance to the pursuit of migrants.
By virtue of General Assembly resolutions 3385 of 12 November 1975 and 31/4 of 21 October 1976, as well as Security Council resolution 376, Comorians are at home in Mayotte.
For the Comorian Nation, the sovereignty of the Comoros over its entire archipelago is not for sale.

We therefore urge the French authorities to undertake a recasting of their political narrative, to review the measures recently announced, and to favour fruitful cooperation and a win-win partnership for France and for the Comoros.
It is indeed imperative to build a harmonious future, taking into account the current geopolitical upheavals and the weakening of traditional alliances.
Development remains at the heart of our national ambition.

Since 2019, the Comoros has adopted the Emerging Comoros Plan, a structuring roadmap aimed at modernizing our infrastructure, energizing our private sector, and offering our youth the decent jobs they deserve.
With a financing need of 5.2 billion dollars over ten years, this plan is the engine of our transformation.

Although tangible progress has been made, with GDP growth rising from 1.9 per cent in 2019 to 3.8 per cent in 2025, the road ahead remains long: we still need to mobilize more domestic and external financing to achieve our objectives.
Faced with the scarcity and rising cost of financial resources, we nevertheless remain hampered by criteria for access to concessional financing that are disconnected from reality.
For a small island State like ours, income indicators cannot obscure our multidimensional vulnerability.
That is why the Comoros strongly calls for a profound reform of the international financial architecture.
Such reform is an imperative to guarantee our right to development and to ensure that multilateral banks finally integrate the reality of our fragilities into their allocation policies.
Strengthened by these encouraging macroeconomic results and by our determination to reach the upper thresholds of middle-income countries, we are now entering a decisive phase.
For the period 2027-2030, we are embarking on a new acceleration phase of the Emerging Comoros Plan.
We invite our bilateral and multilateral partners, as well as the private sector, to join us in transforming this ambition into a lasting reality for the Comorian people.

It is with profound gratitude that I welcome the inscription, during the last session of the World Heritage Committee in Busan, of six Medinas of the historical Sultanates of the Comoros on the UNESCO World Heritage List.
This historic recognition, the result of twenty years of work, honours our nation.
Moreover, my country, the Union of the Comoros, is preparing to host, in one year’s time, for the first time in its history, the Indian Ocean Island Games.

This sporting gathering of the youth of our subregion remains one of the high points for the actors of tomorrow, in search of cohesion and fulfilment, in a world beset by divisions and the rejection of others in their diversity.
We therefore intend to make this event a resounding success for the young people of the Indian Ocean.
At the conclusion of my statement, I issue a call for large-scale action to restore confidence among our Nations, by being fair, just and united.
Let us ensure transformation by making the United Nations, our common home, a more credible Organization and one that offers hope for the future.
It is at this price that we will give ourselves the power to act, in all humanity, for humanity, in its differences and its diversity.
I come from a country made up of ten islands in the Atlantic.
A country aware of its vulnerabilities, but one that has learned that the size of a territory must never determine the size of our dreams.
The history of Cabo Verde is also a history of learning.
We have learned to confront drought and scarcity, to transform the sea from a barrier into a bridge, but, above all, we have learned that a nation’s greatest wealth lies in its people.

We even have a word for this wealth, which is "morabeza", a term that defines the cordiality, determination, and kindness of our people, which the whole world was able to witness a little during this year's Football World Cup.

Amílcar Cabral, one of the great figures of our history, left us a lesson that continues to resonate across generations: “Learn in life, learn from our people, learn from the books and from the experiences of others. Learn always.”

Perhaps this is an ability that the world must rediscover: the ability to learn from history, to learn from one another, and to understand that there can be no lasting development without peace, just as there can be no lasting peace where poverty, exclusion and lack of opportunity persist.
In this spirit, Cabo Verde reaffirms its faith in the United Nations, in dialogue among nations, in cooperation among peoples, and in the primacy of Law over the use of force.

In the face of the wars, inequalities, and crises confronting our world, we reaffirm our unwavering commitment to the Charter of the United Nations, to the sovereignty and territorial integrity of States, to the protection of civilian populations, and to the peaceful resolution of conflicts.
International Law and International Humanitarian Law cannot be applied in a selective manner.
They will only be truly strong and fulfill their role when they are respected and upheld by all.
In our region, terrorism, violent extremism and transnational crimes also remind us institutions and cooperation.
Africa is the continent with the youngest population in the world.
Therefore, investing in our young people, in education, in knowledge, and in the possibility of building a dignified life means also investing in peace.
The world of today is not the world of 1945.
The institutions we created to respond to the challenges of that time need to learn with the world that has changed.
Cabo Verde therefore supports a United Nations that is more effective, more transparent, and more representative.
The UN80 Initiative presents an opportunity to modernize this Organization and strengthen its response capacity.
In this spirit, we also support the reform of the Security Council.

Africa is home to nearly one-quarter of the Member States of this Organization and represents approximately one-fifth of the world’s population, and yet it still lacks the representation it deserves on this Council.
Therefore, we support a more equitable African representation, accordance with the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration.
in A fairer international order also requires fairer and more inclusive institutions.
The election of the next Secretary-General should reflect the same principles: transparency, inclusion, merit and equal opportunities.
But the United Nations is not just a place where we discuss crises.
It is also the space where we build common paths.

The 2030 Agenda, the African Union's Agenda 2063 and the Pact for the Future point us in one direction: sustainable development, centered on the people, capable of transforming global commitments into concrete changes in the lives of populations.
This is also the mission of the new Government of Cabo Verde: to concretely improve the lives of its people.
And we have placed education at the heart of this mission.
Because the school is where a society begins to shape its future.
And Education is a powerful development strategy.

We seek to transform knowledge into innovation, decent employment, and opportunities; to strengthen our education and health systems; and to advance progress in digital transformation, gender equality, the energy transition, water security, and the blue economy.
We want to create more opportunities for our young people and build an economy capable of transforming people’s talent into development.
Development is transforming knowledge into opportunity and opportunity into dignity.

For Cabo Verde and other Small Island States, the climate crisis is not a distant threat; it is a present reality - it’s here: the droughts, desertification, water scarcity, ocean acidification, and rising sea levels.
Just look at what is happening on the island of Sal, where, only two days ago, rising sea waters flooded the avenue in front of the hotels.
It is also a question of justice, because those who have contributed the least to this crisis cannot continue to bear some of its most serious consequences.
Science has shown us the way forward.
We must now translate this valuable knowledge into decisions and actions.
Cabo Verde has tried to do its part.

In September 2024, Cabo Verde launched a call for a Global Compact for Climate Mobility, and in June, in Berlin, 57 countries endorsed the Global Consensus on the Principles to Address Climate Mobility.
At the United Nations, Cabo Verde co-facilitated negotiations on the Political Declaration of the Third Conference on the Oceans and the Declaration on Sea Level Rise.
For a country made up of islands, protecting the ocean is not just an environmental policy.
It is protecting the national territory, the economy, the culture, and the future.
In January 2027, Cabo Verde will take over the Presidency of the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS).

We will take on this responsibility by working for the unity of Small Island States, the implementation of the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda, for fairer financing, for climate adaptation, and for ensuring that the oceans remain at the heart of the global agenda.

And in 2034, we will host the Fifth International Conference on Small Island Developing States, providing an opportunity to share experiences, build common responses, and transform vulnerabilities into opportunities.
There is also pedagogy in the relationships between Nations.
It begins with the ability to listen.
It entails the humility to recognize that no one country alone has all the answers.
And it makes sense when what we learn together is translated into action.
This, after all, is the essence of multilateralism.
In a time of fragmentation, we need to regain trust.
In a time of confrontation, we need to strengthen cooperation.
In a time when force so often prevails, we need to reaffirm the Law.
But our history has taught us to engage in dialogue, to build bridges, and to seek consensus.
It also taught us that no country is too small to have a voice and no challenge is too big to tackle when we work together.
The United Nations must continue to be the space for this collective endeavor.
And I will recall what Amílcar Cabral taught us: “Learn always.”

Today, learning also means understanding that educating a child, providing opportunities for young people, protecting the planet, fighting poverty, promoting development, and building peace are not separate missions.
They are, indeed, different ways of caring for the future.
And perhaps this is the greatest lesson that our times require of us: the future is not simply what we receive.
Rather, it is what we are able to teach, learn, and build together.

Armed conflicts are protracted, transnational organized crime is expanding its capacity for action, the climate crisis is intensifying its effects, development gaps persist, and technological transformation poses unprecedented challenges for our institutions.
At the same time, confidence in multilateralism is weakening precisely when we need it most.
Faced with this reality, Costa Rica reaffirms its conviction that no State can confront common challenges on its own.
Multilateralism is a necessity for preserving peace, promoting sustainable development and protecting human dignity.
But it will retain its legitimacy only if it demonstrates the capacity to produce concrete and tangible results for people.
Costa Rica advocates a United Nations that is more agile, more efficient, more transparent and accountable to its Member States.
An Organization that sets priorities, eliminates duplication, uses its resources responsibly and measures its results.
International peace and security are facing increasingly complex threats.

Transnational organized crime, drug trafficking, trafficking in persons, illicit arms trafficking, money-laundering, cybercrime and illegal mining transcend national borders and undermine democratic stability, development and the rule of law.
Costa Rica knows these threats first-hand.

Illegal mining, driven by transnational criminal organizations in our border area with Nicaragua, has caused serious environmental destruction and creates risks for public health, the economy and regional security.
These organizations contest territories, fuel illicit economies, attack democratic institutions and directly affect the rights and dignity of persons.
Artificial intelligence may well empower cyberterrorism and other crimes that are still unimaginable.
According to Microsoft system usage data, Costa Rica is the country in Latin America with the highest percentage of use of artificial intelligence, at around 58 per cent above the global average.
These threats require greater international cooperation, information-sharing, institutional strengthening and a renewed commitment to international law and international humanitarian law.
Costa Rica has demonstrated that environmental leadership is not measured by the size of a territory, but by the firmness of its commitment to present and future generations.
For decades we have defended a vision in which economic prosperity and the protection of nature are not opposing objectives, but complementary ones.
Climate change particularly affects the most vulnerable, while biodiversity loss, ecosystem degradation, pollution of water resources and pressure on our ocean are accelerating.
They constitute a global crisis that jeopardizes food security, public health and the development opportunities of millions of people.
There can be no lasting security where democratic institutions are weakened, nor sustainable development when human rights are violated.
Our response must place people at the centre.

Costa Rica will continue to defend the dignity and rights of all persons, with special attention to the inclusion, autonomy and effective participation of persons with disabilities, including autistic persons.
In that context, we reiterate our deep concern over the situation in Nicaragua.

The deterioration of fundamental freedoms, the persecution of critical voices, the closure of civic space, religious persecution and reports of human rights violations continue to move the country further away from democratic principles.
As a neighbouring nation that has welcomed hundreds of thousands of Nicaraguans, we maintain our firm commitment to the defence of their rights and to the restoration of the rule of law.
We also observe with concern the situation in Cuba and reiterate our call for full respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms.

We are also continuing to follow closely the evolution of the situation in Venezuela, with the hope that dialogue, respect for the popular will, the restoration of democratic institutions and attention to persons in vulnerable situations will prevail.
Eighty-one years after the adoption of the Charter, the best way to defend the United Nations is to strengthen its capacity to implement its mandates.

We need a United Nations that is more effective, transparent and agile; capable of preventing conflicts, building consensus even in times of deep polarization and providing concrete responses to the challenges of the twenty-first century.
For that reason, Costa Rica has presented the candidature of Ms. Rebeca Grynspan for the post of Secretary-General of the United Nations.

She is a Latin American with political, economic and multilateral experience; a woman of proven leadership who knows the United Nations and understands that to know an institution also means having the courage to reform it.
Her proposal starts from a simple but powerful idea: To defend the United Nations requires having the courage to reform it.
Today we need leadership capable of uniting the membership, strengthening the Organization and renewing confidence in international cooperation.
