We need a United Nations that does what it is called upon to do according to its Charter: maintain international peace and security, respect for Human Rights, and promote development.
Costa Rica firmly believes that the next Secretary-General must be a Latin American woman; it must be Rebeca Grynspan.
Costa Rica abolished its army more than seven decades ago because it believed that International Law could offer greater security than weapons.

We will continue building bridges, forging consensus, and defending the conviction that gave rise to this Organization: dialogue will always be more powerful than confrontation, law more lasting than force, and cooperation the only path toward truly sustainable peace.
The future of the United Nations will not depend solely on the strength of its Charter, but on the collective courage to fulfill it.
Mr. President of the General Assembly; Mr. Secretary General; The advance of expansionism, usurpation, plunder, conquest as well as military and economic aggressions are alarming.
The US government aspiration to impose peace through force is unrealizable.
The fundamental pillars of International Law and the United Nations Organization, such as the sovereign equality among States, are under permanent attack.

The genocidal crime of Zionism against the Palestinian people; the pirate attacks against vessels and the extrajudicial executions in the Caribbean Sea and some areas in the Pacific; the military aggression against the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela and the war against the Islamic Republic of Iran are new expressions of this atrocity.

They are also a reflection of the crisis of identity and relevance imposed on the United Nations Organization, and even on the General Assembly, the most universal, democratic and representative body of the international community.
We are convinced of the need to preserve and strengthen the United Nations, as we make it more democratic and effective; and of placing it closer to the peoples.
As is well known, in Cuba we are facing a multidimensional aggression from the United States government; a permanent, abusive and ruthless hostility that has lasted for almost seven decades already.

Since January, 2026, this aggression has strengthened and become crueler and more dangerous, with the imposition of an energy blockade that, by resorting to intimidation and coercion, prevents any country from exporting fuel to Cuba -an equivalent to a naval blockade-, which is classified by International Law as an act of war.

Through the adoption of successive measures, the government of the United States has been applying new prohibitions on all countries with regard to products and services that cannot be exported or transported to Cuba.
More than 7 thousand containers remain stranded in different ports; many of them are loaded with foodstuffs, medicines and medical devices and have even been paid for by Cuban private companies.
It is an unusual and unprecedented action.

A superpower unilaterally deprives all States of their right to export the commodities that they wish to the country that they wish and continuously and comprehensively violates freedom of trade and navigation.

Added to this is the intimidation of entrepreneurs of different countries so that they abandon, against their will, their investments and businesses in Cuba; the obstacles and tricks to prevent the arrival in Cuba of absolutely legitimate commercial shipments; the pressures to prevent the entry of visitors and tourists; and the efforts aimed at restricting as much as possible Cuba’s legitimate access to financing, technology and markets.

The United States has gone as far as to exert unsuspected pressures on sovereign governments so that they renounce the medical services they requested from us for the benefit of their respective populations and which are offered by Cuban professionals, because the US government is opposed to such cooperation, regardless of the impact and harm this may cause to those populations if they are deprived of free medical care; that is to say, deprived of an elemental human right.
On Thursday last, while the General Assembly was in session, the State Department convened a humiliating meeting specifically with the States that are the recipients of this cooperation.
According to the US Secretary of State, the official policy is to shut down every relief valve, block every possible way out and eliminate any form of survival for Cuba.
The impact of such an iron-clad and ruthless siege has a human face.
The economic warfare is aimed against the people.
It harms the Cuban people as a whole.
It takes a toll on human lives.
It causes individual and collective pain; it causes anguish.
It is a policy deliberately designed to wound the deepest sensibilities of Cuban families; disturb their wellbeing and hurt the dignity of the people.
It is an act of collective punishment; a crime proscribed by International Humanitarian Law.
The obvious short- term goal pursued by such policy is to induce a humanitarian crisis in Cuba, which is also a crime.

The government of the United States and the US State Department have been forced to recognize the suffering inflicted on the Cuban people, but they have the impudence and cynicism to insist in putting the blame on the government of Cuba.

They are following the formula recommended by the State Department since 1960 in the infamous Mallory Memorandum, which established as an official policy, in force up until today, the overthrowing of the Cuban government through the economic suffocation and the extreme suffering of the Cuban people out of material shortages, hunger and desperation.
A few days ago, the President of the United States declared in this room that Cuba was ‘a failed State’.
If that were the case, why did they have to impose a fuel blockade?
Why did they impose secondary sanctions?
Why do they have to threaten, persecute and exert pressures on other States?
He also recognized that his government is putting on Cuba the biggest pressure ever applied against any other State.
A few months before, he had said that “all that is left is to go in and destroy everything.”
The threat of the use of military force against Cuba persists.
This behavior is a violation of International Law and an infringement of the San Francisco Charter.
Should it materialize, it would be a major crime.
It would cause the death of Cuban and American youths as well as huge destruction.
Cuba will exercise, with utmost resolve and energy, its legitimate right to defend itself.
This aggression is being accompanied by a brutal media and cognitive warfare aimed against the Cuban people, the US citizens and the international public opinion.
It is characterized by its gross and brazen attempts to interfere in the internal affairs of Cuba, which is another international crime.

We are often asked what is the US pursuing with such an aggressive behavior, and the question usually surprises us, because the representatives of that government have outrightly declared their purpose to take Cuba, control the country and dominate the economy.

In other words, nullify, through an aggression or economic suffocation, the national sovereignty which several generations of Cubans have struggled for since the nineteenth century -first to achieve it, and later on, after conquering the full freedom in 1959, to tenaciously defend it against the biggest risks, including that of a holocaust.

The US behavior relies on the fallacy, proclaimed early on this year, that Cuba is an unusual and extraordinary threat to the national security and the foreign policy of the United States -a nonsense shamelessly repeated by that government.

In a futile attempt to substantiate such an assertion, the US government inundates its huge communication platforms with false claims using the spokespersons and publications it hires, taking advantage of the increasing control exercised by its government over them.
The US President himself repeated it a few days ago in this room.

Any minimally informed observer would understand the unrealistic and evil intention to portray a relatively small and developing nation like Cuba, with a modest economic performance, as a threat to the biggest nuclear, military, technological and economic power in the planet.

This Organization and its member States have abundant evidence of the fact that we are a peace-loving country; of the efforts of Cuba in favor of international cooperation, understanding and the peaceful settlement of disputes as well as of the active role that we have played in support of the United Nations.
Cuba is not a threat; the blockade is!
We are aware of the immense challenge our country faces in terms of its security, survival, the wellbeing of the people and the destiny of the nation.
We are not facing this challenge passively.
We are doing it firmly and with dignity.
Based on that, we are moving on in a process of changes that would lead to profound transformations of the economic and social model of the country, based on our historical experience.

On July 30 last, during the closing ceremony of the Seventh Session of the National People’s Power Assembly, President Miguel Díaz- Canel referred to the origin of the social and economic transformations that the country is introducing.

He said, and I quote: “In view of the complex situation I have described, how can we prevail in the construction of socialism? How could we find the material and financial resources needed to preserve the social achievements attained by the Revolution? As it already happened on former occasions, when we were faced with particularly complex situations - such as the Special Period-; when, under the guidance, first of Commander in Chief, and later on of Army General Raúl Castro, the economic model was transformed to adapt it to the challenging foreign circumstances demanded by the times, under the leadership of the Party, in a collective and democratic way, in consultation with the people, without compromising the independence, the national sovereignty or the social achievements of the Revolution”, end of quote.
The National People’s Power Assembly has adopted a new program, with new practices, actors and economic concepts.
All of that is being done in accordance with the Constitution in force -.
which was adopted through a free and universal referendum- and the conception of our socialist State of law and social justice.

As was pointed out by the leader of the Cuban Revolution, Army General Raúl Castro Ruz, the most important thing will be “the appropriate and timely implementation process, with well-defined priorities and the conscious participation of the people.”

This process relies on the strengths that we have built; the potential of our human resources and the determination to respond to the needs of the people with the greatest possible social justice, without ceasing in our efforts to defend, with utmost vigor and resolve, the sovereignty and the right to self-determination.

We have always been and we will continue to be ready to engage in a dialogue with the government of the United States to try to find a solution to bilateral differences, on the basis of responsibility, respect, sovereign equality, the observance of International Law, without any interference in the internal affairs of States and without preconditions.
We know that we count on the support of the international community and the solidarity of millions, among them, an increasing number of US citizens.
That is reflected in the numerous gestures and statements in support of Cuba and against the abusive aggression.
It is reflected in the fraternal material assistance received by our people, seeking to mitigate the huge damage caused to the Cuban economy and society.

That spirit of solidarity and empathy is expressed with particular emphasis among Cubans who reside permanently or temporarily outside the national territory and among their descendants, even here in the United States.

Mr. President; We reject the Monroe Doctrine and its Corollaries as much as we refuse every attempt of imperialist militarization, intervention or domination in Latin America and the Caribbean, a region that was proclaimed as a Zone of Peace in 2014 in Havana.
As a Small Island Developing State, we stand in solidarity with our brothers and sisters who share a similar condition and the warning about the worrying and inexorable advance of climate change.
It is necessary to promote a governance that makes a more intensive use of the new ICTs, particularly the disruptive technologies, such as artificial intelligence.
We reject the implementation of unilateral coercive measures.
We express our support to and solidarity with the nations which are victim of them.
We ratify our solidarity with the Government of National Reconciliation and Unity of Nicaragua.
We reiterate our support to the inalienable right of the people of Puerto Rico to self-determination and independence.
The sister nations of Africa and the Caribbean deserve a fair and differentiated treatment, as well as the reparations for the horrors of colonialism and the transatlantic slave trade.
We reaffirm our solidarity with the Saharan people and their right to self-determination.
We ratify our support to the “One China” principle.

We strongly believe that the current trend of international relations of disrespect for International Law and the United Nations, the imposition of the unilateral will of the mightiest over other countries by means of intimidation and coercion, is dangerous and unsustainable.
The law of the jungle cannot be the future of humanity.
To prevent those practices, in addition of promoting peace and justice, the preceding generations founded the United Nations and for decades developed and enriched its activity.
Let us recover its role today, when we are perhaps in time to do so, before the Organization goes down in history as an unrealized dream of great promises.

In the year of the centennial birthday of Fidel Castro Ruz, the historical leader of the Cuban Revolution, let us be confident, as he was, that if we struggle with resolve, a better world will be possible.
Homeland or Death, We Shall Overcome!
Eighty-one years after its birth, that HOPE is being tested.
Technology, including Artificial Intelligence, is advancing at rapid speed.
Climate change is reshaping our societies.
The international landscape is becoming more complex, more contested and more unpredictable.
The international order is not simply changing.
It is being tested in an unprecedented manner.
But, it is in such times of uncertainty, that the foundational values of Multilateralism must be protected: International Law. The UN Charter.
Respect for Sovereignty and Territorial Integrity.
All these are not principles of the Past.
They are principles that transcend time.
The essential ingredient for the Present and for the Future.
The challenge before us is therefore clear: as the World changes, our Institutions must be able to respond to new realities and threats.
While guided by the painful lessons of history AND the vision of the founding fathers of this Organisation.
This is the essence of the theme of the 81st General Assembly: “Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all.”
What must remain constant is the UN Charter as our compass.
Irrespective of Power, Size and Leverage.
For small-sized countries, the principle of equality of States is fundamental.
And it has formed the binding Trust between us.
We rely on an International System in which sovereignty and territorial integrity are respected.
We expect International Law, including the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, to be applied consistently.
We believe in the peaceful resolution of disputes.
AND we demand that the rights of every state are protected.
These, are the integral elements of our Collective Trust.
And this, is the code of conduct of Cyprus’ diplomatic engagement.
And in a rapidly changing world, small and medium-sized States must seek synergies, while continuing to pursue strategic autonomy.
Preserving Trust, also requires Institutions capable of responding to the World as it is today: The United Nations must, therefore, continue to evolve.
The UN80 Initiative is an important part of this effort.
The Pact for the Future, and the 2030 Agenda and its Sustainable Development Goals, are also part of the effort to ensure that Multilateral Cooperation can respond to the needs of our time.
This moment of Reform also comes as Secretary-General, António Guterres, approaches the completion of a decade leading this Organization.
But reforming our structural set-up is only part of the answer.
What is also needed, is the genuine willingness of Member States to contribute and protect the Multilateral System.
After all, States bring different Capabilities, Experiences and Perspectives.
But together, we can help shape them.
There is no doubt that the challenges of today require cooperation and partnerships based on the knowledge of regions and of their realities.
AND The Republic of Cyprus has consistently sought to do exactly that.
And it has built the capabilities for it.
Our geographical position, at the crossroads of Europe, Asia and Africa, places us close to some of the most complex dynamics of our World.
At the same time, it gives us the opportunity to actively contribute to address them.

Following the Hamas terrorist attack of October 7, 2023, and the devastating humanitarian situation in Gaza, Cyprus, in addition to having dedicated more than 25% of its humanitarian assistance budget to Palestine, has put forward the Amalthea Maritime Humanitarian Corridor.
Cyprus could offer something specific: its geographical position, its infrastructure, its excellent relationships with all countries in the region and the will to engage with international partners.
Through cooperation, including with the UN2720 Mechanism, that idea became a proposal, and evolved into a functioning humanitarian route.
One that keeps delivering as we speak.
Cyprus has ALSO played a constructive role in times of Emergency.
When third-country nationals needed to be evacuated from our neighbourhood, my country has served, time and time again, as a safe harbour.
Our infrastructure and our resources, have been made available in order to facilitate safe passage for people in danger.
In the last three years alone, we helped evacuate thousands of citizens from 70 different countries.
AND through CyprusAid, we have provided humanitarian assistance to countries facing natural disasters.
Cyprus was among the first responders following the catastrophic earthquake in Venezuela and the flashfloods in Nepal.

The devastating humanitarian situation in Sudan, and in the wider Sahel region, have also been a priority for my country, with a large percentage of our available earmarked resources directed to the region.
Rising Temperatures, Water Scarcity and Extreme Weather affect us all.
In the Eastern Mediterranean and the Middle East, the interwoven political realities that we are facing, are further amplified by the climate crisis.
Cooperation is therefore the only answer.
This is the purpose of Cyprus’ Regional Initiative on Climate Change: to bring together countries of our region, thus strengthening our collective capacity for adaptation, mitigation and resilience.
ANOTHER manifestation of this, is the Cyprus Regional Aerial Firefighting Station.

Hosted at Paphos Air Base and supported by the European Union, it offers an operational hub for aerial firefighting and rapid response, and a Centre of Excellence for training, interoperability and capacity-building.
Reflecting its emphasis on regional ownership, it brings together partners from the Middle East, North Africa and the Gulf.
This commitment to regional engagement is ALSO demonstrated through the Cyprus Center for Land, Open Seas and Port Security, jointly created with the United States.
In its four years of operation, it has provided specialized training to thousands of government officials from more than 50 countries, from the Middle East, Africa, Central Asia, and Europe.
The ability to bring different interests together was ALSO at the heart of Cyprus’ Presidency of the Council of the European Union, during the first half of this year.
For six months, a country of fewer than one million people, assumed the responsibility of steering the work of a Union of four hundred and fifty million European citizens.
For Cyprus, this was both a Responsibility and an Opportunity: to listen, to negotiate, to build consensus.
And to help the European Union and its Member States move forward on common priorities.
Our size did not diminish the responsibility to lead.
Nor did it diminish our ability to fulfil it.
Our position is CLEAR: In an era of polycrises, isolation is the antithesis of Responsibility and a Luxury we cannot afford.
Cyprus proved to be an Active and Responsible party of the international community.
A contributor in crisis management, an actor in humanitarian assistance, a proponent of regional synergies and a defender of the protection of human rights and multilateralism.
Esteemed Delegates, In these times of transformation, the Credibility of the UN must be safeguarded.
And credibility requires consistency in the application of International Law.
For my country, Cyprus, this is not an abstract principle.
It is a painful, existential reality.
Fifty-two years have passed since the illegal Turkish invasion of Cyprus.
An act of aggression, violating the core principles of the UN Charter.
An ongoing, flagrant violation of International Law, with more than a third of the territory of the Republic of Cyprus remaining under Turkish occupation.
For fifty-two years, the tens of thousands of displaced and their descendants are prevented from returning to their homes.
For fifty-two years, Varosha remains sealed off, with Turkey still in defiance of its clear and specific obligations set out in the relevant UN Security Council Resolutions.

For fifty-two years, we are experiencing violations of fundamental human rights; the destruction of religious and cultural heritage; AND the organized transfer of settlers amounting to demographic change.
Pain and immense suffering are the daily reality of the relatives of the missing persons, that to this day are demanding answers as to the fate of their loved ones.
AND for fifty-two years, the principles at stake have remained the same.
Respect for Sovereignty and Territorial Integrity are not rhetorical vehicles.
Nor are they to be applied selectively, depending on who the perpetrator is.
These principles do not become less important with the passage of time.
Nor do the Resolutions of this Organization.
UN Resolutions cannot be upheld in one case and disregarded in another.
And the Sovereignty and Territorial Integrity of a state cannot depend on its Size, its Power or the Passage of time.
AND This is not only a question for Cyprus.
It goes to the credibility of the International System itself.

If we ask states to believe in Multilateralism, if we expect them to be active contributors, then they must be able to Trust that the principles and decisions of our Institutions will be upheld without exception.
This consistency matters, particularly for States whose security rests on the protection afforded by International Law, rather than on the Balance of Power.

I listened very carefully to the speech of President Erdogan yesterday: references to International Law, to the respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all states, to illegal occupation, to the drama of refugees.
Yet, in relation to Cyprus, Turkey is doing exactly the opposite.
President Erdogan also quoted extensively from the UN Charter.
But politicians are judged not by their words but by their deeds.
Mr. Erdogan, if you want to quote from the Charter, you must first apply it.
The UN Security Council has established the framework for the settlement of the Cyprus problem.
That framework, of a Bizonal Bicommunal Federation with political equality remains the ONLY basis, on which a comprehensive settlement must be reached.
I remain fully committed to achieving a comprehensive settlement.
I am ready to resume negotiations from where they were left off in 2017, building on the substantial work already achieved, within the agreed United Nations framework.
The common ground is there: the relevant Resolutions of the United Nations Security Council, International Law, and the laws, values, and principles of the European Union.
What is now required, is Political Will by all parties.
A genuine willingness to return to meaningful negotiations.
To build on the body of work already achieved.
AND to reach a settlement that reunifies our country and our people.
A settlement that allows Greek Cypriots, Turkish Cypriots, Maronites, Armenians, and Latins, to live together in Peace, Security and Prosperity.
On my side (let me REPEAT it), I am fully committed.
Because Division will not be accepted.
This cannot and will not be the future for my country and my people. Ever.
Our determination to reunify our island is firm.
I therefore call on my Turkish Cypriot compatriots to perceive our future together as the opportunity for prosperity.
AND I call on President Erdogan to give the green light for substantive negotiations within the UN-agreed framework.
I mentioned several times how Change is inevitable.
But the Choices we make in response to Change, are ours.
For countries like Cyprus, the answer must be cooperation with purpose.
Partnerships that deliver when they are needed.
Formed by the belief that in times of need, we must act together.
This is the choice to make.
We can allow divisions to weaken the Institutions we built together.
Or, we can choose to strengthen them.
We can allow differences in power to determine whose voice matters.
Or, we can reaffirm the principles on which this Organization was founded.
For Cyprus, there is no such dilemma: We believe in a United Nations that protects the principles of its Charter and has the capacity to act upon them.
We believe in a Multilateral System in which every state has both rights and responsibilities.
AND we believe that small-sized states have a particular role to play: NOT on the margins of international affairs but as active participants in shaping our common future.

For the Republic of Cyprus, that means Defending the principles on which we depend, Contributing to the institutions in which we believe, Building partnerships for the common good, Taking initiatives to create useful synergies, and Acting responsibly where we can affect change.
Your Excellencies, Despite the challenges because of the Turkish occupation, we remain resilient and steadfast in our faith in the Multilateral system.
Because in the end, the strength of Multilateralism is measured by whether every Member State believes that its voice matters, its rights are protected and its contribution has value.
That is how we restore Trust.
That is how we manage Transformation.
And that is how we build a United Nations that truly delivers for All.
“Restoring trust, managing transformation” is a fitting theme for this year’s session.
It reflects both the scale of the changes our world is undergoing, and the need to navigate them responsibly.
After the Second World War, a robust multilateral system based on rules and global cooperation was built, spanning security, human rights and economic development.
For decades, shifts in global power unfolded within this largely predictable framework.
Power has always been unevenly distributed.
Today, however, we are witnessing profound changes that are reshaping the post-war system.
The task of the international order is not to resist these changes, but to manage them peacefully.

Our shared ambition should be to draw inspiration from the founders of the United Nations: our goal should be to prevent war and destruction, and to build a predictable international order capable of adapting to change, while providing fairness and stability.
This is precisely why we need forums like this one, places where dialogue can prevail and diplomacy can work.
This is why we need rules.
Not because all states are equally powerful, but precisely because they are not.
Rules have value only if they bind everyone, especially those powerful enough to break them.
When rules are cast aside, raw power fills the vacuum.
A world dominated by great-power competition is a volatile world, less able to address the most pressing challenges of our time.
It is a world where a single spark can ignite a fire.
Instead, we should insist that with greater power comes greater responsibility.
Responsibility in the use of force.
But also responsibility to use one’s influence to prevent force from becoming necessary in the first place.
This applies particularly to permanent members of the UN Security Council.
China has the power, influence and responsibility to help prevent conflicts, de-escalate tensions and contribute to ending wars.
This includes using its influence to help bring Russia’s aggression against Ukraine to an end.

That aggression was launched, and continues to be waged, by another permanent member of the UN Security Council – Russia – in violation of the UN Charter and fundamental principles of international law.
Russia’s aggression continues to inflict enormous suffering on the Ukrainian people.
Civilians and civilian infrastructure continue to be attacked indiscriminately.
And the risks are growing day the day.
Russia’s aggressive posture poses a direct threat to European security as a whole.
The immediacy of that threat was starkly illustrated by the recent attempted Russian drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany, only 150 kilometres from the borders of the Czech Republic.
The consequences of aggression reach far beyond Europe.
Russia’s war has undermined global food security, disrupting agricultural production, exports and supply chains.
Its effects are felt in my country, but even more acutely in parts of Africa and elsewhere, particularly in countries that depend on stable and affordable food supplies.
While we need to raise the costs of war for Russia, we must give serious diplomatic efforts a genuine chance.
Diplomacy matters most not between friends, but between adversaries.
That is where the United Nations remains indispensable: as a forum for dialogue, even when agreement seems very distant.
The UN was founded on principles.
They matter in the South China Sea and across the Taiwan Strait.
And they also matter in the Middle East, in Sudan or the DRC.

The current developments in Yemen and Saudi Arabia demonstrate what happens when rules give way to force and coercion, when might replaces right – and how a regional conflict can, in an instant, have consequences for the entire world.
Ladies and Gentlemen, as Secretary-General António Guterres nears the end of his mandate, we commend his efforts to reform and modernize the United Nations.
The next Secretary-General will face a defining task: adapting the United Nations to a world of growing geopolitical rivalry and fragmentation.
We expect her or him to carry forward the UN80 agenda and turn reforms into results.
The success of UN reform will be judged not by new structures or new language, but by whether the multilateral system can deliver, uphold international law and make its rules matter.
The future legitimacy of the United Nations will depend on it.
Nowhere is this more important than in peace and security.
The international community must become better at preventing crises, protecting civilians and defending the rules it has agreed to uphold.
The Czech Republic is ready to do its part.
Let me reiterate that we are seeking a non-permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council for 2032–2033.
If elected, we will contribute actively to its work and shoulder our share of responsibility.
We will continue to help preventing and resolving conflicts through political engagement, humanitarian assistance and practical cooperation.
We will stand for the protection of civilians and critical infrastructure, and for accountability when international law is seriously violated.
And we will remain a strong advocate for human rights and democracy.
We willsupport independent human rights mechanisms, peaceful assembly and free and fair elections.
And we will work to ensure that new technologies strengthen our societies rather than weaken them.
Mr. President, this is also the moment to confront the extraordinary pace of advances in artificial intelligence.
In recent days, the debate has acquired a new sense of urgency and gravity.

The message from the UN’s Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, researchers in leading AI companies, and independent experts is increasingly clear: our ability to govern this technology is not keeping pace with its development.
AI can bring enormous benefits to humanity.
But without effective safeguards, it can also cause immense harm.
We must therefore hold on to a basic principle: human beings must remain in control of technology, not become subject to it.
Technology should advance our common goals, and no system should ever operate beyond human responsibility and accountability.
Nor can we allow an unchecked race to determine the future of AI, with the pressure to move first pushing safety, oversight and responsibility aside.

More than eighty years ago, the Manhattan Project showed how rapidly a scientific breakthrough can transform the balance of power – and how difficult it is for politics and international rules to catch up.
Artificial intelligence confronts us with a different technology and different risks, but with a similar lesson: governance that comes only after the fact may come too late.
If AI is to serve humanity, it must develop within a framework of international rules.
No country, and no company, can meet this challenge alone.
We need common standards, meaningful public oversight and clear mechanisms of accountability.
The choice is not between innovation and rules.
It is between innovation governed by rules and innovation governed by the logic of the race.
Ladies and Gentlemen, artificial intelligence is not the only challenge that no country can manage alone.
The same is true of climate change.
This year has once again reminded us of the growing impact of extreme weather, affecting people and communities across the globe.
In many regions, climate-related challenges are threatening homes and livelihoods.
They are putting pressure on public health, food and water security, increasing living costs and, in some cases, contributing to instability and conflicts.
The most vulnerable are often hit hardest.The Czech Republic has offered its support and stands with those working to rebuild their communities.
But support after disaster is not enough.
We need concerted global action – both to limit further damage and to adapt to changes that are already affecting our lives and will shape the lives of future generations.
Mr. President, let me finish with a message that has not changed over the past year: Most of the challenges we face are global.
No nation can meet them alone.
That is why we need more dialogue, more cooperation and more collective action.
And that is why we must make multilateralism work.

Bundesminister Dr. Johann Wadephul Rede vor der Generalversammlung der Vereinten Nationen 15 Minuten 26.09.2026, New York City Mr President, Imagine if nuclear weapons were developed by private companies.
If stockpiles were located on company grounds.
And launch codes locked away in a safe in a CEO’s office.
When a technology has the power to fundamentally change the world, possibly even determine the fate of humanity – we need to ask: Who controls it?
Today humankind faces another technological revolution that raises exactly these questions.
Engineers have developed a technology that does not need to be launched from a rocket or a submarine to change the course of history.
I am, of course, talking about artificial intelligence.
A technology with seemingly unlimited power.
In the wrong hands, it can upend our economies and threaten our livelihoods.
It has the potential to erode trust within our societies by spreading information that appears real but is, in fact, fake.
A.I. can endanger the infrastructure that keeps our societies running.
And ultimately, it can influence decisions that determine global peace and security.
At the same time, artificial intelligence holds extraordinary promise.
Improve healthcare and education all over the world.
Provide opportunities for economic development, overcome inequalities and help us address challenges that no country can solve alone.
Just imagine a world, where with the help of A.I. we can prevent famine and cure cancer.
This is precisely what makes AI so powerful – for better or for worse.
But there is a critical tension.
Only two major countries are home to the companies holding the vast majority of all global A.I. patents.
That puts an enormous amount of influence in the hands of a very few.
Such power carries responsibility – not only towards customers, shareholders or governments.
And whenever power becomes global, responsibility must become global, too.
The United Nations was created precisely for a moment such as this.
When a challenge is too large for any one nation to address alone.

When risks need to be managed to protect people all over the world, and when opportunities need to be exploited in a way that benefits the largest and the smallest, the richest and the poorest member states.
But today, the United Nations itself is under pressure.
There are great powers that believe they fare better if they ignore the rules enshrined in the UN Charter.
The erosion of international law jeopardises the enormous civilisational progress that the United Nations stands for.
The principle of sovereign equality of all states.
The belief in norms and rules.
The conviction of the dignity inherent in every human being.
The erosion of these principles may serve the interests of a few.
Who believe themselves powerful enough to survive in a world without norms – or to write their own rules.
For us, for the overwhelming majority of the 193 states represented in this General Assembly, this is harmful.
We know that the people of this world will pay the price if the respect for international law erodes.
And if its institutions are under attack.
For some of us, this erosion of the international order is already catastrophic.
If it continues, we all stand to lose.
But this pressure on the international order does not come from political actors alone.
It also comes from the forces of technological revolution.
This poses a crucial question: how do we enable our international institutions to keep pace with the technologies that are reshaping our world?
Faced with this question, it will not be enough to invoke what we still have – or once had – in the United Nations.
Nor will it help if we ignore its weaknesses.
What we need is honesty, realism and cooperation.
Honesty in our analysis, realism in our ambition and cooperation as our method.
We must acknowledge that many of the beams of this common house cannot carry the burden we put on them.
We must decide: which parts of the house do we preserve, and which do we rebuild?
For this endeavor to succeed we need the new Secretary-General to lead a profound process of reform.
Above all, we must close the gap between what we expect from the United Nations and the capabilities we give to the organisation.
First, we need a functioning UN that plays an active role in resolving conflicts – rather than merely managing them.
In times when the Security Council, as the central decision-making body, is paralyzed, this is more difficult than ever.
We need to keep its reform high on our agenda.
Germany stands up for peace and security.
Today, more people than ever are affected by violent conflict.
At the same time, for every member state, resources are limited.
Thus, we have to join forces to bring conflicts to an end.
Today, Germany is the largest supporter of Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression.
This aggression has been condemned consistently by an overwhelming majority here in the General Assembly.
Russia’s war targets the lives of millions of innocent people, the existence of the Ukrainian state and culture and the European peace order.
It puts vital grain deliveries for millions of people at risk, particularly in Africa, Asia and the Middle East.
It shows contempt for the Charter and for the common order on which we stand.
That is why we will continue to urge Russia to finally come to the negotiating table.
I call on every member state to join us in convincing Russia that the future is built at the negotiating table, not on dead bodies in cities and villages.
The day when negotiations finally begin will be a good day for the United Nations.

Germany is also taking on responsibility for peace and security beyond Europe – for example, in Haiti, where we have significantly increased our contribution to the international mission to combat gang crime.
Also, we shall not forget Sudan.
At the Sudan conference in Berlin in April, together with our partners we mobilized more than 1,7 billion Dollars to alleviate the biggest humanitarian catastrophe of our time.
Second, we stand for international cooperation that is peaceful, fair and based on equality.
A new nationalism would be a misguided path.
Whatever its prophets may preach, the truth is, that it would make our lives narrower, poorer and less secure.
Instead, global trade relations need to be diversified and deepened – in the framework of a fair trading order.
No country should have to accept raw materials being used to force obedience.
Or supply chains becoming instruments of pressure.
None of us is powerless in the face of this.
Where we cooperate, we free ourselves from one-sided dependencies and open up new spaces of freedom.
With our partners in the European Union, we have begun this work through new trade accords, cooperation agreements and partnerships.
These partnerships are built on mutual respect, on common rules and a shared respect for international law.
They also take into account the fortunate fact that many countries of the Global South are developing with extraordinary success.
The same principle of partnership and cooperation also applies to technology.
Access to computing power, data, expertise and infrastructure will increasingly shape who can innovate – and who merely has to accept the rules set by others.
Cooperation must therefore create capabilities, not new dependencies.
Third, we want to answer the great global questions of our time together.
No one here – not even the largest among us – can do this alone.
Together with all those who are willing to do so, we will continue our work to address human-made climate change and its devastating effects swiftly and effectively.
We are forced to chart new courses, and we must do it with speed.
But nowhere is the need more pressing than in the area of artificial intelligence.
It is our collective responsibility to ensure that this technology serves human dignity.
This is particularly urgent because technologies are already changing the foundations of our societies.
A.I. is not waiting for our institutions to catch up.
Our institutions have to catch up with reality.
At the beginning of my remarks, I asked three questions: who controls new technologies?
We cannot answer them by simply trusting that those with the greatest capabilities will always act in the interest of everyone else.
We need to ensure that technological progress is guided by a framework that we all have a say in shaping.
That means building the capacity to understand and assess increasingly capable A.I. systems.
It means making sure that all regions can participate in shaping the rules.
And it means moving from voluntary commitments towards increasing transparency, as well as developing common standards.
That is why Germany calls on UN member states to work towards common safety requirements for the most capable A.I. models.
Providers should be required to test these models before release and report serious safety failures.
These requirements should be supported by effective national and regional oversight.
The A.I. industry will have to play its role in this and continue to bear a responsibility in shaping the trajectory of this technology.
At the same time, we need to ensure accountability, in particular when global peace and security are potentially affected.
In the course of this week, we have intensified our conversation about these questions.
How we address A.I. together, is one of the clearest tests of whether we have the strength and the will to build a United Nations for today’s world.
The next Secretary-General can count on Germany along this path.
Our history, our geography and our constitution bind us to the UN Charter and to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
This is at the very core of our statehood.
But one principle will remain: power must be bound by responsibility.
And progress must serve human dignity.
The world has long been in a mode of permanent escalation.
And with it, the UN is navigating stormy waters.
We must decide: are we truly willing to let the boat we all share drift toward capsizing, or will we pool our strength and steer it back on course?
The tools are in our hands.
Together, we can push for renewal and build a peaceful future for generations to come.

PRESS RELEASE DJIBOUTI STATEMENT BY H.E. MR. ABDOULKADER HOUSSEIN OMAR MINISTER FOR FOREIGN AFFAIRS AND INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION, GOVERNMENT SPOKESPERSON OF THE REPUBLIC OF DJIBOUTI DURING THE GENERAL DEBATE OF THE EIGHTY-FIRST SESSION OF THE UNITED NATIONS GENERAL ASSEMBLY SATURDAY, 26 SEPTEMBER 2026 To be checked against delivery PERMANENT MISSION OF THE REPUBLIC OF DJIBOUTI TO THE UNITED NATIONS 866 U.N. Plaza, Suite 4011, New York, NY 10017 • Tel: (212) 753-3163 • Fax: (212) 223-1276 • E-mail: djibouti@nyct.net • Web: www.un.int/djibouti Bismillahi alrahman alrahim At the outset of my remarks, I would first and foremost like to convey to this august Assembly the greetings of His Excellency Ismaïl Omar Guelleh, President of the Republic of Djibouti.
The Republic of Djibouti welcomes the choice of the theme of this session: “Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations Organization in the service of all.”
(3) This theme is particularly relevant in the current international context.

We are living through a critical moment, exacerbated by the proliferation of conflicts, the deepening of existing crises and the emergence of new crises with devastating political, economic, humanitarian and security consequences.

Faced with these challenges, we must reaffirm the essential mission of the United Nations and strengthen renewed multilateralism, more inclusive and more effective, that fully takes into account the interests of all States, large and small.
(4) The region to which my country belongs also continues to face crises whose consequences extend beyond national borders.
Djibouti is following with grave concern the situation in Yemen, whose effects we are directly feeling with the recent arrival on our territory of several thousand people fleeing the violence.
This situation is already placing heavy pressure on the host communities of the Obock region as well as on the reception capacities of the Markazi site.
Djibouti will not be able to shoulder alone the growing needs in terms of shelter, food and essential services.

We therefore reiterate our appeal to the international community to strengthen its support and enable us to respond adequately to this influx, whose number could reach 10,000 persons, according to United Nations estimates.
To prevent the prolongation of this humanitarian crisis, we renew our call for de-escalation and for a lasting political solution in Yemen to preserve human lives.
(5) With regard to Somalia, we remain fully committed alongside the Somali people and Government to consolidating peace and stability.
The international community must preserve the security gains and continue to support the Somali authorities so that they may fully assume their responsibilities and protect their institutions.
In this regard, we recognize the crucial role played by AUSSOM in the stabilization of the country, as well as the decisive support provided by the United Nations, in particular by UNSOS.

We hope that the international community will continue to remain mobilized in order to enable Somalis to assume on a lasting basis their security, sovereignty and the safeguarding of the integrity of their national territory.

(6) With regard to the Sudan, Djibouti, in its capacity as current Chair of IGAD, welcomes that brotherly country’s return to full participation within our regional organization, of which it is a founding member.
We call for priority to be given to de-escalation and the resumption of talks.
Only an inclusive political solution, placing the Sudanese people at the centre of every approach, will make it possible to restore peace and stability on a lasting basis.
We also call on foreign influences to avoid fueling this war through negative interference.
(7) We also once again extend a hand to our Eritrean neighbour.

Djibouti remains convinced that dialogue and negotiation, in full respect for international law, constitute the only path towards a peaceful and definitive settlement of our border dispute, as well as the return of our prisoners of war, who have been held incommunicado for more than eighteen years.

(8) The Republic of Djibouti also reaffirms its unwavering solidarity with the Palestinian people and its full and complete support for their legitimate rights, in particular their inalienable right to the establishment of an independent and sovereign State.
We reaffirm our commitment to a two-State solution, based on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as the capital of the State of Palestine, as the path towards a just and lasting peace.

(9) We strongly condemn the illegal colonization, the violence committed against civilians, in particular by Israeli settlers in the West Bank, forced displacement and any policy aimed at changing the demographic and territorial reality of the Occupied Palestinian Territory.
The situation in Gaza remains a tragedy that requires an immediate response from the international community.
The protection of civilians must be guaranteed, humanitarian aid must reach without hindrance those who need it, and violations of international humanitarian law must cease and must be condemned.
Djibouti will continue to support efforts aimed at putting an end to the suffering of the Palestinian people and ensuring the triumph of justice, peace and international law.
Preserving freedom of navigation in the Red Sea, and more particularly in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, constitutes a major geopolitical and economic issue for regional and global stability.
This vital maritime passage is a lifeline for international trade, and any impediment to its free movement would risk seriously affecting supply chains and energy security.
Although Djibouti has observed no disruption in passage through the Strait to date, the authorities of my country remain particularly vigilant in the face of the current tensions shaking the region.
Mr. President, the climate emergency constitutes one of the most pressing challenges facing our international community.
For Djibouti, an African coastal country, this emergency is inseparable from that of development.
Rising sea levels represent a direct and growing threat to our populations and our ecosystems.
Djibouti, like many developing countries, contributes only marginally to global emissions, yet remains particularly exposed to the consequences of climate disruption.
This situation underscores a profound injustice: the countries that have contributed least to climate change are often those that suffer its gravest consequences.

We must therefore accelerate the implementation of the Paris Agreement and strengthen our efforts in adaptation and resilience, in particular through resilient coastal infrastructure, better protection of marine and coastal ecosystems, early warning systems and simplified, predictable and equitable access to climate finance.
For Djibouti, climate action must not be dissociated from development.
On the contrary, it must help transform our economies, develop renewable energy, create jobs and open up new prospects for investment and innovation.

It is in this spirit that the Government is working to operationalize the mechanisms provided for under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, through a strong, transparent and credible national framework for carbon markets, in order to mobilize new resources, attract investment, promote technology transfer and strengthen national capacities.
Developing countries continue to face high financing costs, external vulnerabilities and limited fiscal space.
Access to climate finance and reform of the international financial architecture therefore remain essential.

In this regard, the Seville Compromise constitutes an important step, and its commitments must now be translated into tangible results, notably through better access to concessional financing, enhanced debt sustainability and increased mobilization of public and private capital in support of development.
We must also strengthen South-South cooperation and triangular cooperation in order to share technologies, knowledge and solutions adapted to the realities of our countries.

Africa must not be viewed merely as a space of climate vulnerability; it must be recognized as an actor capable of innovating, proposing solutions and contributing to the transformation of the global economy.
Beyond climate action, the 2030 Agenda remains at the heart of our vision for development.
Djibouti’s economy is demonstrating resilience, driven in particular by port and logistics activities, trade, telecommunications, energy and investment.
Djibouti intends to consolidate its role as a regional platform while accelerating the diversification of its economy.

By way of illustration, as recently as this week, the launch of works for the modern construction of petroleum products storage and transport infrastructure, in particular oil and gas pipelines in Djibouti, which will link Djibouti and Ethiopia, illustrates this ambition for energy sovereignty and security, regional integration and economic transformation.
But growth must above all translate into jobs, social progress and opportunities, especially for women and young people.
We are continuing our investments in education, health, human capital as well as in the green and digital transitions.

Achieving the Sustainable Development Goals and implementing the African Union’s Agenda 2063 require a collective surge: the climate emergency demands action, development demands investment, and peace and humanitarian crises demand solidarity.
The digital transition and artificial intelligence also offer new possibilities for accelerating development and improving the capacities of our States.
However, their potential can be fully realized only if we bridge the digital divide, facilitate technology-sharing and strengthen the capacities of developing countries.

It is with this in mind that Djibouti supports the intergovernmental “Beyond GDP” process, which seeks to complement traditional economic indicators with measures that better take into account the well-being of populations, social inclusion and environmental sustainability.

Djibouti supports efforts to adapt the United Nations to current challenges and strengthen its effectiveness, but we must make it clear that our Organization does not exist solely to balance accounting ledgers, but to serve our peoples and give effect to the decisions we take collectively.
Any reform must remain guided by the mandates established by Member States and preserve the balance among the three pillars: peace and security, development and human rights.
Lastly, we are following very closely the process aimed at identifying the most qualified person to serve as Secretary-General of the United Nations for the next term.

This selection must be guided by competence, professional integrity, an unequivocal commitment to respect for international law and the ability to carry forward with rigor the reforms on which the Member States have collectively agreed.
I bring greetings to this Assembly from the People and Government of the Commonwealth of Dominica.
This theme speaks directly to the defining challenges of our time.
We are living through an age of profound transformation.
Technology is changing how we work, communicate and understand the world.
Climate change is reshaping economies, communities and entire ecosystems.
Conflicts are destroying lives and displacing families.
Economic uncertainty is deepening inequality, while progress towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals has stalled.
These challenges are not unfolding in isolation.
They are interconnected, global in scale and beyond the capacity of any one nation to address alone.
They demand stronger cooperation and renewed confidence in multilateralism.
Yet, Excellencies, at the very moment when collective action is most urgently needed, this Organization stands at a crossroads.
The question before us, therefore, is whether we possess the courage, solidarity and political will to shape that change and guide our world towards peace, justice and shared prosperity.
The UN already Delivers for All.
I strongly believe that most right-thinking individuals would agree that the UN System has substantially delivered for all countries over the several decades of its existence.

For more than eighty years, this organization has embodied humanity’s highest collective aspiration, that countries, large and small, rich and poor, can work together to prevent conflict, protect human dignity and improve the lives of their people.
The United Nations provides shelter and protection to people enduring conflict, displacement and natural disaster.
It supports education, healthcare, peacekeeping, elections and development in communities that might otherwise be forgotten.
These achievements matter and must never be dismissed or diminished.
What the United Nations does not currently do enough, is deliver at the transformative level.

Too often, humanity, and the institutions we have created to serve us, have had to concentrate on managing one crisis after another, without giving enough attention to the conditions that allow them to persist.
Excellencies, there is no question that managing crises is necessary.
It brings relief, restores hope and saves lives.
Our responsibility must also be to address the root causes of these problems and build systems that are fairer, stronger and better able to serve our people.
The true test of this Organization, therefore, is not only how well we respond after people have suffered.
It is also whether we can work together to prevent that suffering in the first place.
This is not to dismiss what has already been achieved.
It is a call for us to build on that progress, strengthen our cooperation, and deliver the meaningful change that our people expect from us.
A fundamental question that one must ask is “Can the international system still deliver?”
For Dominica, this is not an abstract question.

When a hurricane destroys our infrastructure, when international energy prices rise, when access to capital becomes more expensive, when global markets change or when climate finance remains beyond our reach, the consequences are felt immediately - in our homes, in our businesses, in our schools and hospitals, and in the very lives of our people.
Yet, Mr. President, I do not come before this Assembly to speak only of vulnerability.
I wish to speak of transformation and resilience.
We have chosen not only to rebuild after disaster, but to build differently, build better, build stronger.
We have chosen not only to adapt to climate change, but to demonstrate what a climate-resilient economy and country can look like.
And we have chosen to move from dependence to greater self-reliance.
FROM VULNERABILITY TO RESILIENCE Mr. President, In 2017, Category Five Hurricane Maria demonstrated with devastating force the vulnerability of small island states like Dominica.
The economic and human consequences were enormous.
Hurricane Maria however, also taught us an important lesson: Resilience should never begin after the disaster.
The international community must therefore move from a model that primarily finances reconstruction after catastrophe, to one that invests systematically in resilience before disaster strikes.
For Dominica, this means resilient roads and bridges, resilient buildings, reliable communications, modern water systems, strengthened health infrastructure and disaster-ready communities.
But resilience is not only physical.
A resilient country must have resilient institutions.
It must have resilient public finances.
It must have resilient energy systems and must have resilient food systems.
Above all, a resilient nation must have people who possess the skills and confidence to withstand shocks and move forward.
That is the Dominica that we are building.
THE ENERGY TRANSFORMATION Dominica has begun the transition from imported fossil fuels to renewable energy.
Our geothermal power plant is now in commercial operation, and increasing the renewable share of our electricity generation to approximately 84 percent.
We are well on our way to achieving 100% renewable energy by 2030.
This is more than an energy project.
It demonstrates that small states can lead in the transition to clean energy.
Every barrel of oil that we no longer need to import, strengthens our resilience to international price shocks.
Every unit of clean electricity we produce strengthens our energy security.
Affordable, reliable renewable energy can become a foundation for new industries, new investment, new employment and greater competitiveness.
The lesson is important beyond Dominica.
We need international finance that recognises the transformative nature of renewable energy investment in vulnerable countries.
We need financing mechanisms that allow countries such as Dominica to move faster.
And we need partnerships that allow the energy transition to become an engine of economic development and growth.
Our ambition is not merely to generate clean electricity.
Our ambition is to use clean energy to transform our economy.
Finance Must Change The international community has become very good at recognising vulnerability.
We have become less successful at financing the transformation that vulnerability requires.
Too often, the cycle is predictable: A disaster occurs.
Infrastructure is destroyed and economic activity collapses.
We then mobilise resources to rebuild what was lost, often through borrowing that substantially increases debt to rebuild what we could have made more resilient from the outset.
This is not an efficient financial model.
The best time to build resilience is before disaster.
The best time to finance transformation is before crisis.
And the value of resilience should be measured not only by what we build, but by what we prevent from being destroyed.
Dominica does not come to the United Nations asking to be treated as a victim of vulnerability.
We come asking to be recognised as a partner in transformation.
We must finance potential - not merely manage vulnerability.
And this is not only about Dominica.
It is about whether the global financial system is capable of recognising a different development model.
A model in which resilience is an investment.
And prevention is financially smarter than reconstruction.
That is the proposition we place before this Assembly.
It is time that the international financial architecture evolves.
Dominica joins its voice with those countries that continue to advocate for the use of multidimensional vulnerability as a practical and fair basis in determining access to development finance.
We call for greater and easier access to concessional financing and grants for adaptation.
We call for stronger disaster clauses in sovereign debt instruments.
We call for financing mechanisms that can be activated rapidly when disasters strike.
And we call for a fundamental shift in the way the international community views investment in resilience.
Every dollar spent preventing the destruction of a road, a hospital, a school or a water system is an investment in future development.
Dominica is prepared to serve as a demonstration country for this approach.
We are prepared to work with international partners to show what happens when finance is designed around transformation rather than vulnerability.
Dominica has long spoken of becoming the world's first climate-resilient nation.
Today, I wish to take that ambition further.
We invite the international community to partner with us in making Dominica a living laboratory for climate resilience and sustainable development.
Bring us the technology; Bring us the research; Bring us the investment; Bring us the innovation.
And together, let us demonstrate what a resilient small island economy can look like.

Resilient housing; Smart and renewable energy systems; Climate-smart agriculture; Modern water management; Digital public services; Resilient infrastructure; Nature-based adaptation; And new industries powered by clean energy.
This should not be a relationship based simply on donor and recipient.
It should be a relationship based on partnership, innovation and shared learning.
Dominica has lessons to learn from the world.
But we also have lessons to offer the world.
Transformation Must Create Opportunity Transformation is ultimately about people.
A resilient economy must create opportunity for young people.

Young people want to inherit a country that is not merely protected from disasters, but one in which they can build businesses, work in new industries, participate in the global economy, and build meaningful lives at home.
That is why our investments in energy, connectivity, digital transformation, tourism, agriculture and resilience must ultimately converge around one objective: creating opportunity.
The Wider Challenge to Multilateralism The challenges before us extend beyond climate and finance.
We meet at a time when war continues to devastate communities and ruin lives.
When international law is under pressure.
When trust between nations is strained.
We cannot speak about development without speaking about peace.
We believe in the principles of the United Nations Charter.
We believe in respecting the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states.
We believe in the peaceful settlement of international disputes.
And we believe that international law must apply equally to all nations, and must be applied consistently.
Small states must never become collateral damage in the competition among larger powers.
The security of a small nation is no less important than the security of a large one.
The credibility of multilateralism depends on fairness.
But it also depends on delivery.
The true test of multilateralism is not whether we can agree in this room.
It is whether our agreements can transform lives outside this room.
Restoring Trust That is why I welcome the central challenge of this 81st General Assembly, “restoring trust”.
The world does not need another generation of promises that remain unfulfilled. It needs delivery.
It needs institutions that respond faster.
It needs financing that reaches vulnerable countries more efficiently.
It needs partnerships that produce measurable results.
And it needs a multilateral system that people can believe in again.
For Dominica, restoring trust means closing the gap between international commitments and the lived experience of our people.
It means ensuring that when the world says it supports climate resilience, resources actually reach the communities that need them.
It means ensuring that when we call for sustainable development, financing mechanisms do not make sustainability harder to achieve.
And it means recognising that the challenges confronting small island states are not marginal issues.
They are an early warning of the challenges that the wider world will increasingly face.
The United Nations must remain a place where every country - large or small - can believe that its voice matters.
But the United Nations must also remain a place where ambition can become action.
We must also confront the serious challenges facing the Sustainable Development Goals.

The SDGs represented a promise that, by 2030, we would make meaningful progress in ending poverty and hunger, improving health and education, advancing equality, protecting our planet and building more peaceful and inclusive societies.
Today, that promise is at risk.
Conflict, climate change, debt distress, inflation and persistent inequality have pushed the Goals further out of reach for many developing countries.
But this is not the time to abandon the 2030 Agenda.
It is the time to renew our commitment and concentrate on delivering results that people can see and feel in their daily lives.
For Dominica, we have incorporated the SDG’s as priorities in our National Resilience Development Strategy 2030, our Climate Resilience and Recovery Plan and our wider development agenda.
We see sustainable development in the homes we have built for vulnerable families; in our investment in geothermal energy as cleaner, more affordable and reliable energy.
We see it in our efforts to strengthen education, expand technical and vocational training and better prepare our young people for the world of work.
We see it in our support for farmers, entrepreneurs, agro-processors and tourism operators who are creating jobs and building stronger local industries.
We also see it in our work to protect our forests, marine resources and natural environment.
For Dominica, these resources are part of our identity, but they are also essential to our food security, our tourism product and the livelihoods of our people.
The challenges before us cannot be overcome by any one country acting alone.
They require a strong and effective United Nations, renewed international cooperation and a firm commitment to multilateralism.
We need a United Nations that does more than respond to crises after lives have been lost and communities destroyed.
We need an Organization that works with determination to prevent conflict, advance sustainable development, confront injustice and protect those who are most vulnerable.
We need a system in which every country, regardless of its size, wealth or influence, has a voice and a meaningful place at the table.
We need multilateralism that is not selective in its concern or uneven in its response, but fair, effective and responsive to the needs of all people.
Our development must include young people, women and girls, Indigenous Peoples, persons with disabilities, the elderly and communities that have too often been left behind.
If the United Nations is to deliver for all, it must first see, hear and include all.
Multilateralism is our best hope for addressing challenges that cross borders, threaten our shared future and demand collective action.
We therefore remain committed to peace, climate action, sustainable development and the dignity of every human being.
We remain ready to work with all nations, in a spirit of mutual respect and shared responsibility, to build a fairer, safer and more resilient world.
Mister President Let this Eighty-first Session be remembered as the moment when we collectively renewed our faith in cooperation, and matched our words with action.
Let this Eighty-first Session be remembered as the moment when vulnerability was met with solidarity, promises were honoured and trust was rebuilt through meaningful delivery.

Above all, let this Eighty-first Session be remembered as the moment when this family of nations found the courage to act together and recommitted ourselves to ensuring that no country, no community and no person was left behind.
It helps you find the way; in fair weather as well as in storm.
Eighty-one years ago, the world gave itself a compass.
We named it the United Nations Charter.
It has helped us stay the course, even when the seas have been anything but calm.
It has pointed us toward a world of equal rights, self- determination of peoples and territorial integrity of all states, large and small.
More than a billion people lifted out of poverty.
Colonial empires brought to an end. Independent nations emerged.
Peoples gained the right to shape their own future.
That progress was made possible because we kept consulting the compass.
Today, it seems we are losing our way.
Wars and conflicts are at the highest level since World War II.
Extreme poverty is on the rise.
Extreme weather and climate-related disasters are hitting record highs.
Mistrust, polarisation and divisions are growing, both among states and within societies.
Even the most basic principles of international law, including international humanitarian law, are violated with impunity.
To get back on track, we must turn our attention to the compass.
Respect for the Charter, for human rights, for international law, is not a courtesy we extend when convenient.
These are binding obligations we all agreed to.
Respecting them is the precondition for international peace and security.
We see this clearly in Ukraine.
Russia's illegal war of choice could end tomorrow, if Russia withdrew to its own territory and stopped trying to redraw borders by force.
The vast majority of UN member states and the UN Secretary General support calls for an immediate and comprehensive ceasefire in Ukraine.
It is the only basis for good-faith talks aimed at a just and lasting peace in line with international law, including the UN Charter.
Ukraine has been offering this for a year now.
Denmark's support for Ukraine will remain steadfast.
This is not only a matter of helping Ukraine defend itself.
It is a matter of defending the universal principles upon which this Organisation was built.
In Sudan, the war continues to inflict immense human suffering.
And the international community has been warned of mass atrocities over and over again, but has failed to act.
The responsibility for this horrific war lies in the hands of the warring parties.
Yet, it is fuelled by outside actors and permitted by international inaction.
We must act now to prevent further mass atrocities against the Sudanese people.
We must put our political will and weight behind a stronger demand for peace and accountability.
The warring parties must come to the negotiation table.
And agree on a much-needed truce.
Denmark fully supports the Quintet’s efforts to advance a civilian-led political process and welcomes the improved coordination among mediators.
In Syria, the fall of the brutal Assad-regime offers a historic opportunity to build a brighter future for all Syrians.
Denmark is committed to supporting the people of Syria in a Syrian-led and owned transition.
It is a glimpse of hope in a troubled region.
And a stark contrast to the destabilizing actions of Iran, whose consequences are felt far beyond the region.
Denmark’s position remains clear: Iran must never be allowed to develop or acquire a nuclear weapon.
We strongly support continued diplomatic efforts to restore effective international verification of Iran’s nuclear programme.
And we deeply regret the unwillingness of a few Council members to acknowledge that sanctions measures have been reinstated in full accordance with Security Council resolution 2231.
At the same time, we urge Iran to comply fully with resolution 2817.
Cease attacks against countries in the region and refrain from any actions or threats that undermine freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.
Last year, this Assembly endorsed the New York Declaration – a roadmap toward the two-state solution.
A path to lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians.
Since then, the Comprehensive Plan to end the Gaza Conflict has been endorsed by the Security Council.
Now it must be implemented in full.
We call on all parties to stay committed to the plan.
Yet in Gaza, civilians continue to pay the price.
Far more must be done to secure humanitarian access and long- term peace.
And in the occupied West Bank, settler violence and settlement expansion threaten the daily lives of Palestinians – and undermine the prospects for a future Palestinian state.
As an elected member of the Security Council, Denmark strives to ensure that the Council fulfils its mandate.

This June, the Security Council unanimously adopted resolution 2823 [Twenty-eight twenty-three] on accountability for crimes against UN peacekeepers – led by Denmark and Pakistan, and backed by a record 153 member states.
A clear signal of commitment to the safety and security of the brave men and women who serve under the UN flag.
And a clear demonstration that the Council can still come together and speak with one voice.
Too often, however, the Security Council is blocked by geopolitical divisions. Unable to act.
Meanwhile, the costs of inaction are felt by civilians across the world as the disrespect for international humanitarian law is allowed to fester.
Our collective inability to halt the killings, suffering, and injustices in Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan and beyond, must not prompt us to surrender to a world ruled by brute force.
On the contrary, it must inspire us to work harder to sustain and strengthen the structures, instruments and mechanisms, we have built over the past 81 years.
To Denmark, this includes maintaining our firm support for the ICJ and ICC as core international justice institutions.
This year, Denmark nominated its first-ever candidate for judge at the ICC, reaffirming our unwavering support for the Court at a critical time.
It also means continuing to meet the UN target of providing 0.7 per cent of GNI for official development assistance.
For more than 45 years, Denmark has consistently delivered on this goal.

We do so, not as an act of altruism, but because it is in our shared interest: It creates jobs, opportunities and hope where people live, allowing them to build a future at home, increasing stability and mutual prosperity.
We call on fellow member states to join us.
At the current juncture, however, sustaining an order with the UN at its core, means working for reform.
Reform is how we keep this Organisation fit for the world we live in.
Denmark continues to call for fundamental Security Council reform: we wish to expand the Council with more members in both categories, including permanent seats for underrepresented regions.
And we wish to commence text-based negotiations.
Only then can we begin to redress historical injustices.
Denmark also strongly supports the UN80 reform process.
We applaud the results so far and call for ambitions to be raised.
We must strive to build a more efficient and inclusive UN.
A UN that delivers better – on its core mandates, and on the ground, where it matters most.
To enable this, we call on all UN Member States to meet their financial obligations to the UN.
We need the UN, not for the sake of the UN, but in order to address challenges that face us all.
Because no single country can manage climate change, global health threats, or the governance of emerging technologies on its own.
The climate crisis makes the point starkly.
We see it in droughts and wildfires. In record-breaking heat.
And in the growing pressure on food, water and energy accessibility and security.
