The challenge before us is no longer a lack of solutions.
Therefore, COP31 must be a COP of implementation.
Turning ambition into action and real-world results.
Delivering on the objectives of the Paris Agreement and its 1.5-degree Celsius temperature goal.
With only four years left to 2030, we must also be honest about where we stand with the Sustainable Development Goals.
Both in terms of achievements and challenges.
Let’s make the upcoming SDG Summit a turning point.
2030 must not be a missed deadline.
This year, we will be selecting a new Secretary-General.
The next Secretary-General will take over an organisation under strain and under scrutiny.
To bring the UN safely into the future, we must select a person who can work to restore global trust in the UN and among its member states.

In closing, I am happy to inform you that last week - in this very building - Denmark, Greenland and the United States signed an agreement on security, which strengthens the defence of Greenland, the NATO area and the American continent.
The agreement is good for Greenland, for Denmark, for the USA, and for NATO and Europe.
Progress can still be made, when we consult the compass.
You have brought us together to restore trust and manage transformation.

To achieve this, we now require serenity, clarity, and unity— serenity because the international order is going through a profound transition, clarity because this organization faces an unprecedented financial situation and conflicts that are ongoing, and a technological revolution that is progressing quicker than our ability to govern it, and unity because none of these challenges can be addressed by one country acting alone.
As a developing island country, the Dominican Republic is well aware of vulnerability.
Situations that happen far away from our coasts can directly impact the dinner tables of our families.
The wars in Europe and the Middle East have caused the prices of food and energy to skyrocket.
My country imports all of the fuel that it consumes.
We are not the ones that set the prices; however, the prices impact us without us being able to control them.
And this is why we advocate de-escalation, freedom of navigation, and for a diplomatic solution that prevents nuclear proliferation in the region.

Mr. President, for countries like ours, a rules-based order is a condition for our security and a guarantee that it is the norms agreed on by everyone and not force that resolve disputes between nations.

It's for this reason that it's necessary to restore trust in this organization, and three things are necessary in this regard to achieve it: renewing representation, renewing peacekeeping operations, and renewing support for developing countries.
However, there is no reform that can be successful without resources behind it, and that's why the Dominican Republic is complying and playing our role.
This year, we were one of the first countries to fully pay our contribution to the regular budget.
Renewing representation requires a security council that looks more like the multipolar world of the present, and it also requires thinking about who will lead this organization next.

This year, I affirmed, from this very same rostrum, that it was the turn of Latin America and the Caribbean to provide renewed leadership, and that the time had come for a woman to be Secretary-General of this organization.
The candidates that are running confirm this.
In more than 80 years, no woman has led this organization.
We trust that the Security Council and the General Assembly will rise to this moment.
Ladies and gentlemen, renewing peacekeeping operations, without a shadow of a doubt, is our most urgent task.
Today, transnational criminal networks control territories, they traffic arms and people, and they recruit children.
Haiti, our neighbor, is the clearest example of this.
Since 2021, the Dominican Republic has warned in each and every forum that this crisis is a threat to the peace and security of the region, and particularly for my country.
A year ago, from this same rostrum, I called upon the council to act without delay.
Six days later, the council adopted Resolution 2793 that authorized a banned suppression force with a strong mandate and with the support of a United Nations support office.

I thank the United States and Panama for their leadership, as well as Canada and other donors for their support, Kenya for their commitment, and the commitment of all of the countries who today have their men and women serving in Haiti.
However, the reality does not allow us to wait.
One month ago, in the Haitian community of Kentscoff, in just one night, gangs murdered no less than 47 people, including 5 children.
Close to a million and a half of Haitians have been displaced from their homes.
This assembly cannot resign to seeing massacres become the norm for the long-suffering Haitian people.
What the council approved now requires the means to implement it.
First, the deployment of the force that today is only funded up to a fifth of and only has up to a fifth, rather, of the troops authorized.
Second, fulfilling the arms embargo and sanctioning those who are financing and protecting gangs.
And thirdly, strengthening the police, the armed forces, and the Haitian justice system so that the security can be sustained.
The mandate of the force expires on the 30th of September.
It's for the council now to renew it and for the international community to contribute troops and the resources that are required.
Renewing it without completing it would be prolonging a promise that's not fulfilled.
None of this requires a new decision.
The Dominican Republic has played its role.
We will not practice a diplomacy of mere declarations, but rather a diplomacy of solutions.

We will contribute to building the consensus that made a resolution possible, and we are committing our financial contributions that's proportional for the trust fund of the force and facilitating from our country transit, logistics, and a UN support office.
We are cooperating with the sanctions regime and supporting the personnel of the mission in our hospitals.

We are doing this because this is, above all, a question of national security for our country, and we must repeat this as clearly as possible: there is no Dominican solution to the Haitian crisis, and no state or organization can impose on our country to do it in their place.

We will continue to protect our borders, to implement our migratory laws, and strengthen and equip our armed forces in exercise of sovereign equality that the United Nations recognizes for each state, and all of this fully respecting the international obligations that we freely assumed.

The solution to Haiti lies in Haiti itself, and the obligation of the international community is to make it possible there, in their country, for children to be able to go back to school and for Haitian youth to be able to have a future in their own country, and as soon as the conditions allow it, for the Haitians to be able to vote for the first time in a decade.
Mr. President, the Dominican Republic has worked to fulfill the essential commitments for our people, and we have been able to show results.
We've reduced monetary poverty by 25.8% from 25.8% in 2019 to 14.6% in the first 6 months of this year.
And just two months ago, the FAO confirmed that my country was taken off the hunger map, being the fifth country in Latin America to achieve this.
We have committed to achieving the zero hunger goal by 2028, but we managed to achieve this before that.
For 4 consecutive years, we've received more than $4 billion per year in foreign direct investment, and in 2025, for the first time, more than $5 billion.
And we are forecasting to receive more this year.
Our exports reached a record of close to $16 billion.
These results are a reflection of our legal certainty, institutional stability, and trust, inspired by the trust that different actors have in the Dominican Republic.

Peace, investment in new infrastructure, as well as the hospitality of our people, have led us to receive 7.5 million visitors in 2019, and this year is projected to exceed 12 million, and this figure is only rivaled by Mexico in Latin America.
However, a country's progress shouldn't— progress in a country should not mean that a country is penalized.
Middle-income countries host 3 in every 4 people on the planet and 2 in every 3 people in extreme poverty, and nevertheless, GDP continues to be used exclusively for concessional financing.

So we're calling for a process like the one that was initiated in the Pact for the Future, to achieve a common framework to measure progress beyond GDP, and for international financial institutions to incorporate these criteria in the multidimensional vulnerability index.
Because what can't be measured and what isn't measured doesn't influence decisions, and what doesn't influence decisions does not receive attention.
For a small island country, climate change is not an abstract matter, ladies and gentlemen.

Our vulnerability is not a statistical category; it's the reality that we're experiencing, and that's why we welcome that this assembly has committed to adopting a declaration on sea level rise guaranteeing stability in maritime areas.
The declaration also includes sargassum, which is a scourge that afflicts the Caribbean coast every year, affecting tourism.

Following an initiative by the Dominican Republic, the UN General Assembly and the Assembly for the Environment have adopted the first global resolution on sargassum, which, as a regional problem, recognizes a global challenge.
We will not tire in calling for climate change to be delivered as quickly as storms strike the Caribbean.
In this vein, we have moved to ratify the BBNJ agreement on biodiversity beyond national jurisdiction, and in March, we laid down our ratification instrument.
The ocean is an important source of life and is our most extensive border, and that's why protecting it is a state obligation.
With these concepts, we should be able to build a more representative United Nations that are more efficient and able to fulfill the demands of the people that we serve.
For the whole of humanity who are watching us, it will not be enough to just adopt resolutions.
Rather, the resolutions that matter will be the ones that we duly implement.
Ladies and gentlemen, the urgency before us is imposed by the nature of these new times.
The future is no longer a distant prospect; we are living it alongside the present.

As changes in the conditions of human existence occur with such speed that we no longer need to wait decades before they become part of history, many of our peoples run the risk of living through this era without benefiting from the great advances humanity is achieving.
Let us act now and work together for the well-being of our peoples.
We renew to him our appreciation for his steadfast defence of our Organization whenever some parties sought to undermine it.
3- We meet today while the world, across many parts of the globe, stands at a crossroads.

In many directions, tensions are escalating, trust among States is receding, the scope of crises and conflicts is expanding, polarization is intensifying, exclusionary unilateralism and withdrawal into self are returning at the expense of cooperation, coercive measures are increasingly being imposed, the advantages of dialogue and consensus are being nullified, and the tendency to impose force is making the outbreak of wars the rule rather than the exception.
At times, the principles of international law are suspended, and at other times they are applied selectively, subject only to balances of power and calculations of identity.

In such a dangerous international context, it can by no means be acceptable or normal for war to become a legitimate option in itself, nor for the rules of international law to remain merely a sheet of paper that can be invoked against some but not others.
How can confidence in international law remain when the right of self-defence is granted to some and denied to others, even in the right to survival?
How can confidence in humanity remain if the same reality is used to justify what is imposed on one side while the other is asked to remain silent about it?
If the logic of managing conflicts reverts to what it once was, then what future awaits our collective capacity to preserve peace?
4- The issue, for generations to come, is not only a passing crisis in the international order, but a profound review of the system that emerged after two world wars and of its development.

It is not far-fetched to say that what we are witnessing today compels us to ask whether we have failed to learn the lessons of history, or whether we have never finally grasped those lessons, nor truly overcome the disasters, wars, and calamities that lay at the very core of the purposes for which our international system was established, and the conditions required to enable it to prevent wars and fortify peace on this scale.

The theme chosen by the President of our General Assembly for this session, “Restoring trust and solidarity: improving global governance for present and future generations”, reflects not only the challenges of the current stage, but also places before us a fundamental question: how do we restore trust in an international system whose rules and institutions have been shaken?
And from this hall itself should begin the embodiment of the political will that ought to arise from the very place meant to be its truest expression.

5- Algeria considers that the transformation of the international system is not an institutional luxury, nor a matter that can be deferred; rather, it has become a necessity imposed by the profound changes the world has witnessed, changes that require a more representative, more just, and more equitable international order.
6- The United Nations can no longer continue with the same historical imbalances if we want peoples to trust in multilateral action.

We cannot speak of justice while international decision-making remains hostage to power balances; nor can we ask peoples to place their trust in an international system for the resolution of conflicts while that system remains incapable of ending wars or of safeguarding peace.
7- Reform of the international system has become an urgent necessity.
That need also applies to the Security Council and to its reform, so as to make it more representative, more just, and more effective.

Algeria reaffirms its steadfast support for the Common African Position, and stresses that rectifying the historical injustice done to Africa requires permanent and fair African representation on the Security Council, with full powers.

8- Accordingly, Algeria calls for strengthening the role of the General Assembly through deep reform that makes it more representative and enables it to play a fuller role in confronting selectivity and double standards in the application of international law.
In this context, it is no longer possible to complete the reform of institutions without doing justice to peoples aspiring to determine their own destiny and realize their national projects.

9- If restoring trust begins with reforming institutions, then it certainly cannot be achieved without redressing the grievances of peoples who continue to suffer the gravest forms of denial, exclusion, and marginalization.

10- In this context, my country is following with deep concern the continuation of escalation in the Gulf region, where a conflict is revolving on the backs of the states and peoples of the region, which have found themselves hostage to calculations that are not theirs, and their stability, development and welfare are hostage to interests that are not theirs.

Algeria condemns the violation of the sovereignty of the states of the region and stresses the imperative of respecting their sovereignty and sanctity, reducing escalation, and adhering to international law in dealing with the tensions, differences and conflicts that the region is witnessing.
Algeria also condemns the continuation of Israeli aggressions against the states of the region, particularly Syria and Lebanon, and its efforts to partition brotherly Somalia.
11- It should not remain permissible to extinguish hope for security, peace and tranquillity through the taking of the lives of children and women.

In Gaza, after eleven months of a major humanitarian tragedy that has shocked the world, we welcomed the ceasefire, hoping that this would be the beginning of a political solution that would stop the fire, protect civilians and open the way towards a permanent solution.
12- In Palestine, the humanitarian tragedy continues, and the Israeli occupation continues to claim the lives of Palestinian civilians, among them the innocent.
The scene has become part of the familiar, accepted scene.

Algeria renews its full, unconditional support for the legitimate rights, natural rights and inalienable rights of the Palestinian people, foremost among them its right to establish its independent State with full sovereignty, with القدس الشريف as its capital.

If the question of Palestine places before us a daily test of the credibility of international law, then Africa places before us another test: building partnerships based on solidarity, addressing the residues of crises and their root causes, and giving sufficient attention not to merely managing them, but to peace and development.

Algeria, attached to its African belonging, will continue to support the just causes of the peoples of the continent and to contribute to the path of stability, development and integration, and, at the forefront, support for the Palestinian people, armed with the culture of peace and dialogue in all this, and attached to principled positions.

13- From this standpoint, Algeria’s steadfast principled position supporting the right of the people of Western Sahara to decolonization and to the full exercise of their uncurtailed rights opens onto enabling peoples to exercise those rights in full, rather than perpetuating a distorted practice that entrenches a fait accompli.

14- In this framework, Algeria reaffirms, on the basis of its conviction in the right to self-determination, that the question of Western Sahara can only be resolved through the exercise of that right as enshrined by international legitimacy.

Algeria welcomes the organization, at the beginning of this year, of direct negotiations between the two parties to the conflict, the Kingdom of Morocco and the Polisario Front, under the auspices of the United Nations and with the assistance of the United States of America, which we see as a necessary, sincere and serious path towards a just, lasting and mutually acceptable political solution to the question of Western Sahara.
Algeria also stresses that this path can only proceed within the framework of the relevant United Nations reference parameters firmly established in decolonization.

Any attempt to circumvent this reference framework and to marginalize the representative of the people concerned, namely the Polisario Front, their sole legitimate representative, will only further complicate and aggravate tensions in the region and undermine stability, cooperation and development.

From this perspective, allow me to present to you what we consider essential: First: Algeria affirms that the success of the negotiating track requires the engagement of the parties to the conflict in good faith, with sincere will to reach a just solution, away from the logic of dictates and bargaining.
Respect for the negotiating process cannot be achieved except through seriousness and sincerity.

Second: Algeria warns against depriving the people of Western Sahara, through their genuine and sole representative, the Polisario Front, of their authentic right, for there can be no contribution to a solution without the people concerned being at the heart of it.

Third: In this context, Algeria affirms that, as a result of more than half a century of occupation of their land, the Sahrawis are today torn between voluntary return, local integration, resettlement and exile.

Yet this cannot be reduced to a humanitarian issue; rather, it requires a comprehensive political process in Western Sahara on its land, beginning and ending with the completion of the decolonization process.

This occupation, which is another colonial situation on the continent, cannot in any way diminish the right of the people of Western Sahara to exercise their right to self-determination through a genuine process.

15- The right of peoples to self-determination remains a constant principle in international law, and the passage of half a century cannot transform it from a legal truth into an imposed fait accompli, nor can it deprive its أصحاب of it.

The historical and collective memory of peoples, as well as the African experience, confirm that true peace is not built on the transgression of rights, but rather that the sound and proper treatment of such situations is what responds to and respects the aspirations of their أصحاب.
The United Nations does not need anyone to explain to it the historical facts.
Algeria looks to the Sahel region as one single space in which the challenges of poverty, marginalization and organized crime intersect with the expansion of terrorist networks and groups.
These are challenges that cannot be addressed in isolation from one another, just as they cannot be fragmented.

They are not two parallel tracks; rather, they are two facets of an approach founded on supporting States, addressing the root causes, through dialogue and with respect for the choices of their peoples, their territorial integrity, the reconciliation of the region and the accompaniment of States, nourishing security conditions that make development possible.
Security and development are not two separate paths.
As is the case in the Sahel region, terrorism finds in a fragile environment fertile ground for entrenchment and expansion.

Therefore, Algeria proposes an approach that combines security and development efforts, while respecting the sovereignty of States and encouraging their development, and, faithful to its historic solidarity endeavours and by virtue of its position as a neighbouring sister State, it will continue to extend a helping hand and support political solutions that preserve the stability of the region and open broader horizons for development and progress for the peoples of the Sahel States.

Libya, which has entered its sixteenth year of crisis, remains an example of the conditions that foreign interventions, in their various forms, can create, while at the same time the broad national consensus among Libyans remains an essential element in creating the conditions for a stable and united settlement.
Protracted crises do not find their way to resolution through deepening divisions, but rather through dialogue, reconciliation and the unification of institutions.

Algeria fully supports the sisterly State of Libya in finding a peaceful political solution led and owned by the Libyans, and renews its support for the efforts of the United Nations, trusting in its ability to accompany this process.

For the Libyans alone are capable of rebuilding their State and institutions, preserving its unity, safeguarding their country and guaranteeing their future, whenever they are the sole decision-makers with regard to their country.

With the same convictions, and in response to the same imperatives, Algeria expresses its steadfast support for the legitimate authorities in Yemen and the Sudan, the two brotherly countries, in response to the right of their two peoples to security and stability.
From here we reach a truth: development cannot be revived without security, and stability cannot be built without ending divisions and building the State.

Under the leadership of Mr. Abdelmadjid Tebboune, President of the Republic, Algeria has chosen to be an active participant in the transformations the world is witnessing, turning challenges into bridges towards progress, and making science, knowledge and its resources a driver of its renaissance, for building a productive and diversified economy.
There can be no development without security and stability, unity and cohesion, and this is what forms one of the pillars of peace.

Algeria believes, with complete conviction, that the political, military and social options it has enshrined in its national approach and its Constitution since 2020 proceed from a clear vision and a firm and constant principle: that no one must be left behind in the development process.
This is the true meaning of sustainable development: for ordinary people.

In its voluntary national review presented in July 2026, Algeria showcased what it has achieved over seven years of sustained efforts and what its policies have translated into in figures, as well as the tangible progress made towards embodying the goals of sustainable economic and environmental development.
In doing so, it demonstrated that the essence of development lies in improving people’s dignity in all aspects of public life.

From this understanding of sustainable development, Algeria proceeds from the view that development cannot be complete unless it includes its regional environment and contributes to building a more integrated and capable African space for addressing the challenges of the present and the future.
For the destiny of African peoples is shared, and the continent’s interdependence and the challenge of achieving sustainable development make solidarity and African integration indispensable pillars.
As we discern the features of the accelerating technological revolution, we cannot accept that Africa remain on its margins or be transformed into merely a consumer of its outputs.

Hence the imperative of investing in the African human being and building scientific and digital capacities, so that artificial intelligence may become a lever for development and not a new title for the development gap between North and South.

Therefore, we call for balanced and responsible international regulation of artificial intelligence that ensures justice in access to it, preserves the sovereignty of States, and makes this revolution a shared opportunity for all, not a privilege monopolized by a few.

As for the United Nations, we believe that trust is restored when words match deeds, when the law is one and effective for all, when peoples are able to recover from the tyranny of power politics, and when institutions once again become a common home, not an arena for selectivity.
At the end of the day, we have returned to the question that seemed to begin from it: how do we restore trust?

We restore trust through genuinely multilateral action, not as a slogan but as a course of action; through cooperation, not isolation; through a space in which respect for law is a right, not a privilege; in which development is not the preserve of a few; in which institutions regain the confidence of peoples; and in which the United Nations, at this defining moment, becomes equal to the hopes placed in it before our children and future generations.

That is the alternative, for there is inaction that leaves us all alone, without recourse or means, facing crises we did not choose, and leaving our children to confront what we have failed to resolve.
23. Our responsibility today is not merely to describe the world as it is, but together to shape a better world than the one revolving in the storms of this age.
Let us not walk the path alone, but together among the peoples of the world.
Let us make the restoration of diplomacy to its rightful place a principle, and let us make respect for international law a shared commitment, not an option.
Let us make peace not an absence but a common responsibility for all. Thank you.

General debate of the eighty-first session of the United Nations General Assembly Mr. Secretary-General of the United Nations; Mr. President of the United Nations General Assembly; Excellencies Heads of State and Government; distinguished delegations; ladies and gentlemen: There was a time when, in my country, fear had more authority than the law.
Families experienced it when they stopped going out at night, merchants when they paid in order to be able to work.
Young people to whom a gun was offered before a diploma.
We decided that would not be Ecuador’s destiny, and we have acted with determination.
But along that path we learned something that I have come to share with you: no State defeats alone an enemy that recognizes no borders.
The weapons that reach our streets have crossed several countries.
The money that finances the mafias is laundered far from where the crime is committed.
The routes of drug trafficking, trafficking in persons and illegal mining cross continents.
Criminals have already globalized their cooperation.
They share routes, logistics, finances and technology, without formalities, without distrust and without delay.
It is unacceptable that criminal organizations cooperate among themselves more effectively than States do.
That is the reality that the United Nations must recognize and assume.
For a long time, organized crime was treated as a police problem.
Today we know that it is more than that.
When it controls territories and penetrates institutions, it supplants legitimate authority, erodes the rule of law and destabilizes entire societies.
And when that occurs in several countries at the same time, it ceases to be an internal matter: it becomes a threat to international peace and security.
I say this clearly: we are not asking others to act in place of States.
We are asking for cooperation upon request, with full respect for the sovereignty of each nation and with results that can be measured.

That is why Ecuador today proposes three concrete actions: First, an international mechanism, within the framework of the United Nations, to trace and freeze the illicit financial flows of transnational organized crime.
If money is the fuel of these networks, let us cut it off wherever it circulates.
Second, a permanent platform for the exchange of information among police forces, prosecutors’ offices and financial intelligence units, enabling States to anticipate rather than react.
Third, that the UN80 initiative incorporate transnational organized crime as a conflict-prevention priority, and endow the Organization with the capacity to support States that request it.
These are proposals that Ecuador is prepared to advance, together with all countries that wish to join.
Excellencies: Security is not an end in itself.
It is the condition for a country to be able to flourish, and today we are experiencing a crisis of the soul.
Restoring security means restoring the future.
It means that a young person can choose a university instead of being trapped by a criminal gang.
That a family can open a business without fear.
That a company can invest and create jobs.
That institutions respond to citizens and not to illicit interests.
That is why the success of an economy is measured not only by how much production grows, but by how much poverty it reduces.
It is measured in young people with decent jobs, in children with better education, in citizens who build their future with dignity.
And that measure must also guide the international development agenda.
Middle-income countries face vulnerabilities that per capita income does not reflect.
We ask that access to cooperation and financing be defined by fairer vulnerability criteria, and that the international financial architecture support the efforts of those who undertake reforms.
We believe in open, predictable and equitable trade.
When a producer can export, innovate and grow, there is a family rising out of poverty.
The best social policy is the one that generates opportunities and income for all.
The Galápagos Islands, where Darwin found the clues to the evolution of life, are the heritage of all humanity.
And today they are also threatened by illegal fishing networks that operate with the same logic and the same finances as other organized crimes.
The same is true of illegal mining in the Amazon, which destroys forests and finances the mafias.
Protecting nature is also a security task.
Ecuador will continue to fulfil that responsibility and invites everyone to join in it.
Latin America and the Caribbean is a region of talent, of energy, of food, of strategic resources and, above all, of a youth determined to build a different future.
It is a region that does not come to this Assembly to ask for solutions from others, but to offer its own.
And one of the greatest tests of the future is artificial intelligence.
It can transform education, multiply productivity and close historic gaps.
But it can also deepen inequalities or serve those who seek to weaken our institutions.
We need international governance that makes it possible to innovate without renouncing our values, and that does not leave behind those with fewer resources to access this technology.
Excellencies: Confidence in the multilateral system is undergoing a difficult test.
We receive many questions in the fight against organized crime and very few questions about the number of victims we are having from organized crime.
Many citizens see a gap between what is agreed here and what they experience in their daily lives.
Closing that gap is the task of our generation.
As a founding State, Ecuador believes in the United Nations.
And precisely for that reason, it wants an Organization capable of responding to today’s world, not that of 1945.
To support the United Nations is also the will to transform them.
That is why we support the UN80 initiative and invite it to answer with courage an essential question: What United Nations does the world of today need?
We need a more efficient Organization, with the capacity to prevent, resolve crises and help States in the face of threats that did not exist when it was created.
An Organization whose legitimacy depends not only on the decisions it adopts, but on the way in which it adopts them.
And we need the Charter and International Law to continue to be our common language.
More than eighty years ago, countries understood that peace could not depend on the power of each one, and they built institutions in order to cooperate.
The citizens of the world will not judge this Organization by its declarations.
They will judge it by its capacity to turn commitments into peace and security, into respect for human rights and into real opportunities for development.
By how many lives we truly save.
Mr. President: The mafias have already coordinated.
It is up to us to do better.
Ecuador comes to this Assembly to defend collective solutions, because no country can build by itself a secure, prosperous and sustainable future.
And because when international cooperation works, we are all stronger.
DANIEL NOBOA AZIN Constitutional President of the Republic of Ecuador

The title under which the General Assembly meets this year, “Restoring confidence in the international system: managing transformation and strengthening institutions of global governance,” accurately reflects the challenge facing us today; for our world is changing today at a pace much faster than the capacity of international governance institutions to respond, and the crisis is not in the absence of charters and principles, so much as it is in the widening gap between what we proclaim and what we apply, between those who make decisions and those affected by them.

It is no longer sufficient to content ourselves with a formal multilateralism but rather with an effective multilateralism, in which every State has a fair share of decisions, and every people a voice that is heard, free from exaggeration in opportunities and resources.

Trust in the usefulness of collective action and in the international system has declined, and there is an urgent need to restore recourse to international law and to avoid policies of force and double standards.

It is not by coincidence that the countries of the global South, which comprise the overwhelming majority of the world’s population, are among the parties most harmed by the retreat of the rule of international law, the weakening of the frameworks of global governance and international cooperation, and the role of interlinked UN institutions.

From this standpoint, Egypt believes that restoring confidence in the United Nations requires three basic pillars: justice in representation and decision-making, justice in the application of law, and justice in the distribution of development and transformation opportunities.

This is not a call to rebuild the international system from zero, but rather a call to fulfill its promises and purposes: equality among States, respect for sovereignty, the settlement of disputes peacefully, and enabling international cooperation for the benefit of peoples, and ensuring that all benefit from the fruits of accelerating scientific progress.

Multilateralism remains an indispensable choice, but the effectiveness and sustainability of the international system and the guarantee of its continuity remain contingent upon entrenching justice in the application of the rules.
The real test, Mr. President, is not contenting ourselves with recalling the principles upon which its institutions were established, but acting on their basis without inertia.

.// If the Palestinian question remains the test of the credibility of the international system, then what the Palestinian people have witnessed and continue to be subjected to, of suffering, repression and violations, is the clearest proof of the existing dysfunction.
It must not be allowed to turn into a familiar reality, or into a protracted crisis managed from one round to another.

Stabilizing the ceasefire in the Gaza Strip in accordance with the peace plan of the “Trump” Summit and the Sharm El-Sheikh Summit, ensuring full commitment to it, completing the withdrawal, halting the daily Israeli violations, and enabling the secure and sustainable delivery of humanitarian assistance are not only humanitarian steps, but are also the necessary entry point for the immediate transition to early recovery and reconstruction, by empowering and securing the national committee for the administration of Gaza to directly carry out its work, then to a serious political path that addresses the roots of the conflict and ends it.

In this context, Egypt affirms its categorical rejection of any attempt to displace the Palestinian people from their land, whether from the Gaza Strip or from the West Bank, including East Jerusalem.

./ / The international community bears a clear responsibility to stop all systematic Israeli violations of international law; for peace cannot be built on the uprooting of a people from its land, nor can stability be achieved in the region in the shadow of a policy of managing the occupation instead of ending it.
Every perception that the Palestinian people’s suffering can be ignored, or that the Palestinian State can be prevented from coming into being, is nothing but illusion and fantasy.

:// That goal will remain clear and unambiguous: the embodiment of the independent Palestinian State with sovereignty, contiguous geographically, on the lines of the fourth of June nineteen hundred and sixty-seven, with East Jerusalem as its capital, in the framework of the two-State solution, in accordance with the resolutions of international legitimacy.

This requires preserving the unity of the Palestinian land, empowering the Palestinian people, and the Palestinian political system, to administer their own affairs and build their State, with the international community assuming its responsibility.

It also requires dealing with the rights on the basis that they are non-negotiable, not bargaining chips granted or withdrawn according to balances of power, or Palestinian bidding wars, / / or in cooperation with partners and electoral calculations.

Egypt has borne its responsibility, politically and in action, as it was the largest source for consolidating the ceasefire, and Egypt has worked to open horizons for the humanitarian assistance that reached the Gaza Strip, and Egypt will continue these efforts for reconstruction.
Yet the success of this remains dependent upon an international will that turns legitimacy into decisive political action, and moves from managing the tragedy to ending its causes.
The experience of our region confirms that managing crises instead of resolving them does not create peace, Rather, they are merely postponed explosions, and their cost is multiplied.

Egypt adheres to a clear vision for regional security, at the heart of which are respect for the sovereignty of States and the unity of their territories, rejecting the dismantling of States or the creation of parallel entities to them, and upholding political solutions and national settlements above narrow loyalties and the imposition of force and coercive realities.

However, in every crisis witnessed by the Middle East region in all its breadth, from the Ocean to the Gulf, although the circumstances and details differ, the inclusive and capable national State for all its citizens remains the sole and true foundation, together with legitimate institutions, for stability.

No State can believe that its interests can be secured by undermining the institutions of another State, or that the security of shipping lanes and trade and energy can be ensured through threatening the security of its neighbours, bombing them, violating the sovereignty of States, or through any regional party supporting militias politically and economically, sponsoring the orientations of the national State, or becoming, in the utmost frankness, part of the problem through separatist practices and civil fighting.
Security is indivisible, and can only be achieved through respect for international law.

The responsibility of the international community as a whole for the region’s crises requires that each crisis be addressed within an interconnected regional and security environment, rather than being regarded as an isolated case.

Therefore, Egypt calls for encouraging political settlements and supporting State institutions, in accordance with the principle of national and regional ownership of solutions, national unity and sovereignty, peacebuilding, preventing crises from turning into arenas for regional and international competition over the resources of the peoples of the region, and stopping external interventions.
And in this context, I must clearly reaffirm that water security for Egypt is an existential issue.
It is not merely a resource to be bargained over; rather, it is a lifeline that does not tolerate compromise.
The Nile is not merely an economic resource; the existence of Egyptian society and its development have been linked to it throughout history.
We also believe that transboundary water resources must be an area for cooperation and integration, not conflict.
Egypt believes that water security and development are not two contradictory goals, but rather complementary, if the political will exists, intentions are sincere, and international law is respected.

We do not stand against the right of any people to development; rather, we defend a clear and just principle: that one party’s development must not be pursued through unilateral measures with shared resources, causing harm to others, but through cooperation, good faith, and reaching binding agreements — in accordance with international law — that preserve the rights and legitimate interests of all.

In this regard, Egypt reserves its legitimate right, guaranteed by the Charter of the United Nations and international law, to protect its water security and to preserve its existential capabilities for its people.

With the multiplicity of sources of threats facing our region, whose effects extend beyond borders, the crisis in the brotherly Sudan affects the security and safety of civilians, and in confronting those military confrontations and the risks of dismantling State institutions, brotherly Sudan finds in Egypt a support and a strong backing for its people, for its right to unity, in institutions capable of preserving its resources, and in justice that upholds its dignity.
Justice is incomplete if the institutions that shape the reality of the world they administer remain far removed from fair representation in decision-making.

More than eight decades have passed since the establishment of the United Nations, at the head of its institutions the Security Council, while those institutions still reflect historical balances that reality has overtaken.
Nor can institutions created for a different world retain their full legitimacy and effectiveness unless they reflect the world they are supposed to serve today.

Therefore, Egypt remains committed to a genuine reform of the Security Council that addresses injustice comprehensively, in accordance with broad consensus and in a manner that specifically redresses the historical reality imposed on Africa by the “Ezulwini Consensus” and the Sirte Declaration.
Developing countries also demand an acceleration of the rebalancing of political voice in global economic governance.

The global economic imbalance means that States face, at one and the same time, crises, the green transition, adaptation, job creation and financing, while operating within an increasingly narrow fiscal space, higher financing costs and mounting debt burdens.

Therefore, we believe that reforming the international financial architecture is no longer a luxury but a necessity, and that we are in need of expanding development financing, mobilizing multilateral development financing so that it is more representative, responsive and effective, and addressing debt fairly.

We also need to develop innovative financing instruments, move towards a more concessional lending system, accelerate and increase the capacity of financial institutions and banks, and adopt a more equitable system in assessing countries’ needs and investment risks in them, without transferring risks onto fragile States, in a manner that assists in mobilizing private capital.
States must not be placed before a choice between servicing debt and financing education, health, food and infrastructure.

Development is not a grant, but a right, and investing in it is an investment in stability and in the ability of States to prevent crises before they turn into humanitarian and security crises that cross borders.
At a time when we are working on reforming inherited imbalances, we must not allow their reproduction in the future.
The fifteenth century opens vast horizons for knowledge, innovation and growth.

Artificial intelligence opens vast horizons and can improve services, but it may also create a new and enormous gap linked to the possession of computing power, data and models, as well as skills and financing.

Therefore, managing this transformation requires formulating frameworks for the governance of artificial intelligence and emerging technologies on the basis that technology is a global benefit and not a closed privilege for a limited number of States or companies.

Egypt supports the role of the United Nations and global dialogue in setting principles that combine innovation and responsibility, ensure transparency and accountability, protect privacy, transfer knowledge, respect international law, ensure human oversight, prevent discrimination, develop skills, and finance digital infrastructure and technology, thereby enabling developing countries to be producers and framers of technology, not merely markets for it.
It should also reflect linguistic and cultural diversity, and Arab and African societies and languages should enjoy fair representation in data and models.

Egypt has launched the second edition of its National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, 2025–2030, proceeding from the firm conviction that the safe and responsible use of technology and capacity-building are two inseparable conditions.
The same principle should govern the green transition: there can be no just transition if ambition is detached from justice in means of implementation, and from development and poverty eradication.

Climate action must proceed side by side with granting adaptation, water and food security, creating job opportunities, and giving States, especially in Africa, the priority they deserve, as they are the most exposed to the repercussions of climate change.

From the reality of Egypt’s experience in hosting the Climate Conference in Sharm El-Sheikh, and what it yielded in terms of decisions, we can affirm that the gap no longer lies in diagnosing the problem, but in implementation; in transforming pledges into financing flows and technology projects that reach the countries and communities most in need.
And in a world where geopolitical and technological shifts are accelerating, we must not allow that to lead us to more dangerous arms races.

Egypt renews its adherence to a balanced system for disarmament and non-proliferation, without double standards, and to the goal of establishing a zone free of nuclear weapons and all other weapons of mass destruction in the Middle East.

Collective security is not achieved by the accumulation of instruments of destruction, but by equal rules and obligations applied to all, and by making prevention a priority, not a belated response after escalation occurs.
Egypt, in putting forward this vision, does not merely call for reform of the international order; rather, it places its experience and capabilities at the service of solutions.

Proceeding from its location and heritage—Arab, African and Mediterranean—and from its historical role in the establishment of the multilateral international order, Egypt will remain a bridge to all who seek a more just and sustainable multilateral international system, and a partner to all who seek a more effective one.

We will continue to invest in partnerships with different parties, to remain open to cooperation and the exchange of expertise, and to work with all on solutions that do not impose a single model and that respect the priorities of the North and the South.
Legitimacy is acquired when common ownership is transformed into shared outcomes, and when institutions regain trust.
Transformation is not imposed, but managed; it is not demanded, but built on justice.
Our order regains trust and effectiveness through participation.

Egypt will remain supportive of every effort that restores confidence and contributes to managing the transformations of our world and of the multilateral international order, in a fair and participatory manner, in service of the interests of our peoples and the future of coming generations.

STATEMENT BY THE PRESIDENT OF THE GOVERNMENT OF SPAIN H.E. MR. PEDRO SÁNCHEZ PÉREZ-CASTEJÓN IN THE GENERAL DEBATE OF THE EIGHTY-FIRST SESSION OF THE UNITED NATIONS GENERAL ASSEMBLY New York, 23 September 2026 Ladies and gentlemen, I take this podium with a single objective: to defend what many are trying to destroy.
I have come to vindicate the principles and ambitions that inspired the creation of this organization 81 years ago.
Principles and ambitions that several governments present here despise and intend to dismantle.
Eight years have passed since the first time I addressed this Assembly.
Since then, several things in the world have changed.
And I regret to say that many have changed for the worse.
In 2018, the 193 countries that make up this body had just adopted the 2030 Agenda, and most of the leaders present here proudly wore the symbol of the SDGs.
Nor because we thought it would be an easy path.
We did so because most of us believed in its common promise.
Because we were convinced that peace, sustainability, and equal opportunities are not ideological positions, but an integral part of the future of humanity.
Today, however, these ideas are not only being questioned.
They are being attacked by reactionary entities and governments that want to take us back to a bleak past.
There is no need to point them out.
We all know who they are and what their modus operandi is.
They begin by questioning the rules.
Then they break them, knowing full well that no one will dare to call them to account.
They cut their contributions to multilateral bodies such as this one.
They target their leaders and workers.
They block their capacity to act, only then to describe them as useless entities we can do without.
Theirs is a planned and coordinated attempt at demolition that is presented to us as something unstoppable and necessary.
But in reality it runs counter to the structural currents of history and is built on three mistaken pillars.
The absurd belief that the world is a zero-sum game in which the gain of some necessarily entails the loss of others.
A colossal and shameless ignorance that scorns science and assumes that there are countries so powerful that they can abuse the rest and need no one in order to prosper.
And the third, the worst of all, is cruelty.
A cruelty that no longer even flinches at the sight of the ribs of a starving child or a hospital reduced to rubble.
Over the course of these eight years I have seen these reactionary forces—selfish, ignorant and cruel—grow.
I have seen them remove their masks and take power in many places.
And from there, I have seen them launch illegal wars and massacre innocent civilians.
I have seen them treat millions of human beings as if they were cattle and withdraw their aid from those who suffer most from poverty and disease.
I have seen them pollute the atmosphere and the ocean as if they were their property.
And conspire to destroy this organization and everything it represents.
Witnessing these things has transformed the way I understand the world.
But it has not made me lose hope.
Because over the course of these eight years, I have also seen wonderful things that make me continue to trust in humanity.
I have seen millions of people mobilize in defense of nature, peace and civil rights.
I have seen thousands of activists and public servants stand up to reactionary powers, knowing full well that they were putting their careers and their very lives at risk.
I have seen scientists achieve breakthroughs we thought impossible.
And many governments do the right thing: betting on cooperation, social justice and environmental sustainability.
All this has taught me that humanity is not intrinsically good or bad.
And each year, each day, in every crisis, it must decide how to act.
The United Nations is one of the places where that decision is made manifest at the highest level.
It does not always get it right.
I myself have on several occasions pointed out the contradictions and shortcomings of this body.
But, with equal conviction, I must denounce the fact that most of the voices that today persist in criticizing it are not describing its failure: they are trying to provoke it.

And I must also say that multilateralism is the best instrument humanity has for managing its diversity and its interdependence, especially in a globalized and multipolar world such as the present one.
That is why what we have to do is redouble our confidence in it.
We must renew it and strengthen it.
So that it can play in this century the same central role it fulfilled in the last century.
Doing so will not be easy.
But the good news is that all the guidance we need is here.
In this Charter written by our forebears.
Men and women who had seen the world burn and who, even so, had the courage to imagine a better future.
Those men and women left their wisdom and their hope in this Charter.
And they did NOT ask us to keep it in a display case.
They asked us to comply with it. To defend it.
And to return to it in moments of uncertainty and difficulty.
Today we are going through one of those moments.
And it is our duty to rise to the courage and ambition present in this text.
That is why we must reform the Security Council.
So that all the regions of the world have fair representation.
And to put an end to the veto power of the permanent members.
Because, as this Charter indicates, no country should be both judge and party at the same time.
No matter how powerful it may be.
We must strengthen the other Principal Organs and reorganize the Agencies, Funds and Programmes, equipping them with greater resources and executive capacity.
So that they can have a more decisive impact on the great challenges afflicting humanity.
We must strengthen bodies such as the International Criminal Court, so that they can investigate, prosecute and punish those who violate the rules.
Humanity took centuries to replace the law of the strongest with the force of law, and we cannot be the generation that travels that path in the opposite direction.
For that same reason, we must rebuild the architecture of nuclear non-proliferation and disarmament, to prevent a misguided security policy from dragging us into a new world conflict.
And we must impose strict regulation on the techno-oligarchs to control the operation of social networks and the development of Artificial Intelligence.
Because the future of our children must come before their pockets.
Doing all these things will require commitment. Time. And strong leadership.
Capable of building agreements. Of listening.
Of looking beyond known reality and imagining a better alternative.
My choice for that leadership is clear.
Nine men have occupied the Secretariat-General of this Organization in its eighty years of existence.
Now it is a woman's turn.
Because—ladies and gentlemen—how can an Organization that claims to speak on behalf of all humanity never have had a woman at its head?
How is it going to represent all continents, if for three decades we have not allowed the third most populous to hold this post?

Today, more than ever, when feminism is being attacked and thousands of women are victims of sexism, violence and xenophobia.

Because its citizenry is showing that a crisis can be faced without renouncing decency, maintaining legality and respecting human rights.

Because Spain does not choose the easiest path.

One of the biggest tests for the UN’s relevance is Russia’s aggression against Ukraine.

It seeks to uphold the basic tenets of the international order.
My second observation is that everywhere I travel, I hear the word ‘realignment’.
Whether it is in Europe, Africa, the Middle East, Asia, or the Americas, nations are seeking new alliances and partnerships.
This is a logical consequence in times of uncertainty and transformation.
You seek security where you can get it.
We are seeing an intensification of regional integration akin to what we saw in the immediate aftermath of World War II.
Regional organizations like the African Union, Gulf Cooperation Council, Mercosur, ASEAN or the EU build trust.
When integration is not feasible, other forms of co-operation can prove essential.
We Finns are happy to point to the historic signing of the Helsinki Final Act in 1975.
It brought together 35 nations in the midst of the Cold War and laid the foundations for what would later become the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe.
There were deep disagreements. And outright hostility.
Yet there was room for a process that reduced tensions and built common ground.
I believe regions, such as the Middle East, where conflicts are raging today, may consider something similar.
Even in the face of conflict and grievance, a region may be able to agree on principles that foster co-operation and prevent further conflict.
My third observation is that a new economic world order is taking shape.
Instruments once used for economic integration – including trade, technology, energy, investment, and supply chains – have become instruments of geopolitical competition.
There was perhaps, at times, a naïve belief that interdependence would bring about stability and peace.
Now, the focus on opportunities has been replaced by the focus on threats.
We have entered a world of coercion, where dependencies are vulnerabilities.
Countries seek chokepoints that can be weaponized to pressure others.
No nation, not even the biggest ones, can go it alone.
All coercive actions come at a cost.
And even if a mightier state dominates in one domain, a smaller state can respond in another.
In the new geopolitical environment, the economic order of the post-World War II era is seeking new forms.
The new order must be based on a realistic understanding of the power balance in the world.
We in the West must acknowledge that the Global South and East are an expanding economic and political force.
Many nations around the world have made remarkable advances in competence and know-how.
We should put this collective expertise to work for the global common good.
Countries are right to be wary of dangerous dependencies.
But our focus on threats should not lead us to abandon co-operation.
We should strive for an economic world order built on institutions and agreements.
Multilateralism is also needed in the global economy.
It is all well and good to diagnose the problem: too many nations now compete at the expense of basic rules, and that is why the world has slipped into disorder.
But it matters more to find a prescription which would bring us back to order, stability and co-operation.
Thus, I will offer you three remedies for a world in disorder.
To begin with, we need to go back to the basics of international law.
On my recent visit to India, I came across a quote from Mahatma Gandhi: “The breach of one rule inevitably leads to the breach of other rules”.
These words resonate all too strongly today.
We have moved back to a world defined by raw power and narrow self-interest.
Rules and values seem to be taking a back seat.
Some are ready to throw in the towel, prepared to accept the defeat of the international rules-based order.
International law has been questioned and challenged before.
It has never been a perfect system.
But we must admit that we are at a critical juncture.
Fundamental norms are being questioned in a way that erodes confidence in the entire multilateral system.
Therefore, the first remedy for a world in disorder is rule of law.
Today, international norms are often presented as an obstacle to the pursuit of national interests.
This is both wrong and dangerous.
International law has never been merely an effort to achieve universal justice, but neither can it be reduced to a mere instrument of domination.
It is not only about values, nor only about interests, but about both.
Despite the rhetoric, no major power is likely to give up its ability to shape the rules.
Even when actors claim to abandon rules, they rather seek to replace existing rules with ones more to their liking.
Therefore, we will not face a world without rules.
But we could be facing a world with less predictability, less restraint – a world based on rules that are more permissive for the powerful.
For the collective benefit of the nations in this Hall, we should continue to defend the rule of law and uphold its most fundamental principles.
They include the independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of nations; freedom of navigation at sea; and accountability for the most serious international crimes.
The second remedy is about humanitarian principles.
The world today has an unprecedented capacity to meet humanity’s most pressing needs.
Since the establishment of the United Nations, poverty has declined, access to basic education has expanded, literacy has increased, and child mortality has fallen.
Yet, we are witnessing tyranny, disregard for the vulnerable, and violence against civilians in many parts of the world.
Poverty and distress are still widespread.
For example, Sudan is devastated by war.
Millions have been displaced, and many face famine.
Gaza continues to be one of the world’s most acute humanitarian emergencies, marked by mass displacement, the destruction of infrastructure and a lack of essential services.
Haiti struggles with armed violence and extreme weather events, causing a displacement crisis, a hunger crisis, and a health crisis.
We must not grow indifferent to wars and human suffering, but instead channel our efforts into preventing conflicts, upholding human rights, and strengthening sustainable economies.
Our growing material prosperity should not come at the expense of our ethical responsibilities.
The third remedy is about language and the way we treat each other.
Unfortunately, there is no shortage of examples of those who use dismissive language to describe others and entire groups of people.
Too often, those with the most provocative rhetoric receive the greatest visibility.
Language can foster co-operation, but it can also break trust and turn competition into conflict.
The recipe is simple, but necessary: avoid polarization, strengthen trust, and listen to others.
And that starts here, at the United Nations.
Every Secretary-General is shaped both by their era and by their own actions.
I was reminded of this recently when reading the biographies of former Secretaries-General U-Thant and Kofi Annan, both highly influential leaders who navigated an era of great-power tensions.
Let me put forward a few suggestions for the new Secretary-General’s consideration, whoever she may be, and for the international community at large.
Since my first speech here two years ago, I have consistently called for a reformed Security Council.
The world has changed, so should the UN.
There should be, at least, two new permanent seats for Africa, two for Asia-Pacific and one for Latin America.
No single state should have veto power.
And, if a member of the Security Council violates the UN Charter, its voting rights should be suspended.
The world needs a functioning UN Security Council.
To move forward, we need to break the impasse and be open for creative solutions.
The need for reform also extends to the global economic architecture.
It, too, must be updated to reflect today’s power balance.
We have to make sure international economic co-operation continues to be rules-based, legitimate, and representative.
Multilateral solutions are needed in an increasingly multipolar world.
We must also bring the United Nations back to peace mediation.
The Secretary-General, as Mediator-In-Chief, will have a key role.
The UN’s legitimacy as a mediator is unique.
Together, the UN and its Member States can accomplish what neither can achieve alone.
The UN needs to be at the centre of rule-making and institution-building.
Regional integration and thematic coalitions can and should support it.
Artificial intelligence is the most consequential technology in the history of mankind.
It will impact science, the economy, politics, security, and the very essence of our humanity.
Humans can and should be in the driver’s seat.
We have a choice: we can compete, co-operate or slow down.
For me, co-operation is the best way forward.

This is why Norway and Finland have, together with leaders from nations around the world, launched a call for companies, governments, regional organisations and the UN to develop mechanisms to control frontier models of AI.
My country, Finland, wants the United Nations to succeed and will remain strongly engaged in its work.
Therefore, we are standing for election to the Security Council from 2029 to 2030.
We are motivated by our belief in the UN Charter and the values it stands for.
We will prioritize peace, people, and partnerships.
We are willing to take on the responsibility of the Council membership at a time that calls for more peace.
We want people and nations to thrive.
We believe in dialogue and co-operation.
Finally, let me make a procedural proposal.
The foundations of the United Nations were built in San Francisco over 80 years ago.
Today, we must restore balance to the world order.
We must recommit to the fundamental principles of the international order.
And we must embrace co-operation over conflict.
What the world needs now, is a new San Francisco moment.
A moment where world leaders come together to chart the way forward.
A process to achieve this should start with the new Secretary-General.
I bring warm greetings from the people of Fiji, and from the Blue Pacific Continent.
Fiji assures you of our full support as you guide this Assembly through a period of profound uncertainty and transformation.
Through a decade of turbulence he has defended multilateralism and stood with Small Island Developing States. Fiji thanks him.
The theme of this session — “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All”
— speaks directly to the condition of our world.

We face deepening geopolitical rivalry, armed conflict, climate and environmental crises, economic uncertainty, disrupted supply chains, rapid technological change, and an information environment corroded by disinformation.
These crises do not remain where they begin.
Conflict raises the cost of fuel and food far beyond its borders.
Carbon emitted far from the Pacific takes our shorelines, our homes and our sacred places.
For Small Island Developing States, distance no longer insulates us from global shocks.
Too often, it magnifies their cost.
Trust, therefore, is not restored by declarations alone.

It is restored when commitments are kept, when international law is applied consistently, when institutions listen, and when people can see and feel the results of multilateral action in their daily lives.
PEACE, SECURITY AND THE RULE OF LAW Fiji reaffirms an enduring principle: international law is not optional, and peace cannot be secured by power alone.

For small States, the principles of the Charter — sovereign equality, territorial integrity, the peaceful settlement of disputes — are the safeguard against a world in which size or military strength decides whose rights matter.
When the world asks small States to choose between competing power blocs, Fiji chooses principles.
We choose dialogue over coercion, human dignity over domination, and cooperation over confrontation.
Fiji calls for the peaceful settlement of conflicts wherever they occur.
We urge all parties to protect civilians, respect international humanitarian law, and return to the negotiating table.
The Charter does not apply differently according to who is involved, or where.
Fiji asks the same of every party, in every theatre.
Energy, food security and supply chains are inseparable from peace.
The freedoms of navigation guaranteed under international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, must be respected.
Fiji will continue to serve in United Nations peace operations.

We ask only that they be properly mandated, properly financed and properly supported — and we support renewed investment in prevention, mediation and the quiet diplomacy that stops wars before they begin.
We carry a simple Pacific conviction: the life of a stranger is worth protecting, dialogue is worth pursuing, and peace, however difficult, is always worth building.
THE BLUE PACIFIC AND REGIONAL COOPERATION The Pacific knows the cost of militarization and nuclear testing.
Our ocean carries the memory of decisions made elsewhere but suffered by Pacific peoples.
That memory strengthens our determination that the Blue Pacific remain a region of peace.
The Ocean of Peace Declaration expresses a regional vision grounded in sovereignty, international law and the rejection of coercion.
Our message to all partners is clear: the Pacific welcomes friendship, investment and genuine cooperation — but our ocean must not become a theatre in which others settle their rivalries.
For Small Island Developing States, regional cooperation is not an optional layer of diplomacy.
Separated by vast distances, with small populations and narrow economic bases, what is difficult alone becomes possible together.
We must take it further still — through connectivity, food and energy security, and Pacific-led financing such as something the Pacific has built.
The Pacific Resilience Facility is the first climate and disaster financing facility owned, governed and hosted by the States it serves.
Its treaty entered into force in May, it is seated in Tonga, and its first grants are already reaching our communities.
It exists because a village seawall does not need a three- year accreditation process.
Its initial capitalisation target is five hundred million United States dollars by December, of which one hundred and seventy-three million has been pledged.
I thank those who have come forward, and I ask those able to close that gap to do so.
Cooperation of this kind does not diminish our sovereignty.
It strengthens our ability to exercise it.
RESTORING TRUST AT HOME: CONSTITUTIONAL AND DEMOCRATIC RENEWAL The call to restore trust must also apply within our own nations.
Fiji's democratic journey has not been easy.
We have known political upheaval, constitutional change and periods of deep division.
We cannot change that history, but we can learn from it.
This year Fiji undertook a national review of the 2013 Constitution, informed by consultations across the country.
On 1 September the Commission presented its report to me as Head of State.
That did not end the process; it began the next stage.
The report must now proceed through Parliament and the democratic processes, transparently and in accordance with the rule of law.
What Fiji seeks is not a Constitution for a government, a party or one generation, but a settlement that every Fijian recognizes as their own.
Alongside it, our Truth and Reconciliation process continues.
Renewal strengthens institutions; reconciliation heals divisions.
Together they can carry Fiji from memory to understanding, and from division to trust.
A UNITED NATIONS THAT DELIVERS If the United Nations is to restore trust, it must also be willing to reform itself.
Fiji supports the UN80 reform agenda to make the Organisation more coherent, efficient and effective.
But reform must be judged by a single test: what it improves for people and for Member States.
For Pacific Small Island Developing States, efficiency must not mean distance.
The Multi-Country Offices serving our region are essential bridges between global commitments and island realities.
Reform must strengthen, not thin, our capacity to deliver where need is greatest.
This Assembly will also select the next Secretary- General.
Fiji asks for a process that is transparent and merit-based — and for a Secretary-General who understands the realities of small island States and will act on them.
For too long our circumstances have been well diagnosed and poorly addressed.
The promise to “deliver for all” must also be measured in development.
With 2030 approaching, too many Sustainable Development Goals remain off track.
National income alone cannot capture remoteness, disaster exposure and the repeated burden of rebuilding.
The Multidimensional Vulnerability Index must move from adoption to application.
There is one measure of delivery that reaches Fijian households directly.
Remittances are now Fiji’s third- largest source of foreign exchange.
They pay school fees, rebuild homes after cyclones, and sustain families between harvests.
They are the earnings of Fijians abroad, sent home.
Yet Pacific corridors remain among the most expensive in the world through which to send money.
In May, in this Hall, we recommitted ourselves to bring transfer costs below three per cent, and to eliminate corridors costing more than five.
Fiji asks that this be treated as an obligation and not an aspiration.
Labour mobility must also not become a one-way transfer of the people we have trained.
Fiji does not begrudge any Fijian the chance to build a life abroad.
We ask only that those who recruit our nurses and teachers invest in the systems that produced them.
And this belongs beside what I have said of reconciliation.
Not every Fijian abroad left in search of work.
Some left in seasons of upheaval, when they did not feel that the country was theirs.
They are Fijians still, and so are their children.
A supreme law that belongs to every citizen must belong to them also.
This month, Fiji declared a national HIV emergency.
One in sixty of our adults is now estimated to be living with the virus.
Fewer than four in ten know it.

I say this plainly, because stigma and silence are how this epidemic grew — and because the late Ratu Epeli Nailatikau, our former Head of State and UNAIDS Goodwill Ambassador for the Pacific, spent his last years telling us so.
This is also a security question.
Methamphetamine trafficked into our region by transnational criminal networks is now driving transmission through injecting drug use.
Our borders are ocean, our populations are small, and the profits at stake exceed our national budgets.
A country of under a million people cannot interdict a global supply chain alone.

So Fiji asks three things: that treatment and diagnostics reach small States at prices we can pay; that the Global Fund and UNAIDS be resourced at a level that does not force triage between regions; and that our partners treat Pacific narcotics interdiction as the shared security interest it is.
A nurse who emigrates is a nurse Fiji trained and will not have.
A Fijian who dies at thirty- five of a treatable virus is the same subtraction, made permanent, with the cost of care left behind.
Small States are not losing workers at the margin.
We are losing the capacity to staff our own future.
CLIMATE CHANGE AND THE OCEAN Nowhere is the gap between promise and delivery more consequential than in the climate crisis.
For the Pacific, climate change is not a future scenario.
It is saltwater entering farmland, coastal erosion moving closer to homes, stronger storms damaging schools and roads, pressure on fisheries and food security, and communities facing relocation.
This is a question of science.
It is also a question of justice.
This Assembly has this week addressed the threats posed by sea-level rise.
For Fiji the legal consequences are not abstract.
Maritime zones, once lawfully established and deposited with the United Nations, must remain — notwithstanding the physical changes brought by sea-level rise.
No State should lose its rights, its identity or its seat in this Hall because others have altered its coastline.
Fiji urges this Assembly to carry that principle from declaration into settled international law.
Fiji welcomes the Advisory Opinion of the International Court of Justice on the obligations of States in respect of climate change.
It confirms that climate responsibility is not only political or moral — it is legal.
The task now is implementation: obligations recognised by the Court must be reflected in national commitments, in the conduct of States, and in the outcomes of our negotiations.
Climate finance must move from promise to access, and from announcement to disbursement.
The Loss and Damage Fund must operate at a scale that reflects actual need, and access must be simplified — for small administrations, the cost of applying should never exceed the capacity to apply.
In November, the world gathers in Antalya for COP31.
Before that, Fiji hosts the Pre-COP, and Tuvalu a Leaders’ event, in early October.
To every delegation in this Hall: come to the Pacific.
See what a rising sea means to a village that has nowhere to move.
Then let us go to Antalya and deliver — on adaptation, on finance, on loss and damage, and on the transition away from fossil fuels.
As a Large Ocean State, Fiji’s identity, economy and future are inseparable from the ocean.
