Illegal fishing, pollution, biodiversity loss and warming, acidifying seas do not respect national boundaries — and no island nation can meet them alone.
This year, the Agreement on marine biodiversity beyond national jurisdiction entered into force — a genuine achievement of multilateralism.

Fiji calls for universal ratification, for a first Conference of the Parties that delivers a functioning institution, and for capacity- building and technology transfer that are real rather than aspirational.
And in the deep sea we ask of others only the discipline we ask of ourselves: that no exploitation proceed until the science is sufficient and the rules are sound.
The common heritage of humankind is an obligation owed to those not yet born.
CONCLUSION: THE CHOICE BEFORE US Fiji comes to this Assembly as a small island State, but not with a small vision.
Our size does not diminish our voice.
Our vulnerability does not diminish our agency.
And our distance from the centres of power does not distance us from its consequences.
Transformation will happen whether we manage it or not.
The real question is what kind of transformation we choose.
Will it be governed by law, or by power?
And will this Assembly remain a place where we describe crises — or become an institution that solves them?
Let this Eighty-First Session be remembered not for the depth of our concern, but for the courage of our decisions.
Let us build a United Nations that is trusted because it is fair; relevant because it adapts; and respected because it delivers.
Let us build a Pacific that remains an Ocean of Peace — united in purpose, confident in its identity, and strong enough to shape its own future.
And let us remember that the measure of what we do here will not be found in our speeches.
It will be found in whether a coastal community can remain on the land of its ancestors, and whether a young person can trust democracy and find a future at home.
That is the United Nations Fiji believes in.
And that is the trust we must restore — together.
Since this morning, speeches have followed one another here describing the state of the world.
And I fear I may lack originality in describing it.
For each indeed describes the return of imperialism, of arrogance, the return to force without rules or restraint.

A world, ultimately, of concentration of power where a few think they can undermine the international order in order to expand their borders, where others think they can trample on the sovereignty of peoples in order to dispose of it themselves, and where a few think they can decide the future of the planet, whether in terms of climate or artificial intelligence.
In the end, the question put to us in very simple terms is whether we want to live in this state of nature, with a kind of return to the law of the jungle, or in a civilized international society.

Our duty, more than ever, is to stand firm alongside the United Nations precisely to decide together on the common interest, that is to say, on the side of those who want freely to choose their destiny, their alliances, their development models, their future, on the side of those who refuse to have their sovereignty confiscated by unjust force or by fear, and on the side of hope.
That is the very reason for our organization, this common house that brings together free, equal peoples, founded on the sovereign equality of each of its members.
It is our Charter that prevents the power of some from enabling them to decide for others.
Above all, it is what requires us together to demonstrate our commitment and our ability to act usefully.
You know France's attachment to the United Nations and its determination fully to assume the particular responsibilities entrusted to it by the Charter.

I also want to tell you of my country's commitment to act with each of you to renew the conditions for multilateral action and to demonstrate that we are stronger, more effective, better able to face common challenges together.

Those of today and those to come, which still elude us even as everything around us is changing; I mentioned climate and the environment, it is also true for war and peace, it is obviously true for technologies as for development.

Ultimately, in each of these fields, where the law of the strongest seeks to impose itself, we must defend justice, the common interest, and we must do so in the very interest of each one of us, for it is our Charter that protects this possibility of living together.

So, faced with the course of the world and the fact that what we are living through today is an accumulation of wars that we are unable to resolve, multiplying crises and contemporary challenges that cast a new shadow over new generations, I believe that our duty is not to yield.

In the end, the message I have come to convey today, as I have done for nine years, is one of determination, of optimism in action, but it is to tell you: let us not yield to the spirit of defeat, to fatalism, ultimately to what is in fashion, which would be to resign ourselves to saying that we come to this organization to make speeches but that it no longer serves much purpose; let us set up other organizations where the law of the strongest can prevail and perhaps another peace can be imposed.
But let us not yield to that, even less today than yesterday.
Let us not yield to it in five respects.
Those are the five remarks I would like to make.
First, let us not yield to a kind of fatalism in the face of war and the suffering of peoples.
We must recommit ourselves to finding concrete solutions and building peace.
International law has never claimed to describe reality.
It sets out the limits that sovereign powers have voluntarily imposed on themselves.
So that force is not the only recourse in the event of disagreement, so that even in the face-off of war, the enemy remains a human being.
Those are the lessons of the twentieth century.
Those who wish to forget them today are committing both a moral fault and a political error.
In the Middle East, in Ukraine, in Africa, the industrialization of war crimes, violations of law and the destruction of civilian infrastructure is ushering in a new age of barbarity.

None of us can wish to be the one who dismantles the protective framework of the Geneva Conventions, at a time when attacks are multiplying from Dnipro to Gaza, from Bukavu to El Fasher, with Jordan and the ICRC.

France will therefore continue its efforts so that the global initiative in support of international humanitarian law, already joined by more than 116 States, leads us to renew our commitments together.
We must remobilize to defend our humanitarians, to defend international humanitarian law in this period.

As many of us have often said, it is also because there can be no peace without justice that France continues to provide both political and operational support to international justice, investigation and evidence-gathering mechanisms, in particular fact-finding missions, and that we continue and will continue to support the International Court of Justice and its central role.
We cannot accept the new order of impunity that some would like to build.
This is also why, in the Security Council, France supports reforms that guarantee its effectiveness.

In terms of format, of course, we must open it to new members, to new regions of the world, starting with Africa, but also in substance, the Security Council must be able to act in the face of massive violations of international law.
Who can be satisfied with a procedural deadlock in the face of barbarity?
The French-Mexican initiative on restraining the use of the veto in cases of mass atrocities is more necessary than ever, and I welcome the fact that 128 Member States now support it.
The campaign must continue and must prevail, therefore securing the commitment of each of the permanent members of the Security Council.
But it is not enough to invoke the law and call upon our values in order to fulfil the obligations to which each of us consented by joining the United Nations.
France is ready for that, in coalition with all those who want to act in compliance with the principles of the Charter and who do not accept powerlessness.

Thus, in Ukraine, the coalition of the willing that we have formed with the United Kingdom and Germany brings together all those who are ready to guarantee peace and stability at the heart of Europe, where two world wars began and from which no one can detach themselves.
Many here know better than anyone what the return of war to Europe can mean.
We will yield nothing on this.
The coalition of the willing is carrying this fight.
In the Middle East, we have set up an independent multinational coalition to restore freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.
This must not become an object of blackmail.
It is a cardinal principle of international law, and it is in everyone’s interest that ships pass through the Strait safely and that the energy supply of our countries be ensured.
The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz is a priority.
Respect for international law there is a priority; it is in everyone’s interest, and France will commit itself to it.
In Africa, we bear a collective responsibility in the face of accumulating crises and the absence of responses.
At the heart of conflicts, peace operations must be more effective and, for that, they must have adequate means and be part of better coordination between the United Nations and host States.
I was already referring in 2018 to the role of regional organizations and the organization of better coordination between them and the United Nations.

At the Africa Forward Summit in Nairobi, with more than 30 African heads of State, then at the headquarters of the African Union in Addis Ababa, alongside the United Nations, we stated clearly that the African Union and regional organizations must be able to play their full role in matters of peace and security on the continent.

In November, on the margins of the Paris Peace Forum, we will organize in Paris a replenishment meeting for the African Union Peace Fund, and I call on all potential contributors to make strong and concrete commitments there.
We must not yield, therefore, in the face of wars; we must re-engage and seek to build solutions in compliance with the Charter.
The second principle is not to yield to the constant temptation of double standards, for that is what divides our planet and discredits the coherence of our international order and of our Charter.
How many times have we heard that the sovereignty of peoples applied in Europe, but that when it came to looking at the Middle East or Africa, it could well be dispensed with?
No, we must defend the same principles everywhere and do so in compliance with the Charter, that is to say, with the sovereignty of those same peoples, never by substituting ourselves for them.

Every time a few States, sometimes in the very name of the international order, have sought to substitute themselves for the people in order to change this regime or that system, they have plunged those States into even greater chaos.
No double standards: one life equals one life, peace and security are indivisible, and all are entitled to them.
In Ukraine, for nearly five years, Russia has been waging a cruel war against civilians and occupying the territory of a sovereign country.
France will continue to provide unwavering support for the legitimate aspirations of the Ukrainian people to peace, security and a future.
At the same time, it will spare no effort to ensure that useful negotiations between Ukraine and Russia begin as soon as possible.

We must defend the Ukrainians, and defend them more than ever before the approaching winter, defend them in energy matters, defend them so that they have more interceptors and can protect their civilian population.

That is also why we support the initiative of a double moratorium: a moratorium on energy and civilian infrastructure on both sides, and a moratorium on the Black Sea that will make it possible to release grain and provide an answer to the crucial food security question for so many emerging and developing countries.
This double moratorium is a necessity.
Let us propose it and confront Russia with its own rhetoric.
In the Near and Middle East, too, it is again respect for the sovereignty of each that alone can bring peace and security to all, and that is what we defend.
Respect for sovereignty for the displaced Lebanese whose villages are being destroyed one after another in the south.
Only a fully sovereign Lebanon will be able to lead to Hezbollah laying down its arms and to restoring security for the Lebanese and all their neighbours.
Sovereignty of Lebanon and of its people.
Sovereignty for the Palestinians whose most basic rights are still being violated today.
A year ago, here in this very hall, we were about a dozen States to recognize Palestine.
I hear the cynicism of some: “paper recognition, look at the reality.”
But what credibility do we have if we continue to remain inactive in the face of Gaza?
Some boast of a supposed peace.
But that peace has not reopened the humanitarian routes for a single second.
Must we contemplate this spectacle that brings shame on us all? Never.
Look at what is happening in the West Bank, where every day violations are committed in the name of what?
Hamas has never operated in the West Bank.
It is every day building the impossibility of a project which is respect for the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people to exist.
But at the same time, it is the very conditions of security today and tomorrow for Israel and its people.
Security to which we are attached, existence to which we are attached.

But all those who claim that Israel’s security depends on violating the sovereignty of all its neighbours are making a fatal mistake, weakening Israel’s security for today and for tomorrow, and threatening it.
Sovereignty also for Syria, whose revolution must not be disappointed.
A few months ago, I was in Damascus to bring France’s support for the building of free Syria.
And we must continue these efforts and, there too, enable Syria fully to restore its sovereignty and its unity.
France is committed to each of these struggles.

As we are committed with Italy, with the help of Jordan and a few others, and all the friends of Lebanon, to finding an effective follow-up to our half-century of engagement within UNIFIL, in the service of all the Lebanese and of the sovereignty of their country.
My third conviction is that we must not give in to the division of the world and to this rift that many describe, that some use, between the North and the South.
We will not solve any of the planet’s challenges if we allow this division to take hold.

It is taking hold, it feeds on double standards when they are practiced by some, but we need to reconcile the North and the South in order to meet the challenges, whether climate, health, or development.

It is in this regard that, in recent years, we have multiplied initiatives in response to Covid, with the ACT-A and COVAX initiatives, in partnership with the World Health Organization and the African Union; when it comes to reviving economies, with the International Monetary Fund to reallocate Special Drawing Rights and make it possible to better finance African economies.
And we kept our word by reallocating more than 100 billion dollars in Special Drawing Rights to help African countries.
But we must constantly ensure that we preserve unity and do not set blocs against one another.
That is why it is so important not to allow the global health architecture to fracture.

We must continue to move forward on its reform, but never by weakening the World Health Organization, by making it possible to finalize the pandemic treaty and by supporting WHO and Africa CDC to fight Ebola even more effectively.
We must also know how to reform our official development assistance lucidly and build much more effective solidarity-based investment.
That is the meaning of what we did in 2023 with the Pact for Prosperity, People and the Planet.
That is the meaning of the initiative taken in Nairobi a few months ago at the Africa Forward summit: to build a new consensus on solidarity-based investment.

At a time when so many countries are reducing their transfers and yet the needs of many countries of the South are increasing, we must move faster and more forcefully to help the IMF and the World Bank become more effective, to improve the effectiveness of their instruments, to better mobilize the private sector, to build guarantee mechanisms so that, in emerging countries, middle-income countries and developing countries, we can provide a more effective response.
It is this new financial partnership that we need to build in order to avoid the rift between the North and the South.
In the same way, this North-South partnership depends and will depend on our ability to reopen dialogues on our shared histories, our memories and our cultural relations.

This is what France has sought to do in recent years through work of knowledge and recognition based on joint scientific work, by launching a legislative process that enabled us to begin the restitution of cultural property, to have there too, in a sense, a partnership of memory, culture and history with many countries of the South.
And we are continuing, with Ghana in particular, but also with all partners who so wish, the work to respond to the needs for reparatory justice that have been expressed.
It is a question of respect, and it is also on this respect that the coming together of the North and the South is built.
Beyond development and memory policies, new partnerships also imply having globalization, and world trade, that are more effective and fairer.

This is what we sought to do at the G7 organized by France, by involving several countries of the South, by building through the summit of convergences a dialogue beyond the G7 with China, India, Brazil, the Republic of Korea, Kenya and others, in order to improve our collective organization, to avoid the accumulation by a few of critical minerals and rare earths, and to enable more effective cooperation in trade as in monetary matters.
Fundamentally, as you understand, we have a responsibility not to allow this rift between two blocs to take hold.
The fourth principle is not to give in to fatalism on climate and biodiversity.
We have done a great deal in recent years, since the Paris Agreement, eleven years ago, whose principles remain valid, whose agreements are to be defended and from which we must not depart.
But, like you, I hear the doubt that is arising among some, the questioning of science among others, and so here too, let us yield nothing.
If we want to meet the challenges of the planet, those of climate and biodiversity, we need multilateralism in action.
This is what we sought to do through the One Planet Summit.
This is also what we sought to do collectively, and succeeded in doing, if we look at the issue of the oceans.
A few years ago, everyone was telling us that it was impossible to build agreements to protect our marine areas, our oceans.
Look at what we did a few years ago: protect 30 per cent of our land area and our seas.
We built that agreement, and each year we are improving its implementation.
And then, many told us that, in the end, we would never manage to preserve what represents more than two thirds of our oceans, the high seas, beyond our exclusive economic zones.
We succeeded in bringing that negotiation to a conclusion by engaging, there too, the major powers.
That was the BBNJ Agreement, and within a few months, we finalized the more than 60 ratifications, with the result that this agreement is now in force.

The Nice summit, bringing nations together for UNOC 3 in June of last year, made it possible to accelerate this work, along with several other achievements, and the first COP on the oceans will be held in a few months’ time, in January.
It is tremendous proof of our capacity to achieve concrete results when we mobilize and act together.
And so, let us yield nothing to the fatalism of the moment.
Let us defend our achievements, but let us also defend our principles.
We must defend independent and free science.
Let us protect the IPCC, IPBES, our scientists who alert us, who measure, who assess.
Let us remain committed to the Paris Agreement, to our national trajectories, to our decarbonization and to the objective of carbon neutrality by 2050.
Let us assume our responsibilities, accelerate cooperation and innovation, relaunch work on biodiversity credits and implement our objectives on the protection of forests and oceans.
There is no inevitability, only decisions to be taken by us, today, we who are already the victims of climate disruption, and even more so for our children.

Lastly, let us yield nothing to the state of the world that is emerging on artificial intelligence, through which some would have us believe that only two powers, the United States and China, could decide, or more exactly that a few economic actors could decide everything: decide what innovations they want to pursue, decide, some, to pause, others not, decide whether the innovations they will make will undermine the national security of our States, may tomorrow make it possible to attack our hospitals or our banks, and also decide what the future of our societies will be.
No, no. And this is not something we are just discovering.

As early as 2018, within the G7, with our Canadian friends, we launched the Global Partnership on Artificial Intelligence, anchoring that structure in the OECD to begin the discussion and the need for regulation.
At the Summit for Action on Artificial Intelligence organized in Paris in 2025, followed by India in 2026, and which will be held in Switzerland next year, we argued for two very simple elements.

That each region of the world should be able to equip itself with its own capacities, computing, LLM models, artificial intelligence ecosystems, and that we should be able to develop the possibility of auditing these models and not be dependent simply on a few private actors.
Europe, moreover, was the first, with the AI Act, to establish its principles and in particular the capacity to audit these models.
We must continue along this path.
And in this regard, I want to emphasize one point here.
Our young people and our children.
We waited too long to protect our children and our adolescents from social media.
Everywhere in our societies, we are seeing the consequences.
A decline in the capacity to learn, an epidemic of obesity among some, mental health disorders among others.
The findings are there and the elements of correlation are well established.
That is why several of us launched a major initiative to protect our children and our adolescents from access to social media before the age of 15 or 16, depending on the country.
And Europe has now followed this step, having decided to launch regulation.
And I want here to salute the pioneering character of the Australians, who were the first to legislate in this area.
We are going to pursue this fight to the very end.
But let us not wait for the same consequences when it comes to artificial intelligence.
Starting now, we must protect our children and our adolescents in this regard.
Look at the impact of chatbots on our children.
That is why, with Kenya, Spain and Australia, we brought together the Coalition for Children’s Rights and Protection in the Age of Artificial Intelligence.
As of this afternoon, we are mobilizing it.

And the Paris Peace Forum will be the place where, on 10 and 11 November next, we want to bring together all governments, all organizations, all public and private actors, businesses and academics who want to accelerate this agenda for the protection of our children.
And I look forward to seeing you on 10 and 11 November next in Paris in this regard.
Beyond that, we clearly see that the race for frontier models has begun.

We must continue to invest, each of us in our own regions, in order to take part in it, and France is proud to have an actor that is in the frontier-model race, and we will continue to invest, to support Mistral AI so that we can hold our place and try to have such a model.
But we must also build new forms of cooperation.

And I very deeply hope that all sovereign States attached to their independence—European, Canadian, Brazilian, Indian, Indonesian, African, Gulf States, Singapore, and others besides—that coalition of independents that I have referred to several times, those, in the end, who do not want to become the vassals of one or the other of the two great world powers, will come together to develop an open-source frontier model, by pooling the computing capacity available to them, by pooling their investment capacity to build an open-source frontier artificial intelligence model that we would share.
We must not depend on one or the other, and we must succeed precisely in advancing such an agenda through cooperation.
Lastly, there are areas in which we must clearly establish the new rules of the game.
Artificial intelligence in outer space, in defence, in cybersecurity, as I mentioned, has profound consequences that affect our national security.
We launched this dialogue at the G7 last June in Evian.

Several have now mobilized, and we support the appeal launched by our Norwegian and Finnish friends, and we want to continue, within the framework of the G7, also in close connection with our British friends who will next year have responsibility for the G20, to build precisely an agenda for cooperation on artificial intelligence, to protect the most sensitive elements that affect our national security.

Just as, in the past, we were able to agree to build a new international architecture when it came to chemical weapons or other risks, we must acknowledge that issues are now emerging, when it comes to outer space, defence and cybersecurity, over which we must regain control, which require specific cooperation and a specific framework among Member States, and we must build that cooperation and that framework.
On that, we must yield nothing.
Those are the five principles of action—without claiming to be exhaustive in that regard, but I will stop there—in which France believes and that I wanted to defend before you today.
And fundamentally, on these five points, my message is: yield nothing.

Yield nothing to what is taking hold, which is, fundamentally, a slow division of the world, a spirit of defeatism that is setting in and that would leave some in the abuse of power: abuse of power by empires that threaten the sovereignty of one country or another, abuse of power by a few who concentrate capital capacity and who would have the right either to pollute or to aggregate computing capacity for everyone, abuse of power by a few who would want to concentrate wealth.

Faced with abuses of power, we must recover what is the vitality of our Organization, that multilateralism which is the defence of a common interest, of justice for all, and which is, fundamentally, through unity, justice and cooperation, the only effectiveness, the one that makes it possible to restore a just and lasting peace in our countries, the one that makes it possible to restore unity between North and South, the one that makes it possible to rebuild an agenda for action on climate as well as on technology.
More than ever, we need our United Nations.
At this time, when we have to confront old crises and new challenges, we must indeed continue to act.
We must have the courage to be optimistic, to mobilize and to be useful, to yield nothing to the spirit of the age, for each and every one.
As you conclude your tenure, we honor your advocacy for the most vulnerable, and your tireless efforts in strengthening multilateralism.
The theme of this 81st session "Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all" speaks directly to our realities on our small islands in Micronesia.
We need the benefits of digital innovation, artificial intelligence, energy transition, and institutional reforms.
At the same time, we recognize the challenges of climate change, ocean degradation, pollution, and growing inequality.
Micronesia stands in solidarity with all nations that have endured the recent waves of natural disasters around the world.
The loss of lives, displacements, and destructions remind us of our common vulnerability.
Today’s security landscape is shaped not only by conflict but by climate-driven fragility.
Extreme weather events, sea-level rise, and resource degradation are eroding stability across vulnerable regions, especially the Pacific.
These pressures intensify humanitarian needs, disrupt food and water systems, and strain governance capacities.
For Micronesia, climate impacts are a national security concern.
We underscore the importance of safeguarding maritime security across the Blue Pacific.
Illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing activities, transnational crimes, and environmental degradation threaten not only our economies but the health of our marine environment as well.
We urge the international community to enhance cooperation, share technology, and support capacity-building to ensure that the ocean remains a zone of peace, governed by international law.
The challenges that impede our sustainable development are increasing.
We must respond by implementing science-based emissions reductions, scale up national climate commitments, and accelerate transition to renewable energy.
We demand accessible and predictable adaptation grant financing to support investments in resilient infrastructure.
We must operationalize the Loss and Damage Fund.
Further, we must keep the 1.5°C goal, and sustain methane reductions.

This is not a substitute for long-term decarbonization, but can slow near-term warming, protect vulnerable communities and oceans, and preserve critical time for those on the front lines of the climate crisis.
Micronesia endorses the proposed Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty.
A just and orderly transition away from fossil fuels is now inseparable from the wider geopolitical and economic realities shaping global energy markets.
Instability in the Middle East and volatile fuel prices exposed the vulnerability of SIDS to expensive fuel, unstable supply, and widespread economic fragility.
Shift to renewable energy is an economic necessity.
Solar, wind, and ocean-based technologies can reduce dependence on external fuel markets, strengthen energy security, and lower emissions in line with science.
The world must accelerate the transition to resilient, affordable, and community-centered renewable energy systems.
Our people are the most valuable national resource.
We remain committed to delivering effective public services and advancing Micronesian priorities for our citizens, wherever they reside.
I am pleased to announce the adoption of Micronesia’s National Migration Policy, with the technical support of the International Organization for Migration.
Micronesia will strengthen the protection, engagement, and well-being of its citizens, including members of diaspora.

Micronesia also aligns itself with the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration, and welcomes its comprehensive framework for promoting humane, orderly, and well-managed international migration.
Our people’s health has been increasingly affected by more frequent tropical storms, heat waves, and changing tidal patterns.
We are seeing a rise in illnesses linked to marine life and vector- borne diseases, in particular dengue and Zika.
Already, the burden of non-communicable diseases strains our health system, reduces workforce productivity, and diverts limited resources.

We are strengthening our national health capacity, increasing investments in diagnostics and life- saving medicine, expanding the use of tele-health to access specialist care and medical education, and partnering with neighboring countries to support regular medical exchange programs that augment our treatment capability in-country.
These efforts are essential to safeguard our communities as climate impacts intensify.
The ocean is the heart of Micronesian identity, livelihoods, and future prosperity.
It faces mounting pressures from climate change, sea-level rise, pollution, and unsustainable exploitation.
Micronesia ask for a collective effort to fortify ocean governance, sustainable fisheries management, and effective conservation of marine biodiversity.
Being the first country to sign the BBNJ Agreement, we are among the first movers, comprising six nations to implement the BBNJ.

Micronesia is partnering with GIZ and five co-leading States to develop area-based management tools and marine protected area proposals under the BBNJ framework, translating our commitment to conserve 30 percent of the ocean into concrete, durable protections for areas beyond national jurisdiction.
On deep-sea mining in the international seabed Area, Micronesia employs a precautionary approach.
We stress the need to consolidate comprehensive knowledge, data, and science about the marine environment before any decision is taken on proceeding with exploitation.
Additionally, it is crucial that all stakeholders, including adjacent coastal states, Indigenous Peoples, and local communities in the Pacific, are meaningfully consulted prior to such a decision.
We must address the growing threat of plastic pollution that degrades the Pacific ecosystems and communities.
Marine debris, micro plastics, and associated toxic substances are accumulating on our shores.
Our lagoons, for example, in the State of Chuuk where oil leaks from World War II remnants led to the emergency declaration last year, continue to threaten our livelihood.
These impacts impose disproportionate cleanup and economic burdens on small island governments whose waste-management infrastructure is inadequate.

Our national efforts must be matched by strengthened international cooperation, including technical assistance, predictable financing, and collective action across the full plastics life cycle, to prevent pollution at its source and protect the Blue Pacific for present and future generations.

Micronesia calls on the international community to match local action with global responsibility: through sustained funding, meaningful technology transfer, stricter upstream controls on plastic production, and an end to waste exporting.
Critically, the international community must complete its work on a new treaty to end plastic pollution, including in the marine environment.
With less than five years to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals, the international community must respond with renewed political resolve, scaled-up financing, and accelerated implementation.
The Pacific’s experience underscores this imperative: climate impacts are steadily eroding development gains and placing progress across the Goals further at risk.

The recent typhoon and severe flooding in our States, and more frequent king tides affecting our low- lying islands demonstrate that these are no longer isolated events, but recurring pressures that test the resilience of our communities on the front lines of the climate crisis.
For us, achieving the SDGs requires accelerated action.

Our actions on gender equality continues to address barriers to women’s leadership, economic participation, and access to justice, digital safety, and protection from violence—particularly for women and girls in remote and outer island communities.

We are mainstreaming gender across state and national planning, strengthening survivor-centered services, expanding women’s economic empowerment and decision-making and engaging in preventing gender-based violence and advancing equality.
Our youth are taking active roles in community advocacy, climate stewardship, adaptation and mitigation activities, and services across our nation.

Building on these achievements, our priorities are clear: strengthening youth voices in decision-making; expanding skills training and pathways to decent work; supporting youth-led climate and community action; addressing substance abuse and mental health; and ensuring that young people have the opportunity to lead, serve, and build the future of our nation.
We must implement the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index (MVI) into a modern, coherent, and responsive system that moves decisively from concept to practice.
Doing so would unlock fair access to concessional financing that reflect structural vulnerabilities faced by small, fragile, and highly exposed economies such SIDS.
Micronesia reaffirms its strong commitment to the progress of the UN80 reform initiative.
In addressing the UN Country Team Reconfiguration, we firmly believe that both the Multi- Country Office and the Resident Coordinator system must remain securely in place.
Our distinct geographical landscape features incredibly remote communities.
This lived reality is precisely why the UN80 reform initiative matters so deeply to Micronesia.
For countries defined by distance, dispersion, and vulnerability, reform cannot be an abstract exercise; it must strengthen the UN’s ability to deliver where the needs are greatest.
Our priority is to create a UN architecture that preserves what works, fixes what does not, and ensures that no community, no matter how remote, is left behind.

Micronesia supports an expanded Council that includes Brazil, Germany, India, and Japan as permanent members, alongside permanent representation for Africa, and a dedicated non‑permanent seat for SIDS, ensuring that those most affected by global decisions are finally present at the table.

Digital transformation and artificial intelligence offer significant opportunities to improve public- service delivery, diversify economies, expand market access, and advance climate-resilient development.

Although, we are advancing digital connectivity, private-sector development, and trade opportunities, but without adequate investment, capacity-building, and appropriate governance, these technologies may increase inequalities and further heighten exposure to cyber security threats, misinformation, and risks to data privacy.
We therefore call upon the international community to strengthen financing for resilient digital infrastructure, with ethical and effective guardrails and governance frameworks.
The priorities before us mentioned earlier are interconnected tests of whether the United Nations can deliver for all.
For Micronesia, success must be measured not by declarations, but by tangible improvements in our people’s lives, security, and dignity.
We call for equitable partnership with small island developing States through accessible finance, technology transfer, stronger capacity, and a meaningful voice in global decisions.
In the spirit of KAMORALE, let us choose cooperation over division and build a peaceful, just, and sustainable future in which every nation can thrive.

2. I wish to assure you from the outset of my delegation’s full support and to express the hope that your mandate will be marked by listening, dialogue and the tireless pursuit of compromise in the service of international peace and cooperation.
4. Gabon fully associates itself with the theme of this session: “Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations Organization serving all”.
5. This theme comes at a decisive moment in international history.
Our world is beset by numerous, profound and interdependent crises.
Armed conflicts are tending to drag on, geopolitical tensions are intensifying, inequalities persist, climate disruption is accelerating and humanitarian emergencies are multiplying.

6. To these challenges must be added the economic and social consequences of successive crises, food insecurity, forced displacement of populations, the risks associated with cybercrime and the upheavals brought about by emerging technologies.
7. These realities severely test the capacity of the international community to act in a concerted manner.
8. In this uncertain environment, only one value can still guide us: trust.
9. For Gabon, restoring trust among nations requires, more than ever, a return to the fundamental principles of international law in general, and of the Charter of the United Nations in particular.
10. In this spirit, my country reaffirms its attachment to the principle of non-interference in internal affairs and to respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of States.

11. And on the strength of this affirmation, Gabon once again welcomes the adoption of resolution 2797 (2025), which is giving new momentum to the settlement of the regional dispute over the Moroccan Sahara, on the exclusive basis of the autonomy plan under Moroccan sovereignty.
12. Restoring trust is based above all on concrete action enabling us to address together the global challenges relating to peace and security, climate change, sustainable development and pandemics.
13. Therefore, in the face of human tragedies throughout the world, and particularly in Africa, greater collective engagement is indispensable.
14. This requirement for inclusiveness is necessary, in particular, in the Gulf of Guinea, a maritime area whose importance for international trade is increasing every day.
15. Consequently, Gabon advocates a substantial strengthening of security in this strategic area, the bedrock of shared prosperity.

16. Gabon, in its capacity as a member of the Peace and Security Council of the African Union, underlines the urgency of implementing Security Council resolution 2719 relating to the financing of peace support operations on the continent.
17. Honouring this commitment would help consolidate peace in Africa and strengthen cooperation between the United Nations Security Council and the Peace and Security Council of the African Union.
18. Trust also depends on respect for commitments made within the regional framework.

Under the very high impetus of His Excellency Brice Clotaire OLIGUI NGUEMA, President of the Republic, Head of State, Head of Government, Gabon has made dialogue, peace and respect for its international commitments the guiding principles of its diplomatic action.
19. Managing transformation, as our theme invites us to do, also means knowing how to guide change at the national level.

20. In this regard, under the leadership of the President of the Republic, Mr. Brice Clotaire OLIGUI NGUEMA, Gabon is continuing its transformation at the social, environmental and economic levels, as set out in our National Growth and Development Plan, the PNCD 2026-2030.

21. Gabon’s development plan also places emphasis on improving the living conditions of our populations, notably through new administrative, hospital and educational infrastructure, in line with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
22. In view of the foregoing, my country calls for a renewed partnership based on mutual respect, shared responsibility and concrete commitments.
This partnership must promote the local processing of our natural resources, the diversification of our economy, the transfer of technologies and the strengthening of national capacities.
23. Restoring trust also requires a reform of the international financial architecture, so as to make it more equitable, more inclusive and better adapted to current challenges.
Without this overhaul, it becomes almost impossible to mobilize funds linked to development, particularly those relating to green financing.

25. Therefore, Gabon, a country with extensive forest cover and a low rate of deforestation, a major carbon sequestration sink, calls for better recognition of this contribution to the regulation of the global climate and of the ecosystem services rendered to humanity.
These must be appreciated at their true value and give entitlement to fair, adequate, predictable and sustainable financing.

26. While it is true that digital transformation offers considerable possibilities, it nevertheless entails risks: infringement of privacy, disinformation, cybercrime, as well as the irresponsible use of emerging technologies.
27. The absence of an efficient international legal framework gives free rein to all these abuses, posing a direct threat to the security of our States and to the fundamental rights of citizens.

28. Already suffering from these multifaceted harms, Gabon has had to undertake more appropriate and secure regulation of the digital sector and artificial intelligence, through temporary, proportionate measures motivated solely by the imperative of preserving our fellow citizens.
29. Our objective remains the construction of an open, safe digital ecosystem that respects freedoms, in perfect harmony with our international commitments.
30. For the United Nations to deliver results for all, it cannot ignore the debts of history.
Gabon therefore welcomes the adoption of United Nations General Assembly resolution 80/250 on the slave trade in Africans, characterizing it as the gravest crime against humanity.
31. An organization that delivers results is also an organization that knows how to reform itself from within.
The United Nations must therefore demonstrate its ability to adapt to the international context and to address effectively the challenges facing the world.
32. This determination for institutional transformation must take into account the urgency of reforming the Security Council.
Indeed, Africa must occupy the place that is rightfully its own within this very closed circle of permanent members.
33. For Gabon, there can be no legitimate global governance without the equitable participation of Africa in decision-making relating to international peace and security.
34. Gabon’s vision is that of an inclusive and reformed multilateralism that takes into account the aspirations of peoples, particularly those of women and young people.
It is within this framework that the fundamental right of every State to chart its own path must be guaranteed.
35. It is in the name of this principle that Gabon reaffirms here its support for Cuba.
Gabon joins the repeated calls by many States for the lifting of the embargo.

36. I should like to conclude by saying that Gabon, faithful to its regional and international commitments, and confident in a more serene future for all, based on trust, intends to contribute to building a new global edifice, more peaceful, more just, more equitable and more united.
Learning from our experience of the last one.
It is now ten years since Brexit.
My country has lived through the disruption it brought, and it has given us a unique perspective that I want to share with you today. Britain is back.
We are restoring our stability, building a more dynamic economy a nation that wants to trade with the world and work together to solve the shared problems we face.
But we have also learned that we need to adapt to meet the challenge of these times.
We need to rebalance power in our country and bring it closer to people.

We need to work harder to fight the forces of division and instability which threaten us not just through hard power, but through softer, slower means that sow fear and despair We need to do more to help people with the everyday cost of living, and seize the opportunities that give them hope for the future.
And we need to embrace the incredible potential of technology to improve people's lives.
That's what I want to talk to you about this evening, how the world can come through the turbulence of today to reach towards something better in the decade ahead.
Overcoming the forces of division and instability starts with national security.
So we will keep investing in our defence, meeting our NATO commitments and strengthening European capabilities.
We will be relentless in building up our hard power and deterrence.
But we will not play Russia's game of trading escalatory rhetoric.
Unlike Russia, we do not seek confrontation.
Instead, we will be prepared, but not panicked, clear eyed but cool headed and unflinching in defending our people and our allies.
True resilience depends on this military strength.
But the last ten years tells us that it is also about something deeper as well.
It is about the strength of the social fabric that binds us together.
There is no national security without a strong, cohesive society underneath it.
That's the starting point for everything we hold dear and everything we want to achieve.
But the fact is, it has been under attack in recent years.
We have seen industrial scale assault by hostile actors on the information environment in the UK, and that of many of our allies.
Russian agencies have used every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people's fears.
They've used bots and fake websites, falsified newspaper articles, forged the branding of 28 British organisations, including universities and the BBC.
They've amplified far right narratives, and we have evidence that they tried to interfere with the 2019 general election.
We also know that they have tried to stoke tensions and unrest in the wake of horrific events.
The idea that anyone would try to use such things to their advantage is just repulsive.
But it is what they do.
The Kremlin spends around £1.3 billion each year on manipulating information.

We're talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people's homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community, creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair.
On top of that, we have seen cyber attacks on companies and institutions, and we know that AI will multiply the threat.
We have tiptoed around this for too long.
Over the last decade, we have given too much ground to those who want to run a negative, corrosive narrative about life in Britain, which bears no resemblance to reality Well no more.
We are going to face the new decade in a different way with our eyes wide open.
We are going to be much prouder in standing up for our values and the rule of law.
And we are going to help our people to strengthen their resilience, because faced with this information warfare, security starts in every home.

If you're struggling with the cost of living and your life is not improving, or if you're a young person not in employment, education or training, you are going to be much more vulnerable to this kind of influence.
So part of the challenge is to lift our people up and create the opportunities they need.
When inequalities grow too wide, our societies are at greater risk.
So we will work to make life more affordable for people.
That will be at the heart of a new ten year plan for Britain that we will bring forward later in the year.
And we will put in place the architecture to stem this poisonous tide.

Today, I am asking our security chiefs in the UK to begin work on a new National Centre for information defence, to detect, attribute and disrupt these kinds of hostile state information attacks to support and defend our democracy.
I know this is a shared challenge so we are going to use our experience in the UK and the fact that we have already been through this shock, starting ten years ago, to help other countries.
We have already supported Moldova to protect its elections from Russian interference.
As more elections approach across Europe, more nations are grappling with these issues, some for the first time.

So we're ready to share our understanding of how these actors work and how we can respond, because this is a vital task for our collective security and resilience to overcome division and instability.
We must also find new ways to bring countries together.
We know that we are at our strongest when we unite with others, when we reach across borders to solve shared problems.
Standing here today, I am reminded of the huge human progress that this organisation has led, like the eradication of smallpox or the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
That is the kind of promise and hope that led Britain to host the very first meeting of this General Assembly in London, and led to the world to create this institution.

These United Nations, our United Nations, that is the level of ambition that we need now to renew the UN for our times, to tackle challenges like improving global health and preventing future pandemics, to end the wars that are causing so much suffering and instability, including the terrible conflict in Sudan, and to tackle climate change.
The climate crisis is now a national security threat for countries around the world.
As this summer of extreme heat, wildfires and floods has proved beyond doubt.

Britain will continue to lead with others to fight this threat, to protect our children and grandchildren, to protect the natural world and also to seize the benefits for jobs, growth and reindustrialisation that the clean energy transition can bring.
So we must raise our sights and I believe the United Kingdom has a unique position as an honest broker to help drive this forward.
We have deep ties with our friends in the European Union and seek to deepen them further.
We work with China and emerging powers like India and Brazil.
We sit on the UN Security Council in the Commonwealth, in the CPP.
In a divided world, we have the ability to bring people together and we will.
We are going to step into that role, and we are going to start with one of the most significant challenges and opportunities of our age, frontier AI.
AI brings together so many of the most pressing issues before us.
It is already speeding up cancer diagnosis in the UK, but AI has the potential to go further, not just to help prevent and treat cancer, but to help cure it.
AI will also be the key to economic growth, the route to transforming education, and it will be a vital tool to keep us safe.

I am announcing today that we are developing a new AI defence partnership with the United States to protect our critical national infrastructure, but we know that AI will also be a source of disruption to the way we live and work.
We've all heard the warnings which we must heed.
I know how worried people are, so we have to rise to this moment.
Fundamental decisions on this technology are too important to be left to chance.

They must be taken by elected governments who serve working people, and we need to give people the support they need through this change, ensuring that it becomes an engine for reindustrialisation and opportunity as well.
There is a lesson from the first industrial Revolution, which started in northern England two centuries ago.
It was a time of incredible technological progress, but for workers, the disruption brought huge suffering and exploitation.
Things got a lot worse before they got better.
So this time we need to get it right.
I believe we're more than equal to the task.
The UK has some of the best tech and AI talent anywhere in the world.
And when it comes to guarding against the risks, we have our world leading AI Security Institute working hand in glove with the US and the leading labs on AI safety.
But we need to go further.
Building on the meeting convened by His Majesty King Charles last week, I can announce today that I am going to put AI at the heart of the UK's G20 presidency next year.
I look back at how we responded to the financial crisis back in 2008.
We moved quickly in the G20 and smaller groups to deliver an urgent, practical response.
We came together to agree principles which everyone implemented at home in a way that was right for them. And it worked.
That is the kind of approach we need now.
So we will bring the right people together.
On the key issues, delivering on the potential of AI for good and dealing with the risks.
And we will work towards agreeing a single set of global principles and standards to ensure the transparency and access we need to increase our preparedness and to ensure that AI development is safe.
This will bring together welcome initiatives from others like that proposed by Norway this week.
As His Majesty said, the task before us is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity.
And I want to reassure the British people that ultimately, we will do whatever is necessary to protect them, including bringing forward new laws, if that is what is needed.
They need to know that we will protect their interests and we will.
But on its own, that's not enough, is it?

In this dangerous, turbulent age, it is more important than ever that we give people the power to build their own resilience and do more for themselves, and give them the platform to stand up for what they believe in.
I am working to rebalance power across all regions of the UK, and as part of that, I have set up a second Downing Street office in Manchester.
We call it number ten North.
Outside that office stands a statue of Abraham Lincoln.
It marks the personal connection he made with Manchester and the bond between our two nations, a bond which he described in a letter to the working people of the city as perpetual.
This was not due to some military or material support.
There was no quid pro quo.
It was because Manchester's humble mill workers took a principled stand during the American Civil War in 1862, despite the hardships it brought them.
They refused to touch raw cotton that had been picked by slaves in 1862.
People with little power used it to help those with none.
On the other side of the world, the best change is change like that.

Bottom up change led by people and whatever distorted view social media offers today, the world is still full, full of good and decent people all over the world who are ready to stand up for what is right.
I see that shining through all the time.
Nothing brings the British people together across age, race, and class more than their hatred of injustice, the misuse of power against the powerless.
We will always stand for the underdog against the bully.
That's why we are so united behind Ukraine.
And let me say we salute the Ukrainian people.
They are showing depths of resilience and courage that is an inspiration to the whole world.
I was in Kyiv last month and it gave me a glimpse of life under Russian attack.
I went to a bustling market, just a normal scene from any European city.
The traders singing the praises of their products, pushing into my hands Peaches and plums from Odessa.
But their stalls were out on the street because the market hall had been destroyed.
In the background, there were burned out cars behind us, a building that had taken a direct hit just a few weeks before.
I met people riding the metro home from work, people just getting on with their lives.
But at night, those same metro stations doubling as shelters for thousands of people, from the elderly to little kids, some who have no nothing but war.
People told me about the freezing conditions in the stations last winter, when temperatures dropped below -20 degrees outside.
Meanwhile, Russia was targeting their energy infrastructure, trying to make them suffer even more.
We can't let them do that again this winter.
So we're working to help Ukraine protect their skies and civilians.
We're leading the charge in raising the cost for Russia of continuing this senseless and illegal war.
The Graham bill, which President Trump signed last week, will make a huge difference to that effort.
And we will support Ukraine to repair and protect the heat and power plants that Kyiv will depend upon this winter.
It is right that we provide that support, but we should call Russia out this time and every time.
Everyone in this room knows that strikes on civilian infrastructure are explicitly forbidden, forbidden by international law.
Yet we stand here in the U.N. announcing funding to mitigate the effects of these war crimes, which we reliably expect to be perpetrated yet again by a permanent member of the Security Council.
Russia could choose a different course tomorrow except a cease fire come to the negotiating table.
I urge them to do so.
But until then, we will stand with Ukraine stronger than ever for as long as it takes.
This is about upholding the UN charter and the rule of law.

We will stand firm in the face of any threats and challenges to the rule of law, not just from Russia but from others too, including where they threaten the rights of British territories to remain British, such as the Falkland Islands.
That's why we're also working with France and other partners to support freedom of navigation in the Gulf.
And it's why I have acted on the Middle East.
Just eight weeks into becoming prime Minister, working with my Foreign secretary, Ed Miliband.
I comprehensively reset our position and we built an international coalition of countries to come with us.
The terrorist attack on Israel on the 7th of October 2023 was utterly horrific.
I have condemned it in the strongest possible terms.
We continue to condemn Hamas, and we stand with Israel in the face of the ongoing threats, including from Iran against Israel and Jewish people around the world.
But this does not justify the Israeli government's actions in Gaza or the West Bank.
Far too many people have died, including so many children.
Far too little aid is getting in and it has gone on for far too long.
We will not stand by as the horrific suffering continues to grow and the prospect of a two state solution, the best hope for peace and stability for both nations comes under attack.
Last month, Israel issued tenders for the construction of the E1 Mega settlement, which would drive a wedge through the West Bank and threaten to put a viable Palestinian state beyond reach.

So we have acted by banning trade in goods with illegal settlements, recognizing that the Israeli occupation of the Palestinian territory is unlawful, and sanctioning those taking part in the construction of illegal settlement, we want to see the suffering and death finally come to an.
We want to see Israeli and Palestinian people living side by side in peace and security, and we will do all we can to keep the hope of that possibility alive.
And look, we live in an age of low trust in politics.

If we were to continue to talk about the two state solution, but failed to back those words with deeds, that trust will fall even lower and our enemies will seek to exploit the alienation that follows from that.
So, Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, this is the kind of leadership Britain is here to bring.
We need to recommit together to make the decade ahead of us better than the last.
My message to our partners around the world is this you can count on us.
Count on us to stand up for those long standing British values of fairness and justice, our shared values and for the UN charter.
Count on us to fight racism, discrimination, and the abuse of power wherever we see it.
Just as those Manchester cotton workers did in the 19th century and the country did in the fight against fascism in the 20th century.
Count on us to bring people together, not to point towards old problems, but to work towards new solutions for the 21st century.
Count on us to meet fear and division with unity and hope.
● We meet at a time of considerable change in the international environment.
● Developments in different parts of the world are challenging existing arrangements and raising questions about the future of the international order.
● In this context, maintaining peace and strengthening international cooperation remain key priorities.

● In light of the growing number of global challenges, сoordinated responses to common obstacles, conflict prevention and the achievement of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development are possible only through international cooperation and a shared strengthened commitment to collective action.
● Lasting peace cannot be imposed by force; it must be built through communication and mutual respect.
● Few countries understand the value of peace, stability, and sovereignty as deeply as Georgia does.
● For centuries, we stood at the crossroads of civilizations - open to diverse cultures, peoples, and ideas, while steadfastly preserving our own distinct identity and character.
● Georgia’s statehood has been tested more than once, but these challenges have only strengthened our determination to choose our own path.

● The trials of history have also taught us that sovereignty can never be taken for granted, that stability must be protected, and that the strength of the international order ultimately depends on the same principles being upheld for every nation.
● Our commitment to these principles carries particular meaning for Georgia.
● Twenty percent of our country remains under the occupation of the Russian Federation, while hundreds of thousands of our citizens continue to live in displacement, unable to return to their homes.
● While restoring trust is the major theme of this year’s session, I would like to address our Abkhaz and Ossetian brothers and sisters.
● We have shared a homeland and a history for centuries.
● The divisions of today cannot erase that history, nor should they determine the future of our children.
● We believe that the dividends of peace and economic growth of Georgia should know no artificial boundaries.
● It must reach the people living in our occupied historic regions as well – who remain, and will always remain, part of our shared future.
● The challenges facing our country also remind us that national stability and success cannot be separated from the wider regional context.
● We believe that the South Caucasus should not be defined by the divisions of the past.
● We have consistently sought to act as an honest broker in regional initiatives, fostering cooperation and contributing to peaceful solutions.
● Today, we see a genuine opportunity to turn a new page and build a more peaceful and interconnected region based on shared commitment to a better future.
● This spirit of cooperation must also translate into tangible economic opportunities for the region.
● As an integral part of the South Caucasus and the Middle Corridor, Georgia is well positioned to strengthen connectivity between Central Asia and Europe.
● Our strategic location and direct access to the Black Sea facilitate trade and investment, linking landlocked countries in our wider region to global supply chains.
● Our network of free trade agreements provides access to a market of approximately 2.3 billion consumers.

● To support and further advance connectivity agenda, Georgia plans to invest USD 7 billion by 2032 in major transport infrastructure - modernizing the railway, developing the Anaklia Deep Sea Port, building a new international airport in Tbilisi, and expanding the highway network.
● At the same time, we believe that physical and digital connectivity are two parts of the same strategic agenda.
● Through a Black Sea submarine fiber-optic connection and next-generation data to strengthen secure, resilient, and diversified digital links between Europe and Asia.

● Over the past five years, our economy has grown by an average of 9.3 per cent annually, and this momentum has continued in 2026, with growth reaching 7.9 per cent in the first seven months of the year.
● As the International Monetary Fund projects, Georgia will deliver one of the fastest growth rates in the medium term among regional and European countries, averaging 5.4%.
● With one of the fastest-growing economies worldwide, we are actively building an innovation-oriented, business-friendly environment that supports both local and foreign enterprises.

● Despite the global uncertainty, Georgia’s FDI to GDP ratio is one of the highest among peer countries and averaged over 6% of GDP in 2021–2025, highlighting the confidence of investors in the country’s growth potential.
● Georgia’s FDI outlook is supported by a pipeline of large, multi-year investment projects across transport and logistics, energy infrastructure, tourism and real estate.
● Yet the true measure of success is how it improves people’s lives.

● Strong economic performance must translate into tangible social outcomes - higher output per person, rising real wages, declining poverty, better employment opportunities, and greater economic resilience.
● We are already seeing these outcomes reflected in measurable improvements, including a triple decline in Georgia’s poverty rate, which dropped from 21.3 to 7.1 percent since 2020.
● Yet this achievement is only part of the broader transformation we seek to achieve.

● Over the next five years, our focus will therefore be on narrowing disparities between urban and rural communities, expanding opportunities across every region, and ensuring that the benefits of economic growth are shared widely and that no one is left behind.

● These priorities are fully aligned with Georgia’s commitment to the Sustainable Development Goals and are reflected in our new United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework for 2026–2030.

● Looking further ahead, our ambition for the coming decade is to transform Georgia from an upper-middle-income country into a high-income economy, underpinned by greater economic diversification, a growing share of knowledge-based activities, and broad-based prosperity.
● Georgia remains open to meaningful engagement with every international partner prepared to engage with us on the basis of mutual respect and sovereign equality.
● We believe that lasting partnerships are built through dialogue and never through pressure or coercion.
● The principles of respect and cooperation are also at the heart of effective multilateralism.
● At a time of growing global uncertainty, the United Nations remains indispensable as a forum for dialogue and collective action.
● In this regard, the UN80 Initiative provides a valuable opportunity to strengthen the effectiveness and capacity of the United Nations, while further enhancing its transparency and accountability.
● The choice we make today will shape the world we leave to future generations.
● Let us ensure that we leave them a world that is more peaceful, secure and united than the one we know today.
You assume this solemn stewardship at a time of intense geopolitical fragmentation, deepening inequality, and eroded trust in our multilateral system.
Ghana’s national anthem contains a profound petition.
It asks God to make us "bold to defend forever the cause of freedom and of right."
Those words give my compatriots and I the courage to uphold the Pan- African and anti-colonial heritage bequeathed to us by our forebears.
Another line petitions God to fill our hearts with true humility and make us cherish fearless honesty.

That prayer inspires me today to follow in the footsteps of Kwame Nkrumah, Haile Selassie, Nelson Mandela, and the global icons who have stood at this podium before me and spoken boldly and fearlessly about the state of affairs in our world.
The world may not transform overnight because of the speeches delivered in this August Assembly.
But history faithfully records the truth we choose to speak, and the silence we choose to keep, when we are granted the privilege of addressing this global town hall.
Allow me, therefore, to begin by reintroducing myself to the General Assembly.
I stand before you as President of the Republic of Ghana.
Yet, we too often ascend these heights draped only in the robes of our titles, forgetting that alongside each of us stands a history, a people, and a legacy.
I was born in Damongo, then a modest town in northern Ghana and now the capital of the Savannah Region.
I was born to Mr Emmanuel Adama Mahama of Bole and Madam Abiba Nnaba Suluwu of Busunu, both of blessed memory.
I belong to the foremothers and forefathers who birthed them, who named them, nurtured them, and passed down the enduring values by which I live.
I grew up at the crossroads of several Ghanaian cultures.
I speak Gonja, a Guan language.
I am fluent in Hausa, spoken across the West African savannah and Sahel.
In a very real sense, I belong to all these peoples because their tongues have become my tongue.
Language creates kinship, regardless of the historical complexities through which the kinship was forged.
Every person in this Chamber, and every global citizen listening to these words, possesses an origin.
We carry inherited memories, values, rich cultures, and distinct identities.
Belonging anchors us; it reminds us that we are part of a human story far larger than ourselves.
It is a vital wellspring of dignity and pride.
But belonging also has a dark side.
When weaponised by political expediency, it transforms into nativism, chauvinism, xenophobia and the dangerous prejudices extended to those who are deemed different.
It becomes the pretext for discrimination, displacement, persecution, and war.
Yet for this Organisation, the United Nations, the founding principle remains immutable: Every human being belongs to the human family.
No child’s life is worth less because of the language they speak, the faith they profess, the colour of their skin, or the land of their birth.
This is the unyielding moral foundation upon which the United Nations must stand.
I will return to this issue of belonging at the end of my speech.

Last year, from this podium, I made a solemn pledge on behalf of Ghana, Africa, and the global African diaspora to secure full international recognition of the transatlantic trafficking and racialised chattel enslavement of Africans as the gravest crime against humanity in human history.
Some cautioned that we were reopening old wounds.
But we came not to provoke division or render empty judgment.
True healing requires truth; truth requires acknowledgement; and acknowledgement must lead to meaningful repair.
For centuries, this tragedy was rendered in the passive voice as though millions of African men, women, and children vanished into the shadows of time.
They were hunted, captured, trafficked, bought, sold, exploited, and exchanged for profit.
They were ripped from the families and communities they belonged to.
Their unpaid labour built the cities, industries, banking institutions, and empires of the modern Western world.
Meanwhile, the African continent was left depopulated, with split families, structural disruption, and generational trauma.

On 25 March 2026, the International Day of Remembrance of the Victims of Slavery and the Transatlantic Slave Trade, Ghana had the honour of tabling Resolution A/RES/80/250 in this very August Assembly.
One hundred and twenty-three (123) nations voted to affirm this fundamental truth: the transatlantic slave trade and chattel enslavement were the gravest crimes against humanity.
That resolution was not a mere gesture.

It was adopted because the structural legacies of those historic crimes continue to fuel systemic racism, economic marginalisation, and a global financial architecture weighted against Africa and people of African descent.
Since the passage of the historic resolution, we welcome the positive overtures from many countries and institutions to join the dialogue on reparatory justice and restitution.
The Netherlands, Germany and France have made positive moves to join the conversation on reparatory justice.
But real repair demands structural transformation.

It requires dismantling the persistent engines of exploitation: unfair global trade regimes, predatory resource extraction, discriminatory credit ratings, unsustainable debt burdens, and the continued export of raw materials from Africa while real value addition and job creation occur elsewhere.
The injustices of the past remain embedded in today's power structures.
Africa is home to 1.5 billion people, over 18 per cent of humanity, and constitutes the largest regional voting bloc in this General Assembly.
Yet, Africa remains without a single permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council.
This is fundamentally unacceptable in the 21st century.
Africa must be granted permanent representation on the UN Security Council, complete with all the rights, responsibilities, and veto powers of such membership.
We cannot credibly champion the sovereign equality of nations while preserving a global governance structure designed for the post-war geopolitical realities.
Security Council reform is not a favour to Africa; it is an imperative for the legitimacy, credibility, and survival of the United Nations.
The same systemic inequality permeates the international financial architecture.
Developing nations borrow at interest rates up to eight times higher than industrialised nations.
African and Caribbean nations struck by climate disasters are forced to take on crippling debt to rebuild from floods and droughts they did not cause.
Governments are forced into a tragic choice: to service predatory debt or serve their people.
We need long-term, affordable, and accessible concessionary financing that enables developing economies to invest in human capital, industrialisation, and climate adaptation.
Africa seeks equal partnership anchored in mutual respect.
Our continent possesses the world’s youngest population, vast arable land, unparalleled cultural vitality, and the critical minerals required to drive the global green energy transition.
But Africa will not remain a passive arena for a new scramble for resources.
Critical mineral extraction must not replicate colonial-era exploitation.
We will process our minerals at home, build local industries, create dignified jobs for our youth, and retain the value of our natural resources.
The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), whose Secretariat Ghana is proud to host in Accra, is our engine for intra-African trade, structural transformation, and industrial growth.
As we heal historical wounds, we must address the alarming breakdown of global order today.
We are witnessing a dangerous drift toward unilateralism, lawlessness, and the erosion of multilateral norms.
The United Nations must learn from the lessons of the League of Nations.
The UN Charter must reign supreme over the cynical doctrine that "might makes right."
The veto power must never serve as a license for impunity.
Sovereign equality cannot be a privilege reserved only for nations aligned with global superpowers.
Nowhere is this crisis of credibility more painful than in the ongoing persecution of the Palestinian people in Gaza, the West Bank, and the occupied territories.
We must stop using diplomatic euphemisms to veil the human carnage taking place in Gaza.
How many more innocent lives must be lost before the world acts with decisive moral authority?
The blood of five-year-old Hind Rajab, and the more than 20,000 children killed in this brutal conflict, cries out to the conscience of the world.
Collective punishment, enforced starvation, and mass displacement are flagrant violations of international law.

Ghana remains unwavering in its recognition of the sovereign State of Palestine and its steadfast support for a viable Two-State solution, where Israel and Palestine live side-by-side in peace, security, and guaranteed borders.
At the same time, we condemn all acts of terrorism by Hamas that triggered this conflict.
We insist that all parties unconditionally respect international humanitarian law.
Our moral standards cannot be selective.

In that same spirit of international legality and human solidarity, Ghana reiterates its call for the immediate lifting of the decades-long economic, commercial, and financial embargo imposed on Cuba.
The world must support Cuba’s new Economic and Social Programme.
Measures that inflict collective economic hardship on ordinary citizens run counter to our shared commitment to human dignity and international law.
