We must likewise elevate our global response to the catastrophic conflict in Sudan, which is reported to be the world’s worst humanitarian crisis.
We must also exercise solidarity with nations facing the terrorist scourge, especially the Alliance of Sahel States.
The current Middle East crisis is having a deleterious effect on the world economy.
We call for a return to the negotiating table.
And let me add that no human civilisation deserves to be annihilated, certainly not a member state of the United Nations.
I believe that dialogue can resolve even the most intractable of problems.

Across every conflict, whether in Europe, the Middle East, or Africa, the standard must remain uniform: respect sovereign integrity, protect civilians, ensure unhindered humanitarian access, and hold perpetrators of war crimes accountable.
For those who have declared climate change a hoax perpetrated by geopolitical opponents, the warnings of recent times cannot have been clearer.
Melting glaciers, flash flooding, droughts, record-breaking heatwaves, brush fires, hurricanes and other extreme weather phenomena are unmistakable signals of an overburdened planet.
Climate change is the ultimate test of global equity.
Africa contributes less than 4 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet bears some of the heaviest burden of climate devastation.
We face erratic rainfall, our coastal towns suffer relentless erosion, and our Sahelian regions face accelerating desertification.
On 29 June this year, Ghana and coastal West Africa faced an unprecedented deluge.
Torrential rain, exceeding 160 millimetres, was dumped on seven coastal regions within 24 hours, resulting in 39 deaths and one still missing.
Climate justice demands that developed nations fulfil their long- overdue financial commitments.
Mitigation support must be operationalised with predictable, non-debt-creating grants, not loans that further indebt fragile economies.
Similarly, global health security demands true solidarity.
Pathogens do not respect national borders or GDP.

We must build an equitable global health architecture that guarantees regional manufacturing of vaccines and therapeutics, strengthens epidemic surveillance, and funds resilient public health infrastructure across the Global South in accordance with the demands of the Accra Reset.

Mr President, Excellencies, I agree that even as we demand a place at the table and call for a more equitable and just global order, as African leaders, we must also do what is required to put our own houses in order.
As the legal maxim goes: “Whoever comes into equity must come with clean hands.”
African leadership must be transparent and accountable.
We must fight corruption and ensure that every dollar of our people’s money counts and is used efficiently in their interest.
Ghana is arguably the most stable democracy in Africa.
We believe in the rule of law and have respect for human rights.
We are determined to demonstrate that democracy works.
While progress in a democracy may be slow because it must follow constitutional processes, it is more sustainable because it is built through popular participation and consensus-building.
As Ghana addresses these global imperatives, we are leading by example at home through our transformative "Resetting Ghana Agenda."
Less than two years into my administration, through disciplined governance, fiscal prudence, and an uncompromising fight against corruption, Ghana has achieved a dramatic economic turnaround.
Indeed, some circles describe it as the “Ghanaian miracle.”
Our macroeconomic stabilisation measures have restored growth, drastically reduced inflation, stabilised our national currency, and significantly lowered our public debt burden.

This remarkable economic recovery story has been independently validated by multilateral financial institutions and major international credit rating agencies—all of which affirm that Ghana has moved from economic vulnerability to sustained recovery, resilience, and growth.
But macroeconomic indicators mean little if they do not translate into real improvements in our people's daily lives.
Economic growth must have a human face.
That is why we are pursuing an aggressive national infrastructure agenda under our Big Push Programme to build roads, expand digital connectivity, and construct schools and health facilities.

This strategic investment is opening up the length and breadth of our country, bridging the rural-urban divide, unlocking agricultural potential, and guaranteeing equitable access to basic services for every Ghanaian, no matter where they live.

Through our flagship 24-Hour Economy and Accelerated Export Development Programme, and the soon-to-be-launched ‘New Ghana, New Economy’ policy, we are transforming Ghana into an industrial, high-productivity hub.
We are incentivising round-the-clock commercial operations, driving value addition in agriculture and mining, and creating sustainable, dignified jobs for our vibrant youth and women.

Central to our national reset is a revolutionary expansion of social protection and universal healthcare, delivering on the Sustainable Development Goals, specifically SDG 1 (No Poverty), SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-Being), and SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities).
Ghana has officially launched a historic Free Primary Health Care Programme, ensuring that every Ghanaian can access essential primary healthcare services at the community level at zero cost.

Hailed by the World Health Organisation (WHO) and the United Nations as a benchmark paradigm shift for the Global South, this model is currently being studied by other nations seeking to achieve true Universal Health Coverage.

Alongside our National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS), we have introduced a specialised fund officially named the Ghana Medical Trust Fund (and popularly referred to as MahamaCare) that guarantees Ghanaians suffering from Non-Communicable Diseases (NCDs) such as renal failure, cancer, cardiovascular diseases, and diabetes receive subsidised, affordable, and life-saving care.
I have always believed that democracy must deliver tangible social benefits.

Citizens must experience democracy not only through the ballot box every four years, but through improved access to food, quality education, decent housing, accessible healthcare, and economic opportunity.
Democracy loses its soul when it protects elite privileges while abandoning the vulnerable.
Ghana remains an uncompromising beacon of constitutional democracy, media freedom, the rule of law, and peaceful transitions of power on the African continent.
These domestic achievements set the stage for two historic milestones ahead.
In March 2027, Ghana will celebrate its 70th Anniversary of Independence as the first nation in sub-Saharan Africa to break the shackles of colonial rule.
And in January 2027, Ghana will proudly assume the Chairmanship of the African Union.

We will use our AU Chairmanship to champion continental integration, accelerate the implementation of the AfCFTA, push for peace and security in conflict zones, and ensure that Africa speaks on the global stage with one resolute, undivided, and confident voice.
The daunting crises confronting our world are not insurmountable.
What we lack is not resources or intellect; we lack the political courage to see one another as part of a single human family.
We must see each other not as strategic rivals, economic targets, or demographic threats, but as human beings who belong.
The child in Gaza, Sudan, or Ukraine belongs.
The descendants of enslaved Africans seeking justice belongs.
The indigenous community protecting its ancestral environment belongs.
The small island state threatened by rising oceans belongs.
The poor, the vulnerable, and the marginalised belongs.
They belong to our common human family.
And because they belong, we must safeguard their dignity, enforce their rights, and hear their voices.

When Osagyefo Dr Kwame Nkrumah stood on the eve of Ghana’s independence in 1957, he declared that "the independence of Ghana is meaningless unless it is linked up with the total liberation of the African continent."
Today, from this respected global podium, we must expand that historic truth: The freedom of any nation is insecure unless it is linked to the freedom of all humanity.
Our national prosperity is fragile unless it is shared.
Our global peace is unviable unless it is anchored in justice.
Let this General Assembly recommit itself to a world where belonging is used not to erect walls, but to build bridges; not to exclude, but to unite; not to degrade humanity, but to exalt it.
Let us speak truth with humility.
And let us cherish fearless honesty in the statements we deliver today, and in the choices we make tomorrow.
May God bless our shared world.
May God bless my homeland, Ghana.
And may God bless the United Nations.
It is my hope that the work, under your enlightened leadership, will enable our Organization better to meet the legitimate expectations of the peoples of the world.

It is with a profound sense of pride, but also of humility, that I stand before this august rostrum, on behalf of the sovereign people of the Republic of Guinea, to share with the community of nations the path traveled by my country.
2. Ladies and Gentlemen, Three years ago, from this very rostrum, I delivered, with the frankness that my country and our continent owe to this world, a speech of truth.
I said that the model of governance imported, without adaptation, onto our continent, was struggling to bear the fruits expected by our peoples.
But I return before you today in a different spirit.

Not to denounce, but to share a number of factual elements, with the respect due to this assembly, about the path that the Republic of Guinea has chosen to chart and the results that this choice has produced.
3. The Republic of Guinea has given itself a new Constitution.

Not a Constitution copied from an external model, but a Fundamental Law shaped by the Guinean people themselves, discussed, amended and adopted by referendum, in the image of their own history and their own diversity.

This Constitution has introduced profound innovations in favor of living together: strengthened representation for our local areas and our communities, new guarantees for alternation, participatory governance, and an affirmed recognition of our religious, linguistic, and cultural plurality as the foundation of sacred national unity rather than as a factor of division.

4. On the basis of this Constitution, the Republic of Guinea has organized the entirety of its direct electoral cycle — local, legislative, and presidential elections — as well as the establishment of all the institutions deriving from it, financed one hundred per cent by the Guinean Treasury.

I say this with legitimate pride before this Assembly: none of these elections, throughout the entire extent of our territory, experienced any significant incident on the part of any of the actors in the electoral process.
This is proof, Ladies and Gentlemen, that an African country can organize, on its own, using its own resources, credible, peaceful elections accepted by all.
5. I have not come before this rostrum to present an exhaustive inventory.
But I believe it useful, to support my remarks, to share with you a simple overview of what the Republic of Guinea has accomplished in less than three years:
- more than one thousand kilometres of paved roads, opening up our regions;
- the Simandou megaproject, the largest mining and infrastructure project in Africa, now completed;
- schools and hospitals built across the entire national territory;
- three (03) alumina refineries under construction, to process our bauxite on our own soil;

- the largest gold refinery in Africa, already completed and with production capacity; -A programme for the sustainable and responsible socio-economic development of my country for the next 15 years, SIMANDOU 2040.
6. The Simandou 2040 Programme embodies an ambition for the structural transformation of our economy.
It is not merely a mining project, but a genuine strategic lever for accelerating the development of infrastructure, agriculture, energy, education, health and industry.
These results, achieved in less than three years, are not cited out of vanity.
They illustrate a conviction that I wish to share with this Assembly.
Our greatest wealth, however, remains our youth.
We must offer it quality education, training adapted to the needs of the labour market through the SIMANDOU ACADEMY initiative, as well as real opportunities for employment and entrepreneurship.

7. Excellencies, Heads of State and Government, The recent Guinean experience allows me, with respect, to formulate a conviction: when models of governance are adapted to the historical, social and cultural realities of each nation, rather than imported without discernment, development accelerates.
Let us look at certain countries of the Near East.
They did not wait for an external model to be validated for them in order to build their prosperity.
They were able to draw inspiration from universal experience while adapting it to their own national genius.
In one generation, they have achieved what others took a century to accomplish.
Africa too can take this path.
This is not a rejection of the world or of international cooperation, quite the contrary.
It is a call for a renewed partnership, respectful of the sovereignty of each nation, based on win-win co-construction, rather than on pre-established schemes that ignore our realities.
The Republic of Guinea, for its part, remains and will remain a reliable, open and committed partner of the entire international community, in mutual respect for sovereignties.
8. Mr. President, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, The Republic of Guinea is moving forward.
It is moving forward with its own means, on the basis of its own choices, in the service of its own people.
It is doing so in compliance with international law, in the spirit of the Charter of the United Nations, and in a spirit of frank and non-exclusive cooperation with all its partners.
I express the hope that this Guinean experience may, modestly, inspire broader reflection on the multiple and legitimate paths to development for our continent.

The Gambia assures you of our full support and constructive cooperation as you guide our collective work under the timely theme you have chosen: restoring trust and managing transformation so that the United Nations can deliver for all.
That theme speaks directly to the moment in which we meet.
Few institutions embody the principle of sovereign equality as visibly as this Assembly.
Within these walls, differences in power, wealth and influence may shape the realities our nations confront, but they do not confer a greater claim to membership or participation.
And, perhaps more than anywhere else, this Assembly reminds us of a simple truth: Our differences are real.

That is why this Organization was created with the understanding that disputes must be resolved through dialogue, human dignity must be protected, and that nations must work together if development, peace, and human rights are to be sustained.
In other words, our common future requires common institutions.
Eight decades later, we must ask ourselves whether we have remained faithful to that insight.
And perhaps more importantly: Do we still trust one another enough to act on it?
Because today, Mr. President, trust is being tested.
Wars have become more protracted with devastating humanitarian consequences.

Respect for the United Nations Charter and international law is under visible strain, with developing countries facing intensifying debt burdens, climate vulnerabilities, huge gaps between commitments made and implementation, and a feeling of marginalization and inadequate representation in the global system.

Therefore, the task before us is building a stronger, better equipped, representative, responsive, and effective multilateral system and global financial architecture that delivers for all nations and regions.
The Gambia’s own experience within this Organization gives us grounds for optimism.
We have seen, within this very institution, that multilateralism can still deliver.

During the eightieth session of the General Assembly, The Gambia had the honour of chairing the Second Committee at a time of profound disagreement over some of the most consequential economic and development issues before us.
That experience reminded us that multilateralism does not require unanimity on every issue.
It requires the willingness to remain at the table, to listen, to negotiate, and to have the courage to compromise.

Our experience demonstrated that even in periods of deep disagreement, progress remains possible when Member States approach negotiations with political will, mutual respect and a shared sense of responsibility.
The stakes are perhaps greatest in international peace and security, one of the foremost purposes for which this Organization was created.

If diplomacy can bring countries together to find common ground on difficult questions of global development, then surely, we can summon the same political courage to prevent conflicts, resolve wars and build lasting peace.
The Gambia speaks on this not merely from principle, but from experience.
In 2017, our country stood at a moment of acute constitutional uncertainty.
The democratic choice of the Gambian people faced a grave challenge.

At that critical moment, the United Nations' preventive diplomacy, working in partnership with the African Union and ECOWAS, helped uphold the will of the Gambian people and support a peaceful democratic transition.
We have not forgotten that solidarity.
It taught us that preventive diplomacy is not an abstract concept.
It is a practical instrument for preventing confrontation, creating space for dialogue and protecting institutions.
Sometimes, it can change the course of a nation.
That experience also gives us an obligation.
If the international community could stand with The Gambia at a moment of fragility, then countries facing similar moments should be able to count on the same solidarity.
Across the world, however, conflicts continue to destroy lives, displace populations and reverse decades of development.
Civilians bear the greatest cost, while humanitarian workers operate under increasingly dangerous conditions and the resources available to respond to crises remain far below what is required.
The protection of civilians, respect for international humanitarian law and humanitarian access are not political conveniences.
They are legal obligations and expressions of our shared humanity.

We need stronger early-warning systems that enable us to act before crises escalate, timely mediation before positions become entrenched, and peacebuilding that addresses the conditions that allow conflict to take root.
The question before us must therefore not only be how to end the ongoing wars, but how to prevent the next war from beginning.
Prevention should not have to wait for a crisis to become sufficiently destructive to attract international attention.
It is infinitely less costly, in human, political and financial terms, to prevent conflict than to manage its consequences after violence has begun.
We therefore welcome the Secretary-General’s continued good offices and preventive diplomacy and call for these efforts to be matched with predictable and sustained resources.

Peace must be built and nurtured through institutions that command public confidence, societies in which trust can be restored and justice pursued, and a future in which women and young people have a meaningful voice and economic opportunity is within reach.
The Gambia has experienced the value of peacebuilding firsthand.

Since our democratic transition, the Peacebuilding Commission and the Secretary-General’s Peacebuilding Fund have been steadfast partners in our nationally led efforts to strengthen institutions, advance transitional justice and consolidate peace.
We therefore support a stronger and more responsive Peacebuilding Commission, adequately resourced to support countries emerging from conflict or navigating delicate political transitions.

The implementation of the outcomes of the Peacebuilding Architecture Review must translate into stronger prevention, greater national ownership and closer coordination across the United Nations system.

We also reaffirm our support for United Nations peacekeeping operations and pay tribute to the men and women who serve under the UN flag, including Gambian military and police personnel who have contributed with distinction to international peace and security.
Their safety and security must remain a priority, alongside performance, accountability and strict adherence to international law.
Partnerships between the United Nations and regional organizations, particularly the African Union, must also be deepened with sustained and predictable funding.
The ongoing conflict in Sudan remains a matter of profound concern to The Gambia.
Together with continuing instability across parts of the Sahel, it reminds us that peace cannot be separated from development and governance.

The suffering of civilians in the affected conflict zones globally demands sustained international attention and renewed diplomatic efforts towards de-escalation, dialogue and a durable political settlement.
In the Sahel and other conflict zones, our responses must be comprehensive and holistic.
Security measures are necessary, but they must be accompanied by increased support for democratic governance, institution-building, education, job creation, development and climate resilience.
For millions of people around the world, poverty, lack of human rights, democratic governance, etc. continues to pose great insecurity.
The absence of education, healthcare, decent employment, and the loss of homes and livelihoods to climate change leave communities as vulnerable as conflict itself.
Our understanding of security must therefore extend beyond the absence of war to include the conditions that allow people to live with dignity, opportunity and hope.
In The Gambia, this understanding has guided our democratic journey from 2017 to date.
We have undertaken the difficult work of rebuilding institutions, strengthening the rule of law, expanding access to justice and confronting the legacy of past human rights violations.
Our transitional justice process continues through implementation of the recommendations of the Truth, Reconciliation and Reparations Commission (TRRC).
We have strengthened institutional accountability and established the Special Prosecutor's Office to advance investigations and prosecutions arising from the TRRC process.

We are proud of the progress we have made, but we remain conscious that democracy is never a finished project and requires continuous institutional strengthening, adherence to the rule of law, constitutional order, dialogue, and consensus-building.
On 5 December 2026, the Gambian people will again exercise their sovereign democratic right to choose their President.
This will be another important milestone in our democratic journey, and we need the support of the international community in this regard.

My Government is committed to ensuring that the elections are peaceful, transparent, credible, and inclusive, and are conducted in accordance with our Constitution, national laws, and democratic standards.

This is the democratic path The Gambia remains committed to pursuing: a path in which institutions are strengthened, citizens are heard, differences are resolved peacefully, and democratic gains are consolidated for future generations.
On development, The Gambia's Recovery-Focused National Development Plan, YIRIWA 2023–2027, provides the framework for accelerating our socio-economic transformation.
We are investing in roads, energy, schools, healthcare, agriculture and digital infrastructure, while promoting economic diversification, private-sector investment and value addition.
We are expanding opportunities for women and young people, improving lives and strengthening the human capital upon which our future depends.

The global economic environment remains particularly difficult for developing countries, with declining Official Development Assistance, high borrowing costs, disruptions to international trade, inflationary pressures, food and energy insecurity, narrowing fiscal space, and threats to development gains.
With only a few years remaining to achieve the 2030 Agenda, the time for implementation is now.
Following the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, we must translate the Sevilla Commitments into tangible action.

Developing countries need greater access to affordable, long-term finance; meaningful reform of the multilateral development system; sustainable solutions to debt; stronger international tax cooperation; and decisive action against illicit financial flows.

We also need stronger, more resilient supply chains, greater investment in productive capacity, and a global economic system that gives developing countries a fair opportunity to transform their economies.
Trade must remain an engine of development, and developing countries must be enabled to participate more effectively in regional and global value chains.
This would enable developing countries to invest in education, health, agriculture, climate resilience, and other productive sectors to holistically address their interconnected challenges.
Climate change presents another test of our collective credibility and for The Gambia, it is not a distant threat.
Coastal erosion, changing rainfall patterns, pressure on water resources, food insecurity and environmental degradation are already affecting our communities and livelihoods.

However, we are responding with determination by investing in renewable energy, coastal resilience, mangrove restoration, disaster risk reduction, early warning systems, water security and nature-based solutions.
National electricity access has reached 90 per cent, with universal access targeted by the end of 2026.
We are expanding solar energy in schools and health facilities, modernizing our electricity network and advancing a 150-megawatt solar park.
We have also adopted our first National Disaster Risk Mitigation Plan and are restoring and sustainably managing more than 100,000 hectares of mangroves.

But we urged that our national ambition be supported by international action to make climate finance accessible, predictable and adequate, including through the sustained implementation of the New Collective Quantified Goal on Climate Finance and effective arrangements to address loss and damage, build climate resilience and a fairer international order in which those who have contributed least to the climate crisis are not left to bear its greatest burdens.
Artificial intelligence offer extraordinary opportunities, but opportunity without inclusion can become another source of inequality.
The digital divide must not become the next development divide.
We need the capacity to participate in research, innovation, entrepreneurship, standard-setting and global technology governance.
Technology must serve humanity, and the governance of artificial intelligence must be inclusive, responsible and grounded in international cooperation.
This is particularly important for the world's Least Developed Countries.
As The Gambia prepares to assume greater leadership within the Global Coordination Bureau of the LDC Group, we do so with a clear sense of responsibility.

LDCs continue to face structural constraints, including limited productive capacity, high debt burdens, climate vulnerability, narrow export bases, technological gaps and restricted access to affordable finance.

We will continue to advocate for full implementation of the Doha Programme of Action, with particular attention to productive capacity, structural transformation, industrialization, science and technology, climate resilience and human capital development.
Graduation from LDC status must be a pathway to sustained prosperity and resilience, not a cliff edge leading to the premature withdrawal of essential international support.

South-South and Triangular Cooperation should also remain important complements to North-South cooperation, particularly in knowledge sharing, technology transfer, capacity building and mutually beneficial development partnerships.
Migration is another area where our collective response must be guided by human dignity and shared responsibility.
Migration contributes significantly to economic development, cultural exchange and human progress.
Yet irregular migration continues to expose young people and vulnerable populations to exploitation, trafficking, abuse and tragic loss of life.

We must strengthen cooperation for safe, orderly and regular migration, protect the rights and dignity of migrants and expand lawful pathways for labour mobility as well as investment in young people, women, education, health and social protection to safeguard sustainable development and lasting peace.
With Africa having the world's youngest population, youth employment must remain a development priority.
We need greater investment training, technical entrepreneurship, digital skills and productive employment.
Young people must also have a meaningful voice in the decisions that shape their future.

The Gambia remains committed to expanding women's economic opportunities, strengthening women's leadership and addressing the barriers that limit their meaningful participation in political and public life.
We are also strengthening support for women entrepreneurs, survivors of gender-based violence and vulnerable households.
Ensuring food security, building strengthened and resilient health systems, and pandemic preparedness remain equally urgent.
The Gambia is investing in agricultural productivity, mechanization, irrigation and climate-smart agriculture, while expanding access to improved seeds, fertilizers, credit and support for farmers.
At the global level, we must build food systems capable of withstanding climate, economic and geopolitical shocks.
The Gambia welcomes the calls for reform of the United Nations.
We recognize the constraints facing the organization with limited resources and increasing demands.
Nevertheless, reforms would strengthen the United Nations' capacity to better serve its Member States and the people of the world and correct the historical injustice that continues to prevail.

We need to embark on reforms that strengthen delivery, protect the universal character of the Organization and enable developing countries to participate meaningfully in decisions that shape their future.
The General Assembly must remain at the centre of global deliberation and policymaking, and the structures of the Organization must also reflect the world as it exists today.
For the Security Council, its reform is not simply about expanding membership.
It is about restoring legitimacy and strengthening trust.
We need a Council that is more representative, transparent, accountable, effective and responsive to contemporary geopolitical realities.
The Gambia therefore reaffirms its support for the Common African Position reflected in the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration and commends the position of African leaders in this regard.

The General Assembly's decision to move towards a convention on the prevention and punishment of crimes against humanity is an important contribution to addressing a longstanding gap in the international legal framework.
The Gambia is proud of its leading role, alongside Mexico, in advancing this process through more than three years of patient negotiations.
Our conviction is simple: the gravest crimes cannot be met with silence.
Victims cannot be forgotten, and impunity cannot become an accepted feature of international relations.
Prevention, accountability and reconciliation, healing and sustainable peace.

The continued development of multilateral treaties and the entry into force of the agreement on the conservation and sustainable use of marine biological diversity of areas beyond national jurisdiction also demonstrate what is possible when States negotiate in good faith and persevere.

The Gambia commends Ghana for its historic resolution on the Declaration of Trafficking of Enslaved Africans and Racialized Chattel Enslavement of Africans as the Gravest Crime against Humanity and Togo for the Resolution on Correcting the Map at the General Assembly.
Our credibility is ultimately tested by how we respond to conflicts and crises that remain unresolved for years.
The suffering of the Palestinian people remains a profound test of the credibility of the international system.

We reaffirm the legitimate and inalienable rights of the Palestinian people, including their right to self-determination, membership of the United Nations, and our support for a just, comprehensive and lasting two-State solution, with Israel and Palestine living side by side in peace, security and dignity.
Furthermore, the plight of the Rohingya people must also not disappear from the international agenda.
The Gambia remains committed to accountability, justice and the protection of their fundamental rights and would continue to need the support of you all in this shared collective endeavour.
On Cuba, we reiterate our longstanding call for an end to the economic, commercial and financial sanctions.
Dialogue, engagement and cooperation remain important instruments for improving people's well-being and strengthening peaceful relations among nations.

The Gambia also reaffirms its adherence to the One China Policy and values its partnership with the People's Republic of China, including in development cooperation, infrastructure, South-South and Triangular Cooperation and Partnership.
The leaders of our two countries have raised our bilateral relationship to Strategic Level, and we would continue to grow and deepen this important partnership.

On the question of the Moroccan Sahara, The Gambia supports sustained international efforts towards a peaceful resolution through the United Nations-led political process, and we encourage all concerned parties to engage constructively and in good faith.

The Royal Initiatives of Moroccan Autonomy, the Morocco-Nigeria Gas Pipeline, the Atlantic African Initiative, among others, have provided realistic pathways to a lasting political solution to the dispute over the Moroccan Sahara by giving people the development, human rights, security, and stability they need.

Furthermore, The Gambia welcomes the Kingdom of Morocco’s continued commitment to the ceasefire, full cooperation with MINURSO, and all stakeholders, in line with Resolution 2797 (2025) and other relevant processes.

We urged all stakeholders, i.e., Polisario, the Kingdom of Morocco, Algeria, and the Islamic Republic of Mauritania, to continue working to achieve a sustainable political solution to the conflict, and we support the various initiatives of the United Nations in this regard.

In conclusion, the United Nations and the multilateral system continue to be challenged, but they remain the most reliable guarantor of our collective peace and security and proven mechanisms to confront the challenges facing humanity.
Therefore, the task before us is to make the United Nations and the multilateral system more responsive, more representative and better able to deliver for the people that we serve.

What we leave behind should be a legacy of renewed multilateralism, a reformed United Nations, increased international cooperation and solidarity, and an increased trusted global system that sustains peace, advances development, human rights, democracy, and opens the way to a more secure future for all.
The Gambia stands ready to work with every Member State to renew the promise that brought the nations of the world together.
My country's journey has taught us that countries and institutions can recover from moments of profound uncertainty and further build trust and confidence.
That is the message we bring to this Assembly.
I also commend Miss Annalena Barbosa Barbosa for the dedication she demonstrated during her term of office, and for her efforts to strengthen multilateralism and international cooperation.
Ladies and gentlemen, yesterday September 24th, the people of Guinea-Bissau celebrated the 53rd anniversary of our national independence.
This date of profound significance for our people invites us to reflect on the value of freedom sovereignty, and the dignity of peoples.

It is in this spirit that I bring to this assembly a message of peace, freedom, and fraternity to all the nations of the world in the firm hope that every people may live in peace, fully exercise its rights, and freely chart its own path towards development and prosperity.

We live in an interdependent world marked by growing uncertainty and by challenges that transcend borders climate change, transnational organized crime, terrorism, structural inequalities, the burden of debt, and insufficient financing for development continue to undermine our efforts towards sustainable development.
Devastating conflicts also persist in several regions of the world, as do security challenges, particularly in the Sahel.
In this context, Guinea-Bissau considers it essential to strengthen the international community's support to the most affected countries in the region.

Ladies and gentlemen, the United Nations remains an essential pillar of multilateralism and a privileged forum for dialogue, cooperation and the search for collective solutions to the challenges facing humanity.
It must be acknowledged, however, that in certain circumstances, the expectations that people have placed in it have not always been met with a response commensurate with their aspirations.

This reality should not lead us to question the foundations of the multilateral system, but rather to strengthen the effectiveness representativeness and capacity for action of international institutions.
It is incumbent upon Member States to renew their commitment to multilateralism that is more effective, more inclusive and more responsive to the aspirations of peoples.
We also consider it urgent to reform the architecture of global governance, so that it reflects the geopolitical realities of the 21st century.

It is essential that Africa have more adequate and effective representation in the international institutions that play a central role in shaping responses to the challenges of peace, security and development The reform of United Nations Security Council Council must reflect the legitimate aspirations of the African continent and ensure fairer, permanent and effective representation.

In keeping with the principle of a more inclusive, equitable and representative international order, Guinea-Bissau welcomes the efforts of the United Nations to achieve achieve a lasting political solution to the question of Western Sahara.
We welcome the adoption of Security Council Resolution 2797 of 2025 and view favourably the Autonomy Initiative presented by the Kingdom of Morocco as a basis for resolving this dispute.
Ladies and gentlemen, on November 26th, 2025, during the electoral process, the constitutional order in Guinea-Bissau was interrupted and transitional bodies were established.
A one year transition period was set with the aim of creating the conditions necessary for the restoration of constitutional order.
Within this framework, the constitutional review process has been completed and the new constitution of the Republic was approved by Popular Referendum on August 30th, 2026.
This process is an important milestone in the transition and in the restoration of constitutional order in the country.

The government is committed to creating the conditions necessary for the presidential and legislative elections scheduled for December 6th of this year, to be held in an inclusive, free, transparent and credible manner.

I take this opportunity to express our gratitude to the Economic Community of West African States, ECOWAS, the African Union, the United Nations and our other institutions international partners for their engagement and support in the efforts to ensure a return to constitutional normalcy in our country.
Ladies and gentlemen, three decades ago, Guinea-Bissau had the honor of serving as a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council.

Today, as we reaffirm our commitment to the purposes and principles of the charter of the United Nations and to the promotion of international peace and security, I wish to reiterate that Guinea-Bissau is a candidate for non-permanent membership of the Security Council for the term 2028 2029.
Our vision of the world rests fundamentally on four key words prevention, dialogue, cooperation, peace.
We will work with all Member States to advance essential consensus based priorities for Guinea-Bissau as a developing country, multilateralism and respect for international law are not mere concepts.
Ladies and gentlemen, Guinea-Bissau follows with concern the humanitarian consequences of the measures imposed against Cuba.

We therefore reiterate our call for the lifting of the economic commercial and financial embargo, as well as other restrictive measures that affect the Cuban people and essential sectors of that country's economy.
Over the past decades, this assembly has built consensus and undertaken numerous commitments towards the achievement of common goals Many of these commitments, however, remain unfulfilled.

Enormous gaps persist in financing for development and climate action, alongside high levels of poverty and social inequality, and a growing and unsustainable debt burden on the economies of developing countries in the face of this reality.
We need more multilateralism, effective international cooperation, and more united and determined collective action.
No country, however powerful, can face today's challenges alone.

It is in this spirit of cooperation, solidarity and peace that Guinea-Bissau will continue to work with all member states to uphold the principles enshrined in the charter of the United Nations and to build a better future, a future of peace, development and well-being for present and future generations.

ANTONIO GUTERRES, Secretary-General of the United Nations; Excellencies, Heads of State and of Government and Heads of Delegation; Ladies and Gentlemen: I am honoured to take the floor before this General Assembly in the name on behalf of His Excellency Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, President of Republic of Equatorial Guinea, to convey to you his greetings of peace and those of the Equatorial Guinean people and to reaffirm our adherence and commitment to the Charter of the United Nations.

Mr. President: The theme of this session, “Restoring trust, managing transformation, united nations for all” invites us to reflect on international cooperation in a world subjected to profound challenges.
For Equatorial Guinea, trust is strengthened when commitments and decisions adopted collectively are fulfilled and produce visible results.
The countries of the Global South need cooperation that preserves peace, promotes sustainable and inclusive growth, and expands the capacity of each State to build its own future.
Therefore, cooperation in the twenty-first century must offer opportunities to mobilize financing, transform raw materials develop our own knowledge and technologies.

This vision is especially relevant for Africa, which needs investments that make it possible to develop local value chains, build infrastructure, promote industrialization, strengthen human capital, incorporate new technologies generate employment, especially for the continent’s large young population.
A more productive industrialized Africa will be a stronger partner for the benefit of all than halting its immigration.
When the 2030 Agenda was adopted, the world embraced its deeply human vision: to eradicate poverty, protect the planet and ensure that all people can live with dignity, leaving no one behind.
However, close to the date of its completion, we are far from meeting its goals.
The gaps have not narrowed: poverty persists, inequality is expanding and climate change continues to strike hard.

It is clear that we need an international financial architecture that facilitates productive investments, that takes into account the real vulnerabilities of developing countries and supports the efforts of each nation.
It is therefore urgent to implement the resolutions adopted at the conferences in Addis Ababa in 2015 and in Seville last year.
Mr. President, Development needs peace stability.
Equatorial Guinea defends dialogue, negotiation, mediation and the peaceful settlement of disputes; our own experience demonstrates this.
Equatorial Guinea and the Gabonese Republic constitute a clear example of commitment to peaceful settlement, by submitting their territorial differences to the International Court of Justice.
Today, both States continue to make progress in its implementation through bilateral dialogue.

We express our recognition for the valuable support of the United Nations and the African Union in that process, in which we have demonstrated that it is possible to preserve ties of friendship, cooperation and good-neighbourliness.
Furthermore, Equatorial Guinea has opened its doors to investors and partners from around the world.
We are an African country where you will find stability, tax advantages, opportunities and a partner ready to build relationships of mutual benefit and shared gain.

President, Distinguished delegations: Restoring trust means demonstrating that working together produces results, and managing transformation means turning the challenges of our time into new opportunities.
Africa brings together 54 Member States of the United Nations and represents a fundamental part of the political and demographic reality of the twenty-first century.
We must move towards a more balanced international community, in which Africa participates fully in global decisions and strengthens its capacity to direct its own development.

Equatorial Guinea reaffirms the African Common Position enshrined in Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration, which calls for Africa to have two permanent seats with the right of veto and two additional non-permanent seats on the Security Council.
Mr. President, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen: Respect for international law, sovereign equality and friendship with all peoples guide the foreign policy of Equatorial Guinea.

From this position, we encourage the United States of America and the Republic of Cuba to continue opening avenues of dialogue that will make it possible to end the blockade and build a relationship of mutual benefit.
Moreover, we consider the United Nations to be a universal space for seeking solutions to common problems.
Equatorial Guinea maintains its confidence in this Organization because cooperation among nations remains the surest path to preserving peace and building shared prosperity.
I conclude by expressing that the history of the United Nations shows that peace and prosperity advance when nations work together.

And it is in that sense that Equatorial Guinea will continue to contribute from mutual respect, sovereign equality and dialogue, in order to turn our cooperation into development opportunities for future generations.
I do so at a moment of particular importance, as Greece reaches the end of our second year on the UN Security Council and is preparing to assume its Presidency next month.
12 months ago, as we marked the 80th anniversary of the United Nations, we spoke of the need to reinvigorate multilateralism.
One year later, that need has only become more urgent as we are living through perilous times. Conflicts are multiplying. Tensions are deepening.
And perhaps most alarmingly, we are witnessing a further erosion of restraint in international affairs.
The rules and understandings that have long provided a degree of stability in relations between states are increasingly being tested.
The selection of the tenth Secretary-General presents a historic opportunity for the reinvigoration of the Organization when it is most needed.
The first step in restoring confidence in multilateralism is acknowledging where it has actually succeeded.
Few examples are more powerful than the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.
With 172 parties, UNCLOS provides the binding legal framework within which disputes can be managed peacefully rather than through force.
From the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea to the Indo-Pacific, strategic maritime routes are increasingly becoming arenas of geopolitical confrontation.
Commercial vessels are being targeted and vital trade routes used as instruments of pressure, with grave consequences for supply chains, energy markets and food security worldwide.
Freedom of navigation and uninhibited passage through international straits, as guaranteed by international law, must be championed globally.
It is our collective responsibility to uphold these principles in practice, and to safeguard commercial shipping.
As a leading maritime nation, Greece actively contributes to maritime security through the European Union's Operation ASPIDES in the Red Sea.
This topic will remain a high priority when Greece assumes the Presidency of the Security Council next month, with particular attention being placed to the challenges posed by emerging technologies.
Greece’s geography grants it the natural role of serving as a bridge between Europe and its wider neighborhood to the east and south.
We literally sit at the intersection of the shrinking space between the East and West.
My country is a pillar of stability, connectivity, and peace across the Eastern Mediterranean, the Middle East and the Gulf.
Greece has developed strong strategic partnerships with key countries in the region, including Israel, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Qatar.
We are a bridgebuilder not a troublemaker.
Yet, putting this vision into practice is rarely simple at a time of tectonic geopolitical changes.
In the Middle East, the Gaza Peace Plan, agreed last year, must be effectively implemented.
It is of paramount concern to ensure that Hamas surrenders its arms.
It can have no role in Gaza’s future.
At the same time, reconstruction needs to move forward, with Palestinians themselves taking ownership of Gaza’s future.
Greece will continue to advocate for a two-state solution, with Israel and Palestine living side by side in peace and security.
However, developments in the West Bank remain a source of deep concern.
Actions that are illegal under international law and undermine the viability of a future Palestinian state cannot be allowed to continue.
We strongly argue that this is also to the benefit of the long term security of Israel itself.
Greece has established a durable strategic partnership with Israel, while maintaining strong ties with the Arab world.
It is precisely the strength of this partnership that allows us to engage in an open and candid dialogue.
In Lebanon, there is now a real opportunity to lay the foundations for lasting peace.
The US-facilitated negotiations with Israel are an important step forward and should be sustained.
Greece strongly supports a sovereign, resilient and united Lebanon, and the Government’s efforts to restore the state’s monopoly over arms.
Ultimately, a stronger Lebanese state will serve both domestic security and regional stability.
Therefore, we will continue to deliver concrete assistance to the country, including to the Lebanese Armed Forces.
With the UNIFIL’s mandate ending, joint action is crucial to avoid a security vacuum and maintain an effective international and European presence.
Syria is another key part of the region.
Lasting stability in the Middle East requires a stable Syria.
A Syria that is inclusive, free from foreign interference and regional rivalries, and where every citizen can feel secure.
The new Syrian authorities have taken steps in this direction.
Yet further concrete progress must be demonstrated, particularly when it comes to protecting the rights and security of all religious and ethnic communities.
This includes the Orthodox Christian minority, which continues to face the violence of Islamist extremists.
This search for stability extends to Libya, a neighbor with whom we share many common interests.
A stable Libya, free from foreign interference, would benefit not only the Libyan people, but our entire region.
Greece is ready to support Libyan institutions in border protection and migration.
We remain committed to reaching an agreement on the delimitation of our maritime zones.
Dear colleagues, Let me now turn to our relations with our neighbor, Türkiye.

Over the past three years, we have made a sustained effort to improve our relationship, rebuild trust and keep channels of communication open in order to prevent the escalation of tensions that could lead to unwanted crises.
It is a delicate relationship, and one that carries the weight of history.
Indeed, given the broader regional challenges, the situation urgently calls for a common understanding on how we move forward.
An understanding grounded in full respect for international law and the principles of good neighborly relations.
After all, we cannot change our geography and we are destined to live side by side.

Let me repeat that the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea provides the only institutional framework to solve our only long- standing dispute concerning the delimitation of our continental shelf and exclusive economic zones.
Dialogue is essential for peace and prosperity.
But meaningful dialogue cannot coexist with unilateral actions that challenge the international legal order.
Nor can meaningful progress be made when faced with threats of war in response to the exercise of lawful rights according to international law.
Such actions do not resolve differences.
And they risk undermining the stability of our wider region.
A region which, we should not forget, still bears an open wound: the unresolved Cyprus issue.
Fifty-two years have passed since Türkiye’s illegal invasion and the continuing occupation of part of the island.
A flagrant violation of international law, whose consequences persist to this day.
For the United Nations, Cyprus remains a litmus test of its credibility: of its ability to uphold its own resolutions and the principles of its Charter.
Greece fully supports the efforts of Secretary-General Guterres to create the conditions for the resumption of substantive negotiations.
We sincerely hope that progress can be achieved during his remaining time in office.

And we expect these efforts to continue under his successor with the same objective: the reunification of Cyprus, free of occupation forces, in accordance with the relevant UN Security Council resolutions.
The principles at stake in Cyprus are being tested elsewhere too.
Today, two other major conflicts continue to challenge our ability to defend the values upon which this Organization was founded.
The war in Ukraine is now in its fifth year.
Five years since Russia’s full-scale aggression brought war back to European soil.
The Ukrainian people have shown extraordinary courage defending their freedom.
We strongly condemn attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure.
Diplomacy must now deliver an immediate ceasefire and a lasting peace, anchored in the principles of the United Nations Charter.
Ukraine must have a decisive say in its own future and Europe cannot be absent from negotiations.
Against this backdrop, another devastating war demands our urgent attention.
In Sudan, the nearly four-year conflict has resulted in a staggering humanitarian catastrophe.
Reports of atrocious war crimes continue to emerge, while the conflict is fueling instability far beyond Sudan’s borders.
We should not permit this tragedy to endure.
Foreign interference must also cease with no impunity for war crimes.
Ultimately, the way forward lies in a credible, Sudanese-led political process that reflects the aspirations of the citizenry.
The European Union ought to leverage its capacity to play a more active role in supporting that process and assisting in bringing this destructive conflict to an end.
After all, it has real skin in the game.
Should the devastating war continue, our continent will be the first to suffer from a possible massive new migratory wave.
Greece’s confidence abroad rests on a profound transformation at home.

At a time when the effectiveness of governments all over the world is being challenged by populists and extremists and public trust is being eroded in the echo chambers of social media, Greece serves as an example that sound reform-oriented policies can deliver real results for people and improve their lives Of course, significant challenges remain, but the progress Greece has made is impossible to overlook.
Seven years ago, my country was still emerging from the most painful economic crisis in its modern history, having lost more than 25% of its GDP.
Today, the economy is growing much faster than the European average, while Greece is attracting significant foreign direct investment.
Public finances are solid and our fiscal performance has become a positive example in Europe.
Public debt is declining faster than in any other OECD country.
Structural reforms and the digitalization of the state, which has helped reduce bureaucracy, have transformed the public administration and restored confidence among investors.
A few days ago, two leading rating agencies upgraded their outlook of the Greek economy.
At a time of great turbulence in the global bond markets, this says a lot about the progress that Greece has made.
Not many people would have bet a few years ago that today Greece’s borrowing cost would be lower than that of four G7 countries.
It was made possible by the hard work, resilience and determination of the Greek people.
Economic growth is vital because it expands a nation's strategic leverage.
It enables a state to bolster its defense, a core commitment this government is proud to adhere to, modernize its infrastructure and invest in innovation, all while safeguarding social cohesion.
Economic resilience is, therefore, inherently intertwined with robust institutions and credible deterrent capabilities.
Greece’s ambition is to serve as a nexus through which lasting partnerships are forged.
I was reminded of this vision earlier this year when I welcomed President Emmanuel Macron at the Roman Agora in Athens, to discuss Europe’s place amid a shifting geopolitical landscape.
The Agora was a place where commerce, law and public life once converged.
There, we reflected on how Europe can transform the crisis into an opportunity for its strategic autonomy and improve its competitiveness.

As we prepare to assume the Presidency of the Council of the European Union in the second half of 2027, we will work for a Europe that is more competitive, more secure, more capable of defending itself and more effective in protecting its external borders.
Another lesson, however, is becoming increasingly clear: connectivity is the tangible face of geopolitics.
The region’s energy landscape is fundamentally transformed.
Electricity grids, energy and digital corridors, ports and shipping routes are levers of power. Geography matters.
Our ambition is to translate our unique position into stronger links between Europe, the Middle East, the Gulf and North Africa.

Therefore, we are investing in a new generation of connectivity projects, such as GREGY, which will bring clean electricity from Egypt to Europe, and the Great Sea Interconnector, which will connect the European electricity grid with Cyprus and Israel.
At the same time, we leverage our unique geographic position to become a provider of energy security to our northern neighbors.
And as the prime minister of a leading shipping nation, it is worth remembering a stark fact: More than 90% of global trade is conducted by sea.
If we systematically threaten the freedom of navigation and do not protect vital sea routes, the global economy risks coming to a grinding halt.
And this is something that should be of great interest to every single country represented in this great Assembly I would like to conclude with a few thoughts on the topic of artificial intelligence.
One of my favorite bands when I was growing up was Talking Heads.
Little did I know at the time that David Byrne’s iconic song “we are on a road to nowhere” would ring so prescient four decades later.
For the first time in the history of our species, we have created a technology that openly challenges the supremacy of the human mind as the pinnacle of our evolutionary development.
I will not dwell on the transformational potential of this revolutionary technology, whether in disease eradication, productivity enhancement, or fighting climate change.
However, it is simply impossible to ignore the fact that, at present, the risks of an unchecked and unregulated advance in artificial intelligence could greatly outweigh its potential benefits.

When the people developing the technology tell us openly that, “left unchecked AI could outrun our ability to control these systems” and admit that “we only understand a tiny fraction of what goes on in these models”, alarm bells should ring very loudly for all of us.
In simple words, AI bosses are telling us that they have no idea how recursive self-improvement, the ability of AI to constantly create better versions of itself, actually works.

Add to that the possibility of massive job destruction, the likelihood of unprecedented wealth creation in the hands of very few, and the impact that AI may have on the very nature of human relationships, especially for our kids, and you have all the ingredients of an unprecedented political and social upheaval.
The idea that the big tech companies will find some voluntary arrangement to self-regulate the development of AI is naive.
It flies in the face of everything we know about the history of capitalism.
The prize for the winners is simply too great to believe that benign consideration for the wellbeing of humanity will outweigh the relentless drive of capital to constantly seek better returns.
Given that the leading AI models are being developed here in the United States, this is primarily an issue for the US government to address.
Fortunately, there are precedents from which to draw lessons.

In the 1940s and 50s, the American government heavily regulated another technology so powerful that its creators believed it could bring about either a golden age in human flourishing or the end of the world.
The same needs to happen now.
And it needs to happen fast.
AI companies need to be licensed based on specific requirements: adherence to human values, transparency and, most importantly, safety.
In order for a new plane to fly, it has to undergo a myriad of rigorous tests approved by the regulator.
But the same is not true for a frontier artificial intelligence model.
At the same time, I take the call by leading AI executives for a voluntary pause in the development of their models very seriously.
But only as a temporary measure to buy time for a powerful regulatory authority to be set up.

Liberal capitalism has a history of reining in market excesses, whether it was breaking up powerful monopolies or setting rules and standards to allow the market to operate with an eye on the common good.
The same needs to happen now.

And as much as the cooperation of China and the rest of the world is necessary to address this huge challenge, the fate of artificial intelligence and the impact it will have on humanity as a whole will not be decided in Brussels, Tokyo, or Brasilia, but primarily here, in the United States.
With great power comes great responsibility.
Let us hope our host country will rise to the occasion.
One year ago, standing at this very podium, the Prime Minister of Grenada addressed this General Assembly not only as our Head of Government, but as a proud son of the Caribbean.
He reminded us that our Region continues to literally and figuratively weather storms, yet continues to rise with resilience, dignity and hope.
Today, as I stand before you representing the people of Grenada, I speak of transformation - Because resilience alone is no longer enough.
Our task cannot simply be to survive one crisis after another.
We must transform the conditions that make people vulnerable in the first place.
We must renew our global systems, strengthen our multilateral partnerships and summon the collective will necessary to build a world worthy of the next generation.
And that transformation must begin with people.

Haiti: From Solidarity to Action Grenada joins CARICOM in calling for the timely renewal of the mandate of the Gang Suppression Force, its full and rapid deployment in close partnership with the Haitian National Police, and the provision of the personnel, financing, equipment and logistical support necessary for it to fulfil its mandate effectively with appropriate human-rights safeguards.

These security efforts are essential to creating the conditions for credible, free, fair and inclusive Haitian-led elections, the strengthening of national institutions and the restoration of constitutional governance.
Haiti is not a failed state.
Haiti represents a promise yet to be fulfilled.
It is a promise to the Haitian people that the international community must honour, not with pity - but with purpose; not temporarily - but sustainably.
And even as we respond to the security crisis, humanitarian assistance must remain at the centre of our efforts.
Cuba: Partnership Must Prevail Over Isolation Grenada remains deeply concerned about the continuing hardship endured by the Cuban people.

Our humanitarian conscience cannot be indifferent to the circumstances of ordinary households, particularly children, the elderly and other vulnerable persons, whose difficulties deepen with each passing day that the present impasse remains unresolved.
We call for constructive engagement that places the well-being of the Cuban people at its centre and opens a path towards meaningful relief, improved living conditions and renewed opportunities.
As we speak of transforming our multilateral system, we must also ensure that its leadership reflects the diversity, experience and aspirations of the people it serves.

Grenada therefore proudly joins our CARICOM family in giving our unequivocal support to the candidacy of Ambassador Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of Guyana for the position of Secretary-General of the United Nations.
CARICOM Heads of Government have endorsed her as the region’s candidate, recognising the experience and leadership she brings to this important moment for global multilateralism.
Her distinguished service as Guyana’s Foreign Minister and Permanent Representative to the United Nations, has demonstrated a deep commitment to diplomacy, dialogue and international cooperation.
The Caribbean has long demonstrated that size does not determine the strength of our ideas, the quality of our leadership, or the value of our contribution to the international community.
We believe, Ambassador Rodrigues-Birkett is eminently qualified to serve the entire United Nations membership.

Her election would represent a historic milestone for our Caribbean Region and a powerful affirmation that every region, including Small Island Developing States, can contribute to leadership at the highest levels of our multilateral system.
Restoring Trust Through Transformation We meet at a time of significant global transformation.
The challenges before us are complex, but they also present an opportunity to renew our commitment to cooperation and create practical solutions that improve the lives of our people.
The theme of this session, “Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all,” challenges us to move beyond declarations toward delivery.
For Grenada, restoring trust means demonstrating through our actions that international cooperation produces results.
It means listening to one another.
It means respecting the voices of small states as much as those of large ones.
And it means ensuring that every country has the opportunity to pursue its legitimate development aspirations.
Grenada approaches this General Assembly in a spirit of partnership, optimism and constructive engagement.
We remain firmly committed to the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations, international law, peaceful dialogue and the peaceful settlement of disputes.
In an increasingly interconnected world, cooperation is not merely desirable.
Vision 75: Grenada's Transformation The transformation we advocate internationally must also take place at home.
Grenada is advancing an ambitious long-term roadmap towards our 75th anniversary of independence.
Anchored in our National Sustainable Development Plan 2020–2035, Vision 75 charts a transformational course for our Nation, rooted in sustainability, resilience, equity and opportunity.
At the heart of Vision 75 are five strategic pillars: Education and Skills Training. Healthcare.
The Environment and Energy. And Housing.
These are not simply sectors of government policy.
We are investing in health and wellness, education and skills, food security, renewable energy, digital innovation and environmental sustainability.
We are creating greater opportunities for our young people and preparing them not simply for the jobs that exist today, but for the industries that will define tomorrow.
For Grenada, transformation must always be people-centred.
It means building resilience while creating opportunity.
Expanding our economy while protecting our environment; and, Embracing technology while safeguarding humanity.
SIDS, Climate and Resilience As a Small Island Developing State, Grenada understands resilience.
But experience has also taught us that resilience cannot begin after disaster strikes.
We must invest before the storm.
Build before the damage is done.
And finance resilience before countries are forced to borrow simply to rebuild what they have lost.
This requires greater international cooperation in climate adaptation, disaster preparedness, resilient infrastructure and accessible financing.
Small Island Developing States should not be viewed simply as victims of climate change.
We are also laboratories of resilience.
From Climate Vulnerability to Opportunity Climate action remains one of the areas in which collective effort can make a profound difference.
Grenada remains committed to strengthening resilience and advancing sustainable and low-carbon development.
But ambition without implementation is merely aspiration.
For vulnerable countries, climate commitments must be accompanied by reliable access to the resources required to deliver them.
Climate financing must become more accessible, predictable and responsive.
Our objective should not simply be to help vulnerable countries recover from the next disaster.
Our objective must be to transform vulnerability into resilience and resilience into sustainable opportunity.
Financing Development Differently This transformation must also take place in the international financial system.
Grenada welcomes growing recognition that development and vulnerability cannot be assessed by income alone.
The Multidimensional Vulnerability Index offers an important opportunity to better recognise the structural circumstances of Small Island Developing States.
Our vulnerabilities are shaped by exposure to climate change, natural disasters, external economic shocks and other circumstances that cannot adequately be captured through income per capita.
therefore encourages Member States, development partners and Grenada international financial institutions to advance vulnerability-informed approaches to development financing.

Greater access to concessional financing, climate finance, disaster-risk financing and innovative financial instruments can help countries move from vulnerability to resilience, and from recovery to sustainable growth.
Young People, Technology and AI At the centre of all of this must be our young people.
Their creativity, energy and ideas are among our greatest national and global assets.
Our responsibility is to give them the education, skills, technology and opportunities necessary to shape the world they will inherit.

Digital transformation and emerging technologies, particularly artificial intelligence, offer enormous possibilities for education, healthcare, agriculture, public administration and economic development.
The technologies shaping humanity's future must not create another divide between those countries that can afford to innovate and those that cannot.
And access alone will not be enough.

As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in our economies and societies, we must develop credible AI governance frameworks that encourage innovation while protecting people, privacy, security, democratic values and public trust.
Technology must remain a tool for human development, not a replacement for human responsibility.
We must prepare young people not only to use new technologies, but to question them, govern them, and deploy them ethically.
Global Call to Action Grenada approaches the future with confidence.
We recognise the challenges before us, but we also see enormous possibilities.
Our Vision 75 embodies our determination to build a stronger, healthier, more resilient and more prosperous Grenada.
Our commitment to the Sustainable Development Goals reflects our belief in shared global progress.
And our engagement in this United Nations reflects our conviction that partnership remains one of humanity's greatest sources of strength.
So let this Assembly send a clear message: Let us restore hope in Haiti.
Let us protect children and civilians wherever conflict threatens their future.
Let us choose dialogue over division.
Let us allow cooperation with Cuba and with all nations to be guided by the interests and well-being of people.
Let us ensure that Small Island Developing States have fair access to the financing necessary to build resilience before disaster strikes.
Let us equip our young people to lead the technological transformation rather than become casualties of it.
Let us protect our oceans and our planet.
And let us transform our multilateral institutions so that they deliver not simply promises, but progress.
The measure of this United Nations cannot only be the resolutions we adopt.
It must be the lives we improve.
Grenada stands ready to work with all Member States and international partners in advancing a future that is peaceful, resilient, inclusive and sustainable.
One year ago, Grenada came before this Assembly with a message about resilience and education.
Today, we build upon that message.
Resilience gives us the strength to endure.
Transformation gives us the power to change.
Partnership gives us the ability to do both.
Together, through renewed trust and genuine partnership, we can build a United Nations that delivers.
And ultimately, a world in which no country, no community and no person is left behind.
Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, the international system that has guided our relations over recent decades is undergoing a profound transformation.
Conflicts, geopolitical tensions, declining resources for development and the fragmentation of spaces for dialogue are testing the principles that have guided coexistence among nations.

At the same time, democracy faces a twofold challenge the resurgence of authoritarian tendencies that seek to undermine the will of the people, and the spread of organised criminal networks that infiltrate institutions, corrupt justice systems, capture economies and territories, and erode public trust.
Transnational organised crime is more than just a threat to public security.
It is a direct threat to democracy the rule of law, and the ability of our peoples to freely determine their future.
Criminal networks do not recognize borders.
They are linked through drug trafficking trafficking in persons, illicit arms trafficking, smuggling, extortion, money laundering, environmental crime and other illicit economies.
They exploit institutional weaknesses, inequality, and a lack of opportunities.
Wherever the state is weakened, these structures seek to replace it, intimidate it, or bend it to serve private interests.
In the face of these realities, the fundamental principles that must guide our collective action have lost none of their relevance.
Preserving peace, combating hunger and poverty.
Ensuring equal rights and opportunities, strengthening justice, protecting our planet, and consolidating democratic institutions remain shared responsibilities.
The Sustainable Development Goals continue to provide an essential roadmap.
It is precisely at moments such as this that international law, multilateralism and democracy show their worth.
Law provides us with common rules.
Multilateralism enables us to turn shared problems into concerted solutions, and democracy ensures that power comes from the people and is exercised for their wellbeing.
I address this assembly on behalf of Guatemala, a country that knows from its own experience the value of these tools.
Our history has taught us that democracy, peace and respect for the law are not permanent achievements.
They are built collectively and each generation must preserve them.

A democracy rests on free elections, legitimate institutions, the separation of powers, freedom of expression, public participation, transparency and accountability But it also requires independent and effective institutions committed to the Constitution, the law and the popular mandate.
Public institutions must not serve criminal networks, private agendas, personal loyalties, or political or economic interests that are at odds with the common good.
They must serve the people, the constitutional order and society's democratic interests.
When an institution strays from that purpose, it does more than simply lose legitimacy.
It weakens the democracy it is meant to protect.

Democracy also earns its legitimacy in everyday life When a family is protected from poverty, when a child learns in a decent school, when a woman lives free from violence, when a community is no longer isolated, and when a young person can envision a future without being forced to leave their country.
That is why in Guatemala, we are restoring the state's capacity to reach those who have been excluded from opportunities for far too long.

The intersectional mano a mano strategy brings together health education, housing, nutrition and community development to address poverty at the local level following crop losses caused by climate related events.
More than 450,000 families have received food assistance, while small scale producers have gained access to seeds, tools, inputs and insurance mechanisms.
Public education is central to this effort.
More than 1 million students have participated in initiatives to strengthen reading comprehension.
We have expanded educational opportunities, promoted scholarships, strengthened instruction in national languages, and accelerated the digital transformation of the school system.
In healthcare, we have expanded and refurbished facilities, strengthened regional services, and made progress in the comprehensive treatment of chronic diseases and cancer.
