Alongside the revival of road projects and public works in historically underserved communities, the National Digital Connectivity Plan now provides internet service to 383 public entities.

We have also strengthened early warning systems for earthquakes, tsunamis, floods and volcano hazards, restoring the legitimate presence of the state also means providing security in accordance with the law, strengthening prevention, protecting communities, and pursuing criminal networks rather than only their visible manifestations.
It means improving investigations, institutional coordination, and the tracing of the financial flows that sustain illicit economies.
Guatemala maintains that the charter of the United Nations and international law must remain our common point of reference.
The sovereignty and territorial integrity of states must be respected.
Disputes must be settled by peaceful means.
International humanitarian law must be observed in all circumstances, and international obligations must be fulfilled.
The law loses its ability to protect us when we accept its selective application.
National and international institutions lose legitimacy when they depart from their mandates in response to pressure, calculations or particular interests.
Their authority rests on independence impartiality, transparency and respect for the law.
There can be no there cannot be one rule for the powerful and another for the weak.
Nor can there be victims whose suffering outrages us and others whose suffering we choose to ignore.
For countries such as Guatemala international law does not constrain our sovereignty.
It is one of its principal safeguards.
Guatemala believes in the peaceful settlement of disputes.
We place our trust in dialogue, negotiation and the mechanisms provided for under international law.
Because even the most complex historical differences can and must be resolved by peaceful means.
We are deeply concerned by the persistence of armed conflicts in different regions of the world, and their devastating consequences for civilians.

In every case, our position rests on the same principles respect for the charter and international law, the protection of civilians, safe humanitarian access and dialogue and diplomacy as indispensable paths towards a just, sustainable and lasting peace.
We must not grow accustomed to war.
We must not accept violence as a permanent condition of our time, or allow entire generations to grow up believing that force is the only way to resolve our differences.
This December, we will mark 30 years since the signing of the agreement on a firm and lasting peace, which brought an end to 36 years of internal armed conflict.
After years of negotiation, we chose to replace armed violence with the pursuit of dialogue.
That is why we understand the value of international support and the role of the United Nations.
Our experience allows us to share one conviction.
Negotiation is not a sign of weakness.
Dialogue does not mean abandoning our principles.
Seeking peace must never mean accepting injustice.

We have also contributed to United Nations peacekeeping operations More than 6300 Guatemalan women and men have served under the United Nations flag in peacekeeping operations in different parts of the world.
A country that knows the cost of war must also take responsibility for helping others preserve peace.

Mr. president, we must strengthen the timely exchange of information, operational and judicial coordination, border security with respect for human rights, the protection of ports and transit routes, financial and asset investigations, and the recovery of assets derived from illicit activities.
We must also work together on prevention.
Lasting security cannot be achieved through law enforcement alone.
It requires education, decent work, resilient communities, accessible institutions and opportunities for young people.
It requires us to reduce the social, territorial and economic spaces that criminal structures exploit to recruit, exert control and supplant the state.
Our regional cooperation must be grounded in trust, shared responsibility and respect for sovereignty.
It must not serve private agendas or become an instrument of interests alien to our peoples.
Climate change, pandemics, transnational organised crime, food insecurity, human mobility and technological transformation all demand cooperation.

Guatemala, a country particularly vulnerable to the effects of climate change, knows that adaptation, risk management and the protection of rural livelihoods require national efforts, but also financing and cooperation commensurate with the needs capable of building capacity and delivering results.
Defending multilateralism does not mean defending the status quo.
The United Nations must become more effective, representative, transparent and responsive to people.
It must make better use of its resources, reduce duplication and respond more swiftly without weakening the purposes for which it was created.
Efficiency must strengthen, not erode, its three pillars peace and security, sustainable development and human rights.

Effectiveness cannot be measured solely in administrative terms, but rather by the ability to prevent a war, protect a population under threat, combat hunger, confront transnational criminal networks, or support a state in strengthening its institutions.
We do not need a United Nations that is smaller in purpose.
We need a United Nations that is stronger in results and firmer in defending democratic principles.
That transformation must also reach the Security Council.
Its composition must better reflect the realities of the 21st century and remedy the long standing underrepresentation of entire regions.
When the veto causes paralysis in the face of serious threats to international peace and security, confidence in the entire system suffers.
We also face an important decision for the future of the organisation the selection of the next secretary general.

Guatemala hopes that the process will be transparent and inclusive, and will identify an independent leader able to build bridges, defend the principles of the charter and lead the reform our organisation needs.
The Latin American and Caribbean region stands ready and prepared to shoulder its responsibility to the international community.
The time has come for a Latin American woman to serve as secretary general of the United Nations. Excellencies. Distinguished delegates.

The Republic of Guatemala reaffirms its commitment to the peaceful settlement of disputes and the observance of international law We welcome the fact that the International Court of Justice has set the date for the oral hearings concerning the territorial, insular and maritime dispute with Belize.
For my country, this is more than a procedural milestone.
With the notification of the hearings, the final procedural stage before the court delivers its judgment has begun.
It marks the culmination of a legal dispute that has accompanied the people of Guatemala and successive governments since independence, and whose conclusion we eagerly await.

We recognize that the court's judgment, once delivered, will bring the dispute to an end, and we trust that it will provide legal certainty to both parties and lay the foundations for a new chapter in relations between Guatemala and Belize.

In closing, I wish to say that Guatemala will continue to do its part strengthening democratic institutions capable of meeting the needs of our people, resolutely confronting transnational organised crime, and those who seek to capture institutions defending international law, consistently promoting regional responses based on shared responsibility, and working for a United Nations capable of transforming itself to fulfil the promise contained in the opening words of our charter, we the Peoples.
Restoring trust will depend on our ability to show that even in times of uncertainty and division, we remain capable of building together solutions that none of us could achieve alone.
I wish you every success as you undertake this important responsibility at a moment when multilateralism, and indeed the United Nations, faces profound challenges.

The challenges of our time One year ago, I stood at this very podium and reminded this Assembly that if the United Nations is to remain humanity’s surest hope for a just and peaceful world, it must have the courage to confront aggression and the will to engage fully with the defining questions of our age.

I also argued that we must be bold enough to undertake the institutional reforms necessary to strengthen the Organization, enhance its credibility and enable it to meet the challenges of a changing world.

Indeed, I am pleased that the theme of this year’s assembly, “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All” acknowledges the need for this organization to be made fit for purpose to respond to the challenges and to seize the possibilities of our time.

Today, we confront a climate catastrophe; an energy crisis; food insecurity; biodiversity loss; armed conflicts and geopolitical tensions; the horror of genocide; a spiralling cost-of-living crisis; a mounting debt crisis; widening inequalities within and among nations; and, perhaps most troubling of all, a weakening of multilateralism itself.
Yet if history has taught us anything, it is that even when the world seemed to stand at the precipice, humanity has never been entirely without the means to draw it back from the brink.
We have ended wars that seemed without end.
We have confronted economic calamities that threatened the foundations of societies.
We have overcome dangers that presented existential threats.
Time and again, it has been our inventiveness, our courage and, above all, our willingness to act together that have opened a path where none seemed to exist.
The possibilities of our age This is why I do not wish to linger or lament further upon the difficulties before us.
I wish instead to turn our gaze toward the possibilities that lie beyond them.
For within every crisis lies a summons to solutions, within every disruption an opportunity for renewal, and within every uncertainty the possibility of shaping a better future.
The possibilities before us are immense.
We have the possibility of silencing the guns through dialogue and diplomacy.
The world does not need more sophisticated instruments of destruction; it needs a more sophisticated capacity for peace.

In this regard, I reiterate Guyana’s call for a just and lasting solution to the crisis in the Middle East, one that brings an end to the suffering of innocent civilians and recognises the Palestinian people’s legitimate right to self-determination and to a secure homeland of their own.
We reiterate our support for the two-State solution.

We call as well for an end to the Russia-Ukraine war and the war in Sudan, and for peaceful resolution of all conflicts that continue to consume lives, uproot families and extinguish the hopes of millions in other parts of our world.
We reiterate our call for a viable solution for Cuba, one that is peaceful, people centered, development-focused and allows for the full aspirations of the Cuban people to be realized.
Guyana reiterates CARICOM’s offer to play a meaningful role in achieving this objective.
In Haiti, resolving the multidimensional challenges remains central to achieving democracy, stability, peace and prosperity for the Haitian people.
The sustained support of the international community through the provision of key financial and material resources is critical to realizing these objectives.
Ultimately, the future of Haiti must be Haitian-led and Haitian- owned.
Turning to my own country - Guyana has always advanced the peaceful settlement of the controversy in relation to our border with Venezuela.

Despite the historical truth - clearly outlined in the Arbitral Award of 1899 that determined the full, perfect and final settlement of our border with Venezuela, we endured long and repeated provocations and aggression.
The matter was referred to the International Court of Justice by the Secretary General, acting pursuant to the Geneva Agreement, and the Court twice pronounced on its jurisdiction to hear the matter.
Recourse to the ICJ came after decades of efforts to resolve the controversy bilaterally, including through a mixed commission and the Good Offices of the UN Secretary General.
In full respect for international law, Guyana participated and encouraged Venezuela to participate in the proceedings of the ICJ.

Now that we have both participated in the hearings which were completed in May 2026, we urge Venezuela to abide by the forthcoming ruling in accordance with their obligation under the UN Charter, as Guyana will do.
We look forward to a new era of neighbourly relations in the interest of our peoples, the development of our countries and the stability and prosperity of our region.
In pursuit of a stronger and safer region, Guyana is honoured to be a founding member of the Shield of the Americas, launched by President Trump in March 2026.

Since the founding of this initiative, Guyana has worked closely with the United States and thirteen other like-minded nations that believe in building a Western Hemisphere that values freedom, peace, economic prosperity and have a shared responsibility and commitment to fighting transnational crime and criminal networks.
It is our collective responsibility to never allow our region to be overtaken by gangs or criminal networks.
We understand that it is only through partnership, shared intelligence, and cooperation that we can effectively tackle the threats they pose to our economies and the livelihoods of our citizens.

This week, I was pleased to join members of the Shield of Americas in adopting a Joint Communique which underscores our collective resolve to strengthen the resilience of our region in Economic, Security and Multilateral Coordination.
We stand at the threshold of a new era of technological advancement.

Artificial intelligence, biotechnology, digital communications and other extraordinary breakthroughs offer the prospect of transforming health, education, agriculture, productivity and public services on a scale scarcely imaginable a generation ago.
But the true measure of technological progress will not be how powerful our machines become, but how much more empowered our people become.
Technology must not become the privilege of the few; it must become the servant of all humanity.
We have before us a new opportunity for sustainable development.
Development must not merely make our economies richer; it must make our societies better.
We must not allow further slippage in our pursuit of the Sustainable Development Goals.

We must renew our commitment to them — not as an inventory of promises, but as a covenant with our peoples and a practical blueprint for ensuring that development reaches every citizen, protects generations yet unborn and creates lasting, inclusive prosperity.

One way to arrest this slippage is, as Guyana is doing, to mainstream the Goals into our national development strategies, public policies and budgets, so that they become embedded in the priorities we set and the resources we commit, rather than remaining aspirations.
The SDGs must not only guide our ambitions; they must shape our choices and our national priorities.

In Guyana, we have made significant advances including universal health care, free education, modern infrastructure, accelerated access to affordable housing, opportunities for full employment, acceleration of financing for small and medium sized enterprises, and digitizing service delivery.
Two years ago, at this very podium I committed Guyana to provide global leadership on biodiversity.
In July 2025, under Guyana’s leadership, the Global Biodiversity Alliance was established as an inclusive platform.

In just over one year, the Alliance expanded from 17 to 138 members, bringing together governments, international organization, including the UN, development banks, Indigenous Peoples, local communities, scientists, universities and the private sector.
The second conference of the Alliance, to be held on October 2026, will begin to mobilize the resources and partnerships to deliver its ambitions.
At the same time, we continue to advance our national Low Carbon Development Strategy focused on turning forest stewardship and climate action into a new model for sustainable development.
As we commence this 81st Session, we have the opportunity to build a United Nations that is truly fit for purpose.
The crisis confronting multilateralism can become the catalyst for its renewal.
The United Nations must not be a monument to the past; it must become an instrument for the future.

We need a Security Council that reflects the geopolitical realities of the twenty-first century, not the power structures of 1945; a Council that embraces the emerging multipolarity of our world, including permanent representation from Africa, and Latin America and the Caribbean.
A new multilateralism If the United Nations is to remain humanity’s best hope, then this is not the hour to retreat from multilateralism.
This is the hour to reclaim and to renew it.

For it is in times such as these— when wars rage across borders, when the shadow of existential threats falls across the future of human civilisation, when the old certainties are dissolving before our eyes—that multilateralism must rise.

Multilateralism rests upon the proposition that our destinies are bound together, that the security of one cannot be at the insecurity of another, and that in an interdependent world, cooperation is a necessity; and where there can be no enduring prosperity where inequality deepens, and no just international order where rules are applied selectively.
It is to that truth that this eighty-first session of the General Assembly must recommit itself.
But recommitment cannot mean merely repeating the language of yesterday.
The world has changed, and multilateralism must change with it.

We need a new and invigorated multilateralism—one equal to the turbulence of our age, sufficiently courageous to confront its trials, sufficiently imaginative to navigate its transformations, and sufficiently principled to defend the rule of international law.
To make the United Nations fit for purpose we must make it more transparent, accountable and responsive.
We must strengthen the General Assembly and give greater weight to its deliberative and representative authority.
We must bring greater coherence to a system too often divided by institutional rivalries, bureaucratic silos and competing mandates.
We must ensure that the resources of the UN match the responsibilities we have entrusted to it.
Leadership But institutions do not reform themselves.
They require leadership capable of seeing beyond the present and imagining the institution the future demands.
The United Nations needs leadership that can bring its different organs, agencies and programmes into a greater unity of purpose.
Leadership that can build bridges where division has become habitual; leadership that can defend the principles of the Charter without fear or favour.

The United Nations needs its next Secretary-General to work with all member States to restore confidence in the Organization, mobilise its energies, and turn the language of multilateralism from aspiration into action.
The reform of the United Nations, the restoration of trust and the need to manage transformation is, therefore, inseparable from the question of leadership.
And the choice of its next Secretary-General will be, in no small measure, a choice about the kind of United Nations we wish to leave to the generations that follow.

Guyana’s nominee for UN Secretary General It is in this spirit that Guyana has put forward the candidature of Her Excellency Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett for the office of Secretary-General of the United Nations.
She has served her country, represented the developing world, and worked within the multilateral system with a deep understanding of both its promise and its imperfections.
We believe that her experience, her convictions and her record of service speak directly to the kind of leadership this moment demands.
Her candidature, therefore, acquires special significance amid the profound challenges confronting the United Nations and the international order.

We need leadership capable of restoring trust without compromising principle; of listening without surrendering conviction; of building bridges across the widening chasms between North and South, between large states and small, between the developed and developing worlds.
We need a Secretary-General who will defend the Charter not only when it is politically convenient, but precisely when its principles are under pressure.

The responsibility for recommending the next Secretary-General rests, in the first instance, with the Security Council, and we therefore respectfully place before its members the candidature of Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett.

Endorsed by the Caribbean Community (CARICOM), we invite all to consider her candidacy on its merits and to judge whether her vision, experience, expertise and record can help restore confidence in the United Nations at this critical moment.
Conclusion The United Nations was conceived in hope—and that hope remains alive in the pursuit of peace, security and human progress over the perpetuation of division and war.
This is why we must not abandon multilateralism because it is imperfect; we must renew it because humanity still needs it.

Let us therefore build a United Nations that does not merely reflect the world as it is, but helps create the world as it ought to be—a world where law restrains power, cooperation overcomes division, and every human being can look to the future with hope.

Guyana believes that the choice remains ours as to whether the divisions of our age will define the future, or whether nations can summon the will to build a more peaceful, secure and prosperous international order.
The United Nations must be at the heart of that endeavour—not as an institution looking back at the world it was created to serve, but as one helping humanity shape the world that is yet to come.

STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER H.E. ALIX DIDIER FILS-AIMÉ/GENERAL DEBATE OF THE EIGHTY-FIRST SESSION OF THE UNITED NATIONS GENERAL ASSEMBLY/New York, 25 September 2026 Mr. President of the General Assembly, Mr. Secretary-General, Ladies and Gentlemen Heads of State and Government, Ladies and Gentlemen Ministers; Ladies and Gentlemen Permanent Representatives, Distinguished Delegates, Haitian People, In taking the floor before this General Assembly, I am mindful of the weight of History.

More than 80 years ago, in the aftermath of a war that had plunged the world into chaos, Haiti, a founding Member of the United Nations, joined with the nations of the world in wagering on peace, dialogue and respect for human dignity.

Today, as deadly crises and conflicts multiply, as the climate emergency intensifies, and as new fractures threaten the stability of Haiti and of the world, that founding wager is once again being put to the test.

It is imperative that, in the face of the crises striking Haiti as well as those upheaving so many regions of the world, nations unite around what is essential: peace, security, and the well-being of all peoples.
That is the full meaning of the theme that brings us together this year.
I retain an emotional memory of his visit to Port-au-Prince on 16 June 2026, a powerful testimony of his solidarity with the Haitian people.
In the difficult hours our country is going through, Haiti wishes to express its gratitude to all the partners and friends who continue to stand by its side.

In that regard, I would like to salute the commitment of the United Nations system, and especially that of the Security Council, as well as that of the Organization of American States, CARICOM and the European Union, whose support remains more essential than ever.

I pay particular tribute to the brotherly peoples who, by contributing to the Gang Suppression Force and supporting its full deployment, have chosen to share with us the burden of the struggle for peace and security.
Haiti will forget neither their solidarity nor their sacrifices.

I also wish to underscore the privileged partnership of the United States of America, - the steadfast support of Canada, - the valuable support of partners such as France, Chile and Mexico in the modernization of our national security capacities, - as well as the openness of the Dominican Republic to dialogue and its advocacy in favour of a lasting resolution of the Haitian crisis.

Lastly, we express our gratitude to BINUH, the agencies, funds and programmes present on the ground, as well as to all our multilateral partners for their constant commitment alongside the Haitian people.

Before this august Assembly, I bear the voice of a people who engraved its name in the annals of History by daring to accomplish the unthinkable: to break the chains of slavery and bring into being, on a land won through sacrifice, sweat and blood, the world’s first free Black Republic.
That epic is the eternal proof that no empire is more powerful than a people’s thirst for freedom.
How can one forget the fate and hidden tears of Toussaint Louverture?
Brutally torn from his native land, cast into the icy solitude of a cell in Fort de Joux, deprivation and humiliation overcame Toussaint Louverture.
But his struggle for freedom remained alive through Dessalines, Christophe, Pétion, and all the other founding fathers and mothers.

Toussaint Louverture had predicted it: [Pause] “In overthrowing me, they have cut down in Saint-Domingue only the trunk of the tree of liberty; it will spring up again from its roots, for they are deep and numerous” The tree grew again.
And it will pursue its destiny.
And even though, today, criminal violence threatens its roots and seeks to steal from our children the fruits of that freedom so dearly won, Haiti resists.
It is standing because peoples born of light never abdicate before the forces of chaos.
It is standing because peoples born of sacrifice know the price of freedom, peace and security.
Haiti knows, having learned it in its own flesh, that these achievements are never definitively secured and that, when they are threatened, one must have the courage to defend them.
That is the struggle Haiti is waging today.
And that is why it calls on the world, not to save it, but to stand by its side as it takes its destiny back into its own hands.
Today I bear the voice of Haiti, but also that of those peoples whom our world too often asks to bear the weight of crises they did not create.
For small States like Haiti, the cost of climate disruption has become unbearable.
It is a profound injustice that those who have historically contributed the least to it are nevertheless among those paying the heaviest price, often to the detriment of their own development.
The means devoted to adaptation and resilience must be commensurate with these challenges.
No people should have to choose between responding to the emergency and financing their development.
Access to capital, markets and technologies must be more equitable.
Our international financial architecture must evolve to better respond to the needs and realities of the most vulnerable countries.
Artificial intelligence opens up immense possibilities, but without rules or ethical safeguards, it risks deepening divisions.
Technology must remain an instrument of shared progress, in the service of humanity.
We must remain the masters of technology and never its subjects.
And no people must be left behind.
We must also fulfil the promise of a world where no one is condemned to hunger, deprived of care, displaced by war or a victim of exclusion and discrimination.
That same requirement of dignity must guide the way we look at migration.
For, behind the statistics and the debates, there are women, children and men who carry with them a story, talents, hopes and, sometimes, the burden of exile.
For generations, Haitian women and men established abroad have contributed to the societies that receive them.
From this rostrum, I wish to express our gratitude to the countries that open their doors to them and promote their integration.
Haiti has been a land of welcome, refuge and hope.
We are working to make it so again: a country where one can stay, return, live and build one’s future in dignity.
But I also want to reaffirm forcefully our attachment to respect for the dignity and fundamental rights of all migrants.
Whatever their status, no circumstance can justify their dignity being trampled upon.
Protecting a border and respecting human dignity are not at odds: they must go hand in hand.
A border can and must be protected, without human dignity ever being sacrificed.
The fate of migrants calls us to shared responsibility and lasting responses.
For crises that are allowed to endure fuel displacement and forced migration.
This is the case with the security crisis in Haiti, which has caused the exodus of thousands of Haitians.
The response to this crisis in Haiti lies in the restoration of security, stability and economic recovery.
The Republic of Haiti remains deeply attached to multilateralism and to the ability of nations to join forces when urgency so requires.

At a time when the United Nations must deliver concrete results for all, Haiti can become a model of successful international cooperation, proof of what we can achieve together, in respect for the will of nations and around a vision led by the country itself.
For, however complex it may be, the Haitian crisis is not insurmountable.
We are at a decisive moment.
This moment can no longer make do with half-measures, partially fulfilled commitments or overly timid responses in the face of the scale of the threat.
The massacres, the bereaved families, the women victims of abominable violence, the children deprived of their innocence and the communities driven from their homes must call out to us.
Above all, they must move us to act.
I wish here to honour the memory of all the victims of this violence.
Their loss imposes on us a duty of justice.
I also pay tribute to the police officers and soldiers, Haitian, Kenyan and nationals of other nations, who fell in the service of Haiti.
Through their courage, they wrote, with the ink of their blood, a page in our struggle for security and peace.
Haiti will never forget their sacrifice.
For them, for their families, for those twelve million women, men and children…
Children who ask only to grow up. To dream.
We cannot resign ourselves to seeing the dead and the wounded become mere numbers in our reports.
Because in Haiti, today, one more victim is one victim too many.
We have chosen to strengthen the operational capacities of our national security forces, because Haiti’s security must ultimately rest on the capacities of the Haitian State.
We are recruiting. We are training. We are strengthening.
Through the P4000 Programme, we are continuing the training of 4,000 police officers.
More than 2,000 have already been trained, and a new cohort is due to graduate from the Police Academy next November.
At the same time, more than 1,500 new soldiers have already been trained, and we are putting in place a programme aimed at training 15,000 new soldiers over the next three years.
We have also increased the investment budget of our two security forces.
Our objective is not only to respond to today’s crisis.
It is to build the capacities that will enable Haiti tomorrow to ensure its own security itself, fully and sustainably.

It is regrettable that the Force, called upon to support these efforts on a temporary basis, is not yet fully operational and still has not reached, on the ground, the planned strength of 5,500 members.

That is why, from this rostrum, we insist on the need to renew the mandate of the Gang Suppression Force and for its full deployment, with the personnel, equipment and means necessary for the fulfilment of its mission.
The experience of the Multinational Security Support Mission must serve as a lesson to us: a mandate is not enough.
And there must be the determination to see it through to the end.
But there is another security issue that must concern us collectively: the illicit trafficking of arms and ammunition.
The weapons that kill Haitians, that spread terror in our neighbourhoods and cut down innocent lives are not produced in Haiti.
They arrive through transnational criminal channels that fuel insecurity, strengthen the operational capacity of the gangs and threaten the stability of our entire region.
As long as this trafficking prospers, violence will find the means to perpetuate itself.
Dismantling it is a shared responsibility.
We must therefore go beyond advocacy on behalf of Haiti.
The security of the island also depends on effective control of the border.
[PAUSE] Impunity is another face of insecurity.
We must combat it with the same determination.
That is why we have established two specialized judicial divisions to strengthen the fight against impunity, financial crime, mass crimes and sexual violence.
On 1 January 2027, with the entry into force of our new Penal Code and Code of Criminal Procedure, Haiti will take a historic step in the modernization of its justice system.
For it is not enough to arrest those who terrorize the population.

At the same time, we have reactivated the National Commission for Disarmament, Dismantlement and Reintegration, and launched the Fund for Peace Dividends in Haiti, which I invite our partners to support.
It is imperative to deprive violence of its capacity to recruit by offering our young people credible alternatives and genuine opportunities.
This is where security and development converge and must move forward together.
One cannot be sustainable without the other.
But the lasting well-being of a people cannot remain indefinitely suspended on aid and charity.
We cannot ask security alone to bear the weight of peace.
Economic recovery must be its other pillar.
That is why we welcome the decision of President Donald Trump’s administration to extend the HOPE/HELP trade preferences until 2028.
We are deeply grateful for this gesture of friendship, which constitutes an important step for the recovery of our economy, and we call for a ten-year extension.

We also express our gratitude to the United Kingdom for the Developing Countries Trading Scheme (DCTS) and call on more countries to establish similar mechanisms, capable of transforming market access into trade and investment opportunities.
Haiti needs investment to build its future.
That is why, today, Haiti is calling for a paradigm shift Moving from aid to investment.
And progressively transforming the resources mobilized to manage the crisis into investments capable of creating jobs and sustainable opportunities, especially for our young people and our women.

For when we no longer hear the sound of weapons, we must hear the sound of peace: engines starting up again, construction sites resuming, markets coming alive, women launching enterprises, young people working, the laughter of children playing, and our streets once again finding the rhythm of our music and of life.

Those who have had the privilege of knowing Haiti know what country exists behind the images of crisis: a welcoming and hospitable people, a vibrant culture, unique flavours, magnificent beaches and a heritage of exceptional richness.
We must recreate the conditions for the world to come to Haiti, discover it, invest there, do business there, stay there and return there.
That is also what the peace we want, must, and will build looks like.

Mr. President Security, for which the international community must remain fully mobilized alongside us, must also enable us to honour the second major commitment of the Government that I lead: to return the floor to the Haitian people through elections.

I belong to the generation that knew dictatorship, that had placed so much hope in the democracy that followed 1987, but that has too often seen those hopes run up against political instability and repeated transitions.
It is to break this cycle that I agreed to serve my country with the conviction that:
- this transition must come to an end, - and it will come to an end ...... by a ballot cast in the ballot boxes!
That is why we have launched the electoral process, in keeping with the National Pact for Stability and the Organization of Elections, the fruit of a broad consensus within the political class.

Today, the necessary resources have been mobilized; registration centres are open; women and men citizens are registering; political parties and groups have been accredited, and candidates are completing the formalities necessary for their participation in the vote.
We want free, credible, inclusive and fair elections.
The participation of women is encouraged, and young people are called upon to take their full place in them as voters, candidates and actors in our democracy.
Furthermore, arrangements have been made to preserve the integrity of the process.
Violence, criminal networks, illicit financing and those who support them must find no way to gain access to the ballot box.
For these elections are not only about the next Government.
They are about the future of Haiti.
And that future first bears the face of our youth.
The Haitian crisis is also one of the most painful expressions of the fractures of our time.
This chaos is not an accident of history: it has its roots in centuries of injustice, of which the independence debt remains the heaviest burden.
That is why we welcome the work of the joint Haitian-French commission of historians and await with great attention the publication of its report.
Yesterday, our ancestors wrested freedom from the darkness of servitude; today, our generation will wrest peace from the shadows of violence.
We will restore security to our communities, a voice to our people and hope to our youth.
The challenges are immense, but our determination is even greater.
We showed the world that freedom was possible; tomorrow we will show it that peace is built, defended and will triumph over fate.
More than two centuries ago, Haiti told the world that a people could break its chains.
Today, from this rostrum, Haiti tells the world that a people can also break the cycle of violence, transition and dependence.
Our security will rest durably on our own institutions.
And our development will move from aid to investment, from dependence to partnership, from emergency to prosperity.
The tree of liberty of which Toussaint spoke is still standing.
It is now for our generation to give it the fruits of peace.
This is our promise to our children.
This is our rendezvous with history.
Long live the Republic of Haiti.
I speak here to the nations of the world, but also to my fellow citizens watching at home.
For much of my life, I served as a judge, in Hungary and at the European Court of Human Rights.
That work taught me a simple lesson: The law must apply even to those in power.
Law does not weaken a state by placing limits on power.
It gives citizens a reason to trust the state.
This belief will guide me as President.
I will protect the Constitution, the freedom of our institutions and the dignity of every Hungarian citizen.
The state belongs to those who support the government, to those who oppose it and to those who have lost trust in politics altogether.
A new political majority must not become the new owner of the state.
This April, the people of Hungary voted for democratic renewal.
They expected more than a change of government.
They expect public life to change: a state that serves rather than controls, courts that decide without pressure, a press that challenges power and public money that is used for the public good.
There must be accountability for corruption and abuse of power.
But there must be no revenge.
Justice cannot become a political weapon.
A democratic state cannot repair past wrongs by repeating them with new people in charge.
The same law must apply to those who governed yesterday, those who govern today and those who may govern tomorrow.
A republic begins where power accepts its limits.
That is the republic Hungary must now rebuild.
Trust from our partners will not return because of one election or one speech.
Hungary asks to be judged by what we do.
We will be a reliable member of the European Union, a committed NATO ally and an active member of the United Nations.
These partnerships do not take away our freedom. They protect it.
Hungary will defend its national interests, but it will do so as a partner.
We believe that national interest and international cooperation do not have to stand against each other.
For Hungarians, the reasons are part of our own history.
Seventy years ago, the revolution of 1956 expressed our people's determination to govern themselves.
Our appeals reached the United Nations, but the international community could not prevent our defeat.
Many countries represented here opened their doors to Hungarians who fled their country after the revolution.
We remember both the cost of losing our independence and the help that allowed our people to start again.
Today, Ukraine is fighting to preserve its independence.
Hungary condemns Russia's full-scale war of aggression as a violation of the United Nations Charter and international law.
We affirm Ukraine's right to self-defence, its sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders, and the right of its people to decide their own future.
The freedom Hungarians demanded for themselves in 1956 is a freedom we must uphold for Ukrainians today.
We remember those who have lost their lives in this war, and we want diplomacy to bring the killing to an end.
But a lasting peace must respect Ukraine's sovereignty.
If taking territory by force becomes an accepted way of settling disputes, every smaller country will have reason to worry about its own future.
The principles of the Charter therefore matter to all of us.
Human suffering cannot wait for diplomacy to succeed.
People in conflict need food, medicine and protection now.
Hungary will continue to provide humanitarian aid to people in danger, especially the most vulnerable.
In the Middle East, we call for full respect for international humanitarian law and for aid to reach those who need it safely and without interruption.
Israelis and Palestinians must be able to live in security and dignity.
A lasting peace must give their families reason to believe that their children can grow up without the fear that has marked so many lives.
For people forced from their homes by war or persecution, protection may first mean finding safety in another country.
Hungary's own history gives us reason to understand that need.
At the same time, every state has the right to protect its borders.
Hungary will do so in accordance with international law.
We will fight illegal migration and the criminal networks that profit from it, while respecting human dignity and the protection given to refugees.
But security is not only about borders and wars.
People also need the chance to build a future where they live.
They need homes, schools, health care and ways to earn a living.
Poverty and the lack of opportunity can drive people from their countries just as conflict can.
Hungary will continue to support development that helps communities build that future, based on their own needs and priorities.
We are ready to share our experience in education, health and digital development.
Water is another area where our interests meet.
Drought can destroy crops, threaten food and energy supplies and take away people's income.
Climate change is making these pressures greater.
What one country does can affect the water available to another.
Hungary has experience in water management, sustainable agriculture and climate adaptation, and we are ready to share it.
For many countries represented in this hall, food, energy, education, health and jobs are immediate concerns.
We must give these issues the same serious attention that we ask others to give European security.
International cooperation works best when it responds to people's real needs and when every country has a voice.
Excellencies, The United Nations faces a crisis of trust.
Too often, it fails to act when powerful states or their friends break the rules.
No country should be above the law.
We cannot have one rule for our friends and another for others.
But the answer is not to turn away from the United Nations.
We need it, and we need it to work.
It must be able to act, treat all its members fairly and apply the same principles to everyone.
Hungary is ready to do its part.
We will stand for human rights, support peacekeeping and work with countries across the world to protect people and help diplomacy succeed.
We must also look beyond the problems of today.
Many of the decisions we make now will shape the lives of people who are not yet born.
A school, a strong institution or a safe water system can benefit people for many years.
Future generations must therefore have a place in the decisions we make today.
Hungary supports stronger international action to protect their interests, including the appointment of a United Nations Special Envoy for Future Generations.
The United Nations cannot demand trust.
The same is true of every state and every public institution.
The Hungarian people have asked us to restore their confidence in the future.
We will honour that choice by rebuilding trust at home and by becoming a country others can trust when their own future is at stake.
For Hungary, this is a new beginning.
But the principle behind it is not new: Power earns trust only when it accepts the law.
That is the responsibility Hungary accepts, and the work we are ready to undertake with you.
Eighty-one years ago, from the ashes of the Second World War, Indonesia and the United Nations were born.

We emerged from a world devastated by war, with a shared conviction that never again should humanity leave its future to war and division, and we shared a founding promise: to build a future of peace.

For eight decades, we have worked to turn that promise into progress: nations freed themselves from colonialism, globalization connected our economy, technology transformed our societies, and development improves the lives of billions.
But progress has never been linear.
We have lived through financial crises, a global pandemic, climate disasters, geopolitical rivalries, and conflicts around the world.
With every transformation and every crisis, one lesson remains clear: for peace and prosperity to endure, multilateralism must be resilient.
It must be able to adapt, to respond, and most importantly to deliver.
Because multilateralism that cannot deliver will lose people’s trust.
And without trust, multilateralism will never endure.
Building a resilient multilateralism begins with resilient nations.
And Indonesia has long understood this for decades.

In the 1960s, Indonesia developed the concept of national resilience: to safeguard our identity, to protect our sovereignty and unity, and to sustain our development in the face of challenges and obstacles.
At the heart of our resilience are our people.
A nation is resilient when families can provide for their households, when farmers can produce, when workers can find decent jobs, and when children can learn, grow, and dream about their future.
For Indonesia, this means building greater self-sufficiency in food and strengthening our energy security.
Most importantly, this also means investing in the future of our people: ensuring our children receive quality education, and ensuring our people have access to essential healthcare.
At the same time, we are building an economy that can withstand shocks and create opportunities: more jobs, stronger industries, and greater productive capacity.
Central to our resilience is our ability to manage differences and preserve our unity.
As a nation of more than 280 million people, Indonesia has learned that diversity is not something to overcome.
It is something to manage, respect, and turn into strength, through democratic participation, dialogue and respect for differences, we preserve our unity.
From Aceh to Papua, from Mianggas to Rote, Indonesia is one people.
We also continue to strengthen the promotion and protection of human rights, through our national mechanisms and our commitment to international human rights obligations.
This goes hand in hand with building our national resilience.
Because human rights are not only the absence of violence.
They are also about ensuring that people have food, education and healthcare.
To our neighbours, friends, and partners, let there be no doubt: Indonesia stands strong today, grounded firmly in democracy, human rights, and the rule of law.
And when nations are resilient at home, they have greater capacity to contribute beyond their borders.
A food-secure Indonesia can contribute more to regional and global food security.
A more energy-resilient Indonesia can contribute more to the global energy transition.
A stronger economy opens greater opportunities for cooperation and shared prosperity.
This is how national resilience becomes collective resilience.
And this is how resilience helps us advance the SDGs.
A resilient nation contributes to a resilient region.
Our national resilience will support and complement a region that is stable, peaceful and predictable.
Southeast Asia is home to one of the world’s largest productive-age populations.
It is now the world’s fifth largest economy, supported by a large and fast-growing digital economy.
At the center of this dynamic region is ASEAN.
ASEAN brings together nations with different histories, political systems, levels of development, and national interests.
We do not always agree, but we have made a conscious choice: to stay together.
And we choose to keep talking, even when agreement is difficult.
For almost six decades, ASEAN has managed differences, maintained communication, and continued seeking common ground.
This is the strength that comes from ASEAN unity and centrality.
It enables us to engage all partners, and preserve space for dialogue and cooperation, even as strategic competition intensifies around us.
At the same time, building a resilient region requires the ability to adapt.
This is why ASEAN must continue to evolve, so that it remains fit for purpose and beneficial for its people and the wider region.
Excellencies, Resilience at home and at the regional level must be matched, by a multilateral system capable of supporting and sustaining it.
This is where the United Nations remains indispensable.
The United Nations gives nations the space to resolve differences without resorting to conflict.
It provides common rules, when interests compete.
And it allows us to combine our capacities, when no country can act effectively alone.
This is why Indonesia continues to believe in the United Nations.
But believing in the United Nations also means believing that it must evolve with the world it serves.
Let us be clear: the answer to imperfect multilateralism is not less multilateralism.
It is a stronger and better multilateralism.
A multilateral system fit for the twenty-first century must be more representative, more agile, and better able to deliver.
Institutional transformation will not happen overnight.
But the urgency of today’s challenges requires us to act now.
We must start by strengthening our collective capacity to withstand crises, responding effectively to global crises and humanitarian situations, and sustaining peace, development, and cooperation.

At the same time, international financial architecture must also evolve: to respond better to the needs of developing countries, and to give them greater space to pursue their own development priorities and build their resilience.
But stronger institutions alone will not save multilateralism.
Institutions are only as strong as the principles we are willing to uphold.
International law must be upheld consistently, sovereignty must be respected, and colonialism must be brought to an end.
This is where Palestine remains one of the clearest tests of these principles, and the test of our conscience.
The clear violations of international law in Gaza and the West Bank are reminiscent of our world pre-1945.
A world pre-the UN Charter, pre-the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and pre-the four 1949 Geneva Conventions.
A world where a certain race was almost annihilated.
Indonesia knows what it means to struggle against colonialism, to struggle in a world where international law was weak and might was right.
Our nation’s journey to independence has shaped our consistent support for the Palestinian people and their right to determine their own future.

Indonesia will continue to stand with the Palestinian people until their right to self-determination is fulfilled and until an independent and sovereign State of Palestine is realized, based on the Two-State Solution, in accordance with international law and internationally agreed parameters.
Palestine is not only a question for one region.
It is a test of whether the multilateral system can uphold the very principles it was created to defend, and whether it can deliver when it matters most.
An effective multilateral system also requires effective leadership.

Indonesia’s leadership philosophy, passed down through generations, teaches us that leaders must possess the capability to lead by example from the front, build confidence while standing among the people, and empower from behind.
Leadership is not simply about commanding.
It is about exercising wisdom and giving others the strength to move forward.

Secretary-General António Guterres has led this Organization through an exceptionally challenging period: wars and geopolitical tensions, a global pandemic, humanitarian emergencies, and rapid technological transformation.
Throughout these challenges, the UN continues to provide an important platform for dialogue and collective problem-solving.
The next Secretary-General will carry an equally important responsibility: to uphold the Charter, strengthen the Organization, and to translate multilateralism into concrete results for people.
Effective leadership must also be accompanied with the full commitment of Member States to make multilateralism work.
Indonesia is prepared to carry its share, as our Constitution mandates us to contribute to a world based on freedom, lasting peace, and social justice.
Through diplomacy and mediation, Indonesia has contributed to resolving conflicts in the region and beyond.
We have been among the top tier contributors to UN Peacekeeping Missions, deploying personnel to missions around the world since 1957.
For nearly two decades, Indonesian peacekeepers have served under the UN flag in Lebanon.
UNIFIL may be entering its final chapter, but Indonesia’s commitment does not end with the Mission.
The experience, sacrifice, and dedication of our peacekeepers will continue to shape Indonesia’s contribution to international peace and security.
We will carry our diplomacy forward through humanitarian assistance, through peacebuilding, and through engagement across regions and institutions.
It is in this spirit that Indonesia present its candidature for a non-permanent seat on the UN Security Council for the 2029-2030 term.
Our commitment is clear: Fostering Unity, Advancing Peace.
Fostering unity means rebuilding trust in the multilateral system and keeping channels of dialogue open.
Advancing peace requires us to uphold international law and make effective use of the tools available to us.
Indonesia will work to keep dialogue open, build common ground, and turn shared responsibility into practical cooperation.
We will uphold the UN Charter consistently to maintain international peace and security.
We will bring the same principle that guides our foreign policy: to engage with all and to keep the space for cooperation open.
As President Prabowo Subianto mentioned on this very lectern last year: one thousand friends are too few and an enemy is too many.
The same approach guides Indonesia’s engagement with all partners.
Through ASEAN, G20, D8, BRICS, MIKTA, and the UN, Indonesia will extend the friendship to deliver practical cooperation.
Eighty-one years ago, Indonesia fought against colonialism so we could chart our own future.
Today, we reaffirm our promise for a future of peace we all share.
One year ago, President Prabowo Subianto called upon us to draw closer, not drift apart.
Today, I carry that call forward.
And as we draw closer, let us also make each other stronger.
Strong enough for our nations to withstand crises.
Strong enough for our regions to preserve cooperation.
Strong enough for our institutions to deliver for people.
Because resilience is not simply about surviving the storms.
It is about having the strength to keep moving forward together.
And only through our collective resilience, can the United Nations be strong enough to fulfil the promise we made 81 years ago, a future of peace, for generations to come.
1. We are gathered at this General Assembly, when the United Nations enters its ninth decade.
It was founded to maintain international peace and security, and take effective collective actions to that end.
Members committed to develop friendly relations, and to strengthen universal peace.
2. Yet, even as we meet, conflicts and confrontations remain our primary preoccupation.
The inability to maintain peace, is not just undermining security, but threatening progress, and retarding development.
In a globalized world, the effects of war are felt worldwide.
Countries far from conflicts, are being penalized for no fault of theirs.
Those most impacted, often have the least say.
This Assembly must face up to the true state of affairs.
3. This year, we are witnessing a conflict in the Gulf, one that is exacerbating an already difficult situation.
We remain deeply concerned over continuing hostilities.
The targeting of commercial shipping and seafarers, transiting international waterways, is simply unacceptable.
India calls upon all parties to exercise restraint, de-escalate tensions, ensure protection of civilians, and uninterrupted flow of energy and commerce.
4. The conflict in Ukraine, now in its fifth year, is equally concerning.
As Prime Minister Narendra Modi stated, endless war must give way now, to an end to war.
India supports ongoing initiatives to bring peace.
Even as this is underway, there is an urgent need to address the security of seafarers, and supply of food grains and energy.
India is prepared to do everything possible, to ameliorate this situation, especially with regard to food and energy security.
5. Tensions and violence also regrettably continue in West Asia or the Middle East.
We strongly believe, that a durable and lasting peace, requires a Two State solution.
In the meanwhile, India is contributing to humanitarian assistance, and relief efforts for the Palestinian people.
6. Let us recognize that peace, is not just the absence of war.
If the world is subjected to continuous threats and pressures, then we are really living on the edge of an abyss.
All it takes is one more step to push us over.
Therefore, it is imperative to strengthen stability, security and predictability.
These are crucial elements, of the enabling environment for peace.
If any of them are undermined, peace will inevitably be weakened.
After eight decades of the UN, this should have become our second nature.
7. Instead, what we are actually seeing, is a weaponization of everything.
A mindset of extreme competition has set in, undermining institutions, and establishing chokepoints.
It extends from the world of finance, to constricting market access, disrupting supply chains and withholding technology.
Resources and connectivity have become particularly subject to leveraging.
As a result, nations are now more focused on de-risking and diversifying.
While this may secure their interests to varying degrees, the overall atmosphere is no longer that of trust or goodwill.
8. The predicament of the Global South, is particularly acute.
It faces a 4F crisis – of the security of food, fuel, fertilizer and finance.
The combined impact of a Super El Nino, compounding fertilizer shortages and now impediments to grain movements, all these are cause for alarm.
Moreover, SDG progress is under increasing pressure.
The Global South’s right to industrialize, is also undermined by non-market practices and market denial.
The march of technology, that was meant to instill hope, has now become a source of anxiety.
Misuse of AI is sharpening bias, and diluting mutual respect.
These directions bode ill for the aims and objectives of the United Nations.
9. A persistent threat to peace, has been the scourge of terrorism.
That this could be state-sponsored, with cross-border purpose, makes it a direct affront to the global order.
Governments indulging in such practices must be held accountable.
There must be no dilution in our zero-tolerance approach towards terrorism.
Its financial aspects, in particular, should be exposed and should be countered.
10. Yesterday, a serial practitioner of terrorism, misrepresented facts before this Assembly.
Arguments were invoked to normalize terrorism, and claim immunity from its consequences.
Our right to defend ourselves against terrorism, will be exercised.
Mr. President, friendship and goodwill cannot co-exist with terrorism.
And understandings premised on that, will naturally be called into question.
It is for the perpetrator of terrorism to mend its ways.
11. Given the state of the world, each member of the UN must ask themselves what they can do.
Insofar as India is concerned, its inclusive growth and all-round progress, has advanced the prospects of one-sixth of humanity.
When health, nutrition and education are effectively delivered, when drinking water, electricity, roads and housing are ensured, this veritably lifts the global SDG outcomes.
But today, India has much more than that to offer.
Our digital public infrastructure, is not only ensuring better governance, but is the backbone of delivering socio-economic benefits.
Rapid growth of infrastructure, is visible across all its dimensions.
A continuously improving ease of doing business, ease of living, startup and innovation culture, and focused sectoral missions have all contributed to our economic story.
12. Even as India progresses, we are conscious of our global responsibilities.
We know that many of our experiences and achievements, are replicable elsewhere.
The deep solidarity of the Global South, has always encouraged us to share what we have.
Therefore, we respond more actively, to the requirements of our partners.
600 major Indian development projects in 78 nations, testify to our commitment, a commitment that ranges from infrastructure, manufacturing and agriculture, to IT and to capacity building.
13. Climate action projects and initiatives, have been an important part of these endeavors.
Whether it is clean energy and clean water projects, sustainable agriculture, or the dissemination of best practices and technology, our capabilities and experiences, have been reflected abroad.
African nations and Small Island Developing States, have been our preferred partners in this journey.
Initiatives like the International Solar Alliance, the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure, or the Global Biofuels Alliance are all making steady progress.
14. The turbulence of our times, also demands more from each of us.
India has sent medical shipments to conflict zones, epidemic locations, and after natural disasters.
As a first responder, we were there early, be it the Nepal flash floods or the Venezuela earthquake.
Our limb fitment camps, have given a new hope to many across the world.
Whether to meet food and medicine shortages, energy and fertilizer needs, or creating livelihoods, India has contributed continuously and will do so.
Our capacity-building and experience-sharing programs, have made a real difference across the Global South, especially in Africa.
15. The same international spirit, also inspires our contributions to safeguarding peace.
India has always been at the forefront, of UN peacekeeping operations.
Right now, our contingents are present in 9 out of 11 mandates.
Our troops have stood their ground firmly, and professionally, even under pressure.
We take pride, that an Indian woman combat helicopter pilot, was awarded the UN 2025 Military Gender Advocate of the year.
16. New challenges in the maritime domain, have added to longstanding ones on land.
There have been attacks on commercial shipping, and seafarers in the Gulf, and from the Red Sea to the Black Sea.
Indian seafarers have lost their lives, as indeed have others , from other nations.
India has joined Liberia, and 23 other partners, in an initiative to rally global public opinion, against such unwarranted targeting.
We must ensure, that the safety and security of shipping and seafarers, is never compromised.
Scrupulously observing international law, is an integral element of that endeavour.
17. An issue central to current global conversations, is that of AI.
India hosted the AI Impact Summit this February, gathering together the best minds on that subject.
We view AI as a transformational driver, for human empowerment, economic prosperity and population-scale problem solving.
We believe in the right of each nation, to shape its eco-system, with the development of its own models, and deployment strategies, consistent with its national goals and priorities.
AI will be very much part of our partnership agenda, with the Global South.
18. As technology is democratized, this process is greatly facilitated, Mr. President, by an ethos of mutual respect.
Indeed, care and consideration for the interests, and viewpoints of others, reinforces even the prospects of peace.
And that attitude is best fostered, by an appreciation of each other’s culture, heritage and traditions.
In a globalized world, we must continuously and vigorously, promote international understanding.
Economic rebalancing is well underway; the political one is also visible, and the third facet – cultural rebalancing – must now be taken forward.
19. We are now well on our way, towards a multi-polar world.
The post-1945 order is giving way to new realities.
This process of adjustment, accommodation and acceptance will not be easy.
Much of the turbulence that we witness today, emanates from those very difficulties.
Yet, the march of an intrinsically diverse world, towards a more democratic future, cannot be halted.
Peace in a pluralistic order, requires civil conversations, it requires broad-based consultations, it requires transparent decision-making.
Large sections of humanity, cannot be excluded from that process.
The case for reformed multilateralism only gets stronger day after day.
21. At the conclusion of this General Debate, we hope that all participating delegations, leave with a greater commitment to peace, to development and to prosperity.
This cannot be an imposition, or even a negotiation; it must be a mindset, it must be an outlook, it must be a belief.

In the lawns outside this building, are recorded the powerful words of Mahatma Gandhi, and that should serve as an inspiration for these times, and those words are that there is no way to peace; peace is the way.

Issued by the Government Press Office 24 September 2026 Embargoed until after delivery (approx. 01:00 (IST)), 25 September 2026 National Statement by Taoiseach Micheál Martin to the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly 24th September 2026 President of the General Assembly, Distinguished Heads of State and Government, Secretary-General, Excellencies, A chairde, friends, The United Nations is entering its ninth decade at a moment of great uncertainty and challenge for the global community.
Conflicts are having devastating effects on the most vulnerable.
The impacts of the climate crisis are felt in every corner of our world.
Hard won rights are being rolled back.
Narrow self-interest is breaking the bonds of solidarity which have so often lifted us to meaningful progress.
The international legal order is under tremendous strain.
New and emerging technologies that offer unlimited potential could also, without human intervention, create unprecedented dangers.
In such moments of uncertainty, it can be easy to question our foundations.
To say that international cooperation is too difficult, that multilateralism does not work, that the problems of others are not our problems.
But that would be the wrong conclusion.
Because the answer to a world under strain is not less international cooperation. It is more.
The answer to the weakening of principles is not to abandon them.
And if our multilateral system is not working effectively, the answer is not to walk away from it.
It is to make it stronger, fairer and fit for the world we live in.
And that is what all of us as members of the United Nations need to deliver on.
We should also remember what our collective commitment to the United Nations has achieved.
The multilateral system, anchored in the United Nations Charter, has been the foundation of many of humanity’s greatest achievements.
It has driven advances in poverty alleviation, healthcare, education, social protection, and food and nutrition security.
It has championed human rights and dignity and insisted that accountability matters.
It has given voice to the marginalised.
The people of Ireland understand that we live in an interdependent world; that the challenges we face are interconnected, cross borders, and require collective solutions.
Ireland currently holds the Presidency of the Council of the European Union.
Our stewardship of the EU’s agenda is deeply rooted in the principle of strength with unity.
And this principle is at the heart of our vision for the United Nations.
As well as our unwavering commitment to the pillars which guide its work: peace and security, human rights, and development.
These pillars equally bear the weight of our shared ambition for a better, fairer and peaceful world.
Collectively, however, we are not delivering on their ambition.
We are not staying the course.
At a time when global needs are increasing and becoming more complex, our responsibility to act does not diminish.
The denial of the fundamental human rights of millions of people around the world remains one of the defining challenges of our time.
Renewed pressure on women's rights and gender equality is putting hard-won progress at risk.
Women and girls are being told that their ambitions, their education, their voices and their very presence in public life are unacceptable.
The situation in Afghanistan is one of the clearest examples.
The systematic exclusion of women and girls from education, employment and public life is not something that the international community can simply observe from a distance.
It is a profound human rights crisis.
Girls are being denied the education that should shape their futures.
Women are being denied the ability to work, to participate fully in society and to contribute to the economic and social life of their country.
Their freedoms are being progressively erased.
And the world must not become inured to it.
We must not allow the absence of headlines to become an absence of action.
The women of Afghanistan have not disappeared.
Across the world, women and girls face conflict-related sexual violence, forced displacement, trafficking and discrimination.
Across the world, LGBTQI+ people face growing threats to their rights, safety and dignity.
Ireland remains firmly committed to the universality, indivisibility and equal application of human rights.
That commitment is why Ireland is seeking election to the Human Rights Council for the 2027–2029 term.
And if elected, we will use that seat to defend the principle that human rights belong to everyone everywhere.
Today, Russia’s illegal war in Ukraine is more deadly for civilians than at any point since the start of their full-scale invasion.
Russia’s reckless drone and missile attacks, on Ukrainian towns and cities, continue to intensify.
These are not the actions of a country interested in peace.
Russia could halt its brutal attacks at any time.
Yet it refuses to do so.
Russia’s actions have already had direct global impact, in increased food and energy costs.
This time last year, a bushel of wheat was just over five dollars; this year it is more than seven dollars.
The fact that a permanent member of the Security Council is seeking to change borders by force, in clear violation of the UN Charter, is utterly unacceptable.
Sovereignty and territorial integrity apply equally to all States.
The international community must remain steadfast in our response, in support of the UN Charter and of a comprehensive, just and lasting peace.
Ireland stands in solidarity with Ukraine and will continue to do so.
We will continue to support efforts to hold Russia accountable for its actions.
There can be no impunity for war crimes, not in Ukraine, not anywhere.
That is why Ireland is a steadfast supporter of the International Criminal Court.
Ireland strongly opposes efforts to undermine the Court.
All measures against it should be immediately withdrawn.
The international legal order, founded on our agreements to make the world a safer and more secure place is being challenged.
International law represents the collective lessons drawn from conflict, suffering and atrocity.
The rules and institutions that we have built over generations exist to protect the rights, security and sovereignty of all states and all peoples.
When these principles are disregarded, the consequences extend far beyond any single conflict.
Twenty years ago, the commission on war crimes and crimes against humanity in Darfur saw the international community come together to fulfil our collective responsibility to protect.
Despite the extraordinary efforts of the Sudanese people, the cycle of violence has continued.
