I stand before this international forum, representing, with every feeling of pride and honor, the Republic of Iraq, the cradle of writing and law, and the land of the earliest civilizations, and one of the founding States of the United Nations, to renew my country’s commitment to its Charter and its principles, and to present Iraq’s vision for its future, for its region, and for the world at this delicate stage.

Iraq has dealt with wars and their damage, perhaps more than any other, and with what was imposed upon us in the form of blockade and terrorism, and our people have paid a heavy price in the lives of its sons, its resources, and the opportunities for its development.
Despite those hardships, which over decades turned our country into an arena for wars and conflicts, today we speak with full confidence about our vision for the future.
Iraq aspires to exercise its impact and influence as an effective economic power in the region and as a bridge for dialogue and cooperation among its peoples.
Our vision at this stage proceeds from our national will to restore the prestige of the law, strengthen State institutions, and consolidate citizens’ confidence in them.

And we are moving forward so that the State will be the holder of the decision on peace and war, and so that arms and the instruments of force will remain in the hands of its constitutional institutions.
These are our governing priorities, and the national interest is the compass, until the law becomes the arbiter.

Our executive measures in this field are proceeding in the right direction, because they constitute the foundation for building the State of institutions, protecting sovereignty, consolidating stability, and creating the environment necessary for development and investment.
We are moving, in our relations with our strategic partners, from military cooperation to a new phase of economic and development cooperation, in a manner that serves our common interests.

And with the end of the mission of the international coalition in Iraq, we are determined to build our security and military capabilities, thereby adding to the Iraqis’ victory over الإرهاب a renewed momentum for completing the protection of our land, our people, and our sovereignty.

In order to ensure the sustainability of integration with our international friends, vigilance remains necessary, as does addressing the gaps and calling on all to control the borders continuously, in order to prevent the formation of an environment conducive to extremism.

Our Government is waging the battle against corruption and protecting public funds within the context of institutional reform, and we are proceeding along the path of fundamental and sustainable remedies in order to raise the efficiency of performance and improve services.

As much as we seek to build a strong State and a diversified, modern economy that keeps pace with global digital and technological transformations, we are also working to employ all successful expertise and innovative experiences in the worlds of economics, finance, and business for the renaissance of economic and financial reform in my country, and to provide a safe environment for national and foreign investment.

This vision is based on the great assets Iraq possesses in terms of resources and investment opportunities in energy, industry, agriculture, transport, and technology, in addition to its exceptional geographical location that links the Iraqi economy to the world.

In this context, our vision aims to move Iraq to a stage in which it will be an effective productive partner in the region, through gradually reducing the effects of the rentier economy, strengthening open-market policies, investing in infrastructure, and developing productive and export capacities and services.

From these starting points, we have drawn up the appropriate roadmap toward supporting the private sector and providing the legal, tax, and customs guarantees and facilities necessary for the growth of business and foreign trade, and building effective partnerships with the global market in order to accelerate the wheel of sustainable development.

In the field of global energy, Iraq’s impact stands out directly, as our Government is adopting an ambitious programme to increase crude oil production in proportion to the volume of our proven reserves, to expand refining capacities and the production of derivatives and petrochemical industries, and to develop gas fields.
Our ambition is for Iraq to become a global centre for energy production and to make use of its capabilities to enhance regional and international security and stability in a sustainable manner.
But at the same time, we view with concern the repercussions associated with what it has caused in terms of a crisis in freedom of navigation and maritime shipping, and rising global energy prices.

In order to contain the risks and repercussions for our peoples, we are working to diversify our oil export outlets and to develop energy lines and their corridors linking Iraq, Türkiye, Jordan, and the Syrian Arab Republic to global markets, with the aim of contributing to energy security and diversifying supply routes.
Excellencies, Economic diversification based on genuine partnerships is a strategic central objective in our economic policy.
Therefore, our Government has placed the objective of enhancing economic and industrial development in all fields at the top of its priorities.

From here comes the Development Road project, as Iraq’s vision for comprehensive integration, regional stability, and a strategic corridor for trade, investment, industry, and energy, to be an important gateway linking East and West, starting from the Grand Faw Port to Türkiye and from there to Europe.

We want this project to be available for partnership with all our neighbours and our friends, because we believe that economic interests create prosperity, and when the countries of the region are linked by ports, railways, energy lines, trade, and investments, they will have a greater interest in protecting stability.
From the rostrum of the United Nations, we say to the world: invest with Iraq.
It possesses the resources, the market, the location, and the will to build a new economy.
Our Government is working diligently to formulate partnerships that realize mutual interests, create job opportunities, transfer technology and knowledge, and develop Iraq’s productive capacities.
The security of States and the sustainability of peace are a shared responsibility, based on the Charter of the United Nations, not merely on interests.
And that true stability is not built through wars, but through shared interests that make cooperation more worthwhile than conflict.

Iraq’s vision is based on contributing to moving the region from conflict to integration, from competition to cooperation, and from the depletion of resources to their investment in development, and to consolidating mutual interests.
On this occasion, we extend our hands to all on the basis of respect for sovereignty, non-interference, good-neighbourliness, and adopting dialogue as a means of addressing differences.
Proceeding from these premises, Iraq renews its supportive position for dialogue and diplomacy in order to defuse crises.
and to facilitate the transit of trade across Iraqi territory, and to support efforts by providing major facilities for alternative trade corridors.

Iraq believes that responsibility towards peoples, their security and their stability requires working to end conflicts through negotiation, for the sake of a secure future and to prevent wars from breaking out again.
And there, at United Nations Headquarters, is a copy of the stele of the Babylonian king Hammurabi, in which it is stated: laws were laid down to prevent the strong from oppressing the weak.
Yet in today’s world, we find the weak being wronged because it is the law of the strong, not the force of law, that rules.
Therefore, the question of Palestine remains present in any discussion of stability in the region.

Here, we stress the utmost importance of facilitating the arrival of humanitarian assistance and protecting civilians.
The security that we seek is not confined merely to stopping conflicts, but extends to confronting climate change, its effects of desertification and water scarcity, and the impact on food security.

These are challenges that Iraq faces, and we affirm our adherence to our fair and legitimate water rights, and call for joint management of water resources in accordance with the principles of cooperation, law and international law.

And therefore, we continue to confront organized crime, and, in the context of the risks, to counter its dangers and thwart cross-border drug trafficking through cooperation with all friends, and we call for more exchange of information and international coordination to avert this danger that threatens societies.
Amid all these challenges, the Iraqi human being remains our goal and the ultimate purpose of our efforts.

Relying on the high proportion of youth in our society, we seek to make them a real pillar of the economy of the future, through education, supporting entrepreneurship, diversifying job opportunities, and enhancing the fields of the digital economy, while upholding our constitutional commitment to protecting human rights and freedoms, women’s participation, the care of children, and preserving the national, religious and cultural diversity of our country.

We confidently invite you to further openness towards Iraq, for it is the true partner capable of contributing to the consolidation of security, the enhancement of stability, and the acceleration of development in all fields.
From this rostrum, we say: Iraq has never been on the margins; rather, it is the heart of history and the pulse of the present, and it is worthy of partnership towards the future.

In conclusion, we reaffirm in this context our supportive position for the role of the United Nations through the joint work supporting Iraq embodied by the efforts of the UNAMI mission, and we value its efforts and wish it success in its pursuit of productive cooperation with the Organization and its efforts aimed at mitigating the effects of wars and the repercussions of conflict in the world.
The generation of 1945 had learned, at terrible cost, that while states can choose their actions, they cannot control all the consequences they set in motion.
That lesson is painfully relevant today.
We are living through a period of profound uncertainty. Power is shifting. Conflicts are multiplying.
And there is a growing tendency to treat the rules and institutions of the international system as constraints belonging to another age.
But the United Nations was built precisely for times of uncertainty: to bring rules and restraint to an unpredictable world, and to prevent conflict from descending into catastrophe.
The task of our generation is both to preserve the institutions built by those that came before us, and to also remember the hard-earned wisdom on which they rest.
Today, that wisdom – and the United Nations that embodies it – is under enormous pressure.
This year marks eighty years since Iceland joined the United Nations.
For eight decades, Iceland has held that a small state should enjoy the same protection, rights and voice as a powerful one.
That idea matters more today, not less.
Despite its shortcomings, the United Nations has mattered.
And it has mattered a lot.
UN peacekeeping and peacebuilding operations have helped prevent and contain conflict around the world.
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights transformed our understanding of human dignity.
The Convention on the Law of the Sea became the Constitution of the Ocean, on which countries like mine depend, now strengthened further by the BBNJ Agreement.
The International Court of Justice has helped states settle disputes by peaceful means, through law rather than force.
And the International Criminal Court was created to ensure accountability for the most serious crimes.
The United Nations has advanced gender equality, fought racism and discrimination, delivered humanitarian assistance and helped countries build more peaceful and prosperous societies.
But loyalty to the United Nations cannot mean pretending that everything works perfectly.
Bureaucracy can be cumbersome, decisions slow and resources fragmented.
The Security Council - entrusted with maintaining international peace and security - has too often been paralysed when action was needed most.
Too often, the veto has become a shield against action rather than a tool for preserving peace.
So yes, the United Nations needs reform.
And Iceland fully supports the UN80 reform process.
We need a United Nations that uses resources effectively and responds quickly when people need it.
United Nations that delivers for all.
The deeper challenge, however, is political.
The strength of the United Nations depends on our willingness to uphold the principles and wisdom on which they were founded.
The most basic rules of international relations are being tested.
Not because we no longer know them. We do.
But because increasingly, governments apply them selectively.
Meaning that international law applies - until it becomes inconvenient.
That court decisions must be respected - unless they challenge our own actions or those of our friends.
That sovereignty is sacred - unless someone else's territory stands in the way of our ambitions.
We cannot build courts, celebrate them when they prosecute our enemies, and undermine them when they turn their attention to our friends.
When grave violations go unanswered, they are more likely to be repeated.
And for small states this is existential, not simply a matter of principle.
Russia's brutal war against Ukraine is a clear example.
Russia invaded a sovereign neighbour, seeking to change borders by force and deny another nation the freedom to determine its future.
Ukrainians have paid an unimaginable price.
Behind every destroyed home is a family.
Behind every casualty is someone who was loved.
Ukraine has the right to defend itself, to sovereignty and territorial integrity, and to a just and lasting peace on the basis of international law.
Our support for Ukraine defends a principle on which all our countries’ security depends: That no nation gets to decide the future of another.

In Gaza, we continue to witness repeated violations of the ceasefire and continued suffering among civilians, despite the adoption of the twenty-point Comprehensive Peace Plan and Security Council Resolution 2803.
The suffering of Palestinian civilians cannot become background noise.
Families are still losing their homes.
Parents are still trying to keep their children alive. Again. And again. And again.
We cannot accept Gaza being repeatedly destroyed and rebuilt while the underlying cause remains unresolved.
In the West Bank, illegal settlement activity continues to expand.
Palestinian civilians face settler violence, too often enabled by impunity, inflammatory rhetoric and permissive policies.
Earlier this month, Iceland joined eleven other states in addressing restrictions on trade in goods from settlements that are illegal under international law.
Our objective remains clear: A viable Palestinian state alongside Israel, with both peoples able to live in security, dignity and peace.
We have heard the words “moral cowards” from this podium.
To me, moral cowards are those leaders around the world who refuse to sit down and negotiate a just and lasting peace.
Those who deny access to humanitarian aid for people in desperate need.
And moral cowards are those leaders who repeatedly go against and disrespect international law.
We must not allow the horrors in Ukraine and the Middle East to make other crises invisible.
In Sudan, years of civil war have brought atrocities, mass displacement and grave violations of international humanitarian law.
As humanitarian leaders have reminded us, Sudan does not suffer from a lack of analysis.
It suffers from a lack of action.
Acts that may constitute war crimes and crimes against humanity cannot be met with indifference.
We created the International Criminal Court to ensure accountability for the most serious crimes. Accountability matters.
So does adherence to international law beyond the battlefield.
To be clear: Iceland stands with the ICC.
Obstruction of lawful international transit through the Straits of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb threatens not only countries in the region but global energy markets and food security.
Disruption falls hardest on the most vulnerable.
The freedoms codified in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea are not optional.
For an island nation dependent on open maritime routes, freedom of navigation is fundamental.
Seventy-five years after the 1951 Refugee Convention, we should have hoped that the need for it would be diminishing.
Instead, humanitarian needs and forced displacement have reached staggering levels.
Conflict, poverty, drought, natural disasters and the growing effects of climate change are pushing millions of people from their homes.
And just as needs are increasing, funding is falling.
With development cooperation and humanitarian assistance we are investing in stability, resilience and peace.
Cutting ODA is shortsighted and risks making displacement and conflict worse.
The cost will eventually reach us all.
We must not allow today's crises to push the Sustainable Development Goals aside. Iceland will not.
We also must not forget how much progress has been driven by economic freedom.
Perhaps humanity‘s greatest gift is our capacity to create.
To imagine something that doesn‘t exist and then bring it into being.
Creativity is universal; what differs is whether societies give it room to flourish.
Open, free markets have given people the opportunity to create, exchange ideas, take risks and build better lives for themselves and for others.
Another battle is taking place over what kind of societies we want to be.
Across the world, authoritarianism and political extremism are gaining ground.
We see attacks on democratic institutions, independent media, science and facts in public debate.
Too often, these movements target groups whose rights supposedly matter less.
People who look different, love differently or live differently.
They are our daughters and sons. Our friends. Our neighbours. Our colleagues.
I am deeply concerned by the growing backlash against gender equality and LGBTQI+ rights - including within my own region, Europe.
We hear that equality has gone too far.
That diversity has gone too far.
That some people demanding the freedom simply to be themselves somehow threaten the freedom of others.
Human rights are not a zero-sum game.
Giving a woman equal rights does not take rights away from a man.
Allowing an LGBTQI+ person to live freely does not make anyone else less free. Quite the opposite.
We should be very careful when governments begin telling us that some people's existence threatens society.
History has taught us where that can lead.
And let me be clear: Iceland will not allow others to define our values or dictate the language we use to defend human rights.
Free societies are strongest when people are allowed to be themselves.
But freedom that belongs only to people who fit someone else’s definition of normal is not freedom.
A society that strips people of their dignity will eventually undermine its own democracy.
And nowhere is this backlash more extreme than in Afghanistan, where women and girls have been systematically erased from public life.
Girls are denied education, women are denied basic freedoms.

Statement by H.E. Antonio Tajani, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation UNGA81 General Debate – September 23rd 2026 Mr President, Last year, from this very podium, Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni recalled that 56 conflicts were raging across the world - the highest number since World War II.
Today, those same sources put that figure at 61.
It is the stark truth of the numbers.
Pope Leo XIV issued a warning that Italy has made its own: we must never grow accustomed to war.
Because first we become accustomed to the words, then to images, and finally to the victims.
When war becomes something we grow accustomed to – peace itself risks becoming a mirage.
Against the law of the strongest, we choose the strength of the law.
Against the politics of force, we choose the force of politics.
This is the message Italy brings to the United Nations.
This is the mission of Italian diplomacy: to build bridges, open new paths, and keep dialogue alive even when it seems impossible.
To work for peace, prosperity and growth - because growth creates prosperity, and prosperity, in turn, consolidates peace.
Ukraine, the Middle East, the Gulf, Sudan and the Sahel are not separate crises.
Nor are trade wars, AI competition, hybrid attacks and their economic and social repercussions.
Nor is terrorism in all of its many forms, which we continue to fight in every corner of the world.
These are all different fronts of a single, profound transformation: the world order that emerged after World War II is coming apart.
It did not prevent wars, injustice or suffering.
But today the world balance has been disrupted and history, which someone has declared that it has reached its final chapter, is once again moving at a galloping pace.
But every race needs a finish line.
Our task cannot be to stand and watch the fragmentation of our world, but it must be to build a new framework of rules, responsibility and cooperation capable of governing change.

Change that can happen only through political will, the through dialogue among nations, awareness of peoples and through the ability of multilateral institutions to rediscover a mission equal to the challenges of our time.
through The United Nations cannot simply record the divisions of today.
It must have the ambition to imagine the future.

It must recognize its limitations, overcome its paralysis and instruments, without its abandoning its deepest raison d’etre: to be the place reform where conflict gives way to dialogue, confrontation to diplomacy, and fear to the search for shared solutions.
The United Nations remains the most universal place for pursuing this aspiration.
Not because it’s perfect, but because no other institution can bring together, around the same table, such different interests, cultures, religions and visions of the world.
It is precisely when the world is divided that the value of dialogue grows rather than diminishes.
Italy believes in this institution, in its value and in its central role.
We believe in peace, which remains our guiding star—the guiding principle of Italy’s foreign policy.
It is rooted in our history, enshrined in our Constitution, and integral to our identity.
Dialogue, however, is not a sign of weakness, nor does it mean neutrality.
Italy knows where it stands: our home is Europe, our alliance is with the West, and our values are freedom, democracy and the dignity of every human being.
Yet belonging to the West does not mean retreating behind fortress walls.
It requires us to draw on the strength of our values to engage with others, build partnerships among equals, and mend the fabric of an international system that risks descending into chaos.
The European Union, the G7 and the West—of which we are proud to be part—must not be perceived as walls.
This is the purpose of IMEC, the economic and logistics corridor designed to connect Europe with the broader Indo-Mediterranean region.
The same principle guides our relationship with Africa, a strategic priority for Italy and a major partner for our century.
The Mattei Plan now involves 18 countries and is built on a simple idea: not to decide for Africa, but to decide with Africa.
It is not aid handed down from above, but a partnership among equals—in agriculture and energy, education and training, infrastructure and pharmaceuticals.
Producing vaccines in Africa saves lives, strengthens health systems, creates jobs and supports growth capable of generating stability.
It is in this spirit, and in defense of the right not to be forced to migrate, that we fight human traffickers who prey on poverty.
Agreements with countries of origin and transit help us combat irregular migration, while education, training and access to employment support safe and regular migration.
A world as complex as ours can be governed in only two ways: through shared rules, or through the law of the strongest.
Italy stands for rules, dialogue and diplomacy.
That is why we have condemned, and continue to condemn, Russia’s aggression against Ukraine.

We will continue to support Ukraine for as long as necessary, while working towards a just peace and towards a future in which Russia can once again be a partner in dialogue rather than a threat to Europe.
Russia, as a permanent member of the Security Council, cannot evade its responsibilities.
A ceasefire is not a concession to the other side; it is the first step towards a European security architecture that protects everyone, including Russia.
This is why we view with grave concern the growing hybrid threats posed by Russia against Europe, and why we have expressed our full solidarity with Germany following the attack on Leipzig Airport.
Peace requires openness, but it also requires resolve.
Dialogue without truth is weakness; resolve without dialogue leads to a dead end.
The same principle guides our approach to the Middle East.
Peace can come only through a two-State solution—two peoples, two States.
In Gaza, the truce has slowed the fighting, but it has not yet ended the suffering.
There is not a minute to lose.
The truce must be consolidated, humanitarian aid must be allowed to enter without obstruction, and the disarmament of Hamas must become a reality.
From the very beginning, Italy has mobilized the very best of its humanitarian capabilities.
Through Food for Gaza, we have delivered food and essential supplies provided by our farmers.
We have welcomed and cared for wounded and vulnerable children.
We have opened our universities and research centres to young Palestinians, because a future State also needs a future generation of leaders.
In Lebanon, the stakes extend far beyond the country itself and affect the entire region.
The Washington Agreement of 26 June opened a door.
Italy is proud to continue hosting negotiating sessions in Rome that have helped keep that door open. (Reuters⁠￼)
For decades, Italian troops have served the cause of peace in southern Lebanon through UNIFIL and have helped train the Lebanese Armed Forces.
We have also recently approved new development projects for the area, and we will continue to play our part even after the mission’s mandate comes to an end.
Dear colleagues, Sixty-one active conflicts mean that war is advancing even far from the television cameras.
And as war advances, the principles on which we have built eighty years of international relations retreat: the international prohibition of humanitarian law, and freedom and security of navigation.
Because where goods can move freely, weapons are less likely to do so.
The Strait of Hormuz must reopen.
Dialogue must be revived in the Gulf, and Iran must be called upon to renounce any nuclear threat and any aggressive policy towards other countries in the region.
Attacks on shipping in the Red Sea must cease, as must Russia’s reckless attacks in the Black Sea on shipments of Ukrainian grain destined for Africa.
These crises may seem distant, but their effects reach into every household.
They drive up the cost of energy, grain, bread and fertilizers.
They hurt businesses, agriculture and families.
Food security concerns us all and demands common solutions.
to address Food security and water security are part of the same struggle.
There can be no harvest without water.
There can be no stability without a harvest.
Where water disappears, hunger, conflict and migration advance.
Mr President, dear colleagues, The choice between force and politics is not confined to war.
It extends to the economy, resources and technology—to every sphere in which unrestrained power risks prevailing over the human person.
Politics must once again take the lead in shaping change.
We stand at the dawn of a technological revolution that is already reshaping the way we live, work, produce and make decisions: the artificial intelligence revolution.
The great inventions of the past took centuries to transform the world.
Artificial intelligence is doing so in a matter of years.
Those who control these technologies will enjoy an enormous advantage over those who are left behind.
The risk is that new inequalities, new dependencies and new concentrations of power—or even new forms of domination—will emerge.
Entire professions may disappear or be transformed.
Falsifying and manipulating reality will become easier.
systems operating without human Automated oversight may produce extremely dangerous decisions.

Pope Leo XIV, in the encyclical Magnifica Humanitas, reminded us that no algorithm can take the place of human conscience, and that any technology capable of striking without seeing the face of another person lowers the moral threshold for conflict.
But governing innovation does not mean demonizing it.
Artificial intelligence can open up possibilities that today are unimaginable—in medicine, research, environmental education, manufacturing protection.
Every major technological advance has generated fears, but it has also created opportunities and, over time, greater prosperity.
But neither can we hand over our future to technology without rules.
We do not need bureaucratic cages that only some would respect.
What we need is a balance between transparency, oversight, security and the protection of intellectual property.
We need to share the benefits of innovation and build mechanisms of mutual oversight.
This is precisely the task of the United Nations: to establish common rules before events—or the strongest actors—impose their own.
The United Nations was born in 1945 out of a world in ruins, a world that had learned a simple truth: when each of us stands alone, we all lose.
Eighty-one years later, that lesson is more relevant than ever.
The United Nations was created to prevent violence from becoming the only law.
But to remain faithful to that mission, it must regain its ability to make decisions and, above all, to act.

With this conviction, Italy will continue to advocate for a universal moratorium on the death penalty—a cause rooted in civilization, in the defence of life and human dignity, which we have championed for years here, in this very building.
We are also on the front line in defending individual freedom and women’s rights, and in fighting, among other things, the abhorrent practice of female genital mutilation.
We must have the courage to say it: too often, this Organization appears powerless.
For far too long, its reform has been held back by competing interests.
Italy wants a Security Council that is more legitimate, more representative and more accountable to all Member States.

Not an even more exclusive club, but one of the pillars of the far-reaching renewal of the United Nations that we hope the new Secretary-General will pursue— making this Organization capable of deciding and acting while there is still time to change the course of events.
Italy has always done its part, and it will continue to do so.
We are among the leading contributors to the United Nations budget and among the countries with the largest military presence in international missions.
We place our men and women, our resources and our expertise at the service of peace—in UNIFIL and in every mission in which we participate.
To all our men and women in uniform go the gratitude of the Government, our institutions and the Italian people.
It was a choice—the result of political action.
Amid the ruins, men and women decided to pool coal and steel rather than use them to build new guns.
From that choice emerged an unprecedented endeavor: a Union founded on common institutions, peace, freedom, democracy, prosperity, human rights and the rule of law.
This is the message Italy brings to New York today: peace is not an inheritance secured once and for all.
It is a responsibility we must shoulder every day.
It must be defended with resolve.
It must be built with patience.
And it must be pursued without ever giving up.
Because today, trust is in short supply.
Wars and conflicts are devastating communities and displacing millions.
Climate change is destroying lives, livelihoods and decades of development in a matter of hours.
New technologies, including artificial intelligence, offer extraordinary promise, while presenting risks we have not yet fully understood.
And at the very moment when collective action is most needed, confidence in multilateralism itself is being tested.
The shortcomings of multilateralism cannot be solved by abandoning multilateralism.
For small states like ours, a rules-based international order is not an abstract diplomatic preference.
It is fundamental to our sovereignty, our security and our development.
But neither can we safeguard multilateralism simply by defending it.
We must make it more representative, more accountable, more efficient — and more responsive to the needs and realities of the people it was created to serve.
That is why Jamaica has chosen not merely to call for reform, but to help lead it.
Our Permanent Representative was privileged to co-chair, with New Zealand, the UN80 Initiative’s Informal Ad Hoc Working Group on Mandate Implementation Review.
That work culminated in General Assembly Resolution 80/251 — an important framework for improving how UN mandates are created, implemented and reviewed.
Jamaica now continues that work alongside Norway.
Our objective is straightforward: a United Nations that spends less time sustaining process for its own sake, and more time fulfilling its purpose.
That is the multilateralism Jamaica believes in.
The selection of the next Secretary-General will be one of the most consequential decisions before Member States this year.
Jamaica proudly joins our CARICOM family in supporting the candidacy of Her Excellency Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of the Cooperative Republic of Guyana.
Her candidacy also speaks to something larger.
Small states have long served this international system as bridge-builders, consensus-makers and problem-solvers.
We learn very early that influence does not depend only on size or power.
It can also come from credibility, dialogue, principle and the capacity to bring people together.
These are the strengths which our multilateral system needs now, more than ever.
For Jamaica, the consequences of global challenges are not theoretical.
On 28 October last year, Hurricane Melissa struck our island.
In a matter of hours, the most catastrophic hurricane in our modern history inflicted damage and losses estimated at 56.7 per cent of our GDP.
More than half the value of an entire year of national economic output, damaged or lost through a single event.
Years of fiscal discipline had allowed us to build buffers.
We had put in place disaster-risk financing, including catastrophe insurance and an independently sponsored catastrophe bond.
Those measures gave us immediate liquidity.
But no level of prudent national planning can fully insulate a small developing state from a climate event of that magnitude.
And therein lies the fundamental inequity faced by Small Island Developing States.
In fact, Jamaica’s reforms balanced economic orthodoxy with innovation and expansion of support for the most vulnerable.
And yet one hurricane can still erase decades of progress.
We are deeply grateful to our international partners, our CARICOM family, our Jamaican diaspora and the thousands of individuals and organisations which stood with us in our hour of need.
But Jamaica has not simply resolved to recover.
We have resolved to rebuild better and differently.
Our resilience must not be measured by how much suffering we can withstand.
It must be measured by how well we prepare, how quickly we recover, how intelligently we adapt
That is why the Government of Prime Minister Andrew Holness established the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority — NaRRA.
Its mandate is to drive reconstruction at speed and at scale; to coordinate major infrastructure projects; crowd in investment; and critically, to embed resilience into the Jamaica we are rebuilding.
We are not simply replacing what Melissa destroyed.
We are building the Jamaica that must withstand the storms of tomorrow.
We have also submitted our updated Nationally Determined Contribution, completed our Long-Term Strategy for a low- carbon, climate-resilient future, and advanced our National Adaptation Plan.
But national ambition must be matched by international action.
Climate finance must become more accessible, affordable and predictable.
And the international financial architecture must finally recognise what SIDS have long said: income alone does not and cannot measure vulnerability.
A country does not become less vulnerable to hurricanes and other natural disasters because its per-capita income crosses an arbitrary threshold.
We therefore continue to advocate for the use of measures that go beyond GDP, including multidimensional vulnerability indices, in determining access to concessional and development finance.
Jamaica brings this message to the international community from a position not only of vulnerability, but one of responsibility.
Over the past decade, we have undertaken difficult reforms and made difficult choices.
Our debt, which once stood at more than 140 per cent of GDP, was brought down to 62 per cent before Melissa, with unemployment then at a historic low of 3.4%.
We built macroeconomic stability, strengthened investor confidence and created the fiscal space that ultimately helped us respond to the greatest natural disaster in our modern history.
We are proud and heartened that notwithstanding Melissa, Jamaica’s credit ratings have either been stabilized or upgraded and unemployment still stands at a low of 3.7%.
Those gains did not happen by accident.
They required discipline. Partnership. Sacrifice. Consistency.
Our experience has taught us that the strongest response to a crisis begins long before the crisis arrives — in the choices we make, the institutions we build, and the buffers we create.
Jamaica will continue to take responsibility for the things within our control.
But domestic responsibility must be matched by international solidarity and cooperation.

Developing countries cannot reasonably be expected to simultaneously finance climate adaptation, modernise infrastructure, strengthen social protection, manage debt, absorb external shocks and achieve the Sustainable Development Goals without an international financial system responsive to their realities.
We do not ask to be relieved of responsibility.
We ask for an international system that gives responsible countries the space to succeed.
That opportunity increasingly depends on technology.
Jamaica sees digital transformation and responsible artificial intelligence as powerful tools.
They can enhance productivity, innovation and sustainable development for our people.
Indeed, they can be an equalizing force for the world.
We must therefore not allow AI to deepen old inequalities and create an entirely new global divide.
Developing countries require investment in infrastructure, skills and capacity.

And all countries require governance frameworks that safeguard privacy and intellectual property, ensure data integrity and promote the ethical and responsible use of emerging technologies, without stifling innovation.
The Pact for the Future, the Global Digital Compact and the ABAS provide important foundations.
Our task now as a global community, is to translate commitments into action.
Development also requires peace and security.
For Jamaica and our Caribbean region, transnational organised crime remains a serious threat.

Last year, from this podium, Prime Minister Andrew Holness called for a Global War on Gangs — a coordinated international effort capable of matching the reach, financing and sophistication of transnational criminal networks.
Illicit firearms do not manufacture themselves in our communities. They cross borders.
Criminal networks exploit technology and operate across borders.
Our response must therefore also cross borders.
We call for stronger cooperation in firearms tracing and interdiction, intelligence and information-sharing, financial investigations and law-enforcement capacity-building.
We also urge major arms-exporting states to strengthen export controls and post-delivery verification.
At home, Jamaica has invested heavily in our security forces, strengthened legislation, enhanced intelligence gathering, oversight and transformed policing.
The results are remarkable by any standard.
In 2025, Jamaica recorded its lowest number of homicides in more than three decades.
And in 2026, the Global Peace Index ranked Jamaica the most peaceful country in the Caribbean.
We recognise that there remains work to be done.
Our objective is not merely fewer crimes.
It is a durable ecosystem of peace in which every Jamaican can feel safe, raise a family, do business and fulfil his or her potential and retire in paradise.
Nowhere in our region is the challenge of criminal gangs more devastating than in our sister nation of Haiti.
Jamaica stands firmly with the Haitian people.
We urge sustained international support for the Gang Suppression Force and for the Haitian National Police and armed forces.
This support must include the financial, logistical and operational resources necessary to restore security.
We further call for the Security Council to renew the mandate of the GSF at this imperfect but particularly critical juncture.
We can lose gains, or we can build on progress made.
The international community must send an unequivocal message: armed gangs cannot be allowed to determine Haiti’s future nor that of the region.
Security must create the space for sustained humanitarian relief, developmental and economic progress.
But even more foundationally, security must create the space for political stability, democratic governance and credible elections, led and owned by the Haitian people.
Jamaica remains deeply concerned by the terrible human suffering caused by armed conflicts across the world.
Wherever conflict occurs, our principles must remain consistent.
International humanitarian law must be respected.
International law and the Charter of the United Nations must be upheld.
And diplomacy must remain our first and most persistent instrument for resolving disputes.
Respect for international law — including due regard for the decisions of the International Court of Justice — is indispensable to the peaceful international order on which small states depend.
Similarly, with respect to our neighbour Cuba, Jamaica continues to believe in dialogue and constructive engagement.

We encourage domestic reform and greater integration of Cuba into the international economic system, supported by policies that create pathways for progress and eliminating the dire humanitarian crisis, rather than perpetuating isolation under the blockade.
The suffering of the Cuban people is of deep concern.
Jamaica believes that reparatory justice is, at its heart, about truth, acknowledgement, justice, repair, compensation, development and reconciliation.
Jamaica not only supported the resolution put forward by Ghana on March 25th of this year, we also delivered to Buckingham Palace, a petition framing critical questions on the matter of reparations.
The petition has now been referred to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.
Sixty-four years after Jamaica proudly raised our black, green and gold flag as a politically independent nation, we remain clear-eyed about the world around us.
But we also believe deeply in its possibilities.
The United Nations must change if it is to remain credible.
Jamaica supports the revitalisation of this General Assembly, meaningful reform of the Security Council, and greater coherence, efficiency and accountability across the United Nations system.
Reform is not an act of disloyalty to this institution.
Reform is how we preserve it.
Ultimately however, Mr. President, multilateralism must mean something beyond these walls.

For a small state like Jamaica, its value is felt when our people are safer; when opportunity is expanded; when vulnerability does not become a barrier to development; when countries that have acted responsibly are not penalised for shocks they did not create; and when the voice of a small nation carries the same dignity as that of a large one.
That is why Jamaica remains committed to this institution — not because it is perfect, but because we are grateful for what is has achieved, and we believe in what it can become.
Small states can help lead that effort.

Our own journey has taught us that vulnerability need not mean helplessness; that discipline creates resilience; that partnership multiplies possibility; and that even in moments of profound crisis, nations can choose to build forward.
So let us restore trust through what we do.
Let us manage transformation with purpose.
Let us bring the same seriousness to preventing crises that we bring to responding to them.
And let us never lose sight of the simple idea on which this institution was founded: that nations working together, can achieve what none of us can achieve alone.
That is the United Nations Jamaica believes in.
And that is the United Nations we will continue working to reform and renew.
Perhaps for us that is true.
We are at a unique moment in history.
The scale of knowledge and the speed of change are unprecedented.
Every day brings another crisis, another tragedy, another emergency demanding our attention.
One study shows that average screen attention has fallen from 2.5 minutes in 2004 to just 47 seconds today.
Of course, a screen is not the world, but that says something about our world today that attention has become a scarce asset, and where we choose to direct it has never mattered more.
And in this chamber, attention is more than a cognitive resource.
It determines which conflicts receive sustained diplomacy and which fade from the agenda.

Whether a cease fire holds after the cameras leave, whether humanitarian suffering remains intolerable or becomes familiar and whether the world steps up or scrolls and strolls away, history rarely catches us entirely by surprise.
More often, it catches us focused elsewhere.
Economic disparity, food insecurity, climate change disasters none of these challenged emerged overnight.
The warning signs have been there.
The question is whether our attention lasts long enough to act, and what we neglect has a habit of shaping our future.
Your excellencies, we see the cost of that neglect every day in my region, from Lebanon to Yemen to Sudan, protracted conflict is deepening humanitarian suffering.
And if anyone had any doubt that a crisis in our part of the world stays there, just look at the energy and grocery bills of ordinary families, from Mumbai to Madrid to Minnesota.
The Iran war has shown how quickly instability can disrupt trade, investment and lives beyond the region.
For decades, I've stood before this assembly and warned of the dangers of leaving the Palestinian-Israeli conflict unresolved.
But the international community chose to manage the conflict, not confront it.
And every new Israeli violation was treated as temporary, diverting attention from the reality being created on the ground until temporary became permanent and permanent became policy.

Of course, this is not the world's only injustice, but one of the world's longest running occupations forces a basic question if international law can be ignored for decades, then what exactly is that law worth and how can we enforce it if we won't even call out its violations? In Gaza?
The evidence is overwhelming, and the first 300 days of the so-called cease fire, at least 300 Palestinian children were killed.
Jordan's field hospitals have also been targeted.
President Trump has pushed hard for peace and a path to end this war.
But this Israeli government keeps moving the goalposts, continuing its attacks and destruction of civilian infrastructure, refusing to withdraw and squeezing Palestinians into barely a third of Gaza.
This can no longer be dismissed as temporary military measures or a consequence of war.
Accountability begins when we call things for what they are, an attempt to erase Palestinian life and impose a new territorial reality in Gaza.
And while the world has been focused on Gaza, something extraordinarily dangerous is unfolding in the West Bank.
Some may think we have seen this before settlements, violence, displacement, more of the same, but it is not.
Nor is it simply an escalation.
What was once a creeping process has exploded into something far more aggressive.

Palestinians are being beaten, shot and terrorized, homes torched, property destroyed, families driven from their land and Israel is tightening its grip on more of the West Bank, seizing land, expanding settlements and pushing the Palestinians out.
It is time to see what is happening for what it really is, because when the language is sanitized, the actions become normalized.
Demolishing Palestinian homes to expand illegal settlements is not law enforcement.
Appropriating occupied land is not land registration.
It is de facto annexation, a choking network of checkpoints and barriers is not security infrastructure.
It is a system of subjugation.
Systematic attacks on Palestinian communities are not settler unrest.
The Israeli government criticizes the violence before the international audiences.
They call those responsible a handful of rioters.
They assure us that Israel is a country governed by law.
Yet what's happening on the ground says otherwise.
Israeli soldiers stand by as settlers attacked Palestinians, often protecting the attackers or joining them.
They have blocked ambulances from reaching the injured.
They have targeted international journalists who are trying to say the truth.
And when soldiers watch, enable and sometimes even participate in violence against civilians, this is no longer about a handful of rioters.
And the question is no longer whether a few extremists are breaking the law.
The question is, is this the behavior of a democratic state governed by law?
What is unfolding across the West Bank is not a series of isolated acts.
It is elements of a single policy to compel an entire population to leave their land.
And there is a name for that forced displacement, and that is a war crime.
Your excellencies, if we are to resolve the Palestinian Israeli conflict, the world must abandon some illusions.
The first is that Gaza and the West Bank are separate stories. They are not.
There are two fronts of the same Israeli strategy in both.
Palestinians are being killed in both.
The reality on the ground is being remade as death through destruction.
The West Bank through de facto annexation.
The objective is the same to make a viable Palestinian state impossible.
Another illusion is that this Israeli leadership's rejection of Palestinian statehood is a position that might yet change. It is not.
It is cemented on the ground.
This government has been accelerating settlements and land seizures, but it began long before.
Since Oslo, the map has changed piece by piece, settlement by settlement, and the most dangerous illusion that the Arab world never sought peace.
The Arab Peace Initiative of 2002 offered Israel normalization with 57 Arab and Muslim states, including Iran and Iraq at the time, in exchange for peace and Palestinian statehood.
For over 20 years, that offer has stood.
The obstacle hasn't been the absence of a partner for peace, but the absence of an Israeli government willing to accept it. This Israeli government.
This Israeli government, understands the power of attention, and lately it has not liked the attention it's been getting when confronted with evidence of wrongdoing.
Rather than change the course, it opts for distraction, discrediting its critics.
It is also tried to cast this conflict as a war of religions Islam on one side, Judaism and Christianity on the other. It is not.
This is about whether Palestinians, Muslims and Christians are entitled to the same rights as everyone else.
People across the world are paying attention.
The question now is, will we act because the world's political inaction is not for lack of options.
So let's call it for what it is a choice.
We have tools, sanctions, asset freezes, embargoes, diplomatic isolation, and we have a record of using them elsewhere.
Yet with Israel, resolutions end where they began on paper.
This result is a state without restraint.
This government's sense of impunity has reached terrifying levels.
It no longer feels compelled to ask, can we get away with this?
It already knows the answer, and that is precisely why no one in this assembly should assume its ambitions stop at Palestine.
This Israeli government's expansionist appetite is now a regional threat.
And today Syria is the warning.

The international community is choosing not to see repeated incursions, creeping territorial expansion, new facts imposed on the ground, including around vital water resources, step by calculated step, Israel is testing how far it can go, and every time the international community looks away, Israel learns that it can go even further across borderlines and legal limits.
For Jordan, there is no ambiguity, any threat to our northern border or our water security is a threat to our national security.

We will protect our security, our water and the interests of our people And the question here is, if Israel continues its antagonistic approach in southern Syria, will the international community stand by and let that happen?
Your excellencies, some things demand our immediate attention, others demand sustained attention. Injustice demands both.
Jordan understands this all too well.

We know what it means to live in a region where one crisis arrives before the last one has receded, and we know that we cannot choose between responding to the emergency before us and building the future beyond it.
We are strengthening connections from the Gulf to the Mediterranean as a hub for trade, industry and technology while responding to humanitarian crises.
We are confronting terrorism in the region and beyond, while developing our own defenses and remaining a frontline against threats like narcotics.
We are protecting Christianity in its communities and heritage, in its native and historic land, while promoting the true image of Islam against the voices of hate.
And through it all, we will not abandon our commitment to a just peace.

We will continue to support Palestinian resilience, we will continue supporting Rawa, and we will continue to uphold the Hashemite custodianship and historic and legal status quo at Muslim and Christian holy sites in Jerusalem.
Most importantly, Jordan is striving to build a different model principled, open and steady at a time when certainty is rare and politics can shift by the day.
A country the world can count on, true to our principles, true to our word, ready to talk to everyone and ready to work with anyone seeking peace.
However, our bias towards diplomacy will never supersede our commitment to human values and should not be taken for granted or mistaken for weakness.
My friends within Russia, Sudan Ukraine, or anywhere people live with war, displacement and fear.
Whether crisis began weeks ago or has endured for decades, our principles cannot change with the world's attention.
Military force cannot deliver meaningful solutions.

It cannot feed the hungry, return the displaced, or build peace, nor can it repair our planet, manage mass migration, or guide technological progress that requires institutions that command legitimacy.
Trust between nations, trust in agreements, trust that rules will actually be enforced.
Destroy that trust and every challenge becomes harder.
Preserve it, and cooperation becomes possible.
And in a world competing for our attention, we must be deliberate about where we direct it and vigilant about what seeks to distract it.
The future is shaped not only by what we do, but what we choose to ignore. Thank you. UN.
1. Introduction Mr. President, Excellencies, The international order is experiencing a period of great instability.
The free and open international order based on the rule of law that we have fostered is facing difficult challenges on multiple fronts.
Amid a shifting balance of power and intensifying geopolitical competition, innocent civilian lives are being lost around the world every day.
The “stable post-Cold War era” is now a thing of the past.

The distribution of goods is stagnating, people across the world are suffering from high cost of living, progress towards development goals is not on track, and human rights issues are arising in various places around the world.
Against this backdrop, has the United Nations, now eighty years on since its foundation, been failing to fulfill its role in promoting peace and stability around the world?
We are even hearing such concerns today.

Despite these concerns, the United Nations has never been more important than it is today in bringing about peace and stability to the world, and enabling the international community to overcome new challenges and prosper.
Japan will continue to fulfill its significant responsibilities towards the United Nations.
And I am here today to express that resolve.
This year marks the 70th anniversary of Japan’s accession to the United Nations.
In this milestone year, I would first like to address how Japan has been tackling the challenges facing the international community, working hand-in-hand with the United Nations.
Then, together with you all, I would like to take this opportunity to revisit the role of the United Nations in the international community.
2. Challenges facing the International Community in light of Escalating International Tensions First, let us turn our attention to escalating international tensions.
The situation in the Middle East has been growing increasingly tense, and free and safe navigation is increasingly under challenge in the Strait of Hormuz, which is an international public good.
Japan, in cooperation with the international community, has been continuing to engage in diplomatic efforts with a view to achieving an early de-escalation of the situation across the Middle East.
Furthermore, supply concerns regarding fuel, chemical products, and medical supplies, are causing significant impact on people’s lives and business operations.
Due to disruptions in the supply of fertilizers, the risk of a food crisis is mounting, with Africa and Asia being hit particularly hard.
For many years, we have engaged in dynamic trade in the free and open seas spanning the Pacific Ocean to the Indian Ocean, and together, we have built a strong and prosperous region.
This holds true also in the Atlantic Ocean and Mediterranean Sea.
We wish to extend this to Africa as well, to turn it into a main artery for growth and prosperity.

To that end, exactly ten years ago, former Prime Minister ABE Shinzo advocated a “Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP)” at the Tokyo International Conference on African Development (TICAD) held in Kenya.
However, due to the recent intensification of geopolitical tensions, free trade has been hampered, and stable energy supplies, and supply chains in general, have been disrupted.
Amid this situation, in May this year, I announced the ”Updated Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP)”.
There I appealed that it is essential for countries to acquire the capabilities to freely determine their own futures and resilience across economic, social, and security domains.
Japan places particular emphasis on the following three pillars that embody this idea.
First, Japan is engaged in strengthening the resilience of supply chains for energy and critical materials.

For global energy security, it is crucial to ensure free and transparent energy trade, engage in international coordination on strengthening oil stockpiling, and enhance collaboration between producing and consuming countries.

Japan has also launched the “Partnership On Wide Energy and Resources Resilience Asia (POWERR Asia)” to strengthen energy and resource supply resilience in Asia, and has been promoting cooperation in areas such as stockpiling capacity development and credit provision.
Furthermore, Japan is currently formulating a comprehensive cooperation plan aimed at strengthening the economic and energy resilience of the Gulf countries in the Middle East.
Through this initiative, we will work to further strengthen the collaboration between the Asia-Pacific region, including Japan, and the Gulf countries to ensure a stable global energy supply.
Moreover, concerns about arbitrary export restrictions are growing throughout the international community.
Under this initiative, we are cooperating with countries that produce critical minerals to enable them to play a greater role in mining, refining, and processing.
In June, we established “RISE+” under the World Bank Group and pledged a contribution of 20 million US dollars to help develop the infrastructure essential for critical minerals production.
Second, Japan is devoted to enhancing cooperation towards peace and stability.
Since the end of the Second World War, Japan has consistently and seriously pursued efforts towards nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation.
At the very heart of our aspiration for “a world without nuclear weapons” lies the earnest plea of the hibakusha: the catastrophic consequences of nuclear weapons must never be repeated.
It is Japan’s mission, as the only country to have ever suffered atomic bombings during war, to lead the efforts of the international community towards a “world without nuclear weapons”.

Japan strongly calls for solidarity within the international community to maintain and strengthen the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) regime, to which both nuclear-weapon states and non-nuclear-weapon states are parties.

Furthermore, Japan will persistently advance realistic and practical efforts, including enhancing the transparency of nuclear forces, and promoting a deeper understanding of the realities of atomic bombings.
The situations in Ukraine and North Korea have reminded the world of growing risks and threats posed by nuclear weapons.
There are also concerns regarding the proliferation of nuclear- and missile-related technologies the strengthening of military cooperation between Russia and North Korea.
The security of the Indo-Pacific and the Euro-Atlantic is inseparable.

through The advancement of North Korea’s nuclear and missile programs, as well as its use of malicious cyber activities, including cryptocurrency thefts as a source of funding, are clear violations of relevant Security Council resolutions and pose a serious threat to international peace and security.
The full implementation of Security Council resolutions, under the principle of the complete denuclearization of North Korea, is essential.
Moreover, the issue of abductions by North Korea is an ongoing matter with lives at stake.
The abductees are still denied their freedoms, and their families continue to suffer.
This is a matter of grave concern not only for Japan, but for the international community.
As the abductees and their families are aging, the abductions issue must be resolved immediately.

For the sake of the future of both Japan and North Korea, I am prepared to engage in dialogue and take concrete action to establish a mutually fruitful relationship in accordance with the Japan–DPRK Pyongyang Declaration.
Third, Japan will continue to contribute to the maintenance and development of a free and open international order based on the rule of law.

Any attempts to unilaterally change the status quo by force or coercion are contrary to the principles enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations and must never be tolerated anywhere in the world.
Russia’s aggression against Ukraine is the most obvious example.

A permanent member of the Security Council, with a special responsibility for international peace and security, has initiated an act of aggression against another country, and has vetoed Security Council resolutions concerning its own actions.
In this current situation, it must be said that the Security Council is not functioning for international peace.
Since the end of the Second World War, Japan, as a peace-loving nation, has attached great importance to the rule of law in the settlement of any disputes.

This is demonstrated by Japan’s consistent support for, and its contributions of judges to, various international judicial organs, such as the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the International Criminal Court (ICC) and the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS).
We established a unit for peace mediation within the Government of Japan in March of this year.
Japan will play a more proactive role in the peaceful settlement of disputes.
Furthermore, the maritime order based on the rule of law is currently being greatly shaken in the Strait of Hormuz.

Ensuring free and safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz for all vessels without additional costs, as has been the case, is extremely important not only for the security of the Middle East, but also for the stability of the global economy as a whole.
Similarly, it is essential to ensure stability in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Japan will continue to work closely with relevant countries and the International Maritime Organization (IMO) towards the maintenance of the maritime order in the Middle East.
3. Japan’s Commitment to the United Nations and Multilateralism Next, I would like to set out Japan’s efforts and commitments towards the United Nations and multilateralism.

Since becoming a Member State of the United Nations in 1956, Japan has acted decisively to address global challenges, such as the eradication of poverty, economic and social development, women’s empowerment, climate change, and global health.
We have done so through our Official Development Assistance (ODA), channeled international organizations, and have bilaterally or through deepened our solidarity with the Global South.
To date, Japan has provided ODA totaling over 670 billion US dollars to developing countries and regions, and has dispatched almost 60,000 Japan Overseas Cooperation Volunteers to 99 countries.
Additionally, Japan has been promoting initiatives towards achieving universal health coverage (UHC) across the globe.
Since 1993, Japan has co-organized the TICAD together with the United Nations.
TICAD has served as a platform for reflecting Africa’s voice in the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and for Japan to first put forward the concept of FOIP.
Africa is endowed with a dynamic young population and possesses enormous economic potential.
Japan will continue to promote its diplomacy towards Africa so that Japan and Africa can become more resilient and prosperous together.
For example, we will promote industrial development, job creation, and enhanced connectivity in Africa.
Furthermore, next year, I will host the Pacific Islands Leaders Meeting (PALM) in Yokohama, Japan, which Japan has convened together with the Pacific Islands region since 1997.

Japan aims to further deepen our collaboration with the Pacific Island Countries region and promote the stability and prosperity of the region, including addressing common challenges such as maritime security and climate change.
Several large-scale disasters have occurred and continuously caused extreme damage around the world this year, including in Japan.
Natural disasters are becoming more severe and frequent.
Japan is striving to become the world’s leading nation in disaster risk reduction.

To share Japan’s expertise and technology in disaster risk reduction and contribute to global efforts in this field, I appointed a new Minister of State for International Disaster Risk Reduction Cooperation in my Cabinet reshuffle last week.

I myself, in 2015, as Minister for Internal Affairs and Communications, attended the United Nations World Conference on Disaster Reduction, where the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction was adopted.
Promoting this framework remains one of our top priorities to this day.
It is in Sendai that Japan will host the Asia-Pacific Ministerial Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction in October next year.
To protect the lives of present and future generations, all States must take serious action to tackle global warming.
I believe that climate action and economic growth can go hand-in-hand.
Japan has been advancing Green Transformation (GX) efforts with the goal of achieving net-zero by 2050 by harnessing Japan’s technological capabilities.

Such capabilities include establishing the basis for the production and engineering of materials such as green steel, utilizing the world’s most efficient gas-fired power generation, and popularizing the adoption of energy-efficient data centers.

We will enhance these efforts with a view to strengthening the resilience of the energy supply-demand structure and vigorously advance the Policy Package for Wide Energy and Resources Resilience (POWERR GX).

Furthermore, Japan will contribute to global climate action, including through GX-related efforts, such as the Asia Zero Emission Community (AZEC) that simultaneously achieve decarbonization, energy security and economic growth.

1. Eighty-one years ago, the nations gathered in San Francisco spoke from the ruins of war.
They resolved to save succeeding generations from its scourge.
They reaffirmed faith in human dignity and in the equal rights of nations, large and small.
And they pledged social progress, better standards of life and the economic and social advancement of all peoples.
They were the foundations of a new global order: peace over war, law over force, sovereign equality over dependency, cooperation over division, and human dignity over the ambitions of power.
3. On 16 December 1963, four days after our independence, Kenya took its seat in this Assembly.
We arrived with one vote and the same sovereign rights as every other State.
The promise made in San Francisco now belonged to us as well.
4. And that promise changed the world.
When the United Nations was founded, some 750 million people lived under colonial rule.
At San Francisco, only four African countries were represented while most of our continent remained under colonial rule.
Decolonisation transformed the map of the world, self-replacing determination as peoples once governed from afar took their place in this Assembly as sovereign equals.
5. The United Nations also made a difference where peace had been broken.
It helped Namibia achieve independence, supported Cambodia’s transition from conflict, disarmed combatants in Sierra Leone and Liberia, and helped Timor-Leste take its place among sovereign nations.
More two million peacekeepers have served under the UN flag, proving that peace can be built, protected and sustained.
6. Its impact reached further into the lives of ordinary people.

The United Nations system helped eradicate smallpox, vaccinate generations of children, fight hunger and disease, expand access to education and bring clean water and humanitarian assistance to communities across the world.
Since the year 2000, deaths among children under five have fallen by more than half.
They changed borders, ended wars, defeated disease and transformed lives.
They tell us that multilateralism works when nations summon the will to make it work.
The United Nations has not fulfilled every promise of its Charter.
But without it, our world would have been poorer, more dangerous and less free.
8. That is why Kenya speaks today not from despair in this institution, but from conviction in its possibilities.
Yet conviction in what this institution can be requires us to confront what it has become.
9. Last year, the world recorded 65 state-based armed conflicts; the highest number documented in eight decades of global conflict data.
Thirteen reached the scale of war.
Nearly a quarter of a million people were killed in organised violence.
Interstate conflicts doubled for the second consecutive year; in just two years, their number quadrupled from two to eight.
One-sided violence against civilians reached levels not witnessed since 1994, the year of the genocide in Rwanda.
From Europe to the Middle East, from the Sahel to the Horn of Africa, civilians are paying the price. Cities are destroyed. Families are displaced. Hunger deepens.
Supply chains are disrupted, driving up the cost of food, fuel and essential goods far beyond the battlefield.
Children inherit wars they did not begin and cannot understand.
Too many disputes are no longer being settled; they are being frozen, deferred or decided by force.
This is precisely what the Charter was created to prevent.
It did not ask the United Nations merely to describe war, count its victims and organise relief after diplomacy had failed.
It gave this Organisation a duty to prevent conflict, defend peace and make collective security real.
It also charged it to advance the economic and social wellbeing of all peoples.
Peace and prosperity were never two mandates.
Today, both sides of that promise are under strain.
The crisis of multilateralism is not a shortage of commitments, institutions or rules.
It is the widening distance between the equality this system proclaims and the inequality that is inherent in its structures.
That is precisely why we cannot accept its present limitations.
13. On peace and security, the contradiction is increasingly difficult to ignore.
Every nation in this hall has one vote.
Every nation is sovereign and equal under the Charter.
Yet on the gravest questions of war and peace, five nations possess a permanent power that the other 188 do not.
The equality proclaimed in this Assembly ends at the doors of the Security Council.
That imbalance might have reflected the world of 1945.
It does not reflect the world of today.
Africa has 54 Member States, more than a quarter of this Assembly, yet no permanent voice in the body for the primary entrusted with international peace and security.
We are frequently the subject of its decisions, permanently discussed but permanently excluded.
The problem is not that the world lacks law.
It is that confidence in its consistent application is weakening.
International law cannot be invoked loudly in one crisis, cautiously in another and disregarded when convenient.
Every perceived double standard carries a price, and that price is trust.
Trust cannot be restored by declaration.
It must be earned by consistency.
But the cost of failure is measured in more than lost trust.
It is measured in children driven from their classrooms, children who go to sleep hungry, children who learn the sound of gunfire before they know the safety of peace.
When collective security breaks down, schools close, hospitals collapse, families flee and economies are consumed by war.
Peace is not separate from development.
When the institutions entrusted with peace fail, it is too often the youngest who inherit the consequences.
Africa exposes this contradiction most clearly.
In 1945, most of our continent could not speak for itself at San Francisco because it remained under colonial rule.
Only four African States were represented.
The architecture of collective security was therefore designed at a moment when most Africans had neither a nation at the table nor a voice in shaping the institutions that would govern the peace.
We cannot manage transformation with institutions that refuse to transform themselves.
The test of equality does not end with the institutions that govern peace.
It extends to the institutions that shape prosperity.
The same question confronts us there: does the international system give every nation a fair opportunity to secure the wellbeing of its people?
The Charter did not conceive development as charity.
It pledged social progress, better standards of life and economic and social advancement for all peoples.
Yet for too many countries, the resources required to fulfil that promise are being consumed before they can reach their people.
Global public debt reached a record 102 trillion dollars in 2024.
Developing countries accounted for less than a third of that debt, yet paid about a trillion dollars in interest in that year alone.
Forty-six developing countries now spend more on interest than on either health or education.
Behind these numbers lies a simple reality: the hospital competes with the creditor, the classroom competes with debt service, and too often the creditor is paid first.
Today, 251 million children and young people remain out of school.
Millions more enter classrooms without the teachers, books, meals and facilities they need to learn.
When debt service displaces investment in education, we are not merely balancing budgets.
We are transferring the cost of today’s financial system to the next generation.
But national effort can only go so far when the international financial system makes development itself more expensive.
The countries that most need capital frequently pay the highest price to obtain it.
Developing countries have recently borrowed at rates two to four times higher, on average, than the developed nations.
The question, therefore, is not simply whether finance is available.
It is who can access it, at what price, for how long and under whose assessment of risk.
25. Africa knows the cost of that assessment.

But it must also be measured fairly.
26. We cannot build a fair global economy if the nations with the greatest development needs face the highest cost of development finance.
A road that is commercially viable should not become unviable merely because it crosses an African border.
A power project should not cost more simply because of the passport of the country building it.
Capital must price risk; it must not price prejudice.

This is not an argument against responsibility.
Governments must also do their part to manage debt prudently, strengthen institutions, prepare credible projects, deepen domestic capital markets, honour corruption without contracts equivocation.

Political reform and financial reform are not separate projects.

47. Our responsibility is no less consequential.
We must not wait for another catastrophe to reform institutions whose weaknesses we can already see.

We must not ask our children to inherit wars we could have prevented, debts we could have made sustainable, inequalities we could have corrected and institutions we knew no longer reflected their world.
If we are serious about restoring trust, then rules must apply consistently.
If we are serious about managing transformation, then our institutions must themselves transform.
And if we seek a United Nations that delivers for all, then all must have a meaningful voice, a fair opportunity and a stake in the system.

Let ours be the generation that completes the unfinished work of San Francisco: that makes sovereign equality real in our institutions, makes international law consistent in its application, makes capital serve development and makes cooperation stronger than division.
50. Not a United Nations of some nations.
