The United Nations — Our Family of Nations We meet today at a difficult moment.
Conflicts continue to claim lives and displace communities.
Human rights continue to be violated. Humanitarian crises persist.
Development gains are being reversed in many parts of the world.
Inequality remains entrenched, while climate change places additional pressure on communities already confronting significant development challenges.
Reform should not weaken the organisation, it must enable the UN to fulfil the purposes for which it was created.

to strengthen We also welcome the UN80 Initiative as an important opportunity to strengthen the effectiveness of the United Nations and acknowledge the work under Workstream 2 on Mandate Implementation Review, and recognise the leadership and contribution of Member States, including New Zealand and Jamaica, in advancing this important process.
It is therefore fitting that the theme of this eighty-first session is: “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All.”
This theme is both timely and relevant.
Trust cannot be restored by words alone.
It must be strengthened through implementation, accountability and results that improve the lives of our people.
For Kiribati, the theme reaffirms our shared duty to strengthen the United Nations and ensure it serves everyone.
Ocean Management & Fisheries Kiribati is an ocean nation.
We are a Big Ocean Sustainable State.
Our economy, food security, livelihoods, culture and way of life depend on healthy, sustainable marine resources.
The entry into force of the Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction Agreement marks an important step towards stronger and more equitable ocean governance.

Kiribati is proud to have signed and ratified this Agreement and calls on Member States to recognise the vital importance of our shared ocean and to work collectively to translate the Agreement’s historic ambition into meaningful global action.
CLIMATE CHANGE The sustainability of our oceans and fisheries is closely linked to the changing climate, and the pressures we face on our marine resources are increasingly compounded by its impacts.
Climate change remains one of the most pressing challenges to our development and way of life.
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change Sixth Assessment Report reinforces the urgency of these challenges and particularly the risks faced by small island States.

Through our long-term national development vision, the Kiribati Vision for 20 years, and our national priorities under Te Motinnano policies, we continue to invest in resilient infrastructure, water security, coastal protection, disaster preparedness, renewable energy and community-based adaptation.
Our objective is clear: to continue building a wealthy, healthy and peaceful Kiribati, where our people can live with dignity, in peace and with opportunities.
Renewable energy is increasingly important to Kiribati’s development and energy access.

We therefore see greater investment in renewable energy as an important opportunity to reduce our reliance on imported fossil fuels and strengthen the resilience and sustainability of our energy sector.
But national action must be matched by international action.
We call for greater ambition, stronger support for adaptation and climate finance that is adequate, predictable and accessible, particularly Island Developing States.

The International Court of Justice Advisory Opinion on climate change advances climate justice by affirming that all States have binding duties to protect the climate system and achieve deep, rapid, and sustained greenhouse gas reductions consistent with limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius.
We welcome growing recognition that climate resilience must be locally owned and driven.
The Pacific Resilience Facility is a Pacific-led, Pacific-owned mechanism that strengthens the region’s capacity to finance climate and disaster resilience.
The Pacific’s co-hosting of COP31 with Türkiye later this year further demonstrates the value of local action.
These initiatives also show that strong, genuine partnerships can sustain locally led development.
PARTNERSHIPS FOR DEVELOPMENT Partnership continues to shape international cooperation as we believe that we are stronger when we work together.
At a time when multilateralism faces growing challenges, partnership remains one of our most powerful affirmations, of what we can achieve, collectively.

Kiribati reaffirms its support for frameworks that embody this spirit of partnership, including the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS (ABAS) and the Pact for the Future, which provide important foundations for strengthened international cooperation, solidarity and collective action.
As the 2030 Agenda enters its final years, partnership must remain central to accelerating SDG progress.
Kiribati recently presented its Second Voluntary National Review (VNR), reaffirming our commitment to the 2030 Agenda.

We value our longstanding diplomatic relations with traditional partners and welcome countries seeking new partnerships based on mutual respect, shared interests, transparency, sovereign equality and respect for our national priorities.

This year, following the submission of our second VNR, my Government convened its first “Development Partners Forum” on Kiritimati Island, which we highly value as the world’s largest coral atoll and the first island to see each new day’s sunrise.
The Forum strengthened partnerships between Kiribati and its Development Partners and showcased two flagship projects critical to accelerating economic growth and sustainable development.
Participants included Australia, the People’s Republic of China, the European Union, New Zealand, Japan, the United States of America, the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank, and UN agencies.
We thank our partners and look forward to advancing our shared interests under the Forum’s Outcome document, the “Kiritimati Partnership Accord 2026”.
EDUCATION AND HEALTH Ultimately, development depends on people, our most valuable resource, making education a vital investment.
Kiribati is committed to expanding access to quality, inclusive, relevant education while strengthening skills development, vocational training, digital learning, and opportunities for young people.
We continue to strengthen our health systems across our widely dispersed and remote islands, improve access to essential services and address both communicable and non-communicable diseases.
A healthy and educated population is the foundation upon which every other national priority rests.
WOMEN, YOUTH AND SPORT We cannot speak about development without speaking about women and youth.
Kiribati remains committed to gender equality and empowering women and girls.

Our election earlier this year to the Commission on the Status of Women—the first time Kiribati has secured a seat on this UN body—is a significant milestone, reflecting our determination to advance women’s rights nationally and globally.
We will expand opportunities, prevent violence, and promote women’s economic empowerment and leadership.
Our youth, meanwhile, represent not simply the future of Kiribati.
We must provide them with education, employment, skills, technology, leadership opportunities and spaces where they can contribute.
And one of those spaces is sport.
Kiribati will host the 2030 Micronesian Games, which we intend to use to leave a lasting legacy for our young people.
We invite our regional and international partners to join us in this endeavour.
PEACE AND SECURITY Kiribati is a peaceful nation, yet distance does not make us indifferent to the suffering caused by war and conflict elsewhere.
The people of every nation deserve peace.
We reaffirm that disputes must be resolved peacefully, in accordance with international law and the principles of the United Nations Charter.
For island nations such as Kiribati, respect for international law is fundamental to our security, sovereignty and the stability of the international system.
Kiribati is proud to contribute in our own way to international peace and security, through the service of our police officers under the United Nations flag.
For Kiribati, this is an expression of our belief that even the smallest country can contribute to global peace.
For Pacific peoples, the consequences of nuclear weapons are not merely historical.
Our region still bears the human and environmental legacy of nuclear testing.

As States Parties to the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW), we remain committed to advancing the Treaty’s and the humanitarian objectives and establishing an international trust fund for nuclear-weapons victims.

As Co-Chairs with Kazakhstan of the recent International Meeting on Victim Assistance and Environmental Remediation, we thank the Secretary-General for convening this important meeting and for keeping the needs of affected communities at the center of our collective efforts.
Peace and security must also keep pace with emerging threats in the digital domain.
The East Micronesia Cable landed in Tarawa last year, connecting Kiribati with Nauru and the Federated States of Micronesia, transforming our connectivity and digital development.

With limited redundancy and technical capacity, island States face threats including cybercrime, critical infrastructure attacks, ransomware and online harms that can undermine security and development.
CONCLUSION Your Excellencies, Kiribati comes to this Assembly not simply to speak of the challenges we face.
We come to speak of the future we choose.
I rise before this Assembly at a time when the world is not short of promises, declarations or commitments.
What we need is proof that our institutions can respond to the realities people face.
For Small Island Developing States like ours, that question is immediate.
Saint Kitts and Nevis therefore comes with a clear proposition: trust will be restored not by what we promise, but by what we deliver.
The time has come to move from promise to proof.
I come not only to speak about what the world must do, but to account for what we are doing.

National Delivery Under SISA Mr. President, last year our Prime Minister, the Hon. Dr. Terrance Drew, spoke of our Sustainable Island State Agenda (SISA), our national blueprint for transforming Saint Kitts and Nevis into a more resilient, sustainable, inclusive and prosperous society by 2040.
Today, we return to demonstrate that it is becoming a record of delivery.

Earlier this year, our second Voluntary National Review to the United Nations High-Level Political Forum showed stronger government coordination, closer alignment with the Sustainable Development Goals, and tangible progress for our people.
Water provides one of the clearest measures of that progress.
One year ago, our two-million-gallon-per-day solar-powered desalination plant was nearing completion.
Through semi-airborne drone surveys, we also identified seventeen new potential groundwater sources and, in August, completed drilling at the first rural site.
Together with distribution upgrades, these investments are strengthening water security.
In 2022, only about 25 percent of households had 24-7 water; today, approximately 75 percent do. This is transformation!
On the island of Nevis, we are advancing a 30-megawatt geothermal power development, with drilling expected by early 2027 and Icelandic Drillers contracted to begin the process.
In Saint Kitts, plans for a 50-megawatt solar PV and battery storage project are well advanced.
These investments will reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels and strengthen economic resilience.

We are also strengthening food security through climate-smart support for farmers and healthcare through our locally developed National Digital Health Information System at the Joseph N. France General Hospital.
Sustainability must be practical, people-centred and built to last.
But our experience proves that small states are not powerless.
With investment, partnership and political will, small nations can deliver big solutions.
Saint Kitts and Nevis is not seeking pity; we are advancing partnership.
A Sustainable Island State is not a distant ambition.
Climate Change Yet even as we advance, the climate crisis is moving the goalposts.
This year, our Federation and the wider Caribbean face severe drought; by the end of May, rainfall was 44 percent below the long-term average.
We are investing in resilient infrastructure, but no Small Island Developing State can adapt indefinitely to a crisis the world continues to intensify.
Distinguished colleagues, the science is unequivocal.

The years 2015 to 2025 were the warmest on record, and in 2025 global average temperature remained about 1.43 degrees Celsius above the pre-industrial baseline, while global mean sea level stood approximately eleven centimetres higher than in 1993.
For island nations, this is a question of sovereignty and statehood.
If our coastlines retreat, our sovereignty must not.

Climate-induced sea-level rise must never erase a State's international legal personality, extinguish its UN membership, deprive its people of nationality, or diminish lawfully established maritime zones and sovereign rights.
The International Law Commission has laid foundations for continuity of statehood, sovereignty and maritime entitlements.
This Assembly must turn them into firm guarantees.
International law has spoken with increasing clarity.
Saint Kitts and Nevis welcomed the International Court of Justice Advisory Opinion on States' climate obligations.
Clarification must now become compliance, commitments must become conduct, and promises must become performance.

States must reduce emissions, strengthen adaptation, honour climate-finance responsibilities and cooperate with countries bearing consequences vastly disproportionate to their contribution to this crisis.
Those who contributed least must not pay the greatest price.
Our oceans must also move from promises to protection.
Saint Kitts and Nevis ratified the BBNJ in 2025.

Implementation now matters: large ocean states need access to capacity-building, marine technology, scientific knowledge and financing, while benefits from marine genetic resources must be shared fairly.
For island nations, the ocean is not the space between us and the world; it is our highway, heritage, livelihood and lifeline.
MVI - From Recognition to Application Across climate action, sea-level rise and ocean governance, one reality remains: resilience has a cost.
For decades, Small Island Developing States have argued that income is not the same as resilience.
Per capita income cannot show exposure to hurricanes, drought, pandemics, shipping disruption, energy shocks, conflict or tourism collapse, nor how quickly one shock can erase years of investment.
This year, Saint Kitts and Nevis stood before the United Nations and completed a pilot Vulnerability and Resilience Country Profile under the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index Framework.
We learnt what our grandparents always knew.
A house can look strong from the road and still have rot in the rafters.
Vulnerability is not a statistic, it is a roof that was destroyed in hurricane Beryl.
It is the school that became a shelter.
It is the family rebuilding for the 3rd time in a decade because storms have no patience for GNI per capita.
We are not asking that Gross National Income be discarded; we are asking that it stop being expected to tell a story it was never designed to tell.
GNI can count our coconuts and our cruise ships.
It cannot count our courage and it cannot count the price we pay to simply remain.
It cannot capture the cost of rebuilding the same bridge, clinic or seawall again and again, while nations twice our size and half our vulnerability borrow cheaper than we do.
We therefore call on the World Bank, the IMF, development banks, climate funds and every partner here to incorporate MVI into the architecture of financing.
Not as charity, but as arithmetic and justice made real.
If vulnerability can be measured, it must be considered.
Artificial Intelligence and the Emerging Digital Divide Mr. President, the next great divide between nations must not be digital.
Saint Kitts and Nevis intends to participate.
But we must ask who will shape this new age and who will live with decisions made elsewhere.
At the end of 2025, some 2.2 billion people remained offline.
But the AI divide also concerns computing power, data, research, skills, energy, cybersecurity and capital.
With the global AI market projected to reach about US 4.8 trillion dollars by 2033, developing countries cannot simply consume technologies designed and governed elsewhere.
We must have a place where AI's future is decided.
Saint Kitts and Nevis welcomes the Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence and the Global Dialogue on AI Governance.
Developing countries need affordable computing power, infrastructure, skills and safeguards for privacy, data sovereignty, cybersecurity and rights.
At home, we are advancing a Whole-of-Government Technology Strategy, securing digital identity and digital public services.
Regionally, the Caribbean AI Task Force supports cooperation on governance, innovation and responsible adoption.
Artificial intelligence is already transforming the world.
Saint Kitts and Nevis chooses to help shape that transformation!
CARICOM, Diplomacy and Global Peace As small states, we know a simple truth: alone, we are small; together, we are formidable.
The Caribbean's declaration as a Zone of Peace must retain its force as geopolitical competition moves closer to our shores.
Our response must remain anchored in sovereignty, territorial integrity, international law, peaceful settlement of disputes and diplomacy.
CARICOM supports the International Court of Justice as the lawful path for resolving the Guyana-Venezuela dispute and the judicial process concerning Belize and Guatemala.
We defend international law because, for small states especially, the alternative is a world where power becomes the rule.
Across Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan, Yemen, Chad and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, civilians continue to bear an unconscionable burden.
Saint Kitts and Nevis affirms one standard: international law applied consistently, not selectively; and conscience applied evenly, not conveniently.
There can be no hierarchy of human suffering.
Mr. President, the future of multilateralism also depends on its leadership.
Saint Kitts and Nevis proudly joins CARICOM in endorsing Her Excellency Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of Guyana for the office of United Nations Secretary-General.
Her distinguished record of service, commitment to multilateralism and understanding of the challenges facing developing nations reflect the leadership this moment demands.

Her candidature, as an Indigenous woman from a small developing state, also reaffirms that global leadership must be defined not by the size of a nation, but by the vision, integrity and capacity of those called to serve.
The Atlantic, once a passage of forced displacement and separation, is becoming a pathway of return and reconnection.
Africa-Caribbean cooperation must move beyond sentiment; our shared history must help build a shared future through capital, trade, technology, knowledge, culture and coordinated diplomacy.
South-South cooperation must be felt in jobs, businesses, knowledge transfer and opportunity.
It complements, not replaces, North-South cooperation and the obligations of developed countries.
Greater agency must also include justice.

At the Second Africa-CARICOM Summit, our leaders signed the Addis Ababa Declaration, and this year, the African Union's reparations mechanisms and the CARICOM Reparations Commission held their first joint meeting, establishing permanent coordination.
On 25 March 2026, this General Assembly adopted Resolution 80/250, declaring the trafficking of enslaved Africans and racialised chattel enslavement of Africans as the gravest crime against humanity.
Saint Kitts and Nevis welcomed this historic recognition, but recognition cannot be the destination.
Reparatory justice must move from recognition to remedy and from words to action.
Haiti, Cuba & Taiwan Distinguished colleagues, when we speak of reparatory justice, sovereignty and solidarity, Haiti cannot be an afterthought.
Approximately 1.47 million people are internally displaced, while nearly half the population faces acute food insecurity.
In the very near future, the first round of presidential and legislative elections will take place.
The Haitian people must choose their leaders freely, credibly and safely.

Saint Kitts and Nevis joins CARICOM in calling for the full deployment of the United Nations-authorised Gang Suppression Force and the timely renewal of its mandate, alongside Haitian-led recovery and governance.
Mr. President, we remain deeply concerned about the humanitarian situation in Cuba.
St. Kitts and Nevis has contributed humanitarian relief to the Cuban people, and our very own Nationals studying there.
We welcome the recent measures undertaken by the Cuban Government to improve the well-being of its people and encourage further meaningful action.
We urge constructive dialogue between the Governments of Cuba and the United States.
Engagement, mutual respect and cooperation offer the best path towards improving the lives of the Cuban people and advancing peace and stability throughout our region.
Saint Kitts and Nevis remains steadfast in its friendship with the Republic of China (Taiwan) and support for its meaningful international participation.
Earlier this year, we joined other Member States in requesting Taiwan's observer participation in the Seventy-ninth World Health Assembly.

We continue to support its meaningful participation in the World Health Organization, the International Civil Aviation Organization and other relevant mechanisms, and reiterate that differences across the Taiwan Strait must be resolved peacefully.
To The Young People, The Unseen Majority Mr. President, no generation has a greater stake in our decisions than young people.
Half of the world's population is under thirty, yet 67 million young people were unemployed last year and more than a quarter of a billion were neither in employment, education nor training.
AI, the green transition and climate change are reshaping their future jobs.
Last year, our Prime Minister introduced this Assembly to our ASPIRE Programme - Achieving Success through Personal Investment, Resources and Education - for citizens aged 5 to 18.

Built on savings, investment and financial education, ASPIRE has opened more than four thousand savings accounts, with our Government committing more than US 2 million dollars to give children a financial foundation for adulthood.
We are now piloting our financial education curriculum in schools and training teachers for national rollout.
We are not simply giving children money; we are giving them the knowledge to make money work for them.
Financial independence must not be reserved for those born into wealth.

Conclusion Mr. President, distinguished colleagues, for eighty-one years this institution has represented a bold conviction: that despite our differences, nations can come together around common rules, responsibilities and human dignity.
But institutions cannot live indefinitely on their founding promises.
They must be judged by what those promises produce.
Saint Kitts and Nevis remains ready to do its part and to work with every nation here towards a more peaceful, sustainable, equitable and humane world.
Trust is not something we can demand.
It must be earned: by promising less, delivering more, and letting the proof speak where our words once stood alone.
Let this Assembly be remembered not for what was said here, but for what was done after.
Let our resolve rise faster still.
The United Nations, which has a history of upholding human dignity and pioneering the way for future generations, now stands at a grave crossroads.
The glacial flooding in Nepal that claimed many lives and destroyed the foundations of people’s livelihoods evidences that the climate crisis is a reality of today, not tomorrow.
Persistent armed conflicts around the world, including those in Ukraine and the Middle East, continue to threaten the survival of humanity.
Emerging technologies such as drones are rapidly transforming warfare and posing serious challenges to human rights and the international law-based order.
Tensions surrounding the Strait of Hormuz are undermining the fundamental principles of ‘free and safe navigation’ and heightening the vulnerability of energy supply chains.
“The United Nations was not created in order to bring us to heaven, but in order to save us from hell.”
These words of the second Secretary-General of the UN, Dag Hammarskjöld, compel us to ask ourselves: Is the United Nations today capable of saving humanity from war, poverty, and disaster?
Is the United Nations living up to its promise of restoring peace and achieving sustainable development?
Ironically, the geopolitical crisis brought on by the turbulence in international order has reminded us of the cherished value of multilateral cooperation and international norms.
In an era of fragmentation marked by fierce competition for immediate survival, values such as cooperation, mutual prosperity, and solidarity can sound like hollow outcries.
However, like the founders who, having witnessed the ravages of war, conceived the United Nations, the deeper the crisis, the more we need to return to the basic principles of the UN.
Last year, I proudly announced from this podium that the Republic of Korea, which will be a beacon of light for global citizens, has returned to the international community.

Today, I stand here to make clear the Republic of Korea’s bold resolve to lead the effort to restore the spirit of the United Nations and reconnect the world, as a nation that has risen through the solidarity of the international community.
The worldwide popularity of K-culture serves as an example demonstrating that universal empathy is possible, showcasing the potential of global connection.
The stories and content that grew out of Korea’s unique experience have become a ‘language of solidarity’ that crosses borders.
Just as culture has connected people across borders, so too can nations reunite in the face of common problems.
The Republic of Korea will build on the power of empathy and solidarity that culture has brought to light.
We will harness that power to address the common challenges facing all of humanity.
To that end, allow me to set out the three visions of the ‘K-Initiative’ toward fulfilling this commitment.
First, the ‘Global AI Universal Basic Society.’
The Artificial Intelligence revolution is both a massive opportunity and a crisis for humanity.
While it can be a core driver of new prosperity and sustainable development, it will only deepen inequality and imbalance unless we are properly prepared for it.
Young people around the world, in particular, are facing growing anxiety about their employment and their future as the pace of change becomes increasingly difficult to keep up with.
This boils down to a clear direction for the new era we seek to build.
It is the ‘AI Universal Basic Society’ where everyone can benefit from technological progress.

The Republic of Korea is pursuing an AI transformation that will ensure stronger protection of fundamental rights across fields such as social security, labor, housing, and culture, beginning with our ‘AI Universal Basic Health’ program.
I believe this resonates with the core spirit of the UN Sustainable Development Goals, which prioritizes the guiding principle of “leaving no one behind.”
It also harnesses the AI revolution as a new driver to accelerate the realization of ‘economic, social and cultural rights.’

The Republic of Korea will build the ‘Global AI Hub’ platform to share this vision with the international community, in collaboration with international organizations, multilateral development banks, the business sector, and academia.
The Republic of Korea envisions a ‘Global AI Universal Basic Society’ where no country or individual is left out from access to the basic benefits of AI development.
We will take the lead in shaping AI into a tool for solving the shared challenges we face, such as the climate crisis, public health, food insecurity, and refugee issues.
The climate crisis is often referred to as a ‘global group project shared by all 8 billion people on Earth.’
A single country cannot tackle this challenge alone.
At the same time, abandoning growth cannot bring everyone on board.
The Republic of Korea announced its ‘2035 Nationally Determined Contributions’ as part of its active participation in the Paris Agreement and UN- centered climate action.
The ‘Korea Green Transformation’ strategy aims to convert our industrial structure, creating a virtuous cycle in which carbon neutrality leads to new growth engines and decent jobs.
We are ready to share our experience and best practices with the international community.
Co-hosting the ‘4th UN Ocean Conference’ with Chile in 2028 reflects our commitment to leading discussions on the sustainable development of our oceans.
Third, the coalition for global energy supply chains.
Recently, there have been repeated blockades of sea routes in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.
This has underscored the stark reality that the weaponization of key energy and logistics supply routes can send severe shockwaves to the lives of ordinary people around the world.
Freedom of navigation and safe passage through international straits is a right grounded in international law and serves as a bedrock of the global economy.
Attacks on merchant vessels and threats to the lives and safety of crew members cannot be justified under any circumstances.

While making greater use of existing frameworks such as the International Energy Agency, the Republic of Korea will build a more robust framework of cooperation for energy supply chains to prevent the supply chain crisis from escalating into a broader threat to the global economy and people’s livelihoods.
By nature, these problems cannot be resolved by any one of us alone.
At the same time, we cannot afford to sit idly by and wait for all nations to arrive at a single solution.
The most urgent and realistic path is for countries with the capacity and willingness to supply global public goods to join hands and broaden the scope of cooperation.
I would like to call this a ‘Partnership of Constructive Contributors.’
I am not seeking to propose a new organization, nor an exclusive grouping.

The idea is to respect the functions of the existing international order and the UN, work together in a flexible and open manner in areas where each country has particular strength, and expand our ties of cooperation into new areas.
By continuing to build on the achievements of collaborating ‘separately yet together,’ we can move beyond geopolitical rivalry, deadlock, and fragmentation, and rebuild trust in multilateralism.
The United Nations must evolve with the times.
Agreements reached at the negotiating table must translate into real change on the ground, so that people around the world can feel their impact in their daily lives.
We must reduce duplication across organizations and programs, accelerate decision making, and direct limited resources where they are needed most.
In this spirit, the Republic of Korea supports the ‘UN 80 Initiative,’ which will improve efficiency, prioritize field operations, and deliver greater results.
We also support the reform of the UN Security Council, so that it operates in a more effective, democratic, and accountable manner.

The Republic of Korea will live up to its responsibility and position to deliver results that can be vividly felt by people around the world across the UN's three pillars of peace, development and human rights.

Through the ‘Busan Global Partnership Forum,’ we will continue to support inclusive growth, share Korea’s development experiences such as the Saemaul Undong, and continue to make sustainable and innovative investments.
When it comes to peace on the Korean Peninsula, the Republic of Korea knows firsthand the change that the United Nations has brought about.
Thirty-five years ago, the two Koreas were admitted to the UN as members on this very stage.
It was a crucial turning point that laid the foundation for peaceful coexistence, freeing us from the relentless rivalry and confrontation that followed our division.
One year ago, I stated from this stage that the Republic of Korea would begin a new journey toward ‘peaceful coexistence and shared growth on the Korean Peninsula.’
Today, as we set out on this new journey, I would like to present to the international community the three blueprints for the road to peaceful coexistence on the Korean Peninsula.
First is inclusive peaceful coexistence built on mutual respect.
Based on the respect for each other’s systems and acknowledgement of our differences, we will explore ways for shared growth through cooperation.
We will continue to respect the North on the international stage and seek cooperation wherever possible.
We hope that opportunities will emerge for us to work together in the international community, in areas such as public health, disaster response, and the climate crisis.
Second is stable peaceful coexistence that renders conflict unnecessary.
We will work to institute mechanisms for preventing crisis and managing conflicts.
Reestablishing basic channels of communication and building trust will be the first step toward a stable peaceful coexistence.
Third is responsible peaceful coexistence contributing to world peace.

We will go beyond building a Korean Peninsula free from war and nuclear weapons to promoting stability and cooperation in Northeast Asia, while actively contributing to global efforts to build a world free from war and conflict.
The most critical task is to bring an end to this decades-old war on the Korean Peninsula and establish a lasting peace regime.
For decades, the two Koreas, along with key countries such as the U.S. and China, have recognized the need for a peace regime on the Korean Peninsula and discussed ways to achieve it.
Fortunately, President Trump’s resolve has recently created a hard-won opportunity for change.
I hope the long-suspended dialogue between North Korea and the U.S. can resume without delay.
We will lay the groundwork for this to develop into a dialogue among the parties aimed at ending the war on the Korean Peninsula and transitioning to a peace regime.

I am confident that the dialogue for establishing a peace regime on the Korean Peninsula can provide a valuable framework not only for normalizing relations among the parties concerned, but also for fostering shared growth through multilateral cooperation and promoting stability and cooperation in Northeast Asia.

In this process, we will begin with a stop to further advances in North Korea’s nuclear and missile capabilities, followed by their reductions in the medium term, moving toward a Korean Peninsula free from nuclear weapons over the long term.

I hope that the United Nations, which created a pivotal moment for peaceful coexistence on the Korean Peninsula thirty-five years ago, and the Security Council, which has safeguarded the peace and stability of the international community, will once again play a responsible and constructive role.
As a direct party to peace on the Korean Peninsula, and as a pacemaker, my government will exert every effort to open and sustain the path toward dialogue.
The true performance of UN does not lie solely in the figures and charts of reports, or in the declarations made in conference rooms.

The raison d'etre of UN will be proven only when children's laughter replaces gunfire, when young people can enjoy the opportunity to learn, work, and take on new challenges, and when anyone, anywhere, can choose to live the life they want.
In 2015, the international community adopted the Sustainable Development Goals as our shared commitments for a bright future.
As we approach the 2030 deadline, now is the time to chart a new path forward for the next generation.
It is imperative for young people, our future generation, to define problems together, formulate solutions, and become co-designers who can lead the action.

We need to bring more youth voices into international decision-making by widening opportunities for participation and communication, as well as making bold investments in the potential of the next generation.
The Republic of Korea can testify more vividly than anyone else, to the noble power of solidarity embodied by the United Nations.

Our own experience of achieving industrialization and democratization in the wake of war stands as proof of how the world can bring about miraculous changes with one mind and one heart of the international community.
We are ready to repay that solidarity with greater responsibility and contribution.
We will reconnect a divided world, build a future that leaves no one behind, and chart a course for the next generation to dream of a better tomorrow.
The Republic of Korea stands ready to lead the way toward a peaceful coexistence on the Korean Peninsula, and toward “a United Nations that delivers for all.”

I would also like to congratulate His Excellency Dr. Muhammad Yunus, Chief Adviser of the friendly People’s Republic of Bangladesh, on his election as President of the General Assembly for this session, affirming our support for his wise choice of the theme of this session, “A United Nations that Responds to the Demands of the Future and Manages Transformation Effectively”, and wishing His Excellency every success.
We also commend the efforts of the Secretary-General of the United Nations and his pursuit of strengthening multilateral action and the Pact for the Future.

We hope that efforts will continue, after the end of the Secretary-General’s term, to ensure the continuity of work to improve the performance of the Organization in carrying out the responsibilities entrusted to it and to activate its role by the end of this year, including climate change, the Sustainable Development Goals, industrial development, and the development of its agencies in this regard.

Here, we affirm that reform of the Security Council has become an urgent necessity to preserve international peace and security and to keep pace with the changes that have occurred in international relations since its establishment, so that the Council may become more representative and effective and more transparent in the performance of its responsibilities.

Mr. President, The State of Kuwait and the States of the Gulf Cooperation Council, as well as the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan and the sister Arab Republic of Egypt, have, since last February, been subjected to Iranian aggression involving ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles, in a violation of the international legal order, international law, international humanitarian law, and the Charter of the United Nations, although they were not a party to what was taking place in the region.

These attacks targeted civilian objects, including vital installations, electrical and water facilities, repeated and direct attacks on Kuwait’s oil installations, and caused severe disruption to the basic necessities of life and to vital infrastructure.

These painful attacks also resulted in a number of innocent civilian martyrs and wounded, and inflicted grave material and economic damage in a hostile pattern contrary to Security Council resolutions and global trade.
the harm caused to the economies of the countries of the region and our world, and to global trade and energy security.

Iran is using this paper to obstruct maritime navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, in a flagrant manner that is contrary to international law and the freedom of navigation guaranteed by the relevant international instruments.

The State of Kuwait expresses its great appreciation to the countries that stood by it, showed solidarity with it, and stood with it in this regard, and to the countries that supported Security Council resolution 2817 and the other resolutions issued by the Human Rights Council and the International Maritime Organization, which condemned the Iranian aggression as a threat to international peace and security and called for its cessation, and affirmed the natural right of States to self-defence in accordance with Article 51 of the Charter of the United Nations.

In this context, the State of Kuwait reiterates that the security and stability of the Gulf region are a fundamental pillar of Arab and international security, and that the continuation of Iranian violations undermines this foundation.

Kuwait also renews its support for de-escalation and for reaching a solution, and for the efforts made and the mediation led by the sisterly State of Qatar and the Republic of Pakistan, the friendly one, to spare the region and its peoples the repercussions of war and attacks, in a diplomatic approach that reaffirms the necessity of reaching an immediate ceasefire without restriction or condition, so as to ensure the security and stability of the region and peace for all its peoples.

The State of Kuwait also commends the efforts of all regional and international actors aimed at building sustainable regional understandings, based on commitment to the principles of good-neighbourliness, respect for the sovereignty of States, non-interference in their internal affairs, refraining from the use or threat of force, and addressing the security concerns of the countries of the region, including the Iranian nuclear file, ballistic missiles and armed drones, while emphasizing the need to guarantee freedom of navigation and the safety of maritime passage through the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab al-Mandab Strait, and the right of transit passage through straits in accordance with international law and the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea of 1982.

The State of Kuwait remains committed in its foreign policy to the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, especially respect for the principle of good-neighbourliness and respect for the sovereignty of States, and from this standpoint, it views the Republic of Iraq as a neighbour with which we are linked by brotherly relations and as a partner in security and stability.

Kuwait has been keen, since the fall of the former regime in 2003, to stand by Iraq and support it in facing security and economic challenges, with a view to restoring its role and standing at the regional and international levels, out of the conviction that a secure, stable and prosperous Iraq is a shared interest for Kuwait and for the region as a whole.

Within the framework of its foreign policy and in implementation of Security Council resolutions, the State of Kuwait looks forward to moving relations between the two countries to broader and more expansive horizons through the steps taken by Iraq under the leadership of His Excellency Mr. Ali al-Sudani, Prime Minister, to strengthen the authority of the State and to normalize Iraq’s relations with countries, and the bilateral relationship between the two countries, and to complete the demarcation of the maritime boundary in accordance with the rules of international law and the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea of 1982, signed in 2008, as a legal and practical instrument for regulating navigation and protecting maritime security.

In this regard, the President of the Republic of Iraq has adopted this path, namely enhancing relations with the neighbouring countries and drawing the maritime boundaries, in implementation of the relevant international legal obligations after the demarcation between the two countries, and also in the areas of watercourses, environmental protection, combating terrorism, drugs, and the bilateral security and technical understandings and agreements, including the Agreement on the Regulation of Navigation for 2012, the Protocol on Security Information Exchange, cooperation in the field of combating drug trafficking, and the designation of joint security coordinators.

The State of Kuwait calls upon the Republic of Iraq to continue to implement Security Council resolution 2792, and to persevere in the progress and results achieved in order to realize the hoped-for goal concerning the file of Kuwaiti and third-country nationals who are missing, as well as Kuwaiti property, including the national archives.

Mr. President: The State of Kuwait renews its principled and firm position in condemning the continuing violations by the Israeli occupation forces against the Palestinian people, who are suffering under very difficult humanitarian and living conditions, displacement, arrests, and settlement activity.

We call for the full implementation of the peace plan in all its stages and of the relevant resolutions adopted by the Security Council, for the Israeli occupation forces to cease their military operations, to ensure the flow of humanitarian assistance, and for the return of the Palestinian Authority to the Gaza Strip, while emphasizing that no military operation can displace any part of the occupied Palestinian territory in its entirety, including resolution 2803.

In this context, we commend the decisions and measures taken by the Kingdom of the United Kingdom, France, and a number of States in condemning settlements, imposing a ban on the import of products and goods from the settlements, and imposing sanctions on settlers involved in acts of violence and terrorism against the Palestinian people.

The State of Kuwait affirms that achieving comprehensive, just and lasting peace in the region will remain contingent upon ending the Israeli occupation of all Arab territories and enabling the Palestinian people to exercise their legitimate, inalienable and non-negotiable rights, and to establish their independent State on the 4 June 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital.
The State of Kuwait affirms that any threat targeting the Republic of Yemen and the attacks it is exposed to in this sensitive region, and in this context, ...

As a result of the military escalation taking place in a number of governorates, caused by the Houthi group's attacks on navigation in Bab al-Mandab and in the Red Sea, the State of Kuwait renews its full support for the efforts led by the United Nations aimed at reaching a lasting political settlement led by the Yemenis, in accordance with the agreed references and the relevant Security Council resolutions, in particular resolution 2216.

Any political settlement should preserve the unity of Yemen, its sovereignty, its independence and the safety of its territory, put an end to the suffering of its brotherly people, and open horizons for security, stability and economic development, while preserving the security and safety of international maritime navigation in the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
We also condemn the attacks by the Houthi group targeting the sisterly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and targeting civilian and economic objects in a number of cities.

We affirm in this context that the security of the Kingdom is an integral part of the security of the State of Kuwait and the security of the States members of the Cooperation Council for the Arab States of the Gulf.
The President of the State of Kuwait renews its standing by the side of the Syrian Arab Republic and welcomes the steps and measures that have been taken in the sisterly Syrian Arab Republic.

We reaffirm the importance, in this context, of moving forward with the implementation of Security Council resolution 1974, in a manner that meets the aspirations of the Syrian people, and we stress the importance of respecting the sovereignty of the Syrian Arab Republic and its unity and territorial integrity, lifting from it its isolation and removing it from the list of States sponsors of terrorism.

We also affirm our support for all efforts focused on rebuilding the institutions of the State towards a comprehensive and inclusive political process under Syrian leadership and with the effective participation of all components, in fulfilment of its legitimate aspirations for security, stability and decent living.

In this context, we condemn and reject the repeated attacks and provocations by the Israeli occupation forces inside the occupied Arab territories and what they portend of dangerous escalation; in violation of the 1974 Disengagement of Forces Agreement, and to the detriment of security and stability in the region.

With regard to the Lebanese Republic, the State of Kuwait stresses the importance of the Lebanese State’s constitutional institutions and the necessity of enabling the State of Lebanon to exercise its full sovereignty over all its territory, and of confining weapons to the hands of the State alone.

We also affirm the importance, in this regard, of ensuring the full implementation of Security Council resolution 1701, including our demand that Israel withdraw from all occupied Lebanese territories.

As for developments in the Syrian Arab Republic, the Republic of the Sudan, the Federal Republic of Somalia and the State of Libya, we affirm the necessity of preserving the sovereignty, security, stability, unity and territorial integrity of these brotherly States, adhering to the settlement of disputes by peaceful means and in accordance with the rules of international law and the relevant Security Council resolutions, in a manner that guarantees the security and unity of these brotherly States.

Engaging in political dialogues to resolve conflicts peacefully, and preserving international and regional peace and security, have constituted the fundamental pillar upon which the State of Kuwait has based its foreign policy.

Since its independence, it has based its foreign policy on firm and constant foundations, namely non-alignment, moderation, commitment to the Charter of the United Nations and international law, advocacy of peaceful settlement of disputes through dialogue, and faith that respect for the sovereignty of States and non-interference in their internal affairs are among the pillars of international peace and security.
The State of Kuwait also believes in the inseparable link between security and development.
There can be no security without development, and no development without security.

Through its development and humanitarian diplomacy, Kuwait has embodied this vision through the role of the Kuwait Fund for Arab Economic Development, which was established in 1961 and has, in the firm belief that development is an investment in collective security, financed development projects in countries around the world, especially in areas afflicted by conflict, for development is not achieved by humanitarian aid alone; rather, it also requires support for development paths and the building of societies more capable of resilience, stability and the provision of opportunities.

The State of Kuwait is also moving forward, through Kuwait Vision 2035, with confidence towards achieving the accelerated implementation of development projects, diversifying its economy and sources of income, continuing digital transformation, empowering women and youth, developing its educational system and legislative structure, and enhancing institutional efficiency in governance and transparency, in a manner that strengthens the State of Kuwait’s position as a regional financial and commercial centre and as a cultural leader in the region.

In conclusion, my country has experienced, like many countries of the world, the bitterness of aggression and the harshness of occupation, and our region has suffered for four decades from the wars and conflicts that have swept through it.

This lived experience has led us to become ever more convinced that peace is not a luxury but a necessity, and that dialogue does not diminish rights but preserves them and protects them, and that security is not safeguarded by force alone, but rather by justice, which creates it and sustains it.

As we have come to understand the importance of adherence to international legality and the principles of international law, which protect the sovereignty of States and preserve the rights of peoples, the State of Kuwait, which has believed in them in word and deed, will continue to be a voice in support of peace, a path to stability, and a partner in upholding the authority of the law and recourse to it for the settlement of disputes.
That is because just peace and adherence to international law remain the safety valve for the stability of States and the prosperity of their peoples.
This conviction has become firmly established in us through the experiences we have had.
Respect for sovereignty and non-interference in internal affairs is not merely a legal principle; it is the foundation of a just international order.

The State of Kuwait will remain, as it has always been, a voice in support of wisdom, dialogue, cooperation, openness to all, moderation, partnerships, shared interests and benefits, and support for what is right in a way that makes it a trustworthy partner.

It does so out of its belief that peace is the way to entrench the values of coexistence and to a future in which homelands are stable, rights are protected, and generations enjoy security and prosperity.
2. The theme for this session, “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All,” arrives at a pivotal juncture.
For developing and vulnerable countries, a well-resourced and responsive United Nations is an indispensable anchor.
Restoring trust in our international system requires us to uphold predictable support, honour commitments, and reaffirm our fidelity to the UN Charter.
3. For the Lao PDR, restoring and deepening trust begins with a renewed commitment to inclusive multilateralism, with the United Nations at its core.
When dialogue is guided by mutual respect, transparency, and genuine cooperation, multilateralism yields tangible benefits for all people.
4. Our world continues to confront severe, multifaceted crises: geopolitical tensions, macroeconomic instability, supply chain disruptions, and accelerating climate emergencies.
These headwinds place immense strain on the most vulnerable economies, where rising energy and food prices jeopardize the livelihoods of millions of people in countries in special situations.
5. The ongoing conflicts in the Middle East demonstrate how rapidly confrontation can destabilize global stability.
Sustainable peace cannot be forged through force or unilateral action; it requires diplomacy, respect for sovereign equality and territorial integrity, and strict adherence to international law.
6. The question of Palestine remains an enduring test of multilateral credibility.
We remain deeply concerned by the humanitarian catastrophe and immense reconstruction requirements in Gaza, as well as mounting challenges in the West Bank.

To prevent the two-state solution from slipping beyond reach, the international community must secure a just, comprehensive, and lasting peace, one that fulfils the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people to self-determination through an independent State of Palestine with full membership in the United Nations.
7. In the same vein, the Lao PDR reiterates its principled position against Unilateral Coercive Measures.
The prolonged economic, commercial, and financial embargo against the Republic of Cuba continues to inflict hardship on its people.
We call for the immediate and unconditional lifting of these sanctions, including logistics and energy blockades, and the removal of Cuba from the list of “State Sponsors of Terrorism.”
Such steps are essential first humanitarian measures toward restoring trust and reaffirming the primacy of international law.
8. The gap between commitments and delivery on climate change equally tests the credibility of multilateralism.
Although the Lao PDR has contributed only a small share of global greenhouse gas emissions, our people are increasingly affected by floods, droughts and extreme weather conditions.
9. The Lao PDR remains fully committed to the Paris Agreement and its Nationally Determined Contributions.

However, climate ambition must be matched by adequate, predictable, and accessible climate finance, technology transfer, and capacity-building to enable vulnerable developing states to adapt, build long-term resilience, and pursue low-carbon growth pathways.
10. The Lao PDR welcomes the UN80 Initiative to enhance the coherence, transparency, and effectiveness of the UN System.
Systemic reform must ensure a balanced approach across all three pillars of the Organization: peace and security, sustainable development, and human rights.
11. The implementation of the Pact for the Future and the Global Digital Compact must focus on narrowing the digital divide.
Artificial intelligence and digital technologies must serve human development, strengthen local technical capacities, and respect national development priorities.

12. As an active member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), the Lao PDR reaffirms that a united, integrated ASEAN serves as a cornerstone of regional peace and multilateral stability.
We remain steadfast in supporting ASEAN centrality within the evolving regional architecture, where ASEAN-led mechanisms foster trust and practical cooperation.
13. This year carries special significance as we begin implementing the ASEAN Community Vision 2045 alongside its Strategic Plans across all three community pillars.

It also marks the 50th Anniversary of the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia (TAC)—a foundational framework whose core principles of peaceful coexistence and mutual respect remain fully relevant today.
ASEAN remains the bedrock of Lao PDR’s regional engagement.
14. Despite severe external economic shocks and natural disasters, the Lao economy continues its steady recovery through strong national ownership and strategic international partnerships.
Guided by our Sovereign and Self-Reliant Economic Policy, the Lao PDR has adopted the 10th National Socio-Economic Development Plan (2026–2030).

15. The 10th NSEDP focuses on six core national outcomes: o First: Executing a sovereign and self-reliant economic policy aiming for steady annual GDP growth of 6% or higher; o Second: Developing high-quality human resources capable of driving technological transition; o Third: Improving living standards, ensuring balanced urban- rural development, and alleviating poverty; o Fourth: Protecting natural resources, building climate resilience, and mitigating disaster risks; o Fifth: Enhancing regional and global economic integration and connectivity; and o Sixth: Strengthening the efficiency and transparency of public administration and governance.
16. Central to this strategy is transforming the Lao PDR from a land-locked country into a land-linked regional gateway.

Strategic infrastructure, including the Laos–China Railway, the Laos–Viet Nam Railway project, expanded transit corridors, and access to the sea via Vung Ang International Port are actively driving regional trade and integration.
Our long-term vision towards 2055 aims to firmly establish the Lao PDR as an upper-middle-income nation with sustainable, inclusive growth at its core.
17. This year marks a landmark milestone in our national development.
The Lao PDR remains fully committed to its formal graduation from Least Developed Country (LDC) status, in accordance with relevant General Assembly resolutions.
18. As the UN Secretary-General António Guterres rightly stated, LDC graduation must be “a reward, never a punishment.”
To safeguard our hard-won development gains and prevent structural setbacks, we are executing a robust Smooth Transition Strategy (2026–2029).

We call on our international partners to provide transition support, extend smooth adjustments predictable regarding International Support Measures (ISMs), and expand concessional financing to build enduring economic resilience.
19. The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development remains fully embedded within our national planning.

Restoring trust requires that the human being feel that the law protects him, that development does not exclude him, and that progress does not bypass him.

If restoring trust is a challenge facing our world today, then for Lebanon it is not a slogan we raise, nor is managing transformation an option we discuss; rather, they are the very essence of the mission to which we committed ourselves before our people, before our Arab brethren, and before the whole world on the day I was tasked with heading the Lebanese Government.

Trust is built, decision is regained, and land is liberated.
That is the equation for Lebanon’s recovery.
These are not three separate challenges, but three facets of one issue: restoring a State that its citizens trust, that owns its decision, and that exercises its sovereignty over all its territory.

First, the trust we seek to restore is not trust in words, but in institutions that protect rights, in a judiciary that guarantees justice, in an economy that restores prosperity to the people and to young people their opportunities for a better future.

From this premise, we did not confine ourselves to affirming the exclusivity of arms in the hands of the State and confining the decision of war and peace to its constitutional institutions.

Rather, we translated this commitment into decisions taken by the Council of Ministers, particularly in August and September of last year, and then in March of the current year, after Lebanon found itself in the face of a war it did not choose but that was imposed on it, despite our repeated warnings of the risks of being dragged into it.

Thirdly, our position on the war has been clear from the outset: we want it stopped, and we want to consolidate a ceasefire and the withdrawal of Israel from all Lebanese territory, up to our internationally recognized borders, as reaffirmed once again, in accordance with the 1949 Armistice Agreement, and we want the release of all our prisoners, and a safe and dignified return for our people to their villages and towns, and the reconstruction of what the war has destroyed.

PERMANENT MISSION OF SAINT LUCIA TO THE UNITED NATIONS STATEMENT BY THE HONOURABLE PHILIP J. PIERRE PRIME MINISTER OF SAINT LUCIA AND MINISTER FOR FINANCE, CONSTITUENCY DEVELOPMENT, PEOPLE EMPOWERMENT, JUSTICE, AND NATIONAL SECURITY TO THE GENERAL DEBATE OF THE 81st SESSION OF THE UNITED NATIONS GENERAL ASSEMBLY NEW YORK FRIDAY, 24 SEPTEMBER, 2026 Mr. Secretary-General, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, In 1979, thirty-four (34) years after the creation of this United Nations, my country, Saint Lucia, though small in geography, but large in courage, dignity and conviction, took its seat among the community of nations brimming with hope, optimism and trust in the promise and goals of this body.
Today we meet at a moment of profound international uncertainty.
Conflict is spreading, trust is eroding, development gains are being reversed, and the rules intended to protect humanity are too often applied selectively.
For small island developing states, these crises are not abstract.
Climate change threatens our homes, livelihoods, and very existence.
Debt limits our ability to invest in people.
Digital technologies are transforming our societies, but without safeguards, they can reproduce old patterns of domination in a new form.
And in our own Caribbean neighbourhood, the people of Haiti continue to endure a humanitarian and security catastrophe that demands more than statements of concern.
The theme before us, “Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all,” must not remain a slogan.

Trust will be restored only when promises are matched by action, when commitments are honoured, and when the United Nations delivers meaningful results for every nation, and when there is due regard for multilateral principles not only for the most powerful, but also for the weakest of us as well.
This Assembly should not be a place where the world expresses sympathy without accepting responsibility.
We need action. We need justice.
And we need a renewed international compact based not on power, but on principle; we need multilateralism, not unilateralism.
In the words of a former UN Secretary General, “The United Nations was not created in order to bring us to heaven, but in order to save us from hell.”
Climate Change and Climate Finance For Saint Lucia, climate change is not a distant environmental issue.
It is a direct threat to national security, economic stability, food and water security, and human survival.

Whilst the world focuses on headline-grabbing events like monster hurricanes, melting glaciers and tidal waves, climate change is affecting Saint Lucia daily in small but significant ways, such as the unusual bouts of drought in the rainy season, unprecedented floods in the dry season, and the stifling of our beaches and coastlines by sargassum.
Our people contribute little to global emissions, yet these events constantly set back our people’s development and livelihoods and demand that we find the resources to reverse the damage.

Saint Lucia calls for climate finance that matches the scale of the crisis: expanded grants and concessional funding, faster and simpler access, full support for loss and damage, meaningful debt relief, and financing that reaches vulnerable communities directly.
Eligibility for finance must reflect not only income, but climate vulnerability.
It is about justice, responsibility, and survival.
We must stop confusing loans with solidarity.
A loan is not justice when a small vulnerable nation is forced to borrow to repair damage it did not cause.

A United Nations that delivers for all must deliver for those on the front lines of climate change through accessible finance, concrete support and measurable results, not merely through declarations.

International Crises Saint Lucia laments the continued conflicts and human suffering across the globe, including Ukraine, Sudan and the wider Middle East, including Gaza, and calls for renewed efforts towards peace, stability and respect for international law.

In accordance with their right to self-determination and UN resolutions, in particular Resolution 3236 of 1974, the People of Palestine should be allowed their own State and full membership of the UN, alongside the state of Israel.
Haiti: Responsibility to a Sister Nation We also speak today about Haiti.
Member states of this organisation must act in a manner that will restore the trust of the people of Haiti in the United Nations.
Some member states have failed to meet their commitments and pledges to the Gang Suppression Force in Haiti, whose one-year mandate ends this month.
The Security Council is urged to renew the Force's mandate, and member states to provide the necessary resources to operate effectively and successfully.
While gang violence is the main factor to be resolved in Haiti, the crisis in this country is multidimensional.
The international response must include long-term social and economic assistance that will help restore an acceptable quality of life for the people of Haiti.
That is why the Caribbean Community has been actively engaged in Haiti, a Caribbean Community member state, to assist with a solution to the political and governance dimensions of the crisis.

Through its Eminent Persons Group, comprising three former Prime Ministers, it will continue to facilitate dialogue amongst Haiti’s political and civil society stakeholders as they work towards holding the first round of General Elections this year.
Trust in the United Nations will be restored if the daily lives of the people of Haiti are transformed and enhanced.
CUBA It is in a similar quest for trust and transformation that Saint Lucia believes there should be dialogue and the removal of all obstacles that hinder the true development of the people of Cuba.
Cuba has long been celebrated for its continued contribution to health, education and development across our region and beyond.
Saint Lucia stands with the Cuban people in their hope for a better future, supported by the friendship and solidarity of the international community.

Republic of China (Taiwan) In the same spirit of transformation and consistent with our commitment to the right of all people to self-determination, Saint Lucia supports Taiwan’s full membership in the United Nations.
Reform of the Security Council Saint Lucia believes that a truly inclusive United Nations must ensure that its decision-making bodies reflect the world that they serve.

Saint Lucia advocates for a comprehensive reform of the Security Council to enhance its legitimacy and effectiveness in addressing contemporary global challenges, thereby restoring trust and a more inclusive multilateral system.
Mr. President A 21st-century United Nations Security Council could have been more successful in its responsibility for international peace and security had it not been anchored in the world of 1945.
The prolonged reform process must be concluded quickly to include expanded permanent and non-permanent membership for Africa, the Asia-Pacific, and Latin America and the Caribbean regions.
This reform is essential to restore trust in the United Nations and ensure it delivers peace and security for all.
Saint Lucia pledges its commitment and dedication to work with like-minded nations to achieve the stated reforms.
Saint Lucia wishes to express its endorsement of the candidate of the Republic of Guyana, Ms. Caroline Rodrigues-Birkett, for the post of Secretary General.
Her distinguished record of public and international service speaks directly to the kind of leadership this moment demands.

Reparations and Historical Justice On the 25th of March, 2026, the General Assembly approved one of its most historic and consequential resolutions that declared the trafficking of enslaved Africans and racialised chattel enslavement of Africans as the greatest crime against humanity.

This resolution and the subsequent establishment of the High Level Global Advisory Council on Reparatory Justice is a very significant step in the search for reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and the enslavement of Africans in the Americas and the Caribbean.

Saint Lucia congratulates the Government of Jamaica on its successful petition to the British monarch for him to refer three questions to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council over the legality of the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica.
They are about truth, acknowledgement, repair and transformation.
Reparations are not about seeking charity or revisiting history for its own sake.
History is not behind us when its consequences remain embedded in wealth, power, institutions and opportunity.

Reparations are about addressing the continuing effects of slavery and colonial exploitation, restoring dignity, advancing development and building more equitable relationships with the states and institutions that benefited from these systems.

Digital Colonisation and Digital Sovereignty Digital technology is a new form of power that is rapidly transforming the world, and while it offers enormous opportunities for mankind, it can also create a new hierarchy in which a small number of corporations and powerful states control the systems on which the rest of humanity depends.
We must ensure that artificial intelligence does not widen the gap between the powerful and the vulnerable.
Technology must strengthen aspirations, not quietly erode them.

Saint Lucia therefore calls for strong global standards on data protection, privacy and artificial intelligence; equitable access to digital infrastructure, cybersecurity and affordable connectivity; fair technology transfer; transparent algorithms; protection from surveillance, disinformation and cyber exploitation; and meaningful participation by small states in shaping global digital rules.
The digital future must not be owned by a few.
It must be governed for the benefit of all.
Managing transformation means ensuring that no nation is left powerless in the face of technological change.
A United Nations That Delivers for All Mr. President, my country, Saint Lucia, is small, open, and vulnerable, but our people refuse to impose limits on their aspirations.
History has blessed us with unimaginable natural beauty, ambitious, friendly people, and two Nobel Laureates.
However, an unfair international financial system threatens the very existence of small island states like Saint Lucia.
The rules governing global finance affect our development, and our attempt at economic diversification is hindered by unfair and unequally applied rules.
Oceans of water separate us from the global powers, but our challenges are mainly connected to decisions made in their capitals.
Emissions released from these countries affect our climate.
Weapons and drugs trafficked through international networks instigate violence and gang warfare in our region.
Lack of access to affordable technology slows our development.
We are educating our people to ensure that their skills are relevant.
We are modernising agriculture to ensure our food security.
We are dealing with the scarcity of water due to climate change by exploring new sources of groundwater supply and encouraging the harvesting of rainwater.
We are reducing youth unemployment through the creation of the successful Youth Economy Agency.
We are encouraging the spirit of entrepreneurship by supporting small and micro enterprises, especially women-owned businesses.
We are promoting healthy lifestyles and universal healthcare for the provision of equitable, accessible and affordable healthcare for our citizens.
Mr President, Saint Lucia continues to insist that governance must be about the improvement of the lives of the people.
We have maintained fiscal discipline, reduced unemployment as we continue to create new opportunities and an enabling environment for investment in tourism and other productive sectors.
Saint Lucia believes that a better world is within our reach if we choose cooperation over coercion and ensure that justice and fairness prevail for all.
The 81st Session of the UN General Assembly must be remembered for turning its laudable theme into actionable commitments and those commitments into meaningful change.
As Mahatma Gandhi says, “In a gentle way you can shape the world.”

The people of Saint Lucia remain confident in our collective capacity to shape that better world, even as Saint Lucian Nobel Laureate, Sir Derek Walcott reminds us that “the future happens no matter how much we scream.”
Our task is to meet that future with courage and purpose.
Our other Nobel Laureate Sir Arthur Lewis said, “Economic development requires taking risks and embracing change.”
And with the speed of Julien Alfred, let us embrace that responsibility together and act with the resolve this moment demands.

We did so driven by the conviction that we, as one of the smallest members of the international community, should be part of the most important conversation on global governance, with the participation of all States, big or small, in developing international norms and standards – and also in upholding respect for them.
Sovereignty was a key theme of our domestic discussions resulting in our UN membership.
We joined out of enlightened self-interest - the belief that we need the UN to secure respect for our sovereignty, through upholding international law, as the basis for our security and prosperity.

To this end, we also decided to make our own contribution, to make best use of the opportunity offered to us as a small State, to be an active part of the biggest peace project in the history of humankind.
Our belief in the United Nations remains steadfast.
This is the place where we can make our voice heard, where we can put ideas forward, and where we can gather to try to solve the issues that affect us all.
We have greatly benefitted from our membership, and the UN has consistently been a key platform for our foreign policy.
Our membership has consistently enjoyed high levels of support in our population.
But today we also find ourselves in a moment where instability and uncertainty dominate the conversation.
Our organization no longer seems able to deliver on the key promise of the UN Charter – to save future generations from the scourge of war.
It can no longer count on the unconditional support of its most powerful Members for the guiding rules of international law.
It is increasingly ignored or sidelined in efforts to address both the traditional and new challenges, such as the regulation of Artificial Intelligence.
Legal obligations to pay are turned into tools to exercise political leverage.
As a result, the United Nations has moved down the foreign policy agenda even of States who have a strong history of supporting it.
We can no longer take it for granted that our people will continue their strongly positive views of our organization.
This is the difficult moment in which we find ourselves.
But rather than engaging in doomsday scenarios, we have to find the opportunities hidden in the challenge.
The overwhelming majority of the States present in this room believe in the United Nations.
They want to see positive change, for the UN to emerge stronger, more effective, more relevant.
But we all have to be prepared to be part of the change that we want to see.
Resisting the temptation of collective inertia and of waiting for positive change to happen on its own will require our active political investment.
On the basis of his ideas, our delegations here have done good work that will show positive results over time. This is important.
It shows that we can come together also during times of deep political division.

The steps we have taken are just the beginning of what we need - a political agreement that combines significant structural change with a reliable financial commitment and firm support for the UN Charter from all.
This is also the vision we are looking for in the person that will be appointed as the next Secretary-General.
We hope that this decision will come very soon, in order to give the new Secretary-General the time she needs to prepare for this most unique of jobs.
And we remain convinced that having a woman at the helm of the United Nations is long overdue for an organization that prides itself on its role in gender equality.
At its core, the United Nations is a peace organization.
This is the promise of the UN Charter, and this is what our people expect from the UN – and the reason why they hold it in high esteem.
Over the past year, we have seen a record number of armed conflicts around the world – and a rapidly diminishing role of the United Nations in ending them.
In the Middle East, the UN’s role has been further reduced, in contrast to the central position it has taken up over the years.
In Ukraine, there are few prospects for a peace process even though the aggression has now lasted longer than World War I, without even a nominal role for the United Nations.
In Sudan, the role of the UN is limited to alleviating the enormous suffering of the civilian population, with no prospect of a political solution and an end to the conflict.
We are well aware of the political dynamic in the Security Council, primarily tasked with matters of peace and security – which severely limits the options for UN action.
