But the conversation must not end there.
This Assembly in particular has wide authority over matters of peace and security – and it is universal in composition.
A glance at its history demonstrates its authority in peacekeeping, conflict termination and accountability.
It is time that we make better use of this authority.
The Veto Initiative, which we were proud to spearhead, provides a platform for such action.
What is required is the will to spend our political capital here in this room – on peace rather than force, by dealing with conflict through diplomacy rather than through war.
The United Nations must not accept being reduced to a crisis mitigation organization that distributes States’ contributions to a skyrocketing humanitarian assistance bill.

Instead, we need to see a return to the UN doing political work to prevent, contain and end conflict, through the wide range of peace operations available, and through a strong interplay between a Secretary-General who is proactive and offers creative solutions, backed by the UN membership.
Any successful community must be grounded in the rule of law.
And so it is with the international community: our commitment to the law as the foundation for the conduct of international affairs is grounded both in principle and pragmatism.
The biggest strength of the United Nations is that it is firmly grounded in rules we have all agreed on – and that we have all agreed apply to all of us.
This foundational agreement is increasingly challenged, with alarming trends to dismiss and ignore international law altogether which can only result in a world where might makes right.
This would result in catastrophic human cost, a further proliferation of conflict and have devastating effects on development and on human security.
We hope that both small and medium-sized States will come together in our common interest for a strong multilateral system, on the basis of respect for international law.
This is the moment for us to unify in support of what the United Nations is built on.
Naturally, we are also strong supporters of international courts, the indispensable enforcement mechanisms of international law.
Liechtenstein joined the jurisdiction of the International Court of Justice four decades before we joined the UN.
We have made more submissions to the Court over the past decade than in its entire history before.
We strongly support its work and its competence in both its advisory and dispute settlement functions.
We encourage all to join us in submitting to the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court.

Liechtenstein is also strongly committed to the International Criminal Court, the first permanent international court with jurisdiction over the most serious crimes under international law – genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression.
We will continue to support the Court and its mandate to ensure accountability and its central message - that nobody is above the law.
In joining the ICC, we have exercised our sovereignty and delegated the jurisdiction we have ourselves to an international Court which we have helped create.
We are proud of the way the Court has addressed the challenges to its resilience over the past year, in the face of relentless political attacks and unprecedented sanctions.
We hope that more States will join this project, which is one of the landmark achievements in the history of international treaty-making.
The Rome Statute also criminalizes the supreme international crime – the crime of aggression, which complements the prohibition of the illegal use of force, the core piece of the UN Charter.
At the international level, by signing the UN Charter we have all agreed to refrain from the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of another State.
This is the most ambitious collective commitment to end war that has ever existed.
Amidst accelerating human suffering the world over, it has never been more important for us to implement this commitment.
It has now been many decades since scientists first warned us of the dangers of Climate Change.
Nevertheless, we have continued to run into the climate abyss, leaving the coming chaos for our children and their children.
It is almost impossible to believe that we need to reiterate the facts: the climate crisis is real.
We are seeing its effects every day, from heatwaves that bake the soil, to heavy rains that turned the parched ground into mud.
People are starving in the heat and drowning in the floods.
Crops can no longer be sustainably harvested; animals and pollinators are dying out.
Liechtenstein commits to working with all States to address these harms and to reverse these trends as much as we still can.
We support the Advisory Opinion of the International Court of Justice on Climate Change.
And this week we were proud to join the adoption of a High-Level Declaration on Sea-Level Rise, including a commitment to the continuity of Statehood for all UN Member States.
Only a few years ago, Member States in this debate wondered aloud if their nameplates would be ‘switched off’.
The commitment we made this week is to guarantee that this will not happen.
In the face of seas which inundate whole territories, standing up for self-determination is the least we can do for those most affected.
This week has also seen an intense debate on harnessing the potential of Artificial Intelligence.
But perhaps what we are discovering in these conversations are our own limits to understanding what that potential might be.
Reporting from the most powerful and well-capitalized AI companies tell us that we are on a precipice either of a technology-fueled utopia or an apocalypse.
Whether we achieve one or the other, unfortunately, has been treated as a secondary priority to the ‘AI race’ – one that has no clear finish line – and, for that matter, a dubious prize.
Liechtenstein supports the regulation of Artificial Intelligence.

Unless we have a clear understanding of the methods, processes, and purposes of the huge variety of AI systems, how can we risk the consequences to human rights, to our environment, to the long-term capacities for our critical thinking and ultimately to the future of the human species?
We are already seeing the impacts on civilians as armed forces increasingly integrate AI capabilities into their targeting systems in warfare.
AI tools have to be made for humanity, lest we become the source material for AI systems to use - or merely the victims in its crosshairs.
Many of us standing here this week have mused about the UN’s imperfections or expressed our concerns about its diminished relevance.
The UN is, indeed, in a fragile place.
But very few of us want to live in a world in which the United Nations is rendered obsolete.
On the contrary, we realize how much we need the UN.
In the often-repeated quote, the UN was not built to take us to heaven.
But in an era where it may not even be able to save us from hell, this universal organization retains the unparalleled ability to meet us where we are.
It is up to us to do what we can to bring it closer to carrying out its mission under the UN Charter.
Liechtenstein commits to doing our part with you all in service of multilateralism and of the peoples we serve. I thank you.
Seminal changes are taking place across the world at a pace faster than many institutions are able to adapt or respond.
People across the globe are demanding greater clarity, honesty and action from their leaders and institutions.
The theme of this year’s General Debate — “Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all”
— goes to the heart of this challenge.

The erosion of trust is reflected in unresolved conflicts, humanitarian crises that outpace available resources, increasingly frequent climate disasters, widening inequalities, and technological advances that are moving faster than governance.
Together, these developments have contributed to a growing perception that global institutions are distant from the people they are meant to serve.
Sri Lanka understands this reality deeply.
My country has, on many occasions in the past, experienced the consequences of deficits in trust and breaches of the social contract.

Two years ago, marking a watershed moment in our history, the people of Sri Lanka, representing all communities and walks of life, gave a resounding mandate to the Government of President Anura Kumara Dissanayaka to address these challenges and institute meaningful change.
Since then, our Government has been working with determination to rebuild trust from the ground up.
We are building trust through action — not rhetoric; through delivery, discipline and the courage to confront wrongdoing.
Sri Lanka, too, is therefore undergoing a historic transformation and rejuvenation.

Despite conflicts in several parts of the world, including in West Asia, and climate calamities, including the cyclone that struck Sri Lanka, my country has restored macroeconomic stability following the economic crisis of 2022.
Today, Sri Lanka has been reclassified by the World Bank as an upper-middle-income economy, and ratings agencies have recognised this positive trajectory.
However, these developments do not fully reflect the vulnerabilities of countries exposed to debt and external shocks.
While we work with our global partners to consolidate this hard-won stability, we remain conscious of the critical need to address the hardships faced by vulnerable communities.
Cyclone Ditwah was one of the worst natural disasters in Sri Lanka’s recent history and devastated several parts of our country.
The calamity resulted in the loss of hundreds of lives and affected more than two million people.
Livelihoods were disrupted and critical infrastructure was destroyed.
Having experienced this tragedy, we understand deeply the challenge posed by the Himalayan floods to the people of Nepal and China.
We extend our deepest sympathies to the victims.
These tragic events demonstrate the enormous human and economic costs of climate change.
Sadly, its harshest consequences continue to be borne by countries that have contributed least to global emissions.
The call for action on climate impact is not merely immediate. It is overdue.
Climate justice must become an urgent reality.
For our part, Sri Lanka is on track towards achieving 70 per cent renewable energy by 2030 and carbon neutrality by 2050.
For three decades, Sri Lanka suffered a protracted conflict that caused enormous loss and suffering to all our communities.
Although the guns fell silent 17 years ago, the deep wounds of that conflict remain, and much remains to be done to heal them.
We are determined to prevent a recurrence of such a tragedy and to pursue a path towards national unity and reconciliation.
In this regard, our Government is strengthening national institutions to address outstanding issues.
Throughout these two years, we have remained firm in our rejection of racism and religious extremism in all its forms and manifestations.
We will continue to work tirelessly to build a nation that is more secure, inclusive and united — a nation made stronger by the full richness of its diversity.
In addition to the consequences of natural calamity, Sri Lanka, like many other countries, is experiencing the severe impact of conflicts in West Asia and elsewhere.

As an island nation situated at the crossroads of the Indian Ocean, and as a country with a large number of migrant workers in West Asia, these developments have direct security, economic and social implications for us.
I am pleased to note that, even during these challenging times, Sri Lanka has continued to uphold its commitments to international law and to ensure sanctity of human life and human dignity.

Mr. President In March this year, amidst a highly volatile geopolitical landscape, Sri Lanka found a ship of a party to a conflict in distress close to our territorial waters with many sailors’ life in peril.
We took the difficult path of navigating a wilderness of sensitivities and marshalling our limited national resources to rescue and look after the wounded and sick.
Hard as it was, we went on to rescue hundreds more.
We saw human lives in danger, and we acted - founding ourselves on international law and on humanity.
While safeguarding our neutrality, we placed humanity above all else.

As President Disanayaka has reiterated, “we will never hesitate to protect humanity. If there are actions that must be taken to protect human lives, we will not hesitate to take them under any circumstance”.

This, Mr. President, is the Sri Lanka we wish to bring before the world - a small island nation with a big heart which believes that even in times of conflict and profound division, there remains space for humanity.
And that is also what we wish to see reflected in the world.
We need a world where our capacity to uphold humanity grows faster than our capacity to destroy it.
That is the transformation we should seek.
It is for these reasons that we are pained by the developments in Gaza and the Occupied Palestinian territories.
The global security environment has deteriorated significantly in recent years.
It is difficult to accept that, in a world with so much wealth and knowledge, vast resources continue to be spent on weapons while children face starvation and are deprived of medicine and education.
Sri Lanka remains deeply concerned by the conflicts in West Asia and by the heavy cost being borne far beyond the region.
International law, including International Humanitarian Law, must be adhered to and respected by all parties.
We reaffirm our position that dialogue is the only viable way forward.
Sri Lanka continues to support the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people, including their right to self-determination.
We are among the countries that first recognised Palestine as a distinct State in the 1980s.
We stand in solidarity with the international community in calling for an independent and sovereign State of Palestine, existing side by side with Israel, in peace, within the pre-1967 borders.
We welcome the resolution of the Security Council on a ceasefire in Gaza and urge all parties to uphold it.
Humanitarian assistance must reach civilians without obstruction.
The recovery and reconstruction of Gaza must be an urgent priority.

Sri Lanka is proud of its longstanding contribution to United Nations peacekeeping, in pursuit of global peace and security, having deployed more than 21,000 personnel on numerous missions since 1957.
Our Blue Helmets, through their dedication and service over many years, have earned the trust of local communities and the commendation of UN field missions.

Today, they continue to serve with distinction in some of the most challenging environments under the UN flag — protecting vulnerable civilians, deterring violence and helping war-torn communities transition from conflict to stability.
Sri Lanka has also long championed multilateral disarmament — from our early call for an Indian Ocean Zone of Peace to our leadership at the 1995 NPT Review and Extension Conference.
At a time of rising geopolitical tensions and rhetoric of nuclear escalation, we remain firmly convinced that the only real guarantee against these weapons is their total and verifiable elimination.
As we approach 2030, we must deliver on the Sustainable Development Goals, which remain our collective blueprint for sustainable development.
Sri Lanka once again calls for reform of the international financial system and for fairer rules governing debt and development finance.
We welcomed the Seville Commitment last year, including its call for urgent action to close the four -trillion-dollar financing gap for sustainable development in developing countries.
It is now time to translate those commitments into concrete action.
We remain steadfast in recognising poverty and inequality as factors requiring our urgent attention.
Our national budget last year made historic allocations to the healthcare and education sectors.
We take pride in our longstanding policy of free and universal healthcare and education, and remain committed to strengthening these important pillars of social justice.

While actively implementing all SDGs without discrimination, we fully subscribe to and proactively engage with SDG 16, which underscores the importance of just and inclusive institutions that build and restore public trust and treat all people equally.
Sri Lanka has long championed and contributed towards a fair and peaceful order at sea under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea — a legal regime which we have helped shape.
We also support the work of the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf.
We remain committed to preserving the oceans as a shared space for peaceful and sustainable use, and for international cooperation.
Our nation’s prosperity is closely linked to the Indian Ocean.

As a founding Member of the Agreement on Marine Biological Diversity of Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction, the BBNJ Agreement, we reaffirm our commitment to safeguarding the oceans as a common heritage of humankind for present and future generations.
We look forward to the further operationalisation of the Agreement, complementing the processes of the International Seabed Authority.
One of the key pillars of the decisive mandate given to us by the people of Sri Lanka was to build a transparent and ethical nation.
In delivering on this mandate, we have placed good governance, anti-corruption and institutional transparency at the core of a comprehensive national integrity drive that is being vigorously pursued.
We have seen all too clearly how corruption weakens democracy and destroys trust.
We continue to enforce the law against corruption without fear or favour, irrespective of a person’s background or social standing.
Investigations and prosecutions continue to progress without political interference.
Substantial progress has been made in strengthening the independence of institutions responsible for investigating and prosecuting bribery and corruption.

My President, who addressed this Assembly last year, also highlighted how narcotics and related organised crime have become a menace for many countries, as well as our Government’s comprehensive efforts to address this menace.
One year on, our “United as a Nation” Anti-Narcotics National Programme has made significant progress, including through the arrest of key figures in the narcotics supply chain.

We reiterate our call on the global community to promote meaningful technology transfers, ensure equitable access for developing nations, bridge the digital divide, and build safe, secure and trustworthy systems that leave no one behind.
Sri Lanka is in the process of building a digital future that includes everyone.
We have developed national AI ethical guidelines in line with international frameworks.

We must ensure that emerging technologies and artificial intelligence are developed and used responsibly and consistently with international law, including the well-established principles of international humanitarian law.
Their development and use must contribute to international peace and security while advancing humanity's collective interests.
The interests of humanity must always guide the development and use of these technologies.
For Sri Lanka, the United Nations is an indispensable partner.
The UN has stood with us in challenging times and supported our development.

For many of us in the developing world, the United Nations is also an expression of a fundamental promise: that every nation, large or small, has a voice; that every people has a right to dignity and development; and that, in an interdependent world, no country should be left to confront global challenges alone.
For more than eight decades, amidst its flaws and with much room for improvement, the United Nations has given practical meaning to that promise.

However, genuine faith in multilateralism requires the courage to acknowledge where the system has fallen short, the humility to listen to those who feel unheard, and the determination to make our institutions more effective, more representative and more responsive.
In this regard, Sri Lanka supports the UN80 Initiative as an opportunity to renew and strengthen the United Nations and advance meaningful reform.
Managing transformation cannot mean managing change for some while asking others merely to adapt to its consequences.
The transformation taking place in our world must be inclusive.

It must narrow, rather than deepen, the divides between North and South; between those who shape new technologies and those who merely receive them; and between those who possess resilience and those who are most exposed to global shocks.
My country comes to this Assembly not with the expectation that the United Nations can solve every problem, but with the conviction that there are problems which no country can solve alone.
Our answer must therefore be a renewed faith in multilateralism and a United Nations that listens more closely, represents more fairly and delivers for all.

Your election reflects the confidence of Member States in your steadfast commitment to multilateralism and your vision for a United Nations that is responsive, effective, and capable of delivering for humanity.

Her dedicated leadership, zeal, and tenacity of purpose in strengthening multilateral cooperation during a period of profound global uncertainty gave us hope that the future of this Organization can be secured when all nations work together for the common goal of leaving no one behind.
During his term, the world confronted unprecedented challenges; from the COVID-19 pandemic to the eruption of new conflicts, the catastrophic effects of climate change and unstable trade regimes.

The theme for this Session, “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All,” resonates deeply with Lesotho’s aspirations for a more inclusive, transparent, and results-oriented multilateral system; capable of advancing respect for international law, maintaining global peace and security, accelerating sustainable development, protecting human rights, driving climate action and implementing long-overdue institutional reforms.
Lesotho has restored national peace and security following successive episodes of political and security unrest.
With the support of the United Nations, the African Union, SADC, and other friendly nations, we have reclaimed our rightful place among the comity of nations as a stable and peaceful country.
We therefore attest that preventive diplomacy remains the most effective means of averting conflict and ensuring sustainable peace.
To create an environment conducive to inclusive growth and development, we continue to advance public sector reforms aimed at strengthening democratic governance and the rule of law.
We remain committed to accountability, professionalism and respect for human rights across all of society.
We recognize that sustainable peace requires strong institutions, restored public trust, and an independent judiciary capable of delivering justice impartially and efficiently.
We must acknowledge that climate change is no longer a future threat but a present reality.
Lesotho is increasingly experiencing severe floods and droughts, resulting in unparalleled land degradation and extensive damage to critical infrastructure.
Despite contributing minimally to global greenhouse gas emissions, Least Developed Countries like Lesotho bear a disproportionate brunt of climate impact.
Global warming and rising sea levels pose existential threats, particularly to small island developing states.
We stand in solidarity with these nations and call for greater global action.
To cope with these climate-related challenges, we call upon developed countries to honour their commitments by providing new, adequate, predictable and accessible climate finance.

Further, we urge developed countries to transfer environmentally sound technology and to strengthen capacity of developing countries to effectively mitigate and adapt to the adverse effects of climate change.
Just Energy Transition is therefore an imperative if humanity is to be spared from the existential threat of climate change.

Under the visionary leadership of His Majesty King Letsie III, Lesotho has launched the ’’His Majesty King Letsie III Just Energy Transition Fund’’, designed not only to decarbonize our economy but to transform it from one historically reliant on migrant labour to one rooted in renewable energy exports.
The Fund seeks to attract investment to build new energy generation capacity, unlock energy independence and lay a new foundation for national prosperity that benefits every Mosotho.
We therefore call for partnerships to mobilise the requisite resources for clean energy projects, which can create significant employment opportunities for our youth and women.
Our unique topography also presents opportunities for investment in data centres, which underpin the global digital economy.

We are proud that Lesotho is the first country to pilot the United Nations Blueprint for National AI Strategies and Data Centres, positioning our nation on a pathway to achieve its AI ambitions for economic development.
We are grateful for the UN’s continued support in this digital transformation journey.
The Kingdom of Lesotho remains committed to the 2030 Agenda.
We have accelerated reforms in business development, trade facilitation, public financial management, youth empowerment, and renewable energy.
Yet challenges persist: economic diversification remains limited, youth unemployment stands at 38%, and climate-related shocks and inequality continue to constrain inclusive transformation.
With only three years remaining until 2030, we appeal to the international community to honour their official development assistance commitments which is an essential step in restoring trust.

We further call for reform of the international financial architecture to make it more equitable, fit for purpose, and responsive to the needs of developing countries, as agreed at the Fourth Summit for Financing for Development (FFD4) held in Seville, Spain.
We also urge full implementation of the outcomes of the Third Summit of Landlocked Developing Countries (LLDC3), held in Awasa, Turkmenistan, in August 2025.
The unconditional implementation of these outcomes, together with the Pact for the Future, will undoubtedly help restore eroded trust.
Mr. President, Universal health coverage remains central to our development agenda.
While investments have been made, we continue to face serious public health challenges, including a high burden of communicable and non-communicable diseases and inequalities in access to healthcare.

Lesotho is undertaking reforms to strengthen our healthcare system and invites partnerships to ensure universal access to quality primary healthcare, medicines, vaccines, diagnostics, and robust disease surveillance and pandemic preparedness.
The social and economic costs of cancer are profound.
With support from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Lesotho is developing its first radiotherapy and nuclear medicine facility to provide domestic oncology services.

We therefore call for enhanced cooperation in technology sharing, capacity building, and sustainable health financing to build resilient health systems capable of responding to current and emerging challenges.
Migration is not an abstract concept for the people of Lesotho; it is a daily lived reality.
It is woven into our social fabric as human ambition rooted dignity, opportunity and aspiration.
Migration benefits both home and host countries, contributing to skills development, cultural exchange and shared economic growth.
We must therefore strengthen international cooperation to ensure migration contributes meaningfully to deeper human understanding and sustainable development.
Guided by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, we must guarantee the full enjoyment of human rights by migrants, regardless of status.
Protecting their dignity and fundamental freedoms is not only a legal obligation, it is a moral imperative.
We welcome progress under the UN80 Initiative and appreciate efforts to enhance efficiency, effectiveness, and coherence within the UN system.
As deliberations continue, reforms must remain guided by intergovernmental agreed mandates and Member State priorities.
Any measures undertaken should preserve the UN’s capacity to deliver across all pillars of its work and maintain meaningful impact on the ground.

As we contemplate the future of multilateralism, we must renew our collective commitment to a United Nations that is more inclusive, effective, and responsive to contemporary global challenges and one in which developing countries, particularly African nations, have a stronger voice in global decision-making.

We reiterate our support for comprehensive reform of the Security Council, in line with the Ezulwini Consensus, to make it more representative, equitable, and reflective of current geopolitical realities.
The Kingdom of Lesotho reaffirms its unwavering commitment to the Charter of the United Nations, multilateralism, and the rule of law.
International law remains the cornerstone of sovereign equality, peaceful coexistence, and sustainable development.
The rise in regional conflicts is cause for deep concern.
We call for sustainable diplomatic solutions to secure lasting peace in Ukraine, the Middle East, Sudan and Eastern DRC.

We welcome the ceasefire framework and stabilization arrangements in Gaza and call for sustained engagement to achieve a lasting solution based on the 1967 borders, where Israelis and Palestinians coexist in peace and harmony.
Regarding the broader conflict in the Gulf, we urge all parties to intensify efforts toward a speedy resolution, as its economic impact is dire and devastating.
For humanity cannot continue to bear the high cost of these wars.

We should draw inspiration from the wisdom of Chief Mohlomi, one of our renowned diplomats, who advised Morena Moshoeshoe, the founding father of the Basotho Nation, that “it is better to thrash corn than sharpen the spear.”
As the United Nations, we must continue investing in conflict prevention and building strong democratic institutions grounded in good governance and respect for international law.
My delegation continues to call for the lifting of longstanding unilateral coercive measures on Cuba and Zimbabwe.
These measures are unjust and deprive innocent civilians of their right to development.
In conclusion, Lesotho firmly believes that cooperation, solidarity, and shared responsibility are the only viable path toward a peaceful, prosperous, and sustainable future.
Let us recommit ourselves to a multilateral system that delivers tangible results for humanity, protects our planet, promotes peace and international security and ensures that no one is left behind.
By joining the United Nations, we reaffirmed our strong commitment to the global order based on international law, territorial integrity, state sovereignty, and human dignity.
It was a glorious moment for a nation well taught by historical experience that freedom and independence cannot be taken for granted.
They must be constantly – and consistently – defended.
Today, I am standing here to speak for the same dream that inspired Lithuania in 1991.
The vision of a more just, secure, and peaceful world.
Today, I am backing up the principles of the United Nations which, sadly, are being put under increasing pressure.
Recent years have brought us numerous high-intensity and far-reaching conflicts that dominate the global affairs on a scale not seen in decades.
We witness geopolitical instability in Europe, the Middle East, and elsewhere.
It is made worse by growing nuclear ambitions in the Middle East and Asia, as well as the irresponsible transfer of military-related goods, dual-use items, and sensitive technologies.
In recent months, Iran has continued attacking neighbouring countries, often through its proxies, while actively impairing the freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.
These actions constitute a serious threat to regional and international peace and security.
We reaffirm our full solidarity with the Gulf Cooperation Council states and Jordan.
We call on Iran to halt its nuclear and missile programs, as well as its collaboration with armed groups across the Middle East.
Lithuania commends all efforts to find a solution ensuring the freedom of navigation.
We will contribute with our demining capabilities to the international maritime missions in the Strait of Hormuz.
As regards the situation in the Gaza Strip, my country supports international efforts to maintain and consolidate the ceasefire.
The Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict, including the deployment of the temporary International Stabilisation Force, provides the guidelines to follow.
Lithuania reiterates the importance of full demilitarisation and calls on Hamas and other non-state armed groups to disarm and permanently decommission their weapons.
Humanitarian aid must also be allowed to reach those in need safely, and without obstruction.
To this day, the two-state solution remains the only way towards a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace.
In this light, it is crucially important to abstain from any further actions incompatible with a credible political process.
The one conflict that poses the greatest threat to the world order is Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, supported by its proxies.

In the twelve years since the illegal occupation of Crimea, Russia has escalated from clandestine operations and limited warfare in Eastern Ukraine to massive military operations, mass killings, and, ultimately, the largest drone attacks against civilian infrastructure the world has ever seen.
The current stage of the war, which began with the full-scale invasion in February 2022, has already lasted longer than the First World War.
In the last 55 months, Russia has suffered 1.5 million military casualties.
In the last year, it has gained 0.3 percent of Ukraine’s territory at the cost of over 400 thousand soldiers killed and wounded.
Yet all these enormous efforts, all that blood and tears, basically came to nothing.
Ukraine is still standing proudly as an independent state.
The Ukrainian language, culture, and national identity are alive and thriving.
In all but name, Russia has already lost the war.
Yet its leadership does not allow itself to admit defeat, fearing international legal accountability and possible revenge from its own people.
As the inevitable approaches, the stakes get higher, and the Kremlin regime increasingly finds itself cornered.
How much more Ukrainian civilian lives will be sacrificed on Russia’s war altar?
How many people will be tortured, sexually assaulted, thrown into dark dungeons, never to see the sunlight again?
How many children will be illegally separated from their parents and sent to Russia to suffer indoctrination?
We do not know the answers, yet we must all feel the deep pain brought by this brutal and pointless war.
And we all should join our forces to draw Ukraine’s victory closer.

For it is only Ukraine’s final victory, safeguarding its sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity, that could ensure the global peace, security, and the credibility of the United Nations charter.
What we cannot allow is a brute force prevailing over international law.
We cannot tolerate any longer Moscow’s colonial aspirations, which undermine global food security and driving up food prices.
Russia’s imperial ambitions reach far into Europe, Africa, and Asia.
No country should consider itself immune from this threat.
Naturally, Lithuania witnesses many dangers up close.
In recent months, Russia’s war of aggression has led to numerous violations of our air space by combat drones.
Russia has also intensified hybrid attacks, disinformation, and sabotage efforts.
Where Russia advances, opening Pandora’s box of new techniques for destabilization, other hostile actors follow, learning new skills and ideas.
Attacks on information integrity pose an especially troubling challenge to every society.
Disinformation, foreign information manipulation and interference, and the falsification of history erode trust, restrict civic space, and target journalists and human rights defenders.
As a result, human rights, democracy, and security suffer.
This risk is further enhanced by the development of artificial intelligence.
As we all know, AI has a huge potential for transformation, especially in the field of economy.
Whole sectors, including those related to defence and security, might get radically changed or destroyed almost overnight.
As any instrument, AI is also increasingly used by those seeking to cause harm and destruction.
Lithuania strongly believes that the future of AI must not be determined by authoritarian control, technological coercion, or the malicious use of data.

We are therefore investing in trusted AI capabilities, promoting responsible AI deployment, and advancing the Vilnius Convention – the world’s first legally binding international treaty on artificial intelligence.
By demonstrating how shared principles can be translated into concrete legal commitments, we hope to contribute significantly to the United Nations Global Dialogue on AI Governance.
Lithuania invites the international community to unite in addressing significant legal, ethical, and strategic challenges posed by artificial intelligence.
With even major technology companies sending warning signals that control of AI might slip out of humanity’s hands, the time is ripe for collective action.
Together, we must ensure that AI serves human dignity, sustainable development, and international security, rather than becoming a new instrument of inequality, manipulation, or conflict.
At any cost, human accountability, law, and peace and security must be safeguarded.

international The credibility of the United Nations depends on its ability to respond firmly to aggression, unlawful conquest, forced deportations, and crimes against humanity, and also to coordinate the global response to the growth of AI.
If we are serious about preserving peace, we must defend justice and strongly support those fighting for their freedom.

I am grateful to the Secretary General, His Excellency António Guterres, for his long-lasting service and his focus on reforming the United Nations into a more effective, modern, and responsive organization.
This is the correct path to follow.
No nation can confront today’s challenges alone. Aggression cannot win.
It is only through multilateralism, solidarity, and the unity of all Member States that we can uphold peace, security, and the rules-based international order.
It is also important to learn from the many lessons of history.
Today, too many seem unwilling to recognize and confront the past crimes committed by totalitarian regimes, including Soviet crimes.
We must remember the past so as not to repeat it!
That is why Lithuania is promoting the concept of historical remembrance.
My personal wish is to see the Pan-European Memorial to all victims of the 20th century totalitarian regimes unveiled in Brussels as soon as possible.
There is one lesson Lithuania, having survived and overcome numerous occupations and waves of repression, can share with the international community.
Freedom can be delayed, but it cannot be extinguished; justice can be challenged, but it cannot be defeated.
This, I believe, is a message that goes far beyond an experience of a single person, or a nation.
It speaks to the whole humankind, united in our shared dignity.
At a time of growing global uncertainty and power politics, we need even more multilateralism grounded in international law, the UN Charter, and universal human rights.
We need to resist the law of the strongest collectively, in order not to fall under the yoke separately.
The time to act is now.
And I believe – I want to believe – that we have what it takes to make the world a more just, secure, and peaceful place to live!
When I try to paint an honest picture of the world we live in, one thing strikes me in particular: trust is under growing strain. Trust between nations. Trust between people.
And, perhaps most importantly, trust in our ability to work together.
And yet, I believe that trust is precisely where we should begin.
But because every lasting achievement of the international community has begun with a decision to trust.
This is my first address to this Assembly as Head of State of the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg.
I assumed office less than a year ago.

It is therefore a particular honour to stand before you today, and to reaffirm from this podium the importance Luxembourg attaches to the United Nations and to a rules-based international order grounded in the rule of law.
But this moment also makes me reflect on what the United Nations means from the perspective of my own generation.
As a relatively young man who has had the privilege of travelling the world, I have been fortunate to meet people from very different cultures, backgrounds and traditions.
These experiences have left me with a simple and lasting conviction: We can learn a lot from each other.
And I remain convinced that it is only by working together that we can overcome the many challenges our world is facing today.
I am fully aware of the difficulties confronting us.
But precisely because the world is becoming more difficult, I believe we must resist the temptation to give up on cooperation.
There has never been a time when communication between people in different parts of the world was so easy.
Millions of young people have virtual friends and acquaintances across continents through social media, gaming and countless other forms of connection.
We have never been so connected, and yet we seem increasingly unable to trust one another.
Is it still possible to build a world order in which respect and the willingness to work towards common goals can prevail over the pursuit of self-interest and power?
But it will require determination, dialogue and a willingness to look beyond immediate interests.
And this is why the United Nations matters.
Luxembourg has believed in this principle from the very beginning.

Eighty-one years ago, still deeply marked by the horrors of the Second World War, Luxembourg was among the 51 founding members that came together in San Francisco to lay the foundations of a new international order.
At the time, we were the smallest country represented.
We have prospered in the peace that Europe enjoyed for decades after 1945.
And we have never forgotten that this peace could not be taken for granted.
It was built, generation after generation, by those who chose cooperation over confrontation.
Today, that peace is being challenged once again.
Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine has brought war back to our continent.
It is a stark reminder that peace requires constant commitment, and that the principles on which our international order was built must be defended.
The United Nations itself was born from that choice.
Its Charter called upon us to unite our strength to maintain international peace and security and, above all, to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war.
Eighty-one years later, that promise is under considerable pressure.
But disenchantment should lead us to reform, not to dismissal.
The question is therefore not whether we still need multilateralism.
The question is whether we have the courage to make it better.
This brings me to a question that is particularly close to my heart: What kind of world do we wish to leave to future generations?
We often speak of young people as if they belonged to the future.
In reality, they are already shaping our present.
And we must ask ourselves whether we are preparing a future that is worthy of their trust.
My personal experience has only strengthened this conviction.
This year, I had the privilege of succeeding His Majesty King Carl Gustaf of Sweden as Honorary Chairman of the World Scout Foundation.
My long-standing commitment to the scout movement has taught me a great deal about the strength of exchanges between generations, about solidarity and the values of scouting.
It has also taught me one essential thing: to trust young people is to give them responsibilities and enable them to act.
They are growing up today in a world where the possibilities are extraordinary, but where uncertainty is also profound.
Artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies are already transforming the way we live and work.
The enthusiasm they arouse is also accompanied by real concerns.
The current debates on the most extreme risks of artificial intelligence remind us that technological progress does not come without responsibilities.
Faced with these transformations, we must empower young people to develop their critical thinking and creativity.
That is precisely the role of education: to impart knowledge and skills, but also to teach people to question, to open themselves to others and to take responsibility.
In such a context, I believe one principle must guide us: we must keep the human being at the centre of our decisions.
We must protect the rights, safety and well-being of everyone.
We must also listen to young people and ask them what we can build together with them.

Across cultures and generations, I have seen all that young people are capable of achieving when they are given the trust, the responsibilities and the space they need to act, and when they are encouraged to work together.
That is why Luxembourg supports the United Nations Youth Delegates Programme and the United Nations Office for Youth.
That is also why our commitment to education, science and culture remains so important, notably through our mandate on the Executive Board of UNESCO for the period 2025-2029.
These are precisely the qualities that allow trust to grow.
Luxembourg’s engagement with the United Nations is rooted in its three pillars: peace and security, human rights and development.
Solidarity must also be translated into action.
We continue to devote 1 per cent of our national income to development cooperation and to build long-term partnerships with countries in situations of vulnerability.
We remain committed to the multilateral humanitarian system and to those who provide assistance where it is most needed.
The same responsibility applies to peace and security.
Conflicts affect human beings above all: women and children, older persons, persons with disabilities and all those who are already vulnerable.
The protection of civilians and the defence of human rights cannot become secondary considerations.

Luxembourg has consistently sought to contribute to this effort: through peacekeeping operations and humanitarian action, the protection of children affected by armed conflict, the Women and Peace and Security agenda, and humanitarian mine action in Ukraine.
Our experience as an elected member of the Security Council in 2013 and 2014 showed us that elected members can make a real difference, especially when the permanent members are divided.
That is why Luxembourg seeks the confidence of Member States to serve on the Security Council for the period 2031-2032.

We do so with humility, but also with conviction: the conviction that a small country can bring a different perspective, bring positions closer together and help find common ground when that is most difficult.
That same conviction guides our commitment to human rights.
At a time when respect for human rights is under increasing pressure, we must resist the temptation to regard them as negotiable.
Human rights are neither the privilege of some nor the expression of a particular culture or political system.
They are the foundation of human dignity.
As a member of the Human Rights Council from 2022 to 2024, Luxembourg was able to measure directly the importance of defending human rights through multilateral action.
We continue to support the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, as well as efforts to establish the fate of missing persons in Syria.
Restoring trust also means making our institutions worthy of that trust.
The Security Council must become more representative, more effective and more accountable to the entire membership of the United Nations.
Africa, in particular, should have a stronger voice.
And when the Security Council is paralysed, the General Assembly must be able to play its rightful role.
The United Nations must reform so that it can deliver more effectively, particularly when resources are constrained.
But reform must never become an end in itself.
The purpose of institutions is to serve people.
Ultimately, the test of multilateralism is not how many resolutions we adopt or how many meetings we hold.
It is whether a child is safer because of our decisions.
Whether a young person can receive an education.
Whether a family can live in dignity.
Whether a small country can believe that international law will protect it when power alone cannot.
And this is why Luxembourg will continue to defend multilateralism.
Because we know what happens when it fails.
Climate change reminds us perhaps more clearly than any other challenge that we cannot solve global problems by acting alone.
Small Island Developing States are already experiencing consequences that threaten their very existence.
Luxembourg may be landlocked, but we are deeply committed to this common effort, including by drawing on the expertise of our financial centre in green finance.
Our interests may differ, but our future is shared.
The world is becoming more fragmented.
The international order is under strain.
We need to recognise this reality.
But we should not mistake a world of competing centres of power for a more just or stable international order.
For Luxembourg, the answer is clear.
Our experience has taught us that international law and multilateral institutions give countries, whatever their size, a voice and a place at the table.
It’s not about resisting a changing world, but to make multilateralism fit for that world.
I believe this is ultimately what the United Nations asks of us.
Not that we agree on everything.
Not that we abandon our national interests.
But that we recognise that there are challenges for which no nation, however powerful, can find lasting solutions alone.
We can look at the imperfections of multilateralism and conclude that it no longer works.
Or we can reform it fairly, strengthen it, and make it worthy of the trust that future generations will place in us.
I know which choice I want to make.

Because this is the world I want to leave to my children: a world where dialogue is stronger than confrontation; where respect between nations allows differences to become a source of strength rather than division; where international law protects the weak as well as the strong; If we restore trust, if we listen to the next generation, and if we have the courage to act together, the United Nations can continue to be more than a reflection of the world as it is.
It can remain an instrument for building the world we want to leave behind.
A world worthy of the trust of those who will inherit it.
Young people do not expect us to solve every challenge.
But they do expect us to try.
They expect us to act with responsibility.
And above all, they expect us not to lose faith in our ability to shape a better future.
And that is the promise we should make to the next generation.
I am looking forward to working together for a stronger United Nations and a safer world.
Excellencies, for the past year we have heard it again and again: the world order is breaking down.
The rules-based order that brought stability is under growing strain.
What comes next is not certain, but one thing is certain: the world has changed.
International trade, mobility, technology—what happens far away is no longer far away. Instability travels.
What happens in Ukraine does not stay in Ukraine.
What happens in the Middle East, in the Red Sea, in Sudan—does not stay there.
The same is true of other global threats.
Technology has made distance matter even less.
Artificial intelligence offers enormous opportunities, but in the wrong hands it can also become a powerful tool for deception, disruption, and conflict.
And nature respects no borders either.
Heat waves do not stop at checkpoints.
Rising seas threaten to erase island nations.
That threat means that those island nations may disappear from the face of the Earth.
And far from the ocean, the danger is just as real.
In the mountains, a river can turn into a deadly flood.
These floods sweep away homes, roads, and lives.
We just witnessed the catastrophic flood wave in Nepal, where also 33 Latvian citizens disappeared.
Global climate change does not have borders or citizenship.
Different threats, the same lesson: none of us can face them alone.
We are in the same boat.
Perhaps Noah's Ark is no longer just a biblical story.
Different nations, different realities, but increasingly a shared fate.
And when we share the same boat, we need something that holds us together.
And we already have it: the United Nations Charter and its principles.
Sovereignty, territorial integrity, the peaceful settlement of disputes, respect for human rights, the rejection of aggression.
These principles were not written for an easy world.
They emerged from the devastation of a war, and from the determination not to repeat it.
International peace and security— these words are at the heart of the Charter.
They appear 32 times, and that is no coincidence.
And peace will be relevant tomorrow.
Latvia and its people know what it means to lose sovereignty, what it means to lose freedom.
For 50 years, our independence was denied, but Latvia's right to sovereignty endured.
We restored it through the courage and determination of our people.
And we did not stand alone.
We had friends who never accepted Soviet occupation as legitimate.
Sovereignty and territorial integrity are the foundation of our freedom and our security.
And the same is true for every country represented in this hall.
When one state believes it can redraw the borders of another by force, every border, on every continent, becomes negotiable.
These principles now are being tested in Ukraine.
Russia's war against Ukraine strikes at the very heart of the United Nations Charter.
Schools, hospitals, homes, markets, energy infrastructure.
Russia's attacks reach far beyond the battlefield.
They are directed against the people of Ukraine and their foundations of daily lives.
Drones are used to hunt civilians.
Human lives are treated like targets in a safari.
These are grave violations of international law.
And where crimes are committed, there must be accountability.
Russia is a permanent member of the Security Council.
With that comes a special responsibility for international peace and security.
Instead, Russia is violating the very principles it is entrusted to uphold.
It can leave Ukraine's sovereign territory.
Latvia continues to call for an immediate and full ceasefire.
Members of the United Nations, not every attack on the international order looks like war.
Drones crashing into homes. Airspace violated. Critical infrastructure damaged.
Power stations suddenly in flames. Cyber attacks.
We sometimes call them hybrid threats.
But it sounds as innocent as hybrid cars.
In reality, those threats to international peace and security are as dangerous as conventional wars.
Guarding the eastern border of NATO and the European Union, Latvia faces these threats every day.
Illegal migrants are deliberately exploited and pushed toward our border with Belarus.
Cyber attacks target our critical networks.
Acts of sabotage seek to create fear and instability in our societies.
Russia's shadow fleet exploits legal gray zones and puts our security and environment at risk.
Even in this very building, at the Security Council table, we have heard Russia spread blatant lies and make threats against Latvia and other free and democratic countries.
Distinguished delegates, that brings us back to a fundamental question: what is the United Nations' role if its members are threatened and if its principles are violated?
The United Nations cannot take its relevance for granted.
It must earn it, day by day.
Not through the number of meetings we hold.
Not through the number of resolutions we adopt.
The United Nations must prove that it can still make a difference when it matters most.
Latvia supports the Secretary-General's UNAIDA initiative.
Reform is not about weakening the United Nations.
It is about making it stronger, more focused, and better able to deliver on its mandate.
That must include also the Security Council.
Its composition must better reflect the world of today, not the world of 1945.
Latvia supports an expanded and more representative Security Council.
Excellencies, reform is also about leadership.
This year we will select the next Secretary-General. The choice matters.
The next Secretary-General must defend the Charter with conviction.
He must, or she must, uphold international law.
That is what true leadership means: to speak up for the weak against the powerful.
Dear colleagues, Latvia now serves as an elected member of the Security Council, and we will hold our presidency in November.
Latvia came to the Council with a simple promise: to stand up for international order.
To speak clearly when it is violated.
And to make the voices of smaller nations heard.
That reflects who Latvia is, and that reflects what Latvia believes in.
At the core are real people.
That is why Latvia will continue to do everything possible to help return Ukrainian children deported to Russia.
Those children have been taken from their families, their communities, and their country.
We know such stories from the darkest chapters of history.
Today, those things are happening again.
We support every genuine effort to secure the return of Ukrainian children.
We are very grateful to the First Lady of the United States, Melania Trump, and her efforts to help bring those children home.
These children need to come home now.
The most vulnerable must be protected.
And this includes conflict-related sexual violence. Survivors need justice.
These priorities underpin Latvia's bid for a seat on the Human Rights Council at 2028 elections.
Mr. President, Excellencies, we need a place where every state, large or small, has a voice.
Where threats to peace can be confronted together.
Where disputes can be resolved through dialogue, not force.
Where international law protects the strong and the weak alike.
That was the promise of the United Nations 81 years ago.
It is not a Christmas wish for this year.
We must stand by our principles, always.
But our fundamental purpose has not.
And the fundamental purpose is to maintain international peace and security.
And this organization is worth reforming so that this organization can deliver.
Let us make the United Nations work for peace, for security, and for all of us.

I also commend the tireless efforts of Secretary General Antonio Guterres, since he assumed the leadership of our organization amid the major divisions the world has experienced over the past decade, he has emerged as a voice of wisdom, consensus and pragmatism, defending tirelessly and courageously the United Nations system and international law as the two fundamental pillars for the maintenance of international peace and security.
Mr. Guterres has remained a symbol of multilateral diplomacy and of international cooperation in overcoming the turmoil and obstacles facing our world today.
May God assist him when His Majesty said, and I quote, the world is changing at an unprecedented pace and certainties are steadily receding.
This has led to a blurring of standards and concepts.
Alliances have become open to question.
And its capacity to regulate international relations faces numerous challenges.
End of quote from His Majesty the King We are therefore facing a world whose fundamental features are the following.
First, the escalation of acute and diverse international crises military, economic, energy related and environmental.
Second, the spread of confrontational tendencies as a key determinant of relations between states.
Third, the difficulty of predicting the outcome of crises.
We know when they begin but not when they will end.
Fourth, the diminishing capacity of existing regulatory structures to play the role in preventing and managing crises in this complex international context.
Mr. president, I wish to focus on three areas to which the international community must accord priority.
First, confronting non-state armed groups as a threat to international security and stability.
Second, addressing climate change and its effects.
Third, tackling regional challenges, particularly in the Middle East and Africa.
The role of non-state armed groups that threaten the security and stability of states has grown considerably.
Indeed, they now seek to control maritime corridors and straits and to threaten freedom of navigation.
They also target facilities in a number of countries.
At the global level, more than 200 million people live in areas under the control of armed groups or in contested areas.
Moreover, more than 130 non-state armed groups have been identified as legally classified parties to armed conflicts.
These figures clearly reflect the scale of the spread and proliferation of these groups.
In a world that, over the past two decades has become less secure and less stable.

Further, the close links between these armed groups and separatist militias on the one hand, and terrorist organizations and criminal networks, as well as mercenary elements, on the other hand, are evident to all.
It is therefore a mistake to believe that some of these groups are peaceful or constructive, or that they can engage in the settlement of conflicts.
All these groups use violence to impose a fait accompli and to serve the agenda of those who control them.
They must therefore be dealt with firmly, and responsibility must be assigned to the states that sponsor Harbour Finance and armed them, and provide them with safe haven and support.
The responsibility of these sponsoring states is not merely political, it is also legal, moral and historical.
These groups and their sponsors alike cannot be allowed to become a means of evading responsibility or a tool for carrying out what states cannot do directly.
Hence, deterrent sanctions must be imposed on these groups and their sponsors.
All those who provide them with support, financing or arms must be held accountable.
Mr. president, there can be no way to sustain peace and development without effectively addressing the challenge of climate change, which is no longer a future threat.
It is already affecting water and food security, as well as the stability of territories, economies and the living conditions of populations.
Despite its limited contribution to greenhouse gas emissions, Morocco remains among the countries most vulnerable to the impacts of climate change.

Accordingly, in line with the vision of His Majesty King Mohammed VI, may God assist him The Kingdom has adopted a proactive policy based on the continued construction of dams, the interconnection of water basins, seawater desalination, the reuse of treated wastewater and the rationalization of water resource management, particularly in the agricultural sector.
This national effort forms part of an international commitment to climate action.

On that basis, the Kingdom has set for the period 2026 2035, a target of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by up to 53% by 2035, while placing adaptation and the strengthening of territorial resilience at the top of its priorities.
This effort has extended to the African continent, which suffers from the devastating effects of climate change.

The Royal Initiative to establish three African climate commissions for the Congo Basin the Sahel region and the African island states, has generated promising momentum to strengthen African climate action and coordination among the states of the continent in addressing these challenges.
However, addressing climate change cannot rely on national efforts alone.

It requires the provision of affordable and accessible financing, technology transfer and genuine international solidarity, enabling developing countries to fulfill their responsibilities towards present and future generations alike.

The theme of this 81st session calls on us to assume our shared responsibility for our destiny and that of future generations with lucidity, by placing collective action, the general interest and the good of humanity at the centre of our responses to the profound transformations of the world.
At the same time, we must recognize that the challenges we have been facing for decades, namely food insecurity, disease, armed conflict and natural disasters, are still with us.
Thus, for Madagascar, as for many other nations, the new emerging challenges cannot obscure the prioritizations that must be made.
In the light of intersecting transformations and challenges, the question of trust in our collective action arises with renewed urgency.
Indeed, we must admit, taking into account all the consideration and expectations that we, “the Peoples of the United Nations”, have placed in our Organization, that trust has, over time, eroded.

The most vulnerable populations, struck by the recurrence or persistence of health crises, food insecurity or hunger, the impacts of climate disruption, as well as conflicts aggravated by current geopolitical tensions, sometimes come to feel a certain scepticism as to our collective capacity, within the United Nations System, to provide responses to the scourges that mark our era.
In this regard, the realities on the ground in my country speak for themselves.
In the South of Madagascar, mothers travel dozens of kilometres under scorching heat in search of water in the bed of a dried-up river.
In the East, each year increasingly violent and devastating tropical cyclones sweep away crops, infrastructure and human lives in their path.
In other localities, floods engulf rice granaries, affecting entire regions.
These images illustrate the daily vulnerability of the population.

Faced with these recurrent humanitarian emergency situations, amplified by climate disruption, considerable investments, testifying to the constancy of the commitment of our development partners, are made each year in support of the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) — whether in the fight against hunger, education, or access by vulnerable populations to basic services.
Indeed, Madagascar today hosts 23 agencies of the United Nations System, each of which contributes to supporting our national priorities.
The implementation of the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNDAF) for the period 2024-2028 will mobilize 1.5 billion dollars over five years.
Yet, beyond the commitments and resources mobilized, what matters to us is their concrete translation into the daily lives of our populations.

We acknowledge that, in order to participate fully in the governance of his or her country and benefit equitably from his or her rights, every citizen must be able to grow up in good health, be well nourished and have access to quality education.
Faced with the challenges of a constantly changing world, the government of the Refondation that I lead places food sovereignty, health and education at the heart of its action.

This priority commitment is directed to the entire population and particularly to women and children, while offering our youth the means to build their future with confidence and thus contribute to the development of the nation.
With more than 55 per cent of its population under the age of 25, Madagascar benefits from a tremendous demographic dividend.

Driven by a firm political will to build a bright future for this dynamic youth, we measure the importance of an education system in perfect alignment with the realities of the labour market, a sine qua non condition for sustainable development.

We wish cooperation in this field to move beyond a strictly quantitative approach — measured solely by the volume of infrastructure built or the number of pupils enrolled — so as to adapt fully to economic realities on the ground.

It is a matter of anchoring our action in the sectors of the future (such as agro-industry, renewable energies and digital technology), while recasting our indicators of success to give priority to the concrete acquisition of skills and the rate of integration medium-term professional integration.
However, the achievement of our ambitions cannot be dissociated from the international context in which they are situated.
Can we speak of development when international peace and security are put to the test by the multiplication of crises and the persistence of tensions?
The restoration of confidence depends on the capacity of the United Nations to maintain and restore peace.
We must be concerned that the multilateral system is struggling to contain the escalation of tensions fuelled by geopolitical rivalries.

These are all factors that exacerbate the vulnerabilities we must confront.
Faced with this reality, we must have the courage to acknowledge and accept the limits of the multilateral system in its current form and functioning.
There is an urgent need to initiate concerted and lasting action to guarantee every people its right to pursue its development in dignity and stability.
Far from observing the world as a passive spectator, Madagascar positions itself as an actor fully aware of its strategic place and its responsibilities.
Our country remains a committed and operational partner in the service of peace, development and security.
Maritime security in the Mozambique Channel and the Western Indian Ocean remains at the heart of the regional initiatives in which Madagascar diligently takes part.

We are resolved to intensify regional and multilateral cooperation founded on respect for national sovereignties, while welcoming partnerships that align with our priorities and that constitute genuine levers for development in order to produce tangible results for our populations.
Our commitment remains constant: to cooperate, to act, to produce convincing results, in respect for our sovereignty.
We thus wish to take part in strengthened multilateral and regional mobilization, in order to guarantee the security of our maritime spaces.

What United Nations cooperation should we put in place to support the contemporary transformation of this world?
We must look to the future with greater, more openly embraced ambition.
To guarantee a lasting and measurable impact in the medium and long term, we must take a new step: that of greater, more integrated and better coordinated solidarity.
Madagascar advocates for a multilateral system not only capable of acting but also capable of supporting Member States in their efforts to break the cycles of poverty and insecurity.
My country aspires to an international order founded on the primacy of international law, confident in the virtues of dialogue and diplomatic action.
Our attachment to multilateral cooperation remains unwavering.
Multilateralism constitutes a privileged forum where States unite in collective responsibility.

It enables them to define common and appropriate solutions, both in the face of unpredictable hazards — such as epidemics and climate disasters — and in the face of armed conflicts arising from contemporary geopolitical rivalries or resulting from latent, multifaceted tensions.

History and posterity will judge our Organization by a single criterion: its capacity to accomplish its original mission, to serve all peoples, without exclusion or privilege, in respect for the sovereignty of nations.
It is imperative to restore to the United Nations their full centrality as guardians of peace — a strengthened institution, capable of restoring order and meeting the challenges of our time.

The challenge before us at present is therefore to rethink our cooperation mechanisms through greater synergy between the United Nations agencies and State structures in order to optimize the effectiveness of our actions in the field, but also to provide greater visibility to the concrete results achieved for the benefit of the population.

With this in mind, the success of our agenda depends in large part on the consolidation of governance and the strengthening of institutions — priorities fully integrated into the dynamics of Refoundation in Madagascar.
We acknowledge that it is absolutely necessary to carry out reform of the United Nations so that it may be at the service of all peoples.
We would therefore like to propose the following:

- More inclusive global governance This must begin with the rebalancing of decision-making powers, first and foremost the General Assembly, to which it is necessary to restore its full political strength and its full place at the heart of global governance.
It remains, indeed, the only body where every nation, whatever its power, has a sovereign and equal voice.
We must then correct the historical imbalance affecting Africa’s representation on the Security Council.
Indeed, with its 1.4 billion inhabitants, it cannot remain on the margins of decisions concerning international peace and security.

Africa must be granted permanent representation on the Security Council, in accordance with the Ezulwini Consensus and the Declaration of Sirte, which express a common position based on a demand for justice, equity and representativeness.

There is also a need to strengthen the coherence between the programmes implemented by the offices of the United Nations Resident Coordinators and national priorities: United Nations country teams must be attentive in order to respond precisely and effectively to the priorities defined by host Governments, while avoiding one-size-fits-all approaches.
- A more accessible international financial architecture for effective support for development We must not overlook the reform of the international financial architecture.
This consists in rebalancing access to financing.
The current criteria for the allocation of aid and loans are often based solely on GDP per capita, excluding many vulnerable countries.
The United Nations must therefore take into consideration the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index (MVI) so that access to concessional financing takes account of climate shocks and external debt.
It would also be advisable to support sustainable debt relief.

This consists in advocating for a sovereign debt restructuring mechanism that is faster, more predictable and inclusive, enabling vulnerable countries to invest in the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) rather than repaying unsustainable interest.
There is also a need to drastically simplify the procedures for access to United Nations funds in order to reduce disbursement delays.
For a vulnerable State struck by a crisis, administrative slowness destroys confidence in the effectiveness of multilateralism.
- Effectiveness in the face of climate and humanitarian emergencies The multilateral system that we should put in place should guarantee the fulfilment of climate financing commitments.

It should serve as a catalyst and a guarantor to ensure that developed countries honour their commitments on climate finance (particularly for adaptation and the Loss and Damage Fund) for the benefit of the nations most exposed.
It is also important to link emergency aid to long-term structural investments.

By taking ownership of this theme, we are making a commitment: that of not postponing the essential reforms needed to enable our Organization to act with all the integrity required in the face of the challenges of our time, building on the achievements of the eighty-one years of the United Nations.
If our forefathers were able to build an Organization suited to their time, it is now incumbent upon us to refound it so as to meet the challenges of today and those of tomorrow.
Let us pass on to future generations an Organization that brings together, that protects and that acts.
For its part, Madagascar is preparing, at the national level, a framework conducive to these commitments and to the effective implementation of this transformation.

Indeed, the process of refoundation undertaken following the mobilization of Malagasy youth exactly one year ago is the fertile ground for responsible governance, supported by strong institutions, devoted to the general interest and having restored citizens' trust in the State.
It is a genuine patriotic awakening, driven by a deep conviction that sustainable development requires that every citizen fully find his or her place within the Nation.

To give concrete form to this vision, we have initiated a historic process of inclusive national consultation bringing together all the driving forces of the Nation: young people, women, persons with disabilities, political parties, civil society, the armed forces and the private sector.
We have established a clear timetable.
Our objective is to succeed in holding free, transparent and universally accepted elections before the end of the year 2027.

Indeed, we know that in this endeavour we can count, on the one hand, on the fraternal support of the countries of the southern African region with the unwavering support of the Southern African Development Community (SADC) and, on the other hand, on the support of our bilateral and multilateral partners committed alongside us since the very first steps of this Refoundation.
Long live international cooperation and solidarity, Long live the United Nations.
This year’s theme, “Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all”, captures the task before us.
Trust will not be restored by words alone.
It will be restored by what this Organization delivers for every country, large or small.
Thirty-seven years ago, the Maldives asked this Assembly to face a simple truth: That “Small States can be highly vulnerable to external threats and acts of influence.”

In response, this Assembly adopted Resolution forty-four, fifty- one an initiative led by the Maldives, affirming the importance of protecting the sovereignty and territorial integrity of small States.
That was true then and it is true even today.
Insecurity now travels through sea lanes, supply chains, financial markets, digital networks and new technologies.
Today, sovereignty can be weakened without a single border being crossed.
It can be undermined when external powers limit a State’s freedom to choose.
This is why the Maldives comes before this Assembly with a clear message: “Every State, large or small must have the freedom and capacity to shape its own future.”
And that future begins with peace.
The Indian Ocean must remain peaceful.
It must remain as a region where trade can flow and where States can prosper.
Regional competition among major powers must not limit the choices of smaller States.
Conflict does not have to reach our shores to affect us.
In today’s interconnected world, a crisis far away can quickly become a crisis at home.
Interruption to maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz raises fuel prices.
It affects food supplies and air travel.
The consequences of this are felt across tourism and public finances in the Maldives.
The Maldives condemns the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
