The Strait must remain open and safe.
The Maldives further condemns the attacks on Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman and Jordan.
The Maldives appreciates the diplomatic efforts of Oman, Pakistan and Qatar to de-escalate the crisis and bring the parties to dialogue.
The right to a sovereign future must belong to all.
And nowhere is that right more brutally denied than in Palestine.
Israel's genocide and war crimes against Palestinians continue.
And their actions are not confined to Gaza.
Its military attacks across the region have violated the sovereignty of other States.
Security cannot be built by exporting insecurity.
Nor can any country demand respect for its sovereignty while violating the sovereignty of others.
No State should be shielded from accountability by its power or political alliances.
But condemnation alone is not enough.
Every Member State must ask: What have we done to end this violence?
The United Nations must ask itself the same question.
The problem is not a lack of law.
What is absent, is equal application.
International law cannot bind the weak and bend for the powerful. The same rules. The same standard. No exceptions.
Israel’s genocide in Gaza must end.
Israel’s illegal occupation of Palestine and other Arab lands must end.
Humanitarian assistance must reach Palestinians safely, rapidly and at scale.
And the decisions of international courts and the resolutions of this Organization must be respected and implemented.
For the Palestinian people, a sovereign future means freedom dignity.
And the right to live with security in their own State.
The Maldives will always stand with the Palestinian people and their undeniable right for that future.
That is why I reiterate our call for the recognition of an independent and sovereign State of Palestine, based on the pre- 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital.
And if this Organisation is to restore trust and deliver for all, Palestine must become a full Member of the United Nations.
Conflict is not the only threat to sovereignty.
Forces beyond our borders can also limit a State’s freedom to shape its own future.
For SIDS like the Maldives, none is more consequential than climate change.
For SIDS, climate change is altering the very physical foundations of our nations.
Sea level rise is therefore not simply an environmental concern.
It is a matter of national planning and national security.
It is a matter of sovereignty.
Rising seas may alter our shores.
But they will not erase our statehood.
They will not reduce our rights.
They will not weaken our maritime entitlements.
And they will not diminish our national agency.
Our response must be to adapt innovate and build.
But resilience demands the means to act.
That means finance must reach those who need it.
And on the terms needed to build resilience.
That is why COP31 in Antalya must be a COP of delivery.
Implementation must be the measure of commitment.
We must speed up the 2030 Agenda.
And we must turn ABAS into measurable progress for SIDS.
For island nations, that progress cannot be separated from a healthy and sustainably managed ocean.
Therefore, the first Conference of the Parties to the BBNJ Agreement must deliver from day one.
Ultimately, global commitments matter only when they enable progress at home.
His Excellency President Dr Mohamed Muizzu has set a clear ambition: for the Maldives to become a developed country by 2040.
We are pursuing that goal by raising productivity, diversifying our economy, building resilient infrastructure, expanding renewable energy and investing in our people.
Our future will be built by Maldivians.
But the international system can widen or narrow our choices.
Technology transfer, resilient supply chains and accessible finance expand choice.
Technological dependence, external shocks and unsustainable debt limits it.
This is why reform of the international financial architecture matters.
We must implement the Sevilla Commitment and deliver on its promises on finance, debt, and reform.
Earlier this year, the Maldives joined other developing countries in launching the Borrowers’ Platform.
It must become a lasting mechanism that gives developing countries not just a place in the financial system, but a voice in shaping it.
But for SIDS, greater agency also depends on progress at home.
We must build our institutions, improve stability, and attract responsible investment and meaningful partnerships.
And these partnerships must build national capacity and support national ambitions.
Partnerships must serve national needs strengthen what we have and leave us more capable than before.
Our shared challenges can become shared opportunities.
This is the spirit of President Dr Muizzu’s Maldives First policy.
Partnerships built around respect national interests and mutual contribution.
And the same principle must guide the technological transformation before us.
For small States, AI can close distance.
And it can put better health care, education, and public services within reach.
But these opportunities must be shared.
Every country must have a voice in shaping the global rules for AI.
The digital future should strengthen our ability to serve our people better.
Not create new forms of dependence.
And as the world transforms, so must the United Nations.
The UN80 Initiative is an opportunity to reduce duplication, improve accountability, and focus resources on results.
But efficiency must not be measured simply by what we cut.
It must be measured by what we deliver.
And the United Nations must not retreat from the countries that need it most, in the name of efficiency.
Reform must preserve a meaningful UN presence on the ground, particularly in SIDS.
The UN Development System must respond to the needs of programme countries and remain guided by relevant international frameworks.
The reform process must be Member- State-led.
It must be inclusive and transparent.
This is how reform will restore trust.
By bringing the United Nations closer to the people and the countries it serves.
Reform must also confront one of this Organization’s oldest weaknesses: Unequal representation.
The Security Council cannot reflect the world of 1945 while deciding for the world of today.
It must be expanded in both permanent and non-permanent categories.
SIDS must have a rotating seat.
Africa must receive the representation long denied to it.
And the veto must be abolished.
After all, representation is not merely symbolic.
Who sits at the table shapes what the table sees.
Small States understand how closely climate, finance, trade supply chains and security are connected.
We also know that international law is our strongest safeguard against unequal power.
That principle must remain at the heart of the international system.
The Maldives will take its seat on the Economic and Social Council for the 2027 to 2029 term.
We are seeking election to the Human Rights Council for the 2028 to 2030 term.
And we seek the support of Member States for a seat on the UN Security Council for the 2033 to 2034 term.
We do so because small States must be decision-makers, not decision-takers.
Representation matters not only within the bodies of this Organization.
The process to choose his successor must be transparent and based on merit.
It must draw from the full breadth of talent available to this Organization.
For more than eight decades, every Secretary-General has been a man.
It is time for a woman to lead this Organisation.
A leader who will defend the Charter, without exception.
Who can turn reform into delivery.
And who will listen to all Member States, including the smallest.
The choice we make must meet it.
So, what should this Assembly do?
The Maldives proposes a simple test for a sovereign future.
When we act on conflict, climate, finance, technology, or institutional reform, let us ask: Does this decision expand a State’s freedom to choose?
Does it build national capacity and reduce dependence?
Does it protect sovereignty and independent decision-making?
If the answer is no, we must change course.
And we must hold every State to the same standard.
Let this be the measure of international cooperation.
Not what we promise, but what we make possible.
That is the measure of a United Nations that delivers for all.
In 1989, the Maldives asked this Assembly to protect small States from external threats.
Today, we ask it to protect something just as fundamental: Every State’s freedom to choose its own future.
A future chosen by its people.
A future grounded in international law.
A sovereign future for every State.

GENERAL DEBATE OF THE EIGHTY-FIRST SESSION OF THE GENERAL ASSEMBLY OF THE UNITED NATIONS Statement by the Secretary of Foreign Affairs of Mexico, Roberto Velasco Álvarez I appear before this Assembly on behalf of the first woman President of my country, Dr. Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo, whose government places people at the centre of State action and works, every day, for freedom, democracy, social justice and substantive equality.
Mexico guides its public life by a conviction that I bring to this rostrum today: to make shared prosperity a reality for all people.

That conviction is consistent with the commitments that we all undertook in the Charter of the United Nations, whose first article establishes as purposes the maintenance of international peace and security, the development of friendly relations among nations, and cooperation in solving economic, social, cultural and humanitarian problems, while promoting respect for human rights without distinction of any kind.

Mexico, a culture with more than three thousand years of history, is undergoing a profound transformation that continues the path opened by Independence, the Reform and the Revolution: the three moments when my country expanded the rights of its people.
My country now aspires to a prosperous society, with rights and a dignified life for all.
This is a transformation with clear purposes: to generate shared well-being, strengthen our competitiveness, develop our own capacities and decide our own destiny.

For that reason, my country comes to share the experience of a nation that decided to demonstrate, in practice, that it is possible to improve people’s quality of life by expanding their rights and their capacity to exercise them.
Allow me to highlight the progress achieved.
The first fact is the reduction of poverty.
Between 2018 and 2024, more than 13 million people escaped poverty in Mexico: the most significant reduction in the history of our country.
It is also important to emphasize that in 2025 we had the lowest level of labour poverty in our history.
That effort continues with a social policy of national scope.
In 2026, the Well-being Programmes reach 42.8 million people.
Added to this is sustained investment in infrastructure: health, railways, highways, schools and hydraulic works.
Towards 2030, the Infrastructure Investment Plan for Development with Well-being envisages investments in energy, transport, water, health, education and emerging technologies.

The second fact is security, which President Sheinbaum’s government understands from a comprehensive perspective: one that addresses the causes that push young people towards crime, as well as zero impunity.
In just 22 months, as of July 2026, intentional homicides have been reduced by around 51 per cent.

It is the result of a national security strategy that is strengthened through international cooperation in the face of shared challenges, and which, I respectfully recall, is anchored in four principles: respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity; shared and differentiated responsibility; respect and mutual trust; and cooperation without subordination.
This milestone was not achieved through the logic of war, nor by renouncing human rights or making force the only response.
Mexico combines education and employment for young people with intelligence, investigation, strengthening of institutions and the presence of the State where there had previously been abandonment.
Today we can say with pride that our progress in security distinguishes Mexico on the international stage.
That is why we maintain before this Assembly a truth that we offer to all peoples: peace is neither decreed nor imposed; it is built with social justice.
The third fact focuses on employment.
Since 2018, the minimum wage has accumulated a real increase of 154 per cent and today has reached its highest purchasing power in more than four decades.
We achieved this through dialogue among the government, workers and employers, with inflation under control and with one of the lowest unemployment rates among the economies of the OECD.
What had been denied in theory for decades was demonstrated in practice: paying those who work better does not impoverish economies; it strengthens them.
The fourth fact transformed the very history of my country.
For the first time in two centuries of independent life, Mexico is governed by a woman.
And she did not arrive alone: she arrived with a gender-parity cabinet, a gender-parity Congress and a reform that made substantive equality a constitutional mandate.
Today, the girls of Mexico are growing up knowing that they can go as far as they decide to go.
And the fifth fact is the exercise of a sovereign and independent foreign policy.
Mexico has shown that a country can cooperate closely and respectfully with its partners and, at the same time, fully assert its sovereignty.
That independence is also measured in the protection of Mexican women and men living outside our territory.
Mexico accompanies its community abroad and defends their human rights wherever they may be, always in strict adherence to international law.
Mexico’s transformation has specific recipients: those who have historically been left behind.
Our policies proceed from a clear gender perspective, promoting women’s rights.
They prioritize the poorest, Indigenous Peoples and Afro-descendants, persons with disabilities, children, older persons, and sexual and gender diversity.

Mexico’s foreign policy is anchored in the normative principles of our Constitution, which transcend the government of the day and the international situation and which our people distilled from their history.
We defend the self-determination of peoples and non-intervention, because we know that they are the best guarantee of peace and stability among nations.
We advocate the peaceful settlement of disputes and the prohibition of the threat or use of force.
We believe in the sovereign equality of States, because sovereignty is not measured in armies or material resources: all nations, all peoples, are equal before the law.
We promote international cooperation for development.
We ensure respect for, the protection of and the promotion of human rights, which are also at the heart of our Constitution.
And we strive for international peace and security, the basis for the development of peoples.
Anyone who reviews those constitutional mandates will note that they are the purposes and principles of the Charter of San Francisco, in which the imprint of Mexican diplomacy is evident.

Mexico does not need to adapt its foreign policy to the Charter of the United Nations, for it bears it written in its Constitution: when my country defends multilateralism, it is fulfilling a constitutional mandate.
It is the legacy of Benito Juárez, Venustiano Carranza and Genaro Estrada: three names, one same conviction — law as the only legitimate force among nations.
That conviction admits of no exceptions or selective recipients.

Faced with the international conflicts currently under way, Mexico maintains a firm position: international law must prevail over force, the civilian population must be protected, the territorial integrity of nations must be respected and every dispute must find an avenue in dialogue, negotiation and peace.
That is why Mexico has for decades defended the two-State solution and recognizes the State of Palestine, with the right of its people to live in peace within secure and recognized borders.
Aware that this position would be insufficient without institutions capable of upholding it, Mexico is working to strengthen this house in an environment of global polarization.

Mexico and Norway founded the UN80 Global group in support of the reform undertaken by the Secretary-General, aimed at building, through practical action, a more effective and more transparent United Nations.
With Qatar, Norway and Switzerland, we are promoting the strengthening of the Organization’s mediation capacities.
Every conflict that diplomacy prevents is worth more than all those that force seeks to resolve.
That same commitment begins in our own region.

In Latin America and the Caribbean, Mexico will continue working to preserve the character of a Zone of Peace that our peoples gave themselves, and to strengthen cooperation in forums such as CELAC and the Pacific Alliance.

Our regional vocation also explains a position that Mexico has maintained for more than six decades: solidarity with the people of Cuba and rejection of the embargo and of any unilateral economic measure contrary to the Charter of the United Nations.
We will continue sending humanitarian aid to address the most urgent needs of its population, because the fraternity between our peoples does not depend on circumstances or differences.
That same solidarity calls on us to join efforts to close regional divides on the basis of dialogue and concertation.

Beyond our hemisphere, we are strengthening our ties with Asia and Africa, and the recent modernization of our partnership with the European Union confirms that closeness with some partners has never meant distance from others.

Mexico believes in this Organization, which today faces a challenge of enormous magnitude: to renew itself in fulfilling its founding mandate to save succeeding generations from the scourge of armed conflict, protect human rights, improve the condition of millions of vulnerable people and ensure the primacy of international law.
That renewal also extends to the leadership of the Organization.
We will soon have a new person at the head of the Secretariat.
Mexico states it clearly: in the United Nations too, it is time for women.
Alfonso Reyes, diplomat and humanist, left Mexico a lesson that today we offer to this Assembly: “the only way to be profitably national is to be generously universal”.
That is the calling of our foreign policy.
Mexico knows that no nation builds its future from isolation, and that its sovereignty is strengthened through dialogue and respectful collaboration with all peoples.
Mexico comes to this rostrum with one conviction and leaves with the same one: the legitimacy of institutions depends on their ability to transform, in practice, people’s lives.
As President Claudia Sheinbaum has said, Mexico moves along the path of shared prosperity, with independence, with freedom and always, with dignity.
With that course, we will continue working for a United Nations equal to its founding promise.

PERMANENT MISSION OF THE REPUBLIC OF THE MARSHALL ISLANDS TO THE UNITED NATIONS New York H.E. Dr. Hilda Heine President of the Republic of the Marshall Islands 81st Session - General Assembly General Debate United Nations New York 25 September 2026 Mr. President, Mr. Secretary-General, Excellencies, I ask every nation here - are we still willing to work together?
The principles in the UN Charter, affirmed by each one of us taking our seat in this hall, are now tested not by argument - but by neglect or ill intention.
The credibility and effectiveness of multilateral institutions is imperative for small nations.
It is past time to better turn the urgency expressed in political declarations and resolutions into results, not repetition.
We speak from our own experience when we underscore the importance of acting together.
An institution that takes decisions collectively must also be accountable, collectively.

The United Nations is long overdue to reflect and renew the same spirit with which our Marshallese people first came to the UN, by delivering an apology and acknowledgement of the harm caused by impacts from the 67 nuclear weapons tested on our islands during our time as a UN Strategic Trust Territory - between 1946 and 1958.
The sacred trust of the UN Trusteeship to ensure our well-being was jeopardized by these tests and the lack of due acknowledgement remains a moral failing.
For generations, our families have testified to displacement, illness, contamination and loss, all of them impacts to our core human rights.
As our survivors would say, “this is a song that has been sung far too many times”.

It was in this same building that the UN Trusteeship Council sat in session and voted on Resolutions 1082 and 1493, in 1954 and 1956 respectively, to effectively authorize further nuclear testing over the demands of our local leaders and many citizens.

The United Nations ultimately allowed the testing to continue, but the shock and tragedy of nuclear exposure in the Marshall Islands was a profound driver of the 1963 global ban on atmospheric testing of nuclear weapons.
We acknowledge the ongoing actions, dialogue and complex legacy of the UN’s administering authority, the United States.

But the role of the United Nations cannot pass without comment For us – and for fellow member states – this apology is an opportunity to reflect upon the past, to bring healing and closure to the Marshallese people.
We carry no larger agenda – other than to ensure that the United Nations will do better.
As we face a world in which scientists tell us overshooting the 1.5 degree temperature limit that we agreed in Paris is increasingly likely, we all need to to wake up and act.
Our focus now must be on preventing or minimizing the overshoot, shortening the time we spend above 1.5, and doing everything possible to fight our way back.
As we gather in Tuvalu, Fiji and Turkiye for this year’s climate pre-COP and COP, our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming.
A much accelerated transition away from fossil fuels is the only logical response.
Continued investment in fossil fuels is not only immoral but irrational.
Technologies exist which provide secure, stable, zero-emissions energy.

We are employing them in my own country, where, in the next 18 months, renewable energy will cut fossil fuel use in our remote outer atolls by 88%, giving many access to electricity for the first time.
We must do everything in our power to accelerate the deployment of renewables, and to reduce fossil fuel production and consumption with equal speed.

This includes shipping, where we have the opportunity at the International Maritime Organisation to adopt binding regulations that will place international shipping on a clear path to net zero by 2050 and generate the revenue required to ensure a just and equitable transition.
Mr President, The denials and delays that have slowed the transition away from fossil fuels mean that countries like mine are already experiencing grave challenges.
We have developed our national adaptation plan, working across ministries and with our people to determine how to make a safe future.
Adapting is costly, and takes time, even as we’ve seen schools destroyed by rising seas, salt water poisoning our wells, and disease outbreaks linked to environmental change.
The Marshall Islands, and vulnerable people everywhere, need sufficient, timely and accessible finance for adaptation and loss and damage.
Those who have profited to the detriment of the many must pay.

We have created home grown institutions that are ready and willing to respond, like the Pacific Resilience Facility - a regionally managed platform, and the Marshall Islands Adaptation and Resilience Trust Fund, designed to enable donors to support our adaptation efforts.
Mr. President This crisis has the power to divide us, or to prove that we all remain willing to achieve common goals.
This week the Marshall Islands convened the High Ambition Coalition, a diverse group of countries committed to a rigorous response to the climate crisis.

We are united in the view that the best available science must lead the decisions we make, the importance of a 1.5 degree celcius temperature limit, an urgent transition away from fossil fuels, and the need for adequate and accessible climate finance, especially for adaptation and loss and damage.
As a low-lying atoll nation with no higher ground, sea-level rise is an immediate and stark reality.
This week’s UN High Level Meeting on Sea-Level Rise has helped achieve new understandings in international law.
It is the seas that are rising around us, and not our islands which are sinking.
Our boundaries and baselines of today - the political footprint on the map - will endure in the face of aggressive sea-level rise scenarios.
Our collective stability - and security - as Pacific Islands Forum members, and as a UN member state - will be now better addressed.
As an atoll nation - our tide gauge is proof enough that far more action is needed.

Confronted with rising seas on our most vulnerable shorelines, we completed the Ebeye Seawall and Footpath last week, 1.8 kilometers of ocean-side protection built with support from the World Bank, the Green Climate Fund, and our own resources.

Engineered for rising seas, it now protects 8,400 people and critical energy infrastructure, reduces annual coastal-flooding losses, and anchors resilient future development on Ebeye, including schools, housing, and the proposed new hospital, while providing a safe public space that strengthens community wellbeing.
It cost $75 million dollars, took 70,000 tonnes of rocks, took more than a decade to do - and it is just one island of over a thousand.
We are taking action, and we urgently need strengthened partnership to better protect our islands, before sea-level rise overtakes us.
My nation underscores the importance of the Law of the Sea as a key legal pillar of our future.
Even before we were a UN member, we fought closely both to participate in UN Law of the Sea negotiations, and to secure these rights in our Constitution.
Pacific island leadership, and that of all small island developing states, has defined every multilateral milestone for oceans and fisheries and, we will continue to do so.

As an ocean people, the consequences of getting it wrong are not from distant impacts, but adjacent to our waters - particularly in the North Pacific, both within the International Seabed Authority and unilateral actions.

Collectively-the peoples and voices of Micronesia must be heard - we are joined by Guam, Northern Marianas, Federated States of Micronesia, and Palau - in expressing our alarm at seabed mining actions where the decisions are made before impacts are well-understood, and where adequate safeguards remain undefined.
The Marshall Islands joins 45 nations seeking a moratorium on seabed mining.
Responsible and science-driven regulations need to be in place.
Going on guesswork for global oceans is beyond dangerous.
The Marshall Islands looks forward to the first Conference of Parties to the Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction- to work across silos to advance high seas protection.
We urge wide ratification of the Agreement.
The Marshall Islands looks forward to supporting its Secretariat in a host nation committed to upholding the Law of the Sea as a matter of both principle and law, in words and in actions.
Too often the word geopolitics is considered to refer only to the whims of superpowers, and not the reality of our fragile place between them.
As a region of vulnerable island nations, we rightly define our own security priorities- and they deeply cut across every sector, placing a safe future for our youngest generations beyond grasp.
As fuel and energy costs are rising beyond our ability to respond, impacts from bigger power plays halfway around the world are amplified tenfold in small, remote economies.
The international community is not listening closely to small island developing states, and it is not responding fast enough.
Too often, the purported solutions for island nations don’t seem to know the problems.
The Marshall Islands faces complex challenges in tackling the SDGs, but we are committed with all of our effort to ensure no one is left behind.
Our national planning is now firmly linked to SDG goals and targets and our action proves our commitment.

We have developed direct assistance to vulnerable groups including mothers and early childhood development- and we are also reaching our entire in-country population with quarterly supplemental income and improved access to digital finance tools.
Our aspirations must be better matched by partnership and island-scaled investment and policy innovation.
I must underscore the direct need for data capacity support to measure progress and effectiveness for small island developing states.
If we can’t assess the SDGs, we can’t correct course.
The Marshall Islands affirms the recent Pacific Islands Forum Communique position regarding West Papua, including the 2018 invitation by Indonesia to the UN Human Rights Commissioner.
Further, the Marshall Islands strongly welcomes recent calls for a ministerial summit between ASEAN and the Pacific Islands Forum to take forward our 2023 agreement.
Our two regions can stand united as neighbors and close friends.
The Marshall Islands affirms its longstanding support for Japan - and its G4 partners - to achieve permanent membership on the UN Security Council.
Mr, President, The Marshall Islands expresses its grave concern over increased efforts to spread dangerous disinformation in these halls.
Taiwan, and its 23 million people, are an objective reality, and only its democratically-elected government can represent it.
Appropriate ways must be found for Taiwan’s substantive participation in UN meetings - if the UN is to be truly inclusive and effective.

In years to come, every nation in this hall may be told that aggression or coercion upon Taiwan is an internal matter, somehow justified by an ancient UN seating chart resolution - a resolution which doesn’t even reference Taiwan.
In years to come, we may all be told that it is futile for a small nation to resist a larger one - and that might makes right regardless of the rule book.

We all will experience pressure to accept a false narrative, that UN General Assembly resolution 2758 somehow serves as a legal pretext under the UN Charter for coercion or war, impairing freedom of navigation in one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes.
We will be asked, politely and impolitely, to turn a blind eye and look away.
It is vital that every nation here, including our close partners in our own region, know that appeasement never satisfies an aggressor’s wider agenda, and one taste is never enough.
How the UN addresses this very real security dilemma will be a test of its strength and relevance.
Excellencies, The Marshall Islands stands firm in investing ourselves in this multilateral institution with clear sight of its frustrations and grave errors.
Two years ago, I concluded my statement by reciting an old Marshallese proverb, Wod in Kanol.
It describes the coral reef where different species of fish congregate to feed and seek shelter.

Today, we are not only being called upon to revitalize this 81 year-old institution created from the ashes of global conflict, but we are being challenged to address the complexities of a rapidly changing world.
This United Nations must continue to serve as our primary Wod in Kanol to ensure that no one is left behind.
We do not know exactly what the world in which that young person will live will look like.
But we already know that it will be different from our own.
Artificial intelligence will transform professions, industries and the ways in which decisions are made.
Energy will be governed by a new configuration and a new logic of operation.
Climate change will affect economies, agriculture, cities and the movement of people.
Demographic change will reshape labour markets and social protection systems.
Security will no longer depend on armies and borders, but also on power grids, data centres, cables, satellites, algorithms and trust in the information we receive every day.
And yet today, as we prepare for that future, millions of people are living through war or under the threat of war.
More than one hundred million people have been forcibly displaced.
More than 270 million children and young people are not in school.
This is the paradox of our time.
Humanity has never possessed such immense scientific and technological capabilities.
And yet, it has never been more evident that technological capability does not automatically produce political wisdom.
That is why the real question before this Assembly is not simply how we will manage the crises of 2026.
The real question is this: what kind of international order will we leave to the generation that is entering school today?
For a small country like mine, this is not an academic question.
It is a question of survival.
Thirty-three years ago since we became part of the United Nations the world looked very different.
There was hope that a new era was beginning; an era in which cooperation would gradually replace confrontation.
Our region, however, was living through a very different reality.
Wars were being fought just beyond our borders.
The fear that the violence might spread was real.
And yet, my country chose peace. It chose stability.

It was in those circumstances, on our territory, that the United Nations did something it had never done before: it established the first preventive peacekeeping mission in the history of the Organization.
That experience left a profound lesson in our national memory, a lesson to which I will return towards the end of my address.
Peace does not begin when war ends.
Peace begins when politics is wise enough to prevent war from beginning.
Perhaps that is why small countries sometimes see international politics differently.
Great powers have room for strategic shifts that small sized states simply do not have.
For a great power, a mistaken geopolitical calculation may mean a change of strategy.
For a small sized country, the same mistake can mean a lost decade.
That is why we cannot afford to be indifferent to the rules.
Nor can we afford to believe that the rules will defend themselves.
The world taking shape before us is a world of sharper competition.
Relations among the major powers increasingly shape trade, technology, energy, critical raw materials, transport routes and digital infrastructure.
What we called economic interdependence only yesterday, we increasingly see today also as a matter of national security.
Production is once again becoming a geopolitical question.

States are asking not only where something can be produced most cheaply, but who can be trusted; not only where energy comes from, but whether it will be available when a crisis strikes; not only who develops the next generation of technology, but who will set the rules under which it will operate.
Alliances, too, are changing under the pressure of this same world.
Macedonian citizens know where they belong.
The United States is our strategic partner.
Full membership in the European Union is our strategic commitment.
These are not three separate policies.
They are one geopolitical orientation, an orientation grounded in democracy, collective security, the rule of law and an open economy.
In a time of uncertainty, our response is not strategic ambiguity.
But clarity in our alliances does not mean turning away from the world. Quite the opposite.

It is precisely a state that is confident in its democratic and strategic choices that can engage and cooperate with greater confidence with countries that have different histories, different interests and different political perspectives.
The world does not need yet another division into permanent camps.
It needs competition with limits and rules that all must respect.
And international institutions that remain a space for dialogue precisely when dialogue is most difficult.
That is why the United Nations matter.
Not because they can resolve every conflict. Clearly, they cannot.
Not because every resolution is given effect.
Clearly, that is not always the case.

And that should not discourage us; it should strengthen our determination to protect these United Nations and the rules upon which they are founded, and to stand for multilateralism grounded in values, mutual respect and rules.
Because a world without a place where all states, regardless of their size, can sit under the same roof and invoke the same principles would be even more dangerous than the world we see today.
In 1954, Dag Hammarskjöld reminded us of a thought: The United Nations were not created to take us to heaven, but to save us from hell.
Seven decades later, it is worth understanding the essence of that statement.
We should not demand perfection from the United Nations.
The capacity to prevent and to mediate.
The capacity to protect human dignity.
And, ultimately, the capacity to uphold principles even when applying them is politically inconvenient.
Today, trust in the international system is being jeopardized precisely because too many people have a justified sense that the rules do not apply equally.
That power sometimes takes precedence over principle.
That agreements last only as long as interests remain unchanged.
For small sized states, this is an especially dangerous world.
Our own history has taught us that international compromises are very difficult, and that peace, stability and integration require political courage and hard sacrifices.

And without wishing to sound patronising, if anyone wants to see an example of a country that has repeatedly given up something that naturally belongs to it as a fundamental right—something that many take for granted—all they need is to look at the recent history of my country.

A history marked by challenges, by security risks of regional proportions, by constant compromises and concessions made in the name of peace and cooperation and the higher goals of integration—often at the expense of our most basic understanding of dignity and justice.
We have taken truly difficult decisions.
We have continued forward even when processes lasted longer than one generation of citizens could reasonably have expected.

But precisely for that reason, with the benefit of distance from those decisions and with a clear awareness of reality, I can responsibly say today that trust cannot be a one-way obligation indefinitely.
If small sized states are expected to comply with the rules, then the rules must also provide them with predictability.
If candidates for membership in an organization are required to meet certain criteria, then meeting those criteria must lead to progress.
If we ask citizens to trust institutions, then institutions must demonstrate that their word has value and that their commitments endure.
The rule that applies today cannot be different tomorrow simply because the balance of power has changed.
And a commitment undertaken cannot be a temporary political convenience.
It must be a foundation on which people can plan their future.
We ask our citizens to believe in cooperation, in good neighbourly relations, in compromise, and in mutual respect.

We tell them that lasting peace is worth more than a short-term political victory; that respecting agreements is a sign of strength and wisdom, and that it is the right thing to do, not a sign of weakness; that European and Euro-Atlantic integration means accepting rules that apply equally to all.

But that argument becomes much harder to sustain when citizens see that, in international relations, principle sometimes gives way to power; that criteria can change while the process is already under way; or that some are expected to demonstrate consistency that others do not always demand of themselves.
We cannot tell people, “Trust the rules,” when they can see that the rules do not apply equally.
We cannot convince them that compromise is a virtue, if every compromise produces a new demand.

And we cannot expect trust in international institutions if citizens come to believe that their fate is created more often by the political weight of their state than by the strength of an agreed principle.
This is a question of legitimacy.
Because our authority as elected leaders does not derive from the office itself.
It derives from the people who elect us, who hold us to account, and who every day compare what we tell them with what they see.
And today, they see more than ever before.
We live in an age in which information travels around the world in seconds.
Never before has humanity had access to so much knowledge.
But never before has it been exposed to so much manipulation, half-truths, fabricated images, propaganda and organized disinformation.
That is precisely why politics is entering a new, more difficult and more complex era.
Our task is no longer simply to inform our citizens.
It is not enough to tell them what is true.
We must build institutions they can trust when the truth is uncomfortable for everyone.
It is not enough to speak to them about values.
We must show that those values have meaning and carry a cost—even when defending them requires patience, political capital, or choosing the more difficult path.

We are called upon to convince our societies that cooperation is better than isolation, that the rule of law is better than unilateral behavior, that compromise is better than conflict, and that institutions are better than the rule of sheer force.
But for that conviction to carry weight, we ourselves must be consistent.
Values are not sustained by speeches.
They are sustained when they are upheld precisely at the moment when it is easiest to abandon them.
And this may be the greatest challenge of our time.
The world is changing at extraordinary speed.
The centres of power are shifting. Technology is changing.
Security doctrines are changing. Alliances are changing.

In such periods, there is always a temptation to declare that old principles are no longer practical; that the law must adapt to power; that values are a luxury that can wait until the crisis has passed.
But that is precisely when we need them most.
Because if, in times of change, we abandon the rules that protected us in times of stability, we will not gain greater freedom.
We will inherit a world in which every subsequent decision depends on who has more power at that particular moment.
And such a world is especially dangerous for small sized states.
That is why our duty as leaders is not to promise our people a world without injustice, without disappointment, and without conflicting interests.
Such a world does not exist.
Our duty is far more demanding.
To preserve faith in the rules even when it is clear that the rules are being broken.
To defend cooperation even when confrontation appears more popular.
To sustain trust in institutions not by asking people to look less closely and ask fewer questions, but by making institutions more worthy of their trust.
And not to allow disappointment with the imperfections of the international order to lead us towards something far worse: a world in which there is no order at all.
That, in my view, is one of the greatest political and moral responsibilities of our generation.
It applies to the international system.
We will not abandon the European idea because the European path has been difficult.
The European Union remains, for us, our natural political, economic and institutional home.
And we have work to do at home.
We must strengthen the rule of law.
And strengthen our citizens ’confidence in their own state.
That is our responsibility, and we will not shift it to Brussels.
At the same time, we expect European integration to remain a merit based-process based on measurable criteria—not a process in which bilateral issues can continually move the goalposts.
We are not asking for an easier path.
We are asking for a path governed by rules.
We are not asking for lower standards.
We are asking for standards to remain standards.

This is equally important for Europe’s credibility at a time when its geopolitical weight will increasingly depend on its ability to translate its commitments into tangible political outcomes, and on its resolve to uphold the values it espouses and to remain steadfast in advancing them, despite the many challenges it faces.
The future international order will not be shaped only on battlefields or in diplomatic halls.
It will also be shaped in laboratories. In schools. In factories. In energy grids. In data centres.
And in the ability of societies to make sense of the changes that technology is bringing.
Artificial intelligence is no longer a subject of the future.
It is infrastructure for the present.
Today, the world is once again recognizing the value of resilience. Of reliable energy. Of infrastructure.
Of nearby and trusted supply chains.

For us, the intensive development of Corridors VIII and X is part of a broader European vision: to better connect the Adriatic, the Black Sea, the Aegean and Central Europe; to provide goods, energy and people with more routes and greater connectivity; and to ensure that the region becomes interconnected in infrastructure rather than remaining on the geopolitical periphery.
Our geography does not have to be our destiny.
It can become our advantage if we build the institutions and infrastructure that transform our geographical position into connectivity.
At the same time, we must also approach migration differently.
Migration begins where there is no security, no employment, no education, no access to water, no prospects, or no confidence that tomorrow will be better than today.
It is not simply a matter of borders.
Responsible policy must bring together security, human dignity, development and the real needs of labour markets.
Climate policy, too, will have to become more grounded in reality.
But if we make it socially unsustainable, we will lose the political support that is necessary to implement it.
If we make it technologically dependent on a handful of sources, we will create new challenges while addressing old ones.
If we expect poorer countries to move at the same pace without providing them with equal access to capital and technology, we will create injustice instead of a transition.
That is why future climate policy must, at the same time, be environmental policy, economic policy and social policy.
Mr. President, All of this brings us back to the central theme of this session: trust.
Trust is not a sentiment that can be created by adopting a resolution.
It is built when an institution delivers on the purpose for which it was established.
That is why reform of the United Nations is necessary.
So that the Organization can become more capable.
So that it can deliver greater results.
And certainly not to replace the responsibility of national states.
But to act where collective action is needed.
Multilateralism does not begin in New York.
It begins with the quality of the states that come to New York.
We are a small sized country.
But we refuse to let the smallness of our territory define the scale of our ambition.
Our ambition is to become a serious state.
A state that its allies can trust.
A state in which young people can plan their future.
A state that respects the diversity and multicultural character of its society.
A state confident enough to defend its own identity without denying the identity of others.
A state that knows its history but is not imprisoned by it.
And a state that does not expect others to build it in its place.
That, to me, is modern sovereignty. Not isolation. Capability.
This year, Secretary-General António Guterres reminded us that the Charter begins with the words: “We, the peoples.”
And he added: “Not we, the powerful. Not we, the victors.”
In those few words lies the reason why a small sized European country continues to believe in this Organization, even when it is disappointed by it.
Because the alternative to a world governed by rules is not a world in which everyone is free.
It is a world in which the strongest are the freest.
And everyone else depends on their goodwill.
Such a world may appear effective for a moment.
Some three decades ago, the United Nations came to our country with a new idea: that the international community does not have to wait for violence to begin before it acts.
Today, we once again need that same political wisdom.
We must not wait for technology to create new inequalities before we establish rules.
We must not wait for young people to leave before we build societies in which they see a future worth staying for.
We must not wait for institutions to lose all public trust before we reform them.
And we must not wait for the world to become fully divided into opposing blocs before we rediscover the value of dialogue.
That child with whom I began will be fourteen years older when the world enters 2040.
None of us today can promise that child a peaceful world.
But we can leave that child something else.
A world in which power is not the only argument.
A world in which knowledge is not the privilege of the few.
A world in which alliances create security, rather than new lines of fear.
A world in which technology serves humanity.
And a world in which a small state has the right to the same dignity, the same rules and the same voice as a great power.
That is the promise worth renewing.
Not because we are naive about the world as it is.
But because we are realistic enough to understand what happens when the world is left to power alone.
Macedonians and the Macedonian citizens will share their burden of responsibility.
• Ladies and Gentlemen, Mali welcomes the theme of the eighty-first regular session of the General Assembly, namely “Restoring trust, accompanying transformations: a United Nations that serves all”.

This theme is relevant and timely because, beyond the reflection it prompts on how our Organization can regain its credibility and effectiveness in an international context of multiple crises and challenges to multilateralism, it above all calls for restoring trust among Member States in order to find common and appropriate solutions to the many challenges of our time.

For its part, Mali reaffirms its unwavering attachment to a reformed multilateralism, based on the strict respect for the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations, in particular the sovereign equality of States, respect for the territorial integrity of States, the prohibition of the use of force, mutual respect and non-interference in the internal affairs of States.
By moving away from these principles, we inevitably move closer to cycles of conflict.

We all know this: flagrant violations of international law, its selective application, the persistence of the policy of double standards in the management of crises throughout the world, and the abusive use of force, of threats, and policies of hegemony, subjugation and domination, in violation of the Charter of our Organization, have considerably eroded the trust of the world’s citizens in international institutions, in particular the United Nations.

Accordingly, Mali calls for the lifting of unilateral coercive measures, which undermine the sovereignty of States and endanger the lives and well-being of the populations of the thirty or so countries affected by these sanctions.

To all these practices that weaken current global governance is added the slowness of anticipation on the part of the United Nations, which obliges it, after the fact, to stand by powerlessly as an observer of the crises shaking the world.

This is the case in the Sahel, which has, for more than a decade, been confronted with a security crisis caused in particular by the military intervention of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) in Libya in 2011.

A military adventure with unmanaged risks, NATO’s military action in Libya considerably worsened the security, political, humanitarian and human rights situation in our region, notably through the spread of terrorism and violent extremism.
In the face of this grim picture, it is legitimate to question the effectiveness of the levers available to our Organization.

That is why we welcomed the strategic review process of the United Nations Office for West Africa and the Sahel, which should lead to an arrangement more consistent with the realities and concerns of the populations concerned.

The Government of Mali reiterates its firm condemnation of international terrorism and of its foreign State sponsors, which finance, arm, provide logistics and intelligence for this organized transnational crime.

Following the initial statements by Ukraine, which as early as 2024 acknowledged its support for terrorist groups operating in the Sahel, that country publicly reiterated, at the Summit level, its interference in Africa.
Today, beyond our States, other independent sources corroborate these unacceptable actions by Ukraine.

In the face of history, the international community, and Africa in particular, cannot continue to maintain a guilty silence in the face of Ukraine’s acts of aggression, with their enormous consequences for African countries and beyond.
We are not deceived: Ukraine is only the visible part of the iceberg of the destabilization of our countries.

Terrorism, sustained and supported, manifests itself in armed, economic and media forms, particularly through organized and systematic disinformation, of which our countries are victims at the hands of certain media nostalgic for a bygone colonial past.
The complex and coordinated attacks of 25 April and 04 July 2026 in several localities in Mali, which caused numerous victims, constitute proof of a dangerous connection.

Unsurprisingly, the scenario played out in 2012 is being repeated, with armed terrorist groups and so-called separatist armed groups forming an avowed terrorist coalition against the Malian institutions and populations.

Regional and international responses, including the deployment of international forces, have not made it possible to contain these complex security crises and the massacres of the populations of the Sahel.

This is why Their Excellencies Captain Ibrahim TRAORE, President of Faso, Head of State and President of the Confederation of Sahel States (AES), General of the Army Assimi GOITA, President of the Transition, Head of State of the Republic of Mali, and General of the Army Abdourahamane TIANI, President of the Republic of the Niger, Head of State, took the historic decision to create, on 6 July 2024 in Niamey, Niger, the Confederation of Sahel States, in order to take charge of the destiny of our countries.
From its creation to the present day, the AES Confederation has made it possible to achieve real and encouraging progress in its various areas of action.
I reaffirm here the determination of our three Heads of State to continue and intensify this fight against terrorism, in all its forms and manifestations.

The delegation of Mali fully endorses the statement to be delivered by His Excellency Mr. Karamoko Jean-Marie TRAORE, Minister for Foreign Affairs of Burkina Faso, on behalf of the Confederation of Sahel States (AES), comprising Burkina Faso, the Republic of Mali and the Republic of the Niger.

Malian Forces, acting alone and within the framework of the Unified Force of the AES, as well as with the support of the Russian Federation, are today on the front line of the fight against imposed terrorism, a proxy hybrid war whose stakes go beyond our area and threaten other regions.
I also salute all the partners who continue to support Mali and the countries of the Sahel in this difficult context.

Victory over terrorism, this global existential threat, calls for the pooling of efforts and resources, but also and above all for a shared understanding of the terrorist phenomenon, because, contrary to what some want us to believe, there is no good terrorist and bad terrorist.

To reinforce this momentum, the three member countries of the AES Confederation remain open to cooperation with all partners who so wish and who respect the cardinal principles that now govern public action in our countries, namely respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our States, respect for our strategic choices and partnerships, as well as taking into account the interests of our populations.
We have no injunctions to receive; rather, we expect sound and sincere collaboration and partnership.

In this dynamic, Mali, in accordance with the principles and goals of its foreign policy, will continue to place its diplomatic action within the dynamic of promoting good-neighbourly relations, respect for sovereignty, mutual respect, non-interference in the internal affairs of other States, and the peaceful settlement of disputes.
I take this opportunity to bow my head to the memory of all the victims of cowardly terrorist barbarity, and who heroically fell on the field of honour.

Furthermore, I pay vibrant tribute to our defence and security forces for their courage, their professionalism and their unfailing commitment to defending the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our countries and to protecting our civilian populations.

I wish particularly to salute the memory of General of the Army Sadio CAMARA, Minister of Defence and Veterans, whose legacy, marked by patriotism, courage and sacrifice, will continue to inspire many generations of Malians.

To strengthen the security measures essential to the lasting return of peace in Mali, the Government is resolutely working to implement a comprehensive, integrated and coherent strategy for the stability and prosperity of the country.

Through this strategy, the State keeps its hand extended to all those who are ready to lay down their arms and rejoin the Republic, in accordance with the conclusions of the Inter-Malian Dialogue and the National Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation.
Already, thousands of former combatants who meet the conditions have either joined the ranks of our defence and security forces or taken up civilian functions.
The sovereignty of Mali is dear to us and is not negotiable.

It is not limited to the defence of the territory but must also enable our country to control its economic choices, control and develop its natural resources, strengthen its productive economy and create more opportunities for its youth.
It is in this spirit that the Government remains committed to implementing the Mali Kura Vision 2063 and the National Strategy for Emergence and Sustainable Development (SNEDD 2024-2033).
These two programmes, both ambitious and structuring, aim to respond, in a coherent and sustainable manner, to the legitimate aspirations of the Malian populations.

They constitute the pact of the generations and reflect the determination to build a sovereign State, a competitive economy, a just society and a country where every citizen will be able to fulfil themselves and flourish in dignity.
The Government has placed economic recovery and the well-being of the populations at the heart of its action, indispensable links in achieving lasting peace and stability.

Thus, through appropriate reforms, in addition to political governance, the Government has considerably improved economic governance, in particular the efficient management of public affairs and the increased mobilization of domestic resources.

Public expenditure is now being directed towards structuring investments in productive sectors and in support of better access for populations to basic social services, training and employment for young people and women.

This ambition also entails strengthening the local processing of our natural resources, developing national production capacities and making Malian youth a major actor in our economic and social transformation.
Mali intends to continue its national Refoundation, in order to durably guarantee security, justice and well-being for all its daughters and sons.
At the regional and international levels, the Government of Mali remains very attentive to the evolution of the situation in Africa and in the rest of the world.
In this regard, Mali encourages efforts towards the rapid and lasting resolution of the various conflicts on the Continent.
With regard to the situation in the Middle East, Mali reaffirms its full support for the brotherly Palestinian people in their legitimate struggle to exist as a full-fledged State.
Let us face the facts: the international order is at the hour of major upheaval and profound change.
Ignoring this will move us further away from the most appropriate solutions.

The question is no longer whether we are moving towards a multipolar world, but rather who the major actors of the various poles will be and how these actors intend to cooperate to respond to the aspirations of the Peoples of the planet that we share.

In this new complex and turbulent international environment, Mali intends to pursue a foreign policy based on the sovereign equality of States, the diversification of its partnerships, the defence of its national interests and constructive engagement.
Our objective is to achieve the strategic autonomy of Mali, the AES and Africa, both in the field of security and in that of development.
This strategic autonomy is not synonymous with rupture but rather aims to make Africa a credible and indispensable partner for the stability and prosperity of the world.

Climate change and desertification constitute, for Mali and for the Sahel, a factor of economic, social and environmental vulnerability which not only directly affects agricultural activities and livelihoods but also constitutes a threat to peace and security.
Thus, Mali invites Member States to place emphasis on adaptation, access to climate financing and endogenous technologies, as well as on solutions adapted to Sahelian realities.
We advocate better articulation between combating desertification, food security, water management, risk and conflict prevention and the resilience of territories.
The world is experiencing exceptional technological advances, among them generative artificial intelligence, another challenge at the heart of the passionate debates of our day.
It is a strategic technology that offers considerable possibilities and also presents risks.
But we must be clear-sighted: AI must not be only a technology that we consume.
It must become a technology that we master, that we adapt to our realities and that we contribute to developing.
This ambition implies defining our priorities and putting in place an appropriate legal and ethical environment.
For Mali, digital and technological sovereignty now constitutes an essential dimension of national sovereignty.
In particular, we must invest in the skills, research, innovation and infrastructure necessary so that our young people can participate fully in this transformation.
That is why the Head of State has established the Mali Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics, which promotes the country’s digital sovereignty.

On issues of international migration, Mali, as both a country of origin, transit and destination for migrants, renews its commitment to international cooperation and considers that human mobility is an asset for humanity.
It calls for respect for the rights of migrants, in accordance with the relevant provisions of international conventions.
In conclusion, Mali recalls that our multilateral framework, embodied by the United Nations, is at a crossroads.
The time has come for us to assume our common and shared responsibility for a reformed United Nations, fairer, more representative and truly at the service of all peoples, without distinction.
This is the essential condition for restoring the confidence of Member States and Peoples in the Organization.

This implies, in particular, strengthening representativeness within multilateral institutions and making the voice of Africa heard more strongly in the bodies where decisions are taken that commit the future of our world.
Mali reaffirms its readiness to contribute to the common efforts of the international community for a peaceful world, safer, fairer, more prosperous and more united.
Dear friends, the chosen theme for this year's General Assembly is restoring trust, managing transformation.
I don't think that there could be a more appropriate framing for our discussions of this week.
Properly, the lack thereof is the greatest challenge currently facing our world.
The erosion of trust that has gripped our societies runs deep.
Where once people embraced trust, now people are gripped by suspicion, suspicion of governments, suspicion of institutions, suspicion of businesses, even.
All too often suspicion of each other.
I am talking about suspicion, not skepticism. Skepticism.
The legitimate questioning of those who hold power over people's lives is the lifeblood of a democratic society. Suspicion.
However, the assumption that others are automatically looking out for their interests and not those of the common good is poison to any democratic society.

No community can succeed if we blindly believe that our neighbors are out to do us down just as no country can succeed if it blindly believes that its neighbors, even those it may long have considered and seen as friends, are out to get it.
Which means restoring trust, rebuilding alliances, remaking friendships must be the central mission for all of us here at home and abroad.
It must also be the central mission of the remaking of this United Nations To change.
We know we need to change how the United Nations works, how it takes decisions, and how it delivers on the ground.
But we can only make that change, achieve that transformation if we believe that change is possible.
Nobody ever successfully renovated the House without the faith that however hard the work, however many setbacks faced along the way, the end result would be a real improvement on what went before.
So we need to show faith that however hard the work, however many setbacks faced along the way, the end result of transforming this house, this home of all the nations, will be a real step forward.

And as this United Nations embarks on its ninth decade of service, the need for a step change in how the international community works together solves problems together is arguably needed more acutely now than ever before.
That erosion of trust is leading to the corrosion of the international order, not the improvement of the international order, but the destruction of the international order.
An international order that, for all its flaws and failures, has seen more children escape hunger, more families live in peace, and more children grow into old age than any era before it.

To destroy the international settlement, without any idea of what comes next would be an act of wanton destruction that would rightly never be forgiven or forgotten by the tens of millions whose future it would betray.
So let us be bold and let us say it loud and clear.
Now more than ever, is a moment for more cooperation, not less.
That is the only way that we will manage to find paths to progress on the all too many, all true, all too intractable conflicts blighting our world today.
In Malta, the smallest member state of the European Union, we have always been a bridge between Europe and the Middle East.
So allow me to focus on two of those conflicts on our doorstep. Firstly, Ukraine.

It is all too easy and all too great a mistake for us to fall in the trap that repelling the invasion of Ukraine becomes another never ending conflict, a grinding tragedy on the corner of our continent about which we can do nothing.
Malta will never accept that despair.
Europe must never accept that despair.
The world must never turn its head away in despair.
Malta remains as adamant in our condemnation of that invasion today as we were on day one in February 2022.
And Malta is equally as adamant that a just and lasting peace must guarantee Ukraine's sovereignty within its internationally recognised borders.
That will only come about through a diplomatic process that the Ukrainian people can have full trust in.
They will only have such trust if the process follows a full and unconditional cease fire and the full participation of Ukraine and its people in the subsequent peace talks.

Rightly the Ukrainian people will never have trust in any search for a settlement which involves their government being frogmarched to the table, one arm tied behind its back, whilst the guns still blaze.

The issue of trust is clearly also central to the very worrying situation in Gaza The people of Israel need to have trust that Hamas will be disarmed, and that they will play no future role in the governance or security structures of Gaza.
But the people of Gaza need to have trust that there is a path to a just peace.
It is impossible to build that trust with a humanitarian situation as acute as that being experienced in Gaza right now.
Malta's voice remains unwaveringly with the global calls for safe, sustained and unhindered humanitarian access throughout Gaza in accordance with international law.
We firmly believe that the Gaza peace plan provides the best path towards ending the conflict and advancing credible political progress.
To achieve that progress, all parties and I emphasize all parties must fully respect and implement the objectives and commitments set out in the plan.
And naturally, no progress can be made.
If there is any question of the forced displacement of any of the Palestinian population.

Indeed, it is incumbent on each and every one of us in the international community to rebuild the trust needed to underpin the conditions where genuine progress can be made towards a negotiated and lasting two state solution.
Unfortunately, that seems at the moment.

But nor is this the moment to shy away or run away from the only goal that will guarantee the people of Israel and Palestine living side by side with the peace, prosperity and stability that they both deserve.

Sadly, any progress towards a long term solution is being endangered by the situation in the West Bank settlement expansion, running directly counter to the resolutions of this General Assembly and designed to undermine the Palestinian territorial integrity, must stop and stop now.
So too, must the violent settler attacks on Palestinian communities increasing at an alarming rate.

These are all essential preconditions to a just and lasting peace, as is a credible and reformed Palestinian Authority that can demonstrate to citizens of both Palestine and Israel that it has the transparency, the accountability, the institutional effectiveness, and, above all, the democratic legitimacy to be a truly effective partner for peace.

Malta stands ready to play its part in building the capacity of both a renewed Democratic Palestinian Authority and the robust civil society that must underpin it, not just in Ukraine, Gaza and Israel, but across the world.
Be it the conflict in Sudan, the ongoing violence in Myanmar or the instability across the Sahel.
It is evident that diminished trust means diminished chances of finding solutions.
You could put it as starkly as no trust equals no peace.
Of course, no matter the conflict, each with its own individual and particular circumstances, there is no easy way of building trust.
But equally, there is no easy way of avoiding the need to build trust.
We all know from our lives as much as from the experiences of our own countries, just how hard it is to rebuild trust when it has evaporated.
Yet we also know the consequences if we give up trying, and the rewards that can come.
If, however, slowly and however tentatively, we can start.
If it is hard enough to build trust human to human face to face, it can be, of course, infinitely harder to build trust.
Of machines, of the technology shaping all our lives.
Yet the challenge of how we can manage to trust that technology and the organisations behind it is rapidly becoming the most pressing challenge of our age.
The sheer spread and the sheer power, the sheer speed of artificial intelligence is mind blowing.
It appears to be moving far too fast for anybody let alone governments, to manage to keep pace.
It can seem, whether from the perspective of a leader, consumer or parent, to be overwhelming.
This is the biggest change and the biggest challenge that any of us will experience in our lifetime.
So much so that we barely have the words to describe how monumental a disruption it is proving to be.
The usual phrases step change, paradigm shift just don't seem to capture the scale.

And we should also be under no illusion that the currently existing rules, the traditional models of governance are in any way or manner up to grappling with the revolution that we are living through.

Which is why, if we stand any chance of helping to build citizens trust in these advanced technologies, we need to begin by being honest and transparent that governments, just as individuals, we are still finding our way, that we don't have all the answers.
What we do have, what we must have, is the will and determination to act and the right values to underpin those actions.
And of course, it almost goes without saying that no state, however micro or mighty, has any chance of getting a grip if they try to go it alone.
We only stand a chance as humanity.
On getting a grip on technology that seeks to ape our humanity.
Acknowledging that the rules need to be set globally and they need to be stuck to.
Even as they develop, as the tech develops.
If we are to stand any chance of securing public confidence that AI can enhance and not destroy humanity, we need a set of international rules that reflect international law.
So Malta, my country, wholeheartedly supports the implementation of the global Digital Compact and wider UN efforts to strengthen international digital cooperation.
To fragment is to fail, and that applies equally to fighting the new threats from the new frontline in global conflict and disruption.
Cyber attacks, attacks on critical infrastructure, disinformation, the cutting of the underwater cables that connect us all to each other.
They are constant and existential threats.
For a small nation like Malta, a small island in the Mediterranean that relies on our connections to the rest of the world.
Tackling them must be a priority.
The priority for this United Nations.
We need to embrace every emerging technology that can help us fend off those threats and build our digital resilience today.
The guardians of our democracy, of our freedoms are just as likely to be found coding at a keyboard as marching in uniform.
Both must work in lockstep together.
Security will always, of course be physical.
Yes, but now it must also be digital.
The change must then be reflected in the way we work together to achieve our different and common goals.

I know that I am preaching to true believers, Mr. President and Mr. Secretary General, when I say that there must be no letup, no slowing down in the relentless, relentless drive for reform of how disunited nations and its agencies does its business and delivers its services, to take our foot off the gas would be to let down the millions who need this United Nations to do better, be better at tackling the problems that blight their lives.
That is why the goal of this General Assembly, a United Nations that delivers for all, is so important and so urgent.
If we are to have any hope of renewing the trust of the citizens with serving global institutions and the global order.
We have to show that those institutions, this institution, can indeed deliver deliver in ways that change tangibly lives for the better.
We must never lose sight and never lose faith in the values that brought us together in the first place. As nations united.
Malta is and always, of course, will be a passionate advocate and promoter of and passionately committed to multilateralism.
At the core of all we do must be the code and conscience of the founding charter of this United Nations.
But the implementation of those values, the way we turn those fine words into fine actions, must always be a process of constant evolution.
We can never stand still if we are to keep cooperation alive.
So Malta remains thoroughly committed to the implementation of the pact for the future and all of its associated actions.
Reforms must, yes, remain Member State driven and firmly anchored in the intergovernmental process, and efficiency must not come at the expense of effectiveness on the ground.

Malta solidly backs a strong and effective resident coordinator system as the key anchor of UN action at a country level, and I can't reiterate often enough or restate strongly enough, that the only effective antidote to the cancer of cynicism and suspicion is effective and concerted action to tackle the greatest threat to our people and our planet.
And alongside spreading conflict and the dangers of uncontrolled technology, the greatest threat to us all, and especially island nations like Malta, is man made climate change.
I say, and I express this to all of you.

Just look at the weather extremes we have been experiencing in Europe, particularly during these last weeks, to do nothing, to stand by and just wash our hands of it would be a moral and practical betrayal of the citizens, of the millions of citizens who put their faith in us, that we won't flinch from the biggest problems and the toughest solutions and decisions needed to tackle them So we must not stand by.
Stand firm against the torrent of disinformation that fuels the deniers.
Stand firm against the vested interests that seek to block effective action.
Stand firm against the naysayers who say that.
To those cynics, I want to point out an instance that shows how hope can triumph over defeatism.

And I go back to 1967 when representing the then geographically smallest member state of the Europe of the United Nations, a member state that had been a member of the United Nations for less than three years, Arvid Pardo spoke up in this General Assembly in a stirring speech, Malta's permanent representative made a passionate plea to the world's common humanity.
He may have been speaking on behalf of a very small nation, but he had a very ambitious vision.
Pardo Pardo called for the world to treat the resources of the oceans beyond their own borders as the common heritage of mankind.
His demand for a law of the sea was prescient, but to achieve it took persistence.
In fact, it took 27 years before it came into being.
What motivated Malta's action, then, is what motivates Malta's demands now?
Doing nothing meant leaving the world's oceans to the mercy of the world's biggest, strongest and richest nations.
Taking action showed that, and I quote, they belonged to all of humanity.
Those living and those who still had to be born.

That spirit was evident was evident when, in 1988, right at the start of the concern about global warming, Malta proposed the United Nations General Assembly resolution that recognized climate change as a global problem, requiring collective and global solutions suspicion of collective action won't be counteracted by retreat.
It will only be overcome by the strength to turn convictions into action.

The phrase dare to dream has become perhaps the world's most common motivational phrase, imploring us that all we have to do is have the courage to dream, and those dreams will almost automatically become reality.
