And yes, we should all indeed dare to dream, to inspire ourselves, to turn hope into achievement, but to turn initial aspirations into sustainable attainment takes something more than just dreams It takes trust.
Trust that by working together, we achieve more than we could ever achieve alone.
It is that belief in the power of trust which underpins the values that brought me into public life.
It is that belief in the power of trust, even now when it can seem a commodity in all too short supply, that convinces me that ultimately it trust will prevail.
That ultimately, we as a world will find the courage to dial down the disbelief and crank up the confidence. If we don't.

If we don't realise that mutual suspicion can only lead to mutual destruction, if we don't realise that closing our minds to those who don't share our worldview limits our chances of solving the world's biggest problems.
If we don't realise that limiting dialogue only to those who are like minded in reality can only drive us further apart, we face a very bleak future indeed.
I refuse Malta refuses to believe that such a future is any more inevitable than it is desirable There is only one simple antidote to the destructive power of suspicion.
It is one that may not, as of yet, have appeared on many motivational bumper stickers, but it is one that must be our lodestar.

So I say to my fellow leaders, as much as I say to my fellow citizens of this planet, let us dare to trust, dare to realize that even those who we disagree with the most must become a part of the solution, and not a prolonger of pain.

It is my honor to address you today as President of Montenegro, a Balkan and Mediterranean country, a credible NATO Ally, steadily advancing towards membership in the European Union, and deeply committed to regional cooperation and effective multilateralism.
In Montenegro, we have an old and simple saying: a person’s word carries weight.
This implies that a promise creates responsibility.
And what is true between people should also be true between nations.
In the opening words of the UN Charter, the nations of the world made perhaps the most important promise of all: “to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war.”

Eight decades later, as conflicts take lives and displace millions, geopolitical rivalries place the international system under growing pressure, and new challenges test our collective capacity to respond.
So, how well have we kept our pledge?
This is best told in numbers: In 2025, the world witnessed more armed conflicts than in any year since 1946.
Sixty-five active conflicts, 8 of which between states.
More than 240 thousand lives lost to organized violence, the deadliest toll in three decades.
About 120 million people driven from their homes, roughly 1 in 70 people.
So, are we leaving a better world to the generations after us, or have we eroded trust in our collective capacity to evade conflicts and confront the challenges that face the world.
Trust is not built through declarations.

Trust is built when commitments are honored, when rules are applied consistently, when institutions act with responsibility, and when people can see that international cooperation produces tangible results in their lives.
Twenty years ago, shortly after peacefully restoring our independence, Montenegro took its seat in this Assembly as a full member of the United Nations.
This year therefore holds special significance for us.
We celebrate twenty years of our UN membership as a sovereign country.
A child born in Montenegro that year is now twenty years old.

A generation has come of age witnessing Montenegro’s transformation from a newly independent state into a country helping shape the Balkans defined not by the conflicts of the past, but by the opportunities of the future.
On the geostrategic front, Montenegro has paved the path towards our future in the EU, which is now within reach.
Our goal is clear: by 2028, to see Montenegro’s flag stand among the member states of the European Union.
In 2017, Montenegro joined NATO, strengthening not only our own security but also contributing to the stability of our entire region.
We have kept good relations with our neighbors and demonstrated that a multi-ethnic, multi-religious and multicultural society can turn diversity into confidence, belonging and common purpose.
At home, we have transformed our economy and strengthened the democratic institutions on which lasting prosperity depends.
Much work remains ahead of us, but the foundations have been laid for a society in which talent and effort open doors; and a country where young people can imagine their future at home.
For us, the European Union is not simply a destination we wish to reach, but a value-based journey that we have embarked on.
When the European perspective of the Balkans was reaffirmed at the Thessaloniki Summit in 2003, the world looked very different.
Multilateralism and international cooperation were expanding.
The European Union was one of the most attractive political projects in the world and would welcome thirteen new member states over the following decade.
At the same time, the Balkans was still emerging from the devastation and divisions of the 1990s.
More than two decades later, we live in a profoundly different international environment.
The international order is entering a new and uncertain phase.
This is why enlargement of the European Union is an act of strategic foresight.
It is one of the best investments Europe can make in peace, security and long-term stability.
Montenegro is proud to stand today at the forefront of that process, ready to serve as an example for other candidate countries.
Not because our journey has been without difficulties.
But because our journey demonstrates something essential: progress is possible. Reforms matter.
And democratic political culture pays off.
Earlier this year, leaders from across Europe gathered in Montenegro for the European Union–Balkans Summit.
For Montenegro, that gathering carried a meaning far beyond protocol.
It demonstrated how far our country has travelled and how close our European future has become.
It also sent an important message about our region: The future of the entire Balkan region lies within the European Union.
Our region has carried the weight of division for too long.
A new chapter is being written through cooperation, connectivity, economic opportunity and European integration.
My generation has a responsibility to help complete that chapter.
These responsibilities are not important because of the titles they carry.
They are important because of what they allow us to contribute — to reconciliation, connectivity, democratic resilience and the European future of our region.
And lasting reconciliation cannot be built on denial, selective approaches to justice or the glorification of those convicted of war crimes.
It requires respect for the judgments of international courts and equal dignity for every victim, regardless of their identity or background.
And in a world searching for proof that cooperation still works, Montenegro is contributing to the vision that the Balkans become that proof.
The principles that guide us at home guide us here, in this very organization.
Our engagement within the United Nations system is guided by the same principles.

Montenegro is a reliable, credible and predictable partner, committed to an effective multilateral system with the UN Charter at its core, aligned with the European Union’s Common Foreign and Security Policy and working closely with our NATO Allies and EU partners in support of international peace and security.
This commitment comes at a time when the United Nations itself is facing a profound test.
Conflicts are eroding trust in the international system.
Climate change is testing the resilience of states and societies.
Artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies are creating risks at a speed that national frameworks alone cannot adequately address.
It must be more effective multilateralism.

Montenegro therefore strongly supports the UN reform agenda and the ambition to build a United Nations that is more effective, more agile, more accessible, financially sustainable and fit for the challenges of our time.

This reform must strengthen the UN’s ability to deliver where it matters most: in preventing conflict, protecting human rights and freedoms, advancing sustainable development and responding effectively to humanitarian crises.
This responsibility extends to the Security Council itself, which must become more effective, representative, accountable and transparent.
And the exercise of the veto must carry the weight of conscience, above all when the world is confronted with mass atrocities and the large-scale loss of civilian life.
The Charter of the United Nations must remain our common reference point.
Montenegro will be a constructive partner in those efforts.
Excellences, Montenegro remains committed to supporting Ukraine and welcomes all credible diplomatic efforts aimed at bringing the war to an end.
We believe that a just and lasting peace must be achieved through dialogue and diplomacy.
In Gaza, our responsibility begins with the protection of human lives.
Civilians must be protected and humanitarian assistance must reach those in need safely and without obstruction.
Palestinians deserve dignity, freedom and a viable state of their own.
Montenegro supports a negotiated two-state solution, with the State of Israel and an independent and viable State of Palestine living side by side in peace, security and mutual recognition.
The disarmament of Hamas remains an important element of a sustainable settlement, while full respect for international humanitarian law must guide us throughout.
But human dignity cannot have different standards.
The same commitment to international law applies to freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, a route whose security has implications far beyond the region.

Disruptions affect energy markets and global trade, but they also affect food security through the supply and price of fertilizers and other critical agricultural inputs, with particularly serious consequences for vulnerable import-dependent countries.
At the same time, we must not allow conflicts that receive less international attention to become forgotten conflicts.
In Sudan, Myanmar, Haiti and elsewhere, civilians continue to endure violence, displacement and profound insecurity.
Dear Colleagues, Human rights are at the heart of the society we are building at home and of the international order we promote abroad.
Human dignity is universal and indivisible.

That means protecting the rights and freedoms of every person, combating discrimination and hate speech, and safeguarding the independent institutions, free media and civil society on which democratic societies depend.
Montenegro is proud of its multi-ethnic, multi-religious and multicultural character.
We understand that diversity is not a challenge to be managed.
It is a strength to be protected.
Montenegro sits where the Mediterranean meets the Balkans — a small country shaped by different cultures, religions and identities.
Our history has taught us that living together cannot be taken for granted.
It has to be renewed by every generation.
Perhaps this is why we understand so well that trust is not the absence of differences.
Trust is the ability to live with those differences without allowing them to become divisions.
At a time of growing polarization, societies do not become stronger by making everyone the same.
They become stronger by building institutions in which every citizen can recognize the same fairness and the same dignity.
The choices we make today on peace, technology and climate action will shape the lives of generations yet to come.
The Pact for the Future reminds us of precisely this responsibility: the decisions we make today must not undermine the possibilities of those who will live with their consequences tomorrow.
But future generations should not only be the subject of our decisions.
They should have a voice in making them.
Montenegro has heard the call from young people to move from participation to real influence in decision-making.
Young people are not simply beneficiaries of public policy; they are partners in shaping it.
And education is our most powerful investment in young people, equipping them with knowledge, critical thinking and values they need to shape a better world.
This is also personal to me.
I know what education can make possible.
I was born and educated in Montenegro.
And it was education which gave me the opportunity to study and work abroad, to learn from other countries and institutions, and ultimately to return home to serve my country.
It shaped my belief that the place where a child is born should never define the limits of what that child can become.
Coming from a small country, one can sometimes assume that greater size brings greater vision and greater wisdom.
But the United Nations reminds us of a simple truth: vision and wisdom are not measured by the size of a country, but by the ideas we bring and the responsibility with which we act.

Our responsibility is to expand those possibilities: to build schools that inspire, institutions that recognize talent, economies that reward ideas and work, and societies in which young people have a reason to stay and those who left have a reason to return.
Artificial intelligence will increasingly shape those possibilities.
But AI presents not only an extraordinary opportunity; it also creates a responsibility to ensure that technological transformation remains human-centered and rights-based.
Technology must remain at the service of humanity — not the other way around.
Climate change demands the same long-term responsibility.
Montenegro carries the identity and responsibility of an ecological state.
Our mountains, rivers, forests and the Adriatic Sea are not simply natural resources.
They are part of our national identity and of the legacy we will leave to future generations.
But climate change is also a question of global fairness.
Those who have contributed the least to this crisis are too often the first and hardest hit by its consequences.
No country can solve this challenge alone.
This is one of the clearest reasons why effective multilateralism remains indispensable.
Twenty years ago, Montenegro entered this hall at the beginning of a new chapter in our history.
We have built our institutions, secured our place on the global stage, strengthened our economy and democracy, and brought our country within reach of membership in the European Union.
Our transformation is not complete, but its direction is clear.

When the next generation of Montenegro stands in this hall twenty years from now, I hope they will be able to say that we used our moment well: that Montenegro completed its European journey, our region left old divisions behind, and we stood firmly in defense of the rules and principles that protect peace.
But above all, I hope they will be able to say something much simpler: We gave them more opportunities than we had ourselves.
Because that is ultimately the responsibility of leadership — not simply to manage the present, but to expand the possibilities of the future.
At the beginning of this address, I spoke about the meaning we attach to keeping one’s word.
Perhaps that is also what the United Nations needs most today.

Not new promises for every new challenge, but renewed confidence that the promises we have already made still carry weight: to uphold the UN Charter, to protect human dignity, to preserve peace, and to leave those who come after us more possibilities than we inherited ourselves.
Montenegro will continue to do its part — at home, in our region and here, at the United Nations.
This session of the General Assembly is convening on the eve of the 65th anniversary of Mongolia’s full-fledged membership in the United Nations.

In 1961, Mongolia made history by raising its national flag with the golden Soyombo at the United Nations and becoming the 101st member of the United Nations, the guarantor of global peace and security and the beacon of hope and trust for the world's nations.

Mongolia welcomes the convening of the eighty-first session of the United Nations General Assembly under the theme “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All,” reaffirming its belief in the central role of the United Nations in fostering mutual trust, mutual respect, and cooperation among the nations and peoples of the world.
Mongols say, “If you do your best, fate will do the rest.”
The United Nations is an organization based on the trust and commitment of each Member State, and the UN is strengthened by their dedication and sustained efforts.
Therefore, it is incumbent upon us, Member States, to uphold the mission of the United Nations with a sincere heart.
Rather than simply expecting support and assistance, we must remain deeply conscious of our own responsibilities and duties and dedicate our wholehearted efforts to strengthening the United Nations.
It is through trust and hope, dedication and commitment, and engagement and participation of every Member State, that we can strengthen the United Nations.
A stronger United Nations, in turn, will deliver more efficiently towards global peace, security, and sustainable development, thereby creating conditions for all Member States to benefit.

As the conflicts and confrontations flash across the world, the walls of distrust rise higher, and the chasm of misunderstanding grows deeper, it is becoming crucial to shape and develop international relations not through a form of multi-polarity that risks driving the world toward division, but through a multi-pillared principle that respects the pluralism inherent in each nation's history, culture, civilization, core national interests, and chosen path of development.

Eight centuries ago, our ancestors established the great "Pax Mongolica," promoting, for the first time, the idea to the world that nations could mutually recognize one another's values and that peoples of diverse civilizations and faiths could coexist.
This historic contribution of the Mongols to the advancement of humankind continues to be recognized by the international community.

Let us strengthen multilateral cooperation through the multi-pillar principle inspired by the ideas of "Pax Mongolica," so that we may restore our trust and hope through shared responsibility, reform the United Nations with a common purpose, and build a better, more peaceful world through the strength of our collective action.

Despite the remarkable heights of development and progress humanity has reached, our planet is currently confronted with more than 90 armed conflicts, around 30 of which are international, demonstrating that global peace and security remain unstable and that geopolitical and geostrategic competition continues to intensify.
This results in the disruption of global economic supply chains, a rise in thein the prices of energy, fuel, raw materials, and food, as well as economic strains on nations around the world.

All of this is weakening the international order established since the Second World War, changing the universally recognized norms of international law, and undermining the stability of multilateral relations and cooperation.

Mongolia shares the view expressed by United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres in his Annual Report on the Work of the Organization that in a world marked by turbulence, division and uncertainty, the United Nations is more necessary than ever.

Hence, Mongolia underscores the tangible progress made under Secretary-General’s UN80 initiative to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of the United Nations in response to the challenges of our time, and reaffirms its active support for this initiative.
The effectiveness of the United Nations, the decisiveness of its actions, and the ability of nations to unite their efforts will ultimately depend upon us, the Member States.

that Mongolia is confident the soon-to-be-appointed Secretary-General will steadfastly uphold the purposes and principles of the United Nations and international law, ensure that the voices and positions of all Member States are equally heard and reflected, and provide strong leadership in restoring trust and managing transformation within the United Nations.

Believing that reform of the Security Council should be at the core of broader United Nations reform, Mongolia maintains its principled position in support of expanding the number of both permanent and non-permanent members of the Security Council, ensuring equitable representation of developing countries in the Council, and promoting greater openness and transparency in its work.
Mongolia is one of the 58 countries that have never served as a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council.

Therefore, Mongolia aspires to actively participate in the work of the Security Council and contribute to finding collective solutions to the problems and challenges facing the international community.

In manifestation of this aspiration, I officially announce from this rostrum today that Mongolia is presenting its candidature for a non-permanent seat of the UN Security Council for the term 2048-2049.

On behalf of the people of Mongolia, I extend my heartfelt gratitude to the United Nations and its system organizations for their valuable contributions to our country’s development and progress and their longstanding constructive cooperation over the 65 years since Mongolia’s accession to the United Nations as a full-fledged member.

Mongolia has been contributing with honor to the efforts on strengthening international peace and security, advancing social and economic development, and protecting human rights - the core pillars of the United Nations.
For instance, more than three decades ago, in pursuit of its foreign policy to ensure national security through political and diplomatic means, Mongolia declared its territory nuclear-weapon-free.
Since then, Mongolia has consistently pursued policies and taken actions to verify this status legally.

In this spirit, the United Nations General Assembly adopts, on a biennial basis, the resolution entitled "Mongolia's international security and nuclear-weapon-free status," initiated by Mongolia in 1998.

Furthermore, Mongolia has made tangible contributions to global efforts to maintain international peace and security through its active participation in United Nations Peacekeeping Operations and other international missions, having deployed more than 23,000 military and police personnel to hotspots around the world since 2002.Even today, our troops are serving in the "Gang Suppression Force" multinational police and military mission deployed to Haiti.

Mongolia has been actively advancing the implementation of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1325, “Women, Peace and Security,” and has become one of the few countries to have reached 15 percent women’s representation among its military personnel serving in United Nations Peacekeeping Operations.

Since 2006, when Mongolia deployed its first female peacekeeper to the UN mission in Western Sahara, Mongolian women have made valuable contributions to global peace over the past two decades through their courage, resilience, and ingenuity.
In this connection, Mongolia plans to host the second international conference on "Women's Participation in UN Peacekeeping Operations" in Ulaanbaatar in 2027.

I am pleased to highlight Mongolia’s active leadership within the United Nations in advancing the interests of landlocked developing countries, drawing greater international attention to their special needs and unique circumstances, and cooperating with these countries to ensure that their voices are heard on the global stage.

Mongolia has launched several important initiatives in this regard, including serving as one of the founding members of the Group of Landlocked Developing Countries at the United Nations and the establishment of the International Think Tank for Landlocked Developing Countries in Ulaanbaatar.

To translate the Awaza Programme of Action into tangible outcomes, it is essential for landlocked developing countries to align the Programme with their national development agendas and make full use of available resources and opportunities to accelerate regional integration and cooperation.

We also call upon the international community, banks, financial institutions, and development partners to provide credible assistance to landlocked developing countries through their support and collaboration.

As the deadline for the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development approaches, the 2026 SDG report shows that only 36 percent of the Sustainable Development Goals are on track or making moderate progress, while 15 percent are regressing.

It is deeply regrettable that, according to the latest report of the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, released at this critical time, global military expenditure has reached an all-time high of 2.9 trillion USD.

It is time for all of us to ponder and reflect with common sense on what progress could have been achieved in the development of human society if this huge budget and funds had been spent on tackling pressing issues such as combating global warming and climate change, and improving education, health, food security, and advancement of women and children.
According to the Sustainable Development Report 2026, Mongolia has achieved 68.8 percent of the SDGs, reflecting the tangible results of our efforts and the progress we have made in recent years.

As a country experiencing the adverse impacts of climate change first-hand, Mongolia has remained steadfast in contributing to global collective efforts to protect and preserve our natural environment.

In this regard, Mongolia is successfully implementing a series of national policies and initiatives, including the “Billion Trees,” “Food Revolution,” “White Gold,” “Blue Gold,” and “Healthy Mongolian,” aimed at restoring degraded land, expanding forest resources, protecting soil, water and pastureland, ensuring food supply and security, and supporting sustainable rural development.

Mongolia’s “Billion Trees” National Movement goes far beyond tree planting and afforestation; it is a comprehensive, nationwide initiative aimed at combating desertification and land degradation, scaling up land restoration, expanding forest resources, protecting soil fertility, water resources and biodiversity, mitigating the adverse impacts of climate change, improving food supply, and creating employment opportunities.

Furthermore, the United Nations General Assembly resolution initiated by Mongolia proclaiming 2026 as the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists provides an opportunity to raise global awareness of the importance of rangeland ecosystems, support the livelihoods of pastoralists, strengthen sustainable food systems, conserve biodiversity, and preserve the cultural heritage of nomadic peoples.
In this regard, Mongolia, with its millennia-old tradition of nomadic pastoralism, took the initiative to convene the Global Pastoralist Gathering and Conference in Ulaanbaatar.
The Gathering brought together around 400 herders from 57 countries, whose opinions and fruitful discussion of challenges and solutions culminated in the adoption of the Ulaanbaatar Declaration.

Moreover, in August, Mongolia successfully hosted the seventeenth session of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification in Ulaanbaatar, under the theme “Restoring Land, Restoring Hope.”
Restoring Mother Nature to its pristine state and creating conditions for future generations to live in a healthy environment with confidence and contentment must be a noble duty of humanity.
Mother Nature and healthy soil are the guarantee of humanity's existence, and the foundation of food and water resources, livelihood, and sustainable development.
Healthy soil means healthy food, and healthy food means healthy people.

Therefore, desertification, land degradation, and drought should not be viewed merely as environmental issues but should be addressed holistically in connection with food supply and security, water resources, livelihoods, sustainable development, and global peace and security.

In this spirit, as the Presidency of UNCCD COP17, Mongolia has advanced the Steppe Action Agenda, built upon three interconnected flagship initiatives: the Rangelands Flagship Initiative, the Water-Land Nexus Initiative, and the Nature-based Solutions for Sustainable Infrastructure Initiative.
Particularly, we regard the Rangelands Flagship Initiative as a landmark global movement that opens a new chapter in the history of rangeland conservation.

This initiative is special in raising global awareness that the protection, sustainable management, and restoration of rangelands are of strategic importance for building resilience to climate change, ensuring food security, and maintaining balanced ecosystems.

The nomadic way of life that we Mongols have inherited and carried forward over thousands of years embodies a comprehensive set of values and wisdom for living in harmony with nature and preserving it in its pristine state.

Today, we Mongols aim to share with the world our cultural heritage and the traditional knowledge and experiences gained from living in harmony with nature, thereby contributing to enhanced adaptation and resilience to climate change.

Mongolia consistently adheres to the principle of resolving any conflicts through diplomacy and multilateral dialogue, while maintaining longstanding friendly relations with the countries of the region.
Building on this distinctive advantage, Mongolia held the 11th International Conference of the Ulaanbaatar Dialogue on Northeast Asian Security this year.

The Ulaanbaatar Dialogue has evolved into a unique platform for strengthening trust and confidence-building across Northeast Asia, facilitating multilateral discussions among government delegates and scholars, not only on traditional security challenges such as political and disarmament matters, but also on a broad range of issues including energy, infrastructure connectivity, green development, and humanitarian cooperation.

Furthermore, as an active member of the United Nations, Mongolia has contributed to international cooperation to advance gender equality, strengthen women’s political participation and leadership, and increase their representation at decision-making levels.

In recent years, Mongolia has established a tradition of hosting international events dedicated to women in our country, including the International Conference on Strengthening the Role of Women in Peacekeeping in 2022, the Female Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in 2023, and the World Women’s Forum in 2024, in collaboration with the United Nations, and the World Women Entrepreneurs’ Forum in 2025.

Hence, I am confident that the World Women Parliamentarians’ Forum, to be held in Ulaanbaatar on October 12-13 this year, will substantially contribute to strengthening women’s political leadership and inter-parliamentary cooperation, thereby advancing gender equality and accelerating progress towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals.
I cordially invite you to participate in this important event at a high level and with broad representation.
Mongolia will continue to serve as a solid bridge for partnership, cooperation, and solidarity in advancing women’s social and political leadership and participation at all levels.

Mongolia has consistently championed and supported numerous initiatives within the international community aimed at preserving and promoting cultural heritage, traditional knowledge, and the shared values of humanity.

For instance, in 2025, at Mongolia’s initiative, a United Nations General Assembly resolution proclaiming World Horse Day was adopted, which recognizes the invaluable contribution of horses to the history, civilization, and socio-economic development of peoples around the world.

Moreover, last July, the Cemetery Complexes of the Xiongnu Nobility, Mongolia’s first statehood, were inscribed in the UNESCO World Heritage List, reflecting international recognition of their historical and cultural significance.
It is my pleasure to underline that Mongolia is serving for the first time as a member of the UNESCO World Heritage Committee for the term 2026-2029.
Moreover, this year marks the 820th anniversary of the Great Mongol Empire founded by Great Chinggis Khaan, Man of the Millennium, King of Kings.

The United Nations General Assembly resolution adopted on the occasion of the eight hundred years of Mongolian statehood highly values and emphasizes the contribution of Mongols to the history of humankind by “recognizing the richness of nomadic civilization and its important contribution to promoting dialogue and interaction among all forms of civilization, and that nomadic civilization influenced, inter alia, societies across Asia and Europe and, in turn, absorbed influences from both East and West in a true interchange of human values, the important role in the development of extensive trade networks and the creation of large administrative, cultural, religious and commercial centers.”
This demonstrates that these historical contributions embodied progressive ideas that could serve as a foundation for today’s collective efforts to safeguard peace and stability.

For example, the renowned Mongolist Władysław Kotwicz, in his work “Mongols are the promoters of the idea of global peace from the early 14th century,” noted that Öljeitü, Il-Khan of the Mongol Empire, in his letter sent to King Philip IV of France in 1305, eloquently underscored the value of harmonious relations among nations and peoples in the thoughtful words, “What could be better than true concord?”
History is the foundation upon which we reflect on the past, shape the present, and build the future, and it is the memory of our statehood.

Scholars advise that studying the establishment of “Pax Mongolica” by Great Chinggis Khaan and his successors, as well as the history of its foreign policy and diplomacy, offers good practices and enduring lessons.

Hence, we, the Mongol people, who are guarding the sacred hearth of the Great Mongol Empire, wish to call upon from this mighty rostrum of the United Nations that if the nations of the world can bring together their efforts, it is possible to establish a Pax Globalica, a Global Peace, embodying the vision of the Pax Mongolica, which, eight centuries ago, laid the foundation for nations to coexist in peace and for humanity to flourish.

The role and contribution of the United Nations in further strengthening mutual understanding, mutual trust, and mutual respect among world nations, and in fostering a peaceful world free from war and conflict, where all can prosper together, are becoming increasingly critical than ever.

Therefore, let us work together to empower the United Nations, the guarantor of world peace and security and a source of hope and trust for the nations of the world, into a strong and respected Organization capable of bringing Pax Globalica!
May the eternal blue sky bless humankind forever with peace across the world.

The theme for this session, "Restoring Trust, Managing Tansformation: a United Nations that Delivers for All," strikes at the heart of our current global reality.
We live in an era of deep fractures.
Global systems are failing to manage rapid technological, economic, and environmental shifts equitably.
For the United Nations to remain relevant, it must transform into an institution that delivers tangible progress for the most vulnerable, leaving no nation behind.
I would, therefore, like to highlight six opportunities for restoring trust, managing transformation and, thereby ensuring a United Nations that delivers for all.

The first opportunity is accelerating sustainable development and economic transformation: Mr. President, the timeline for the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development is rapidly drawing to a close, yet the promises of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) remain dangerously out of reach for millions.
For Malawi, the pursuit of wealth creation, self- reliance and economic transformation is not merely a political aspiration; it is an urgent survival strategy.
Because of this, we have remained steadfast in implementing the SDGs, in alignment with our long-term development vision, the Malawi 2063.

President, I am happy to report that Malawi successfully presented our third Voluntary National Review during the 2026 ECOSOC High-Level Political Forum, thereby reaffirming our commitment to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Malawi 2063, as well as our desire to accelerate sustainable development and economic transformation.
The review revealed that even though we face numerous structural challenges, we have made some progress on many of the SDGs.
Mr. President, our goal is to systematically transform our economy by modernizing agriculture, expanding mining and accelerating digitalization.
However, national efforts alone cannot dismantle the structural barriers built into the global economic architecture.

Developing nations require deliberate, scaled investment in industrialization, sustainable infrastructure and regional value chains to transition from primary commodity exporters to diversified, industrialized economies.
In addition, we cannot achieve sustainable development while drowning in debt.
Malawi, therefore, calls for immediate, comprehensive debt relief and restructuring.
The current international financial architecture forces developing nations to choose between servicing predatory debts and investing in health, education and climate resilience.
We also call for a massive scaling-up of concessional development financing.
We need targeted investments in our key productive sectors, namely agriculture, industrialization and infrastructure development as follows:-
(a) Agricultural modernization through mechanization and commercialization to guarantee food security;

(b) Building local industry so that we stop exporting raw materials, and create decent jobs for our youth, who make up nearly 40 percent of the Malawi population; and connect Malawi to regional and global markets.
We, therefore, call upon our international partners to align their support with national blueprints like the Malawi 2063 in order to generate meaningful job creation and shared prosperity.

The second opportunity is strengthening climate action and resilience: Mr. President, Malawi contributes negligibly to global greenhouse gas emissions, yet we remain on the frontline of the climate crisis.

In recent years, devastating cyclones, prolonged droughts and increasingly erratic weather patterns have destroyed infrastructure, devastated crops, displaced thousands of our citizens and inflicted severe damage on our economy.
This year, we face the added threat of El Niño-related extreme weather, which risks further undermining livelihoods, food security and economic stability.
As such, we are fighting back by embedding climate resilience into our national development planning and strengthening locally driven adaptation measures.
However, our efforts are continually outpaced by the scale and speed of climate change.
Climate shocks repeatedly destroy infrastructure, decimate agricultural production, exacerbate food insecurity, and erode hard-won development gains.
The global community must therefore move beyond rhetoric and translate commitments into meaningful action.
We call for the full and effective operationalization and capitalization of the Loss and Damage Fund.

Major historical and current emitters must honour their climate- finance commitments by providing accessible, predictable, grant-based and highly concessional financing, rather than relying on debt-creating instruments further burden vulnerable countries already struggling to cope with the consequences of a crisis they did little to cause.
Malawi, therefore, calls for enhanced, predictable and easily accessible climate finance, with greater emphasis on adaptation and disaster-risk reduction.
We need sustainable investment in early-warning systems, climate-resilient infrastructure, sustainable land management, climate-smart agriculture and locally led adaptation.
Climate change is an existential threat to Malawi's development and to the hard-won gains we have made.

Mr. President, the third opportunity is to reform global governance and strengthen multilateralism: The current global challenges underscore a fundamental truth: our multilateral framework is fractured because its foundational architecture is obsolete.
The institutions designed in 1945 no longer reflect the geopolitical and economic realities of 2026.
Malawi reaffirms its unwavering commitment to multilateralism, but it must be a multilateralism that is inclusive, fair, and democratic.
We call for an urgent comprehensive reform of the United Nations Security Council to correct the historical injustice done to Africa.
Africa deserves permanent representation with full veto privileges, as articulated in the Ezulwini Consensus.
Furthermore, the international financial architecture, specifically the IMF and the World Bank, must be radically overhauled.

The current system traps developing nations in cycles of unsustainable debt, forcing governments to choose between servicing foreign loans or funding basic education and healthcare for their citizens.

Mr. President, because Malawi strongly believes in multilateralism, we take responsibility when called upon by the international community to participate in causes that further the aims of this organisation.
Malawi remains firmly committed to the rule of law, accountability and the peaceful resolution of disputes as indispensable foundations of an effective multilateral system.
It is in this spirit that Malawi has presented the candidature of Lady Justice Tujilane Chizumila for election as a Judge of the International Criminal Court for the term 2027–2036.

Justice Chizumila is a distinguished jurist with extensive judicial and legal experience at the national, regional and international levels, including her service as a Judge of the African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights.
Her candidature reflects Malawi’s commitment to strengthening international justice through experienced, independent and highly qualified judicial leadership.

As States Parties prepare to elect six judges to the International Criminal Court in December 2026, Malawi respectfully seeks the valued support of States Parties for the candidature of Lady Justice Tujilane Chizumila.

We are confident that her extensive judicial experience, commitment to the rule of law and demonstrated service to justice and human rights would enable her to make a meaningful contribution to the work of the Court.
Malawi looks forward to the support of fellow States Parties for her election and to continuing our collective efforts to strengthen the institutions of international justice.
Mr. President, the fourth opportunity for restoring trust, managing transformation, and thereby ensuring a United Nations that delivers for all, lies in strengthening global health security.
Economic transformation and sustainable development are impossible without a healthy population.
The vulnerabilities exposed by recent global pandemics continue to linger, reminding us that global health security is only as strong as its weakest link.
Malawi is making strides toward achieving Universal Health Coverage and strengthening our primary healthcare systems.
However, systemic global inequities in healthcare access, medical manufacturing and vaccine distribution remain glaringly unresolved.
True global health security demands decentralized pharmaceutical manufacturing capabilities, unrestricted technology transfers and intellectual property waivers during health emergencies.
My delegation appeals to all of us here to finalize a robust, legally binding Pandemic Treaty that guarantees equity, solidarity and immediate resource sharing for the Global South.
We also call for collaboration in efforts to build long-term resilience against pandemics, through investments in our domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing capacity.
By producing essential medicines within Africa, the entire world gains through stronger health security and stable supply chains, especially through faster outbreak response.
Mr. President, the fifth opportunity is to promote human rights, peace and international security: Malawi firmly believes that development, peace and human rights are inextricably linked.
We remain deeply committed to upholding the constitutional rights of all our citizens, strengthening our democratic institutions and maintaining an uncompromising stance against corruption.
Further, we strongly defend the right to development as an inalienable human right.
True freedom cannot exist in conditions of extreme poverty and systemic economic exclusion.

On the global stage, we view, with great alarm, the proliferation of violent conflicts, unconstitutional changes of government, geo-political fragmentation and acts of racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related intolerance.
Mr. President, the Malawi nation is not standing aloof as all these alarming developments occur.
Malawi continues to play its part in global peace operations, deploying our brave men and women to United Nations peacekeeping missions to safeguard stability on our continent.
In this regard, let me reiterate the calls for immediate cessation of hostilities in all active conflict zones worldwide.
Global resources currently being funneled into destructive warfare should, instead, be redirected towards eradicating poverty, building schools and financing sustainable development.
We also reaffirm our solidarity with global efforts to combat racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance.

The last, but not least, opportunity is in advancing economic diplomacy and strategic partnerships: Mr. President, in alignment with the Malawi 2063, our foreign policy prioritizes robust economic diplomacy.
Malawi recognizes navigating the complexities of the 2020s requires a paradigm shift away from traditional, paternalistic foreign aid, toward genuine reciprocal economic diplomacy.
For this reason, we are actively strengthening bilateral and multilateral partnerships to attract foreign direct investment, enhance international trade, and mobilize development assistance.
Further to this, Malawi highly values South-South and triangular cooperation.

Collaborative initiatives with fellow developing nations allow us to share cost-effective technologies, best practices, and home- grown solutions in climate-smart agriculture, renewable energy, and digital governance.
We will continue to deepen these alliances to accelerate our national development priorities.
Mr. President, as we take steps to grasp these opportunities, we must also recognize the emergence of Artificial Intelligence, which presents both opportunities and threats to humanity.
Malawi welcomes the transformative potential of AI as an expression of human ingenuity and as an increasingly important tool for accelerating sustainable development.

For developing countries, including Malawi, AI offers opportunities to strengthen agricultural productivity and food security, improve healthcare and education, enhance climate resilience and disaster preparedness, expand financial inclusion, and improve the efficiency of public services.

Malawi believes, however, technological advancement must remain human-centred: Artificial Intelligence should complement and enhance human capabilities rather than diminish the indispensable role of people in shaping their own development.

At the same time, Malawi recognises that the rapid expansion of Artificial Intelligence presents significant challenges, particularly for developing economies with fragile labour markets and limited technological infrastructure.

Automation could disrupt employment and widen existing inequalities, while unequal access to computing capacity, data, digital infrastructure, skills and financing risks creating a new technological divide between and within countries.

Malawi therefore calls upon the United Nations to continue promoting an inclusive, ethical and development-oriented global framework for AI governance—one that safeguards human dignity and employment, builds the technological capacities of developing countries, facilitates equitable access to AI technologies and ensures that the benefits of innovation contribute directly to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals.
No country should be left behind in the emerging AI-driven global economy.
Mr. President, in conclusion, restoring trust requires honesty, accountability and action.
Managing transformation requires courage, vision and solidarity.
The choices we make today will reverberate for generations to come.
We can choose to retreat into isolationism and protectionism, or we can choose to summon the political courage required to build a fairer, more resilient and inclusive world.
Malawi stands ready to play its part.
We are transforming our economy, reforming our institutions and investing in our people.
But we cannot do it alone in an unfair global environment.

We stand ready to work hand-in-hand with all member states to bridge the divides, restore trust in multilateralism and deliver a sustainable dignified future for all humanity Let this 81st Session of the General Assembly mark the turning point where the United Nations transitions from a forum of speeches to an engine of delivery.
Let us build a United Nations that delivers wealth instead of poverty, resilience instead of vulnerability, and peace instead of conflict.
A United Nations that truly delivers for all.

The theme of this session, “Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that works for all”, is perfectly in keeping with the concerns of peoples who aspire to peace and progress while bombs and other instruments of mass destruction constantly bring death and desolation in all parts of our planet.
How can trust be restored and transformation managed in the world so that the United Nations effectively bring peace and happiness to all peoples?
I recall that our previous session called on us to act “better together”.
But it imposes on us a duty of assessment, to measure what has been accomplished and to recognize what has not.
For trust is not built through the accumulation of promises, but through their effective implementation for the benefit of peoples.
Trust is not decreed. It is built. It is earned.
And it requires truth and justice.

How can trust be restored when, for decades, the idea of a poor Africa has been fostered through propaganda, condemned to survive thanks to the assistance of a supposed international generosity, while its wealth is stolen and/or sequestrated for the benefit of other agendas?

How can this trust be restored when the international institutions, supposed to protect us, have become the instruments of a world order where some peoples count and others merely survive, and where international law is variable in application?

What is to be said of the crimes committed in Libya, Iraq, Palestine, Iran, Lebanon, Cuba, Venezuela, and the Sahel, in the name of supposedly universal values and which remain unpunished, while sovereign nations are threatened with sanctions for having simply wanted to decide their destiny?
The Niger is following with deep concern the tragic situation prevailing in Palestine, particularly in Gaza, where civilians are paying an unbearable human price.
We call for the effective protection of civilian populations, unimpeded humanitarian access and the search for a just and lasting peace.
The Niger reaffirms its support for a two- State solution, enabling the State of Palestine and the State of Israel to live side by side in peace, security and dignity.
How can trust be restored when, 81 years after San Francisco, Africa, with its 1.4 billion inhabitants and 54 States, still has no permanent seat on the Security Council?

Through my voice, the Niger reaffirms its attachment to the Ezulwini Consensus and requests that this historical anomaly cease to be a subject of sterile debates and finally become the object of a concrete decision.
Our Sahel is in a war of liberation against a conspiracy aimed at its recolonization!
What is happening in the Sahel is neither a simple armed rebellion, nor a religious war, nor a fatality arising from our own weaknesses.
What some call “terrorism” in our region is a cynical engineering of recolonization, clothed in the rags of extremism, but whose real motivation lies elsewhere: in the coveting of our resources.
The uranium of the Niger, the gold of Mali and Burkina Faso, the lithium, gas, oil and so many other riches continue to make the former colonial powers salivate.
They want us to believe that we are incapable of governing ourselves, of producing, of thinking and of defending ourselves.

They want to convince us that we have neither science, nor intelligence, nor sovereignty to build anything valuable by and for ourselves and that, consequently, we should accept the tutelage of Emmanuel Macron’s France and its allies; a France which very often acts through local proxies, networks and complicities.
For centuries, self-depreciation, fear and resignation have been instilled.

They continue to seek to set in permanent conflict communities which, since time immemorial, have lived in harmony within the same space and which have created peaceful mechanisms for the settlement of disputes, in particular joking kinship.
This perfidious undertaking to destabilize the central Sahel, led by France with the active complicity of Ukraine, is now documented.
This criminal undertaking has been exposed since the military and politico-media elites who justify it in the name of the interests of their own countries have, they- themselves, lifted the veil.
I say it solemnly from this rostrum: the Sahel sees. The Sahel hears.
The Sahel remembers and the Sahel understands.
Our Sahel is determined to defend its freedom, its resources and its dignity, whatever the cost.
A people that has decided to be free cannot be recolonized either by fear, by cunning, or even by savage violence.
The AES, the culmination of a long historic struggle by our peoples against colonization and neocolonialism, is henceforth an irreversible process towards the sovereignty of our countries.
We must be fully convinced of this: the century in which we live marks the end of the old hegemonies and the awakening of forces hitherto subjugated.
The AES is for Africa, its historic and contemporary diasporas, what light is to darkness.
For this human community present in the four corners of the world, it is a source of hope and dignity.
I say this before the world, so that the world may understand.

The AES is the result of a movement that comes from the depths of the ages; it is a profound, lasting, irrepressible and irreversible change which, blunting the sharp claws of imperialism, abolishing the slave trade and slavery, overthrowing colonialism and neocolonialism, is carrying the peoples of Africa towards independence, sovereignty and freedom.
I affirm that our Refoundation is directed against no one.
It expresses our determination to rely on ourselves, to have full control over our resources, as well as responsibility for our choices and our alliances.
Our Organization must hear this truth: the sovereignty of our States is not negotiable.
Our resources belong to our peoples.
Our future will no longer be decided elsewhere.

Ladies and Gentlemen, This is the place to salute the courage of our defence and security forces and to pay tribute to all our civilian and military martyrs who lost their lives in the struggle for our full and complete freedom.
We remain open to any security cooperation that takes into account our strategic interests, reciprocal interest and respect for our sovereignty.

With Burkina Faso and Mali, Niger is developing, within the Confederation of Sahel States, cooperation focused on defence and security, diplomacy and development, meeting a requirement for solidarity among peoples facing common challenges.
On 16 September 2023, in Bamako, Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso signed the Liptako-Gourma Charter, giving birth to the Alliance of Sahel States.

On 6 July 2024, in Niamey, our three Heads of State, President Assimi Goïta of Mali, President Ibrahim Traoré of Burkina Faso and President Abdourahamane Tiani of Niger, took a historic step by creating the Confederation of Sahel States.

Two years later, the institutional structure of this Confederation is virtually complete: a unified force of five thousand men is conducting the coordinated fight against the mercenaries operating across our three territories; a Confederation Investment and Development Bank is financing our projects and programmes with our own means; a confederation biometric passport has been in circulation since 29 January 2026; a common television channel, a press agency and a radio station are carrying our voice.
More recently, from 26 to 29 August 2026, the first sessions of the Confederation Parliament were held in Niamey, thus completing our institutional architecture.
It has never waged war and will not wage war against another country; but it is determined to defend itself and to control its natural resources.

We have chosen a transformation based on national responsibility, the enhancement of our resources, the strengthening of our institutions and the tangible improvement of the living conditions of our people.

Since 26 July 2023, Niger has been inexorably advancing towards the full recovery of its sovereignty, under the leadership of the National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland (CNSP) and its President, His Excellency General of the Army Abdourahamane TIANI, President of the Republic, Head of State.
This transformation breaks radically with policies imposed from outside and disconnected from the real needs of the population; it is rooted in the social values of the people of the Niger.

Aware of the challenges it faces, the Government has chosen to mobilize the resources necessary to finance agriculture and the basic social sectors through funds from the voluntary contributions of the women and men of the Niger, in addition to the revenue derived from the exploitation of our mining and petroleum resources, revenue that previously escaped the control of the State.

Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen, A few days ago, on the night of 28 to 29 August 2026, after two previous unsuccessful attempts to attack Diori Hamani International Airport in Niamey, a third attempt at destabilization, orchestrated by obscurantist and colonialist forces, targeted our institutions.
Like the previous ones, it was failed, thanks to the loyalty of our Armed Forces.
It failed thanks to the solidarity of our allies and to the categorical refusal of the Nigerien people to return to subjugation.
Niger has emerged from it united and determined.
The necessary investigations are under way in order to establish the circumstances, responsibilities and the internal and external support linked to this attempt.

At the conclusion of this procedure, Niger reserves the right, in accordance with the Charter of the United Nations and international law, to have recourse to the competent mechanisms to defend its sovereignty.
In that regard, we ask that any concern of a Member State relating to its security be examined with diligence and impartiality, without differentiated treatment.
The credibility of our Organization also depends on its ability to make the voices of all its Member States heard.
Niger seeks confrontation with no country.
It extends its arms to all partners who wish to build a new relation, based on equality, reciprocity and mutual interest.
For more than half a century, Niger’s uranium lit the cities of Europe, while ours remained in darkness.
That injustice has now come to an end.
In June 2025, the State of Niger regained control of the Société des Mines de l’Aïr.

Our resources are now managed by us and for us, and Niger intends to market its uranium on the international market, in full transparency and in strict compliance with its obligations regarding the non-proliferation of nuclear weapons.

In the same spirit, in 2024 our country became an exporter of crude oil thanks to the pipeline linking AGADEM to the Atlantic coast, the longest on the African continent, making Niger one of the fastest-growing economies on the continent in 2025.
That revenue goes to the security, agriculture, electrification, water, education and health of our fellow citizens.

And the Solidarity Fund for the Safeguarding of the Homeland, fuelled by the voluntary contributions of millions of Nigeriens, says everything about a people that has understood that sovereignty has a price, and that it is ready to pay it.
After three years of breaking with the old order, the progress observed on the ground is remarkable.
Our economy recorded growth of 7 per cent in 2025, driven above all by oil and agriculture.

Inflation, which had reached 9.1 per cent in 2024, fell back to -4.7 per cent, thanks in particular to exceptional agricultural production and a targeted reduction in fuel tariffs and the price of cement.
The Major Irrigation Programme, initiated by the President of the Republic and allocated 526.7 billion CFA francs, aims to develop 21,200 hectares of new irrigated perimeters.
The results recorded at this level are very satisfactory because, for the first time in decades, our country has not experienced a food shortage nor called on foreign aid.
Through this programme, we intend to halve our cereal imports by the end of 2027, insha’Allah.
As regards health, we have reduced by 50 per cent the costs of services in public health facilities.
Certain services are free of charge, in particular childbirth, care for children from 0 to 5 years old and dialysis.
The rate of assisted childbirth rose from 36 per cent in 2022 to 42.5 per cent in 2025, and that of prenatal consultations from 32.7 per cent to 38.2 per cent.
Education is free and compulsory for all children in public schools.
Moreover, a 20 per cent reduction in school fees in private institutions was decided in July 2025.

Those orientations, contained in the Programme for the Refoundation of the Republic (PRR) 2025-2029, constitute the reference framework for all State interventions in favour of the structural transformation of our economy.
Those results are very encouraging, despite the scale of the challenges, because they are ours and have been obtained with our own means.
Three years ago, some predicted the collapse of Niger under the weight of sanctions and isolation.
It is standing because its people refused to bow their heads.
It is standing because it found, within the Confederation of Sahel States, a family in the full African meaning of the term.

It is standing because the People’s Democratic Republic of Algeria, a brotherly and neighbouring country, chose to accompany it through a substantial investment in the exploitation of its natural resources and through constant support for its defence system.
With Algeria, we also maintain dynamic cooperation in the fields of health, education, energy, water resources and agriculture.
To that must be added major structuring projects such as the tripartite gas pipeline and the Trans-Saharan Highway.
Above all, Niger is standing because it has regained possession of its soil, its subsoil and its voice.

Our country is also standing because it speaks within our common organization, the United Nations, which counts among its members countries with which we have fruitful cooperation based on mutual respect.
Allow me to say that Togo, Türkiye, the Kingdom of Morocco, the Russian Federation and the People’s Republic of China are among our friends.
The security, development and dignity of our peoples cannot be considered separately.
We believe in international relations based on cooperation, dignity, sovereignty and mutual respect.
Our conviction is that no country, however powerful it may be, can arrogate to itself the title of policeman of the world.
In conclusion, Niger respects the choices of others and asks no one to share its own; it asks everyone to respect them.
It intends to exercise fully its sovereignty over its natural resources, and will never again accept any restriction imposed from outside on its sovereign right to choose its partners freely.
That right is inalienable; it is not negotiable.

We proclaim that confidence will be reborn when each nation, large or small, is treated with the same consideration; when the right to sovereign equality, territorial integrity, the free choice of partnerships and non-interference is respected.
It is on this condition that confidence will be restored, that transformation will be fair and that the United Nations will truly deliver results for all.
2. None of us can pretend that conflicts within our borders or in lands far beyond them do not exact a price from us.
Such is the reach of our interdependence.
Such is the urgency of this session’s sacred duty to restore trust in the international institutions we established to reconcile our differences and advance our common interests.
3. The persistence of conflict across the world recalls the purpose for which the United Nations was founded: to spare succeeding generations the devastation of war.
We must therefore return to the founding principles of dialogue, mutual respect and collective responsibility.
Nigeria stands by the Charter and its promise of a world in which diplomacy prevails over coercion, cooperation over isolation and international law over the arbitrary exercise of power.
4. The reform of this institution must begin with the reconstitution of the Security Council, for the world of 2026 cannot remain captive to the distribution of power in 1945.

Africa cannot continue to fill the Council’s agenda while remaining absent in from accordance with the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration, at least two permanent seats for Africa, with all the rights and responsibilities of permanent membership, including the veto for as long as it exists, and five non-permanent seats in total.
The authority to speak for humanity carries an obligation to represent it.
5. Nigeria stands ready to assume greater responsibility on the strength of obligations honoured and sacrifices made over decades in the service of peace.
From Liberia and Sierra Leone to Darfur, Mali and The Gambia, we have committed international solidarity personnel and required action.
Through ECOWAS, the African Union and our Gulf of Guinea partnerships, we continue to advance mediation, democratic governance, counter-terrorism and maritime security.

6. Our foreign policy rests on the same conviction that guides our sound macroeconomic economic management, private-sector development and strategic public investment, we seek to give sustainable development practical meaning commitments.
This purpose binds our national advancement to our continent’s progress and to our responsibility to contribute to a peaceful, equitable and prosperous world.
7. We understand that governments and multilateral institutions earn trust when their decisions improve lives.
Yet none of these gains will matter if we turn a deaf ear to the threats gathering around our borders and farther afield.
We inhabit the only planet known to sustain human life, and as long as that scientific fact holds, we cannot pretend that we are insulated from conflicts elsewhere.
Geography offers no exemption from the consequences of a fractured world.
8. We reject the false choice between development and climate action.
Developing countries must industrialise, eradicate poverty and expand energy access through low-carbon pathways supported by technology transfer, capacity building and climate finance.
Africa contributes less than four per cent of greenhouse gas emissions, yet bears disproportionate consequences.
Nigeria remains committed to the Paris Agreement and an equitable energy transition that reflects historical responsibility and capacity while protecting people’s right to development.
9. Under our Energy Transition Plan, we are working towards net-zero emissions by 2060 while expanding access to affordable, reliable and sustainable energy.
This effort combines renewable energy, clean cooking and gas as a transitional fuel with climate-smart agriculture and nature-based solutions.

Finance must be governed by equity and shared responsibility rather than charity, with international commitments translated into accessible, predictable and funded mechanisms enabling developing adequately countries to pursue climate action without compromising development objectives.
10. We refuse to surrender our technological future to paranoia.
An invention can be destructive or beneficial, depending on the purposes it serves and the judgement of those who use it.
A knife can take a life in the hands of an assailant and save one in the hands of a surgeon.
We can deploy artificial intelligence to wage war or use it to transform healthcare, education, agriculture, governance and economic productivity.
Much of the anxiety surrounding AI reflects the distrust we have allowed to grow among us.
11. Nigeria is investing in digital public infrastructure, broadband connectivity, innovation ecosystems, research institutions and technology entrepreneurship.
We invite the world to work with our inventive, resourceful and enterprising young people to direct AI towards humanity’s advancement rather than its destruction.
13. One of the greatest obstacles to sustainable development is inadequate financing.
Many developing countries devote substantial resources to debt servicing at the expense of education, healthcare and infrastructure.
Nigeria therefore calls for reform of the international financial architecture, wider access to concessional financing and debt sustainability frameworks that recognise developmental needs.

We also support innovative financing through private capital, blended finance, South-South cooperation and strategic partnerships for sustainable development, climate adaptation and resilient infrastructure.
14. Nigeria further recognises the African Continental Free Trade Area as one of the continent’s most transformative opportunities.
It can strengthen regional value chains, expand intra-African trade, promote industrialisation and attract investment.
Africa must move beyond its historical role as an exporter of raw materials towards greater value addition, manufacturing, technological innovation and knowledge-driven growth.
Our abundant natural resources must become engines of shared prosperity rather than sources of perpetual dependency.
15. No nation, however formidable its defences, can secure itself completely against dangers sustained beyond its borders.
Terrorism, organised crime, cyberattacks and illicit finance exploit the gaps between our national responses, drawing strength from the divisions that weaken collective action.

Nigeria’s prolonged struggle against Boko Haram, ISWAP and other armed groups has taught us that military victories require enduring foundations in education, economic opportunity, accountable governance and communities whose rights and dignity are protected.
Development cannot take root where violence repeatedly uproots livelihoods, and peace cannot endure where injustice and exclusion replenish the ranks of those who threaten it.
16. Our common security therefore demands cooperation equal to the reach of the threats before us.
We must exchange intelligence, strengthen institutional capacity, interrupt the financing of violence and prevent weapons from crossing borders that our responses too often fail to cross.
The turmoil in the Sahel illustrates how insecurity in one territory can imperil its neighbours, displace populations and frustrate commerce, regional integration and democratic governance.
As a founding member of ECOWAS, Nigeria upholds regional solidarity and African leadership in resolving these challenges, reinforced by principled international partnerships.
17. Nigeria remains committed to the peaceful settlement of disputes under the United Nations Charter.
The conflicts in Sudan and other war-torn countries demand urgent diplomacy to address their humanitarian, economic and geopolitical international consequences.
All parties must uphold humanitarian and human rights law, protect civilians and facilitate humanitarian access.
Negotiated settlements must respect sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Within and beyond our continent, no claim to security can justify starving children, denying relief to civilians or erasing communities from the land they call home.
18. We should all be afraid of a world in which we can no longer tell the victim from the aggressor.
When our investment in propaganda shields perpetrators from justice to the point that telling the truth becomes a crime, the promise of this institution stands betrayed.
19. We place our faith in diplomacy because military victories alone cannot secure lasting peace.
Dialogue, reconciliation and inclusive political processes must give people a stake in ending violence and preserving the agreements that follow.
The United Nations must therefore strengthen peacekeeping and give greater attention to peacebuilding, mediation, institution-building and sustainable development.
Prevention must command greater resources and political attention.
20. Africa is ready for the future.
Our resilience, our ingenuity, our youthful population, our natural wealth and our expanding markets can make us a major driver of global growth in this century.
The African Continental Free Trade Area offers exceptional scope to deepen regional integration, accelerate industrialisation and strengthen our place in global value chains.
Developing countries must be recognised as indispensable partners whose contributions to global solutions and shared prosperity extend far beyond their need for assistance.
21. Such a partnership requires a United Nations that evolves with the aspirations of present and future generations.
Institutions that adapt preserve their relevance; those that resist change imperil it.
Nigeria remains optimistic because history shows that countries acting with common purpose and determination can overcome obstacles once considered insurmountable.
Our generation has the privilege of shaping the future and the responsibility to answer for it.
Those who follow us will judge our courage in reforming outdated institutions, building cooperation across divisions, protecting the planet and directing technology responsibly.
22. Nigeria pledges to choose cooperation over confrontation, dialogue over division, hope over fear and partnership over isolation.
These choices must shape institutions that respond to the legitimate aspirations of all nations.
Restoring trust requires us to honour our obligations to one another and to manage the changes before us with justice, wisdom and compassion.
23. The world looks to this Assembly for leadership, and our debates must lead to action worthy of that expectation.
Nigeria believes that the humanity we share is stronger than the divisions we have made and that cooperation remains wiser than conflict.
A reformed, inclusive and effective United Nations is indispensable to the peaceful, just and sustainable future generations deserve.
Whatever our world differences, we must remember that humanity is our oldest citizenship, and peace is the inheritance we owe every child.

Nicaragua is addressing the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly with the strength of the peace that we think is possible in our country and throughout the world, where the human family can opt for the urgent need to live in harmony in all possible ways.
This is critical to address poverty and to live in dignity, freedom, and fraternity.
We bring to this forum, of all peoples and states of the world, the legitimate aspiration of families from the entire world,
and in particular in Nicaragua, to live peacefully and safely, to strengthen the work that will allow all of us to establish better societies,
to defeat extreme poverty, to live in harmony and in complementarity, which is so critical to allow all societies to progress,
and so that also we can care for and increase our resources and natural riches, which will be of benefit to everyone.
The conflicts assailing the world are, as we know, the enemy of the well-being to which we are all entitled.
In the words of our Rubén Darío, we are in favor of peace, peace, peace, to make headway on the goals laid out, and in particular by this organization which gathers us together.
We need to defeat extreme poverty, and we also need to achieve well-being for all, to bring about a better world, which is so urgent a task.

The scourges of our time are the greatest threat and greatest danger to our societies because they deprive us of our heritage, and we see major crimes linked to drug trafficking and organized crime, which are forms of terrorism, which assail us and make us sick.

Against this intimidating backdrop, our purpose, our vote, our commitment has been and remains clear, and we aspire to gather with more peoples around the urgent need to curb these afflictions and to bring about safety and to provide education, food, health, peace, and development for all.
We would like warmly to greet all delegations who are present here, and we hope that you will join our commitment to address these challenges and to alleviate the suffering that we have mentioned.

There are many proposals that we have mentioned, and we wish to stress the strength that the BRICS countries, for instance, have shown in striving for better living conditions for their people and the right of all to achieve sustainable development in a complementary way.

We would like to recognize and pay tribute to all brothers and sisters throughout the world who believe in ideals, principles, and values that are valuable to us all as humanity, to continue moving towards achieving the most important significant battle, which is to achieve peace, so that we can defeat poverty once and for all.
It is in this battle that we all have to wage to achieve peace.

In this context, we wish to express our unwavering solidarity with the heroic people of Cuba, and we also recognize the principles and values expressed by the people and government of the People's Republic of China, in particular the One China principle, which is non-negotiable.
We also fully share the struggle against fascism and the right to peace waged by the Russian Federation.

Distinguished delegates, I wish to express to you all in this forum the commitment for us all to live together in a fraternal and solidarity-based way, to achieve dignity and shared responsibility for all.
Speech by Prime Minister Rob Jetten at the United Nations General Assembly, 24 September 2026, New York Mr President, Your Excellencies, Anne Frank was a teenage girl without power or influence.
But she had a pen and a diary.
A diary that would make its way into the world, and inspire millions of people.
