Papua New Guinea comes to this Assembly with profound respect for the Charter of the United Nations and for the principles and purposes upon which this great institution was founded.
The United Nations reminds us that whether we are big or small nations, rich or poor, developed or developing, powerful or less powerful, we are all members of one international community.
The challenges confronting humanity do not recognise the size of our economies, the strength of our militaries or the boundaries on our maps.
No nation can address them alone.

We must therefore continue to work together, respecting the sovereignty of nations, upholding international law and the United Nations Charter, resolving our differences peacefully, and recognising that every nation, regardless of its size or economic strength, has a voice and a place in this Assembly.
For Papua New Guinea, and for the small island nations of the Pacific, multilateralism matters.
The United Nations provides a place where the smallest nations can sit alongside the largest, where our voices can be heard, and where we can work together on the common challenges facing humanity.

At a time when our world has confronted war, displacement, poverty, inequality, climate change and many other challenges, he has consistently called for peace, human dignity, international cooperation and respect for the principles of the United Nations He has demonstrated the qualities of a global statesman and has used his office to speak for humanity, including those whose voices are too often unheard.
Your advocacy reminds us that beyond our national borders, political differences, cultures and beliefs, we belong to one human family and share one Earth.
It is in that spirit of our common humanity that I wish to speak about human rights, human freedom and, particularly, freedom of conscience, thought, religion and belief.
At the heart of human rights is a simple truth: every human being has inherent dignity and is entitled to fundamental freedoms.
From my Christian perspective, these freedoms are not gifts bestowed upon humanity by governments, institutions or powerful nations.
They are God-given rights inherent in every human life.

And because these rights belong equally to every person, we have a responsibility to respect and protect the rights of others, including those who may not look like us, speak like us, worship like us or believe what we believe.
The strength of a nation, a government, an economy, a technology or a religion should never be used to suppress the fundamental rights of another human being.
The might of military power must not suppress the weak.
The might of economic power must not suppress the poor.
The might of technology must not diminish human dignity or freedom.
And the might of a religious majority must never be used to suppress those who belong to a religious minority.
Human rights have their greatest meaning when they protect those with less power, minorities, vulnerable communities and individuals whose beliefs may differ from those of the majority.
We must therefore learn to live together with mutual respect.
We do not have to agree on everything.
We do not have to share the same religion, culture, political system or worldview.
But we must respect the humanity and fundamental freedoms of one another.
This principle is especially important when we speak about religion.
Papua New Guinea is a Christian nation, believing that Jesus Christ is our Lord, Saviour and soon-coming King.
Christian principles have profoundly influenced our country, our communities and our institutions.
But our Christianity must never become an excuse to deny another human being freedom of conscience.
Section 45 of our Constitution guarantees every person freedom of conscience, thought and religion, and the practice of his or her religion and beliefs.
Our Constitution also protects people against being compelled to participate in religious observance and against attempts to force religion or irreligion upon another person.
Faith that is forced is no longer faith.
I believe freedom of choice is a God-given right, implanted in the conscience of every human being.
Our moral consciousness comes from God.
He calls people through love while allowing every person to exercise the freedom of choice He has given them.
True faith therefore cannot be imposed by force, fear, law or persecution.
A person must be free to believe.
A person must be free to worship.
A person must be free to change his or her belief.
And a person must also be free not to profess a religion.
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights recognises this principle in Article 18, the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion.
History teaches us what happens when governments, institutions or majorities use religion to suppress those who believe differently.
Human beings have been persecuted, expelled, imprisoned and killed because of their faith.
Humanity must learn from this history.
A Christian-majority nation must protect people of other religions.
A Muslim-majority nation must protect people of other religions.
A Hindu-majority nation must protect people of other religions.
A Buddhist-majority nation must protect people of other religions.
And every society must respect the rights of those who choose not to profess a religion.
The size of a majority does not diminish the human rights of the minority.

The United States of America, where this Assembly meets, expressed this principle more than two centuries ago through its First Amendment, which prohibits laws “respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof.”
Government should neither impose faith upon its people nor prevent people from practising their faith.
Papua New Guinea supports this principle.
But the strength of our Christianity should not be demonstrated by suppressing another person’s beliefs.
It should be demonstrated by having the confidence to allow every human being freedom of conscience.
Humanity can be diverse in culture, religion and thought, yet we must be united in respecting and tolerating our differences.
Papua New Guinea knows something about diversity.
We have more than 800 languages and many different cultures and traditions.
Yet for 51 years as an independent nation, we have remained together as one Papua New Guinea.
But our experience demonstrates something important: Diversity does not have to mean division.
People can speak different languages and still belong to one nation.
People can come from different cultures and live under one Constitution.
And people can worship differently and still be neighbours, colleagues and fellow citizens.
Papua New Guinea therefore calls upon all Member States to defend freedom of conscience, thought, religion and belief.

And I respectfully extend this call to every nation that calls Papua New Guinea a friend, every nation with which we have a bilateral partnership, and every nation that seeks friendship and engagement with us.
Ensure that religious minorities are not persecuted, suppressed, intimidated or discriminated against because they practise a religion different from that of the majority.
Whether a country is predominantly Christian, Muslim, Hindu, Buddhist or follows another religious tradition, the faith of the majority must never become an instrument for persecuting the minority.
This message is not directed at one country, one religion or one region.
It is a principle that must apply equally to all of us.
Because human rights cannot be selective.
We cannot demand respect for our own rights while denying those same rights to others.
And we cannot ask the world to respect our beliefs while refusing to respect the freedom of conscience of another human being.
But there is a wider principle here.
This is ultimately about human dignity.
If we recognise the dignity of every human being, then we must also consider the conditions in which people live — and the Earth we will leave to our children.
The United Nations General Assembly has recognised the human right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment.
What value is freedom if a child has no clean water to drink?
What value is development if we destroy the environment that sustains human life?
And what inheritance are we leaving our children if our forests disappear, our oceans become polluted and our climate becomes increasingly unstable?
There is one reality that transcends every political, economic and religious difference between us: We have only one Earth.
There is no other known habitable planet presently within the practical reach of humanity to which billions of people can simply relocate if we destroy this one.
This Earth is our common home.
Whatever our religion, nationality or political system, we breathe the same atmosphere.
We depend upon the same global climate.
And ultimately, we share the consequences of what humanity does to this planet.
Think about the children of the world.
A child born today did not create climate change.
That child did not choose the wars of this generation.
That child did not create pollution or environmental destruction.
Yet that child will inherit the consequences of the decisions we make today.
We must therefore be custodians not only of the present, but also of the future.
Future generations cannot stand before this General Assembly today and argue for themselves.
We must consider them when we make decisions about war and peace, development, energy, forests, oceans, minerals and the global economy.
Papua New Guinea understands this responsibility.
We are custodians of great tropical forests, extraordinary biodiversity and a vast ocean space.
For us, the environment is not an abstract international discussion.
It is where we grow our food.
And it is the inheritance we must pass to our children.
In our interconnected world, decisions made in one country can affect people thousands of kilometres away.
Greenhouse gases do not recognise national borders.
Pollution carried by oceans does not stop at immigration checkpoints.
Wars can disrupt food, fuel, energy, trade and supply chains far from the battlefield.
Economic decisions made in the world’s largest economies can reach an ordinary family in a small developing country.
A mother buying food can feel the consequences.
A farmer buying fuel can feel the consequences.
A small business facing higher transport costs can feel the consequences.
And developing countries trying to build roads, schools and hospitals can feel the consequences.
This is why leadership in powerful nations carries responsibilities beyond national borders.
With greater power comes greater responsibility.
Papua New Guinea respectfully asks the leaders of the world’s major powers to remember the ordinary people whose lives can be affected by decisions made far away from them.
When wars disrupt food, fuel and trade, families far from the battlefield can experience higher prices and economic uncertainty.

When the climate changes, communities that have contributed relatively little to global greenhouse-gas emissions can nevertheless face rising seas, extreme weather, threats to food security and damage to livelihoods.
My appeal to leaders everywhere is simple: Put human welfare ahead of war.
Put humanity ahead of narrow geopolitical interests.
Choose dialogue and peaceful settlement wherever possible.
Remember ordinary families when making major economic decisions.
Balance commercial interests with the welfare of people.
Use technology to advance human dignity, not diminish it.
Protect our planet while pursuing development.
And place the interests of our children and future generations at the heart of the decisions we make today.
Leadership is not measured only by the power a nation possesses.
Leadership is also measured by the responsibility with which that power is exercised.
Papua New Guinea does not claim to have all the answers.
We are a developing nation with challenges of our own.
But perhaps our position as a Pacific nation allows us to remind the larger powers of a simple reality: No nation is so powerful that it can live apart from the Earth.
And no nation is so small that its people should be forgotten when decisions affecting humanity are made.
The military strength of a nation does not make the rights of another nation less important.
The size of an economy does not make the dignity of a poorer person less important.
Technological advancement does not diminish our obligation to protect human freedom.
And the size of a religious majority does not reduce the rights of a minority.
Power in all its forms must be exercised with responsibility.
And perhaps Papua New Guinea can offer one simple thought to this Assembly: You do not have to believe what I believe in order for me to defend your human rights.
Let mosques call their faithful to prayer.
Let people search their own consciences.
Let powerful nations exercise their power responsibly.
Let nations resolve their differences peacefully wherever possible.
And let no State compel the human soul.
We may have different religions, political systems, cultures and national interests.
We may be big nations or small nations.
We may be rich or poor.
We may possess different levels of military, economic and technological power.
But beneath those differences, we share something greater.
And we must leave our children a world better than the one we inherited.
Papua New Guinea will remain proudly Christian.
But we will also remain committed to freedom of conscience, thought and religion.
For ultimately, faith cannot be commanded by government.
Faith must come from the heart.
God has given humanity the capacity to choose, and that freedom must be respected.
And God has entrusted this Earth to our generation only for a time.
Let us use our leadership wisely.
Let us uphold the Charter of the United Nations.
Let us respect the rights and dignity of every human being.
Let us work together — big nations and small.
Let us ensure that power, whether military, economic, technological or religious, is never used to suppress the rights of others.
Let us protect our common home.
And let us remember always the generations who will follow us.

Amid the challenges we face as a developing nation, we are growing our economy, opening our country through enabling infrastructure, working to provide quality education and health services for all, moving towards cleaner energy, conserving our forests and oceans, strengthening our independent judiciary and free-market economy, and opening our doors to genuine foreign investment.

I want to assure this Assembly that my Government is working to ensure that none of our 11 million people is left behind as we pursue development, opportunity and a better quality of life in our God-given homeland.
May God bless Papua New Guinea.
May God bless all nations and all peoples.
May God protect our children and the generations yet unborn.
And may the United Nations continue to defend peace, human dignity, freedom and the Earth that we all share.
The 81st session of the UN General Assembly begins at one of the most difficult—in my view—moments since the Organization’s founding.
Poland was, in fact, a founding member of the UN.
From the very beginning of the UN’s existence, we have been faced with a question—a question about the foundations of the international order that we help shape within our Organization.
Despite many achievements, we must not forget that at the very root of its creation lies a fundamental flaw that continues to undermine the system’s credibility to this day.

The UN was established in response to the greatest tragedy in human history— World War II—but it was not founded on a simple and fundamental principle: that every wrongdoing must be met with accountability, and sometimes with just punishment.
For Poland, this is not an abstract issue.

At the very moment the foundations of the UN were being laid, my nation—a victim of two totalitarian regimes—was under the domination of one of them—Soviet Russia—and, after several years of devastating occupation, of the other— Germany.
Thousands of Polish heroes who fought for the freedom of Europe and the entire world were, at that time, imprisoned, tortured, and sentenced to death.
The UN already existed at that time.
Poland has never received redress for that period and those wrongs.
It sent a signal that violations of international law, aggression, and imperialist policies could go unpunished.
It is precisely this lack of justice—this sort of original sin of the postwar order—that creates space for the return of old aggressive ambitions and methods of operation.
The aggressive policies of certain states today are therefore not a phenomenon detached from history.
They are a direct consequence of it.
A state that has not been held accountable for its actions is more likely to resort to the same tools again.
That is why it is so important that we today—as the international community—restore the full meaning of the principle of accountability.
Without it, there will be no lasting peace, and international law will remain nothing more than a declaration devoid of real power.
Today we must show courage, while remembering, that sometimes courage alone is not enough; that without prudence, courage can lead to disaster.

Prudence in this case means not only knowing what we want—a return to principles, a return to peaceful free and sovereign states—but also courageously pursuing that goal, calling aggression by its name and condemning those who disrupt the world order, without turning a blind eye when they violate the rules.

cooperation among For many years, representatives of my country have been trying, in this chamber and in the Security Council, to point out that a situation in which a permanent member of the Council—Russia —attempts, unsuccessfully but with ruthless persistence, to conquer a neighboring state and destabilize the entire region—is a violation of the principles we all uphold as signatories to the Charter of the United Nations.
Russia is destabilizing the situation in Europe through open aggression, hybrid operations, acts of subversion and sabotage, and by ignoring successive resolutions of this Assembly.
It displays the same imperial arrogance that in the past led to unimaginable suffering and the tragedies of two world wars.

That is why we are determined to counter the threats that the Kremlin’s aggressive policies are posing to us with increasing audacity.
As a representative of a country neighboring Russia, I want to make it clear: we are not the ones seeking confrontation.
We are strengthening our alliances, developing our military, and modernizing its equipment—not to wage war, but to prevent it.
Our goal is deterrence and defense—the defense of two values that also form the foundation of the United Nations Charter: freedom and sovereignty.
We continue to view the North Atlantic Alliance as the guarantor of European security.
NATO remains united in the overarching goal of defending our community on both sides of the Atlantic Ocean—in Europe and America, on its eastern flank and along its northern border.
We therefore welcome with satisfaction the strengthening of security in the Arctic region, which is now a reality thanks to the agreement signed yesterday between our allies.
we must, however, make it clear: modern security threats are not limited to conventional military actions.

Russia is carrying out actions aimed at undermining the foundations of international stability, striking at global food security through attacks on ports and ships transporting grain, as well as by deliberately provoking crises that affect millions of people outside of Europe.

At the same time, a large-scale hybrid war is being waged, involving sabotage, cyberattacks, and destabilization operations on an unprecedented scale—including an artificially induced migration crisis.
These are planned, coordinated, and consistently executed actions.
Their goal is to weaken states, undermine public trust, and shatter the unity of the international community.
We are not dealing with isolated incidents, but with a sustained, well-thought-out strategy.
And that is precisely why the response to these actions cannot be ad hoc or half-hearted.
It must be firm, consistent and united.
For if aggression—whether military or hybrid in nature—is not met with an adequate response, it becomes an invitation to repeat it.
Even if today we have reservations about the effectiveness of the Security Council, we respect the achievements of the United Nations in maintaining and building peace in many parts of the world.
The role of UN peacekeeping operations in preventing the resurgence of conflicts is undeniable.

Poland advocates for stable funding of peacekeeping missions and for granting them more transparent mandates that also take into account tasks related to the protection of the population and support for the reconstruction of state institutions.
Poland also fulfills its commitment to global security through its participation in UN peacekeeping operations.
Polish “blue helmet” soldiers are currently serving in Lebanon, carrying out their duties with dignity despite the difficult security situation throughout the region.

We will support efforts to de-escalate conflicts, protect civilians, and uphold international humanitarian law, and work toward the implementation of a two-state solution ensuring the peaceful coexistence of Israel and Palestine.
This is precisely why the response to contemporary threats cannot be limited solely to reacting to crises.
It must be based on clear principles and reliable partnerships.
Our historical experience is different— marked by the struggle for our own freedom and resistance to domination imposed by force.
In international relations, we advocate an approach based on mutual respect, sovereignty, and the equality of states.
Poland does not seek an advantage over others.
On the contrary—it builds cooperation that strengthens all participants.
In a world of growing geopolitical rivalry, we need more partnerships that create real value rather than deepening dependencies.
That is why Poland consistently works toward a model of international cooperation that gives countries room to develop, strengthens their resilience, and allows them to make sovereign decisions.
It is in this spirit that we view our role in the global economy and our engagement in international initiatives.
Today Poland is the world’s 20th-largest economy.

Our path to becoming a developed nation was not a matter of chance, but the result of consistent reforms—including the fight against corruption—responsible policies, and the efforts of the entire society.
We view this experience not as a reason for complacency, but as a commitment to share with others.

As we engage in the work of the G20, we view this forum as key to rebuilding trust in international relations and developing responses to the most important challenges of the modern world—from economic security, through supply chain resilience, to the stability of the trading system.
In this context, an important step toward a more representative governance structure was the decision to expand this format so that every region could be represented.
In 2023, the African Union was admitted to the G20.

It has strengthened the voice of the African continent and better reflects the actual processes taking place in the global economy and the real needs of partners, rather than just the interests of the most powerful.
Now is the time for the voice of Central Europe—which has been absent from this forum until now—to be heard in the G20 as well.
This is a region that is developing dynamically and has a slightly different perspective and set of experiences compared to its Western partners.
Poland wants to be the voice of this region—as a country that understands both the challenges of development and the importance of stable rules of the game in the international economy.

The response cannot consist solely of economic measures.
We also need to rebuild our institutions and culture.

Yes, the family—mother and father—and an appreciation for their roles are the first step toward overcoming the demographic crisis!

Let us do everything we can to ensure that culture and the mass media promote having children, not aborting them!

I believe that the UN can be an organization where we can work together to develop ways to gradually overcome the demographic crisis, as well as other related challenges, such as illegal migration, which often takes the form of human trafficking.
However, illegal migration itself cannot be the answer to demographic challenges—for it breeds misery, tensions, and unrest.
That is not the way forward!

strengthening the resilience of nations and building stability, however, cannot overlook one more dimension of responsibility—the responsibility for the world we will leave to future generations.

Poland supports environmental protection efforts, recognizing their impact on security, including food security.
Caring for the natural environment is undoubtedly our duty, but fulfilling this duty must not lead to the weakening of our economies or the shifting of problems beyond our borders.

Pushing for ambitious environmental policies without considering their global consequences may result in deindustrialization, longer supply chains, and the relocation of production to countries that do not apply comparable standards.

This path does not lead to genuine climate protection—it merely leads to the export of emissions to other parts of the same globe, accompanied by job losses in the country of origin and the erosion of production capacity.
We need solutions that combine environmental responsibility with competitiveness economic and economic security.

In this spirit, it is worth recalling the message of St. Francis of Assisi, who saw nature not as a resource to be exploited, but as a gift entrusted to humankind—“our common home”—for which we are responsible as its guardians and stewards.
We cannot leave the protection of our environment to fanatics.
Care for nature is much older than left-wing concepts; it stems from an ethic that took shape long before the emergence of post-Marxist ideologues.
For concern for creation and concern for humanity are inextricably linked.
That is why humanity and human dignity must remain at the center of our reflection on the future of the world.
Human rights are not an afterthought in international politics.
They are its foundation and also stem from ethical principles older than our Organization.
Violating them always leads to violence, destabilization, and conflict.
History—including the history of my country—teaches us this unequivocally.
The social movement that led to the fall of the communist government imposed on Poland was called “Solidarity.”
It was an expression of the courage of people who—despite repression and the lack of freedom—refused to live under a system based on lies and violence.
We may differ in our assessments of the extent to which the crimes of the communist system have been addressed.
This debate is still ongoing in my country.

But that is precisely why we should pay tribute to all those people, especially the workers, thanks to whom we have a free world today, and who do not boast of their wealth and status—gained at the expense of others—but remain faithful to their values and commitments.

Last year we meaningfully celebrated the 80th founding anniversary of the United Nations.

As we marked the watershed in UN history reviewing its past eighty years and looking ahead into the future, mankind ardently desired and aspired to put an immediate end to the current chaos of international relations and regain peace and stability.

Unfortunately, however, what the world witnessed every day for the last one year was a harsh reality rampant with unprecedented mutual distrust and confrontation, infringement on sovereignty, and military conflicts that led to extreme unrest and disorder globally.

The new year started with the most despicable, world startling act of state-sponsored terrorism, followed by worldwide outbreaks of other appalling incidents and events which anyone with common sense and knowledge can hardly imagine.
Crises causing insecurity and instability increased further with wars and bloody conflicts.

The effects of disaster-prone abnormal climate gave rise to a succession of extreme high temperature, droughts, heavy rains and floods in many countries and regions, seriously threatening the survival of mankind.
This, coupled with the spread of communicable diseases and hike in oil prices, worsened the socio-economic crisis.
Humanity desires that the United Nations should fulfill its mission and responsibility as an organization established to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war.
Regrettably, however, the Organization still fails to recover from functional paralysis owing to the high-handedness and unilateralism of a handful of countries pursuing only chauvinistic interests.

All the crises the international community is faced with point to one clear fact – that infringement on sovereignty, threat to security interests, and denial of right to development of other countries are bound to breed regional instability and crisis and lead to aggression and war.

In order to overcome all the existing crises and challenges and promote peace, security and sustainable development, all member states should seek appropriate solutions to problems while strictly complying with the intrinsic purposes and principles of the UN Charter and giving priority to unity and cooperation among nations.
The historic 9th Congress of the Workers’ Party of Korea was held with splendor in February this year in Pyongyang, the capital city of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.
The Congress reviewed with pride the achievements made over the past five years and set out new innovative goals for overall development in the next stage.

During the last five years, the existence and development of humankind were severely constrained by the global pandemic, abnormal weather conditions, geopolitical confrontation and the entailing economic crisis.
They were harsh times for our State, too.
Yet, we have thoroughly and consistently maintained the characteristic principle and approach of self-reliance.
We overcame all difficulties and challenges before us and ultimately made remarkable advances by leaps and bounds.
The five-year plan for the development of the national economy was successfully accomplished.
The economic foundation for production boost was reinforced.
Policies for the people that our government invariably pursues are implemented at a higher level.
We are seeing the upward trend of comprehensive development conducive to simultaneous and balanced growth in all sectors, fields and regions of the country.

As the first-hand witnesses of the above realities, all our citizens have become all the more confident that the path we have trodden is the most accurate path and that self- reliance and self-sustenance of our choice are the surest shortcut to prosperity.

Under the unique leadership of Comrade Kim Jong Un, President of the State Affairs of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, our people have now confidently embarked on new massive projects aimed at building on the successes in pioneering an era of comprehensive development and leading it to new heights.
The path ahead of us is laden with numerous challenges and difficulties presented by inhumane acts of certain forces that disfavor the DPRK’s very existence, let alone her development.
Yet we will surely attain all that we plan to, relying entirely on our own efforts, regardless of changes in the situation.
This is the confidence that every Korean is assured of.

The sovereignty, security interests and territorial integrity of sovereign states are ruthlessly trampled upon and the international law and order feebly collapse due to the unilateral high-handedness and tyranny of a hegemonic state.
Such a grim reality of international relations teaches us a serious lesson.
A lesson that fair advocacy and earnest desire for compliance with the law and order alone can hardly defend anything.

Like in other parts of the world, a serious landscape of confrontation between justice and injustice and between hegemonic forces and independence forces is being witnessed in Northeast Asia this year.

The Korean peninsula and its vicinity, in particular, are faced with an extreme instability and further aggravated tension on a level different from that of last year due to the persistent hostility towards the DPRK and ever-increasing military confrontation of the U.S. and its followers.
The U.S.-Japan-ROK military alliance, unmistakably aimed at the DPRK, is being evolved by the United States into a more offensive and aggressive military bloc with a nuclear element.

The U.S. is conspiring with its allies to systematically amend and update the anti-DPRK nuclear war scenarios and to steadily cultivate and master their performance capability through provocative war rehearsals of all hues and military build-up.
This year alone, the U.S. staged a series of bilateral and multilateral military exercises including "Freedom Shield" and "Freedom Edge", simulating a real war scenario.
It didn’t even bother to cover up its dangerous attempt at military confrontation against the DPRK.

The U.S. has approved and is encouraging Seoul’s ambition to possess nuclear- powered submarines, while relocating and deploying different military hardware including the latest missiles and drones on the Korean peninsula and in its vicinity.
The current military inclination is further aggravating the already vulnerable security landscape in the region.
On the other hand, Japan, an A-class war criminal that inflicted untold sufferings and disasters upon mankind in the last century, is taking advantage of the present international turbulence.

It accelerates its attempts at rearmament with an unprecedented commitment including the revision of the Peace Constitution, abandonment of “exclusive defence”, reformation of the military structure and arms build-up.
Such actions are casting war clouds over the entire region.
Under the signboard of “counterattack capability”, Japan has buckled down to the development and possession of long-range attack weapons that put neighbouring countries within a striking range.
Its ambition run counter to its obligations as a defeated nation; they are in shameless disregard of the UN Charter and pose a grave challenge to global peace.
The global military and political context is worsening day by day and the unlimited abuse of power has become a commonplace.

Under such circumstances, the risky military threat of the U.S., Japan and the ROK go beyond precedent and continue to break the worst records in their scale, intensity, nature and the dangers, creating security instability on the Korean peninsula on a level different from previous years.

Nevertheless, no physical conflict has occurred on and around the Korean peninsula, a hot spot of the world, and the security index is being maintained at a higher level than any other part of the globe.

We owe it to the fact that the DPRK has a war deterrent in place powerful enough to break anyone’s will to start a war of aggression against the DPRK and that we are thoroughly containing and managing the hostile forces’ intention to use force.
Thus the regional balance of power maintained by the DPRK’s self-defensive capabilities effectively curbs the risk of an armed conflict.
No one can deny such an obvious fact.
It further highlights the immutable truth that a just power means the national sovereignty and prestige and a fundamental guarantee of peace and stability.

The Head of State of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea stated that our national sovereignty and security have firmly been ensured by virtue of great strength so far and will invariably be so in the years ahead.
The DPRK’s nuclear deterrent is the absolute might and irresistible force designed, from A to Z, to safeguard the sovereignty, security and peace against aggression and threat from outside.

I would like to reiterate the official position of the DPRK government: the status of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea as a nuclear weapons state, that has been uncompromisingly and permanently fixed both physically and legally with absolutely no turning back, can never be reversed in any circumstances or by any means, no matter how hard and loudly the hostile forces may deny in chorus with all sorts of rhetoric.

The DPRK will continue to strictly control and manage every external threat by dint of her supremacy in overwhelming strength and be all the more faithful and committed to our mission as a responsible nuclear weapons state to firmly defend national sovereignty and fundamental interests and to guarantee peace and security of the region and beyond.
Large-scale natural calamities claimed tens of thousands of lives in different parts of the world this year.
The international community came to realize once again that climate change is a pressing issue that calls for a joint action.
AI and other new cutting-edge technology are transforming every domain of human life, offering great opportunities.
But at the same time, they also carry risks of being misused for sinister purposes.
Highly volatile present era urgently calls for strengthened UN capable of handling challenges and crisis facing humanity in conformity with the common interests of mankind.

The most pressing issue to be addressed is none other than building the UN into a UN for all, faithful to the purposes and principles enshrined in the Charter and fully guaranteed of impartiality and objectivity in the face of the arbitrary practices of the anti-peace forces that are abusing the UN as a tool for implementing their hegemonic strategy.
The United Nations should no longer be misused for the sinister political purposes of specific forces.
The United Nations should firmly secure its authority and future by promoting equality and cooperation among sovereign states.
It’s about time the UN undertook a reform.

Not the reform centered on specific countries but the one aimed at democratization of the United Nations in the true sense of the word so that the organization would represent the views and interests of the entire membership evenly and equally.
Gone are the days when an individual member state unilaterally imposed its will on the rest of the world and dominated the international political arena.
Instead, multilateralism and multipolarization have emerged as an irresistible aspiration and trend of the times based on justice and equity.

The DPRK will always be with the anti-imperialist, independent countries aspiring after the building of a just and peaceful world and is committed to undertaking the historic mission of leading the movement for global independence under the uplifted banner of independence.
This year marks the 35th year of the DPRK’s entry into the UN.
The DPRK joined the UN out of the desire to defend peace and security of the region and the world and to achieve common prosperity of mankind together with the entire UN membership.
To this end, we have remained faithful to the purposes and principles of the UN Charter.

As a UN member state, the DPRK government maintains its invariable stand to actively work towards the establishment of genuine international justice and a new fair international order in compliance with the UN Charter and international law.

In particular, I affirm that the DPRK government led by the present Head of State of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea will direct positive efforts to promote international justice, co-prosperity, and peace and security of the region and beyond while firmly defending her national sovereignty, security interests, and the right to development.

81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly – General Debate Statement by the Prime Minister 24 September 2026 Mr. President Rahman, Whom I congratulate on your election; Mr. Secretary-General António Guterres, To whom I pay tribute for ten years of tireless work in defence of the Charter of the United Nations, international law and multilateralism; Heads of State and Government, Over the last decades, the international order, focused on promoting stability, has been essential for prosperity and for socioeconomic progress in our societies.
The wars and geopolitical tensions that mark this time have had a terrible human impact, call that international order into question and, consequently, the prospect of prosperity.
Therefore, we must explore every opportunity for dialogue, for diplomacy and for peace.
In the Middle East, the humanitarian tragedy must cease and we must move towards the two-State solution – with Israel and Palestine coexisting as two sovereign States in peace and security.
The aggressive conduct of Iran and its associated armed groups must come to an end, including attacks on neighbouring countries, on merchant ships and on civilian infrastructure.
Just as the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz must end and freedom of navigation must be guaranteed, including safe and toll-free passage, also in the Red Sea.
In Europe, we must achieve a just and lasting peace, that puts an end to Russia’s brutal and illegal aggression against Ukraine.
Ukraine is a partner that has had the full support of Portugal and the European Union.
In the Sudan, we must put an end to the most dramatic humanitarian crisis we face.
We must also be firm in combating the global threats of terrorism and nuclear weapons.

And in the face of the new challenge of artificial intelligence, we must find together the virtuous balance between innovation and regulation – one that allows its potential to be harnessed in favour of humanity, but that avoids the distortion of our essence.
The energy crisis and the escalation in fuel prices that we face, as a result of international conflicts, affect all our peoples. Everyone is harmed.
From Asia to Europe, from Africa to the Americas, there is no country that is immune to it.
They have a serious economic and social impact and are already having undesirable consequences.
For all of us and also for the parties directly involved.
This is a senseless crisis because it is bad for everyone.
We must put an end to this kind of collective masochism.
And we must do so quickly in order to close this chapter, which is a chapter that generates losses for all.
We all have a duty to learn from the lessons of the crisis of the 1970s and to avoid what happened then.
We will all also be judged by the way in which we were able to deal with this challenge.
On the one hand, it is urgent to put an end to the conflicts that drag on.
And on the other, from now on, we must debate and decide on complementary ways to mitigate the impact of this energy crisis and avoid its prolongation.
It is my conviction that it would also be beneficial to discuss the mechanism for setting the international price of oil.

Not that I have a concrete solution, which is very complex and difficult, but we should ask whether it makes sense for us all to be so dependent on the speculative factor and the volatility of financial and futures markets, which make their effect felt across all production, even when the instability originates only in one part or in a limited period of that production.
We also bear the intergenerational responsibility to accelerate the energy transition in order to reduce dependencies and mitigate the effect of climate change.
I share with you that Portugal feels at first hand the devastating impacts of climate change.
This is happening in the multiplication of forest fires, in the phenomenon of coastal erosion, in the degradation of marine ecosystems.
And also, now and often, with new, unpredictable extreme phenomena, storms, winds and sudden flooding.
That is why we have a strategic perspective on the energy transition.
More than 70% of our energy production comes from renewable sources.
We have brought forward to 2045 the target of carbon neutrality.
We maintain close collaboration and continued support for countries especially vulnerable to climate change.
And we are investing in innovative solutions, such as debt-for-green-investment conversion agreements.
Climate change and freedom of navigation also have in common a priority of our policy: the sea and the oceans.

The protection of the marine domain, of its diversity, combating the warming of the waters, the threat of sea-level rise and guaranteeing universal freedom of navigation are essential priorities of the ocean agenda, an agenda that concerns us all.
These are shared responsibilities and opportunities that require a collective effort that must also unite us all.

Mr. President, Despite everything, the United Nations are a political masterpiece of humanity, they will always be under construction and will always reflect what their Members are able to decide at each moment.
The results in the maintenance of peace and security will, to a large extent, be whatever the members of the Security Council – in particular the permanent members – are able to decide.
For the United Nations to fulfil the objectives we have defined, we must also converge in making it more agile and more effective.
Therefore, first and foremost, we must honour our commitments financial resources.

And we must equip the United Nations with the appropriate means so that peacekeeping missions — which Portugal is very proud to be part of — can make a difference in the places to which they are deployed.
We must strive to make the Security Council more representative, which entails permanent seats for Africa, for Brazil and for India.
This representativeness of the United Nations and its organs must also be linguistic.
The Portuguese language is the most widely spoken language in the Southern Hemisphere, with almost 300 million speakers throughout the world.
It therefore deserves a greater role also in the United Nations.

It is a language of culture and business, which, across four continents, unites the members of the Community of Portuguese-speaking Countries (CPLP), which this year celebrates 30 years, and is manifestly a space for dialogue and cooperation, founded on a common history and a shared language.
From January, Portugal will bring to the Security Council, as a non-permanent member, a global vocation and a culture of dialogue and bridge-building.
We are deeply grateful for the trust placed in us by all and we are very conscious of the responsibility that follows from it.
We know well the challenges faced by the Least Developed Countries and the Small Island Developing States.
In the Security Council, Portugal will be committed to three major priorities: Prevent, Cooperate and Protect.
Prevent crises and conflicts with a serious human impact, which unfortunately are raging on several continents, and which are many, and not only those that are often in the news.
For us there are no first- or second-class conflicts.
All call upon us, all concern us, all mobilize us.
Cooperate and develop our Partnerships, in a Council that is more transparent, more representative and more democratic.
And Protect human dignity, by combating poverty and safeguarding fundamental rights, food security and the future of the new generations.
The most collective response is the multilateral response.
And the United Nations is and must continue to be the centre of the multilateral system.

That is why Portugal faces the future with renewed commitment to the mission of the United Nations, with confidence in our collective capacity and in the hope that it is together that we can build and leave a better world.
And we will succeed in leaving to those who will be here after us a better world than the one we found.
1. People do not want declarations. They want solutions.
The theme of this Assembly challenges us: “restoring trust, managing transformation and making the United Nations deliver for all”.
It is a good theme and I enthusiastically endorse it.
But let us be honest, dear friends: people no longer want themes.
Our people want solutions to their problems.
For that reason, I do not come to this podium to recite beautiful phrases, full of grandiloquent words, that do not redound to the benefit of our citizens.
I come to speak about concrete problems.

And I come to speak on behalf of a country that rose up from the most heartrending war in the Western Hemisphere – the War of the Triple Alliance – which brought mourning to no fewer than four sister countries.
A country that today is one of the fastest growing in the world.
Paraguay’s contribution is not a theory: it is an experience.
Facts teach us that war is abominable, that peace is the only objective, and that we have to stop watching and talking, and start acting.
And Paraguay arrives at the concert of nations with a conviction that it does not negotiate: the dignity of the human person must be at the centre of every decision.
That is why we defend freedom, democracy, the sovereignty of States, respect for human rights and the peaceful settlement of disputes.
That is why we uphold human life from conception and recognize the family as the fundamental nucleus of our society.
Because where human dignity is forgotten, humanity itself disappears.
Human dignity, from conception to the end of life, is the foundation of our presence on this earth.
There is an ever more visible distance between the commitments we undertake and the results we achieve.
When that distance grows, trust weakens.
And that trust is not recovered with mere declarations or slogans.
It is recovered by facing problems without fear, and by proposing solutions, offering results.
2. I begin with my neighbourhood: Venezuela The first problem I want to speak to you about here is one that is in my neighbourhood.
Everyone knows it: it is called Venezuela.
Before coming to New York, I visited Caracas, even though Paraguay and Venezuela have their diplomatic relations suspended.
For that reason, my decision to visit the Caribbean country surprised quite a few, and many people have questioned me – even harshly – about that decision.
I therefore take this opportunity to say it loud and clear, with complete clarity: I did not go to Venezuela to validate a regime, I did not go to validate absolutely anything.
No, gentlemen: rather, quite the opposite.
Paraguay loves democracy, and believes that the Venezuelan people deserve democracy as well.
The reason why I went to Venezuela is because for 25 years South American leaders spent their time launching lovely lyrical words, thunderous declarations, themes and slogans about Venezuela.
They were 25 years of watching, waiting and condemning – from a comfortable distance – but without doing anything for the Venezuelan people. We watched. We spoke.
And meanwhile our Venezuelan brothers and sisters suffered.
That is why I went to Venezuela a few days ago, to take a second step, after the first – difficult but very important – step of the fall of the dictator Maduro.
Because Paraguay can be useful for that second step: Venezuela’s step towards a democratic and pluralistic transition.
Today Venezuela is going through a new reality.
The defence of our values cannot mean indifference in the face of that reality.
That is why Paraguay has opened a channel of dialogue with the Venezuelan authorities and is already working, through actions, for a Venezuela where power resides in its only sovereign: the people.
To engage in dialogue is not to renounce principles nor to forget the past.
It is to have the courage to look ahead and act.
We cannot wait for the United States or some northern power to solve our problems: we have to do it ourselves.
I want for Venezuela what my country achieved after thirty-five years of dictatorship in 1989: a real democratic transition.
I do not want a photo.
I do not want a communiqué.
I want, we want, a transition.
A transition with institutions, with security, with an economy and with a people once again integrated into the international community and in our case integrated into MERCOSUR.
Paraguay’s leadership does not confuse dialogue with the indifference.
To speak is a way of standing with the Venezuelan people.
It is also a way of jointly combating transnational crime that respects no borders and harms the entire region.

Today I ask all my Latin American brothers and sisters, but also these United Nations: let us unite to help Venezuela, that beautiful country, once again become integrated into the world and have a democratic government that respects human rights.
In the words of the Latin poet Publius, “I am human, nothing human can be foreign to us”: the suffering of the Venezuelan people is the suffering of the Paraguayan people, it is the suffering of all.
And what applies to Venezuela applies perhaps even more forcefully to Nicaragua, to Cuba and to Haiti, countries that have lived too long in the darkness of authoritarianism, violence, and sadness.
Let us bring light to those sister peoples.
Because where there are free elections, there is hope.
But we must not remain at the level of discourse: we have to act.
3. The Middle East, Hormuz and Israel Of course, my region is not the only one with problems.
Problems in the world are everywhere.
Paraguay observes with deep concern what is happening in the Persian Gulf.
When the Strait of Hormuz is closed, the price is not paid by the powers or the richest.
It is paid by the most unprotected: the most vulnerable citizens.
The food and energy security of millions of people depends on that passage remaining open.
That is why today I make a fervent appeal for the immediate cessation of attacks, the full opening and free navigation of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, and a return to negotiations.
Human dignity, dear friends, does not change because we change continents: it is always the same.
And it is that human dignity that must guide not only our speeches, but our actions.
4. The coming strait: Taiwan and microchips Hormuz is the problem that confronts us today.
But I want to tell you here that tomorrow the problem may be much worse—far, far worse.
I am referring to the ominous shadows that are gathering in the Indo-Pacific, and particularly in the Taiwan Strait.
What happens there is not a mere regional matter. No, sir.
It affects Japan, all of East and Southeast Asia, and—above all—the world economy.
It affects the microchips that drive industry, defence and artificial intelligence.
Whoever pretends that this is “far away,” or too distant, simply has not understood the twenty-first century.
If oil was the fuel of the twentieth century, microchips are the fuel of the twenty-first century.
What is at stake in that potential conflict is no small matter: the very future of humanity is at stake.
I want to tell you that, in the face of this problem, Paraguay is not neutral.
Paraguay stands—I say this loud and clear—with Taiwan.
And it does so not out of convenience, but quite the opposite: it does so because of the deep values that we share.
Democracy, the rule of law, human rights and peace.
Seventy years of uninterrupted diplomatic relations is not a mere number, or a mere calculation of expediency: it is a tribute to the true friendship between our peoples.
That is why I reaffirm here today my support for the full and meaningful participation of the Republic of China (Taiwan) in the United Nations and its specialized agencies.
Taiwan has concrete contributions to make to peace, development and human rights.
Excluding it does not strengthen the system: it deprives it of capacities that can benefit everyone.
And it is a stain on these United Nations.
But the problem, make no mistake, is not only Taiwan.
What is gathering there, in that area, is far too dangerous for everyone.
Friends: Let us not remain with words, with slogans: let us move to concrete action.
I assure you that, at that negotiating table, of peace, of concord, you will find Paraguay in the front row, ready to help.
The Council that is no longer enough But the world’s problems do not end in a single region or place: they go to the very heart of the international system.
The United Nations, I will not be the first or the last to say it, needs renewal, a new impetus.
The fine motto of this Assembly proposes “United Nations for all”.
A fine motto, without a doubt.
But I fear that it is not enough.
That is why I ask you today, respectfully, but firmly: how are we to have United Nations “for all” if it is led by a Security Council of “a few”?

Worse still, it is a Council designed eighty years ago, for another era, for other scenarios, for other situations, and which demonstrates with all too great frequency that it simply does not serves the problems of today.
That original design, a child of its time, has had many achievements. Without a doubt.
And today I recognize and celebrate them.
However, as the great Nobel Prize in Literature laureate Bob Dylan would say: “things have changed”.
And the Organization, dear friends, also has to change.
Otherwise, this beautiful idea, that of the United Nations, will simply be overtaken and limited to being a stage for fine speeches, and few facts for people.
There are those who conclude from all this that multilateralism has failed.
Paraguay reaches a different conclusion: the United Nations remains indispensable.
It is the only system that allows all the countries of the world to coexist.
But it must be more effective in preventing conflicts, protecting people and ensuring respect for the rules that the States ourselves have agreed upon.
Our vocation for peace is summed up in the phrase of a distinguished Paraguayan, Manuel Gondra: “As we cannot make the just always strong, we must strive to ensure that the strong are always just.”
Paraguay wants to assume greater responsibilities in this system.
But this system, as it stands, does not work.
That is why we believe that the election of the next Secretary-General will be a fundamental decision.
The time has come for that leadership to correspond to Latin America and the Caribbean.
Our region has a vocation for peace, dialogue and multilateralism, and it has candidates capable of assuming that responsibility.

We need a Secretary-General who restores the political leadership of the Organization, who strengthens preventive diplomacy, who acts before crises become irreversible and who listens to the States and the peoples whom he serves.
The Security Council, in short, must cease to be a photograph of the world of 1945.
It must listen more to this Assembly and not become paralyzed when peace is threatened.
We need a United Nations for 2026, or 2050, not for 1945.
So that we may truly be able to deliver for all.
6. An enormous challenge: AI This Assembly also calls on us to manage transformation.
There is no need to say here what the great transformation of our time is.
Every great era of humanity has had its driving force.
The transistor drove the digital age.
No force of our era is as profound as artificial intelligence.
It is already showing its power in war, in the economy and in everyday life.
Unlike tools that merely transmitted what we said, these systems take part in what we decide.
Paraguay today feeds one hundred million people; with this tool it could feed one billion.
It can shorten by years distances that took generations.
This transformation can no longer be stopped, and no one should be excluded from it.
We are not blind to the risks; but fear cannot guide us.
Like a child, artificial intelligence repeats what it learned from whoever trained it.
If it learned to deny freedom, that lesson will not arrive as a law that we can debate.
It will arrive concealed, in the minor task, in the gesture that no one regards as a decision.
Democracy endures so long as the decisions that govern us can be traced back to the will of those who are subject to them.
When that thread is cut, the popular will risks being replaced without being defeated.
Protecting that thread does not mean renouncing the benefits.
It means not ignoring the risk that matters.
Artificial intelligence must serve human dignity and not replace it, as the Holy Father’s recent encyclical Magnifica Humanitas reminds us.
The values that these systems carry are not a technical limit.
They are a decision by whoever trains them.
And the future demands of us that that decision be freedom, democracy and equality before the law, and that whoever makes it be accountable for it.
7. A message of optimism, not resignation It might seem that up to this point I have spoken only of an endless number of problems and challenges.
That this is a pessimistic speech.
No, dear friends, not at all.
I am simply convinced that the only way to change reality, to have a better world, is first of all to accept reality. To face problems.
Not to sweep them under the rug, beneath speeches.
That is why I also come to deliver a message of optimism.
Things can change, the world can be better, peace is not a pipe dream: it is a real possibility.
And my country can speak of this, because it knows very well the harsh reality of Erasmus of Rotterdam’s phrase: “war is sweet only to those who have never experienced it”.
Paraguay experienced it, all too painfully, in the flesh.
We know what happens when multilateralism does not work: people die.
The land is stained with blood.
The price is paid not only today, but across generations.
That is why my country knows that multilateralism, dialogue, are the only alternative.
Today I come here to defend all these ideas firmly, so that they become reality.
Extremism in the defense of multilateralism is not a vice, but a virtue.
Let us be extremists, dear friends, in the defense of multilateralism, concord, peace.
Just as Paraguay rose from a bloody war, the world can do so.
That Paraguay which was, after the military hecatomb, a true “open-air cemetery,” today lives a different reality.
Paraguay has risen, and is ready to take its place in the world.
We rose with effort, with openness to the world and with the stubbornness of a people that did not choose its geography, but did choose its destiny.

Today Paraguay is experiencing one of the best economic moments in its history—in fact, the best—and it has become an example for other countries in macroeconomic stability, sustained growth and the fight against poverty.
As a result, in December 2025, Standard & Poor’s awarded us the second investment-grade rating, the first country to achieve that distinction in more than a decade.
In the last quarter of that year, unemployment fell to 3.6 per cent, the lowest level in our records.
Growth only matters if it is felt in households: decent employment is one of the best social policies that a State can offer.

Not only that, Paraguay has reduced poverty to numbers never seen before: in less than twenty years, we have gone down from 58% poverty to 16%, doing so faster than all the countries of the region Because people matter.

Moreover, the future is bright, not only because our electricity matrix is abundant, stable and one hundred per cent renewable, but because our region possesses land, energy, critical minerals and—most importantly—its wonderful people.
8. Closing: Paraguay chooses its destiny Mr. President: As I come to the end of this statement, I want to return to the idea with which I began.
People no longer want only slogans.
They want solutions to their problems.
And, above all, they want peace.
They want freedom, security, democracy, prosperity and opportunities for their children.
And we, who have the responsibility of leading our countries, must rise to those expectations.
Paraguay knows that the road is very difficult, but not impossible.
We believe that it is possible to build a world in which cooperation produces results.
In which democracy is not an empty promise.
In which technology is at the service of humanity.
In which development reaches those who need it most.
And we believe that Paraguay has much to contribute to that future.
We are a country that did not choose its geography, but did choose its destiny.
A country that faced adversity and decided to rise.
A country that has energy, resources, talent and, above all, an unbreakable will to progress.
We are a country that stopped asking what we lack and began to ask how far we can go.

The Paraguay that integrates into the world, that opens its doors to opportunities, that defends its sovereignty, that opts for peace, freedom and democracy and that wants to grow without leaving anyone behind.
And that Paraguay has a message for the world: We come to demonstrate what we are capable of doing.
Today we once again choose dialogue over confrontation.
The United Nations will not regain trust because we declare it so in this hall.
We must be firm and unequivocal in the defense of multilateralism, democracy, peace and, above all, human dignity.
And before this Assembly, I want to say it with absolute clarity: Paraguay is ready to do its part.
Because our history taught us to endure and our future calls upon us to build.
Dear brothers and sisters from all over the world: I close these words with a request, with an exhortation, almost a prayer.
“Let us be extremists in the defense of multilateralism, of democracy, of peace, and, above all, of human dignity”.

Only thus will future generations be able to look back and say that we fulfilled our mission, that we restored trust in humanity, that we managed transformation for the better, with a United Nations that delivers for everyone.

In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful Mr. President of the General Assembly, Dr. Khalil Al-Rahman, His Excellency Mr. António Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations, members of the delegations, ladies and gentlemen heads, For the second consecutive year, the Palestinian delegation has been denied obtaining the entry visas necessary to reach New York and participate in person in the meetings of the United Nations General Assembly.
We reject these unlawful punitive measures, and we reject the accusations and justifications on which they were based.

We affirm that we have fulfilled our commitments, completed a comprehensive national reform programme, and continued our commitment to international law, the renunciation of violence and terrorism, and the two-State solution and peace based on resolutions of international legitimacy.

We also affirm that it is not permissible to punish the Palestinian people and their leadership because they demand an end to the occupation, or because they resort to the United Nations, the International Court of Justice, and the International Criminal Court.
Our recourse to international law, and to its institutions, is a peaceful and civilized choice, not an act hostile to peace.
Preventing the Palestinian delegation from reaching United Nations Headquarters is inconsistent with the obligations incumbent upon the United States as the host country of the Headquarters.

From here, we call on the United States administration to reverse these sanctions and restrictions, return to the language of dialogue and mutual respect, and work with us and with the international community in order to implement the two-State solution based on international legitimacy and to achieve peace, instead of punishing the side that chose international law and politics and diplomacy as a path to attaining its rights.

Mr. President, Member States, Today I address you while our Palestinian people are confronting one of the most dangerous stages in their history, after long decades of historical injustice, uprooting, asylum, occupation, and deprivation of their natural right to self-determination, freedom, and independence.

Our people have been subjected at the hands of the Israeli occupying forces, in the Gaza Strip, to killing, destruction, starvation, and attempts at forced displacement, and to a war of genocide unprecedented, which has left behind a collective inhuman tragedy, destroying neighbourhoods, cities, camps, institutions, mosques, churches, hospitals, schools, universities, and the future of entire generations.
It has targeted every element necessary for life.

And in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, settlement expansion is accelerating, the judaization of Jerusalem is intensifying, the bonds of the West Bank are being severed and Jerusalem isolated, and settler terrorism is escalating under the protection of the occupation forces.

The crimes of land theft, house demolitions, checkpoints, and incursions continue under a system of laws, measures, and practices based on racial discrimination, ethnic cleansing, and State terrorism.

Ladies and gentlemen, for a long time we have warned the international community, through the United Nations General Assembly and the Security Council, that these Israeli policies, which are outside international law, would destroy the two-State solution.
And this is what is now happening.

Today we warn of an even greater danger that requires international measures to stop it: the danger is no longer confined to undermining the two-State solution and preventing the embodiment of the Palestinian State; rather, it has come to threaten the life and very existence of the Palestinian people on the land of their homeland.

What is taking place in Gaza, and what is taking place in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, are not separate events, but rather a malicious colonial plan aimed at making Palestinian life more difficult on their land and driving them to forced departure from it.
We warn: do not allow another Nakba and massacres like those that happened in 1948.
Do not allow the terrorist gangs protected by the Israeli occupation forces to burn Palestinian homes while their inhabitants are sleeping inside them.
And do not allow our children to live in fear and under threat.
I ask you again: how long will some States continue to remain silent about Israel or to supply it with the weapons that it uses against our people!?
The world has seen the exorbitant cost in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank.

What, then, is the international community waiting for in order to protect the Palestinian people, end the Israeli occupation, and implement the two-State solution based on international legitimacy, instead of a threat from the coming extremism in Israel, which is aimed at expansion through what is called “Greater Israel” and at erasing the Palestinian presence?

Mr. President, Member States, We welcomed President Donald Trump’s plan with the same points, and we also welcomed Security Council resolution 2803 and the road map for implementing the second phase, in order to stop the aggression against our people, end its humanitarian tragedy, secure the withdrawal of the occupation forces from the Gaza Strip, and reconstruct it.
But with deep regret, we have not seen any of this materialize on the ground, and the Israeli aggression and killing continue to claim the lives of men, women, and children in Gaza.
Nearly a year has passed since the adoption of resolution 2803 and the formation of the Security Council bodies, and there remains only one year of the transitional period set until the end of 2027.
Therefore, we call for accelerating the implementation of the second phase and not wasting any more time.
The transitional phase must not turn into a permanent or open-ended situation with no clear political or temporal horizon.

Rather, it must lead to the reunification of the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, under the ولاية of the State of Palestine, its legitimacy and institutions, and in accordance with the principle of one State, one Government, one law, and one legitimate weapon.
