In that vein, Senegal is presenting its candidacy to a non-permanent seat on the Security Council for two 2032 2033.
However, beyond reform, the organisation also needs experienced leadership to steer its work in these times of crisis and uncertainty.
The UN needs a secretary general able to speak to one and all, able to listen and to build bridges between member states.
That is the vision embraced and espoused by Macky Sall, former president of the Republic of Senegal.
Here I wish once again to express my support for his candidacy.
I wish to reiterate Senegal's request that you, as Member states, support his candidacy.

Ladies and gentlemen at a time when our organisation is seeking to rebuild trust, Senegal continues to believe in the vision of a world based on peace, justice, the dignity of each and every human being and human brotherhood.
The world does not need unilateral posturing.
It needs a fairer, more inclusive and more effective multilateralism.
Addressing our challenges requires bridges and not walls, dialogue and not confrontation.
Cooperation and not isolation and not might.
That is the very spirit in which Sen Senegal will host the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar 2026.
This first This is the first Olympic event in history to be held in Africa It will be held from the 31st of October to the 13th of November.
It will welcome athletes from 206 national Olympic communities.
It will welcome young people from across the world.
And in doing just that, Senegal will do much more than host a sporting sporting competition.
We will host a generation that wish to come together rather than stand apart, one that wishes to build together rather than pit themselves against each other.
That is our promise to those young people, and it is the Olympic promise.

And ultimately that is the promise of the United Nations that is making strength out of our differences make making wealth out of our diversity, and making our human community the very bedrock of peace.
Madam president, excellencies, our world is undergoing a profound disruption characterised by great power, contestation, the wars in Ukraine, the Middle East, Africa.
We're witnessing the rise of trade barriers.
Supply chain disruptions, worsening climate change, and a new industrial revolution driven by digital technologies, biotechnology and renewable energy.
This means we face both great peril and great promise.
Yet we are in a more polarised and fractured world, and one that may be unable to protect the global commons at precisely the moment that we need that protection.
Our inter-state relations are increasingly dictated by raw power, where the outcomes are determined on the basis of size, leverage and coercion.
And this poses obviously, a clear and present danger for smaller states like Singapore.

But the point I wanted to make is that even the more powerful states would ultimately pay a price, because hard power on its own cannot secure supply chains, protect populations from pandemics, or stabilise a warming planet.
Even big powers need partners to secure their long term national interests.
The bilateral and regional arrangements can complement global frameworks, but on their own, they cannot replace shared rules that apply universally.
A system built on individual coercive bargains would inherently be more volatile and more unstable.
And therefore, our thesis today is that multilateralism offers a different bargain, one that is, in every state's enlightened national interest.
These shared rules and norms provide predictability.
They constrain the capricious exercise of power, and they maximize autonomy even when power is unequally distributed.
Actually the multilateral system today still works more often than the headlines would suggest.
The World Food Program feeds over 100 million people a year.
The common ICAO standards enable 100,000 flights to operate safely every day with the ITU, our telecommunications networks and the internet continues to operate safely, smoothly on a planetary scale.
The question is, therefore not whether we need multilateralism, but how to make it fit for purpose.
First, we all have to consistently comply with international law and the norms of multilateralism.
Second, we need to reform existing institutions where needed.
And third, we need to collectively formulate new rules and create new institutions for new technologies.
Let me deal with the first point.
The consistent compliance with international law.
Consider Unclose, the UN convention on the law of the sea.
In fact, UN clauses, one of the great achievements of multilateral law making.
It was concluded under the presidency of Professor Tommy Koh of Singapore, who called it the Constitution for the oceans.
For over four decades It has set out the legal framework for activities in all our oceans and seas.
But the current war in the Persian Gulf has put us close to a severe stress test.
The Strait of Hormuz is closed.
We have to collectively reject this transit passage through straits used for international navigation is a right for all of us.
It's not a privilege subject to fees and tolls.

And this is customary international law, which means it is binding on all states whether or not they consider themselves parties to enclose how we deal with the Strait of Hormuz will have implications for navigational rights and freedom around the world.
At stake is the legal architecture for freedom of navigation and overflight, and we cannot allow any single country to exercise a veto on these navigational rights and freedoms.
Beyond the legal and political implications, the economic impact is also very stark.
The Strait of Hormuz carried around a fifth of the world's oil supplies, as well as critical supplies for other industries everywhere.
Its disruption has meant higher energy prices for all of us broken disrupted supply chains and stranded seafarers.
And this is why shared rules like enclose matter.
Defending them is not just a matter of principle or debate.
It is in our collective interests.
The largest economies depend on the open sea lanes as much as the smallest.
And we in Singapore hold ourselves to the same standard.

The Strait of Singapore is less than two nautical miles at its narrowest and yet nearly a quarter of the world's seaborne trade passes through the Strait of Singapore Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia.

The three littoral states of the Straits of Malacca and Singapore have worked with other users of these traits to keep the straits open, secure and accessible to everyone for decades, including through the cooperative mechanism on the safety of navigation and environmental protection in the Straits of Malacca and Singapore.
Madam president, excellencies, the second point is that we should and must reform existing institutions and processes where necessary.
In fact, free trade is another success story of the post-war multilateralism.
Lower trade costs in these decades have boosted global real GDP by an estimated 6.8%, and in the case of low income countries, by around 33%.

Under the GATT and subsequently the WTO, disputes even between unequal powers could be settled by adjudication rather than the exercise of unilateral coercion But we all know the multilateral trading system has frayed.

This year's WTO conference in Yaoundé could not even reach consensus on several key issues, including the moratorium on the customs duties for electronic transmissions, which lapsed tariffs and supply chain restrictions have also returned as instruments of coercion.
The consequences of all this cannot be overstated for Singapore.
Trade is three times our GDP.
For many in this hall, access to markets and technology are absolutely essential for our development.
When the rules governing trade are eroded, all of us will pay the price.
I know that consensus amongst 193 states is difficult, but it remains the gold standard.
And I would ask all of you to recollect the BB, NJ agreement which entered into force this year.
This is clear evidence that even in this time, we can still build common rules for shared challenges.
And Singapore is proud that our ambassador, Vina Lee, presided over the negotiations that concluded this agreement by consensus.
Having said that, even when consensus is elusive, we cannot allow collective action to be held hostage or to be paralysed.
We need more flexible coalition of states and partners who are willing and able to move forward, whilst remaining open to others to join when they are ready.
Such coalitions already serve large and small economies alike The Rcep, the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, is the largest trade agreement in the world.

The Cptpp, the Comprehensive and Progressive Trans-Pacific partnership now stretches from Asia to Latin America to the United Kingdom, and in July 19th, small and medium sized trading nations of the Future of Investment and Trade Partnership met in Auckland.
Not to negotiate a grand bargain, but to systematically reduce trade frictions and to strengthen supply chain resilience.
Excellencies, this is not a retreat from multilateralism.
It is a pragmatic and flexible effort to sustain cooperation when broader agreement is not yet possible, while remaining open for those who are ready to join later on.
The objective remains the same to preserve the benefits of cooperation, widen participation over time, and ultimately bring these arrangements into the multilateral global architecture.
Third, we must collectively formulate new rules and be prepared to create new institutions, if necessary, for new technologies.

Artificial intelligence, which we've heard so many times from the podium this week, is arguably the most urgent frontier AI offers with extraordinary potential, but its capability is advancing faster than our appreciation of its risks.
There are fundamentally three categories of risk.
First, the loss of control of autonomous systems.
Second, that rogue actors could use AI to create bioweapons or other weapons of mass destruction or mass disruption.
Domestic disruptions are only just emerging.
But excellencies, the genie is already out of the bottle.
It is too late to call for a halt, especially given the superpower rivalry and the huge financial incentives for companies who already have frontier models.
But let me offer a metaphor of driving a high performance car to drive a high performance car quickly and safely.
But equally, you need good brakes.
And especially if you are going to go beyond your neighborhood or cross boundaries, you need effective shared rules, traffic lights, insurance norms of behavior, seat belts.
Every one of us has to continue to invest in science, the talent, and the infrastructure that will drive AI forward. For small states.
This entails especially developing our people, equipping them with the skills necessary to master and deploy AI quickly, widely, at scale and safely.

The real productivity gains from AI comes not from the IT department, but from our businesses and workers having the skills, the tools and the wherewithal to engineer their work processes. Workflow by workflow. It is.
That's where the cutting edge of value creation arises.
But having said that, every powerful engine needs good brakes, safeguards as the capabilities of AI advance, our safeguards must keep pace.
We need rigorous testing and evaluation before deployment.
We need clear limits on what autonomous systems can do and mechanisms to intervene when they behave in ways we do not intend.

And since the risks from AI do not remain confined behind borders, it means we also need rules of the road that will form a shared global understanding of how we will collectively confront this challenge.
Just as all of us instinctively understand traffic lights the same way, whether we're here in New York or in Beijing, Moscow or Singapore.
Most importantly, human beings must ultimately remain in control and accountable.
Let me give you an extreme thought experiment.
Do you want the nuclear button to be in the hands of a human being or an AI?
The scarce resource today is not legal architecture or technology. It is trust.
Trust that the risks will be disclosed, that testing will be comprehensive and credible, and that cooperation will be inclusive and not be used to secure unilateral advantage.
The technology has already become an arena for strategic competition precisely when international cooperation is most needed.
Any durable international approach must give all states, all states a meaningful stake.
Not only those who already have the most advanced models, or the deepest pockets, or the largest set of armaments.
So the question is how do we build trust?

Even where states have differences on governance, I believe it is possible for us to work together to collectively understand the capabilities and risks of AI models, to develop comparable methods for testing and evaluation, and to report serious incidents quickly across borders.
We are not starting from zero.

If you carefully go through what we already have today, the UN's Independent International Scientific Panel on AI already helps to establish a common understanding based on evidence The global dialogue on AI governance can help to translate that common understanding into common objectives, and the Itu's AI for Good Global Commission brings together leaders from government, industry and international institutions to discuss challenges and to come up with practical solutions.

We must urgently establish common rules and safeguards for AI, and we should build on the many ongoing discussions in different formats and groupings And here I want to make a point The UN, the United Nations has a critical role to play in building convergence, because this is the only apex international institution with universal membership.
We must explore all options, including the idea of a UN framework Convention on AI safeguards.
We may also need an international institution that can perform for AI some of the functions that currently exist for institutions that perform this.

This function of setting common technical standards and the examples are the International Telecommunications Union, which provides all the International Atomic Energy Agency, which provides verification.
Ultimately, the global Commons are best protected by collective action agreed through an inclusive process, and Singapore commits to contribute where we can.
This week we joined the call for greater safety and security of frontier AI models, and I'm glad that this was led by Finland and Norway.
We will continue to contribute through platforms such as the Digital Pillar for the Forum of Small States, and by making our governance frameworks and testing tools available to all.
But the work of building trust and laying the ground for global cooperation must begin now.
Ultimately, powerful engines and good breaks and common rules do not stop us or slow us down.
They give us the assurance and the confidence so that we can move faster and more effectively for the benefit of all our peoples.
Madam president, excellencies, effective multilateralism requires institutions that can deliver, and that begins with a reform of the UN itself.
I welcome the progress of the UN initiative.
But reform must be strategic. Not not merely.
Fiscal reform must strengthen the equal standing of all members.
The goal is not a smaller UN for its own sake, but one that delivers better and more equitably.
In this session, we will appoint the 10th Secretary General of the UN.
No one today under the age of 80, has lived in a world without the United Nations.
But the UN has to earn the confidence of successive generations, and it does this through what it delivers, not what it declares on paper.
The next Secretary general must lead a UN that turns multilateral cooperation into practical results and communicates.
This results in an effective way to all our people.
He has been a consistent voice for the charter, for our climate and oceans, and for the rules that hold the global commons together.
Finally, Madam President, effective multilateralism requires all countries to be prepared to contribute to the institutions that sustain it.
For Singapore, this begins with international law.
The rule of law requires institutions to give it effect.
Currently, the International Court of Justice has its fullest docket in its history, at precisely the moment when the relevance and effectiveness of international law is being questioned.
States continue to bring their most serious disputes before the world's principal judicial organ.
That's actually a good sign that demonstrates trust in the peaceful settlement of disputes and we must safeguard that trust.

Singapore has nominated our ambassador for international law, Rina Lee, for election as a judge of the ICJ and as a tiny small state, Singapore has been a beneficiary, has been an active practitioner and a builder, a contributor to international law.
We now ask for the chance to serve the cause of the rule of law.
Madam president, this is the case for multilateralism It's not some pie in the sky idealism, but a hard headed recognition that cooperation ultimately serves all of us.
For every state, large or small a world governed by rules is infinitely better than one governed simply by the exercise of hard, crude power.
In 1945, the founders of the UN hoped that the rules could restrain power.
If we want to keep that hope alive, we must defend those very same rules that continue to serve us consistently everywhere across the globe.
We have to adapt to a changing world, and we have to build new rules, new institutions and new processes where the challenges demand.

Statement by the Prime Minister of Solomon Islands Hon Matthew Cooper Wale, MP 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly UN Headquarters, New York, 25th September 2026 “Please chexk against delivery” Secretary-General of the United Nations, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, I stand before this Assembly conscious that I speak on behalf of a nation and a people whose future is being shaped in halls like this one.
I bring warm greetings from the people and Government of Solomon Islands, a nation of nearly one thousand islands stretching across as many miles of the Blue Pacific.
Our people hold the same hopes as people in every land: to live in peace, and to raise their children in dignity.

Your unwavering advocacy on climate action and your repeated visits to our region told the world a simple truth: that the Pacific matters, and that our challenges, and how the world responds to them, remain a litmus test for us all.
We meet at a time when multilateralism is under serious strain, and when the notion that might is right appears to be making a return.
Yet we continue to gather, in forums and dialogues around the world and here in the General Assembly, the pinnacle of multilateralism.
That, in itself, is cause for hope.

National Priorities For my people, what is said in this hall is measured not in declarations but in results: classrooms with teachers and books, clinics with medicines, roads that reach markets, and villages that thrive.
That is the lens through which Solomon Islands engages with the world.
My government is delivering a programme of national transformation.
We are providing universal free education, so that no child is turned away from school because their family cannot afford the fees.
We are strengthening our health system, with a renewed focus on tackling the scourge of non-communicable diseases, eradicating malaria and building a new national referral hospital.
We are prioritizing energy and other transformative infrastructure, expanding roads, ports, airports and telecommunications to connect our scattered islands into one national economy.
We are reforming our public finance systems so that every dollar delivers for our people.
And we are pursuing constitutional amendments to strengthen our democracy.
This is the agenda by which our people will judge my government.
International Peace and Security Over the past year, the international community has faced many challenges.
Protracted armed conflicts, an energy crisis and disruptions to global trade have been compounded by destabilization orchestrated by those who pursue their own selfish ambitions.
For small island economies, these are not distant events.
Every rise in the price of fuel is felt in the cost of shipping, electricity, food and essential services, placing a heavy burden on communities that have no buffer against external shocks.
These tensions confirm what Solomon Islands has long understood: peace and security are inseparable from development.
Neither can be secured without the other.
There are no winners in war, only graves, orphans and the long labour of rebuilding what conflict has torn down.
There is no substitute for dialogue, diplomacy and peaceful negotiation.
Solomon Islands calls on all parties to armed conflicts to protect civilians, return to the negotiating table and act in full respect of international law.
And it is why the world needs a stronger, more agile United Nations, one equipped to respond to the realities of today.
Transnational Crime, Illicit Drugs and Ocean of Peace The Pacific faces a grave and growing threat.

Transnational criminal networks are using our ocean as a highway for illicit drugs, undermining our sovereignty and national security, destroying young lives and tearing at the fabric of our communities.
Behind every statistic stands a family, a community, and a young life robbed of its promise.
We will not allow criminal networks to profit from the vulnerability of our people.

We are amending our Dangerous Drugs Act to introduce stiffer penalties as a deterrent, and we are strengthening law enforcement to prevent and detect these crimes and to hold perpetrators accountable.
In August this year, Solomon Islands acceded to the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime, a clear demonstration of our resolve to confront this threat.
These are costly and demanding undertakings, and no Pacific country can win this fight alone.
We call for stronger international cooperation, greater information sharing, sustained investment in the capacity of our law enforcement agencies, and support for prevention and rehabilitation.
Our vision of a peaceful and secure Pacific extends beyond transnational crime.
As enshrined in the Ocean of Peace Declaration, our region must remain free of nuclear weapons and free from destabilizing external influence.
In keeping with that vision, my government has proposed a treaty that would bind Pacific Island countries and like-minded partners to a firm, shared commitment to keep the Pacific an Ocean of Peace.
Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technologies Artificial intelligence and emerging technologies present both unprecedented opportunities and serious risks.
They can accelerate sustainable development, transform education and health care, strengthen disaster preparedness, and open new economic pathways for developing countries.
But a widening digital divide threatens to leave developing countries further behind.
For my government, digital transformation is not about technology for its own sake; it is about connecting our scattered islands and opening the modern economy to every Solomon Islander.

The completion of 161 telecommunication towers across the country will lift national broadband coverage from 56 to 86 per cent, expanding access to information, education and digital financial services.
The benefits of AI must be shared by all, not concentrated among a few.
Its risks, including its use for non-peaceful purposes, must be governed by all, not left to a few.
Solomon Islands therefore recognizes the need for an inclusive and transparent international governance framework on AI.
Climate Change Year after year, Pacific leaders have stood at this podium and urged the world to act on climate change.
And yet global action continues to fall short of what the science demands.
With every passing COP, the impacts grow more severe.
Our islands are being lost to the sea.
Disasters are more frequent and more is under threat, and devastating.
Solomon Islands knows this reality first-hand.
This year, Tropical Cyclone Maila, a Category 5 storm, tore through our communities, destroying homes, schools, infrastructure and livelihoods.
My government has just approved US$9.38 million for shelter recovery.
That is money our essential services urgently need, now diverted to deal with the impacts of this climate extreme.
Like many Pacific Island countries, we are trapped in a relentless cycle of response, recovery and rebuilding.
This is not sustainable, nor is it just.
My people did the least to cause this crisis, yet they pay its earliest and heaviest price.
That is the moral ledger that lies before this Assembly.
Last year, the International Court of Justice confirmed in its landmark advisory opinion that States have legal obligations to protect the climate system.
Major emitters must make deep emission cuts and transition away from fossil fuels.
Climate finance, including support for loss and damage, must be grant-based and channelled through our national budget systems.
Project-based financing of climate action is unsustainable and out of step with the scale of a crisis we did least to cause.
Vulnerable countries should not have to choose between climate action and educating their children, caring for the sick or securing food and water.
Yet that is the choice we face with every dollar we spend.
We therefore call for the full capitalization of the Pacific Resilience Facility and an ambitious and timely third replenishment of the Green Climate Fund.
Our region has long led on climate action, and we will continue to lead.
The Pre-COP31 meeting, to be hosted in the Pacific by Australia in partnership with Fiji and Tuvalu, will bring the reality of climate change directly into the heart of the global process.
I call on all Parties and partners to come to that meeting, and to COP31, with stronger commitments and concrete action.
The communities on the frontline of the climate crisis deserve nothing less.
Sea-Level Rise Solomon Islands welcomes the convening of the Second High-Level Meeting on Sea-Level Rise and the adoption of the first political declaration on sea-level rise.

Every day, our people are defending their coastlines, strengthening their resilience, protecting their food and water security and their cultural heritage, and, where there is no other choice, relocating.
But we cannot do this alone.

I call on this Assembly to match the courage of our Pacific communities with collective international resolve: to scale up adaptation and resilience finance and to support communities facing climate mobility needs.
Ocean The ocean is not simply a resource; it is our identity, our heritage and our future.
It sustains our livelihoods, our culture and our economy.
We do not own the ocean; we belong to it.
We hold it in solemn trust for generations not yet born.
Yet our ability to benefit fully from our own ocean is undermined by illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, which costs our region US$300 million every year.

Solomon Islands is fighting back, working with the Forum Fisheries Agency and partners including Australia, France, New Zealand and the United States to strengthen surveillance and enforcement across our waters.
SDG 14 remains among the least funded of all the Sustainable Development Goals.
With just four years left until 2030, the fourth United Nations Ocean Conference must raise the bar on ocean finance and secure the ocean's place in the development agenda beyond 2030.
Solomon Islands welcomes the entry into force of the BBNJ Agreement and the preparations for the first Conference of the Parties in January.
We look to that Conference to establish, without delay, the Secretariat and the institutional arrangements to implement the Agreement.
Plastic pollution is poisoning our ocean and our food.
As negotiations resume in Bangkok, Solomon Islands calls for an ambitious, legally binding treaty that addresses the full life cycle of plastics, from production to disposal.
Youth, Women and Persons with Disabilities Our people are our greatest asset.

With more than half of our population under the age of 25, my government is prioritizing legal frameworks that empower young people, advance gender equality, and strengthen the protection of women and children against domestic violence.

We welcome global progress in advancing the rights and full participation of women and persons with disabilities in the economy, and Solomon Islands is committed to accelerating that progress at home.
There can be no sustainable development without equal opportunity for all.

International and Domestic Cooperation Our development partnerships play an indispensable role in infrastructure, maritime connectivity, health and expanding education, and in improving the lives of Solomon Islanders.
South-South cooperation remains an important complement to Official Development Assistance.
Partnerships among developing countries have enabled us to share expertise, technology, innovation and practical solutions suited to our circumstances.
The support of Papua New Guinea, Indonesia, India and our Pacific family embodies the true spirit of South-South solidarity, and we value it deeply.
We also acknowledge the partnership of multilateral organizations, non-governmental organizations and our private sector in supporting development work in Solomon Islands.
At home, my government is working hand in hand with our churches to build stronger and more inclusive communities.
Cooperation and partnership, at every level and across borders, are critical to nation building, and my government remains fully committed to them.
Financing for Development As a Small Island Developing State, our vulnerability remains a fundamental reality.
A single natural disaster can erase years of investment and progress and push a nation backwards.
The Multidimensional Vulnerability Index captures the special circumstances of SIDS in a way that income measures alone cannot.
We call on international financial institutions to integrate the MVI into their financing decisions for SIDS without further delay.
Last year, the world spent more than US$2.9 trillion on its militaries.
That is more than sixteen times all official development assistance.
In less than 18 days, the world spends more on arms than developed countries provide in a full year of climate finance.
In the same year that military spending reached its highest share of global output since 2009, development aid had its steepest fall on record.
Bilateral aid to the least developed countries fell by a quarter.

Redirecting even a small share of this spending would fully capitalize the Pacific Resilience Facility and the Loss and Damage Fund, secure the Green Climate Fund's third replenishment, and meet the ODA targets. The resources exist.
What is missing is the will.
The time to act is now.
LDC Graduation Solomon Islands is due to graduate from Least Developed Country status in 2027.

As part of our preparations, my government is pursuing an ambitious and proactive agenda that uses public-private partnerships to unlock investment in transformative projects, special economic zones and key sectors.
A second tuna cannery at Bina Harbour, upgraded airports, agricultural treatment facilities to support trade, and expanded road networks and maritime ports will shift the trajectory of our economy.
At the same time, my government is strengthening our financial institutions and frameworks to improve revenue collection and accountability, so that we can sustain our development priorities.
These reforms reflect our commitment to a strong and resilient economy that delivers decentralized, people-centred development across the country.

Our ambition is clear: to graduate from LDC status with confidence, to strengthen the foundations of our economy, and to ensure that development delivers lasting opportunities for every Solomon Islander.
UN Reform As the United Nations marks its eighty-first anniversary, it must continue to evolve to meet today's challenges while remaining faithful to its founding principles.

The UN80 reform process must strengthen the Organization's effectiveness and relevance without diminishing its presence, services or support in the most vulnerable regions, where assistance is needed most.
Reform must enhance delivery, not reduce it.

The United Nations is not perfect, but it remains the cornerstone of multilateral diplomacy and the indispensable platform through which nations preserve peace, advance sustainable development, uphold international law and protect human rights.

Solomon Islands looks to the next Secretary-General to lead with vision and to ensure that the Secretariat is accountable to all Member States, serving the interests of small and large States on an equal footing.

Security Council Reform Solomon Islands reiterates its support for comprehensive reform of the Security Council to make it more representative, transparent, accountable and reflective of today's realities.
A Council with a dedicated seat for Small Island Developing States would strengthen the legitimacy and effectiveness of the entire multilateral system.
The veto is a relic of 1945.
Too often, it has been used to shield violations of international law and to entrench the double standards that fuel conflict.
At a minimum, the veto must never again be used in situations of genocide, crimes against humanity or war crimes.
Peacekeeping It is with great pride that Solomon Islands is once again contributing personnel to United Nations peacekeeping in South Sudan.

Despite our small size, our participation reaffirms our enduring commitment to the Charter, to international peace and security, and to the noble work of peacekeepers serving communities affected by conflict.
Solomon Islands looks forward to increasing its peacekeeping contribution in the coming year.
Decolonization Leaving no one behind demands that we complete the unfinished work of decolonization.
Solomon Islands reaffirms its longstanding support for the right to self-determination of the Kanak people of New Caledonia and the Maohi nui people of French Polynesia.

The United Nations decolonization process must offer more than hope; it must provide practical pathways to the full emancipation of peoples in Non-Self-Governing Territories, and to their freedom to determine their own political future and development aspirations.
In the same spirit, I turn to West Papua, whose people are our Melanesian brothers and sisters.
Solomon Islands respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Republic of Indonesia, and we value our friendship with its Government and people.
It is precisely because of that friendship that we speak with candour.
Reports of human rights violations in West Papua have persisted for far too long.
They must be independently verified, not left in dispute.

We therefore renew the call of Pacific Islands Forum Leaders for the Government of Indonesia to facilitate, without further delay, the long-awaited visit of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights to West Papua.
Such a visit is an act of confidence between friends, and an affirmation that there is nothing to fear from the light.
Closing Mr. President, in closing, the challenges of our time demand renewed solidarity, stronger multilateralism and genuine commitment to the principles of the UN Charter.
But institutions do not have hearts; people do.
Charters do not keep the peace; the men and women who honour them do.
Beyond every declaration and commitment, each of us carries a profound responsibility: to be agents of peace, champions of goodwill, and keepers of the fragile bonds of friendship among nations.
The world has never needed that spirit more than it does today.
Our Constitution was established "under the guiding hand of God," by a people "conscious of our common destiny."
We believe that is true not only of Solomon Islands, but of this whole family of nations.
We live in a time when division has become the calling card of the day.
Neighbours are asked to choose sides.
Small States are too often treated as prizes to be won rather than partners to be heard.
But the destiny of nations does not finally rest in this general assembly, nor in any capital, however powerful.
King Solomon, among the wisest rulers of antiquity, wrote: "There are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless, the counsel of the Lord, that shall stand."
That truth does not make us passive.
It makes us humble, and it makes us accountable.
So I call on my fellow leaders to do three things.
First, let us ask for wisdom before we ask for advantage.
When Solomon was offered anything he wished, he did not ask for riches, or long life, or the defeat of his enemies.
He asked for "an understanding heart," so that he might judge his people well.
I can think of no better prayer for every leader in this room.
Second, let us stay at the table.
The same king taught that "in the multitude of counsellors there is safety."
That is the oldest case I know for what this Organization is meant to be: many nations, large and small, sitting together, because none of us sees far enough alone.
Third, let us measure greatness rightly.
Not its arsenal, not its alliances, but its justice: how it treats the poor, the displaced, and the small.
Let us choose cooperation over division, dialogue over confrontation, peace over hostility, and action over inaction.
And let us lead as people who know we will answer for it one day.
Our national motto teaches us that “to lead is to serve”.
In that spirit of service, Solomon Islands stands ready to do its part, as a willing partner and a committed Member of this Assembly.
Nearly twenty-five years ago, Sierra Leone completed disarmament and formally declared its civil war over.

The formal declaration matters, but peace became real in more practical ways: in the families that returned home, in the communities that learned to live together again, in the citizens who chose the ballot and in institutions that slowly earned back confidence.
The United Nations stood with us through disarmament, elections and the long work of peacebuilding.
We know what international cooperation can make possible because we have lived it.
That experience taught us that trust cannot be commanded by declaration.
Trust grows when promises are honoured, when the law protects everyone, when institutions serve their people, and when citizens can see a future for themselves.
Sierra Leone brings that lesson to this Assembly at a time when trust between nations, in institutions and in multilateral cooperation is under profound strain.
In this year’s theme, “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers FOR ALL,” the words “FOR ALL” carry its defining moral weight.
The words “FOR ALL” ask not only whether the United Nations can act, but also whom its actions reach, whose voices shape them, and whose dignity they protect.
15. An institution may act quickly and still fail those it was meant to serve.
16. Delivery worthy of the UN Charter must reach those furthest from power and recognise the equal worth of every nation and every human life.
That is the standard by which the world will judge us.
Trust is the currency of multilateralism.
Trust is gained when the law protects the vulnerable as firmly as it restrains the powerful.
International law must not change with geography or bend according to the identity of the accused.
In the Middle East, the UN Charter and international law must guide us.
Civilians must be protected, humanitarian access ensured, aggression and occupation ended, and freedom of navigation safeguarded.
The inalienable right of the Palestinian people to self- determination must be realised through a viable State of Palestine living alongside the State of Israel in peace and security.
That same commitment to peace requires progress on nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation through diplomacy.
In Sudan, civilians continue to endure atrocities and displacement, underscoring the cost of delayed action.

The credibility of international law also depends on who has a voice in applying it.

37. Africa seeks its rightful place because the Council cannot be fully legitimate or effective while an entire continent remains permanently absent from its highest level of decision-making.

Before this session concludes, Member States should have a consolidated model, which we committed to in the Pact for the Future.
Sierra Leone speaks with the authority of service.

Through ECOSOC, Sierra Leone will champion a development system that responds more effectively to Africa’s priorities.
Restoring trust and delivering for all must also embrace the unfinished cause of reparatory justice.

For Sierra Leone, this history is neither abstract nor distant.
From Bunce Island, in our own river estuary, thousands of Africans were forcibly transported across the Atlantic into enslavement.
Freetown, our capital, would later become a home for formerly enslaved and liberated Africans.
This history is woven into our nation's identity.
However, the consequences did not end with abolition.
Their legacy continues to be reflected in enduring disparities in wealth, power and opportunity across our world.
Reparatory justice is therefore not a plea for charity.
It calls for acknowledgement, formal apology, the return of cultural heritage, fair redress and guarantees of non-repetition.
Sierra Leone stands with Africa, the Caribbean and the wider African diaspora in advancing this cause, not to remain captive to the past, but to build a more just and equitable future.
The same principle of fairness applies to Africa's critical minerals.
59. Critical minerals are indispensable to the global energy transition, yet too much value is still added elsewhere.
Processing at source, fair value chains, technology transfer and local industry would turn natural wealth into skilled work, stronger economies and hope for our young people.
The green transition must not reproduce the extractive terms of the past.
For the youth, this is immediate.
A young person without work, opportunity or a stake in the future becomes vulnerable to the recruiter, the smuggler and the dangerous journey across the Mediterranean.
Jobs, skills and dignity are therefore part of any serious policy for peace and development.
Sierra Leone does not ask of the world what it does not demand of itself.
We carry these same principles into our work at home.
Through Feed Salone, we are increasing domestic food production and strengthening food security.
Through Free Quality School Education, we are widening the path from the circumstances of a child's birth to the possibilities of that child's future.
In 2024, we enacted the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act and subsequently championed the proclamation of 27 November as the International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage.
68. A girl in Sierra Leone is no more or less precious than a girl anywhere else.
Protecting her childhood, education and freedom is part of what development means.
69. A girl’s future, like the future of every young person, will be shaped by forces already remaking our world: climate change, artificial intelligence and the energy transition.
The meaning of ‘FOR ALL’ becomes more urgent as we decide how these transformations will be governed.
71. Artificial Intelligence can improve education, healthcare, agriculture and public administration.
It can also widen inequality if infrastructure, knowledge and rule-making remain concentrated in a few countries.
73. Developing nations must help shape the standards that will govern technologies affecting their people.

In Shenge, on Sierra Leone's southern coast, families watch the sea take land, fishing grounds and the graves of their ancestors.

Those who contributed least to the climate crisis are bearing some of its greatest costs.
78. Accessible and predictable climate finance, support for adaptation, and effective arrangements for loss and damage are obligations of justice.
They are also investments in global stability.
Fairness in transformation depends on the institutions that govern it.
Sierra Leone therefore supports the UN80 Initiative and wider reforms that make this Organisation more effective, accountable and responsive.
Efficiency matters and reform must preserve the capacity to act.
The choice of the next Secretary-General offers another test of institutional effectiveness and equality.
In eighty years, every Secretary-General has been a man.
The women put forward for this office have placed their competence beyond dispute.
86. What remains is the will of this Organisation to live by the equality it asks of others and entrust a woman with its highest office.
87. Our insistence on a capable United Nations comes from experience.
For Sierra Leone, this Organisation is part of our living history.
It stood with us when our country was broken and helped us make peace durable.
In this Hall, a Small State has the same vote as a great power.
Imperfect as it is, that equality remains one of humanity’s boldest promises.

Sierra Leone will continue to contribute personnel to United Nations peace operations, uphold international law, support mediation and peacebuilding, defend the rights of women and girls, and serve as a bridge wherever Member States seek one.

In this regard, Sierra Leone has nominated Professor Charles Chernor Jalloh, a distinguished international jurist, endorsed by the African Union and ECOWAS, for election as a Judge of the International Court of Justice.
93. We respectfully seek Member States' support on 3 November.
The United Nations was created in a world of unequal power, yet it rests on a radical idea: nations differ in size and strength, but their peoples do not differ in human worth.
95. A United Nations that delivers ‘FOR ALL’ makes that equality felt beyond this Hall.
96. Nearly twenty-five years ago, Sierra Leoneans placed their trust in peace because they believed tomorrow could be different.
People around the world are asking something similar of us now.
They need reason to believe that cooperation still works, that law still matters, and that promises made here will be honoured in their lives.
Let this session give them that reason.
The words 'FOR ALL' should not remain at the end of this year’s theme.
They must become the measure of our work.
1. While we speak of peace, security and international cooperation, thousands of people are dying as victims of war, hunger, violence, disease and injustice.
It would seem that we have lost our sense of humanity.
2. It is not a future tragedy.
It is happening now while we are here.
3. At this moment, there will be mothers, fathers, children and families asking themselves something that is neither abstract, nor diplomatic, nor geopolitical.
It is an elementary question, with the deepest humanity: Where are the United Nations?
4. That question, perhaps more than any other, is the reason why we are here.
And for that reason I would like to ask those of us in this Assembly, do we today have an Organization that continues to be relevant and has the conviction to confront the challenges of our humanity?
5. We are living in an extremely complex era in which changes and challenges occur in a matter of seconds.
These changes and challenges overwhelm us.
6. But the most vulnerable, the voiceless, those who suffer the most, yearn for something much simpler; but fundamental: peace, security, employment, and a dignified future for their children.
7. And that is the greatest contradiction of our time.
8. We have more capabilities than ever, but also challenges that no State can confront on its own.
9. As the United Nations, we have to commit ourselves and work to redefine the international order so that it prioritizes the common well-being of humanity.

10. We need a multilateralism that is capable of listening, but also of deciding; that preserves principles, that respects the sovereignty of States, but that understands that no State can resolve on its own problems that no longer recognize borders.
11. Because the credibility of the United Nations is not built only with resolutions.
Its legitimacy is attained when the Organization is truly capable of preserving and guaranteeing a dignified future for people.
12. And this is something that El Salvador knows very well.
13. For decades, my country was known for a reality that seemed impossible to change.
The entrails of violence penetrated deeply into our society.
14. An entire nation resigned itself to the fact that that reality was what we were condemned to live.

15. After decades of institutional indifference, in 2019 the Salvadoran people placed their trust in Nayib Bukele, a young leader who dared, like no one before, to challenge that to which an entire generation believed itself condemned and to transform the country’s profound reality.

16. El Salvador went from recording homicide rates of 103 homicides per 100 thousand inhabitants, among the highest in the world, to reaching radically different levels, 1.3 per 100 thousand inhabitants, becoming one of the benchmark cases most closely watched internationally in the area of security.

17. The International Monetary Fund has indicated that the improvement in security has strengthened the country’s confidence and economic activity, and estimates that the Salvadoran economy will grow by 4.5 per cent in 2026, driven by investment, private consumption, remittances, tourism and capital inflows.
18. However, it would be a mistake to reduce that transformation to a figure.
19. Because behind a figure there are faces.
a. There is a mother who no longer fears that her son will return home.
b. There is a shopkeeper who can open his business.
c. There is a worker who can move through his city.
d. There is a child who can play on a street that previously did not belong to him.
20. And there is something even deeper.
A society that recovered hope, grounded in the possibility of imagining a different future.
21. That is what recovering security really means.
a. It does not mean only reducing crime.
b. It means giving space back to freedom.
22. And when a society recovers the freedom to walk, to work, to undertake, and to live without fear, a second transformation begins: the recovery of confidence.
23. That explains why El Salvador is today a point of reference for countries seeking support and answers in the face of their own security challenges.
24. Not because our path can be copied mechanically.
25. However, there is a lesson that we believe can be universal; no nation should be obliged to accept collapse and governmental incapacity to manage as its destiny.
26. El Salvador does not come to this Assembly to say that we have solved all our problems.
27. Today we come to say something much deeper.
28. With determination, we have shown that a problem that seemed irreversible can be confronted and transformed.
29. And I want to be clear; in keeping with the vision of my President Bukele, security is not the final destination, it is the point of departure.
30. In El Salvador we have placed education at the centre of our national transformation, because we believe that transforming a school is, ultimately, transforming a life. Transforming the homeland.
31. With initiatives such as Two Schools a Day, we are comprehensively renewing public education from early childhood through secondary education.
32. In health, we have infrastructure, modernized equipment and created digital care through Doctor SV in order to bring quality care to every forgotten corner of our country.
33. The vision of our First Lady, Gabriela Rodríguez de Bukele, is profoundly human.
That every girl, boy and young person may grow up in freedom, fully develop their potential and have the real opportunity to build the life project they choose.

34. Now our efforts as a country are focused on turning security into investment; investment into employment; employment into social mobility; technology into opportunities; education into capabilities; and stability into prosperity.

35. By leading, together with Estonia, the global dialogue on the governance of artificial intelligence, El Salvador reaffirmed that this technology must expand capacities and create opportunities to build environments capable of competing in the future.
36. The transformation my country is experiencing has taught us that security, development and human dignity are not separate compartments.
a. Without security, development becomes fragile.
b. Without development, security can hardly be sustainable.
c. And without dignity, neither of the two has any true meaning.
37. The international community must understand that solving global challenges goes beyond a resolution on paper.
38. A multilateralism that does not force countries to choose permanently between sovereignty and cooperation.
39. Today, we have before us a historic and inexcusable challenge.
To make multilateralism once again synonymous with “capacity for action”.
40. El Salvador considers that the reform of the United Nations should not be limited to reorganizing structures.
41. We need an agile, representative, effective and transparent Organization; one that is capable of resolving, with the speed that contemporary problems demand, contemporary problems.
Enough already with personal and national interests prevailing over global needs and crises.
42. We expect this same commitment from the next Secretary-General of the United Nations.

43. A leadership with absolute independence, with capacity for dialogue, with moral authority, with knowledge of the international reality and with the will and reforming conviction for the benefit of humanity.

44. In a short and historic period of 7 years, El Salvador has taken a firm step toward changing its reality, recovering its security, its spaces, its confidence and its dignity, while also fighting for its sovereignty.
We are determined to defend it, because it has cost us too much blood to recover it.
I am convinced that each and every one of my compatriots would be willing to defend our Homeland and our sovereignty with the greatest commitment and sacrifice.
46. Today, El Salvador wishes to place before this Assembly 4 fundamental lessons: a.
That nations are not condemned to repeat their past eternally.
That difficult problems are not necessarily impossible problems.
That the size of a country does not determine the size of its responsibility.
And that the future does not necessarily belong to those who have more power.
47. It also belongs to those who dare to transform with determination.
48. El Salvador’s invitation to this General Assembly is simple.
a. Let us not resign ourselves.
b. Let us not accept that war, poverty and violence are inevitable.
Let us not accept that this Organization is condemned to immobility.
And let us not accept that the differences between nations are more powerful than what we have in common.
49. Today we must ask ourselves a vital question for the present and future of our Nations: What world do we want to build so that humanity may prosper?
50. El Salvador has already made a decision about its own future; and I do not say this lightly.
51. Today we come to say it loud and clear: not with words, but with deeds. Transformation is possible.
We are doing it and we will not take a step back.

For more than seventeen centuries, we have survived not through military power, territorial expansion or economic might, but through dialogue, respect for the law, neutrality, and the conviction that the sovereignty of a small State is no less valuable than that of a great power.
Our history has taught us a simple lesson: when power is not enough to protect you, rules matter.
When you cannot impose your will, dialogue matters.
And when the world is divided, institutions that bring States together matter.
This is why multilateralism is not an abstract concept for San Marino.
It is a fundamental principle of our foreign policy, and, in many ways, a lesson drawn from our own history.
Our commitment to cooperation and shared rules is also reflected in our relationship with the European Union.
The forthcoming signing of the Association Agreement with the European Union on 19 October will mark a milestone for our country.

It represents a historic step towards closer cooperation, shared rules and greater integration with the European Union, while fully preserving our sovereignty, identity and institutional specificities.
For San Marino, this is not simply an agreement about economic relations.
It is a long-term choice to deepen our engagement with Europe while preserving the distinctive character of our Republic.
It is a choice that reflects a principle at the heart of our history: cooperation does not diminish sovereignty.
For a small State, cooperation, rules and dialogue are precisely what allow sovereignty to be exercised and protected.
Today, that principle is under extraordinary pressure.
Eighty-one years ago, the United Nations was created to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war.
Yet today, conflicts are multiplying. Inequalities are deepening.
Food and water are increasingly being used as instruments of pressure.
And the rules that have governed international relations for decades are being challenged.
We are witnessing the use of force against sovereign States.
We are witnessing violations of international humanitarian and human rights law.
At such a moment, the answer cannot be less multilateralism.
And it must be a multilateralism that works: one that protects the weak as well as the strong; one that applies the law equally; and one that gives every State, large or small, a meaningful voice.
San Marino supports the priorities of your programme and stands ready to cooperate fully with you and with all Member States in the year ahead.
There can be no world in which might makes right.
Sovereignty, territorial integrity, political independence and self-determination matter.
These principles are not optional and they cannot depend on the size of a country or the power of a government.
There can be no impunity for violations of international law.
The law must apply to all.
For San Marino, this is not an abstract principle.
For small States, international law is our protection.
A rules-based international order allows every State, large or small, to have an equal voice and equal legal standing.
This is why San Marino strongly supports the Secretary-General’s UN80 initiative.
The United Nations must become more effective, more efficient and more responsive.
And reform must include the Security Council.
The Council must better reflect today’s world.
It must be more representative, transparent and accountable.

San Marino is also a member of the Uniting for Consensus group and supports its efforts to promote a comprehensive and balanced reform of the Security Council, based on greater regional representation, equitable geographical distribution and wider access to elected seats.
Reform must strengthen the voice of all Member States, including small States, and it must be achieved through broad consensus.

We support efforts to restrain the use of the veto, including the French-Mexican initiative and the ACT Code of Conduct in involving mass atrocities, alongside the General situations Assembly veto initiative.
We also reaffirm our full support for the International Court of Justice.
Its orders and judgments are legally binding.
Respect for the Court is respect for the international legal order.
The next Secretary-General will carry a vital responsibility.
The United Nations must remain relevant and credible.
Above all, it must remain capable of protecting people and upholding the Charter.
San Marino stands ready to contribute.
I now turn to one of the most painful crises of our time.
The situation in the Middle East demands clarity.
San Marino unequivocally condemns terrorism, including the horrific attacks of 7 October 2023.
But we must be equally clear on another point: the Palestinian people have an inalienable right to self-determination and to their own State.
Statehood is not a reward for terrorism.
At the same time, nothing can justify the collective punishment of civilians.
The suffering in Gaza cannot become the new normal.
We call for a permanent ceasefire and for full, safe and unhindered humanitarian access.
Humanitarian assistance must reach those who need it.
UNRWA and other humanitarian organizations must be able to operate.
We call for the permanent disarmament of Hamas and other non-State armed groups, and for the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the Gaza Strip.
We support the Palestinian Authority and its reform efforts, including democratic elections.
We urge Israel to release withheld clearance revenues and to facilitate correspondent banking services for the Palestinian Authority.
These developments undermine the possibility of a viable Palestinian State.
The Status Quo of Jerusalem’s holy sites must be respected.
All communities, including Christian communities, must be protected.
Last year, San Marino endorsed the New York Declaration for a two-State solution.

Following a unanimous mandate from our Parliament, the Great and General Council, San Marino recognized Palestine as a sovereign and secure and internationally recognized borders and in accordance with relevant United Nations resolutions.
There is no alternative to two States living side by side in peace, security and mutual recognition.
The window for that solution is narrowing.
The consequences of the conflict extend far beyond Gaza and the West Bank.
Escalation across the region threatens international peace and security.
We are deeply concerned by hostilities involving Iran and by threats to maritime security in the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz.
Freedom of navigation is essential to global stability.
International law, including UNCLOS, must be respected.
In Lebanon, we call for full respect for sovereignty and for the implementation of Security Council resolution 1701.
In Syria, we support an inclusive and peaceful political transition that respects sovereignty, protects civilians and strengthens institutions.
Peace cannot be imposed by force.
Europe is also facing a war that continues to cause immense human suffering.
San Marino condemns Russia’s ongoing aggression against Ukraine.
They are violations of international law.
No State can be allowed to redraw borders by force.
San Marino therefore reiterates its call for a full, immediate and unconditional ceasefire, leading to a comprehensive, just and lasting peace.
Any peace must respect Ukraine’s sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders.
From Ukraine to Gaza, from Sudan to Syria, from the Sahel to Afghanistan, civilians continue to pay the highest price.
International humanitarian law was created precisely for these circumstances.
It does not disappear in times of war.
It is not suspended by political convenience.
San Marino strongly condemns the use of explosive weapons in populated areas and calls on all States to implement the Political Declaration on Explosive Weapons in Populated Areas.
Those who deliver humanitarian assistance must also be protected.
Aid workers and journalists are not legitimate targets.

San Marino also reaffirms its commitment to the Australia-led Declaration for the Protection of Humanitarian Personnel, and calls on all parties to armed conflict to respect and protect humanitarian personnel and to ensure that assistance can reach those in need.
San Marino therefore reaffirms its commitment to the Geneva Conventions, the Genocide Convention and the Rome Statute.
And we reiterate our unwavering support for the International Criminal Court.
The Court exists because the gravest crimes cannot go unanswered: genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Accountability is not an obstacle to peace.
It is part of lasting peace.
to Protect, which must Recent political pressure and coercive measures against the Court, its officials and those who cooperate with it are deeply concerning.
States Parties to the Rome Statute must defend the independence and integrity of the Court.
San Marino also reaffirms its historic commitment to the abolition of the death penalty, which it abolished in 1865.
This reflects our enduring conviction that human dignity must be protected even in the face of the gravest crimes.
Justice cannot depend on political power.
Five years ago, the Taliban seized power in Afghanistan.
Five years is too long for half of a population to be denied its rights.
Afghan women and girls continue to face systematic restrictions on education, employment, movement, public participation and access to justice.
Girls remain excluded from secondary and higher education.
Women are increasingly excluded from public life.
San Marino calls for the full restoration of the rights of Afghan women and girls.
Participation in public life is a right.
These rights do not disappear because a government chooses to deny them.
The international community must continue to stand with Afghan women and girls.
Humanitarian access must also remain unhindered.
Children are being killed, maimed, abducted and recruited.
They are losing their homes, their schools and their futures.
San Marino remains firmly committed to the Children and Armed Conflict agenda and supports the work of the UN Special Representative for Children and Armed Conflict.
We have endorsed the Safe Schools Declaration, the Paris Principles and the Vancouver Principles.
We call on all States to strengthen the protection of children in armed conflict and to ratify the Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child.
The return of nuclear threats is another source of grave concern.
There can be no acceptable nuclear threat or acceptable use of nuclear weapons.

The modernization and expansion of nuclear arsenals, together with growing military expenditures and the rapid development of artificial intelligence and cyber capabilities, increase the risk of escalation.
The consequences of nuclear use would be catastrophic.
San Marino remains committed to a world free of nuclear weapons.
We support the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons.
We also proudly uphold the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, which San Marino has signed and ratified.
Diplomacy must prevail over deterrence through fear.
Peace and security cannot be separated from development.
Nor can development be separated from human rights.
Conflict destroys development gains. Poverty fuels instability.
We must also not overlook the devastating humanitarian and socio-economic situation in Cuba, where prolonged hardship is placing an immense burden on the daily lives of the Cuban people.
We must therefore treat peace, security, human rights and sustainable development as parts of the same agenda.
The SDGs remain our common commitment.
The Pact for the Future provides an opportunity to strengthen multilateralism and accelerate implementation of the 2030 Agenda.
We need implementation, financing and accountability.
We also need a fairer and more inclusive international financial architecture, supported by adequate resources and greater financial stability for the UN itself.
The triple planetary crisis - climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution - is already affecting peace and security.
Environmental degradation fuels food insecurity, water scarcity and displacement.
The Paris Agreement must be fully implemented.
The 1.5-degree goal must remain within reach, the transition must be just and no country should be left behind.
Food security must also remain at the heart of our collective efforts.
Conflict and climate shocks are driving hunger and malnutrition.
San Marino believes that reducing food loss and waste is one practical contribution to a more secure and sustainable food system.
We are also entering a new technological era.
Artificial intelligence and emerging technologies offer enormous opportunities, but they also create new risks.
It must not be used to undermine human rights, international peace or international humanitarian law.
The rules must keep pace with innovation.
And where new technologies create new risks, our responsibility is not to look away, but to govern them.
Multilateralism is not an outdated idea.
It is the only framework capable of managing an interdependent world.
No country can address today’s challenges alone, protect itself from climate change alone, prevent the proliferation of nuclear weapons alone or regulate global technology alone.
And no country can build lasting peace alone.
We need cooperation and institutions that work.
And we need the political courage to uphold the rules we have created together.
For more than seventeen centuries, San Marino has shown that a small State can preserve its independence through dialogue, respect for the law and engagement with the international community.
This is why San Marino will continue to defend the United Nations Charter, international law, human rights and multilateralism.
At a time when the world is tempted by division, we must choose cooperation.
When force challenges law, we must stand firmly by the law.
And when despair is growing, we must choose peace.
San Marino will do its part.
Together, we must ensure that the United Nations remains what it was created to be: a shield for the vulnerable, a forum for dialogue and a guardian of peace, dignity and international law.
Indeed, his successor will have extremely large boots to fill going forward.
For generations, the United Nations has represented humanity’s shared determination to replace conflict with dialogue, domination with cooperation and despair with hope.
Yet today, many of the ideals and values we once collectively defended are being questioned and challenged.
Respect for international law is becoming increasingly selective.
Conflict, geopolitical rivalry and mistrust are becoming defining features of our time.
Uncertainty, unfortunately, has become the new normal.
I remember the sense of optimism that accompanied the transition from the Millennium Development Goals to the Sustainable Development Goals in 2015.
There was genuine hope that we were beginning a new chapter-one in which no person, no community or no country would be left behind.
Eleven years later, we must have the courage to admit that the world is not where we expected it to be.
Progress towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals by 2030 stands at 36%.
Conflicts between and within States are increasing.
Humanitarian needs are rising while the resources available to meet them are rapidly declining.
Nationalism, intolerance and political polarisation are weakening the spirit of international cooperation.
At the same time, the climate crisis continues to destroy lives, livelihoods and public infrastructure, particularly across the developing world.

According to the United Nations, over 40% of the global population are vulnerable to the destructive effects of Climate change and governments in developing countries spend over 10% of their GDP to respond to this.
These painful fiscal trade-offs come at the expense of investment in education and health which should never be the case.

For millions of vulnerable people, global development can sometimes appear to be moving from one framework to another, from one set of promises to the next, without sufficient transformation in their daily lives.
New declarations and targets have value, but they cannot become a substitute for effective implementation.
This is why this year’s theme is both timely and necessary.
Trust in the UN will not be restored through declarations alone.
It will be restored when our institutions act consistently, uphold international law and produce results that people can see and experience.
The United Nations Charter is founded on sovereign equality, territorial integrity, peaceful coexistence, human rights and the dignity of every person.
The most important word in this year’s theme is “ALL.” Not some people.
Not a select group of nations.
Not only those with the greatest economic or military might.
The promise of the Charter belongs equally to every human being and every Member State.

Yet, the United Nations has increasingly become associated with political gridlock in the Security Council, prolonged negotiations without tangible outcomes and a weakening capacity to mobilise collective action in response to threats to international peace and security.

This should concern all of us, not because the United Nations is not important, but precisely because it is indispensable and appears absent from the global solutions for peace and stability in this dangerous and unpredictable time.
The Security Council must become more representative, transparent and effective.
Africa remains unrepresented in the permanent category and not represented enough in the non-permanent category.
This historical injustice against 54 sovereign states cannot be postponed indefinitely.
Somalia supports the Common African Position and meaningful African representation in both categories of the Council.
Given that many of the discussions directly concern African States, they have the right to full representation on equal par with all other Permanent Security Council members.
Reform is not an attack on the United Nations.
Reform is necessary to protect its legitimacy, renew confidence in its institutions and ensure that it remains capable of responding to the realities of our time.
Somalia currently proudly serves as a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council and as a member of the African Union Peace and Security Council.
We carry these responsibilities with great seriousness, humility and determination.

In both institutions, Somalia works to uphold the principles of the United Nations Charter and the Constitutive Act of the African Union, strengthen cooperation between the United Nations and the African Union, prevent conflict and support peaceful, African-led solutions with global benefits.

Respect for national sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity is not an abstract principle for Somalia: It is a foundation for peace and stability in our country, our region and the wider international community.
Therefore, Somalia firmly rejects unilateral actions that undermine its sovereignty, unity and internationally recognised borders.
Disagreements between nations must be resolved through dialogue and in accordance with international law and not through actions that create new tensions or threaten regional stability.
Somalia stands firmly with the Palestinian people and their legitimate right to self-determination and statehood.
We reaffirm our support for a just and lasting peace based on the two-State solution, with an independent and viable Palestinian State along the 1967 borders.
A just resolution of the Palestinian question remains essential to lasting peace and stability in the Middle East and beyond.
UN Political reform must be accompanied by institutional administrative and operational renewal.
For nearly two decades, we have discussed the need to make United Nations operations more agile, coordinated, cost-effective and capable of delivering measurable results.
Some progress has been made, and we recognise the dedication of the many United Nations personnel working under difficult conditions around the world.
However, we must also be honest: the results have not yet matched our collective expectations.

In countries like mine, where the United Nations has maintained a substantial presence for more than three decades, operations can become more effective by aligning more closely with our national priorities and using credible national systems.
The majority of UN assistance continues to be delivered through parallel structures, fragmented projects and off-budget arrangements in Somalia.
This makes it difficult for governments to plan, coordinate resources, measure results and build the institutions required for long-term stability.
Let us be clear: Somalia is not calling for the United Nations to withdraw.
We are simply calling for a more accountable, strategic and result oriented partnership where Somali institutions are in the lead when it comes to implementation.
Indeed, Somalia wants a partnership in which international assistance reinforces rather than replaces national leadership.
This partnership is one in which national institutions are strengthened rather than bypassed and both governments and international organisations are mutually accountable for results.
The base argument of past UN agencies development thinking that countries like Somalia lack capacity must be condemned permanently to the dustbin of history.
We now have capable people, institutions and policies that are proudly guiding our national transformation.
We must also ask ourselves why we continue to mobilise vital resources to respond to crises while investing far less in preventing them.

The UN office for Disaster Risk Reduction estimates that every $1 invested in proactive measures, resilient infrastructure, or early anticipatory action saves between $3 and $15 in future damages and response costs.

Therefore, we cannot remain trapped in a cycle of financing the consequences of conflict while neglecting peacebuilding or responding to humanitarian emergencies while under-investing in resilience and anticipatory action.
El Niño is strengthening and is likely to bring another period of significant climate stress across the world with disproportionate impact on nations like Somalia.
We must learn from what happened before and be better prepared and not simply respond after the destruction it leaves in its wake as a community of nations.
Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen, Somalia is successfully leading on its own national development.
Our government is implementing the National Transformation Plan, strengthening public financial management, expanding domestic revenue, and investing in the capabilities of our national institutions.
For over five decades, our people have dreamed of choosing their leaders through their votes.
The last such election was held in 1969.
Today, we are determined to change that history.
Through constitutional reform, we are laying the foundation for universal suffrage, accountable institutions, and a multi-party-political system that allows every Somali citizen to have a voice.
We engaged all Somali political leaders, Federal Member states, civil society, women, youth, and the diaspora to take part constructively in our hopeful political transition.
Our aim is to become an effective democracy where differences are resolved through dialogue, law, and elections, not violence.
We invite the United Nations and our international partners to support this transition by helping to strengthen democratic institutions but always respecting our ownership of Somali democracy.
This is a new progressive chapter where political power is determined by citizens guided by constitutional law and safeguarded by the rule of law.
That is how we are building a durable Somali state.
Ours is a democracy where every citizen has a voice, where every vote has value, and where every government is accountable.
That is our commitment to our people and to the world.
Somalia also continues to confront international terrorism with determination and with the support of our international partners.
