We are strengthening our national security institutions, improving force generation, developing intelligence capabilities and expanding security cooperation with our neighbours and the rest of the world.
But the fight against terrorism in Somalia must not be understood as Somalia’s responsibility alone.
We stand on the front line of a struggle that directly affects regional and international security.
We therefore call for predictable and sustainable support for Somalia’s security transition, including adequate financing for the African Union Mission in Somalia.
The transition towards full Somali security responsibility must be properly resourced, phased and firmly anchored in capable Somali institutions.
Following debt relief, Somalia’s economy continues to grow on the foundation of strong reforms.
Our real GDP growth this year is 3.1% despite all the global shocks we are experiencing.
We also continue to strengthen public financial management, increase domestic revenue, enhance budget transparency and deepen our financial sector.
We are actively working to improve the investment environment to create opportunities for all our people.
We also continue to strategically increase investment in education, health and human capital despite the pressures created by geopolitical tensions, recurrent climate shocks and rising global prices.
A serious example of regional tensions negatively impacting Somalia’s development is the issue of the Strait of Hormuz.
For Somalia, disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz have serious economic and humanitarian consequences.

As an import-dependent country reliant on the Middle East for much of our food, fuel and trade, Somalia is already facing rising prices, inflation and increased transport and insurance costs while drought linked to climate change is affecting over 6 million people.
The disruption has also contributed to an estimated 40% decline in our customs-based domestic revenue, a critical source of financing for Somalia's economic reforms, growth, and poverty reduction.

Ensuring free and fair navigation through the Strait is therefore essential to protecting vulnerable economies like Somalia and sustaining stability, advancing development, and delivering basic services.
In Somalia, we have created institutions capable of translating international commitments into national results.

These include the National Climate Fund through which Somalia is mobilising and coordinating urgently needed climate finance, the Independent National Human Rights Commission, established to strengthen the protection and promotion of human rights and the Somali Disaster Management Agency which is on the frontline of responding to humanitarian crises.

Somalia’s membership of the East African Community, our leadership in the Horn of Africa Initiative, our ratification of the Agreement Establishing the African Continental Free Trade Area and our continuing efforts towards accession to the World Trade Organization demonstrate Somalia’s commitment to regional integration and a rules-based international order.
Therefore, the promise of sustainable development cannot be fulfilled without reform of the international financial architecture.

In the same way that the Security Council must reflect today’s political realities, international financial institutions must effectively respond to today’s economic and environmental realities with relevant, affordable and accessible financial products which can be disbursed in a timely manner.
In conclusion, Somalia is proudly playing an active role in global stability both at home and within the key existing multilateral structures of global governance.
We are also rebuilding our economy and unwaveringly committing to democracy and people centred, people led and people owned development.
As we march forward with purpose and determination, we invite Africa and the rest of the world to remain our steadfast companions on this journey.
On the UN, indeed the UN remains vital to global governance and multilateralism.
Managing transformation requires courage and cooperation.
Delivering for all requires fair representation, accessible resources and measurable results especially for developing countries.
I agree that we need to restore trust in the United Nations, but I am less certain about the extent to which we can manage a transformation that has, in many respects, already taken place.
The international system as we knew it has collapsed.

Today, we are witnessing emergence of a new order, increasingly structured around two principal centers of power, alongside a growing number of strong regional actors with considerable political, economic, military technological capabilities, seeking to shape their own environments and influence broader global developments on their own terms.
We are therefore entering a period marked by a more complex less predictable distribution of power, in which the risk of potential conflict is greater than it has been for decades.
This is no longer confined to conventional armed conflicts between states.

Confrontations are increasingly taking the form of economic pressure, technological restrictions, competition for resources and markets, cyberattacks, disinformation attempts to influence other societies.
Cultural and identity-based divisions are also becoming more pronounced, increasingly exploited for political purposes further deepening mistrust among peoples.

The boundary between peace and conflict is becoming ever less distinct, while consequences of confrontation among global and regional powers increasingly affect even those countries that are not directly involved.
For small and medium-sized countries, just like the Republic of Serbia, such an environment represents an enormous challenge.
The space for independent decision-making is narrowing, while pressure on states to choose sides is steadily increasing.
At the same time, disagreements among the most powerful actors are increasingly paralyzing the very institutions should be protecting all countries equally.
The traditional system of international justice seriously undermined whenever interests prevail over law and the same rules do not apply to everyone.
The greatest problem of today is not the lack of rules or political principles, but the fact that they were not respected in the past or now.

You will notice, dear friends, that today, with the exception of a few countries, everyone speaks of and invokes the UN Charter, the spirit of the Charter, and the principles on which the world order that was in force until recently was based on.

It is as though they want to tell us, “Never mind, it doesn’t count” — that the fact that in the past we tore down and violated that Charter, by which we opened a Pandora’s box which is impossible to be closed, and today we would like, without consequences, to return to the future.
They would like revitalize observance of the very same principles that powerful and great countries trampled so brutally.

How many times over the past two days, from this rostrum, have you heard calls and appeals for observance of the principles of international public law, particularly when it comes to the conflict in Ukraine, while the majority of those same countries shamelessly and recklessly remain silent about the fact that they themselves participated in trampling the Charter and destroying the foundations of the international public- law system — and today they would, at any cost, like to return to those principles now that they see that more powerful and stronger ones have resorted to the very same violations they themselves carried out when they were the most powerful and the strongest.

Here I am referring to all the countries that recognized the unilaterally declared independence of the so-called Kosovo and, without any basis whatsoever in international legal documents, attempted to seize 14 % of the territory of the Republic of Serbia.
To many of you, this may sound like a distant past, but the wounds inflicted on international public law are becoming ever deeper and more severe.
To be completely precise, the order based on respect for the UN Charter and the law founded upon it no longer exists.
It was destroyed by those who tore apart the territories of other countries for the sake of their own political and economic interests.
They did so unscrupulously, recklessly, and shamelessly.

Do you know, esteemed friends, what was, in fact, the reason — the sole official and formal reason — for the attack on the territory of the Republic of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, carried out by 19 NATO countries?
They told us they had attacked a sovereign, free, and independent country in order to prevent a potential humanitarian disaster.
The humanitarian disaster did not occur, and I have still not managed to hear or see where a similar example has occurred anywhere in the world.

The attack against that small, yet free and freedom- loving country, Serbia, of which I am the proud president, was carried out with the intention of finally destroying the UN order established after the World War II, and of formally and informally confirming the dominance of at that time unison Western world, of America and Europe.
Do you know which countries took part in decision-making in the UN Security Council to bomb an independent and sovereign country that had attacked no other country?
Not a single soldier, not a single police officer from Serbia had set foot on the territory of any other country, and yet the decision was made.

I am certain that most of you, dear friends, who are among those best informed about world politics, no longer remember much of this either — and especially not the fact of who in the UN Security Council voted for that decision, or perhaps in the General Assembly.
Do not even try, because it is impossible for you to remember. Why?
Because such a decision was never made in the first place, and to make things even worse, no one ever even attempted to make such a decision.
They were so arrogant and so powerful that they trampled everything in their path.
From the Clinton administration to the administrations of numerous European countries.

That is precisely why Serbia supports actions of the Administration of President Donald Trump and sees in his work an opportunity for establishing a more just order in the world and more responsible attitude towards Serbia as a close American ally from both World Wars.
And what they did not know or understand at the time was this: they trampled Serbia, but they did not defeat it.
Serbia rose like a phoenix from the ashes.
And today, through its example, it shows everyone in the world how the international public order is preserved and how international public law is protected.
Nevertheless, consequences of that brutal attack against Serbia are enormous and particularly visible here the UN General Assembly.
Admittedly, they are even more visible on the numerous battlefields around the world. Why?
Well, because the principles, of any kind, no longer exist.
Those who once trampled them have no moral right to speak about them.

And to make the situation even worse, and the hypocrisy even more visible, it is precisely those very people and those very countries who have assumed the position of supreme teachers of moral and every kind of protection of the values of the modern world.

The most difficult thing for us in Serbia is when we see in our surroundings the resurgence of Nazism elevated the position of social prominence, especially in the Republic of Croatia, which is proud of its Nazi past and of the use of Nazi slogans and symbols today.

The Serbian people, as people who suffered the most from Nazi hands, cannot accept the revival of the most terrible ghosts from the past responsible for the death of hundreds of thousands of Serbs, Jews, and Roma in monstrous concentration camps like Jasenovac.
That is precisely why moral lectures coming from such sources are completely unacceptable to the Serbian people and Serbia.

In addition, for four and a half years now, I have been listening to lectures how many in the West remain the last beacon of democracy in the world, the protectors not of Ukraine’s, but of the rules and principles of international law.

And when they raise their voices, thinking that they are being highly moral and that their positions are the only right ones, we simply smile and ask ourselves: “And how did you treat Kosovo and Metohija and the territorial integrity of Serbia which is guaranteed by the UN Charter and the Resolution of the UN Security Council 1244?”
To that, either there is no answer, or they supposedly give us some well-intentioned advice and tell us not to look to the past, but to the future.
When we ask them, “Do you also say to Ukraine that the territories they are fighting for are not important?”, we end the pointless conversation and move on to another subject.
And I want to warn all of you.
All of you here who belong to the Global South.
Pay the utmost attention while signing all the agreements with great powers.
That is how we signed the famous Brussels Agreement in 2013, wishing to resolve problems between Serbs and Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija by compromise.

All obligations that were to be met by Serbia have been met, and the only one that the was to be bet by Albanians, the one about the establishment of Community of Serb Municipalities, has not been met to this day.
It is interesting that the Agreement was accepted not only in the presence of the EU but it was also confirmed with the signature of the EU, but it meant nothing.
As President of Serbia, for 10 years I have been facing all possible tricks and pressures give up on full implementation of what was signed.
It is a lesson to us Serbs, but also to all others in the world who want to protect their country.
In spite of everything, Serbia will defend its country, its territorial integrity, the UN Charter and the UN Security Council Resolution 1244.
I wish to thank, individually, every of 107 states that has not recognized the unilaterally declared independence of the so-called Kosovo.
We know that many of those states have been subjected to pressure, and we know that maintaining a principled position sometimes far more difficult than it appears from the outside.
Thank you for being consistent in not recognizing the independence of a part of Serbia’s territory.
Serbia is on its European path and it will have to do many more things in order to become a full-fledged member of the EU.

Although full- fledged membership to the European Union remains a strategic priority, we cannot ignore prolonged enlargement fatigue, both among certain EU Member States and among the candidate countries themselves.
Serbia’s European path is a clear illustration of the length and complexity of this process.
We obtained candidate status in 2012 and opened accession negotiations in 2014 – more than twelve years ago.
The citizens of Serbia therefore rightly expect a clearer perspective and more tangible results from a process in which our country has participated for more than a decade.

At a time when the next enlargement of the European Union does not appear likely in the near future, we have sought to remain constructive and to propose practical ways of overcoming the current impasse.

We have therefore proposed that the Western Balkans be gradually integrated into the EU Single Market and granted access to the Schengen Area even before attaining full membership in the European Union.
This would neither serve as a substitute for membership nor diminish our ambitions.

Rather, it would provide a concrete and pragmatic way forward, enable the citizens and economies of the region to experience tangible benefits of European integration, and help overcome deadlock in which the enlargement process has remained for far too long.

However, a stable and integrated Europe, of which Serbia is a part, and our European path do not mean renouncing the traditional friendships thanks to which Belgrade is one of the few European capitals from which one can fly directly to the United States of America, the People’s Republic of China and the Russian Federation.

I owe special gratitude for the support during COVID Pandemics as well as paramount investment in Serbia to the President of the People’s Republic of China Xi Jinping, hoping that his talks with the President Trump will be productive and that they will contribute to the stabilization of the developments in the world.

At the same time, we nurture ties with traditional friends and partners in Africa, Asia and Latin America, with whom we recently marked in Belgrade the sixty-fifth anniversary of the First Conference of Non-Aligned Countries, held in our capital in 1961.
Our openness reflects our development strategy, our history our understanding of the world.
Serbia believes that states can have a clear course and interests of their own without closing the door to those with whom they do not agree on everything.
After all, a world in which we speak only to those who think as we do would have little need for diplomacy.
Freedom and independence in making decisions are the highest values for Serbia.

We must anticipate the consequences of a world in which force is once again being presented ever more openly as the most reliable instrument of policy; in which military budgets are growing, conflicts are multiplying, arms-control mechanisms are weakening, and channels of communication are disappearing precisely when they are needed most.
We must therefore ask the essential question: Where is the United Nations in such a world?
The Security Council is often blocked precisely in the crises in which it should be most active.
Other parts of the UN system face financial pressures, overlapping mandates, bureaucratization and the justified demand of Member States to see more concrete results.
These are real problems, and there is no benefit in glossing over them.
Yet it by no means follows that we need the United Nations less.
We may need it more than ever; it simply must be more effective, more focused and more prepared to address the issues for which it was created.

Over the past eight decades, states have not come to this building because they shared the same interests, but because they understood that the cost of settling disagreements by force of arms was too high.
That is why multilateralism came into being and why we are here today.
Serbia supports the United Nations and reform of the UN system so that the Organization may become more effective and better adapted today’s realities.

We advocate a more representative UN Security Council through greater representation of developing countries, particularly those from the African continent, as well as more inclusive regional representation and the addition of another seat the Eastern European Group.
However, without a genuine return to the principles on which we have already agreed, I do not expect progress in terms of this Organization’s concrete results.
Peace is not the only test of our ability to manage change.
We are in the midst of a technological transformation whose full reach we are only beginning to understand.
Artificial intelligence already changing economy, education, medicine, security, the labour market and the way states function.
It can bring enormous benefits humanity.
It can also deepen existing inequalities, enable new forms of manipulation and create security risks that we could not even have imagined only a few years ago.

During our leadership cycle the Global Partnership on Artificial Intelligence – GPAI, which Serbia chaired in 2025, one of our priorities was to ensure that technological progress remained connected with security, human rights, the rule of law, accountability and bridging the digital divide.
The Belgrade Ministerial Declaration received support of 44 Member States and the European Union and affirmed the need for safe, sustainable and human- centered artificial intelligence.
The more powerful technology becomes, the more responsible those who manage it must be.

We may have cutting-edge algorithms, quantum computers, unmanned systems and artificial intelligence capable of processing in a matter of seconds what once took us years, but if, at the same time, we allow the fundamental rules of the international order to be applied selectively, technological progress will not make the world safer.
It will merely make us more technologically advanced in a world that is becoming politically less predictable.
If we wish to manage the coming transformation responsibly, we must first reinforce the foundations on which the international order rests.

Those foundations are simple: sovereign equality of states, respect for territorial integrity, the prohibition of the use of force except the cases expressly provided the UN Charter, and the obligation not change the rules from one case to another.

Esteemed colleagues, To those of you who know Serbia and our region, as well as those less familiar with this part of the world, I wish to express my gratitude to all who have honored Serbia by confirming their participation in the specialized exhibition EXPO 2027, to be held next year in Belgrade under the theme “Play for Humanity: Sport and Music for All”.

Cultures, science, sport, technology, business and young people from all parts of the world will come together in Belgrade, and I look forward to our hosting a large number of the states represented in this Hall today.
At the outset, I spoke about trust and responsibility, and that is where I wish to conclude.
We will not restore trust through grand declarations if we then continue to act as before.
Each of us must begin with our own decisions.

Serbia endeavors to do so by preserving peace in its neighborhood, participating in peacekeeping missions far from its borders, assisting others when they are in danger, speaking even with those with whom it disagrees, and fulfilling the commitments it undertakes.
What will restore trust in international law and in the United Nations is more actions such as those.
The theme of this Session, “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All,” speaks directly to the experience and aspirations of South Sudan.
As the world’s youngest nation and the 193rd Member of the United Nations, South Sudan understands both the promise and the responsibility of multilateralism.

South Sudan also understands that trust is fundamental to peace: trust among citizens; trust between citizens and their institutions; trust among nations; and trust between Member States and the international institutions created to serve them.
South Sudan remains committed to the United Nations and to the purposes and principles of its Charter.

We recognize and appreciate the contribution the United Nations has made to South Sudan, from humanitarian assistance and the protection of civilians to peacebuilding, development and institutional support.
However, restoring trust also requires honest reflection.
Our experience has shown that international institutions can sometimes be slow to adjust to changing circumstances on the ground.
Approaches designed to respond to conflict must be capable of evolving as nations move toward peace, recovery, institution-building and national ownership.

For South Sudan, therefore, restoring trust must mean strengthening partnership between the United Nations and Member States, respecting national ownership, recognizing progress while acknowledging remaining challenges, and ensuring that international engagement ultimately strengthens the capacity of nations to assume responsibility for their own future.
To understand where South Sudan seeks to go, one must understand where South Sudan has come from.
The history of South Sudan did not begin with independence on 9 July 2011.
It was shaped by more than half a century of struggle, sacrifice, displacement and an unwavering desire for freedom and self-determination.
Dr. John Garang de Mabior summarized the aspirations of that struggle when he spoke of “freedom, liberty, equality, justice, human rights and democracy.”
Those aspirations did not end with independence.
They remain part of the ongoing work of nation-building.
The Comprehensive Peace Agreement of 2005 provided the political framework that transformed decades of armed struggle into a peaceful exercise of self-determination.

South Sudan therefore continues to recognize the indispensable contribution of IGAD and our African brothers and sisters, as well as the support of the Troika, the United States, the United Kingdom and Norway and the wider international community.
South Sudan also remembers the extraordinary contribution of churches and faith leaders.
During some of the darkest years of conflict, the churches remained with the people.
They educated children, assisted displaced communities, mediated disputes and kept alive the belief that reconciliation was possible.
That tradition continued with the historic Ecumenical Pilgrimage of Peace to South Sudan by His Holiness Pope Francis, the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Moderator of the Church of Scotland.
Their message reinforced something South Sudan has learned through painful experience: Peace requires political agreements, but lasting peace also requires reconciliation, forgiveness and courage.
His Excellency President Salva Kiir Mayardit belongs to the generation that carried the struggle for liberation.

Following the passing of Dr. John Garang, President Kiir assumed responsibility for safeguarding the Comprehensive Peace Agreement and leading the people of South Sudan toward the referendum on self-determination.
In January 2011, the people of South Sudan spoke overwhelmingly through the ballot.
And on 9 July 2011, President Salva Kiir Mayardit stood before the people as the flag of the Republic of South Sudan was raised for the first time.
Fifteen years later, South Sudan has travelled a difficult road.
South Sudan experienced internal conflict shortly after independence.
Implementation of the Revitalized Peace Agreement has taken longer than originally anticipated.
Economic and humanitarian challenges remain significant.
The Government does not deny these realities, but neither should these challenges be allowed to erase the progress made or define permanently the identity of South Sudan.
Throughout the transition, President Kiir has repeatedly made one commitment clear: he will not take South Sudan back to war.
This commitment has guided his approach to the peace process and remains fundamental to his vision for the next chapter of South Sudan.
The mission before President Kiir today is therefore different from the mission of the liberation years.
The liberation struggle sought to give the people of South Sudan the right to determine their destiny.

The responsibility today is to consolidate peace, strengthen institutions and create the conditions through which the people of South Sudan can once again determine their political future through democratic means.
When the people of South Sudan voted for independence, they were voting for more than the creation of a new State.
They were voting for a dream:
• They dreamed of peace after generations of war;
• They dreamed of schools for their children;
• A government whose authority ultimately derives from the will of its people.
The difficulties of the last fifteen years have not extinguished those dreams.
They remain alive among the people of South Sudan.
And it is precisely for this reason that His Excellency President Salva Kiir Mayardit remains committed to paving the way towards general elections scheduled for December 2026.
These elections are intended to mark the conclusion of the transitional period and provide the people of South Sudan the opportunity to democratically choose their leaders.
We recognize that important work still in progress.
Civic and voter education must reach communities.
Women and young people must participate meaningfully.
Refugees and internally displaced persons must not be left out.
And an environment must be created in which political competition can occur peacefully.
The Government remains committed to working towards these objectives.
For too long, South Sudan has often been seen internationally through the lens of conflict, humanitarian need and political crisis.

President Kiir’s vision is to create the conditions in which the world can once again see the people of South Sudan for who they truly are: a resilient people who struggled for freedom, voted peacefully for independence, and continue to aspire for peace, dignity, democracy and prosperity.
The people of South Sudan must increasingly speak for themselves.
And they must speak through the ballot.
• from liberation struggle to the Comprehensive Peace Agreement - to the Referendum - to independence;
• from conflict to peace; and now
The message of President Kiir remains clear: South Sudan must not return to war.
Political disagreement must be addressed through dialogue.
Political competition must never again become armed confrontation.
The ballot must replace the bullet.
South Sudan recognizes that conducting peaceful elections requires security and strong institutions.
The Government bears the primary responsibility for protecting its citizens, maintaining public order and safeguarding the electoral process.
South Sudan therefore continues to call for constructive engagement with the Security Council concerning restrictive measures, including the arms embargo.
South Sudan’s objective is not militarization.
The objective is to develop professional, unified, disciplined and accountable security sectors operating under civilian authority and the rule of law.
South Sudan believes that accountability and national capacity should reinforce one another.
We therefore call for the lifting of all restrictive measures.
Sanctions must remain instruments for achieving clearly defined objectives; they should not become permanent substitutes for political engagement and institution-building.
South Sudan remains grateful for the contribution of the United Nations Mission in South Sudan.
We recognize the men and women who have served under the United Nations flag, particularly those who have lost their lives in the service of peace.
As South Sudan advances its transition, however, international engagement must also evolve.
President Kiir’s vision is not for South Sudan to remain indefinitely dependent upon international peacekeeping.
The objective must be a South Sudan capable of sustaining its own peace.
South Sudan therefore calls for greater emphasis on peacebuilding, institutional development and continuous capacity building.
We are keen on establishing partnership:
• Invest in South Sudan’s police and judiciary;
• Invest in women and young people; and
• Invest in the institutions that will sustain peace long after peacekeepers have departed.
The ultimate measure of successful peacekeeping should be the establishment of conditions under which peacekeeping is no longer required.
South Sudan therefore seeks a responsible transition from managing crises towards building lasting national capacity.
Peace cannot be sustained without development.
At independence, South Sudan inherited extremely limited infrastructure and institutional capacity.
Nation-building, state-building and service delivery have therefore had to proceed simultaneously.
His Excellency President Salva Kiir Mayardit has placed particular emphasis on agriculture, infrastructure, education, healthcare and economic diversification.
South Sudan possesses millions of hectares of arable land, significant water resources, livestock, fisheries, natural resources and one of the youngest populations in the world.
South Sudan therefore seeks to transition progressively from humanitarian dependency to self-reliance and to towards sustainable development and investment.
For a farmer, a road to market is development.
For a child, a functioning school is development.
For a mother, access to healthcare is development.
For a young person, employment is development.
And for South Sudan, development is one of the strongest foundations for lasting peace.
We therefore invite international partners and responsible investors to look beyond South Sudan’s current challenges and recognize its potential.
Do not ask only what South Sudan needs.
Ask what South Sudan can offer.
South Sudan continues to face severe consequences from climate shocks despite contributing minimally to global emissions.
Recurrent floods, drought, displacement and food insecurity are affecting millions of South Sudanese.
South Sudan therefore reiterates its call for predictable and accessible climate financing, investment in adaptation, resilient infrastructure, renewable energy, agriculture and technology transfer.
Climate justice must be reflected not only in commitments, but in implementation.
Women and young people remain central to President Kiir’s vision for South Sudan.
The Revitalized Peace Agreement provided for 35 per cent representation of women in public institutions.
South Sudan continuous on working to translate that commitment into meaningful participation at all levels.
South Sudan also has an overwhelmingly young population.
These young people should not inherit the conflicts of previous generations.
They should inherit the opportunities technology, entrepreneurship, agriculture and sports, that is the future they deserve.
But the South Sudanese diaspora should not be viewed only through the history of displacement.
It is also an extraordinary national resource.
Our national basketball team, the Bright Stars, demonstrated this before the world.
South Sudanese whose journeys had taken them across different countries and continents came together under one flag.
Under the leadership of Luol Deng and the South Sudan Basketball Federation, South Sudan qualified for the FIBA Basketball World Cup and subsequently for the Olympic Games.
They showed the world another image of South Sudan: not conflict; not displacement; but talent, discipline, unity and excellence.
This experience offers a model for national development.
South Sudanese doctors abroad can contribute to healthcare.
Entrepreneurs can invest and create employment.
Technology professionals can connect South Sudan to the digital economy.
And successful South Sudanese around the world can mentor another generation.

To the international community, we need to create strong partnership that would enable our South Sudanese Diaspora to transfer their skills and professional experience; in order to contribute to the ongoing development in the Republic of South Sudan.
To the South Sudanese Diaspora, our message is simple: South Sudan needs you. Bring your knowledge. Bring your experience. Bring your investment. Bring your networks.
Where physical return is not possible, allow your skills and experience to contribute to South Sudan.
The same spirit that brought South Sudanese athletes from around the world together under one flag can help bring South Sudanese expertise together for one national purpose.
South Sudan’s greatest resource is ultimately its people, both at home and abroad.
South Sudan stands in solidarity with the people of Sudan.
South Sudan and Sudan share history, families, economic interests and one of the longest borders in the region.
South Sudan therefore reiterates and continues to support all efforts leading to the consolidation of peace in Sudan.
South Sudan knows from experience that military confrontation ultimately requires a political solution.
Even the longest conflict must eventually reach a negotiated settlement.
South Sudan therefore supports regional and international efforts aimed at achieving peace in Sudan.
Outstanding matters arising from the Comprehensive Peace Agreement, including border issues and the final status of Abyei, also require continued peaceful engagement between South Sudan and Sudan.
Restoring trust also requires reform of the institutions of global governance.
The composition of the Security Council does not adequately reflect realities of today; Africa with fifty-four Member States remains without permanent representation on the Council.
South Sudan therefore reaffirms its support for the Common African Position reflected in the Ezulwini Consensus and Sirte Declaration.
Africa must be appropriately represented in both the permanent and non-permanent categories.
Similarly, developing countries must have a stronger voice in international financial institutions and in decisions concerning development financing, debt, climate and technology.
Fifteen years after independence, South Sudan remains a young nation undertaking the difficult work of building a State while consolidating peace and delivering development.
The journey has not been easy.
But South Sudanese have never been a people defined by easy journeys.
The generation of liberation fought for freedom.
The generation of the Comprehensive Peace Agreement secured the pathway to self-determination.
The people of South Sudan chose independence through the ballot.
And His Excellency President Salva Kiir Mayardit carried the responsibility of leading South Sudan through the Referendum and into statehood.

Today, President Kiir’s vision is directed toward another historic responsibility: to preserve peace, strengthen national institutions and pave the way toward elections through which the people of South Sudan can determine the next chapter of their nation.
This is ultimately about completing the promise of independence.
A South Sudan at peace with itself.
A South Sudan governed through strong institutions.
A South Sudan where political competition does not lead to war.
A South Sudan where women participate fully.
Where the diaspora contributes to national development.
And where children grow up knowing South Sudan not through memories of war, but through the possibilities of peace.
Dr. John Garang once challenged the people of South Sudan to “unite and dream together.”
That dream did not end with independence. It continues.

And today, the responsibility of President Salva Kiir Mayardit, his Government, the political leadership and indeed every South Sudanese is to transform that dream into a functioning, peaceful and prosperous Republic.

To our international partners who stood with South Sudan during the struggle for peace, during the Comprehensive Peace Agreement, during the Referendum and at independence, we say: Stand with South Sudan again.
But let this next chapter be a partnership that strengthens national ownership.
A partnership that recognizes progress while helping address remaining challenges.
And a partnership that enables South Sudan progressively to stand on its own.
For South Sudan, restoring trust means delivering on the promise of peace.
Managing transformation means moving from conflict to institutions, from dependency to national capacity, and from transition toward democratic governance.
And a United Nations that delivers for all must ultimately help nations develop the capacity to deliver for their own people.
South Sudan remains committed to the United Nations.
South Sudan remains committed to Africa.
South Sudan remains committed to peace.

And under the leadership of His Excellency President Salva Kiir Mayardit, South Sudan remains committed to the long journey of transforming the sacrifices of liberation into the peace, dignity, development and democratic future for which the people of South Sudan have waited for generations.
That is the promise of independence.
That is the responsibility of this generation.
And that is the future South Sudan seeks to build.
May the Lord Almighty bless the people of South Sudan.
And may the Lord Almighty bless all nations represented in this Assembly.

We are living in a context marked by conflicts, geopolitical rivalries, economic uncertainties, climate change, inequalities, forced displacement, transnational crime and rapid technological transformations....
No State can face challenges of this magnitude alone.

For Sao Tome and Principe, this reality reinforces the importance of an international order founded on the Charter of the United Nations, on international law and on the sovereign equality of States, with principles applied in a universal and consistent manner.
As a small island nation, we assert ourselves as a consolidated democracy and a State based on the rule of law, grounded in peace, stability and coexistence among citizens.
It is on the basis of this experience that we reaffirm our confidence in dialogue, diplomacy, cooperation and the peaceful settlement of disputes.
For small island developing States, geographical, economic, financial and social vulnerabilities are aggravated by the effects of climate change...
In Sao Tome and Principe, these impacts are already affecting coastal areas, infrastructure, marine resources and livelihoods, despite our negligible contribution to global emissions.
This reality reflects a profound climate injustice.

Sao Tome and Principe therefore reaffirms its commitments under the Paris Agreement, its Nationally Determined Contribution and the National Adaptation Plan, underscoring that their implementation requires adequate, predictable and accessible resources.
We also maintain that the vulnerability of small island States should be assessed beyond per capita income, taking into account their specific characteristics and structural constraints.
In this context, we call for the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index to be translated into concrete criteria for access to concessional financing.
We also advocate the full operationalization of the Loss and Damage Fund and simpler and more effective access to the Green Climate Fund......
The limited institutional capacity of vulnerable countries cannot become an obstacle to access to the instruments created to support them.

In the case of Sao Tome and Principe, this issue is of particular relevance following graduation to the category of middle-income countries, which constituted an important milestone and recognition of the progress achieved in the human development index....
However, it requires appropriate transition measures capable of consolidating these gains and protecting the country from external shocks.
Consequently, it is within this effort at consolidation that the energy transition is situated, which is, for us, an economic, financial, social and environmental necessity.
In an island economy dependent on fuel imports, the cost and reliability of electricity have an impact on all sectors.
The implementation of our energy transition programme and the National Energy Compact should contribute to a cleaner, more accessible, secure and stable system,....
but will require investment and international partnerships.
Excellencies; Food security and strengthening productive capacity are urgent priorities.

We want to reduce dependence on imports, increase domestic production and ensure better access to markets for farmers, so that a greater share of the value generated by quality products such as cocoa and coffee remains in the country.
If the land is essential to our food security, the sea and our biodiversity constitute one of the greatest horizons of our development.
UNESCO's recognition of our territory as a World Biosphere Reserve confirms the exceptional value of our natural heritage and reinforces the responsibility to protect and enhance it.
We want to transform this wealth into opportunities for sustainable development, through fisheries, the blue economy, research and nature tourism that generates employment and income for communities.

At the same time, in the face of the threats of illegal fishing and transnational crime, Sao Tome and Principe will continue to work with States of the region and international partners to strengthen maritime security and promote a sustainable blue economy, preserving our resources for future generations.
The preservation of these resources and the construction of sustainable development ultimately depend on people and on the opportunities afforded to them.
The future of Sao Tome and Principe lies in the ability to generate opportunities for the next generation.
Our priority is to ensure that young people have conditions to study, work, undertake, innovate and carry out their life plans in the country.
In a nation of our size, every talent counts and every young person is an indispensable force for national progress.
Likewise, the Sao Tomean diaspora is also an essential part of our human wealth and a strategic partner of the country.

We will continue to strengthen its ties with Sao Tome and Principe and to create conditions so that its contribution to investment, entrepreneurship, the transfer of knowledge and national life may become ever greater.

Creating opportunities and ensuring truly inclusive development requires strong institutions, capable of ensuring peace, justice, respect for human rights and the participation of all in the life of the country.
There is no sustainable development without these conditions, nor without the full participation of women and men in political, economic and social life.
It is in this context that the year 2026 is of particular importance for São Toméan democracy.

On 19 July, our citizens took part in the presidential elections, which were conducted in a peaceful and transparent manner and led to the re-election of His Excellency Carlos Vila Nova as President of the Republic. ….
On 27 September, the São Toméan people will once again go to the polls for the legislative, municipal and regional elections and massively exercise their right to vote.

These elections are marked by important innovations, notably automatic voter registration and the first application of the Parity Law, representing a significant step in strengthening inclusion and the participation of women.
With 41.4 per cent of actual candidacies, above the legal threshold of 40 per cent, women will be able to assert a growing presence in decision-making spaces.

Sao Tome and Principe reaffirms its commitment to the constitutional order, political pluralism, fundamental freedoms and respect for the sovereign will of citizens, while pursuing reforms aimed at strengthening justice, security, gender equality, human rights and confidence in institutions.
Inclusion and equality must also guide the response to the great transformations of our time.

Faced with the rapid advance of artificial intelligence and the digital transition, Sao Tome and Principe advocates international cooperation that enables developing countries to gain access to the technology, knowledge, infrastructure and financing required.
We advocate responsible technological governance, centred on human dignity, transparency and fundamental rights, so that innovation translates into better opportunities and services for all.
Excellencies, The experience of Sao Tome and Principe as a small democracy also influences the way in which we view representation at the international level.
Africa today occupies a demographic, economic and political place that still does not find adequate correspondence in the institutions where the most far-reaching decisions are taken.
It is in this area that the reform of the Security Council is imperative.
This is not a concession to Africa.
It is a matter of legitimacy, justice and effectiveness.
An institution responsible for international peace and security cannot remain indefinitely based on a distribution of power inherited from another era.

In this effort towards greater historical justice and representation, Sao Tome and Principe therefore welcomes the recent decisions that recognized the historical gravity of the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and promoted a cartographic representation that is more faithful to the dimensions of the continents, correcting distortions that visually reduced Africa.

It is necessary for these recognitions to be translated into an international order in which Africa participates fully in defining the future and does not remain merely in the position of responding to decisions taken elsewhere.
Peace remains the raison d'être of the multilateral system.

Sao Tome and Principe is following with concern the conflicts in Ukraine, the Sudan, the Sahel, the Great Lakes, the Horn of Africa and the Middle East, calling for strengthened diplomacy and the protection of civilians, in accordance with the Charter of the United Nations and international law.
We also advocate respect for international humanitarian law, full access to humanitarian assistance and the release of hostages.
We reaffirm our support for a two-State solution, enabling Israel and Palestine to coexist in peace and security, on the basis of international law and the relevant United Nations resolutions.

We are also following with concern the persistence of the economic, commercial and financial restrictions affecting Cuba, and we call for their lifting, for the benefit of the development and well-being of the Cuban people, and we express our solidarity.

Excellencies, Sao Tome and Principe will remain faithful to the Charter of the United Nations, international law, peace, human rights and multilateralism, asserting itself as a voice of dialogue and moderation and a partner committed to stability in the Gulf of Guinea.
On the eve of the elections in STP, it is important to recognize the path travelled.

In a challenging context, the Government has initiated reforms and made progress in infrastructure, the energy transition, digitalization and the attraction of investment, creating conditions to mobilize the resources indispensable to the most pressing needs of our population, notably in access to health, water, sanitation, justice and security, in protecting the environment as well as in the development of indispensable infrastructure.

The challenge before us is to transform these advances into concrete and lasting results, consolidating the foundations of more inclusive, sustainable and resilient development, it being essential to guarantee continuity and governmental stability.
Our vulnerabilities, as a Small Island Developing State, do not define our horizon.

We therefore reaffirm our determination to transform challenges into opportunities, through strategic partnerships based on shared responsibility and mutual benefit, also reaffirming our capacity to contribute to peace, defend the principles of the Charter of the United Nations and participate, responsibly, in the construction of solutions to the challenges we face collectively.

We call on all Member States so that, together, we may continue to build a more representative, more supportive and more just international order, founded on respect for the sovereignty of States, on international law and on equality of opportunity.
It is in this spirit of peace, dialogue and hope that Sao Tome and Principe will continue to assume its responsibility in the international community.
We also remember with warmth your visit to Suriname, expressing the importance of the United Nations’ engagement with our country and the Caribbean region.

Standing before this Assembly, I am reminded that, while some efforts have been made from this rostrum over the past year, these have not yet matched the scale of the challenges confronting our world.

We will have to increase and strengthen efforts and commitment to the process of transformation and strengthening of the UN in order to restore the trust that our organization will really be capable of delivering peace, inclusion and development in the world.

THE UNITED NATIONS AND MULTILATERALISM Suriname is firmly committed to the upholding of International Law, as we depend on a rules-based international order, without which, like many other vulnerable nations, we simply cannot exist as sovereign countries.

The consistent application of international law and the strengthening of its institutions is also essential to maintain international peace and security, protect human rights and ensure sustainable development for all.

INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY As mentioned before, the international community is experiencing profound uncertainty, including energy and food security crises, leading to intensified displacement of many people globally.
Armed conflicts continue to claim innocent lives, while geopolitical tensions escalate.
Children are living through unimaginable horrors.
The United Nations has not been able to prevent this or end the continuation.

Other developments, for example in the Strait of Hormuz, demonstrate how quickly wars can affect energy markets, suddenly and steeply increasing the cost of energy, adversely impacting economic and social developments in our countries.
Common people suffer when food and energy prices rise, so the quality of life of our people is directly threatened, even by wars in regions far from their home.
Suriname, therefore, calls for a renewed commitment to the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, namely the peaceful resolution of disputes.
Dialogue is paramount for safeguarding a solid and proven UN system.
The people of Cuba, a Caribbean country, are adversely affected by the current situation in their country.
Suriname calls on the parties involved to remain committed to dialogue and negotiation, to end the economic, commercial and financial embargo.
We plea for continuing of negotiations in order to prevent further escalation and to reach a resolution, that will benefit the people of Cuba.
We also call for sustained international support for Haiti to restore security, constitutional order and democratic governance.
Suriname supports solutions that place the Haitian people at the center.
The UN80 process rightly emphasizes mandate rationalization, institutional coherence and efficiency.
Reform must protect and improve the United Nations' capacity to deliver and also make the system easier to navigate.
It should not reduce support where it is most needed.
Equally important, is the overdue reform of the Security Council, hence Suriname reiterates its call for making it more representative, more accountable and more capable of acting.
Africa, the Republic of Suriname supports your demand, for just permanent representation.
Likewise, we underscore the relevance of a dedicated representation for Small Island States and Low-Lying Coastal Developing States.

CARICOM AND REGIONAL LEADERSHIP Regional and international partnerships remain indispensable to achieve our economic and social objectives as Suriname continues to actively engage in various regional bodies and mechanisms including CARICOM, CELAC, ACTO and Brasilia Consensus.
As Suriname prepares to be the Chair of the Caribbean Community (CARICOM) in 2027, we are also committed to further strengthen our partnership globally in different areas of shared interest.
Our regional priorities are practical: food and energy security, climate resilience, improved connectivity, and movement of skilled people, transportation of goods and services.
These are essential to economic integration and to our ability to withstand external shocks.
The pursuit of restorative justice gained new momentum with the adoption of the resolution on Slavery and Transatlantic Trafficking of Enslaved Africans, in this Hall in March of this year.
This development is relevant for Suriname.
And equally important for the countries of the Caribbean region.
The discussion is no longer about whether slavery and colonialism have caused lasting consequences.
We know we are living them.
We increasingly must focus on how to overcome these effects and on the question of what form reparation should take to achieve that.
How will countries that have benefited from slavery and colonialism compensate the affected.
It is therefore that the CARICOM ten-point plan for restorative justice is now of eminent importance.
SURINAME: CLIMATE LEADERSHIP AND CULTURAL HERITAGE Suriname occupies a unique position.
We are carbon- negative and remain the world’s most forested country with over 90 per cent forest coverage.
High Forested and Low Deforestation countries, like Suriname, should not first have to lose forests, before climate finance institutions recognize the value of protecting them.
Conservation costs cannot be borne only by the countries protecting ecosystems whose benefits are shared globally.
I will continue my plea for just and effective climate finance, because our forests are under even more pressure than when I addressed this meeting last year.
I stated that the forest faces competition of rich natural resources like gold, diamonds and other precious minerals.
We are now confronted, however, with a new threat of people who also want to clear parts of our rainforest for large-scale agriculture.
At this very moment my government is introducing legal and institutional measures to better protect our forests and the immediate living environment of the Indigenous Peoples and Tribal Communities.
Their knowledge and participation are important at all stages of development.
Last year at this rostrum I noted that Suriname is diversity.

At a time when diversity is too often manipulated as a source of division, Suriname has chosen the path to recognize the distinct histories of its people while strengthening their unity and their shared responsibility for the future.
Our experience affirms that diversity, when grounded in equality, mutual respect and meaningful participation, is not an adversity; it is a source of national resilience and prosperity.

Last month, the Republic of Suriname observed its first National Heritage Month under the theme, "Hoe wij hier ook samen kwamen, hoe wij samen verder gaan”, meaning “However we came here, united we move forward”.
This initiative was conceived not merely to celebrate our culture, but as a deliberate national undertaking centered on growing inclusion, mutual respect and unity.
This process is also relevant for the global community.

SURINAME: ENERGY TRANSITION AND SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT The development of Suriname’s offshore natural resources including oil and gas, will present significant opportunities to accelerate national development and improve the well- being of our people.
Yet, we are equally conscious that oil and gas cannot and should not become the only foundation of our economy.
We must transform temporary resource wealth into lasting national prosperity using resource revenues strategically to strengthen our economy and make it more resilient, through diversification.
Additionally, we will need to improve our energy security.
Although we are preparing for gas to shore, renewable energy will be part of our national energy mix.
Besides the expected economic and energy transition, we must also prepare for the transformation driven by artificial intelligence.
Only if we can implement AI responsibly, Suriname will be able to benefit from the opportunities of this technology and mitigate its risks.
With only four years left to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals, we may question whether we were too ambitious or if we should have done much more.
Political will, international peace and accelerated implementation are required, supported by financing, technology and partnerships that produce measurable results.
Equally important is to have a mechanism in place for global commitments after 2030.

CLOSING: RECOMMITMENT TO THE CHARTER AND CALL TO ACTION Mr. President, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, Finally, as the United Nations approaches change in its highest leadership, current realities and approved mandates require the next Secretary-General to portray strong commitment to multilateralism, dialogue, and the rule of law.
Many capable candidates, including women leaders who have taken up the challenge, have been put forth and for the first time in history we have a female candidate from the Caribbean.
We are at that time in history where trust in the United Nations must urgently be restored.
We make efforts to protect our forests, use our natural wealth responsibly, strengthen the Caribbean Community and promote dialogue.
We will do what we can and call on more influential members of the United Nations, to help maintain peace.
Only a United Nations, capable of safeguarding international peace and security will deliver for all.
For some, security means protecting borders.
For others, it means food, water, energy, or the future of their children.
Many countries face all of these challenges at once.
That is why a world ruled mainly by power, rather than by rules, would be dangerous for everyone.
For smaller countries such as Slovakia, this is especially clear.
But no country, large or small, is truly safe in a world where international law is ignored and institutions are weakened.
Sadly, we no longer need to imagine such a world.
We can already see parts of it around us.
The idea that every country should have a voice is under pressure.
And when rules are weakened, when cooperation is replaced by confrontation, all of us become more vulnerable.
But we still have a choice.
The international system we have built is not perfect.
At times, it does not deliver as quickly as people need.
But the solution is not to destroy it.
The solution is to make it work better.
Slovakia is firmly anchored in the United Nations, NATO and the European Union.
But we also believe that institutions must produce real results.
Over the past year, Slovakia has hosted several international meetings and offered space for dialogue.
Where we can be useful, we are ready to help bring parties together and support diplomacy within the UN framework.
Because when diplomacy stops, confrontation fills the space.
That is why, when we speak about the United Nations, I believe in evolution rather than revolution.
The world has changed, and the United Nations must change with it.
The Security Council should better reflect today’s realities and give a stronger voice to countries and regions that are still underrepresented.
Countries from the region often understand a crisis best.
Giving them a stronger voice can help us act earlier and prevent escalation.
Slovakia sees its engagement in UN reform as part of its responsibility to this Organization, including through UN80 and the implementation of the Pact for the Future.
Our responsibility to the wider international order is also reflected in our candidacy for the Security Council for 2028 and 2029.
We would be grateful for your trust and support.

If elected, Slovakia will focus on four priorities: International law and the UN Charter; Accountable security institutions; The protection of strategic resources and critical infrastructure; And the security challenges linked to digitalization and artificial intelligence.
I fully share the concern of the United Nations about the inequalities that can be created by unequal access to artificial intelligence.
It is in our common interest that innovation benefits all of humanity, not only the strongest economies or the biggest companies.
If AI is available only to a few, new divisions will appear.
Entire communities may be left behind.
The growing use of AI-powered weapons and autonomous systems also requires urgent attention.
One principle must remain clear: machines should never be allowed to make life-or-death decisions on their own.
Just as the international community developed rules for nuclear, chemical and biological weapons, we also need strong international frameworks for new technologies.
The United Nations can and should play a leading role in this effort.
AI is not only a potential threat on the battlefield.
It is already having a negative impact on society, especially in education.
An entire generation of young people is being affected.
Recent assessments show declining test scores across the vast majority of countries.
This is a concerning trend that deserves open and serious discussion on international platforms such as the United Nations.
At the same time, we should not see AI only as a risk.
It can also be a tool for peace.
It can help us analyze information, identify patterns and overcome language barriers in real time.
It can support better decisions, faster responses and more effective prevention.
With responsible use, proper human oversight and good governance, we can move this technology away from the battlefield and towards diplomacy, mediation and conflict prevention.
Every conflict we prevent saves lives. It protects development.
Once violence begins, every solution becomes harder, more costly and more painful.
There is no need to reinvent the wheel when we reform international institutions.
AI may be revolutionary, but we did not need to reinvent the personal computer in order to build it.
The same is true in global politics.
We should improve what already exists, not start again from zero.
But let's ask ourselves a simple question.
What if we, as world leaders, simply started following the UN Charter again?
Would reform even matter if we finally did our best for global peace?
Too many conflicts are still driven by the belief that political problems can be solved by force, by changing borders, violating sovereignty and ignoring international rules.
We need to reject this logic.
Leadership is not shown by the willingness to escalate.
It requires the courage to de-escalate.
International rules may sound abstract in this hall.
But on the ground, they are very real.
They can mean the difference between life and death.
When these rules are ignored, civilians suffer. Communities are destroyed. Millions are displaced.
Supply chains are disrupted. Prosperity is lost.
And there is an even deeper danger.
If violence becomes normal for the next generation, diplomacy itself will become harder.
What is difficult to solve today may become impossible tomorrow.
That is why our most urgent task must be clear: stop the violence, keep diplomacy alive, and prevent today’s conflicts from becoming tomorrow’s normal.
The war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year, continues to bring destruction close to Slovakia’s border.
Attacks on civilian areas and critical infrastructure remain unacceptable.
A ceasefire is still distant and lasting peace even further away.
We should support every serious diplomatic effort that can help end Russia’s war against Ukraine and build a safe future for our neighbor.
Our commitment to international law and human dignity cannot stop at Europe’s borders.
The same basic principles must guide us in the Middle East.
International humanitarian law must be respected.
Humanitarian aid must reach those who need it, including in Gaza.
There can be no justification for terrorism, antisemitism, anti-Muslim hatred or calls to violence.
Israelis and Palestinians both deserve to live in security and dignity.
Slovakia continues to support a negotiated two-state solution, with Israel and an independent Palestinian state living side by side in peace and security.
Other conflicts that are currently out of the spotlight must not escape our attention and our efforts to solve them.
Take for example the civil war in Sudan that has triggered the world’s largest humanitarian crisis.
Excellencies, The first words of our Charter are “We the peoples of the United Nations”.
Today, we need that sense of shared responsibility again.
Armed conflicts have reached levels we have not seen since the Second World War.
Civilians continue to pay an unacceptable price.
What we need now is the will to use them.
This year, the United Nations will choose its next Secretary-General.
Slovakia supports a transparent and inclusive process based on merit, with due regard to regional diversity and gender balance.
The next Secretary-General will inherit an organization under serious security, geopolitical, institutional and financial pressure.
But the future of the United Nations will not depend on one person alone.
It depends on all of us.
On our will, courage and determination.
We “the people of the United Nations” should not leave the next generation a world where violence is normal and diplomacy is the exception.

Allow me to begin my speech by quoting the sentences that I delivered on behalf of Slovenia, on behalf of vast number of current and former heads of states and governments who signed our declaration for this rostrum in 2012.
I quote: » This year's theme of the United Nations Assembly is peaceful resolution of disputes...
Last year we celebrated the sixtieth anniversary of the entry into force of the Convention on prevention and punishment of the crime of genocide.
The Convention was the fruit of the tireless efforts of the Polish jurist of Jewish descent, Raphael Lemkin...
I would like to remind you that since the end of the Second World War alone; there have been more than 80 countries witnessing mass atrocities.
At least 53 million innocent people lost their lives.
Behind these numbers are concrete men and women, as well as children.
They had a future, but they were not allowed to live that future.

For this reason, I call on the Member States of the United Nations, regional organizations and the United Nations system to develop a new approach and a strategy for the prevention of genocide and other mass atrocities...

In addition, an intergovernmental forum of like-minded states should be established in order to propose a United Nations resolution that would give a clear mandate for preparation and adoption of an appropriate legal mechanism – legal mechanism that would give the concept of the "responsibility to protect" a new tool, a legal mechanism that will enforce the prevention of crime, a mechanism that will enable a faster and more effective response to acts of genocide and other mass atrocities...
I would like to inform you that this initiative also comes from international civil society.
The Institute for Cultural Diplomacy has gathered thousands of supporters at international non-governmental organizations, among lawyers, students, journalists and others...
As early as 1946, Raphael Lemkin declared: "Our heritage is the result of the contribution of all nations."
All nations, as well as the United Nations as a whole, have great responsibility, as well as an enormous opportunity to prevent atrocities in the future.
We cannot escape history, but we can learn something from it...
I firmly believe that the mistakes we made yesterday we do not want to repeat tomorrow.
We took responsibility for this world from our fathers, and we have a great responsibility to make it better for our children.
I call on you to improve it by joining all our efforts for a world free from genocide and other mass atrocities.
After 14 years, I note that, despite the great initial support, our initiative has not been realized.

It has been drowned in new crises, in the incompetence and ignorance of the individuals and institutions responsible, and in the double standards that have further marked the behavior of our United Nations.
Today, we are even further away from the goal we tried to achieve 14 years ago.
The theme of this year's session is therefore actually very well chosen. Restoring trust.
A United Nations that is here for everyone.
Because: Trust begins with a simple question: do we apply our principles consistently, or only when it is politically convenient?
The United Nations was founded on universal principles: sovereignty, equal dignity, the rule of law, the peaceful settlement of disputes, and the protection of human rights.
But principles lose their meaning when they are applied selectively.
For decades, the United Nations has devoted significant institutional attention to the question of Palestine.
The General Assembly has adopted resolution after resolution, while the Security Council and Human Rights Council have repeatedly addressed the situation.
Let me be clear: the search for peace and security in the Middle East is of profound importance, and the suffering of Palestinian and Israeli civilians deserves serious and sustained consideration.
But are we applying the same standard of urgency when victims are elsewhere?
Last year alone, over four thousand eight hundred Christians were killed because of their religion.
More than three hundred million Christians around the world suffer discrimination and persecution.
In Iran, the criminal theocratic regime has brutally murdered tens of thousands of its own citizens this year alone.
After 1948, more than one million Jews fled or were expelled from Arab countries, many amid persecution and violence.
For more than a decade, Nigerian communities have faced mass killings, kidnappings, the destruction of villages and places of worship, and the displacement of hundreds of thousands of people.
In return, this body produced a single Security Council resolution. Not seventy. Not seventeen. One.
So, we must ask: if every civilian life matters, why does our urgency seem so different from one crisis to another?
This does not mean caring less about one crisis but caring more consistently about all of them.
We must also be willing to ask difficult questions about how Palestine is discussed and used politically.
A majority position does not, by itself, determine what is right.
The right of a democratic state and its people to defend themselves against terrorism must be recognized and upheld.
Civilian suffering is tragic and must be addressed, but it can never justify terrorism or the pursuit of political objectives through violence.
At the same time, criticism of government policy must never become a cover for antisemitism.

If civilian lives are equal, our attention should be guided by the scale, duration and severity of suffering - not primarily by geography, political alliances, media visibility or political influence.
These principles must also guide our approach to Belarus.
We condemn the authorities’ systematic repression, arbitrary detention and persecution of political opponents, human rights defenders and independent voices.
All political prisoners must be released immediately and unconditionally, and those responsible for human rights violations must be held accountable.
Slovenia stands with the Belarusian people and supports a peaceful democratic transformation founded on free and fair elections, the rule of law and full respect for human rights.
Belarus belongs in a free and democratic Europe.
Selectivity does more than distort our attention.
Over time, it destroys institutions themselves.
The United Nations cannot defend the rule of law while silently watching its own mandates, procedures and institutions become instruments of political convenience.
The rule of law must never become merely rule by law.
It requires rules to be applied impartially, consistently and transparently.
When the same principles are invoked strictly in one case and conveniently overlooked in another, we do not strengthen international law.
And when institutions created to protect universal standards are instrumentalized for political purposes, we weaken the very multilateral system they were created to defend.
This inconsistency is particularly difficult to ignore when we consider Iran.
Executions, including those involving political prisoners, young intellectuals and others who oppose the regime, demand serious attention.

Yet there is often no sufficiently serious condemnation of these executions or of the broader violations of human rights under a system that seeks complete control over social, political and economic life.

The abuse of religion to justify or reinforce such control is another example of how principles can be distorted when institutions and political power are placed above the rights and dignity of individuals.
Human rights cannot depend on whether the victims are politically convenient to defend.
The United Nations must therefore defend not only its institutions, but also the integrity of the principles those institutions exist to serve.
Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is a flagrant violation of the United Nations Charter and a direct assault on the sovereignty and territorial integrity of a Member State.
Russia's occupation and attempted illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014 challenged a fundamental rule of our international order: territory cannot be acquired by force.
As Mustafa Dzhemilev, the leader of the Crimean Tatars, reminded us at yesterday's Crimea Platform Summit, the international response to Russia's aggression in 2014 was too little, too late.
The full-scale invasion of 2022 was the consequence.
The Russian leadership chose this war.
Ukraine is defending its people and its independence.
For Slovenia, sovereignty and territorial integrity are fundamental to our own security.
If a powerful state can seize its neighbour's territory by force, every smaller state becomes less secure.
The United Nations has documented torture and executions of Ukrainian prisoners of war by Russian forces, as well as grave abuses in occupied territory.
Prisoners of war and civilian detainees must return home.
Ukrainian children forcibly transferred or deported must return to their families.
Our goal must remain a just and lasting peace, based on the United Nations Charter and Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Ukraine must participate fully in decisions concerning its future.
Any settlement must provide credible security guarantees against renewed aggression.
Slovenia will continue to support Ukraine on its European path.
Ukraine's future belongs in the European Union.
A permanent member of the Security Council, entrusted with a special responsibility for international peace, is waging a war of aggression against another Member State.
Russia's permanent seat cannot place it above the Charter.
Its veto cannot erase aggression or responsibility for international crimes.
If this Organization wants to restore trust, it should begin by applying its own principles consistently.
First, this Organization should strengthen transparency around its responses to crises.

We should establish an independent mechanism, answerable to this Assembly as a whole, that annually compares the scale, duration and severity of major crises with the scale and nature of the international response.
Not to dictate political verdicts, but to make it impossible for us to remain unaware of our own patterns of selectivity.
Second, we should strengthen safeguards against the political instrumentalization of United Nations mandates and institutions.
Their credibility depends on transparent procedures, consistent criteria and equal standards of scrutiny for all Member States.
The multilateral system was created to prevent power from replacing principle.
We must not allow political convenience to reverse that relationship - so that principle becomes merely a language used by institutions when it serves political interests.
The answer is not to weaken multilateralism.
It is to protect it from instrumentalization.
A United Nations that delivers for all cannot mean an organization that responds loudly to some crises and quietly to others.
If we want to speak credibly of the United Nations that delivers for all, then we must be prepared to ask a difficult question: does it really deliver for all?
For states whose concerns receive little international attention.
For families struggling to build a future.
We will restore trust when a crisis matters because human beings are suffering, not because the politics surrounding it are convenient.
And we will restore trust when the institutions of multilateralism are strong enough to serve universal principles rather than political convenience.
But restoring trust is not only about correcting what is wrong today.
