It is about deciding what kind of international system we are willing to pass on to those who come after us.
Mr. President, A United Nations that cannot uphold its own principles has no standing to ask the world for its trust.
What we owe the people of the world is not sentiment.
It is an institution consistent enough, and far-sighted enough, to be worthy of their trust.

Sweden's National Statement at the General Debate of the 81st Session of the General Assembly of the United Nations Delivered by Foreign Minister of Sweden Maria Malmer Stenergard, 25 September 2026 *** Madam/Mister President, Excellencies I want to tell you about my grandmother, Alice.
Growing up in rural Sweden, as the seventh of eleven siblings, her opportunities were very different from those of her brothers.
Her parents expected her to focus first and foremost on family life.
Yet she was curious, capable and determined to build a life of her own.
A job at a local bank gave her not only an income, but also independence and confidence.
There, at the bank, she met many women with little to no experience with finances and were left vulnerable when circumstances changed.
She wrote in her diary about some of the women she met – many of whom were recently widowed – coming to the bank in tears because they didn’t know anything about their own family finances.
Some didn’t know how to fill out a withdrawal slip.
One woman came to the bank holding two safe-deposit keys without knowing which bank they belonged to.
My grandmother was as independent as a woman in that time and place could be.
But she worried deeply about the consequences for the women who were not.
During her life she witnessed extraordinary progress.
But two generations later, far too many women are still entirely economically dependent on men.
1(12) In the 1940s and 50s, Swedish women joined the labour market in large numbers.
This was not only a matter of principle – it also came from the realisation that our economy needed women in the work force.
Women’s economic empowerment is a matter of freedom.
When women work and earn their own money, their self-determination grows.
Gender equality is not only the right thing to do, it’s the smart thing to do.
Each generation must fight for equality.
In 1919, the same year my grandmother was born, Sweden decided that women should have the same right as men to vote.
That very same year, women in Afghanistan were also granted the right to vote.
More than a century later, the contrast between women’s freedoms in our two countries is as striking as it is saddening.
It is a painful reminder that progress is never irreversible.
Rights once gained can be lost.
It is up to us to protect them, for women and girls everywhere – and for generations to come.
When Sweden joined the UN in 1946, the world was emerging from the devastation of war.
The lesson from that catastrophe was clear: peace must not be taken for granted.
Defence of sovereignty and territorial integrity have been at the heart of Swedish foreign policy ever since.
Eight decades later, these principles are once again being challenged.
Bad faith, conflict and utter contempt for our common rules are weakening the institutions that we built together.
2(12) The number of armed conflicts is growing.
And civilians are paying the price.
In Ukraine, Sudan, Yemen, Palestine, Lebanon, Myanmar, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and many other conflict zones, millions are suffering.
Russia’s aggression against Ukraine is a blatant violation of international law.
It strikes at the heart of the very principles upon which the United Nations was founded.
Sweden’s support for Ukraine is felt deeply throughout our entire society.
It comes from our people, our civil society and the business community.
We will support Ukraine for as long as it takes.
Russia has not only violated the UN Charter, it has repeatedly violated international humanitarian law and human rights law.
Attacks targeting civilians, forcible transfer and deportation of children, conflict-related sexual violence and torture – the list is far too long.
Ensuring accountability for these violations is crucial.
If there is anything that we have learnt from history, it is that there cannot be a just and lasting peace without accountability.
Sweden stands firmly behind the ICC, its independence and integrity, and recognises its vital role not least in Ukraine.
Russia must also be held accountable for its breaches of the Chemical Weapons Convention, both on and off the battlefield.
Russia’s war of aggression against a peaceful neighbour is one of the biggest strategic mistakes and moral failures of the 21st century.
Four and a half years after launching its full-scale invasion, Russia has failed to achieve its objectives.
Its economy is under strain, and its casualty numbers are devastating.
Ordinary Russians are withdrawing their funds from the bank, and a substantial share of Russia’s young people are dying on the front lines.
The impact of Russia’s war of aggression extends far beyond Ukraine.
Russia intensified its systematic attacks on civilian infrastructure and on vessels in the Black Sea this summer.
To President Putin and Mr Lavrov I say this: the path to peace is clear, the choice should be easy.
Withdraw your troops. End this war.
Sweden has been an active contributor to the United Nations for 80 years.
But as a staunch partner, we will continue to push for a UN that is more effective, more transparent and better equipped to uphold the principles of its charter.
Sweden’s first peacekeepers, 300 of them, served this organisation during the Suez Crisis in 1956.
Since then, more than 80 000 Swedes have followed in their footsteps.
We have a long tradition of supporting mediation through the UN.
It began in 1948 with the UN’s first mediator, Sweden’s Folke Bernadotte.
We have long been a major donor of development assistance.
And we remain devoted to tackling global development challenges and contributing to urgent humanitarian efforts.
But development assistance alone will not be enough to meet the challenges before us.
Reducing emissions to curb climate change is a common and global challenge, and is necessary to safeguard and increase development gains in the coming decades.

Sweden will continue to promote climate action based on urgency and opportunity – urgency based on what science tells us, opportunity based on the economic growth, jobs and strengthened competitiveness that climate transition brings.
Given the state of the world, changes are necessary to ensure the UN’s central role in international affairs and its ability to address today’s challenges.
Sweden strongly supports the Secretary-General’s UN80 initiative and expects all UN entities to engage fully, with a clear focus on improving delivery at country level.
We also expect Member States to give the UN adequate resources.
Assessed contributions must be paid in full and on time.
As members, we also need to carefully consider institutional reforms and align mandates with available resources.
UN80 is an opportunity to strengthen the UN’s impact across all three pillars, and to reinforce the international system firmly grounded in the UN Charter and international law.
Sweden remains firm in its defence of the UN’s normative mandates on human rights, gender equality and sexual and reproductive health and rights.
Everyone has the right to live freely and with dignity.
To be who they are and to love whom they choose.
Sweden will always stand up for that freedom, and for equal rights of all.
A balanced expansion of the Security Council would strengthen its credibility and the legitimacy of its decisions.
Sweden would like to see permanent and non-permanent seats added, and a fairer representation of all continents on the Council.
Africa, home to 1.3 billion people and the largest regional bloc in the United Nations, has no permanent seat.
This is neither logical nor fair.
Furthermore, the veto should never be used to prevent the UN from acting against serious violations of international law or in humanitarian disasters.
We must continue to strengthen our United Nations.
To make this organisation stronger and better equipped to prevent conflict and meet the challenges of tomorrow.
5(12) We must continue to find common agreements, based on the fundamentals.
Every country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Prohibition of the use of force.
Respect for international law, human rights and humanitarian principles.
It is our shared responsibility to ensure that the UN remains relevant, effective and resolute.
That it becomes greater than the sum of its parts.
To show once again that we can turn the page on conflict and chaos and move toward peace and prosperity.
Madam/ Mister President This year also marks 65 years since Secretary–General Dag Hammarskjöld died.
Sweden continues to support the UN investigation aimed at clarifying the circumstances surrounding Secretary–General Hammarskjöld’s death.
I would like to conclude with the words of Mr Hammarskjöld: “It is no news to anybody, but we sense it in different degrees, that our world of today is more than ever before one world.

The weakness of one is the weakness of all, and the strength of one – not the military strength, but the real strength, the economic and social strength, the happiness of people – is indirectly the strength of all.”

WE CONGRATULATE THE PRESIDENT OF THE 81ST SESSION ON ASSUMING THIS OFFICE AND EMBRACING A THEME THAT IS BOTH TIMELY AND IMPERATIVE: "RESTORING TRUST, MANAGING TRANSFORMATION: A UNITED NATIONS THAT DELIVERS FOR ALL".

EIGHT DECADES LATER, THE WORLD CONTINUES TO LOOK TO THIS ORGANISATION AS A SANCTUARY WHERE NATIONS CAN ASSEMBLE, WHERE DIFFERENCES CAN BE RESOLVED THROUGH DIALOGUE, AND WHERE HOPE CAN BE TRANSFORMED INTO TANGIBLE ACTION.

TO ORDINARY PEOPLE ACROSS THE GLOBE, THIS ASSEMBLY MUST NOT BE PERCEIVED MERELY AS A FORUM WHERE THE WORLD DISCUSSES ITS PROBLEMS, BUT AS AN ORGANISATION THAT ACTIVELY SOLVES THEM.

THE TRUE TEST OF INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION IS WHETHER A CHILD IN A CONFLICT-AFFECTED COMMUNITY CAN LIVE WITHOUT FEAR; A YOUNG PERSON CAN FIND DECENT EMPLOYMENT; A FAMILY CAN AFFORD FOOD; AND A DEVELOPING NATION CAN ACCESS THE FINANCE REQUIRED TO BUILD ITS FUTURE.
RESTORING TRUST AMONG NATIONS TRUST AMONG NATIONS HAS ERODED ON MULTIPLE FRONTS.

MULTILATERAL COMMITMENTS HAVE TOO OFTEN GONE UNMET, FINANCING PLEDGES HAVE NOT YET BEEN FULFILLED AND DEVELOPING COUNTRIES FACE TRILLIONS OF DOLLARS IN ANNUAL INVESTMENT GAPS TO ACHIEVE THE SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT GOALS.
FURTHERMORE, BILLIONS OF PEOPLE RESIDE IN COUNTRIES WHERE GOVERNMENTS ARE FORCED TO SPEND MORE ON DEBT SERVICING THAN ON HEALTHCARE OR EDUCATION.
RESTORING TRUST CANNOT BE ACHIEVED THROUGH DECLARATIONS ALONE.
IT REQUIRES THAT PROMISES ALREADY MADE BE HONOURED, AND THAT OUR INSTITUTIONS DEMONSTRATE THE CAPACITY AND WILL TO RESPOND TO CHANGING GLOBAL REALITIES.
SINCE THE EZULWINI CONSENSUS WAS ADOPTED IN 2005, SADLY AFRICA STILL HAS NO PERMANENT SEAT ON THE UN SECURITY COUNCIL AND YET THE CONTINENT REMAINS A GLOBAL STRATEGIC PARTNER IN THE WORLD STAGE.
THE QUESTION IS, HOW MANY MORE YEARS SHOULD AFRICAN LEADERS TRAVEL TO NEW YORK AND STAND BEFORE THIS ASSEMBLY AND CALL FOR FAIR REPRESENTATION IN THE UN SECURITY COUNCIL.
MR PRESIDENT, WE ARE BEING DEPRIVED OF THE OPPORTUNITY TO CONTRIBUTE TO GLOBAL SECURITY ISSUES.

PREVENTING AND RESPONDING TO CRISES WE MEET AT A TIME WHEN MULTIPLE WARS AND ARMED CONFLICTS CONTINUE TO CLAIM LIVES, DESTROY INFRASTRUCTURE AND DISPLACE COMMUNITIES ACROSS VARIOUS REGIONS OF THE WORLD.
BEYOND THE IMMEDIATE HUMAN TRAGEDY, THESE CONFLICTS EXERT A HEAVY ECONOMIC TOLL.

THEY ALSO DRIVE UP ENERGY AND TRANSPORTATION COSTS, DISRUPT GLOBAL SUPPLY CHAINS AND EXACERBATE THE RISING COST OF LIVING FELT BY PEOPLE EVERYWHERE.
PEACE AND INTERNATIONAL SECURITY PEACE REMAINS THE INDISPENSABLE FOUNDATION UPON WHICH ALL DEVELOPMENT IS BUILT.
WHERE THERE IS WAR, DEVELOPMENT IS REVERSED.
WHERE THERE IS INSTABILITY, INVESTMENT WITHDRAWS.

ON AFRICAN CONTINENT, CONTINUED INSTABILITY VALIDATES THE URGENT NEED TO STRENGTHEN AFRICAN-LED PEACE PROCESSES.

UNCONSTITUTIONAL CHANGES THE AFRICAN UNION’S AGENDA 2063 AND ITS ASPIRATION TO 'SILENCE THE GUNS' REFLECT OUR CONTINENT’S RESOLVE TO END CONFLICT AND CREATE STABLE CONDITIONS REQUIRED SUSTAINABLE GROWTH.

OUR CITIZENS MUST NOT BE VIEWED MERELY AS BENEFICIARIES OF DEVELOPMENT; THEY MUST BE FULL PARTICIPANTS AS KEY PILLARS OF OUR SUSTAINABLE GROWTH.

THE KINGDOM OF ESWATINI STANDS READY TO WORK WITH ALL MEMBER STATES, THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM, REGIONAL ORGANISATIONS INTERNATIONAL PARTNERS TO ADVANCE PEACE, DIALOGUE, SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT AND HUMAN DIGNITY FOR ALL.
You assume this high office at a defining moment for our Organisation and for humanity.
You have consistently championed a United Nations that is more effective, responsive, and grounded in the needs of the people we serve.
The theme of this session strikes at the core of our contemporary global crisis: trust has eroded, yet structural transformation is urgently upon us.
In a world increasingly fractured by geopolitical rivalry, the answer cannot be a retreat into isolationism.
It must be a revitalized commitment to multilateralism.
The United Nations must prove that dialogue can bridge division, that international law must prevail over force, and that collective action achieves what unilateralism never can.
Seychelles approaches the world guided by an enduring, foundational principle: we are a friend to all, and an enemy to none.
Our commitment to non-alignment is not passive indifference; it is an active choice for peace.
It is the conviction that principled diplomacy, mutual respect, and international law are the true foundations of global stability.
Small states like ours do not seek strategic competition—we seek shared solutions.
This requires a multilateral system that is principled yet practical, ambitious yet accountable, and representative yet effective.
In short, a United Nations that delivers for all.
If multilateralism is to deliver, it must first secure the peace upon which all human progress depends.
Without peace, sustainable development is an illusion.
Conflict destroys lives, uproots communities, and diverts vital resources away from healthcare, education, and climate resilience.
We must reject the normalization of perpetual conflict and the selective application of international law.
International law must apply equally to all—without exception, bias, or double standards.
This principle is vital to maritime security.
The oceans are the lifeblood of global trade.
When maritime routes are threatened by piracy, geopolitical friction, or armed aggression, the shocks ripple far beyond regional waters, devastating vulnerable island economies.
Freedom of navigation and maritime security must be preserved under international law.
Small and vulnerable states should never bear the collateral economic costs of conflicts in which they have no part.

It is an honour to address this Assembly for the first time, as Thailand marks 80 years of membership in the United Nations.
When Thailand joined this Organization, the post-war international order was still taking shape.
Today, it is being reshaped once again.
Many of its old certainties are giving way.
But what comes next is not yet settled.
We are seeing many transformations taking place.
Strategic competition is becoming sharper and international rules are under strain.
At the same time, technology is transforming our societies, while climate change is testing our resilience.
Our institutions, however, are struggling to keep pace.
Confidence in our ability to work together is weakening.
That is why this year’s theme speaks directly to the task before us.
Managing the transformation requires trust: trust between countries, trust in the rules we share, and trust that our institutions can deliver.
But trust cannot be taken for granted.
Trust weakens when principles are applied selectively.
When countries have little say in decisions that shape their future.
And when promises made in this Assembly fail to improve lives beyond it.
Rebuilding trust means addressing each of these concerns.
We must uphold common principles consistently.
We must give countries a genuine stake in the international system, including a stronger voice for the Global South.
And we must take shared responsibility for turning commitments into results.
The UN’s purposes remain as relevant as ever: to promote peace and security, human rights and dignity, sustainable development and cooperation among sovereign equals.
But we cannot build lasting peace if security is assured for some and denied to others.
Universal human rights lose their meaning when applied selectively.
Development loses its purpose when prosperity remains in the hands of a few.
For Thailand, peace means more than the absence of war.
It requires dialogue to settle differences and respect for international law, so that all countries can live with security and dignity.
The situation in Palestine continues to demand our attention.
It reminds us that the principles we uphold must protect people when they need them the most.
That is why human rights must be universal in practice.
As a member of the Human Rights Council, Thailand believes that our work must reach beyond resolutions and make a real difference in people’s lives.
Development must be people-centered and sustainable.
Growth must improve people’s lives today without closing off the opportunities of tomorrow.
Consistent application of principles gives countries the confidence that they will be treated fairly.
But that confidence must also extend to how decisions are made.
Countries need to know that their voices count.
Today the UN’s membership has become nearly universal.
But representation has not evolved at the same pace.
An international system cannot command trust if large parts of its membership feel they have too little say in shaping it.
The United Nations must reflect today’s world, not the distribution of power eighty years ago.
That is why Thailand supports Security Council reform that gives developing countries and underrepresented regions, particularly in the Global South, a greater role in decision making.
Asia, too, must be better represented.
For all its economic weight, Asia must be able to help shape global decisions and carry more responsibility for the outcomes.
And representation must also mean that women have a meaningful voice in the decisions that shape our common future.
They are already at the forefront of this Organization’s work – from development to peacekeeping.
As the United Nations considers its next Secretary General, maybe it is time that this representation be reflected at the highest level.
Representation and effectiveness must advance together.
We commend Secretary-General António Guterres for his commitment to reform, including through the UN80 Initiative.
We stand ready to work with his successor to carry this work forward.
Having a stronger voice in global institutions means countries working together on the problems closest to them.

The United Nations must remain the centerpiece of the multilateral system.
But we cannot expect it to do everything.
It cannot settle problems when Member States are not willing to act.
Regional institutions can help turn that willingness into cooperation.
They bring countries together around shared challenges and translate global principles suited to local realities.
In this way, regionalism becomes a building block of effective multilateralism.

It has grown from five to eleven members.
But we have learned to manage differences and preserve space for cooperation.
For Thailand, that practical cooperation means serving as a trusted platform.

Our conviction is that together we should combine Asia’s diversity for co- creation, bringing together the different strengths of our countries to promote shared prosperity.

A greater voice must come with a willingness to contribute.

You bring to this house the wisdom of 5 billion people (60% of the world's population), representing some of the world's oldest and most sophisticated civilisations.

Then came the end of the Cold War, bringing us euphoria, celebrations, new promises of peace.
The Berlin Wall collapsed, Apartheid ended.

We are gathering in this Hall of Nations, countries large and small, some insanely rich, too many shockingly poor.

Some possess non-threatening antiquated guns while few others have perfected their nuclear arsenals, now 100 times more destructive than the ones dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945.
As primitive as they were then, these experimental bombs incinerated two cities and almost all living beings in them.
Those unfortunate ones who survived the blast died long, painful deaths.
Russia, US, China, France and the UK, all members of the Nuclear Non-proliferation Treaty (NPT) were joined by four countries not members of the NPT -- Israel, India, Pakistan.

Dismantle your nuclear capabilities and lose the only deterrence you have against a nuclear power deciding to bomb you into submission.
So, let's get used to this reality, a regime like no other in the world, with nuclear weapons.
On June 30th, 2019, President Trump travelled to the DMZ in the Korean peninsula.
The mysterious Swiss-educated leader of North Korea, half the age of the American President, walked halfway and the two leaders engaged in an embrace that promised peace.
This is what leaders do to advance peace.
President Trump did the right thing.
We cherish and embrace our friends, never ignoring them or excluding them from the table.

We talk to enemies to prevent wars, and perhaps we become partners in peace.
Those countries amassing nuclear weapons keep us all living near imminent catastrophe.
On any day, by accident, miscalculation, computer error, madness, or foolish strategic design, we could become the last human generation.

All the while, the brandishing of these weapons reinforces adversity and fear, which create a very high barrier to achieving the rational cooperation necessary to fulfil our responsibility to future generations, the imperative to protect the natural world upon which we all depend, and the moral imperative to eliminate the suffering of poverty.
Is this the best we can do?
Trillions of dollars are invested in perfecting forms of death instead of investing a fraction of these trillions in clean water, food, schools and clinics for fellow human beings.

No thought was given to the tens of millions of fellow humans pushed back to extreme deprivation by the COVID-19 pandemic, the Ukraine/Russia war, and as if the innocent bystanders on the periphery had not suffered enough, we are presented with another catastrophe: the Iran war and disruption of vital waterways for trade.
We know the madness of the Iranian leaders seeking regional supremacy, pouring fuel into the fire of religious extremism in neighbouring countries to destabilise wealthy, stable, monarchies.
Iranian leaders launched unwarranted attacks against neighbours, destroying civilian industries and infrastructure.

So is Iran going to launch waves of drones and missiles against US bases across Europe?

President Trump: be audacious, unpredictable, visionary, invite all nuclear powers and all major conventional military powers and industries, without exception, to a Summit in some town in Portugal, to talk on No First Strike, enhanced regular communication between leaders of the nuclear powers, and commitment on reduction of nuclear weapons towards total deactivation and destruction of nuclear arsenals over a decade.

Behind each of the dead is not a statistic — it is a mother who will spend the rest of her life searching for a face in a crowd that will never appear.
It is a boy hiding in silence, learning before he can read that the world outside his door wants him dead.
It is a girl, pregnant by the men who came to destroy her home, carrying inside her both the violence done to her and a life she never chose.
We tell ourselves we would never look away if we truly saw it.
And yet we saw Rwanda and Bosnia happen right under UN watch.
We see it every day, live, in our pockets, in vivid colour — and still, somehow, life goes on normally.
We grow inured to the killing of Palestinians.
This is not a lack of information.
We can live stream it all as it happens.

All this happens before our eyes, but from the powers that can make the difference between life and death, there is no response. And worse.

We witness diplomatic acrobatics to brush off the bombing of a school or a hospital, saying that it does not really violate international law because terrorists may be hiding in the basement of the building.
Worried that we have started treating a catastrophe as something we can simply coexist with.

Worried that total force now sounds more viable than diplomacy.
This very institution was founded on a promise.
All through the archives here, resolutions say a ceasefire must hold, a border must not be crossed, a civilian must not be a target.
Many of those promises have remained unmet, raising concern that the phrase "never again" has lost all meaning.
I do not have a plan that will end a war by nightfall.

Every time we let the suffering of people become background noise, we let ourselves forget how small the distance really is — how little separates your daughter, granddaughter, niece, from the girl in the refugee camp you saw on the news last night.
How many children, right now, are learning that a world at war is normality.
The more we linger in this fog, the harder it becomes for that hiding child to believe the world is not his enemy.
These tragedies are not somebody else's tragedy.
They are what we allowed, what we still allow, and what we will all answer for.

No country, regardless of size or power, can address today's interconnected challenges alone.
Leadership is not merely discovering the angriest instinct of the electorate and amplifying it.

[Sovereignty and the United Nations] We live in a world more connected than ever.

We meet amid deepening division, geopolitical competition and rising conflict.
For Tonga, navigating such stormy currents is not new.
As descendants of voyagers, “we have been in the survival business much longer than most appreciate.”
Under King George Tupou I, Tonga preserved its independence during an era of colonial expansion.
Our Constitution of 1875 secured Tongans’ rights and freedoms more than seven decades before the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
It reflects our fierce determination to chart our own course.
That is the essence of our sovereignty.
Multilateralism allows us to project the power of our ideas, rather than the might of our power.
Tonga participates as an equal under the founding principle of the United Nations Charter: the sovereign equality of states.
This is how we must approach our theme, “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All.”
Enduring trust is restored when commitments produce results.
True transformation is realised when our communities, economies and ecosystems can anticipate change and recover with greater strength.
Small Island Developing States must not bear disproportionate costs for challenges they did little to create.
[United Nations Reforms] Too much of the international architecture still reflects the world of 1945 rather than today’s realities.
If the United Nations is to remain the principal vehicle through which sovereign nations confront global challenges, it must transform.
We need a United Nations that enables innovation and expands meaningful access to investment and technology, especially for Small Island Developing States too often excluded from both.
We need a stronger General Assembly and institutions that respond effectively to the needs of the majority of their members.
We cannot keep negotiating climate, biodiversity and the ocean in separate processes when they form an interconnected ecosystem requiring coherent solutions.
Global processes must recognise the ocean–climate nexus and address these challenges together.
International commitments must also be capable of implementation nationally.
We need a more inclusive and representative Security Council, equipped for today’s challenges and prepared to recognise the triple planetary crisis as a profound threat to peace and security.
We need an international financial architecture that delivers timely, accessible financing to those most in need.
Internationally pledged commitments must be acted upon urgently.
Sovereign equality must be reflected in how these institutions listen, decide and deliver.
The next Secretary General must understand these realities.
It is in this spirit that Tonga has nominated Ambassador Ivonne Baki of Ecuador.
Her vision for a renewed and reformed United Nations speaks to the needs of vulnerable states.
To restore trust, every Member State, large or small, must have a voice in shaping this Organisation’s future and a stake in its success.
[The Blue Pacific and an Ocean of Peace] The Pacific region spans one third of the Earth’s surface.
Through the 2050 Strategy for the Blue Pacific Continent, we have set our own course and identified our priorities.
Our Blue Pacific must be defined by those who call it home.
For Tonga, investing in the ocean and nature is foundational to our development ambition.
Protecting and restoring them builds climate resilience, strengthens food security and enables a sustainable blue economy.
The financing and partnerships we build around ocean and nature based solutions will help determine our future and sustain our people.
We declared our region an Ocean of Peace in 2025.
It sends a clear message: the Pacific must not become a staging ground for military escalation or a battleground for major power rivalry.
Our Ocean of Peace is more than the absence of conflict.

Our most pressing threats are already reaching our shores: transnational crime, illicit drugs, illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, cyber threats, and the unresolved consequences of nuclear testing and radioactive contamination.
We will use innovative technologies and work closely with trusted security partners to confront these threats, including through stronger regional cooperation and maritime awareness.
We are committed to protecting the rights of marginalised people and ending violence against women and girls.

In doing so, we completed the universalisation of the latter treaty in the Pacific.
[Climate Action and Resilience] On climate, the Pacific is already drowning in a crisis that others continue to postpone addressing.
The United Nations Environment Programme’s Limiting Overshoot report warns that exceeding 1.5 degrees Celsius could occur within the next few years.
Crossing that threshold must not become an excuse for abandoning it.
We must limit the extent and duration of any overshoot, peak as low as possible and return below 1.5 degrees as quickly as possible.
Every fraction of a degree matters.
The Pacific loses an estimated US$500 million each year from cyclones and floods.
Early warning systems give communities time to prepare and can reduce these losses.
This sum may seem modest in global terms, but it is a heavy burden for Pacific nations.
The financing to prevent such losses still falls short.
The Pacific Resilience Facility, our own mechanism for financing community resilience, needs a further US$328 million in pledges to reach its initial capitalisation target of US$500 million.
Weather Ready Pacific, our regional mechanism supporting Early Warnings for All, needs a further US$160 million to reach its target.
Tonga’s Climate Trust Fund, which provides funding directly to communities and disbursed its first grants this year, also needs significant support.
We call on partners to invest in these Pacific-designed and Pacific-owned solutions.
Tonga stands behind the 2026 Pacific Islands Forum Leaders’ Belau Declaration and calls on all major emitters to act urgently.
Climate action is a legal obligation.
Meeting those obligations will require difficult decisions rooted in science.
Climate leadership is not a popularity contest.
Seven of the nine planetary boundaries have been breached by human activity.
Climate inaction is not an option.
Tonga is accelerating its transition away from fossil fuels, expanding renewable energy and encouraging the shift to electric vehicles.
For us, decarbonisation also means greater energy security and protection from global fuel price shocks.
Explicit fossil fuel subsidies, estimated by the International Monetary Fund at US$725 billion, must be phased out.
International financial institutions and multilateral development banks must recognise the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index in eligibility and allocation decisions.
The index must help unlock affordable and timely support before disasters strike.
By any credible index, Tonga is among the world’s most vulnerable countries.
We call on all nations, especially the world’s largest emitters, to attend the Pre COP31 meetings in Fiji and Tuvalu this October.
Come to the Pacific and confront what 1.5 degrees means for our water, our food, our homes and our people.
We welcome the General Assembly’s Declaration on Sea Level Rise, a significant achievement for the preservation of sovereignty and the first common text on sea level rise agreed by all Member States.
Our resilience must account for every hazard confronting our islands.
In recent years Tonga has endured cyclones, flooding, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions and tsunamis.
The developing El Niño intensifies weather patterns and strains water and food security.
We need integrated warning, preparedness and response systems that protect communities against the full range of these risks.
[Protecting Our Ocean, Unlocking Prosperity] Tonga has committed to protecting at least 30 per cent of our ocean by 2030.
Our ratification of the Agreement on Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction extends that commitment beyond our waters, supporting the protection of marine biodiversity on the high seas.
Its implementation must be fair and take account of the circumstances of Small Island Developing States.
Our task is to navigate a course that safeguards the ocean and unlocks its value for our people.
This principle underpins Tonga’s Ocean Strategy: responsible management of ocean resources, stronger marine protection and a sustainable blue economy whose benefits reach our communities.
It is in this spirit that we intend to convene a Polynesian Ocean Summit in Tonga in May 2027, moving from shared ambition to practical action.
We will bring governments, communities, scientists and partners together to strengthen ocean governance and generate lasting benefits for our people.
Our responsibility does not stop at the boundaries of our Blue Pacific Continent.
Born in Tonga’s warm waters, it migrates to Antarctica to feed on krill before returning to the Pacific to breed.
Tonga’s sanctuary protects whales here, but their survival depends on healthy ecosystems at both ends of that journey.
What happens in the Southern Ocean near Antarctica is felt in Tonga’s waters.
We invite partners to join us with practical commitments that recognise the interconnectedness of these ocean corridors.
[Energy Security and Technological Change] The same principle extends across our development: interconnection must not become dependency.
For Tonga, resilience means taking greater control of the forces shaping our future and turning the resources within our geography into greater self sufficiency.
When we import fossil fuels, we also import their volatility.
Moving away from them is both a climate imperative and an energy security necessity.
We are expanding renewable generation, improving energy storage and strengthening our electricity grid while exploring sources suited to our islands, including geothermal energy.
Tonga is not short of ambition: 70 per cent renewable electricity by 2030 and 100 per cent by 2035.
We welcome partnerships that help turn these goals into reliable and affordable power.
The forces shaping our future are increasingly technological.
Digital connectivity and rapid technological advancement are transforming how we live.
They offer significant opportunities for large ocean sovereign states, but risk creating new inequalities and dependencies.
Those who benefit last from global change often bear its highest costs.
We continue to live with that injustice through climate change.
We cannot again be asked to adapt only after the systems have been built and the rules written.
For Tonga, submarine cables and satellite links are foundational infrastructure connecting our islands to global opportunities.
Digital skills and secure, resilient systems must support it.
We will protect children online and retain sovereignty over our national data.
Tonga does not need to be first in artificial intelligence, quantum computing or every technology that follows.
But we will not simply endure global transformation.
We will exercise sovereignty by helping shape the rules and norms that govern it.

We are looking beyond conventional development models, seeking new forms of finance through the responsible valuation of our natural and ocean assets while exploring the potential of frontier technologies.
We will form the right partnerships and direct innovation towards our priorities in climate forecasting, public health, ocean management, clean energy and disaster preparedness.
The Pacific’s data, ocean, biodiversity, critical minerals and traditional knowledge must not power the next technological revolution while returning only a fraction of their value to our people.
Small Island Developing States need meaningful access to emerging capabilities and a voice in how these technologies are governed and shared.
[Conclusion] From experience, Tonga knows its challenges, and we will meet them with the determination that has always defined our people.
We also know our strengths as a large ocean sovereign state.
We are not asking for charity.

We simply ask that others do theirs: uphold the 1.5C degree threshold; help us protect the planet we all share and the ocean that connects us; ensure that everyone benefits from technological advancement; recognise the imbalance between the funds committed to our collective development challenges and those prepared for conflict; and uphold the rules and institutions that allow every nation to participate as an equal sovereign.
That is the promise at the heart of the United Nations.
Not that all nations would be equal in power, but that no nation, however powerful, is more sovereign than another.
That is the multilateral system Tonga believes in: an international rules based order founded on the United Nations Charter and the equality of nations.
That is the multilateral system we must preserve.

6. Tuvalu extends its deepest sympathies and condolences to all communities worldwide that are affected by ongoing armed conflicts and recent natural disasters, including the devastating floods in Nepal and Myanmar, the earthquake in Colombia, and the tragic loss of lives at sea in Vanuatu.

Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that deliver for all
15. The theme for this session “restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all”, resonates well with the moment of time we find ourselves in right now.
16. There is no denying that the architecture of multilateralism and international law founded on the UN Chater is under enormous stress.
17. And restoring in trust is critical, particularly for small island developing states like Tuvalu, whose sovereignty and future are anchored in that very architecture.

18. Tuvalu therefore stands in solidarity with fellow Member States in contributing to the restoration of that trust and advancing the necessary reforms and transformations that will enable the United Nations to deliver for all.
Managing Transformation: Protecting Our Land, Preserving Who We Are
20. Tuvalu, like other countries, is being challenged by various enforced transformations that threaten our land, values, knowledge and cultures.
21. Climate change is transforming our physical environment.
22. Technology is transforming how we communicate, govern and preserve knowledge.
23. Artificial intelligence is changing the way economies and society function.
24. The challenge is not to stop transformation.
25. Rather, the challenge is to manage transformation in a manner that protect people, preserve what is valuable, and give every country the capacity to determine its own future.

26. In response to the transformation to Tuvalu’s physical environment caused by rising seas, the Tuvalu coastal adaptation project (TCAP) has already reclaimed on the capital island of Funafuti, 15.3 hectares of elevated and flood free land as part of the reinforcement of the island’s coastal areas.
27. A further 10 hectares is being reclaimed which is significant adjustment for a country with only around 26 square kilometres of land area.
28. While we work to protect our physical territory, we are also contemplating preserving the intangible foundations of our nation, our traditional values, knowledge and cultures.
29. In that regard, we have two digital initiatives.

30. The first is the Tuvalu Digital Nation Initiative that utilizes digital technologies to sustain our sovereignty, institutions and our capacity to deliver services to ensure that our national identity is not lost in the transformation.
31. The second is the Tuvalu Digital Ark Initiative which seeks to preserve Tuvalu’s culture and historical heritage in digital form.
32. Mr. President UN Political Declaration on Sea-Level Rise
33. Less than twenty-four hours ago, Member States endorsed in this very building, the landmark United Nations Political Declaration on Sea-Level Rise.
34. A monumental and gratifying achievement for Tuvalu, because Tuvalu was at the forefront of global efforts demanding for such a declaration.
35. For Tuvalu, sea-level rise is not a future threat, it is a present reality.
36. Tuvalu is therefore overwhelmed with joy and warmly welcome the commitments the Declaration entails namely: (i) (ii) (iii) (iv)
(v) It affirms the continuity of statehood and sovereignty despite sea-level rise.
It safeguards the permanence of maritime zones and rights established under UNCLOS.
It recognises and protects the rights, dignity, culture, identity, and heritage of affected peoples.
It commits to strengthened adaptation and resilience.
It calls for accessible, predictable, and needs-based climate finance.
(vi) And it supports science, technology, data, and knowledge systems that enable informed decision-making and long-term planning for vulnerable countries.

37. The Declaration affirms that Tuvalu’s nationhood is not negotiable, that our maritime rights are not erasable, and that our people should never be forced to choose between their homeland and their future.

39. For the sustainable development goals (SDGs), Tuvalu is seriously concerned that the world is not on track to achieve them, because the consequences of such shortfall will be acutely felt by small island developing states.

40. Of the SDGs, Tuvalu underscores the urgent need to accelerate progress on SDG 14, Life Below Water which is the least funded and progressed, yet it is the most fundamental to the survival and prosperity of small island developing states.

41. Tuvalu calls on Member States to expedite implementation of the commitments of the Third United Nations Ocean Conference and to build momentum towards the fourth conference in the Republic of Korea in 2028.
44. Tuvalu acknowledges the efforts of the international community to address the climate crisis, but the pace and scale of global actions remain insufficient.
45. With a temporary overshoot of the 1.5°C target now inevitable, a fast, fair, just, and orderly transition away from fossil fuels is even more urgent and require serious attention.

46. Although the science may be clear that methane mitigation is the only scalable, near-term solution capable of rapidly slowing global temperature rise and buying time for long-term CO₂ decarbonization strategies to take effect.
47. Tuvalu would insist that CO₂ mitigation must also remain a top priority and that both methane mitigation and CO₂ mitigation should be vigorously pursued simultaneously.

48. Therefore, the Tassiriki Call for a Fossil Fuel Free Pacific and the Funafuti Call for Climate Justice and Climate Action are critical Pacific-led instruments championing Pacific regional survival and global climate actions.

49. Towards that objective, Tuvalu is determined to play its part in driving greater ambition, including hosting the Leaders’ Segment of the Pre-COP31 next month, and co-hosting with Ireland in Tuvalu next year the Second Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels.

50. Tuvalu reminds states of their legal obligations to take appropriate action to protect the climate system from greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, as failure to do so constitute an internationally wrongful act as confirmed by the ICJ Advisory Opinion.
51. Tuvalu welcomes the operationalisation of the Loss and Damage Fund and call on countries to honour their pledges and commitments.

52. Adequate, predictable, and timely financing is essential to ensure the Fund can fully deliver on its mandate and provide meaningful support to those most vulnerable to climate related loss and damage including non-economic loss and damage.
53. Finance, therefore, must be provided as grants at the scale required to address the climate impacts already unavoidable and the increasing loss and damage caused by further warming.
54. Tuvalu stands ready to work with all nations to advance climate ambitions, strengthen resilience, and ensure that no country is left behind.
55. Tuvalu’s message is clear: the world must act now decisively, collectively, and with urgency to protect the future for generations to come.
Ocean Governance and the Blue Pacific
57. The ocean is central to Tuvalu’s identity and sustainable development.
58. The ocean has sustained Tuvalu for generations and remains at the heart of our existence, our future and our resilience.
59. Tuvalu may have only 26 square kilometres of land, but we are custodians of some 750,000 square kilometres of ocean, which makes Tuvalu a large ocean state.

60. This year, Tuvalu soft-launched its first ever National Ocean Policy, a comprehensive framework to strengthen our stewardship of marine the permanence of our maritime zones, protect biodiversity, and place the ocean at the centre of our resilience and sustainable development.
62. For Tuvalu, ocean governance is not simply an environmental policy.
63. It is also an issue of economic security, food security and climate security.
64. Tuvalu has ratified the BBNJ Agreement and looks forward to contributing to the first Conference of the Parties of the Agreement next year.

65. Tuvalu’s objective towards the implementation of the BBNJ is simple in that the ocean areas beyond national jurisdiction belong to our shared future and must be the governed responsibly based on science, equity, approach and effective international precautionary cooperation.
66. Mr. President Financing Resilience at the Speed of the Crisis
67. Tuvalu, like other small island developing states, is highly vulnerable to climate and economic shocks, but the international financing architecture to respond effectively to those shocks.
68. Earlier this year, Tuvalu declared a national state of emergency due to prolong electrical power disruptions caused by fuel shortages, escalating energy costs and infrastructural deficiencies.

69. Although, Tuvalu did receive with gratitude external assistance, the timing and scale of those responses were slow and insufficient, and this is why access to rapid-disbursement and crisis-response financing is essential for the stability and resilience of small island developing sates.

70. Tuvalu, therefore, continues to urge the international community to adopt financial approaches that match the urgency of the crisis with simpler and faster access to climate finance, scaled-up adaptation funding, accessible loss and damage finance, and rapid-disbursement crisis mechanisms.

72. In the Pacific, Pacific Leaders have adopted the Pacific Resilience Facility as a regional financing mechanism to help our communities respond effectively to the growing impacts of climate change.

73. Tuvalu calls on the international community and our development partners to support the full capitalisation of the Pacific Resilience Facility, to enable Pacific-led and Pacific-owned solutions to build resilience where it matters most.
75. Adaptation and building resilience against the impacts of climate change will reduce the severity of climate change but will not eliminate all consequences of climate change.
76. One of those consequences is people deciding to migrate and set up home elsewhere.

77. Although relocation is not part of Tuvalu’s climate change strategy, it is inevitable that some Tuvaluan may decide to migrate and it is incumbent on the Government to ensure that they do so with dignity.
78. Tuvalu has therefore endorsed the Global Principles for Climate Mobility, which are rights-based, people-centred and grounded in international law.
79. We invite all Member States and partners to join us in advancing this framework of cooperation and common ambition.

82. Yet too many communities remain outside the structures designed to serve all humanity.

90. Tuvalu also supports the call for necessary reform of the is more UN Security Council representative, inclusive, transparent, and accountable, and better align with the reality of the twenty-first geo-political landscape.

92. To conclude, I wish to assure this Assembly that Tuvalu stands in solidarity with the rest of the Member States to play its part in restoring trust and managing transformations to ensure the United Nations delivers for all.
93. Tuvalu has shown that small nations can lead in climate adaptation and resilience, ocean stewardship, digital innovation, mobility with dignity, and the advancement of international law.
94. Tuvalu’s ability to lead is not determined by the extent of our vulnerabilities but national leadership cannot substitute for global responsibility.
95. The United Nations and its charter are the bedrock of international cooperation and multilateralism, and they must be guarded with all seriousness and integrity.

96. Tuvalu will continue to stand firm in its efforts to safeguard its sovereignty, the health of the ocean, and the integrity of its people despite climate change and other global transformations because they are worth fighting for.
97. And Tuvalu invites this Assembly to stand with us in that fight.
Tuvalu mo te Atua, Tuvalu for God.

Support for Multilateralism The theme "Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All" speaks directly to the anxieties of our time and also to the hopes of small states like mine.
As we have heard from many speakers in this chamber, trust in the multilateral system is broken.
Hope has retreated while cynicism and doubt have grown.
Nevertheless, we hear the insistent calls for justice, peace, and for a rules- based international order that applies to all nations.

Mr. President, I come here for the first time representing my country Saint Vincent and the Grenadines with a clear mandate and a commitment that governance must be transparent; that individual actions must consistently reflect integrity; and that public resources must be used to improve the lives of ordinary people.
We are a small, democratic, multi-island Caribbean nation committed to multilateralism and the peaceful resolution of disputes.
Those principles serve us well and we believe should bind us all in this chamber.

Vulnerability We in St. Vincent and the Grenadines experienced firsthand the vulnerability of living on the frontlines of climate change, having experienced only two years ago the sudden destructive power of a category 5 hurricane.
We also feel the enormous strains imposed on our small, open economy by distant wars that have disrupted supply chains, and by decisions made in places where our voice is never heard.
Yet, we will not let vulnerability define us or limit our ambitions.
We will be resilient and will work individually and collectively to transcend our vulnerability.
So, Mr. President, we come to this august Assembly not as mere petitioners, but as partners seeking to play our part in making our world a better place.
I come at this point in the debate having had the privilege of listening to other leaders who spoke before me.
And Mr. President I must tell you, I was moved by the hopeful vision, fiery passion and boundless generosity and caring of many of the speakers.
They lifted my spirit and, I am determined that that is where my spirit shall remain.
I owe it to the people who sent me here to be hopeful.
I owe it also to people whom I have never met, who come from places I have never been but who, nevertheless, are my brothers and sisters.
And so that brings us to the task at hand.
We all know that the United Nations has its flaws.
But we must not seek to abandon it like a motherless child.
It is what we have made it.
Some, no doubt, are more culpable than others, but in one way or another, we are all involved.
We speak of culpability not merely to point a finger of blame, but to understand better where the solutions may lie.
We believe profoundly that more than ever, humanity needs the United Nations.
Try to imagine a world without it.
Where would we go to have the conversations we are having now and had earlier in the week?
And that is only the beginning!
As a global institution, the United Nations is fundamentally an inclusive space where every nation can play a role in addressing our common problems.
A retreat from multilateralism undermines the interests of small States and, indeed, of everyone.
But we acknowledge that our support for the United Nations must be matched by our willingness to embrace reform to make it more effective.
Trust cannot be built or restored by declarations alone.
It is only when ordinary people see that cooperation makes their lives safer, richer and happier that trust will be restored!
UN REFORM Mr. President, let us restore trust through organizational reform and greater inclusiveness.
The United Nations governance model designed in 1945 cannot adequately address the security and economic challenges of today.

Therefore, we join with other nations in calling for reform, specifically of the Security Council, to include a permanent member from the continent of Africa with all the attendant rights and privileges.
Failure to do so would only confirm that the current composition is not about governance and fairness, but about power.
Further, as we proceed with selecting our next Secretary-General, let us be more open and inclusive.

Saint Vincent and the Grenadines is pleased to join other Caribbean Community members in endorsing the candidacy of Her Excellency Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of Guyana and of the region of Latin America and the Caribbean.

Mr. President, as this is my first visit here, like a tourist I walked the halls of this historic building and admired on the walls the impressive portraits of the nine men who have served as Secretary-General since 1946.

And while I appreciated the outstanding caliber and service of those men I, nevertheless, could not resist thinking that after eight decades, surely the time has come for an equally capable woman to be Secretary-General.
We believe Ambassador Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett is well-suited to be that person.
Climate Finance Reform Mr. President, for Small Island Developing States (SIDS), climate change is not a distant forecast.
It is a present danger and recurring financial emergency.
We suffer the scourge of sargassum seaweed that damages our tourism, and we worry about the growing problem of Sahara dust that seriously degrades air quality across the Caribbean islands.
And we worry constantly about hurricanes!

In July 2024, Hurricane Beryl struck SVG and demonstrated once again how a few hours of extreme weather can destroy homes, livelihoods and infrastructure built over many years, and set back a country.
Small states cannot continue borrowing merely to replace what climate- related disasters repeatedly destroy.
We cannot continue to walk up the down escalator, pretending it is development.

Mr. President, we renew our call for the full operationalization of the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index, so that access to concessional financing is not constrained by per capita income but reflects the real climate risks small island states face and their limited capacity to respond to such large events.
We also call for the swift implementation of reforms set out in the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS.

Further, we support the continuing work of the Bridgetown Initiative to reform the international financial architecture, including automatic debt-service suspension clauses when disaster strikes, expanded and re-channeled Special Drawing Rights, and multilateral development banks that lend like development partners rather than like commercial creditors.

Mr. President, we must also accept that affordable, patient, concessional capital is not charity to small states; it is justice for states that contribute the least to the climate crisis yet bear the highest costs.
Peace and Security Mr. President, let us restore trust through the pursuit of peace and security.
Trust in the international system begins with the conviction that everyone matters, and that the security of small states is as precious as that of great powers.

International conflicts far from our shores--in Ukraine and the Middle East-- continue to have devastating consequences for our daily lives, disrupting agricultural trade and global food stability and driving up fuel prices and shipping premiums.
We therefore join with others here and call for an immediate end to the war in Ukraine with full respect for state sovereignty and territorial integrity under the UN Charter.
And Likewise, we call for a permanent ceasefire in the Middle East, the protection of civilians, and the realization of a two-state solution guaranteeing peace and security for Palestine and Israel.
A CARIBBEAN ZONE OF PEACE Mr. President, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines does not stand alone.
We stand with our brothers and sisters of the Caribbean Community, CARICOM, which is not just a trading bloc but a family whose members in these uncertain times need each other more than ever.
For us in the Caribbean, peace and security are paramount concerns in our diplomatic efforts.

Therefore, as we seek to restore trust, we reaffirm that Latin America and the Caribbean must remain a Zone of Peace, where disputes are settled through peaceful means with adherence to international law and the UN Charter.
We urge that the territorial dispute between Venezuela and Guyana be resolved in this manner.
Within our hemisphere, other unresolved challenges require immediate, principled engagement.
HAITI Haiti remains our urgent concern.
Nearly four decades ago, the Trinidadian calypsonian, David Rudder, sang a lament to Haiti.
His words are still relevant today.
I quote: “When there is anguish in Port-au-Prince, it’s still Africa crying.
We’re outing fires in faraway places when our neighbors are burning.
I refuse to believe that we good people will forever turn our hearts and our eyes...away.
The insecurity of the Haitian people, plagued by gang violence and political uncertainty is a pain felt across our region.
We support the efforts of CARICOM and of this organization to help fund and provide security, to build up critical institutions, and create a viable path to general elections.
We must confront the reality of arms trafficking, including assault weapons that are terrorizing Haitian communities, and communities across the Caribbean.
We don’t make these weapons in the Caribbean.
They are manufactured in industrial nations and smuggled across borders into our region and countries.
We, therefore, call on all countries to take decisive actions to stem the illicit flow of weapons and ammunition across borders and into the Caribbean.
CUBA Mr. President, Cuba has long been a valued member of our Caribbean family.
For more than three decades, this Assembly has said that the economic embargo imposed on Cuba must end.

Whatever disagreements exist, the collective punishment of an entire population, denying medicine, denying trade, denying fuel, denying ordinary development, cannot be reconciled with the Charter we all signed.
My government adds its voice to the call, renewed year after year in this very hall, for that embargo to end.

VENEZUELA When devastating earthquakes struck Venezuela earlier this year, claiming thousands of lives, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines stood up in solidarity, contributing emergency assistance through a coordinated CARICOM relief effort.
Mr. President, when tragedy strikes, we must act as our brothers' and sisters' keepers.
This too builds and restores trust among nations and strengthens the UN.

TAIWAN Mr. President, friendship is also a form of trust, and I wish in this august body to recognize our country’s 45 years of diplomatic ties and friendship with Taiwan that has seen us work together in development, in disaster response, education and in public health.
Taiwan has shown time and again that they are prepared to be a responsible member of the international community.
We renew our call for Taiwan's meaningful participation in the United Nations system and its specialized agencies.
Reparatory Justice Mr. President let us also restore trust through support for Reparatory Justice.
The past is not past when its consequences still shape who is rich and who is poor in the world today.

The Caribbean Community has, for over a decade, advanced a Ten-Point Plan for Reparatory Justice, seeking acknowledgment, repair, and genuine partnership to address the historic injustices of the enslavement of African people and the near-annihilation of our indigenous populations.

We are encouraged that in March 2026, this assembly strongly adopted a resolution sponsored by Ghana and supported by the African Union and CARICOM, declaring “The Trafficking of Enslaved Africans and Racialized Chattel Enslavement of Africans as the Gravest Crime against Humanity”.
This is a hopeful and historic event, and after the follow-up conference in Accra in June, momentum grows, so necessary actions must follow.
When the continent from which our enslaved ancestors were taken and the islands to which they were brought in chains spoke with one voice, this Chamber listened—the world listened.
We expect that more steps will follow from discussions that will be held as part of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda in November.
CONCLUSION Mr. President, we ask how the United Nations can restore trust while managing transformation.

In summary, trust is restored when the smallest and most vulnerable nations feel they are included and that their concerns met; Trust is restored when a national debt is restructured to be fairer; It is restored when hurricane response arrives in time and when the benefits of new technology such as Artificial Intelligence is shared rather than hoarded or priced out of reach; it is restored when an embargo denounced in this chamber is finally lifted; when peace in a conflict is secured; and when an historical wrong is made right.
Mr. President, we remain hopeful that, with necessary changes in the organization and in the mindset of those of us who shape its work, the UN will live up to its name.

However, we must manage this era of transformation with courage, honesty, and fairness, and including equally the concerns of all the peoples of the world, who despite our individual protestations, are inevitably part of our shared humanity.

Always seeking a horizon in favor of the country.

An orderly, institutional and verifiable process, to build a country that is freer for all, more prosperous and more reconciled with itself.

For the rebirth of our nation.
For the rebirth of our people.

There will be elections in Venezuela.
We have already initiated a political dialogue with sectors of the opposition that will lead to a process on equal conditions for all.
The Venezuelan people, with their ancestral wisdom, will determine the right moment, and their institutions will be prepared to guarantee that inclusive and transparent process.
A country that is not subject to economic restrictions of any kind so that its right to development is guaranteed.
The rest and the spasmodic reactions from within and from outside form part of the spectacle that Venezuelans no longer want to see.
Venezuela must abandon the path that allowed extremism and intolerance to prevail over democratic and peaceful coexistence.
And there I ask for international support, so that you may in good faith back the changes that Venezuela needs, with respect for the self-determination of my people.
Venezuela wants to breathe freely, to exercise its rights as a sovereign nation, without any kind of interference.
Venezuela wants and must be respected.

I come to assume, going forward, a historic responsibility: that of leading Venezuela from a stage of uncertainty and conflict toward a stage of full democracy, recognized by its own people and by the world.
A new stage of well-being for the rebirth of Venezuela.
To my people I say: this is not the end of a speech, it is the beginning of a commitment.
To the international community I say: Venezuela is ready to walk hand in hand with those who believe in respectful international engagement, without interference or prejudgment.
To the young people, who have grown up seeing a fractured country and who many times decided to leave in search of what they could not find here: I say to them that it is worth believing again.
This is the time to build the country to which many will want to return, and not only the one from which many wanted to flee.
And to every Venezuelan who today, amid the material or human loss left by the earthquake, wonders whether it is worth remaining standing: I answer yes.
That the strength of this people is not measured in easy moments, but precisely in moments like this.
That from every catastrophe we have experienced as a nation, we have always emerged more united than we were before it happened.
Venezuelans: I do not promise you an easy path.
The recovery of the country will take time; the reconstruction of the national soul will be our priority.
We will walk united as one nation that decided, after pain, to choose hope.
On 16 December it will be 200 years since the anguished call of the Liberator Simón Bolívar to the people of Venezuela to save it from dissolution, division and civil war.

He said: "Venezuelans!.. You will be consulted so that you may say when, where and on what terms you wish to hold the Great National Convention. There the people will freely exercise their omnipotence, there they will decree their fundamental laws. Only the people know their own good and are masters of their fate; but not a powerful man, nor a party, nor a faction. No one but the people is sovereign."

Nor a party, nor a faction: let us all together bring our effort to bear for the rebirth of the prosperous Homeland that our daughters and our sons deserve May God bless Venezuela, and may the unity of its people be, from now on, our greatest banner.
Let us go together to build the rebirth of Venezuela.

Throughout nearly a decade of formidable challenges, he has steadfastly upheld the values of the Charter, while working alongside Member States to strengthen the role and effectiveness of the United Nations.
Mr. President, Excellencies, The world is undergoing profound shifts in the international order, with many risks and uncertainties.

The tendency towards the use or threat of force and the arms race, particularly the modernization of nuclear weapons and the development of new technology weapons, are heightening the risks of confrontation, miscalculation and conflict, even of large-scale wars.
At the same time, the global economy is becoming increasingly fragmented, amid mounting barriers to trade, investment and technology.
Supply-chain disruptions and economic instability are narrowing development opportunities for many countries.

Climate change, natural disasters, pandemics and emerging technological risks continue to pose direct threats to people’s lives and livelihoods, as well as to the development and stability of many nations.
Shifts in the balance of power and development inequalities are placing growing strains on international relations.
Instability is further exacerbated when competition goes unchecked, commitments are left unfulfilled and international law is applied selectively.
An erosion of trust is further impeding efforts at cooperation.
What should concern us is not only how the international order is changing, but where that change will take our world.
Change is inevitable, for it is part of the objective course of history.
Conflict and confrontation, however, are not inevitable.
From our own history, Viet Nam understands profoundly the cost of war, the value of independence, and the power of reconciliation and cooperation.

Over the past eight decades, despite its limitations, the United Nations has helped sustain dialogue, advance decolonization, uphold the right of peoples to self-determination, and support development.
What we seek is a more equitable, democratic and inclusive international order, where every country has a voice and every nation has the opportunity to develop.
In that spirit, I wish to put forward four major priorities: First, we must restore the UN Charter and international law.
They must be respected fully, consistently and without selectivity.

All States must respect one another’s independence, sovereignty, territorial integrity and right to choose their own path of development; refrain from interference in internal affairs; and refrain from the threat or use of force inconsistent with the UN Charter.
Restoring trust does not require countries to erase their differences, but rather to manage those differences responsibly.
Competition must be kept under control.
Commitments must be honored and fully implemented.
responsibly common restraint and In every conflict, civilians must be protected, international humanitarian law must be respected, and humanitarian access must be ensured.

Viet Nam supports the right of the Palestinian people to self-determination and the two-State solution, with an independent State of Palestine living peacefully alongside the State of Israel, in accordance with international law and relevant United Nations resolutions.

In the Asia-Pacific, nearly six decades of ASEAN’s development have demonstrated that countries can transform suspicion into trust, confrontation into dialogue, division into cooperation, and individual strength into collective strength.

In that spirit, Viet Nam remains steadfast in its commitment to resolving disputes, including those in the East Sea, by peaceful means and in accordance with international law, particularly the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.
Viet Nam is resolute in safeguarding its sovereignty, sovereign rights and jurisdiction.
The seas and oceans must remain spaces of peace, cooperation, connectivity and sustainable development.
In the same spirit of peace and respect for peoples’ right to development, Viet Nam has always stood in solidarity with the State and People of Cuba.
We call upon the United States to end the unilateral embargo and sanctions and the energy blockade against Cuba, and to remove Cuba from the list of State Sponsors of Terrorism.
We also call upon the international community to support Cuba in overcoming the sanction-driven crisis.
Second, we must advance development that is equitable, humane, inclusive and sustainable.
International commitments must be translated into action and bring people lives of peace, security, dignity and happiness.
It is for this reason that the Pact for the Future and the 2030 Agenda, our promises to present and future generations, must be implemented earnestly and in full.

Commitments on financing for development, including the Sevilla Commitment, must be translated into concrete measures: expanding access to long-term financing at affordable cost, supporting countries burdened by debt, and amplifying the voice of developing countries in international financial and monetary institutions.
The multilateral trading system must be strengthened in an open, equitable and transparent manner, ensuring development opportunities for all countries.
Climate action must be accorded its rightful place in development cooperation, particularly through adaptation finance, technology transfer and a just energy transition.
Development must be people-centered and leave no one behind.
Growth must go hand in hand with social progress and equity, environmental protection and the safeguarding of people’s livelihoods, particularly in vulnerable countries and communities.
Global progress must uphold the spirit of humanity in relations among nations, safeguard their legitimate interests, and respect differences in history, culture and development conditions.
Third, we must proactively shape technology governance so that progress serves humanity and our common development.
Science, technology, digital transformation and artificial intelligence are opening up unprecedented opportunities, while also presenting new challenges.
The future of technology does not automatically guarantee equity.
Technological progress must help narrow divides and expand development opportunities, rather than create new forms of dependency or new sources of conflict.

We need to develop inclusive, safe, transparent and accountable principles and governance frameworks to ensure that technology serves people, while respecting national sovereignty, digital sovereignty and the right to development.

Developing countries must be able to participate substantively in rule-making, receive support for infrastructure and digital capacity, and enjoy equitable access to the benefits of scientific and technological progress.

Viet Nam’s hosting of the Opening for Signature of the United Nations Convention against Cybercrime in Ha Noi in 2025 reflects our desire to make substantive contributions to global digital cooperation.

Viet Nam stands ready to work with partners to strengthen cooperation and build capacity in preventing and combating cybercrime, so that people may live safely and benefit from technological progress.

Viet Nam also stands ready to support international initiatives on green and digital transformation and the development of effective governance frameworks, so that science and technology can truly become drivers of shared development.
Fourth, we must strengthen multilateralism and the central, indispensable role of the United Nations.

The strength of the United Nations does not lie in its ability to replace the responsibilities of States, but in its legitimacy and capacity to build consensus, establish norms, develop rules, and mobilize global efforts to address common challenges.

For the United Nations to adapt to the transformations of our time, Viet Nam supports efforts to reform the Organization, particularly the General Assembly, the Security Council and the Secretariat, with a view to enhancing effectiveness, prioritizing structural reform and streamlining the apparatus, while fully harnessing the Organization’s advantages in advancing global agendas and safeguarding the interests of developing countries.
Viet Nam’s nearly half-century journey alongside the United Nations mirrors the transformation of our own country.

From being primarily a recipient of invaluable assistance during the years of reconstruction and Doi Moi, Viet Nam today is increasingly making proactive contributions to our common endeavors, while deepening and broadening our substantive relations with the United Nations.

Vietnamese military personnel and police officers have served, and continue to serve, in United Nations peacekeeping operations, carrying our nation’s aspiration for peace to places where peace remains fragile.
Our tradition of independence and self-reliance provides the foundation for Viet Nam to strengthen its strategic autonomy and proactively pursue international integration.

Looking towards our goal of becoming a developing country with modern industry and upper-middle income by 2030, and a developed, high-income country by 2045, Viet Nam is establishing a new development model based on productivity, quality and added value; with science, technology, innovation and digital transformation as key drivers; and with economic growth closely linked to cultural development, social progress and equity, and environmental protection.
Autonomy also means proactively adapting and cooperating with the world on an equal footing.

Viet Nam therefore pursues the consistent foreign policy of independence, autonomy, self-reliance, peace, friendship, cooperation and development, and of multilateralization and diversification of external relations.

Viet Nam will remain steadfast in upholding the UN Charter and international law, promoting dialogue and the peaceful settlement of disputes, and deepening its participation in United Nations peacekeeping operations.

Viet Nam is working together with fellow Member States to build a united, self-reliant and resilient ASEAN, and is actively preparing to host APEC in 2027, contributing to peace, cooperation and development in the region and the world.

As a member of the United Nations Human Rights Council, Viet Nam champions dialogue and cooperation in promoting and protecting human rights and in ensuring that all people can share in the fruits of development.
Viet Nam stands ready to share its experience in poverty reduction, agricultural development and climate change adaptation, and to work with partners to broaden cooperation for common interests.
The direction of such change will depend on the choices we make and the responsibilities we shoulder today.
Viet Nam chooses peace, cooperation and development.
We will work steadfastly with all nations to strengthen the United Nations, uphold international law, and translate our shared commitments into tangible benefits for our people.
Viet Nam believes that, with a strong United Nations, together we can build a more peaceful, equitable, inclusive and better world for all.
On this journey, Viet Nam will remain an active member, a trusted partner and a responsible nation, ready to contribute to the common endeavors of the international community.

I bring with me the voice of a nation of more than 80 islands of many indigenous communities and languages, and a nation whose identity has been shaped by the ocean, by kastom, by faith, by resilience and, above all, by our commitment to peace.
Your visits to our region reflect an understanding that the concerns of small island development states deserve to be heard at the higher level.
You have stood consistently for multilateralism at a time when multilateralism itself was under enormous pressure.
Vanuatu hopes that the next Secretary General will carry forward that same commitment to all member states, large or small.
