Vanuatu comes to this 81st session of the General Assembly with a simple message: The world needs the United Nations more than ever, and the United National must deliver for the people who depend on it.
The theme of this session — “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All” — therefore comes at an important moment.
The 81st session opened against a backdrop of profound geopolitical uncertainty and rapid transformation.
For Vanuatu, developments in international system are never distant or abstract.
Their effects reach our villages, our markets, our schools, our hospitals, our oceans and our homes.
THE INTERNATIONAL POLITICAL AND SECURITY ENVIRONMENT The international political and security environment is becoming increasingly difficult.

We are witnessing geopolitical competition, strategic rivalry, armed conflicts, growing military expenditures, economic fragmentation, technological disruption and a weakening of confidence in multilateral institutions.
The rules that were designed to provide predictability and stability are increasingly being tested.
The prohibition against the use of force is being challenged.
International humanitarian law is being tested.
The peaceful settlement of disputes is being undermined.
And the authority of international institutions is being questioned.
For small States, this is deeply concerning.
Small States do not possess the military, economic or technological capabilities of major powers.
We do not have the ability to impose our will through coercion.
Our security depends fundamentally on something else: International law, multilateral institutions, diplomacy and the equal sovereignty of States.
This is why Vanuatu has a profound interest in the success of the United Nations.
The Charter begins with a commitment to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war and reaffirms the equal rights of nations large and small.
It establishes sovereign equality, peaceful settlement of disputes and the prohibition of the threat or use of force as fundamental principles of international relations.
These are not merely legal concepts for Vanuatu.
When international law is respected, a small State has protection.
When the Charter is respected, a small State has a voice.
When disputes are resolved peacefully, a small State does not have to choose between submission and confrontation.
And when sovereignty is respected, independence has meaning.
We therefore cannot accept a world in which international law applies differently according to the size, military strength or economic power of a State.
The Charter must apply equally to all.
The security environment is also changing in ways that are particularly important for the Pacific.
The Pacific Islands are increasingly viewed through the lens of strategic competition.
There is growing interest in our maritime spaces, our sea lanes, our resources and our geopolitical location.
But we also say clearly: The Pacific must not become an arena for great-power competition at the expense of Pacific priorities.
The security of the Pacific is not simply about military deployments or strategic competition.
For us, security also means: • food security;
• and the security of our people from the impacts of climate change.
For Vanuatu, a cyclone that destroys a school is a security issue.
A rise in food and energy prices as recently experienced by Middle East conflict is a security issue.
A disrupted shipping route is a security issue.
A cyberattack against critical infrastructure is a security issue.
Sea-Level rise also raises fundamental questions on sovereignty, identity and security.
Vanuatu joins its Pacific colleagues in affirming the continuity of statehood and the preservation of maritime zone and sovereign right in the face of sear level rise.
The rights and dignity of affected persons must remain at the center of international response.
These are the realities faced by small island development states.

We therefore call for a broader understanding of international peace and security — one that reflects the realities of small island developing States, and we hope that these security issues are well understood here at the United Nations.
THE INTERNATIONAL ENVIRONMENT AND VANUATU'S DOMESTIC REALITIES What happens here in New York does not remain here in New York.
The decisions taken by major powers affect the smallest economies.
A conflict thousands of kilometres away can increase the price of fuel in Vanuatu.
A disruption in international shipping can increase the price of food in our islands.
A change in global interest rates can increase the cost of borrowing.
A crisis in international development finance can delay a school, a hospital, a road or a climate-resilience project.
And global economic uncertainty can affect tourism, investment, employment and government revenue.
For Vanuatu, therefore, foreign policy and domestic development are inseparable.
Our international diplomacy is ultimately about our people.
It is about whether a child in Tanna can attend school.
Whether a farmer in Malekula can bring produce to market.
Whether a family in Torba has access to reliable electricity.
Whether a community in Penama can recover quickly after a natural disaster.
And whether our young people can find meaningful opportunities at home rather than being forced to leave in search of them.
This year, as Vanuatu celebrated its 46th Independence Anniversary, we reflected on how far our country has come since 1980.
Our independence was not given to us in a golden plate.
It was achieved through the determination, courage and sacrifice of our people, supported by our brothers and sisters in the Pacific.
At our Independence celebrations, we were reminded once again of the importance of solidarity — including the historic support of Papua New Guinea during our struggle for independence.
Our 46th Independence anniversary was therefore not simply a celebration of the past.
It was a call to build the future.
The message of our national celebration was one of unity, national pride, resilience and determination to build a stronger, more prosperous Vanuatu for future generations.
And this is important in the context of our discussion today.
Vanuatu has experienced cyclones, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, economic shocks and other disasters.
Resilience is not simply something Vanuatu speaks about.
It is something our people practise every day.
But resilience also requires international solidarity.
A small island country cannot finance all of its resilience needs alone.
We cannot rebuild every road, bridge, school and hospital after every disaster from domestic resources alone.
We cannot absorb indefinitely the economic consequences of external shocks.
And we cannot protect our people from a changing climate without meaningful international cooperation.
Therefore, when we speak about climate finance, development finance, disaster resilience and sustainable development, we are not asking merely for charity.
We are asking for partnership, fairness and the fulfilment of international commitments.
That partnership must include predictable and accessible finance for adaption and for addressing loss and damage.
Access to such finance must be made easier for the small island state and must respond to the needs of our communities.
We invite partners to support the Pacific Resilience Facility in bringing the necessary resources to support resilience efforts in the Pacific.
At the same time, keeping 1.5 Degree Celsius is vital for Pacific.
In light of the International Court’s Advisory Opinion, we urge all members to give effect on their legal obligations through stronger climate actions and international cooperation.
We are also deeply concerned by the developing strong El Niño event in the Pacific, which threatens to bring more extreme heat, disrupted rainfall, drought and flooding across our region.

For Pacific Island countries, these are not simply meteorological events; they affect food and water security, agriculture, fisheries, health, livelihoods and the resilience of already vulnerable communities.
The international community must act before disaster strikes.

We call for stronger regional early-warning systems, pre-positioned humanitarian assistance, rapid access to climate and disaster financing, and greater investment in resilient infrastructure and food and water security.
The Pacific does not ask the world to prevent El Niño; we ask the world to help us prepare for it, withstand its impacts and recover with dignity.
The Ocean is central to Vanuatu’s identity, culture, food security and prosperity.
Protection of it is essential for the future of our people.
Climate change, damage to the ocean and the loss of biodiversity are linked.
Vanuatu welcomes the entry into force of the BBNJ Agreement.
It is an important achievement for ocean governance and multilateral cooperation.

For a nation whose identity, culture and prosperity are inseparable from the ocean, the BBNJ Agreement represents an important step towards protecting marine biodiversity beyond national jurisdiction and ensuring that the benefits of our common ocean heritage are shared fairly and sustainably.
Vanuatu stands ready to contribute to its effective implementation and to strengthening international cooperation for the protection of our oceans for generations to come.

Since the Agreement entered into force on 17 January 2026, following its ratification by more than sixty States, including Vanuatu and our Pacific neighbours, the international community has moved into a critical implementation phase.

Vanuatu looks forward to that first Conference of the Parties advancing the operationalization of marine protected areas, environmental impact assessments and the fair and equitable sharing of benefits from marine genetic resources, and we call on all States yet to ratify the Agreement to do so without delay.
The Implementation of the BBNJ Agreement must respect sovereign rights and take full account of the special circumstances and capacity constraints of small island developing states.
It must enable countries to participate effectively and equally benefit from it.

The hosting of the inaugural Melanesian Ocean Summit in Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea, this year arrives at a critical juncture where, on one hand, we are faced with daily mounting challenges of the detrimental effects of climate change, the alarming degradation of our marine biodiversity, pervasive marine pollution, and the overexploitation of our vital marine resources.

Yet, some of these global issues have already escalated to a level where ensuring sustainability for future generations has become a critical concern, highlighting the urgent need for improved management of our ocean resources.
In today's world, science and technology and economic opportunities MUST also work closely with our traditional custodians in our vast coastal area to maintain respect for nature.

Our culture and tradition are deeply rooted in the ocean and hence our collective wisdom and collaboration to address the core issues affecting our people's livelihoods today and reshape the future of our ocean and the communities is extremely paramount.
MANAGING TRANSFORMATION — WITHOUT LEAVING SMALL STATES BEHIND The world is entering a period of extraordinary transformation.
Artificial intelligence is changing economies and societies.
Digital technologies are changing the way governments operate.
And climate change is transforming the physical environment in which many of our societies exist.
The question before us is not whether transformation will occur.
The question is: Who will shape that transformation, and who will benefit from it?
For Vanuatu, the answer must be clear.
Transformation must not create a new hierarchy between those who possess technology, capital and influence and those who merely experience the consequences.
We need an international system in which developing countries and small States are participants in transformation — not simply consumers of decisions made elsewhere.
AI offers enormous opportunities for education, healthcare, public administration, agriculture, climate forecasting and economic development.
But without appropriate governance, it could also deepen existing inequalities.
Small States need access to technology.
We need access to data and computing.
And we need a meaningful voice in establishing the international norms that govern emerging technologies.
The digital future must not become another form of dependency.
V. SMALL STATES: DEPENDENT, BUT NOT POWERLESS There is a tendency to describe small States primarily in terms of our vulnerabilities.
We depend on imported fuel, food and manufactured goods.
And, yes, in many respects we are dependent on the international system.
But dependence must not be confused with powerlessness.
Indeed, history has shown that some of the most important developments in international law and global governance have emerged because small and vulnerable States refused to remain silent.
Vanuatu is proud of its contribution to the global climate debate.
We are proud of our advocacy for climate justice.
We are proud of our role in advancing the recognition of the legal dimensions of climate change.
And we remain committed to ensuring that the voices of those most vulnerable to climate change are heard in international decision- making.
Our experience demonstrates an important principle: Influence is not determined solely by population, territory or military power.
It can come from moral authority.
It can come from international law.
And it can come from the ability to bring different regions and groups together around a common cause.
This is the strength of the General Assembly.
Every Member State has a voice.
Every Member State has a vote.
And every Member State — large or small — has a responsibility to contribute.
The General Assembly is the most representative body of the United Nations, bringing together all 193 Member States on the basis of sovereign equality.
For countries such as Vanuatu, this principle is fundamental.
HUMAN RIGHTS, SELF-DETERMINATION The imposition of coercive economic measures, including unilateral sanctions, against developing countries is unfair and unjust.
Such measures are in violation with the principles enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations and adversely affects sustainable development outcomes of countries such as Cuba.
In this respect, we consistently call for the uplift of the economic embargo on the Republic of Cuba.
Peace and security cannot be separated from human rights.
Vanuatu remains deeply concerned about reports of serious human rights violations affecting Indigenous Papuans in West Papua.
United Nations Special Procedures have also raised concerns regarding Indigenous rights, displacement, cultural rights, environmental impacts and the treatment of human rights defenders in Papua.
The call from the Pacific Forum Leaders for the UN Human Rights Commissioner visit to West Papua remains unheeded and needs to be action.
Vanuatu reaffirms its unwavering support for the decolonisation of Kanaky-New Caledonia, which remains a Non-Self-Governing Territory under the purview of the United Nations.

We reiterate the inalienable right of the Indigenous Kanak people to self- determination and call for a peaceful, inclusive, transparent and credible process, consistent with the Charter of the United Nations and relevant General Assembly resolutions.
We remain concerned by persistent socio-economic disparities affecting the Kanak people, including inequalities in employment, education, income and access to economic opportunities.

These longstanding structural imbalances continue to constrain the full and equitable enjoyment of economic, social and cultural rights by Indigenous Kanaks, notwithstanding the Territory's considerable natural resources and economic potential.

Reports from the FLNKS, supported by independent assessments, point to the enduring effects of economic marginalisation and uneven development, which may be understood as forms of structural violence insofar as they limit meaningful participation in, and equitable benefit from, the Territory's development.
Addressing these disparities is essential to fostering social cohesion and advancing a just, inclusive and sustainable decolonisation process.

In this regard, Vanuatu calls for the full implementation of relevant United Nations resolutions on the Question of New Caledonia and encourages continued engagement and constructive dialogue among all stakeholders, including the administering Power and representatives of the Kanak people.

We further reaffirm the important role of the Special Committee on Decolonization (C-24) and the Fourth Committee in advancing the realisation of self- determination and ensuring that the rights, aspirations and interests of the Kanak people remain at the centre of the decolonisation process.

At the end of August, the Vanuatu Government initiated proceedings against France before the International Court of Justice concerning sovereignty over Umaenupne and Umaeneg/Leka islands – or Matthew and Hunter as they are called in English - and the maritime boundaries between Vanuatu and New Caledonia.

These islands are an integral part of Vanuatu’s territory, grounded in customary governance, longstanding historical connection, indigenous ownership and seen as a part of our duty as ancestral custodians to protect and preserve.
We recognize France as a steadfast champion of the international rules-based order and, under the leadership of President Macron, a strong supporter of international judicial institutions.
France has stood alongside Vanuatu in advancing global climate action, including through its support for our initiative before the International Court of Justice.
We greatly value this partnership and France’s leadership on issues of international importance.
It is in that same spirit of mutual respect and commitment to international law that we respectfully invite France to consent to the jurisdiction of the Court VII.
A UNITED NATIONS THAT DELIVERS FOR ALL Trust is important for the United Nations credibility.
It cannot be restored through declarations alone.
Trust must be earned through action.
People will trust the United Nations when they see it preventing conflict.
They will trust it when international law is respected.
They will trust it when humanitarian assistance reaches those who need it.
They will trust it when development commitments become real projects.
They will trust it when climate finance reaches vulnerable communities.
They will trust it when small States are heard.
And they will trust it when the international system treats all nations with equal dignity.
For Vanuatu, restoring trust also means restoring confidence in multilateralism itself.
We must resist the temptation to conclude that because the international system is imperfect, it is therefore irrelevant.
The UN80 reforms currently implemented are paramount to rebuild trust again at the UN and therefore needs to be managed diligently.
Vanuatu supports efforts to strengthen the United Nations.
But reform must preserve what is most important: the principle of sovereign equality.
The United Nations cannot become an institution where the voices of the most powerful States dominate while smaller States are expected merely to follow.
Reform must strengthen the General Assembly.
It must make international institutions more accessible to developing countries.
It must address the financing and capacity constraints facing small delegations.
It must improve the implementation of international decisions.
It must ensure that the development pillar remains resourced and that implementation on the ground is effective and efficient.
And it must ensure that international law remains central to the international system.

Vanuatu calls for a UN Security Council that is more representative, transparent and accountable, with membership and working methods that reflect today’s realities and give all regions a meaningful voice.
But reform cannot be limited to institutional structures.
The deeper reform we require is political: a renewed commitment by Member States to the principles we have already agreed to.
The Charter does not need to be reinvented.
CONCLUSION: THE UN CHARTER AS OUR COMPASS Mr. President, Excellencies, For Vanuatu, the United Nations Charter remains our compass.
It tells us that nations are sovereign equals.
It tells us that disputes must be settled peacefully.
It tells us that force must not be used against the territorial integrity or political independence of States.
It tells us that nations must cooperate.
And it reminds us that the ultimate purpose of the international system is not power for its own sake.
It is peace, justice, human dignity, development and cooperation And it is a better future for succeeding generations.
These principles are particularly important to Vanuatu because we know what independence means.
Our independence is not merely the absence of colonial rule.
Independence means the right of our people to determine our future.
And it means having an equal place in the family of nations.
That is why Vanuatu will continue to defend the multilateral system.
That is why we will continue to defend international law.
And that is why we will continue to speak for the principle that every nation — regardless of size — matters.
We meet at a difficult moment in international affairs.
There are wars that remain unresolved.
There are communities facing humanitarian catastrophe.
And there is declining confidence in international institutions.
Yet I remain convinced that this is precisely the moment when we must choose cooperation over confrontation.
We must choose dialogue over division.
We must choose law over force.
We must choose solidarity over indifference.
And we must choose multilateralism over fragmentation.
Vanuatu comes from a part of the world where our ancestors navigated vast oceans using the stars, the winds, the currents and knowledge passed from generation to generation.
Today, the international community is navigating another uncertain ocean.
The United Nations Charter is that compass.
It provides the principles by which we can navigate a world of competing interests while preserving our common humanity.
The theme of this 81st session — “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All” — reminds us of what is required.
But ultimately, restoring trust will depend not on the words we adopt here, but on the actions, we take when we leave this hall.

Let us therefore build a United Nations that is strong enough to prevent war, fair enough to protect the vulnerable, courageous enough to defend international law, and inclusive enough to give every nation a meaningful voice.
Let us build a United Nations where the concerns of a small island nation in the Pacific and all over the world can stand alongside those of the largest powers of the world.
Let us not allow division to rule our era.
And we chose to renew our faith in the idea that together, nations can build a better world.
Vanuatu stands ready to do its part.
Samoa e, tapua’i maia se’i fai so tatou sao i upu fai o malo aufa’atasi, aua o faiva e tapua’ia, o faiva ia e a’e manuia.
The chosen theme for the general debate, “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All,” could not be more timely.
It speaks to the reality of the world we face today; a world shaped by uncertainty, disruption and rapid change, but also by hope, innovation and opportunity.
For Samoa, the theme is a promise the world must keep; Can trust be restored?
The answer lies in the first words of our UN Charter - WE THE PEOPLES.
We must always put PEOPLE at the centre of our decisions.
For us, this is underpinned by the core values of our Samoan culture the fa´asamoa and our faith, such as respect, dignity, love, protection and service.
Every decision in this Hall shapes the world that every child inherits.
We meet at a pivotal moment in history.
Profound and transformative changes are not only necessary, but inevitable.
Across many societies, people are increasingly asking whether global institutions are delivering on the promises made to them.
We must prepare ourselves to face the challenges ahead with resolve, and use the opportunity to herald in much needed reforms for the benefits of all and leaving no one behind.
For Samoa, multilateralism remains the cornerstone of our international engagement.
Only through genuine cooperation and mutual trust can we craft solutions that no single nation could achieve alone.
The UN80 initiative has merits but also its risks, if not fully assessed and understood.
Any reform must strengthen delivery on the ground, by eliminating duplication, improving coherence, and accelerating impact.
Critically, such reforms must not weaken the operations of the UN Multi- Country Offices or the Resident Coordinator system.

Whilst Samoa reaffirms its unwavering commitment to the United Nations as the premier forum to address global crises, we also caution against premature decisions taken without the full consideration and endorsement by member states.
Excellencies Climate change remains the single greatest threat to Samoa and the global community.
Its impacts are more extensively felt by SIDS due to our special circumstances.
As the ICJ advisory opinion puts it, climate change is not merely an environmental concern, but “an existential problem of planetary proportions” that requires urgent global action.
The United Nations General Assembly welcomed the unanimous ICJ Advisory Opinion, and affirmed its importance as an authoritative contribution to the clarification of existing international law.
Climate finance is the bridge between ambition and action.
It must be scaled up, easily accessible, devoid of burdensome conditions, and responsive to the needs of the most climate vulnerable.
Resources intended for education, health, water and social protection are now diverted to disaster recovery.
Small nations are being asked to finance both development and survival.
No nation should have to borrow its way out of a crisis it did so little to create.
The world is facing a growing development financing crisis.
The gap between commitments and delivery continues to widen.
Too often, we simply rebrand and recycle old ideas while failing to deliver tangible progress.
Meanwhile multilateralism is under siege, and international financial commitments are being eroded.
The current international financial architecture was designed for a different era.
It struggles to adequately recognise vulnerability and fails to fully account for the realities faced by SIDS.
A fairer financial system is not only in the interests of developing countries.
It is in the interests of global stability and shared prosperity.
The implementation of the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index (MVI) in financing decision-making is essential if we are to genuinely address the financial challenges facing developing countries.
We look forward to the pilot project to demonstrate the MVI can help developing countries in their financing challenges.
On debt, we need to build a sustainable, equitable, and fair debt regime, starting with a robust mechanism for debt restructuring.
Debt forgiveness must be linked to measurable progress on resilience-building.
Investment in resilience today will reduce the costs of disasters tomorrow.
Samoa supports the incorporation of state-contingent clauses in debt instruments, allowing for suspension during crises.
Energy is both a driver and accelerator for Samoa’s sustainable development ambition.
Energy security has become a defining issue for many small island nations.
While we have one of the highest shares of renewable electricity in the Pacific, Samoa remains heavily dependent on imported fuels.
Successive energy crises, and the 2026 fuel crisis exposed the economic cost of our energy dependence.

We are working towards a whole-of-system transformation that delivers electricity that is reliable and affordable, reduces our dependence on imported fuels, strengthens resilience and supports sustainable development.
The clean energy transition is also an opportunity for Samoa to build a smarter, more resilient and investment-ready energy system.

The digital transformation – including AI and data analytics – offers real opportunities to drive an inclusive, just energy transition, particularly through off-grid solutions and smarter energy planning.
Excellencies The ocean defines who we are as Pacific people. It connects us. Sustains us.
Yet our ocean faces increasing pressures from pollution, biodiversity loss, overexploitation and the impacts of climate change.
Pursuing economic growth has come at a grave cost to our marine ecosystems.
Coupled with the unchecked exploitation of deep seabed mineral resources, our oceans face a crisis of limitless proportions.
These planetary changes leave no middle ground.
Weak governance frameworks threaten what remains.
Without urgent action, small island states face a future without land and no usable ocean.
It is time to transform how we value and interact with the ocean - from a resource we exploit to one we protect and cherish.
We must do more on this front.
Samoa has ratified the BBNJ Agreement, and we remain actively engaged in negotiations towards a global treaty on plastic pollution, particularly to protect our marine environment.
We remain committed to implementing the Apia Commonwealth Ocean Declaration, the 2026 Pacific Islands Forum Leaders’ Ocean Statement, and our own Samoa Ocean Strategy.
These are critical to the implementation of SDG14.
Our maritime domain is increasingly exploited by transnational criminal networks involved in illegal trafficking, including illicit drugs moving through our region.
Illicit drugs enter homes, harm young people, fuel violence and place increasing pressure on communities and essential services.
Non-communicable diseases represent one of the most serious development challenges to Samoa´s public health and economic productivity.
In response, we are shifting towards prevention through strengthening health literacy, reforming school nutrition and food environments and early intervention programmes.
This includes our Early Childhood development framework, a multisectorial roadmap to ensure every child from pregnancy to age five receives nurturing care, protection and early learning.
In many of our Pacific countries, our water systems are highly vulnerable to disruption.
These realities demand that the global water agenda fully recognize the special circumstances of SIDS.
First, climate-resilient water systems must be scaled up urgently Second, access to finance must be significantly improved.
Third, capacity and partnerships must be strengthened.
Finally, we need a transnational water governance regime informed by the outcomes of the various water conferences held over the last 8 years.
Samoa remains a peaceful country, steadfast in our commitment to human rights and justice.
We remain concerned by the ongoing wars in Ukraine, Gaza, and Iran.
The terrible loss of civilian lives, displacement of people as well as the destruction of infrastructure and the environment is something we do not condone.
The continued supply of weapons to fuel conflicts must end.
We also reiterate our longstanding call for meaningful reform of the Security Council to ensure that it remains effective, credible and representative of today’s realities.
It is imperative that the UN resolves disputes peacefully and strengthens international peace and security.
The world needs a stronger commitment to peace. Not more division. Not more conflict.
At its heart, Samoa’s development journey is about investing in people.
We are strengthening social protection, investing in youth, supporting women and persons with disabilities, and building a resilient economy.
These efforts are championed through our District Development Program, delivered across all fifty one districts. Empowering our communities.
Our greatest source of resilience will not be our infrastructure or our institutions alone.
It will be our people: healthy, skilled, educated and empowered.
This is why the Aiga or family is at the heart of our pathway for development of Samoa.
His legacy will continue to guide our collective efforts in advancing peace, dignity, and sustainable development for all.
Before I am a leader, I am first and foremost a mother.
History may record our titles, but our children will inherit our choices.
This is why, now more than ever, the United Nations matters.
We must continue to stand, as One United Nations Family.
Life itself has become at risk.
It should be noted that this ancient country, with its civilization, its history, and the suffering of its people, must once again stand before us and ask: for how long?
For twelve full years, its great people have lived under instability and a prolonged crisis, while political calculations have extended this suffering and deprived Yemen’s children of a normal life.
A whole generation was born under war, and grew up between hunger, fear and weapons, learning the alphabet of pain before learning the alphabet of childhood.

For twelve full years, Yemen’s children have lost a world that today stands with the Yemenis only in adding to their misery, while the coup by the Houthi terrorist militias against the State of Yemen has continued, after twelve full years of war, deprivation, recruitment of children, confiscation of rights, freedoms and resources.

The Yemeni Government has dealt responsibly with the various international and regional initiatives, and has made major concessions in good faith for the sake of bringing peace and ending the suffering of the Yemeni people.
Meanwhile, the Houthi militias met those efforts with obstinacy, and turned the truce into an opportunity to expand their military fronts at the expense of citizens’ livelihoods.

The latest of these efforts was what had been undertaken by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and the Sultanate of Oman to formulate a road map towards peace, while the Houthi militias met it by escalating in the Red Sea and obstructing it, and the Yemeni Government welcomed it, but the militias transformed the security of one of the world’s most important maritime passages, Bab al-Mandab and the Red Sea, into a bargaining chip used by Iran to export its influence and negotiations to the world.

There is no room for doubt that if this coup has been able to continue all these years and extend to neighbouring States and international waterways, it is because of the support that the Houthi militias receive from the Iranian regime in weapons, expertise and military technologies.

The world has long hesitated in designating the Houthis as a terrorist group, and gave them a precious opportunity to consolidate their influence; when leniency is used in the face of an armed group, it only emboldens it.

We have seen how firmness in confronting this group is critical, and we value what the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, by leading the Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen, has provided in decisive efforts to deter this group and support the Yemeni Government, thereby contributing to protecting the security and stability of the region and the world.

The Houthi militias have also tested the firmness of the United States administration in dealing with them, and we believe that the right approach is one that understands the nature of this phenomenon accurately.
Therefore, we appreciate President Trump’s understanding of this equation: the equation of firmness, which is the only language understood by the terrorist group.
We also appreciate every friendly State that stands in that firm position.
International legitimacy and its resolutions are with us, and we reaffirm that peace cannot be made by resolutions alone, but by will.
Peace is not the absence of war; it is not an endless marathon of negotiations that produces nothing but more terrorism.

What is needed is a firm hand that deters those who threaten the security of States and their stability, so that Iran’s agenda is not allowed to override the interests of Yemen and the Yemenis, or our battle with the world.

The threat to maritime security, and to one of the world’s most vital waterways, begins in Tehran before reaching Bab al-Mandab, and is represented in the sectarian ideological thinking and expansionist ambition that have long shaped Iranian behaviour.

To address manifestations without addressing results is not enough, for the Houthis in Yemen are not the beginning of the story but one of the manifestations of a comprehensive project that transcends borders.
What the Houthi militias are undertaking in Yemen does not require more concessions; as the world has become reassured, what is required is a serious stand against this Iranian militia.
The threat to international peace and security is no longer confined to Yemen alone, after its ambitions have crossed beyond it.
It is no longer possible to build security in the Red Sea, Bab al-Mandab and the Gulf of Aden as long as it remains hostage to the will of a militia linked to an external project.

Iranian support is not the only thing that heightens the danger of this militia, the Iranian arm’s-length militia; there is also a wider international gateway that benefits from every step it takes, and that gateway is the direct and indirect support networks and the use of mercenaries.

The years have proven that this danger extends across the region and beyond, and that in the absence of deterrence and amid the language of appeasement, the threat persists beyond the borders of States and grows at Yemen’s borders and in the Red Sea, nourished by organized smuggling networks, Iranian groups and militias, and networks of trafficking and organized crime, thereby threatening States and international security.
Restoring the sovereignty of the Yemeni State and securing Bab al-Mandab are two inseparable issues.

Supporting the Yemeni Government and strengthening its economic, security and military capacities are one path, and protecting this vital waterway is a regional and international responsibility in which Yemen alone cannot bear the burden.
Every State whose economy depends on freedom of navigation bears responsibility for these threats and for piracy.

The safe path to secure this waterway cannot be achieved so long as a militia remains in control beyond the State and outside it, because the issue is not solely Yemeni; rather, it directly concerns the protection of one of the most important maritime passages.

As we commend the initiative of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and appreciate the efforts made by the Special Envoy and the brotherly countries, the protection of maritime navigation and the security of the region cannot be achieved while Yemen is denied the return to stability, supplies, exports, and the freedom of safe passage through the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait.

The world has from this platform been repeatedly told what should be clear to them: there can be no security against evil, and no lasting stability, so long as this painful scene remains in Yemen, with all its devastation, misery, and open wound, in a region of such strategic importance to the world, with its internal and external dimensions, at a cost to development, with military formations, displacement, victims, and conflict, and with the suffering of Yemenis and the fragmentation of the Yemeni political map.

There, on the other side, the armed Yemeni groups, and behind them those lying in wait for the security of the region or for the world, are present in Sana’a, Sa’dah, Hudaydah, and Dhamar, while the world looks on; and in the field, the scenes of the Yemen tragedy are all too visible, and I am among those who speak on behalf of the people, the earth, sovereignty, the future, and dignity.

Ladies and gentlemen, had our people wished to surrender to the dark fate and to withdraw from their State, that would have been easier for us; but because we shall not abandon our State, and because we shall not relinquish our matter and our right, the armed coup has prolonged the collapse.

More than ten years have passed without every hand being extended to Yemen, a great country, despite the potential it possessed, and today the Iranian militias still believe that they are striking at Yemen through the latest criminal wave in our country and from among us.
Yet our suffering and your suffering are one, and our battle has never been for Yemen alone, nor for its future alone.
Rather, our battle is against schemes or agendas beyond the State and its institutions.
Our battle has been against the overthrow of the State by Iran’s agents.
The suffering is that of all Yemenis.
We struggle for the sake of all of us together, and for the States and the nation as a whole.

Yemen cannot accept the injury of any one of its sons, nor can our struggle be against those who are not aggressors; rather, it is so that Yemen may be rebuilt, prosper, secure its rights, and preserve its life, dignity, future, and decision, so that Yemen may remain the State, the human being, freedom, the future, and sovereignty.

What we ask is that the international community fulfil its responsibilities, that it understand the seriousness of the Houthi project and its manifestations, that it not create peace at gunpoint or make concessions in the face of militias, and that it support the Yemeni Government seriously in putting an end to the danger of the Houthi gatherings, restoring protection to its ports and maritime passages.
This is what we want from the international community, not a policy of appeasement that endangers Yemen, the region, and international peace and security.

We want a Yemen free and at peace, a Yemen of work, similar to the rest of the world, a Yemen for partnership and cooperation; that is the Yemen we want the world to see, not Yemen as a state of war and a project for one party at the expense of Yemenis and their institutions.
Distinguished guests, our region, the focus of security, the Arab island, and the Horn of Africa, have for years depended on restoring the role of their States.
They are determined not to remain permanently exposed to crises, but rather to strengthen security in their States, peoples, sovereignty, and future.

Again, we affirm to the world, and to the Yemenis and the international and regional community, our full support for the State, and we also affirm Yemen’s standing in the Kingdom’s conscience, given the reliance placed upon it.

For this, in all frankness, and on behalf of our Government, we express our great appreciation and gratitude to the Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques, his Government and institutions, for the Kingdom’s leadership of the Arab coalition, and we call upon the world that the Kingdom shall continue to be a steadfast support for the sake of Yemen’s security and prosperity, and that its role will remain present in the memory of the Yemeni people and in the conscience of the Yemeni human being.
Yemen can give to the world when it regains its security and prosperity.

As for our Yemeni people, we renew our affirmation before the world that Yemen will remain steadfast, investing its history and sacrificing its present and future in order to consolidate the values of justice, peace and human dignity in our region and in the world.

I express our gratitude, in this firm forum, for the appreciated role of the sisterly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, its leadership and people, and the burdens it has borne alongside Yemen and its people, from the beginning of the Iranian aggression through its militias against our country, and from the phase of supporting legitimacy to the targeting of the territory of the Kingdom, its people, its land and its sacred sites, in defense of the security of the Two Holy Mosques, the blessed sanctuary, and the protection of its land, its airspace, its capabilities and its peoples.

The Republic of Yemen renews its steadfast support for the right of the Palestinian people to self-determination and the establishment of their independent State with East Jerusalem as its capital, and for all efforts aimed at ending the suffering of the Palestinian people.

We express our concern at and support for the suffering of the Yemeni people, and we condemn the crimes of the Iranian-backed terrorist militias against civilians and the obstruction and piracy they have practiced against humanitarian organizations; for they have caused the aggravation of human suffering for the sake of extortion and domination.
Peace and justice, for Yemenis inside and outside, are a memorial to all the Yemenis in their homes, their displacement and their exile.

As the delegate said, and as the Yemeni poet Abdullah Al-Baraduni affirmed, “From the most dangerous things that happened to Yemen is that it no longer belongs to itself, but to Iran and to those attached to it, the wanderers.”
And as has been said: “Yesterday belongs to the sword and the people, and tomorrow belongs to the people and the sword.”
Long live free Yemen, secure, for every people of the world, and let there dawn in the world a secure life for our great Yemeni people, a path to justice.

We express our appreciation to the United Nations, its Secretary-General and his Special Envoy and all its agencies, for their efforts for the sake of the peace for which we have all longed… it must come, and it has great peace and great meaning, and we renew the covenant to the United Nations concerning it.
Yemen will remain secure and prosperous, open to life and to the peoples, free from those who bargain over it and trade in it, before the United Nations and the world.

We also value the positions of brothers, friends and allies in support of Yemen, backing efforts to restore the State, peace and stability, the references, and support for all efforts directed at achieving a comprehensive political settlement, the protection of civilians, and the establishment of humanitarian access.
Time will remain our witness, and greater and more enduring our struggle and our steadfastness in the pledge.
A day where we reassert that diversity is not a cause for division but celebration.
Our strength is in our diversity.
Sixty years ago, in the chambers of this Assembly, the United Nations adopted a resolution condemning apartheid as a crime against humanity.
The demise of apartheid freed the people of South Africa from racial segregation and slaughter, domination and deprivation, humiliation and exploitation.
But it was not only the people of South Africa who were unchained when apartheid collapsed.
The end of apartheid also marked the end of a system that exported violence and instability across southern Africa.
Indeed, the fall of apartheid is a glorious story that attests to what multilateralism can deliver.

Since democratic South Africa took its place in this Assembly, we have pursued a foreign policy anchored in Ubuntu and international law, dialogue and multilateralism, and in the understanding that our fate is tied to the fortunes of our region and continent.
Millions more South Africans have access to education, electricity, water and sanitation, housing and social protection than they did at the dawn of our democracy.
We have built a united nation of a diverse people, steeled in their determination to never let history repeat itself.
In November 2025, South Africa classified gender-based violence and femicide as a national disaster, recognising that dealing with this scourge demands exceptional measures.
We have built a vibrant democracy capable of self-correcting and stepping back from the brink.
A democracy strong enough to withstand and resist attempts at external supervision and tutelage.
After the 2024 election, political parties put national stability above narrow interests and formed a government of national unity within two weeks of the announcement of the results.
Since the dawn of our democracy, we have held no fewer than seven free and fair national elections.
As we speak, South Africans are preparing once again to exercise their democratic right, this time in local government elections.
Again, the will of the people will prevail.
The promise of democracy and international cooperation wanes when we cannot demonstrate that they can address inequality and insecurity.
Compelled by our unenviable position as the world’s most unequal society, South Africa made inequality a key focus of our G20 Presidency in 2025.
Today, the top 10 percent own roughly 75 percent of global wealth, while the bottom 50 percent own only 2 percent.
This extreme concentration of wealth at the top and poverty at the bottom is neither inevitable nor insurmountable.
Together with Brazil, Norway and Spain, South Africa calls on this Assembly to throw its weight behind the establishment of an International Panel on Inequality.
We know that inequality is at the heart of the rising appeal of politics founded on hate and exclusion.
Across the world, citizens who have seen little improvement in their economic fortunes are turning to ideas diametrically opposed to the values of the UN Charter.

As we mark the 25th anniversary of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, South Africa reaffirms its commitment to confronting racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and all forms of intolerance.
We are determined to confront racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and all forms of intolerance through our Constitution, our laws and our institutions.
Dealing with the root causes and challenges of irregular migration is a shared responsibility of all countries of the world.

We approach our leadership of a regional bloc that is home to a quarter of Africa’s population – the Southern African Development Community (SADC) – with a firm resolve to champion greater regional integration, industrialisation and trade.
We want to increase trade among our countries so that our citizens can share in the prosperity of our region and our economies are better prepared to absorb the shocks of unilateralism.
If multilateralism works at regional level, then citizens have greater reason to believe it can work globally.
Our governments face a difficult choice: whether to meet the needs of their citizens or satisfy the expectations of creditors.
In the last year alone, African countries spent roughly the same amount on servicing debt as is needed to close our infrastructure financing gap.
This grim reality inspired South Africa’s G20 Presidency to focus on debt sustainability.
The Africa Expert Panel report calls for an end to incrementalism.
It supports multilateral efforts to establish a Borrowers’ Club to counter-balance the power of creditors and calls for greater debt transparency and greater scrutiny of credit rating agencies.
To us, Mr President, unsustainable debt betrays the promise of development and destroys the prospects for democracy.
With only 36 percent of the Sustainable Development Goals showing sufficient progress, we are running out of time!
Africa and much of the Global South need multilateral action to free resources absorbed by debt service and redirect them towards development.
We must close the financing gap for the 2030 Agenda and meaningfully advance implementation of the African Union’s Agenda 2063.
Climate disasters and extreme weather patterns threaten our people, our prosperity, and our hard-won development gains.
In the last year, two million people in SADC suffered the combined and debilitating impact of floods, cyclones, wildfires, and disease outbreaks.
Our responses are severely constrained by a climate finance architecture stacked against developing nations.
Global action on disaster resilience and predictable financing for a just energy transition is essential if international cooperation is to deliver for all.
Our continent has the world’s largest reserves of critical minerals.
These critical minerals can help bridge the gap between wealthy and poor nations and overcome the indignities of poverty and underdevelopment.
We insist, Mr President, that indeed Africa must have a stake in shaping the rules that govern the development and deployment of Artificial Intelligence.
We have a youthful population ready to play a key role in the beneficiation at source of critical minerals and on research and innovation for artificial intelligence.
Restoring trust in multilateralism demands that we demonstrate, as the United Nations, that the peaceful resolution of conflicts is still our mantra.
Unfortunately, much of what we see runs counter to this.
In the last two years, the world spent more on military budgets than on resourcing this important body tasked with maintaining global peace.

We are reminded that meeting the SDGs by 2030, including ending hunger and expanding access to safe water and sanitation, would require no more than 5 percent of the 2.9 trillion US dollars spent on arms.
The result of the choice we are making is an arms race and a world as divided as it is dangerous.
We see the consequences in Sudan, which is today the worst humanitarian crisis in the world.
We see the consequences in the Eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, Iran, Ukraine and elsewhere.
Humanitarian workers are caught in the crosshairs of today’s conflicts.
When they are not being obstructed from reaching civilians in need, they are being killed in the line of duty.
To restore respect for international law, we must protect those who deliver humanitarian assistance.
That is why South Africa endorsed the Declaration for the Protection of Humanitarian Personnel, supported by nearly 120 states from all regions of the world.
Mr President Eighty years ago, the first resolution of the General Assembly called for the elimination of nuclear weapons.
Later this year, South Africa will preside over the First Review Conference of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons.

As the only country in the world to have voluntarily dismantled its nuclear weapons programme, South Africa stands ready to share this experience as a demonstration that, with political will, credible and verifiable nuclear disarmament is achievable.
In our view, restoring trust in multilateralism will not happen without meaningful reform of global governance, principally the UN Security Council.
African citizens are growing weary of their continent being consigned to the periphery of global governance.
Africa is home to nearly one-fifth of the world’s population and African countries together account for more than a quarter of UN member states.
Yet over the past decade, 70 percent of UN Security Council resolutions have concerned conflicts on the African continent.
If the future belongs to the young, then surely a continent that will be home to one in four of the world’s youth by 2030 deserves a bigger seat at the table.
South Africa therefore reaffirms its support for the Ezulwini Consensus and its call to end Africa’s relegation to the margins of global decision-making.
Permanent seats for Africa in the Security Council, with all the prerogatives of permanent membership, are long overdue.
Nowhere is the need to uphold our shared humanity more urgent than in Palestine.
The rights, dignity and humanity of Palestinians cannot be treated as conditional.

The State of Israel’s continued violations of international and humanitarian law constitute genocide, and we remain steadfast in our view that the international community must act decisively to end this impunity.
In our support for a just and lasting peace and a two-state solution, in accordance with UN resolutions, South Africa is unwavering.
We are steadfast in our longstanding solidarity with the people of Western Sahara.

We reaffirm their inalienable right to self-determination and support a just, lasting and mutually acceptable political solution consistent with international law and the principles of the United Nations Charter.
We are also deeply concerned by the wielding of economic weapons to coerce countries into abandoning their chosen development trajectories.
The suffering of the Cuban people should command our deepest solidarity.
We reiterate our call for an end to the blockade on the Cuban people.
The designation of Cuba as a State sponsor of terrorism, is similarly unfounded, and it should be removed from that list.
Unilateral coercive measures have negative spillover effects that seriously undermine third countries.
Similarly, we also call for the urgent removal of sanctions against Zimbabwe.
Our current reality demands that we act collectively to protect existing international institutions of justice from sanctions and intimidation.
These institutions fulfil important mandates for the benefit of humanity.
As I conclude, Mr President, South Africa leaves this podium with an important refrain: The South African nation is the creation and heritage of the international community.
South Africa today stands tall in the family of nations because the United Nations delivered on the promise of its Charter.

As Member States we must continue to support this organisation, our organisation, because as President Nelson Mandela said in his inaugural Address to the United Nations General Assembly on 3 October 1994: “The millions across our globe who stand expectant at the gates of hope look to this Organisation to bring them peace, to bring them life, to bring them a life worth living” I thank you.

Zambia salutes His Excellency António Guterres for reminding us that the answer to a more divided and multipolar world is not less multilateralism, but a stronger, fairer and more representative United Nations.
The theme of this session, “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All,” is both timely and necessary.
Trust is the foundation on which international cooperation is built upon.
Yet today, trust in institutions, trust among nations and, most importantly, trust between the institutions that serve the people, is under strain.
Trust means that the founding principles of the United Nations Charter must be respected.
For Zambia, trust begins with keeping promises.
Trust means that international agreements must be honoured.
Trust means that development commitments must be financed.
Trust means that the voices of developing countries matter, in word and in deed.
Trust means that the global system must not protect the interests of the powerful, at the expense of the vulnerable.
And trust means that when the world agrees on a goal, we must have the commitment to implement it.
The world is undergoing profound transformation.
Technology is changing economies and societies.
Geopolitical competition is altering global trade and investment patterns.
Conflicts are causing massive displacements and humanitarian suffering.
And yet, Developing countries continue to confront a financing system that does not adequately reflect and respond to their development needs.

The question before us is therefore, not whether transformation will happen, but it is rather how we manage transformation, who benefits from it, and whether our multilateral institutions are capable of delivering meaningful results for ordinary people.
For Zambia, our answer is clear: we must restore trust by achieving results, and we must manage transformation by ensuring that no country and no-one is left behind.

Zambia's Democratic Journey and the 2026 Elections Article 21 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights affirms that, “the will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government,” expressed through periodic and genuine elections.
It is in this spirit that Zambia recently concluded its general elections, through which our people exercised their constitutional right to choose their leaders.
We thank the people of Zambia for their participation in the democratic process and for renewing their confidence in our leadership.
We also express our sincere appreciation to the international Election Observation Missions for their invaluable support and contribution to Zambia’s democratic process.
It is important to emphasize that Zambia is not at war.

Zambia is a peaceful, stable and sovereign nation, and the peaceful atmosphere that characterized the country before, during and after the elections is a clear reflection of our people’s enduring commitment to peace, democracy, national unity and constitutional governance.

Despite the political differences that naturally accompany a democratic election, Zambia has demonstrated that such differences can and must be managed peacefully and through the established constitutional and legal institutions.
Our democratic process should never be mistaken for conflict or instability.
We therefore reaffirm our unwavering commitment to preserving Zambia’s long-standing tradition of peace.

We will continue to ensure that political differences are addressed through the due process of the law and will take all necessary measures, within the confines of our Constitution and laws, to prevent political disputes from degenerating into violence, armed mobilization, insurgency or the emergence of militia groups.

In this regard, we extend a sincere invitation to cooperating partners, international development institutions, investors, the private sector and Zambia’s friends around the world to continue working with us in advancing our Grow Zambia Agenda.
Zambia needs partnerships, investments, innovation, technology, skills and sustained development cooperation in order to unlock its full potential.

We encourage our cooperating partners to view Zambia through the lens of the peace and stability that define our country, and to deepen support for programmes that promote inclusive economic growth, job creation, infrastructure development, human capital development, agriculture, energy, health and other priority areas of national development.
Our message is clear: Zambia is at peace, Zambia is open for partnership, and Zambia is ready to grow.
Zambia: A Stable Partner for Investment and Trade Peace and stability provide the foundation for economic development.

Zambia is positioning itself as an attractive destination for investment and trade, with opportunities in mining, critical minerals, agriculture, agro- processing, manufacturing, energy, infrastructure, tourism and digital services.

Our ambition is to move beyond the export of raw materials and primary commodities towards value addition, industrialization, job creation and technology transfer as key enablers of our economic transformation agenda.
We welcome investment that creates jobs, develops skills and builds sustainable value chains.
Our message to investors is: Come to Zambia. Invest with us. Produce with us. Trade with us. Grow with us.
Zambia is open for investment Climate Change and Environmental Resilience; Water and Sanitation For Zambia, climate change is not an abstract concept.

Our people continue to experience the devastating effects of droughts, floods and changing weather patterns, with significant impacts on agriculture, food security, water availability, energy generation and livelihoods.
The effects of activities transcend our borders and yet our people and the coming generations may pay a heavy price.
Zambia recognizes that countries such as ours cannot finance the climate transition alone, nor should they.
This is a collective moral responsibility of the international community, especially the highest contributors to carbon emissions.
This is to mitigate the effects of climate change and protect lives and livelihoods.
Those who have contributed least to climate change must not be left to bear its greatest costs.

We therefore call for predictable, accessible and affordable climate finance, technology transfer, and greater investment in adaptation and resilience, consistent with the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities.
For Africa, adaptation is not optional.

Our farmers require climate-resilient agriculture; our communities and cities need resilient infrastructure; our energy systems must become more diversified; and our water resources, forests and ecosystems must be protected.
Zambia is ready to contribute to global climate solutions, but those that have contributed least to climate change must not bear a disproportionate share of its costs.
Water security is integral to climate resilience and sustainable development.
Zambia therefore attaches great importance to international cooperation on water and has actively participated in the preparatory process for the 2026 United Nations Water Conference.

Together with Finland, Zambia is co- chairing the Interactive Dialogue on Water for Cooperation, focusing on transboundary and international water cooperation, scientific cooperation and inclusive governance.

We remain committed to strengthening water security, climate resilience and sustainable management of natural resources, while working with the international community to ensure that climate and water action delivers tangible benefits for our people and future generations.
Health, Human Capital and Inclusive Development Africa's youthful population is one of our greatest assets and represents an enormous opportunity for global prosperity.
According to demographic forecasts, one in every 4 youths on the globe will be African, by 2050.
We have a wealth of young Africans with the potential to become entrepreneurs, scientists, engineers, farmers, innovators, artists and future leaders.

Our responsibility is to equip them with quality education, relevant skills, access to technology, entrepreneurship opportunities and decent employment, so that they can become active drivers of economic transformation and sustainable development.
We are alive to the fact that we should ensure that we keep this youthful and productive population healthy in order to harness positive dividends.

In the health sector, Zambia has increased domestic budgetary allocations from approximately 7 percent to over 10 percent, enabling the recruitment of health workers, expansion and modernization of health infrastructure, and improved availability of essential medical supplies.

Recognizing continued vulnerability to epidemics, Zambia calls for the expedited conclusion of negotiations on the Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing Annex under the WHO Pandemic Agreement, alongside strengthened access to technology and preparedness capacities to detect and respond to future health threats.
Zambia is further making efforts toward building capacity for local Vaccine Manufacturing.

In Zambia, we have taken decisive steps to expand access to education through the enactment of the Free Education Act, and the strengthening of the school feeding programme, ensuring that more children can access education and remain in school without the burden of fees or hunger standing in their way of learning.
Zambia is equally committed to promoting gender equality and economic empowerment of women and girls.
We are expanding opportunities in education, skills development, entrepreneurship, financial inclusion and leadership.

For the first time in our history, Parliament now provides for proportional representation of women, young people and persons with disabilities, reflecting our conviction that their voices and experiences must be heard in shaping the decisions that affect our nation.
We are also strengthening efforts to end child, early and forced marriage by keeping girls in school and addressing the social and economic factors that place them at risk.

Zambia has demonstrated that progress is possible, reducing child marriage prevalence from 29% to 23.9% in four years through comprehensive legal reforms, free education, school re-entry policy, multisectoral support systems like the Keeping Girls in School initiatives and targeted economic investments such as our expanded Constituency Development Fund.
We need to continue building on these successes.
We therefore invite Member States to unite behind our global and continental commitments to drive domestic action.
By investing in our people, particularly women, girls and young people, we are investing in Zambia's future.
When we empower our people, we strengthen our nation; and when we invest in Africa's young people and women, we invest in the prosperity of our continent and the world.

Our commitment is to build an inclusive society in which every citizen, regardless of gender, age or disability, has an opportunity to participate fully in our country's economic and social transformation.

Sustainable Development and the 2030 Agenda The Sustainable Development Goals remain the most comprehensive expression of our shared ambition to eradicate poverty, reduce inequality and build a sustainable future.
Yet we must acknowledge that progress is uneven.
The world cannot continue to adopt ambitious commitments while developing countries struggle to finance their implementation.

For Zambia, the SDGs must translate into tangible improvements in the lives of our people: a child receiving quality education; a mother accessing safe healthcare; a farmer having reliable water and markets; a young person finding decent employment; a family having access to electricity; a community having accessible roads; access to clean water and sanitation; a small business gaining access to finance.
Sustainable Development Finance and Reform of the Global Financial Architecture Sustainable development cannot be achieved without addressing the persistent financing gap facing developing countries.

High borrowing costs, limited fiscal space and heavy debt-servicing obligations continue to constrain countries’ ability to invest in climate action, health, education, infrastructure and other development priorities.
We cannot expect countries to deliver more for their people while resources available are increasingly consumed by the cost of debt.
This is not sustainable, nor is it compatible with our collective commitment to leave no one behind.
Zambia has undertaken significant fiscal reforms and made progress in restructuring our debt, to restore macroeconomic stability and create fiscal space.
This demonstrates our willingness to make bold decisions when needed.
At the same time, we are strengthening domestic resource mobilization by expanding the tax base, modernizing tax administration and combating illicit financial flows.
We cannot continue to lose resources essential to Africa’s transformation while being asked to mobilize greater financing for development.
Africa’s resources must work for Africa’s development.
We support enhanced international cooperation on transparency, beneficial ownership, asset recovery and the prevention of illicit financial flows.

We equally support stronger international tax cooperation through the UN Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation, to ensure fairer taxing rights and strengthen domestic resource mobilization for development.

Zambia therefore calls for greater access to affordable and long-term development finance, increased climate finance—particularly for adaptation and resilience—and innovative financing mechanisms to mobilise private investment for sustainable development.
Africa needs a fairer and more responsive global financial architecture that enables developing countries to finance development as an investment in our shared future.
Multilateralism, Geopolitics, Peace and Security The United Nations remains indispensable to international peace, security and sustainable development.
However, its institutions must evolve to reflect today’s geopolitical, economic and demographic realities.
Zambia therefore supports meaningful UN reform, particularly of the Security Council, including permanent African representation in line with the Ezulwini Consensus and Sirte Declaration.
We also support reforms to global economic and financial governance, that give developing countries a greater voice in decisions affecting them.

Zambia welcomes the UN80 Initiative as an opportunity to strengthen multilateralism and build a more effective, efficient, equitable and fit-for- purpose United Nations and acknowledge the commendable progress achieved so far.
As efforts are made to attain a more efficient and nimbler United Nations, we must not lose sight of the most important aspect – the effectiveness of the UN in delivering on its mandates.
With each crucial question, we must ask ourselves if the reforms will make the world safer and uplift the lives of the most vulnerable in society.
We take note of the proposed mergers of some key institutions and emphasize on the importance of protecting their mandates.
We further note the changed landscape for international cooperation that has seen significant declines in official development assistance, which has also affected important UN programmes.
We, therefore, call on member states to protect these institutions we trust by ringfencing crucial core funding.

In the face of rising geopolitical tensions and protracted conflicts, we reaffirm our commitment to dialogue, diplomacy and the peaceful resolution of disputes in accordance with the UN Charter and international law.
We further support African-led solutions and stronger cooperation between the UN, African Union and regional organizations to advance conflict prevention, peacebuilding and collective security.
Conclusion Zambia remains committed to peace, democracy, multilateralism and sustainable development.
We believe that restoring trust requires delivery; that sustainable development requires genuine international partnership; and that managing transformation requires inclusion.

We call for an equitable global system that provides developing countries with affordable financing and policy space to transform their economies, strengthens climate action through adequate finance, expands opportunities for young people, and reforms international institutions to reflect today’s realities.

Let us together strengthen peace through dialogue, respect for human rights, democracy and the rule of law and ensure that the commitments made in this Assembly, translate into tangible improvements in the lives of our people.
Zambia stands ready to work with all nations to restore trust, manage transformation and build a more peaceful, prosperous and equitable world.
I wish to thank Miss Annalena Baerbock for her effective leadership of the 80th session and their contribution to the UN aid reform process.
We commend his defense of multilateralism as well as efforts to advance dialogue for conflict prevention and resolution, sustainable development and the pact for the future.

Mr. president, we meet during a pivotal moment when the world is facing numerous interconnected and complex crisis conflicts are spreading, climate shocks are intensifying and technology is advancing faster than the rules that govern it.
As the current crop of leaders, it should concern us that today, somewhere a child is born into war, a families displaced by conflict.
A farmer loses another harvest to drought, and the young person wonders whether technological progress will expand opportunity or deepen inequality.
These experiences reveal a common truth.
Humanity's challenges are increasingly interconnected, and no nation can overcome them alone.
The trust deficit among nations has continued to erode the gains that cooperation fostered within the United Nations system.
We must therefore choose between purposeful reform or unmitigated repression.
Trust will be restored when conflicts are prevented.
Development commitments are fulfilled, and all nations are fairly represented in global institutions.
It ensures that all have an equal voice under international law, and an equal role in shaping our shared future.

Undoubtedly, the charter remains our common compass sovereign equality, political independence, territorial integrity, non-interference, peaceful settlement of disputes and international cooperation must be applied universally, not selectively.
International law cannot be a shield for some and a sword against others.
The United Nations has a sacred duty to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war.
Our experience in southern Africa has taught us that dialogue is a shared fortitude and not a weakness.
In the African tradition, the meeting place is not where courage is abandoned.
It is where wisdom is summoned.
Lessons can be drawn from the heritage based approaches to peace building and conflict resolution from communities across the world, including within Africa.

Military action may alter the battlefield, but durable peace is built through inclusive political processes that restore confidence, address grievances and allow affected communities to shape their socioeconomic and political destinies.

Mr. president, Zimbabwe's grateful for the confidence placed in us through our election to the Security Council for the 2027 to 2028 term, my country will assume this responsibility in January 2027 with humility, independency and a readiness to serve, guided by our foreign policy of being a friend to all and an enemy to none.
Accordingly, my country will prioritize for priorities in the Council.
Firstly, the promotion of preventive diplomacy, mediation, a peaceful dispute resolution while tackling the underlying causes of insecurity.
Secondly, we shall advocate for the strengthening of cooperation between the United Nations and the regional organizations such as the African Union and its Peace and Security Council.
In this respect, we call for the full implementation of resolution 2719 to ensure predictable, adequate and sustainable financing for authorized African Union led peace support operations.

Thirdly, our nation believes that our rich heritage and natural resource endowments must advance industrialization, modernization and the green agenda for the prosperity of all and not to finance conflict As such, Zimbabwe shall support Africa silencing the guns agenda and strong action against terrorism, organized crime, illicit arms flows, and illegal resource trafficking.
Finally, women and young people must shape peace.
From the outset, the support of Zimbabwe will also be extended to the women and youth peace and security agendas.
The current times demand peace keeping that is grounded in clear political strategies, realistic mandates and adequate resources.
Those most affected by the decisions of the Security Council should not be the least heard.
There is need not only give a voice, but consider the views of the countries and regions on the Security Council agenda towards our shared aspirations for enduring peace and sustainable development.
Mr. president, restoring confidence in collective security requires the Security Council to move beyond the outdated geopolitical realities of 1945.
The long standing position of Africa is outlined in the Ursuline Convent.
Africa is united, sovereign and independent.
Institutional legitimacy depends on the consistent application of international law, sovereign equality and the inalienable right to self-determination of all within the comity of nations.
Unilateral coercive measures as a manipulative foreign policy tool are outdated in a global era, which should be encouraged on solidarity, mutually beneficial partnerships and shared prosperity.
I urge us to use this defining epoch in the history of our August organization to protect the United Nations Charter.
The tendencies where our resolutions and international law are ignored should no longer be excused.
Mr. president, peace cannot endure without development.
